topic: Indus Valley Civilization - Geography, Social Organisation & Architecture
text:
INDUS VALLEY CIVILIZATION

Flourished from 2600 BCE to 1900 BCE

GEOGRAPHY & SETTLEMENTS

  • Located in the Indus River Valley (present-day India and Pakistan)
  • Vast and extensive civilization
  • Major cities:- Harappa, Mohenjodaro, Dholavira, Lothal
  • Planned urban centres with grid-like street layout
  • Sophisticated drainage systems and public wells

SOCIAL ORGANISATION

  • Well-structured society
  • Hierarchical system with distinct social classes
  • Evidence of a ruling elite and priestly class
  • Skilled artisans, traders, and labourers
  • Evidence of communal living and shared public spaces
  • Possible evidence of gender equality and absence of social discrimination

ARCHITECTURE & CRAFTSMANSHIP

  • Advanced urban planning and architecture
  • Use of standardised bricks in construction
  • Large public buildings, granaries, and reservoirs
  • Elaborate drainage and sewage systems
  • Intricate and well-designed houses with courtyards

details.summary: Overview of the Indus Valley Civilization covering period (2600 BCE–1900 BCE), geography, major urban centres, social structure, and key architectural characteristics.

mcq.question: Which of the following features characterized the urban planning of the Indus Valley Civilization?
options: Radial street layouts and mud-only structures
Grid-like street layout and sophisticated drainage systems
Unplanned organic settlement growth without public wells
mcq.explanation: The Indus Valley Civilization featured planned urban centres with grid-like street layouts, sophisticated drainage systems, public wells, and standardized bricks.

topic: Political Systems and Rise of Monarchies (Mahajanapadas)
text:
Key developments in the political structure during the Later Vedic and Mahajanapada periods:

  • Emergence of powerful monarchies (Mahajanapadas).
  • Kingship based on hereditary succession.
  • Sabha (council of elders) and Samiti (assembly of people) functioned for decision-making.
  • The Sabha gradually became more aristocratic in nature.
  • Rise of powerful monarchies like Magadha under the Nandas and Mauryas.

details.summary: Overview of the political transformation during the Mahajanapada era, focusing on hereditary kingship, institutional governance (Sabha & Samiti), and the rise of Magadha.

mcq.question: Which of the following assemblies in ancient India was known as the council of elders and became increasingly aristocratic over time?
mcq.explanation: Sabha was the council of elders which originally served decision-making roles alongside Samiti, but over time became more aristocratic in nature.

subject: History
content:
Key developments in the political structure during the Later Vedic and Mahajanapada periods:

- Emergence of powerful monarchies (**Mahajanapadas**).
- **Kingship** based on *hereditary succession*.
- **Sabha** (council of elders) and **Samiti** (assembly of people) functioned for decision-making.
- The **Sabha** gradually became more aristocratic in nature.
- Rise of powerful monarchies like **Magadha** under the **Nandas** and **Mauryas**.

### Key Exam Facts
- **Summary:** Overview of the political transformation during the Mahajanapada era, focusing on hereditary kingship, institutional governance (Sabha & Samiti), and the rise of Magadha.

The Eightfold Path of Buddha consists of eight practices essential for liberation and spiritual development in Buddhism:

  • Right View: Understanding the nature of reality and the Four Noble Truths
  • Right Intention: Cultivating wholesome and compassionate intentions
  • Right Speech: Speaking truthfully, kindly, and avoiding harmful speech
  • Right Action: Engaging in ethical conduct and avoiding harm to oneself and others
  • Right Livelihood: Pursuing a livelihood that is honest and non-harming
  • Right Effort: Cultivating wholesome qualities and abandoning unwholesome ones
  • Right Mindfulness: Being present, aware, and attentive to the present moment
  • Right Concentration: Cultivating focused and tranquil states of mind through meditation

topic: Religious History & Ashoka's Policy of Dhamma
text:
RELIGIOUS HISTORY

Ashoka's Policy of Dhamma: Ashoka embraced Buddhism and promoted a policy of Dhamma (righteousness).

  • Encouraged moral conduct, non-violence, and respect for all religions.
  • Edicts were inscribed on pillars and rocks, propagating Dhamma and outlining ethical principles.

  • Mesosome: Infolded plasma membrane structure.
  • Flagellum: Long helical structure that helps in movement of bacteria.
  • Pilus & Inclusions: For attachment and storage.

text:
Vegetative Propagation

Vegetative propagation is a method of reproduction in plants where new individual plants are produced from the vegetative parts (roots, stem, leaves) rather than reproductive structures (flowers).

Plant Parts Overview

  • Reproductive Part: Flower → involved in sexual reproduction.
  • Vegetative Parts: Leaf, Stem, Roots → not involved in sexual reproduction.

1. Artificial Vegetative Propagation

Methods used to propagate multiple plants artificially include layering or grafting.

  • Examples: Sugarcane, Roses, Grapes.

2. Natural Vegetative Propagation

Natural propagation occurs through specialized structures of vegetative parts:

  • Leaves: Bryophyllum — Buds are produced in the notches along the leaf margins. When these buds fall onto moist soil, they develop into new individual plants.
  • Stem: Turmeric, Ginger.
  • Runners / Stolon: Grass runners, Strawberry.
  • Bulbs: Onion, Lily.
  • Other Natural Examples: Potato.

Diagram Description: Illustrated diagram showing plant anatomy separating sexual reproductive parts (Flower) from vegetative non-reproductive parts (Leaf, Stem, Roots), alongside a detailed leaf of Bryophyllum showing marginal buds growing along its notches.

mcq.question: In Bryophyllum, vegetative propagation takes place through which of the following plant structures?
mcq.explanation: Bryophyllum reproduces vegetatively through adventitious buds produced in the notches along the margins of its leaves. When these buds fall on soil, they develop into new plants.

text:
Reflex Action is an immediate, automatic, and involuntary response to a stimulus without conscious thought by the brain.

Pathway of Reflex Arc:

  • Stimulus Received: Detected by Receptors (e.g., heat or pain receptors in the skin).
  • Sensory Neuron: Transmits the nerve impulse from receptor to the spinal cord (CNS).
  • Relay Neuron (Interneuron): Located in the spinal cord; processes the signal and transfers it to a motor neuron.
  • Motor Neuron: Transmits the impulse from the spinal cord to the effector.
  • Effector: Target organ or tissue (e.g., muscle in arm) that acts on the signal.
  • Response: Final action executed (e.g., moving hand away from heat).

Key Exam Notes:

  • The Brain is NOT involved in directing a Reflex Action, but information regarding the action will reach the brain.
  • The vertebral column (backbone) protects the spinal cord.

Diagram Overview: Schematic diagram illustrating the reflex arc involving a hand touching a hot pot, heat/pain receptors, sensory neuron, relay neuron inside the spinal cord (CNS), motor neuron, effector muscle, and message transmission path to the brain.

details.summary: Explains the pathway of a reflex arc from receptor to response, detailing sensory neuron, relay neuron, motor neuron, effector, spinal cord protection by the vertebral column, and the indirect role of the brain.

topic: Human Brain - Protection, Anatomy, and Functions
text:
The Human Brain is the central control unit of the body, protected by three essential layers/structures:

  • Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF)
  • The Meninges: Divided into Dura mater (outer), Arachnoid (middle), and Pia mater (inner).
  • Cranium (Skull): Bony protection encasing the brain.

Major Regions of the Brain and Their Functions

1. Fore-Brain

  • Receives signals from sensory organs (eyes, ears, skin, nose, tongue).
  • Controls voluntary movement and utilizes past experiences.
  • Fore-brain is the main thinking part of the brain.
  • Regulates senses such as Sight, Smell, and Hearing.
  • Includes key structures like the Cerebrum, Hypothalamus, and Pituitary Gland.

2. Mid-Brain

  • Connects the fore-brain to the hind-brain.
  • Controls certain involuntary actions.

3. Hind-Brain

  • Cerebellum: Main function is maintaining balance and equilibrium of the body. Controls precise actions like walking in a straight line, riding a bicycle, and picking up a pencil.
  • Pons: Regulates the sleep cycle and breathing rate.
  • Medulla (Medulla Oblongata): Controls involuntary actions, including:
    • Blood pressure
    • Salivation
    • Vomiting
    • Heartbeat
    • Coughing
    • Respiration rate

Diagram Context: Cross-sectional view showing Cerebrum, Mid-brain, Hind-brain (Pons, Medulla, Cerebellum), Hypothalamus, Pituitary Gland, and Spinal Cord.

details.summary: Detailed structural and functional breakdown of the human brain into Fore-brain, Mid-brain, and Hind-brain, along with its protective coverings (Cranium, Meninges, Cerebrospinal Fluid).

mcq.explanation: The Medulla (Medulla Oblongata), located in the hind-brain, controls involuntary actions such as blood pressure, salivation, vomiting, heartbeat, and respiration rate.

text:
Hormones in Animals

Hormones are chemical messengers secreted directly by endocrine glands into the bloodstream.

  • Respiratory Control Mechanism: Contraction of the diaphragm and rib muscles leads to an increased breathing rate.

Key Endocrine Glands and Their Functions

  • Thyroid Gland:
    • Requires Iodine to synthesize Thyroxin Hormone.
    • Regulates metabolism for overall body growth.
    • Iodine Deficiency: Causes Goitre disease, characterized by a swollen neck.
  • Pituitary Gland:
    • Stimulates growth in all organs.
    • Deficiency in Childhood: Leads to dwarfism.
  • Pineal Gland:
    • Regulates sleeping patterns (circadian rhythm).
  • Pancreas:
    • Acts as both an endocrine and exocrine gland.
    • Secretes Insulin, which helps regulate blood sugar levels.
    • Diabetes: Managed by taking insulin injections.
  • Adrenal Gland:
    • Regulates physiological responses such as heartbeat rate.
  • Gonads (Puberty at 10-12 years):
    • Testes (Male): Produces Sperms and secretes Testosterone.
    • Ovaries (Female): Produces Ovum and secretes Oestrogen.

details.summary: Overview of major endocrine glands in animals (Thyroid, Pituitary, Pineal, Pancreas, Adrenal, Testes, Ovaries), their hormones, functions, and deficiency disorders such as Goitre, Dwarfism, and Diabetes.

Growth hormone deficiency from Pituitary Gland

topic: Plant Movements: Nastic and Tropic Movements
text:
1. Growth Independent Movements (Nastic Movements)

Movements in plants that are not growth related.

  • Thigmonastic Movement: Movement occurring in response to touch.
  • Example: Touch-me-not plant (belongs to the Mimosa family).

2. Growth-Related Movements (Tropic Movements / Tropism)

Plant responses and movements that are directly growth related.

  • Phototropism: Response in relation to light.
    • (+ve) Phototropism: Growth towards light (e.g., stem / shoot).
    • (-ve) Phototropism: Growth away from light (e.g., root).
  • Geotropism: Response in relation to gravity.
    • (+ve) Geotropism: Growth towards gravity (e.g., roots).
    • (-ve) Geotropism: Growth away from gravity (e.g., stem).
  • Thigmotropism: Growth response to touch of an object.

content:
**1. Growth Independent Movements (Nastic Movements)**

Movements in plants that are *not growth related*.

- **Thigmonastic Movement:** Movement occurring in response to touch.
- **Example:** Touch-me-not plant (belongs to the *Mimosa* family).**

2. Growth-Related Movements (Tropic Movements / Tropism)**

Plant responses and movements that are directly *growth related*.

- **Phototropism:** Response in relation to light.**(+ve) Phototropism:** Growth towards light (e.g., **stem / shoot**).
- **(-ve) Phototropism:** Growth away from light (e.g., **root**).
- **Geotropism:** Response in relation to gravity.**(+ve) Geotropism:** Growth towards gravity (e.g., **roots**).
- **(-ve) Geotropism:** Growth away from gravity (e.g., **stem**).
- **Thigmotropism:** Growth response to touch of an object.

### Key Exam Facts

Genetics is the branch of biology concerned with the study of heredity and variation.

Father of Genetics: G.J. Mendel (Gregor Johann Mendel), who conducted fundamental genetic research using the pea plant.

Classification of Traits (Variations):

  • Somatic Variation (Acquired Traits):
    • Acquired after birth during the individual's lifetime.
    • Non-heritable (not passed to progeny).
    • Examples: Tattoos, driving skill.
  • Gametic Variation (Inherited Traits):
    • Present by birth due to changes in germ cells.
    • Heritable (passed from parents to progeny).
    • Examples: Hair colour, eye colour, skin colour.

Ploidy Status:

  • Haploid (n): Contains a single set of chromosomes.
  • Diploid (2n): Contains two sets of chromosomes (paired).

Important Exam Fact: All human cells are diploid (46 chromosomes / 23 pairs), except gametes which are haploid (23 chromosomes).

Reproductive Cycle Flow:

  • Gamete Formation: Egg cell (haploid, 23 chromosomes) and Sperm cell (haploid, 23 chromosomes) are produced via meiosis.
  • Fertilization: Egg (23) + Sperm (23) fuse to form a single-celled Zygote (diploid, 46 chromosomes).
  • Embryo Formation: The single-celled zygote divides repeatedly via mitosis to form a multicellular Embryo (46 chromosomes per cell).

topic: Genetics - Alleles, Dominant/Recessive Traits, and Genotypes in Pea Plants
text:
Alleles: Different varieties or alternative forms of a gene located on maternal and paternal homologous chromosomes.

  • Dominant Allele: The stronger gene variant that expresses its phenotypic trait even when paired with a different allele. Represented by a Capital letter (e.g., T or V).
  • Recessive Allele: The gene variant whose effect is masked in the presence of a dominant allele. Expresses its trait only in a homozygous condition. Represented by a Small letter (e.g., t or v).

Example Study: Garden Pea (Pisum sativum) Flower Colour

  • Violet Flower (V): Dominant allele
  • White Flower (v): Recessive allele

Zygotic Genetic Conditions (Genotypes & Phenotypes):

  1. Homozygous Dominant Condition (VV): Both alleles are dominant. Expresses Violet colour (Pure condition).
  2. Homozygous Recessive Condition (vv): Both alleles are recessive. Expresses White colour (Pure condition).
  3. Heterozygous Condition (Vv): Contains one dominant and one recessive allele. Expresses Violet colour (Hybrid condition).

details.summary: Notes explaining the concept of alleles, dominant versus recessive traits, and zygote genotypes (homozygous vs heterozygous) using flower colour in Pea plants (Pisum sativum) as an example.

mcq.explanation: In a heterozygous condition (Vv), the dominant allele (V) masks the recessive allele (v), resulting in the dominant phenotype, which is Violet.

topic: Classification of Diseases, Deficiency Diseases, Viral & Bacterial Diseases
text:
Diseases Overview

Diseases can broadly be categorized into Congenital Diseases and Acquired Diseases based on their occurrence and timeline.

1. Congenital Diseases

  • Present since birth.
  • Caused by structural or functional abnormalities, such as an imbalance of chromosomes.

2. Acquired Diseases

Developed after birth and categorized into:

  • Communicable Diseases: Transmitted from one person to another (e.g., caused by Bacterial or Viral pathogens).
  • Non-communicable Diseases: Not transmitted from person to person (e.g., Heart Attack, Diabetes).

3. Deficiency Diseases

Caused by a lack of essential nutrients in the diet:

  • Kwashiorkor: Deficiency of Protein (leads to stopped body growth in children).
  • Marasmus: Deficiency of Protein.
  • Goiter: Deficiency of Iodine.
  • Anaemia: Deficiency of Iron.
  • Hypokalemia: Deficiency of Potassium (causes fast heart beat).
  • Rickets: Deficiency of Vitamin D.
  • Scurvy: Deficiency of Vitamin C.

4. Diseases Caused by Viruses

  • Examples: Cold, Flu, Smallpox, Measles, Mumps, AIDS, Ebola, Chicken pox, Rabies, Hepatitis, Polio, Dengue, MERS.
  • Important Note: Antibiotics are NOT useful against viruses. Use vaccines for prevention/protection.

5. Diseases Caused by Bacteria

  • Examples: Cholera, Gonorrhea, Syphilis, Pneumonia, Diphtheria, Tetanus, Tuberculosis, Leprosy, Pertussis (Whooping Cough), Plague, Scarlet Fever.

details.summary: Comprehensive classification of diseases into congenital and acquired, listing key deficiency diseases, viral diseases with treatment nuances, and bacterial diseases.

Map Analysis: Natural Vegetation of India

The provided map illustrates the geographical distribution of various vegetation types across the Indian subcontinent, including India, Pakistan, China (Tibet), Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Sri Lanka, and the Andaman & Nicobar Islands.

  • Coordinate Range: The map covers approximately 68°E to 96°E longitude and 8°N to 36°N latitude.
  • Key Geographical Features: Arabian Sea, Bay of Bengal, Tropic of Cancer, Indian Ocean, and the Himalayan range.

Types of Vegetation (Legend):

  • Littoral and Swamp Forest (Dark Grey): Found along the coastal belts, particularly in the Sundarbans region (West Bengal/Bangladesh border) and along the eastern coast.
  • Montane Forest (Dotted Pattern): Located in the high-altitude regions of the Himalayas in the north.
  • Tropical Thorn Forest (Light Grey): Dominates the arid and semi-arid regions of western India (Rajasthan, Gujarat) and extends into the Deccan Plateau.
  • Tropical Deciduous Forests (Medium Grey): Covers the central and eastern parts of the Deccan Plateau and the northeastern states.
  • Tropical Evergreen and Semi Evergreen Forests (Dark Grey): Found in the Western Ghats (coastal strip of Kerala, Karnataka, Goa, Maharashtra) and the northeastern hill regions.

Definition of Mixture

A mixture is a combination of 2 or more substances.

Examples of Pure Substances

  • Gold
  • Cu (Copper)
  • O2 (Oxygen)

Classification of Matter

  • Pure Substance
    • Elements: Cannot be broken down to simpler substances.
      • Copper
      • Oxygen
      • Iron
      • Hydrogen
      • Mercury
    • Compounds: Have fixed composition. Can be broken down into elements by chemical or electrochemical reaction.
      • Water
      • Methane
      • Sugar
      • Salt
  • Mixture: Has no fixed composition.
    • Homogeneous (Uniform composition):
      • Sugar in water
      • Salt in water
      • Sulphur in carbon disulphide
      • Water in Alcohol
    • Heterogeneous (Non-uniform composition):
      • Sand & salt
      • Sugar & salt
      • Water in oil

text:
Definition of Solution

  • A solution is a homogeneous mixture.
  • It can be formed by mixing solid, liquid, and gases (e.g., CO2 gas).

Properties of Solutions

  • Particles do not scatter a beam of light (Tyndall effect is absent) because the size of particles is very small.
  • The path of light is not visible.
  • Components cannot be separated physically.
  • Particles cannot be seen by naked eyes.

Examples

text:
1. Finding the number of moles in 52g of Helium (He)

  • Formula: no. of mole = given mass / molar mass
  • Calculation: 52 / 4 = 13

2. Mass of 0.5 mole of N2 gas

  • Conversion: N → 14, N2 → 14 × 2 = 28
  • Calculation: no. of mole = 0.5 / 28 = 14 g

3. Molecular mass of HNO3

  • Calculation: 1 + 14 + 16 × 3 = 63 u

4. Number of particles in 46g of Na atoms

  • Formula: no. of mole = (Gr. m / m.m) = (no. of p. / Av. no)
  • Calculation: 46 / 23 = x / (6.022 × 1023)
  • Result: x = 12.044 × 1023

5. How many moles are in 28g of N atom

  • Calculation: no. of mole = 28 / 14 = 2

Decomposition Reaction

  • A single reactant breaks down to give simpler products.

Example 1: Decomposition of Ferrous Sulphate

2FeSO4 (s) --Heat--> Fe2O3 + SO2 + SO3

  • Reactant: Ferrous sulphate (green)
  • Products: Ferric oxide (Reddish Brown solid), SO2 (gas), SO3 (gas)

  • (White) silver chloride turns grey in sunlight.

2AgBr (s) --sunlight--> 2Ag (s) + Br2 (g)

  • Both reactions (AgCl and AgBr) are used in black & white photography.

Example 4: Decomposition of Ferrous Sulphate Crystals

FeSO4·7H2O (green) --Heat--> Colour change to White

  • 108C water is released.

Example 5: Decomposition of Limestone

CaCO3 (s) --Heat--> CaO + CO2

  • CaO is known as Quick lime.
  • Used in manufacture of cement.

Example 6: Decomposition of Lead Nitrate

2Pb(NO3)2 (s) --Heat--> 2PbO (s) + 4NO2 + O2

  • Reactant: Lead nitrate (red violet)

CaSO4·½H2O + 1½H2O → CaSO4·2H2O

Gypsum → CaSO4.2H2O → Plaster of Paris (POP) → CaSO4.½H2O

On heating gypsum at 373 K (Δ), it loses water to form calcium sulphate hemihydrate (Plaster of Paris):

CaSO4.2H2O — 373 K, Δ → CaSO4.½H2O

gypsum → calcium sulphate hemihydrate

On adding water back, POP reverts to gypsum:

CaSO4.½H2O + 1½H2O → CaSO4.2H2O

(POP) → gypsum

topic: Metals & Non-Metals – Properties of Metals (Mind Map)
text:
Metals & Non-Metals

The central node of the mind map is Metals, with the following branches/properties:

  • Basic oxides – Metals form basic oxides.
  • Lustre – Metals in their pure state have a shining surface.
  • Malleability – Metals can be beaten into thin sheets.
    • Most malleable metals:
      • Gold
      • Silver
  • Sonorous – Metals that produce a sound on striking a hard surface.
    • School bells are malle.
  • Ductility – Metals can be drawn into thin wires.
    • 1 gm of gold → about 2 km wire.
    • Most ductile metal: Gold.
  • Good conductors of heat
    • Best conductors of heat:
      • Silver
      • Copper
    • Poor conductors of heat:
      • Lead
      • Mercury
  • High melting points
    • But Gallium and Caesium have low m.p. (melting point).
  • Hard
  • Solid at room temperature
    • Except Mercury – liquid at room temperature.

details.summary: Handwritten mind map listing the physical properties of metals: they form basic oxides, show lustre (shining surface in pure state), are malleable (beaten into thin sheets; gold and silver most malleable), sonorous (produce sound on striking; school bells), ductile (drawn into thin wires; 1 g of gold gives ~2 km wire; gold most ductile), good conductors of heat (silver and copper best; lead and mercury poor), have high melting points (except gallium and caesium which have low m.p.), are hard, and are solid at room temperature (except mercury which is liquid).

topic: Reaction of Metal Oxides with Acids and Classification of Oxides
text:
General Reaction of Metal Oxides with Acids

  • metal oxide + Acid → salt + H2O (metal oxide is basic)

Example Reaction:

  • CuO + 2HCl → CuCl2 + H2O
  • The product CuCl2 is Greenish Blue in colour.

Classification of Oxides (Diagram described in words):

  • Metal oxide → Basic
  • Non metal oxide → Acidic
  • Both Acidic & Basic → Amphoteric oxides

Examples of Amphoteric oxides:

  • Aluminium oxide
  • Zinc oxide

Reactions of Aluminium:

  • 4Al + 3O2 → 2Al2O3
  • Al2O3 + 6HCl → 2AlCl3 + 3H2O (AlCl3 is the salt)

Solubility of Metal Oxides in Water:

  • Most metal oxides are insoluble in water.
  • Exception: Potassium oxide and Sodium oxide.
  • These two dissolve in water to produce Alkalis.

details.summary: Metal oxides are basic and react with acids to form salt and water (e.g., CuO + 2HCl → CuCl2 + H2O, greenish blue). Oxides are classified as basic (metal), acidic (non-metal) or amphoteric (both, e.g., Al2O3, ZnO). Most metal oxides are insoluble in water except potassium oxide and sodium oxide, which dissolve to form alkalis.

Redox is feasible

✓ Fe + CuSO4 → FeSO4 + Cu
(Iron more reactive than copper)

✓ Zn + FeSO4 → ZnSO4 + Fe

(Iron less reactive than zinc)

details.summary: Displacement reactions demonstrating the reactivity series. Iron displaces copper from CuSO4 (Fe is more reactive than Cu). Zinc displaces iron from FeSO4 (Zn is more reactive than Fe). Iron CANNOT displace zinc from ZnSO4 (Fe is less reactive than Zn). A more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from its salt solution.

mcq.question: Why does the reaction Fe + ZnSO4 → Zn + FeSO4 NOT occur?
options: Iron is more reactive than zinc
Iron is less reactive than zinc
Zinc is less reactive than iron
mcq.explanation: Iron is less reactive than zinc, so it cannot displace zinc from zinc sulfate solution. A less reactive metal cannot displace a more reactive metal from its salt solution.

text:
Time offset rule:

  • every 15° E = +1 hr
  • 15° W = -1 hr

Diagram (circle of longitudes with time offsets):

  • Top arc marked West on left and East on right with longitudes 0°, 15°, 30°, 45°, 60° on each side.
  • Time offsets around the circle: West side −4, −3, −2, −1; centre 0; East side +1, +2, +3, +4.

Compass / direction diagram:

  • Vertical axis: N (top) to S (bottom).
  • Horizontal axis: time W [−] on left, time E [+] on right.
  • Centre labelled Prime meridian (0° long.)

details.summary: Each 15° of longitude corresponds to a 1-hour time difference. East longitudes add time (+) and West longitudes subtract time (−). A circular diagram shows 0° at the centre with ±1 to ±4 hour offsets at 15° intervals up to 60°, and a compass diagram shows West as negative time and East as positive time with the Prime Meridian (0°) at the centre.

Rules when moving toward the IDL:

Toward EastToward West
Gain dayLose day
Lose timeGain time

Rules when crossing the IDL:

West to EastEast to West
Gain a day
Ex: 24 → 23		Lose a day
Ex: 23 → 24

Key relation: 24 hr lose = 1 day gain

topic: Earth's Revolution, Solstices, Equinoxes and Tropic of Cancer
text:
Diagram: Earth's Revolution Around the Sun

The diagram shows the Earth at four key positions in its orbit around the Sun, illustrating the changing seasons and the tilt of the Earth's axis (NP - North Pole, SP - South Pole).

  • Top Position: Vernal Equinox (21 March) — Sun rays fall vertically on the Equator. NP tilted neither toward nor away from the Sun.
  • Left Position: Summer Solstice (21 June) — Vertical ray on Tropic of Cancer overhead at 23.5°N. Summer in N. Hemisphere, Winter in S. Hemisphere.
  • Bottom Position: Autumnal Equinox (23rd Sep) — Sun rays fall vertically on the Equator again.
  • Right Position: Winter Solstice (22 Dec) — Vertical ray on Tropic of Capricorn at 23.5°S. Winter in N.H, Summer in S.H.

Key Annotations from Diagram:

  • At Summer Solstice (21 June): Continuous sun rays on North Pole for 6 months; continuous daylight; N. Hemisphere gets more heat; Summer in N. Hemisphere.
  • At Winter Solstice (22 Dec): Continuous sun rays on South Pole for 6 months; continuous daylight; S. Hemisphere gets more heat; Summer in S.H; Winter in N.H.
  • At Vernal Equinox (21 March): Arrows show sun rays coming downward toward the Earth from the Sun.
  • At Autumnal Equinox (23rd Sep): Arrows show sun rays going downward from the Earth toward the Sun.

Tropic of Cancer — 23.5°N

Tropic of Cancer is located at 23.5°N latitude. At the Summer Solstice (21 June), the vertical ray of the Sun falls on the Tropic of Cancer.

Tropic of Capricorn is located at 23.5°S latitude. At the Winter Solstice (22 Dec), the vertical ray of the Sun falls on the Tropic of Capricorn.

topic: Earth's Revolution, Solstices, Equinoxes and Tropic of Cancer
text:
Vernal Equinox (21 March):

  • The Sun is positioned directly above the Equator.
  • Day and night are approximately equal in length across the globe.
  • Marks the beginning of spring in the Northern Hemisphere.
  • In the diagram, the Earth is shown at the top position with sun rays (arrows) pointing downward toward the Earth.

Summer Solstice (21 June):

  • The vertical ray of the Sun falls on the Tropic of Cancer (23.5°N).
  • Longest day in the Northern Hemisphere; shortest day in the Southern Hemisphere.
  • Summer in N. Hemisphere; Winter in S. Hemisphere.
  • North Pole receives continuous sun rays for 6 months (continuous daylight).
  • The Earth is shown at the left position in the diagram, tilted with NP toward the Sun.

Autumnal Equinox (23rd September):

  • The Sun is positioned directly above the Equator again.
  • Day and night are approximately equal in length across the globe.
  • Marks the beginning of autumn in the Northern Hemisphere.
  • In the diagram, the Earth is shown at the bottom position with sun rays (arrows) pointing downward from the Earth.

Winter Solstice (22 December):

  • The vertical ray of the Sun falls on the Tropic of Capricorn (23.5°S).
  • Longest day in the Southern Hemisphere; shortest day in the Northern Hemisphere.
  • Winter in N. Hemisphere; Summer in S. Hemisphere.
  • South Pole receives continuous sun rays for 6 months (continuous daylight).
  • The Earth is shown at the right position in the diagram, tilted with NP away from the Sun.

Diagram Description — Earth's Orbital Positions:

The handwritten diagram shows the Sun at the center with the Earth at four orbital positions connected by curved arrows showing the direction of revolution (counterclockwise as viewed from above the North Pole):

  • Top (Vernal Equinox, 21 March): Earth with NP at top, SP at bottom. Sun rays (upward arrows from below) directed toward the Earth. Label highlighted in orange: vernal Equinox (21 March).
  • Left (Summer Solstice, 21 June): Earth tilted with NP toward the Sun. NP receives continuous sun rays. Label highlighted in orange: summer solstice (21 June). Annotations: 'summer in N. Hemisphere', 'get more heat', 'continuous sun rays on North pole for 6 months', 'continuous daylight'.
  • Right (Winter Solstice, 22 December): Earth tilted with NP away from the Sun. SP receives more heat. Label highlighted in orange: winter solstice (22 Dec). Annotations: 'winter in N.H', 'get more S.H heat', 'summer in S.H', 'Tropic of Cap. (23.5°S)', 'cont sun rays on South pole for 6 months', 'continuous daylight'.
  • Bottom (Autumnal Equinox, 23 September): Earth with NP at top, SP at bottom. Sun rays (downward arrows from above) directed toward the Earth. Label highlighted in yellow: Autumnal equinox (23rd Sep).

Central Diagram: The Sun is drawn at the center with radiating lines representing sunlight. Arrows between positions indicate the direction of Earth's orbital motion.

Important Note: The diagram clearly shows that at solstices, one pole is tilted toward the Sun (receiving direct sunlight) while the other is tilted away. At equinoxes, neither pole is tilted toward or away from the Sun.

topic: Refraction and Day-Night Duration on Equator
text:
Why the length of days on equator is always more than Night:

  • Refraction (atmospheric refraction causes sunlight to bend, making the sun appear above the horizon even when it is geometrically below it).

If there was no atmosphere:

  • No refraction
  • day = Night (day and night would be equal in duration)

details.summary: Atmospheric refraction causes the length of days on the equator to always be more than night. Without an atmosphere, there would be no refraction, and day and night would be equal.

Side labels on the right of the diagram: upper mantle (red), inner mantle (red), outer core (blue), inner core (blue).

Discontinuities of the Earth

The note lists the internal discontinuities (boundaries between the layers of the Earth):

  • 1) Conrad discontinuity (written "conard") – within the crust.
  • 2) Moho discontinuity – crust–mantle boundary.
  • 3) Gutenberg discontinuity – mantle–outer core boundary.

Diagram 1 description: A cross-section showing the Indo-Australian plate (continental crust) and the Pacific Plate (oceanic crust). The denser oceanic crust of the Pacific Plate sinks beneath the continental crust at the subduction zone, descending into the mantle, with a volcano erupting above the subduction point.

topic: Earthquakes: Epicenter, Focus, and Seismic Wave Properties (P-wave, S-wave, Body & Surface waves)
text:
Earthquake Terminology & Wave Classification:

  • Epicenter: The point on the Earth's surface directly above the focus.
  • Focus / Hypocenter: The point within the earth where an earthquake rupture starts (energy release point).

Two types of waves:

  • Body Waves: Generated due to release of energy at focus & move in all directions. Include:
    • P - waves (Primary waves)
    • S - waves (Secondary waves)
  • Surface Waves: Body waves interact with the surface rock & generate a new set of waves, mainly L - waves.

* Note on Velocity: The velocity of wave changes as they travel through materials with different densities.

* Note on Density: Denser material ↓ higher is the velocity.

P - Wave (Primary Wave)

  • Move faster
  • 1st to arrive at surface
  • Similar to sound waves
  • Travel through:
    • gaseous
    • liquid
    • solid
  • Velocity order: S > l > G (Solid > liquid > gas) with max velocity in solid.
  • Longitudinal wave (sound)
  • 1.7 times faster than S wave
  • Vibrate parallel to the direction of propagation.

S - Wave (Secondary Wave)

  • 2nd to reach
  • Transverse wave
  • More destructive than P wave
  • Travels only in solid
  • Perpendicular to the wave direction in the vertical plane
  • Doesn't pass through core

details.summary: Comprehensive notes on seismic waves generated during earthquakes. Covers the distinction between body waves (P-waves and S-waves) and surface waves (L-waves). Key physical properties of P-waves (longitudinal, fastest, travels through solid, liquid, and gas, vibrates parallel to propagation direction) and S-waves (transverse, slower, travels only through solids, cannot pass through the Earth's core, more destructive). Also highlights how wave velocity increases with the density of the medium.

mcq.question: Which of the following seismic waves is a transverse wave, travels only through solids, and cannot pass through the Earth's liquid core?
mcq.explanation: S-waves (secondary waves) are transverse waves and cannot propagate through liquids or gases, meaning they cannot pass through the liquid outer core of the Earth.

topic: Seismic Waves – Epicenter, Focus & Two Types of Waves
text:
Diagram (Earthquake Wave Propagation Model): A 3D rectangular block representing the Earth's crust is drawn with a set of concentric circles radiating from a central point inside the block. The central point is labelled Focus / Hypocenter (the point of origin of the earthquake within the Earth). A vertical line connects the focus to a point on the top surface of the block, which is labelled Epicenter (the point on the surface directly above the focus).

Two Types of Seismic Waves:

  • Body Waves – generated due to the release of energy at the focus; they move in all directions. Sub-types:
    • P-Waves
    • S-Waves
  • Surface Waves – generated when body waves interact with the surface rock and generate a new set of waves. Sub-type:
    • L-Wave

text:
P-Wave (highlighted):

  • Move faster than other seismic waves.
  • 1st to arrive at the surface.
  • Similar to sound waves.
  • Travel through gaseous, liquid and solid media.
  • Velocity order (max velocity): S > L > G (Solid > Liquid > Gas).
  • It is a longitudinal wave (like sound).
  • 1.7 times faster than S-Wave.
  • Particles vibrate parallel to the direction of wave propagation.

details.summary: P-waves are the fastest, first-arriving longitudinal seismic waves that travel through solids, liquids and gases, vibrating parallel to propagation and moving 1.7 times faster than S-waves.

text:

  • Very fluid lava.
  • Because of this fluidity, these volcanoes are not steep.
  • Low-explosivity type.

  • Develops into a cinder cone.

text:
Lava is broadly classified into two types on the basis of its silica content:

  • Acidic Lava
    • Contains more silica
    • Viscous (high viscosity)
    • Lighter in color
    • Creates a dome structure
    • Examples:
      • Stromboli, Italy
      • Puy de dome, France — described as the light house of the Mediterranean Sea
  • Basic Lava
    • Contains less silica
    • Less viscous (low viscosity)
    • Darker in color
    • Creates a flat-top structure
    • Example: Mauna Loa, Hawaii

details.summary: Lava is divided into Acidic Lava (more silica, viscous, lighter in color, forms dome structures; e.g. Stromboli in Italy and Puy de dome in France, the light house of the Mediterranean Sea) and Basic Lava (less silica, less viscous, darker in color, forms flat-top structures; e.g. Mauna Loa in Hawaii).

text:
Volcanoes are classified into three categories based on their eruptive activity:

  • Active Volcanoes — erupt regularly
    • Japan — Sukurajima
    • Hawaii Island — Kila, Mauna Loa, Mauna Kea
    • Indonesia — Tambora, Sumeru, Merapi, Dukano
    • Italy — Stromboli, Mount Etna
    • India — Barren Island
  • Dormant Volcanoes — erupted in the near past but have the potential to do so
    • India — Narcondum (near North Andaman)
    • Indonesia — Krakatau
    • Japan — Fujiyama
    • Italy — Vesuvius
  • Extinct Volcanoes — haven't erupted in human history and will not erupt in the future
    • Tanzania — Mt. Kilimanjaro
    • Ecuador — Chimborazo
    • Argentina — Aconcagua
    • Myanmar — Popa

text:
Intrusive Igneous Landforms are formed when magmatic material cools and solidifies within the Earth's crust at deeper or shallow depths before reaching the surface.

1. Batholiths

  • Magmatic material that cools in the deeper depth.
  • Cooled portion of magma in deeper regions.
  • Develops into large dome-shaped bodies.
  • Composed primarily of granitic bodies.

2. Laccolith

  • Large dome-shaped intrusive bodies.
  • Connected by a pipe-like conduit from below.
  • Surface expression: Associated with composite volcanoes.
  • Example: Karnataka plateaus.

3. Lapolith / Lopolith

  • Saucer-shaped intrusive body.
  • Concave to the sky body.

4. Phacolith

  • A lens-shaped mass of intrusive igneous rock.
  • Deposition on syncline or anticline structures (troughs and crests).

5. Dyke (Vertical)

  • Magma solidifies perpendicular to the ground.
  • Forms a distinct wall-like structure.

6. Horizontal Bodies (Sills & Sheets)

  • Near-horizontal intrusive igneous sheets.
  • Thinner horizontal bodies are called Sheets.
  • Thick horizontal bodies are called Sills.

7. Stock

  • A smaller batholith-like intrusive structure.

topic: Ocean Floor Relief Features & Continental Shelf
text:
Ocean Floor Relief Features are classified into major and minor divisions based on depth, slope, and geological structure.

Diagrammatic Representation: Illustrates the sequence of underwater topography: Continental Shelf → Continental Slope → Continental Rise (gradient 0.5–1°, covered with clay and silt) → Abyssal Plain (plane area) along with features like Volcanic Islands, Mid-Ocean Ridges, Rift Valleys, and Oceanic Trenches. The boundary of the continental slope indicates its end.

4 Major Divisions of Ocean Floor:

  • 1. Continental Shelf: The shallowest part of the ocean floor.
  • 2. Continental Slope: Connects the continental shelf to the ocean basin.
  • 3. Deep Sea Plain (Abyssal Plain): Extensive flat regions of the ocean basin floor.
  • 4. Oceanic Deeps: The deepest trenches and chasms in the ocean floor.

Key Characteristics of Continental Shelf:

  • Shallowest part of the ocean floor.
  • Average gradient of 1° or even less.
  • The point of steep incline at the edge is also called the Shelf Break.
  • The Siberian Shelf in the Arctic Ocean is the largest shelf in the world.
  • Serves as a rich source of fossil fuels.
  • Acts as a good fishing ground due to shallow sunlight-penetrated waters.

Minor Relief Features:

  1. Hills
  2. Seamount: Isolated volcanic peaks 3000–4500m tall (e.g., Hawaiian Islands).
  3. Mounts
  4. Guyots: Flat-topped submerged mountains (plateau).
  5. Trenches: Formed at convergent plate boundaries.
  6. Canyons
  7. Peak
  8. Ridge: Underwater mountain chains formed at divergent plate boundaries.

details.summary: Detailed overview of major ocean relief features (Continental Shelf, Slope, Deep Sea Plain, Oceanic Deeps) and minor features (Seamounts, Guyots, Trenches, Ridges) with key facts about the Continental Shelf.

text:
Problem 2: A train accelerates from 36 km/h to 54 km/h in 10 sec. Find acceleration and distance.

Given:

  • u = 36 km/h = 36 x 5/18 = 10 m/s
  • v = 54 km/h = 54 x 5/18 = 15 m/s
  • t = 10 sec

Calculation:

  • v = u + at
  • a = (v - u) / t
  • a = (15 - 10) / 10 = 5/10 = 0.5 m/s^2
  • s = ut + 1/2 at^2
  • s = 10 x 10 + 1/2 x 0.5 x (10)^2
  • s = 100 + 25 = 125 m

details.summary: Solved example calculating acceleration and distance for a train.

mcq.question: In the train problem, what is the calculated acceleration?
mcq.explanation: Using a = (v-u)/t, the acceleration is (15-10)/10 = 0.5 m/s^2.

  • d = 40 m

Calculation:

  • v^2 - u^2 = 2as
  • 400 - 25 = 2 x a x 40

text:
Problem 3: A bullcart at rest accelerated uniformly to a speed of 144 km/h in 20 sec. Then distance?

Given:

  • v = 144 km/h = 144 x 5/18 = 40 m/s
  • u = 0 (at rest)
  • t = 20 sec

Calculation:

  • a = (v - u) / t
  • a = (40 - 0) / 20 = 2 m/s^2
  • s = ut + 1/2 at^2
  • s = 0 + 1/2 x 2 x 400
  • s = 400 m = 0.4 km

text:
Key Milestones in the Making of the Constitution:

  • The idea of a constituent assembly for India was put forward for the first time by MN Roy in 1934.
  • The demand for a constitution was first accepted by the British in August 1946.
  • The constituent assembly was set up as per the Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946.
  • The first meeting was held on 9 December 1946 with Sachidanand Sinha as its provisional president.
  • On December 11, Dr. Rajender Prasad was elected as the president of the constituent assembly.

details.summary: Timeline of the formation of the Constituent Assembly, including key dates and figures like MN Roy, Sachidanand Sinha, and Dr. Rajender Prasad.

mcq.question: Who was the first to put forward the idea of a constituent assembly for India?
mcq.explanation: The idea was put forward for the first time by MN Roy in 1934.

content:
**Key Milestones in the Making of the Constitution:**

- The idea of a constituent assembly for India was put forward for the first time by **MN Roy** in **1934**.
- The demand for a constitution was first accepted by the British in **August 1946**.
- The constituent assembly was set up as per the **Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946**.
- The first meeting was held on **9 December 1946** with **Sachidanand Sinha** as its provisional president.
- On **December 11**, **Dr. Rajender Prasad** was elected as the president of the constituent assembly.

### Key Exam Facts
- **Summary:** Timeline of the formation of the Constituent Assembly, including key dates and figures like MN Roy, Sachidanand Sinha, and Dr. Rajender Prasad.

text:
Salient Features of the Indian Constitution:

  • It is the lengthiest written constitution of all the written constitutions of the world.
  • The constitution of India has borrowed most of its provisions from the constitutions of various countries as well as the Government of India Act 1935.
  • The constitution of India is neither rigid nor flexible but a blend of both.
  • It is a federal system with unitary bias. The term "Federation" has nowhere been used in the constitution; rather, "union of states" is mentioned.
  • The constitution of India has opted for the British Parliamentary System of Government rather than the American Presidential System. This model is also called the "Westminster" model of Government.
  • The Indian constitution establishes a judicial system that is integrated as well as independent.
  • The constitution of India stands for a secular state.
  • The Indian constitution provides for only a single citizenship.
  • The Indian constitution contains elaborate emergency provisions to enable the president to meet any extraordinary situation effectively.

details.summary: Key characteristics of the Indian Constitution, including its length, federal nature, parliamentary system, secularism, and emergency provisions.

mcq.question: Which model of government has the Indian Constitution opted for?
mcq.explanation: The constitution of India has opted for British Parliamentary System of Government, also known as the Westminster model.

content:
**Salient Features of the Indian Constitution:**

- It is the lengthiest written constitution of all the written constitutions of the world.
- The constitution of India has borrowed most of its provisions from the constitutions of various countries as well as the **Government of India Act 1935**.
- The constitution of India is **neither rigid nor flexible** but a blend of both.
- It is a **federal system with unitary bias**. The term *"Federation"* has nowhere been used in the constitution; rather, *"union of states"* is mentioned.
- The constitution of India has opted for the **British Parliamentary System** of Government rather than the American Presidential System. This model is also called the **"Westminster" model of Government**.
- The Indian constitution establishes a **judicial system** that is integrated as well as independent.
- The constitution of India stands for a **secular state**.
- The Indian constitution provides for only a **single citizenship**.
- The Indian constitution contains **elaborate emergency provisions** to enable the president to meet any extraordinary situation effectively.

### Key Exam Facts
- **Summary:** Key characteristics of the Indian Constitution, including its length, federal nature, parliamentary system, secularism, and emergency provisions.

text:
Definitions and Properties:

  • The centre of the reflecting surfaces of a spherical mirror is a point called the pole. It lies on the surface of the mirror.
  • This sphere centre is called the centre of curvature of the spherical mirror (C).
  • Centre of curvature is not a part of the mirror.
  • The centre of curvature of a concave mirror lies in front of it, it lies behind the mirror in case of a convex mirror.
  • A straight line passing through the pole and the centre of curvature of a spherical mirror is called the principal axis.

Formula: The radius of curvature is found to be equal to twice the focal length. R = 2f

- The centre of curvature of a concave mirror lies in front of it, it lies behind the mirror in case of a convex mirror.
- A straight line passing through the pole and the centre of curvature of a spherical mirror is called the principal axis.

**Formula:** The radius of curvature is found to be equal to twice the focal length. **R = 2f**

text:
More to Know:

If an opaque object on the path of light becomes very small, light has a tendency to bend around it and not walk in a straight line - an effect known as the diffraction of light. Then the straight-line treatment of optics using rays fails. To explain phenomena such as diffraction, light is thought of as a wave, the details of which you will study in higher classes.

Again, at the beginning of the 20th century, it became known that the wave theory of light often becomes inadequate for treatment of the interaction of light with matter, and light often behaves somewhat like a stream of particles. This confusion about the true nature of light continued for some years till a modern quantum theory of light emerged in which light is neither a 'wave' nor a 'particle' - the new theory reconciles the particle properties of light with the wave nature.

details.summary: Explanation of diffraction, the limitations of ray optics, and the quantum theory of light which reconciles wave and particle properties.

mcq.question: According to the modern quantum theory of light, light is:
options: Neither a wave nor a particle
mcq.explanation: The text states that the new theory reconciles properties, stating light is neither strictly a 'wave' nor a 'particle'.

Then the straight-line treatment of optics using rays fails. To explain phenomena such as diffraction, light is thought of as a wave, the details of which you will study in higher classes.

Again, at the beginning of the 20th century, it became known that the wave theory of light often becomes inadequate for treatment of the interaction of light with matter, and light often behaves somewhat like a stream of particles. This confusion about the true nature of light continued for some years till a modern quantum theory of light emerged in which light is neither a 'wave' nor a 'particle' - the new theory reconciles the particle properties of light with the wave nature.

### Key Exam Facts
- **Summary:** Explanation of diffraction, the limitations of ray optics, and the quantum theory of light which reconciles wave and particle properties.

text:
All cells contain the following organelles:

  • Cell Membrane: It is innermost layer of cell envelope that is semipermeable in nature. It is a bilayer consists of protein and lipids mainly. Most popular theory "fluid mosaic model" is given by Singer and Nicolson.
  • Ribosome: They are composed of RNA and proteins and are not surrounded by any membrane. The eukaryotic ribosomes are 80S while the prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S. S stands for sedimentation coefficient; it is a measure of density and size.
  • Nucleus: It is largest principal cell organelle of cell, which contains all genetic information for controlling all essential processes related to metabolism and transmission. The nucleus contains chromosomes which are visible as rod shaped structure only when the cell is about to divide. Chromosomes are composed of DNA (Deoxyribonucleic acid) and protein. Functional segments of DNA are called genes. CHROMATIN - composed of nuclear acid and histone protein. It is entangled mass of thread-like structures. NUCLEOID - Undefined nuclear region lacking nuclear membrane containing only nucleic acids. Present in organisms like bacteria.
  • Cytoplasm: The clear jelly-like fluid that fills the cell providing protection for it's contents.
  • Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER): The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is a large network of membrane-bound tubes and sheets. There are two types of ER - rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER) and smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER). RER looks rough under a microscope because it has particles called ribosomes attached to its surface. The ribosomes, which are present in all active cells, are the sites of protein manufacture. The SER helps in the manufacture of fat molecules, or lipids, important for cell function. Some of these proteins and lipids help in building the cell membrane. This process is known as membrane biogenesis. SER plays a crucial role in detoxifying many poisons and drugs.
  • Goldi Bodies (Golgi Apparatus): First described by Camillo Golgi, consists of a system of membrane-bound vesicles (flattened sacs) arranged approximately parallel to each other in stacks called cisterns. The material synthesized near the ER is packaged and dispatched to various targets inside and outside the cell through the Golgi apparatus. Its functions include the storage, modification and packaging of products in vesicles. The Golgi apparatus is also involved in the formation of lysosomes.

subject: General Science
text:
Definition and History of Science

Science in a broad sense existed before the modern era and in many historical civilizations. Modern science is distinct in its approach and successful in its results, so it now defines what science is in the strictest sense of the term.

Science in its original sense was a word for a type of knowledge rather than a specialized word for the pursuit of such knowledge. In particular, it was the type of knowledge which people can communicate to each other and share. For example, knowledge about the working of natural things was gathered long before recorded history and led to the development of complex abstract thought.

Historical Examples:

  • Construction of complex calendars
  • Techniques for making poisonous plants edible
  • Public works at national scale (reservoirs, dams, and dikes)
  • Buildings such as the Pyramids

However, no consistent conscientious distinction was made between knowledge of such things, which are true in every community, and other types of communal knowledge, such as mythologies and legal systems.

Etymology and Scope:

The word Science comes from Latin word "scientia" meaning "knowledge" and in broadest sense it is any systematic knowledge-base or prescriptive practice being capable of resulting in prediction. Science is a branch of knowledge or systematic study of various operations, structure and behaviour of physical and natural world through observations and experiments.

Relevance to Exams:

It plays an important role for Exams like IAS, CDS, NDA, AFCAT, State PSC, SSC and other similar competitive exams. The questions in different competitive examination are such that to test the aspirants general awareness of a variety of disciplines.

3.1 Difference Between the Living and Non-Living

  • Life is a distinguishing characteristic of physical entities having biological processes from those that do not have such processes.
  • Living things are a complex organization of physical molecules, that perform various biological and chemical reactions in metabolism, reproduction etc., constituting an organism.
  • Non-living things, on the other hand, does not show any of such characteristics.

Characteristics of non-living things:

  • Non-living things are made up of atoms.
  • Non-living things do not show growth or reproduce.
  • Non-living things do not respond to external stimuli.
  • Non-living things are all around as like a chair, a pen, a book etc.,

Characteristics of living things:

  • The basic units of living things are cells. These cells contain a nucleus, protoplasm and cell membranes. They from the basic and most important characteristics of living beings.
  • They obtain and use energy in ways like photosynthesis, metabolisms etc.,
  • Living things grow and develop.
  • Living things reproduce.
  • Living things interact with the external environment and respond to external stimuli.
  • Living things adapt to their environment.

- **6. Sixth Schedule:** Provision related to Administration of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram
- **7. Seventh Schedule:** Division of Power between Centre and State through Union List, State List and Concurrent List
- **8. Eighth Schedule:** Languages recognized by Constitution. Total 22 languages are there.
- **9. Ninth Schedule:** Land Reforms and Abolition of Zamindari System
- **10. Tenth Schedule:** Anti Defection Law
- **11. Eleventh Schedule:** Panchayat
- **12. Twelfth Schedule:** Municipalities

### Key Exam Facts
- **Summary:** A comprehensive list of the 12 Schedules of the Indian Constitution and their respective subject matters, ranging from state names to anti-defection laws.

subject: Physics
text:
The Ray Model of Light

When light rays encounter an object, they can be reflected, absorbed or transmitted.

  • Reflection occurs when light bounces off a surface.
  • Absorption happens when materials take in light, often converting to heat.
  • Transmission is when light passes through a transparent material, like glass or water.

Ray diagrams assist us in tracing the path of light for someone seeing a point on an image of an item. Lines represent the incident and reflected rays with arrows in a ray diagram. It also aids us in determining the direction of travel of light. Rays for the incident and reflected rays are represented on the diagram.

details.summary: Overview of how light interacts with objects (reflection, absorption, transmission) and the utility of ray diagrams.

mcq.question: What happens when light passes through a transparent material?
mcq.explanation: Transmission is when light passes through a transparent material, like glass or water.

content:
**The Ray Model of Light**

When light rays encounter an object, they can be reflected, absorbed or transmitted.

- **Reflection** occurs when light bounces off a surface.
- **Absorption** happens when materials take in light, often converting to heat.
- **Transmission** is when light passes through a transparent material, like glass or water.

Ray diagrams assist us in tracing the path of light for someone seeing a point on an image of an item. Lines represent the incident and reflected rays with arrows in a ray diagram. It also aids us in determining the direction of travel of light. Rays for the incident and reflected rays are represented on the diagram.

text:
SIGN CONVENTION FOR SPHERICAL MIRRORS:

  • (i) The object is always placed to the left of the mirror.
  • (ii) All distances measured from the pole of the mirror.
  • (iii) All the distances measured to the right are taken as positive while those measured to the left are taken as negative.
  • (iv) All the distances measured upwards are taken as positive while those measured downwards are taken as negative.

details.summary: Standard rules for assigning positive and negative signs to distances in spherical mirror calculations.

mcq.question: In the sign convention for spherical mirrors, distances measured to the right are taken as:
mcq.explanation: All the distances measured to the right are taken as positive.

content:
**SIGN CONVENTION FOR SPHERICAL MIRRORS:**

- (i) The object is always placed to the left of the mirror.
- (ii) All distances measured from the pole of the mirror.
- (iii) All the distances measured to the right are taken as positive while those measured to the left are taken as negative.
- (iv) All the distances measured upwards are taken as positive while those measured downwards are taken as negative.

### Key Exam Facts
- **Summary:** Standard rules for assigning positive and negative signs to distances in spherical mirror calculations.

text:
2nd Law of Motion

  • Rate of change of momentum of an object is proportional to the applied unbalanced force in the direction of force.
  • Relation between position & time.
  • Momentum (p) = mv
  • Both direction and magnitude.

Formulas:

  • a = change in velocity / time = (v - u) / t
  • F = ma (F: change in mom)
  • F = m(v - u) / t
  • F = (mv - mu) / t
  • F ∝ a
  • Force = kg ms-2 or Newton

details.summary: Explanation of the 2nd Law of Motion, definition of momentum, and derivation of the force formula F=ma.

mcq.question: What is the SI unit of Force?
mcq.explanation: The notes explicitly state Force = kg ms^-2 or Newton.

content:
**2nd Law of Motion**

- Rate of change of momentum of an object is proportional to the applied unbalanced force in the direction of force.
- Relation between position & time.
- **Momentum (p) = mv**
- Both *direction* and *magnitude*.

**Formulas:**

- a = change in velocity / time = (v - u) / t
- F = ma (F: change in mom)
- F = m(v - u) / t
- F = (mv - mu) / t
- **F ∝ a**

text:
India's Extent: India extends from Kashmir to Kanyakumari in the south and Arunachal Pradesh in the east to Gujarat in the west.

  • India's territorial limit extends to 12 nautical miles (21.9 km).
  • The northern part of the country lies in tropics whereas southern lies in sub-tropics.
  • 82.30-degree E is the standard meridian of India. It is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of Greenwich Mean time.
  • There is 30 degrees / 2 hours difference between eastern and western most parts of our country.
  • It has a coastline of 6100 km in mainland, and 7517 km in the entire geographical coast of mainland plus islands.

details.summary: Overview of India's geographical boundaries, standard meridian, time difference, and coastline length.

text:
Diagram Description: A cross-sectional diagram of the ocean floor showing the transition from the continental margin to the deep ocean. Key features labeled include the continental shelf, continental slope, volcanic island, mid-ocean ridge, trench, and rift valley. The boundary between the shelf and slope is indicated.

Continental Rise: Composed of clay + silt. It has a gradient of 0.5 - 1°.

Deep Sea Plain: Described as a plane area.

4 Major Divisions of the Ocean Floor:

  • Continental Shelf
  • Continental Slope
  • Deep Sea Plain
  • Oceanic Deeps

Continental Shelf (Highlighted):

  • It is the shallowest part of the ocean.
  • Average gradient is 1° or even less.
  • It has a very steep slope.
  • Also called shelf break.
  • The Siberian shelf in the Arctic Ocean is the largest in the world.
  • It is a source of fossil fuels.
  • It is a good fishing ground.

Minor Relief Features:

  • Hills
  • Sea mounts
  • Mounts
  • Guayots (Plateau)
  • Trenches (Convergent plate boundary)
  • Canyons
  • Peak
  • Ridge (Divergent plate boundary)
  • Seamount (4500m tall) - Example: Hawaiian Islands

Preamble refers to the introduction or preface to the constitution.

  • N.A Palkhivala called “Preamble” as the 'identity card of the constitution'.
  • It is based on “Objective Resolution”.
  • It has been amended only once by 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act which added three new words – Socialist, Secular and Integrity.
  • Preamble is a part of constitution according to Keshavanand Bharati Case.
  • It is non- justiciable that is its provision are not enforceable in courts of law.

This text is followed by notes explaining key aspects of the Preamble.

content:
Preamble refers to the introduction or preface to the constitution.

- N.A Palkhivala called “Preamble” as the 'identity card of the constitution'.
- It is based on “Objective Resolution”.
- It has been amended only once by 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act which added three new words – **Socialist, Secular and Integrity**.
- Preamble is a part of constitution according to Keshavanand Bharati Case.
- It is non- justiciable that is its provision are not enforceable in courts of law.

text:
LAWS OF REFRACTION OF LIGHT

  • The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal to the all lie in the same plane.
  • The ratio of sine of angle of incidence to the sine of angle of refraction is a constant, for the light of a given colour and for the given pair of media. This law is also known as Snell's law of refraction.
  • If i is the angle of incidence and r is the angle of refraction, then sin i / sin r = constant.

details.summary: The laws of refraction state that incident, refracted rays and the normal lie in the same plane, and Snell's Law defines the constant ratio of sines of incidence and refraction angles.

subject: Physics
text:
REFRACTIVE INDEX

  • The value of the refractive index for a given pair of media depends upon the speed of light in the two media.
  • Light travelling from medium 1 into medium 2, as v1 be the speed of light in medium 1 and v2 be the speed of light in medium 2.
  • The refractive index of medium 2 with respect to medium 1 is given by the ratio of the speed of light in medium 1 and the speed in medium 2. This is usually represented by the symbol n21.
  • This can be expressed in an equation form as n21 = v1/v2.

details.summary: The refractive index of a medium is a measure of how much the speed of light changes when entering that medium, defined as the ratio of light speeds in the two media.

Do You Know?

Litmus solution is a purple dye, which is extracted from lichen, a plant belonging to the division Thallophyta, and is commonly used as an indicator. When the litmus solution is neither acidic nor basic, its colour is purple. There are many other natural materials like red cabbage leaves, turmeric, coloured petals of some flowers such as Hydrangea, Petunia and Geranium, which indicate the presence of acid or base in a solution. These are called acid-base indicators or sometimes simply indicators.

text:
• The pH of a neutral solution is 7.
  • Values less than 7 on the pH scale represent an acidic solution, more than 7 represents base solution.
  • The atmosphere of Venus is made up of thick white and yellowish clouds of sulphuric acid.
  • Our body works within the pH range of 7.0 to 7.8.
  • When pH of rain water is less than 5.6, it is called acid rain.
  • During indigestion the stomach produces too much acid, people use bases called antacids. These antacids neutralise the excess acid. Magnesium hydroxide (Milk of magnesia), a mild base, is often used for this purpose.
  • Tooth decay starts when the pH of the mouth is lower than 5.5. Tooth enamel, made up of calcium hydroxyapatite (a crystalline form of calcium phosphate) is the hardest substance in the body.
  • Bee-sting leaves an methanoic acid which causes pain and irritation.
content:
- The pH of a neutral solution is 7.
- Values less than 7 on the pH scale represent an acidic solution, more than 7 represents base solution.
- The atmosphere of Venus is made up of thick white and yellowish clouds of sulphuric acid.
- Our body works within the pH range of 7.0 to 7.8.
- When pH of rain water is less than 5.6, it is called acid rain.
- During indigestion the stomach produces too much acid, people use bases called antacids. These antacids neutralise the excess acid. Magnesium hydroxide (Milk of magnesia), a mild base, is often used for this purpose.
- Tooth decay starts when the pH of the mouth is lower than 5.5. Tooth enamel, made up of calcium hydroxyapatite (a crystalline form of calcium phosphate) is the hardest substance in the body.
- Bee-sting leaves an methanoic acid which causes pain and irritation.

subject: Biology
text:
Plastid

  • Are present in only plant cells.
  • It is of various types namely chromoplasts and leucoplasts.
  • CHROMOPLASTS - they are the colored plastids.
  • Chromoplast containing the pigment chlorophyll is called as CHLOROPLASTS. Chloroplasts are important for photosynthesis.
  • Chromoplasts also contains yellow and orange pigments.
  • LEUCOPLASTS - they store oil, starch and protein granules.
  • Plastids also have their own DNA and ribosomes.
  • Leucoplasts are further divided into few types- Amyloplasts, Elaioplasts and Aleuroplasts.
  • Amyloplasts store carbohydrates (starch).
  • Elaioplasts store oils and fats whereas Aleuroplasts store proteins.

details.summary: Plastids are organelles found exclusively in plant cells, categorized into chromoplasts (colored, including chloroplasts for photosynthesis) and leucoplasts (colorless, for storage of oil, starch, and protein). Plastids possess their own DNA and ribosomes.

text:
Lysosomes

  • Lysosomes are membrane bound sacs filled with enzymes. These enzymes are made by rough endoplasmic reticulum.
  • These help to keep the cell clean by digesting any foreign material as well as worn-out cell organelles. Foreign materials entering the cell, such as bacteria or food, as well as old organelles end up in the lysosomes, which break complex substances into simpler substances.
  • Also called as “SUICIDAL BAGS OF CELL”.

details.summary: Lysosomes are enzyme-filled, membrane-bound sacs produced by the rough endoplasmic reticulum. They function in cellular waste disposal, digesting foreign materials and worn-out organelles, and are known as the 'suicidal bags of the cell'.

subject: Biology
text:
Mitochondria

  • Are known as “POWERHOUSE OF CELL”.
  • Mitochondria have two membrane coverings. The outer membrane is porous while the inner membrane is deeply folded. These folds increase surface area for ATP generating chemical reaction.
  • The energy required for various chemical activities needed for life is released by mitochondria in the form of ATP (Adenosine triphosphate) molecules.
  • ATP is called as the “ENERGY CURRENCY OF THE CELL”.
  • They have their own DNA and ribosomes.

details.summary: Mitochondria, the 'powerhouse of the cell,' have a porous outer membrane and a folded inner membrane that increases surface area for ATP production. They release energy as ATP, the 'energy currency of the cell,' and possess their own DNA and ribosomes.

subject: Geography
topic: Peninsular Block, Northern and Northeastern Mountains, Himalayan Subdivisions, Kashmir and Northwestern Himalayas
text:
PHYSIOGRAPHY

(Refer to the accompanying map of India showing major physiographic regions.)

PENINSULAR BLOCK

  • It is formed mainly of "gneisses and granites".
  • It is part of "Indo- Australian" Plate.
  • It has been subjected to various vertical movements and block faulting.

THE NORTH AND NORTHEASTERN MOUNTAINS

  • The great Himalayan range include the Great Himalayas and the Trans-Himalayan range, the Middle Himalayas and the Shivalik.

HIMALAYAS ARE FURTHER DIVIDED INTO FOLLOWING SUB DIVISIONS

(Refer to the accompanying map showing the regional divisions of the Himalayas, including Punjab Himalaya, Kumaon Himalaya, Central Himalaya, and Assam Himalaya.)

  1. KASHMIR & NORTHWESTERN HIMALAYAS
  2. HIMACHAL & UTTARANCHAL HIMALAYAS
  3. DARJILING & SIKKIM HIMALAYAS
  4. ARUNACHAL HIMALAYAS
  5. EASTERN HILLS AND MOUNTAINS

KASHMIR AND NORTHWESTERN HIMALAYAS

  • It comprises of ranges like the Karakoram, Ladakh, Zaskar and Pir Panjal.
  • Valley of Kashmir and Dal Lake lies between the great Himalayas and Pir Panjal range.
  • Kashmir Himalayas are famous for "Karewas".
  • Important fresh water lakes like Wular lake and Dal Lake and salt water lakes like Pangong Tso and Tso Moriri are also found in this region.
  • This region is drained by river Indus.
  • It also consists of longitudinal valleys k/a "Duns" e.g. Jammu dun and Pathankot dun.

(Refer to the detailed map of Kashmir and Northwestern Himalayas showing Karakoram, Ladakh, Zaskar, Pir Panjal ranges, and major rivers like Indus, Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Sutlej, along with passes like Zojila, Bara Lacha La, Shipki La.)

  • KAREWAS are thick deposits of glacial clay and other materials which are useful for cultivation of "Zafran" a local variety of Saffron.
  • Srinagar is located on the banks of Jhelum River.
  • JHELUM is the only river in its youth stage to form meanders.
  • ORDER OF RANGES FROM NORTH TO SOUTH IS:
    • KARAKORAM
    • LADAKH
    • ZASKAR
    • PIR PANJAL

"Bugyals" are summer grasslands in the higher reaches.

details.summary: This document provides an overview of the Physiography of India, focusing on the Peninsular Block, the Northern and Northeastern Mountains, and a detailed look into the Kashmir and Northwestern Himalayas. It covers geological formations, major mountain ranges, their subdivisions, important lakes, rivers, and unique geographical features like Karewas and Duns. It also highlights the order of ranges from North to South in the Kashmir region and defines 'Bugyals'.

content:
**PHYSIOGRAPHY**

*(Refer to the accompanying map of India showing major physiographic regions.)*

**PENINSULAR BLOCK**

- It is formed mainly of "gneisses and granites".
- It is part of "Indo- Australian" Plate.
- It has been subjected to various vertical movements and block faulting.

**THE NORTH AND NORTHEASTERN MOUNTAINS**

- The great Himalayan range include the Great Himalayas and the Trans-Himalayan range, the Middle Himalayas and the Shivalik.

**HIMALAYAS ARE FURTHER DIVIDED INTO FOLLOWING SUB DIVISIONS**

*(Refer to the accompanying map showing the regional divisions of the Himalayas, including Punjab Himalaya, Kumaon Himalaya, Central Himalaya, and Assam Himalaya.)*

- KASHMIR & NORTHWESTERN HIMALAYAS
- HIMACHAL & UTTARANCHAL HIMALAYAS
- DARJILING & SIKKIM HIMALAYAS
- ARUNACHAL HIMALAYAS
- EASTERN HILLS AND MOUNTAINS

**KASHMIR AND NORTHWESTERN HIMALAYAS**

- It comprises of ranges like the Karakoram, Ladakh, Zaskar and Pir Panjal.
- Valley of Kashmir and Dal Lake lies between the great Himalayas and Pir Panjal range.
- Kashmir Himalayas are famous for "Karewas".
- Important fresh water lakes like Wular lake and Dal Lake and salt water lakes like Pangong Tso and Tso Moriri are also found in this region.
- This region is drained by river Indus.
- It also consists of longitudinal valleys k/a "Duns" e.g. Jammu dun and Pathankot dun.

*(Refer to the detailed map of Kashmir and Northwestern Himalayas showing Karakoram, Ladakh, Zaskar, Pir Panjal ranges, and major rivers like Indus, Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Sutlej, along with passes like Zojila, Bara Lacha La, Shipki La.)*

- **KAREWAS** are thick deposits of glacial clay and other materials which are useful for cultivation of "Zafran" a local variety of Saffron.
- **Srinagar** is located on the banks of Jhelum River.
- **JHELUM** is the only river in its youth stage to form meanders.
- **ORDER OF RANGES FROM NORTH TO SOUTH IS:**KARAKORAM
- LADAKH
- ZASKAR
- PIR PANJAL

**"Bugyals"** are summer grasslands in the higher reaches.

### Key Exam Facts
- **Summary:** This document provides an overview of the Physiography of India, focusing on the Peninsular Block, the Northern and Northeastern Mountains, and a detailed look into the Kashmir and Northwestern Himalayas. It covers geological formations, major mountain ranges, their subdivisions, important lakes, rivers, and unique geographical features like Karewas and Duns. It also highlights the order of ranges from North to South in the Kashmir region and defines 'Bugyals'.

text:
Distance and Displacement

  • The distance covered by a body is the actual length of the path travelled by the body between the initial position and final position.
    • It is always positive.
    • It is a scalar quantity which has magnitude only.
    • Its unit is metre.
  • The displacement of a particle is the change in position of the particle in a particular direction and is given by a vector drawn from its initial position to its final position.
    • Displacement may be positive, negative or zero.
    • It is a vector quantity and its unit is also metre.
    • The magnitude of displacement may or may not be equal to the path length travelled by an object.
    • Displacement ≤ Distance

Diagram (a): A particle starts from A and reaches B through points C, D and E. AB is the displacement and (AC + CD + DE + EB) is the distance travelled.

Diagram (b): A particle starts from A and reaches C through point B. AC is displacement and distance covered is (AB + BC).

- It is a vector quantity and its unit is also metre.
- The magnitude of displacement may or may not be equal to the path length travelled by an object.
- Displacement ≤ Distance

*Diagram (a): A particle starts from A and reaches B through points C, D and E. AB is the displacement and (AC + CD + DE + EB) is the distance travelled.*

subject: Physics
text:
Speed

The path length or the distance covered by an object divided by the time taken by the object to cover that distance is called the speed of that object. Its unit is m/s or km/h.

Speed = Distance travelled / Time taken

  • An object is said to be moving with a uniform speed, if it covers equal distances in equal intervals of time.
  • An object is said to be moving with a variable speed, if it covers equal distances in unequal intervals of time or unequal distances in equal intervals of time.

details.summary: Definition, formula, unit, and types of speed (uniform and variable).

**Speed**

**The path length or the distance covered by an object divided by the time taken by the object to cover that distance is called the speed of that object.** Its unit is m/s or km/h.

Speed = Distance travelled / Time taken

- An object is said to be moving with a **uniform speed**, if it covers equal distances in equal intervals of time.
- An object is said to be moving with a **variable speed**, if it covers equal distances in unequal intervals of time or unequal distances in equal intervals of time.

### Key Exam Facts
- **Summary:** Definition, formula, unit, and types of speed (uniform and variable).

subject: Physics
text:
Average Speed

  • If a motion is the ratio of the total distance travelled by the object to the total time taken.
    i.e. average speed, vav = (s1 + s2 + s3 + ...) / (t1 + t2 + t3 + ...)
  • If the body covers equal distances with different speeds, then vav = (2v1v2) / (v1 + v2)

When the speed of an object is constantly changing, then the speed at a particular moment or instant of time is called the instantaneous speed of that object.

subject: Physics
text:
Velocity

The rate of change in position or displacement of a body with time is called the velocity of that body. It is a vector quantity.

Velocity = Displacement in particular direction / Time taken

  • A body is said to be moving with uniform velocity, if equal displacements of the body take place in same direction in equal intervals of time.
  • If a body moves in such a way that its speed or the direction or both changes with time, the body is said to have variable velocity.

details.summary: Definition, formula, and types of velocity (uniform and variable).

content:
**Velocity**

**The rate of change in position or displacement of a body with time is called the velocity of that body.** It is a vector quantity.

Velocity = Displacement in particular direction / Time taken

- A body is said to be moving with **uniform velocity**, if equal displacements of the body take place in same direction in equal intervals of time.
- If a body moves in such a way that its speed or the direction or both changes with time, the body is said to have **variable velocity**.

### Key Exam Facts
- **Summary:** Definition, formula, and types of velocity (uniform and variable).

subject: Physics
text:
Average Velocity

  • If a body is defined as the net displacement divided by the time taken for displacement.
    vav = (x2 - x1) / (t2 - t1)
    As net displacement = x2 - x1 and time taken = t2 - t1
  • Average velocity could be zero, positive or negative but average speed is always positive for moving body. When a particle returns to the starting point, its average velocity is zero but average speed is not zero.

details.summary: Definition and formula for average velocity, with an important note on its relation to average speed.

subject: Physics
text:
Relative Velocity

  • When two bodies are moving in the straight line, the speed (or velocity) of one with respect to another is known as its relative speed (or velocity).
  • When two bodies are moving in the same direction, then relative velocity = v1 - v2. When the two bodies are moving in opposite directions, then relative velocity = v1 + v2.

details.summary: Definition of relative velocity and formulae for bodies moving in the same or opposite directions.

content:
**Relative Velocity**

- When two bodies are moving in the same direction, then relative velocity = v1 - v2. When the two bodies are moving in opposite directions, then relative velocity = v1 + v2.

### Key Exam Facts
- **Summary:** Definition of relative velocity and formulae for bodies moving in the same or opposite directions.

Introduction to Cells

  • The cell is the fundamental unit of life. It is the basic structural and functional unit of all living things.
  • Cells from the basic life unit irrespective of the nature of the organism – either unicellular or multicellular and either plant or animal cell.
  • The cells of common structure and function combine to form a tissue.
  • Tissues form organs and cooperation of organs constructs an organism.

Cell Structure:

  • Cells can be of any shape and size predetermined to perform specific functions.
  • The major constituents of a cell can be classified into two – Cell wall and protoplasm.
