text:
Methods for Reducing Friction

  • By using lubricants e.g. grease, oil, etc.
  • By using ball or roller bearings, which changes sliding into rolling.
  • By using soap solution.
  • By using powder.
  • Friction due to air is considerably reduced by streamlining the shape of the body moving at high speed in air. e.g. aircraft, jet-planes, fast cars are streamlined.
  • The tyres are provided with treads which increases the friction between the tyres and the road.
  • Note: Pulling is easier than pushing. While pushing, there is one component of force that acting downward on the object adds to the weight of the body hence there are more friction opposing the effort. Whereas on pulling, the vertical component of force is against the weight of the body and friction is less overall friction. So, it is easy to pull than push.

SELECTION CRITERIA

Selection will be done on the basis of Written Test, SSB and Medical Examination have been given below.

STEP 1 Written Test

  1. The AFCAT Question Paper will have 100 questions. All questions will be of three marks each. For every correct answer the candidate will get three marks and for every wrong answer one mark will be deducted under negative marking. The total time allotted for the paper is two hours.
  2. Each Question Paper will have questions from the following topics:-
  • (a) General Awareness – History, Sports, Geography, Environment, Civics, Basic Science, Defence, Art, Culture, Current Affairs, Politics, etc.
  • (b) Verbal Ability in English – Comprehension, Error Detection, Sentence Completion, Synonyms, Antonyms and Testing of Vocabulary.
  • (c) Numerical Ability – Decimal Fraction, Simplification, Average, Profit and loss, Percentage, Ratio and Proportion and Simple interest.
  • (d) Reasoning and Military Aptitude Test – Verbal Skills and Spatial Ability.

If you have successfully cleared Step 1, you will receive a Call letter to report to any one of the Air Force Selection Boards located at Dehradun, Varanasi, Gandhinagar, Mysore and Kanchanrapara. STAGE I TESTING

  • Officer Intelligence Rating Test
  • Picture perception and Discussion Test

Stage I is a screening test. Those who qualify Stage I are eligible to undergo Stage II testing. Stage I disqualified candidates are routed back after announcement of results.

text:
Functions of Cytokinins:

  • They stimulate cell division, cell enlargement, and cell differentiation.
  • They prevent aging of plant parts.
  • They inhibit apical dominance and help in the growth of lateral buds into branches.

(iv) Ethylene:

  • Ethylene is a gaseous hormone. It is found in ripening fruits, young flowers, and young leaves.

Functions of Ethylene:

  • It induces ripening of fruits.
  • It promotes senescence and abscission of leaf and flowers.
  • In cells, it only increases the width not the length.

(v) Abscissic acid:

  • Abcissic acid also known as Dormin is a naturally occurring growth inhibitor found in a wide variety of plants. It is synthesized in leaves.

Functions of Abscissic acid:

  • It induces dormancy of buds and seeds as opposed to Gibberellin, which breaks dormancy.
  • It promotes the senescence of leaf i.e., the fall of leaves happens due to abscissic acid.
  • It inhibits seed germination and development.
  • It causes the closing of Stomata.

details.summary: Overview of the functions of Cytokinins, Ethylene, and Abscissic acid (Dormin) in plant physiology.

text:
Germination of seeds:

  • Seed germination is the return of metabolic activities and growth of the seed tissue to give rise to a new plant by the development of the embryo.
  • There are two types of seed germination
  • Epigeal germination - In epigeal germination hypocotyl (the region below cotyledons) elongates and cotyledons come out above the soil surface. Examples: seeds of pumpkin, mustard, tamarind, and french bean.
  • Hypogeal Germination - In hypogeal germination the epicotyl (the region above cotyledons) elongates and cotyledons remain below the soil surface. Examples: Most monocots seed like rice, wheat, maize, and coconut.

Five factors affect the seed germination - water, temperature, oxygen, light and growth hormones.

Photoperiodism:

  • The effect of duration of light on the growth of plants is known as photoperiodism.
  • On the basis of light required by the plants for flowering, the plants are classified into the following three categories:
  • Short-day Plants - Some plants produce flowers when exposed to a light for a shorter period than usual. These are called Short-day Plants. Cosmos, Dahlia, Soyabean, are short-day plants.
  • Long-day Plants – Some plants, flowers when exposed to a light for a period longer than usual. Gulmohar, radish, spinach, are long-day plants.

Pilot Aptitude Battery Test (PABT)

PABT is a unique test aimed at assessing a candidate's aptitude to be trained as a pilot. It is used as an independent selection device to induct potential officers into the Flying Branch of the Indian Air Force.

Components of PABT:

  • Instrument Battery Test (INSB)
  • Sensory Motor Apparatus Test (SMA)
  • Control Velocity Test (CVT)

Instrument Battery Test (INSB) is a paper-pencil test, while the other two (SMA and CVT) are machine tests.

INSB Details: Comprises two parts. It assesses assimilation of briefing and the ability to read and interpret dials of an instrument panel of an aircraft. Candidates scoring minimum criteria are subjected to the machine test.

text:
Simple Squamous Epithelium

  • In cell lining blood vessels or lung alveoli.
  • Transportation of substances occur through selectively permeable surface.
  • The lining of oesophagus and lining of mouth is also covered with this.
  • When epithelial cells are arranged in layers to avoid wear and tear they are called STRATIFIED SQUAMOUS EPITHELIUM e.g. Skin.

Columnar Epithelium

  • They are present where absorption and secretion occur as in inner lining of the intestine.
  • In respiratory tract the columnar epithelia also have cilia, hairlike projections. These types of epithelia are called CILIATED COLUMNAR EPITHELIUM.

Cuboidal Epithelium

  • Forms the lining of kidney tubules and ducts of salivary glands, where it provides mechanical support.
  • Sometimes a portion of epithelium folds inwards and a multicellular gland is formed. This is called GLANDULAR EPITHELIUM.

content:
**Simple Squamous Epithelium**

- In cell lining blood vessels or lung alveoli.
- Transportation of substances occur through selectively permeable surface.
- The lining of oesophagus and lining of mouth is also covered with this.
- When epithelial cells are arranged in layers to avoid wear and tear they are called **STRATIFIED SQUAMOUS EPITHELIUM** e.g. Skin.

**Columnar Epithelium**

- They are present where absorption and secretion occur as in inner lining of the intestine.
- In respiratory tract the columnar epithelia also have cilia, hairlike projections. These types of epithelia are called **CILIATED COLUMNAR EPITHELIUM**.

**Cuboidal Epithelium**

- Forms the lining of kidney tubules and ducts of salivary glands, where it provides mechanical support.
- Sometimes a portion of epithelium folds inwards and a multicellular gland is formed. This is called **GLANDULAR EPITHELIUM**.

text:
Connective Tissue

Blood, ligaments, tendons, bones and cartilages are types of connective tissues.

  • Ligaments: Two bones are connected to one another through ligaments. The tissues of this are very elastic and have considerable strength.
  • Tendons: Tendons connect bone to muscle. Tendons are fibrous tissue with great strength but limited flexibility.
  • Cartilage: It has widely spaced cells. The matrix is composed of proteins and sugars. It smoothens bone surfaces at joints and is present in the nose, ear, trachea and larynx.
  • Areolar Tissue: It is found between the skin and muscles around blood vessels and nerves and in the bone marrow. It fills the space inside the organs, supports internal organs and helps in repair of tissues.
  • Adipose Tissue: Fats are stored in adipose tissues which are present under the skin and between internal organs. The tissues are filled with fat globules. Storage of fats also lets it act as an insulator.
  • Bone: It forms the framework that supports the body, also anchors the muscles and supports the main organs of body. Composed of calcium and phosphorus compounds.
  • Blood: Blood has fluid matrix called plasma in which RBC, WBC and platelets are suspended. The plasma contains proteins, salts and hormones. Blood flows and transport gases, digested food, hormones and waste materials to different parts of body.

details.summary: Detailed classification of connective tissues including ligaments, tendons, cartilage, areolar, adipose, bone, and blood, describing their structure and functions.

mcq.question: Which connective tissue acts as an insulator and stores fat?
mcq.explanation: Adipose tissue stores fats and its storage of fats allows it to act as an insulator.

content:

Blood, ligaments, tendons, bones and cartilages are types of connective tissues.

- **Ligaments:** Two bones are connected to one another through ligaments. The tissues of this are very elastic and have considerable strength.
- **Tendons:** Tendons connect bone to muscle. Tendons are fibrous tissue with great strength but limited flexibility.
- **Cartilage:** It has widely spaced cells. The matrix is composed of proteins and sugars. It smoothens bone surfaces at joints and is present in the nose, ear, trachea and larynx.
- **Areolar Tissue:** It is found between the skin and muscles around blood vessels and nerves and in the bone marrow. It fills the space inside the organs, supports internal organs and helps in repair of tissues.
- **Adipose Tissue:** Fats are stored in adipose tissues which are present under the skin and between internal organs. The tissues are filled with fat globules. Storage of fats also lets it act as an **insulator**.
- **Bone:** It forms the framework that supports the body, also anchors the muscles and supports the main organs of body. Composed of **calcium and phosphorus** compounds.
- **Blood:** Blood has fluid matrix called plasma in which RBC, WBC and platelets are suspended. The plasma contains proteins, salts and hormones. Blood flows and transport gases, digested food, hormones and waste materials to different parts of body.

### Key Exam Facts

text:
Muscular Tissue

  • They consist of elongated cells, called muscles fibers which are responsible for movement in our body.
  • Muscles contain special proteins called CONTRACTILE PROTEINS which contract and relax to cause movement.

Types of Muscles:

  • Voluntary Muscles: Their movement can be controlled by our brain. Also called as skeletal muscles or striated muscles. The cells of these are usually long, cylindrical, unbranched and multinucleate.
  • Involuntary Muscles: They are not controlled by brain or as per our wish. E.g. movement of food in alimentary canal, relaxation of blood vessels, iris of eye, in ureters, in the bronchi of the lungs. The cells are long with pointed ends and uninucleate. Also called as unstriated muscles or smooth muscles.
  • Cardiac Muscles: Muscles of heart show show rhythmic contraction and relaxation throughout life. These involuntary muscles are called cardiac muscles. Heart muscle cells are cylindrical, branched and uninucleate.

details.summary: Description of muscular tissue, its contractile proteins, and the three main types: voluntary (skeletal), involuntary (smooth), and cardiac muscles.

mcq.question: Which type of muscle is cylindrical, branched, and uninucleate?
mcq.explanation: Cardiac muscles are described as cylindrical, branched, and uninucleate.

content:
**Muscular Tissue**

- They consist of elongated cells, called muscles fibers which are responsible for movement in our body.
- Muscles contain special proteins called **CONTRACTILE PROTEINS** which contract and relax to cause movement.

**Types of Muscles:**

- **Voluntary Muscles:** Their movement can be controlled by our brain. Also called as **skeletal muscles** or **striated muscles**. The cells of these are usually long, cylindrical, unbranched and multinucleate.
- **Involuntary Muscles:** They are not controlled by brain or as per our wish. E.g. movement of food in alimentary canal, relaxation of blood vessels, iris of eye, in ureters, in the bronchi of the lungs. The cells are long with pointed ends and uninucleate. Also called as **unstriated muscles** or **smooth muscles**.
- **Cardiac Muscles:** Muscles of heart show show rhythmic contraction and relaxation throughout life. These **involuntary muscles** are called **cardiac muscles**. Heart muscle cells are cylindrical, branched and uninucleate.

### Key Exam Facts
- **Summary:** Description of muscular tissue, its contractile proteins, and the three main types: voluntary (skeletal), involuntary (smooth), and cardiac muscles.

text:
Nervous Tissue

  • Cells of the nervous tissue are highly specialised for being stimulated and then transmitting the stimulus very rapidly from one place to another within the body.
  • The brain, spinal cord and nerves are all composed of the nervous tissue.
  • The cells of this tissue are called nerve cells or neurons.
  • A neuron consists of a cell body with a nucleus and cytoplasm, from which long thin hair-like parts arise.
  • Usually, each neuron has a single long part, called the axon, and many short, branched parts called dendrites.
  • The signal that passes along the nerve fibre is called a nerve impulse.

subject: Biology
text:
Day-neutral Plants

  • Flowering in these plants is not affected by a light period.
  • Examples: Cucumber, Tomato, and Sunflower are day-neutral plants.

Vernalisation

  • Vernalisation is the process of accelerating the process of flowering by subjecting or exposing the plant to low temperature.
  • For example, by applying a temperature ranging between 1-10° C to certain variety of wheat, rice and cotton, growth of seedlings is accelerated and flowering occurs earlier.
  • Plants whose life cycle are completed in two seasons (biennials) can produce flowers in one season if their seeds are pre-treated to a low temperature.

Plant movements

Tropic Movement:

  • Growth of plants towards or away from environmental factors is called tropic movements.
  • Phototropism: Induced by light i.e., bending of branches and stems towards the light.
  • Geotropism: Induced by gravity, e.g. growth of roots towards gravity.
  • Thigmotropism: Movement caused by contact.
  • Hydrotropism: Induced by water, i.e., growth of roots towards source of water.

Turgor Movements:

  • It is the movement due to the change in volume of water inside a cell.
  • When more water is present in the cell, it expands and becomes rigid or hard. Such a cell is said to be turgid.
  • When the cell retains less water, it is not fully expanded and remains soft. This is called flaccid condition.

Reproduction in plants:

  • Reproduction is the process by which individuals produce their offsprings and pass on genetic information to the next generation.
  • Plants reproduce both sexually and asexually.

Asexual reproduction in plants:

  • Asexual reproduction occurs when a single parent is involved in the process.
  • The different means of asexual reproduction in plants are,
    • Budding – This is the method of reproduction of unicellular plant species like yeast. The unicellular organism produces a protrusion on its cell wall called Bud. The bud gets its own nucleus replicated from parent nucleus. The bud then gets detached and develops into a new plant.
    • Fragmentation – When some plants fragment into certain smaller pieces. Each piece develops into a new plant. This method of reproduction is called fragmentation. Example – Spirogyra.

text:
Religion

  • The chief male deity was Pashupati Mahadeva (Proto shiva), which is represented on a seal surrounded by elephant, tiger, rhino and buffalo (all facing in different direction) and two deers appearing in the background.
  • Female deity i.e. Mother Goddess—depicted in various styles.
  • Symbolic worship was also there—Phallus worship, Yoni worship.
  • Evidence of fire worship was also found at Lothal, Kalibangan and Harappa.
  • Animal (Unicorn Bull) and tree worship (Pipal) also found there.
  • The harappans also believed in evil-powers and might have used amulets as protection against them.

text:
Social Life

  • It was a highly developed urban way of life.
  • Society principally consisted of middle class urban people. Presence of various classes like priests, merchants, craftsmen, peasants and labourers can be seen.
  • The dress of the men consisted of two garments, the upper and the lower cotton garments, which were generally used. Wool was also used. Different kinds of necklaces have been discovered. Bracelets were used quite commonly. The vanity case found at Harappa reveals, that the Harappan women knew the art of wall painting.
  • They domesticated buffaloes, bulls, oxens, sheep, asses, goats, elephants, pigs and dogs.
  • Harappans produced wheat, barley, pulses etc. In some areas evidence of rice have been found.

subject: History
text:
Trade and Commerce

  • Internal (in India) as well as external (foreign) trade prevailed during Harappan Civilisation.
  • No metallic money but barter system was practiced.
  • Agriculture, industry and forest produce provided the basis for internal and external trade.
  • Weights and measure of Harappa were made of limestone, steatite etc. They were in the multiples of 16.
  • The inter-civilizational trade is evident from the mention of word 'Meluha' (probably Indus valley) in the Sumerian literature. Mesopotamian cylindrical seals have been found from Mohenjodaro.

text:
Art and Craft

  • Harappans used stone tools and were well acquainted with bronze. Bronze was made by mixing copper (from Khetri) with tin.
  • Bead Making and jewellery of gold, silver precious stone were made. Cotton fabrics were used in summers and woolen in winters.
  • Both men and women were very fond of ornaments and dressing up.
  • Pottery both plain (red) or painted (red and black) pottery was made. Pots were decorated with human figures, plants, animals and geometrical patterns and ochre was painted over it.
  • Seals were made of steatite pictures of one horned bull, buffalo, tiger, rhinoceros, goat and elephant are found on the seals. They marked ownership of property.

The Alaknanda River meets various tributaries at different points known as Prayags (confluences) before forming the Ganga River at Devprayag.

The Five Holy Confluences (Panch Prayag)

  • Devprayag: Bhagirathi + Alaknanda (Forms the Ganga River)
  • Vishnuprayag: Alaknanda + Dhauliganga
  • Nandprayag: Alaknanda + Nandakini
  • Karnaprayag: Alaknanda + Pindar
  • Rudraprayag: Alaknanda + Mandakini

details.summary: The confluences of the Alaknanda river with other Himalayan rivers to form the Panch Prayag, culminating in the formation of the Ganga at Devprayag.

mcq.question: At which Prayag do the Alaknanda and Mandakini rivers meet?
mcq.explanation: Alaknanda and Mandakini rivers meet at Rudraprayag.

content:
The Alaknanda River meets various tributaries at different points known as **Prayags** (confluences) before forming the Ganga River at Devprayag.

### The Five Holy Confluences (Panch Prayag)

- **Devprayag:** Bhagirathi + Alaknanda (Forms the Ganga River)
- **Vishnuprayag:** Alaknanda + Dhauliganga
- **Nandprayag:** Alaknanda + Nandakini
- **Karnaprayag:** Alaknanda + Pindar
- **Rudraprayag:** Alaknanda + Mandakini

### Key Exam Facts
- **Summary:** The confluences of the Alaknanda river with other Himalayan rivers to form the Panch Prayag, culminating in the formation of the Ganga at Devprayag.

subject: Physics
text:
The human eye can suffer from several defects of vision, which can be corrected using appropriate lenses.

  • Myopia is also known as near-sightedness.
    • A person can see nearby objects clearly but cannot see distant objects distinctly.
    • A person with this defect has the far point nearer than infinity. The image of a distant object is formed in front of the retina.
    • This defect may arise due to (1) excessive curvature of the eye lens, or (2) elongation of the eyeball.
    • This defect can be corrected using a Concave lens.
  • Hypermetropia is also known as far-sightedness.
    • A person can see distant objects clearly but cannot see nearby objects distinctly.
    • The near point, for the person, is farther away from the normal near point.
    • Image forms behind retina.
    • This defect arises either because i) the focal length of the eye lens is too long, or (ii) the eyeball has become too Small.
    • This defect can be corrected by using a convex lens of appropriate Power.
  • The power of accommodation of the eye usually decreases with ageing. It is difficult to see nearby objects comfortably in presbyopia.
    • It arises due to the gradual weakening of the ciliary muscles and diminishing flexibility of the eye lens.
    • Sometimes, a person may suffer from both myopia and hypermetropia. Such people often require bifocal lenses. A common type of bi-focal lenses consists of both Concave & Convex lenses. Upper portion consists of a concave lens & lower part is a convex lens.

Diagrams:

  • Myopia Diagrams: Illustrate (a) Far point of a myopic eye, (b) Myopic Eye showing image formation in front of the retina, and (c) Correction for Myopic Eye using a concave lens.
  • Hypermetropia Diagrams: Illustrate (a) Near point of a Hypermetropic eye, (b) Hypermetropic eye showing image formation behind the retina, and (c) Correction for Hypermetropic eye using a convex lens.

details.summary: Detailed explanation of Myopia, Hypermetropia, and Presbyopia, including their causes, symptoms, and corrective measures with lens types, along with descriptions of related diagrams.

The human eye can suffer from several defects of vision, which can be corrected using appropriate lenses.

- **Myopia** is also known as *near-sightedness*.A person can see nearby objects clearly but cannot see distant objects distinctly.
- A person with this defect has the far point nearer than infinity. The image of a distant object is formed in front of the retina.
- This defect may arise due to (1) excessive curvature of the eye lens, or (2) elongation of the eyeball.
- This defect can be corrected using a **Concave lens**.
- **Hypermetropia** is also known as *far-sightedness*.A person can see distant objects clearly but cannot see nearby objects distinctly.
- The near point, for the person, is farther away from the normal near point.
- Image forms behind retina.
- This defect arises either because i) the focal length of the eye lens is too long, or (ii) the eyeball has become too Small.
- This defect can be corrected by using a **convex lens** of appropriate Power.
- The power of accommodation of the eye usually decreases with ageing. It is difficult to see nearby objects comfortably in **presbyopia**.It arises due to the gradual weakening of the ciliary muscles and diminishing flexibility of the eye lens.
- Sometimes, a person may suffer from both myopia and hypermetropia. Such people often require **bifocal lenses**. A common type of bi-focal lenses consists of both Concave & Convex lenses. Upper portion consists of a concave lens & lower part is a convex lens.

**Diagrams:**

- **Myopia Diagrams:** Illustrate (a) Far point of a myopic eye, (b) Myopic Eye showing image formation in front of the retina, and (c) Correction for Myopic Eye using a concave lens.
- **Hypermetropia Diagrams:** Illustrate (a) Near point of a Hypermetropic eye, (b) Hypermetropic eye showing image formation behind the retina, and (c) Correction for Hypermetropic eye using a convex lens.

subject: Physics
text:
Dispersion: The splitting of light into its component colours is called dispersion. Different colours of light bend through different angles with respect to the incident ray, as they pass through a prism. The red light bends the least while the violet the most. Thus the rays of each colour emerge along different paths and thus become distinct. Isaac Newton was the first to use a glass prism to obtain the spectrum of sunlight.

Diagram: A prism dispersing white light into a spectrum of colours (VIBGYOR).

subject: Physics
text:
The Electromagnetic Spectrum is the range of all types of EM radiation. Radiation is energy that travels and spreads out as it goes – the visible light that comes from a lamp in your house and the radio waves that come from a radio tower are two types of electromagnetic radiation.

The spectrum is ordered by increasing wavelength and decreasing frequency:

  • Gamma Rays: Shortest wavelength (~10 pm), highest frequency (~30 EHz). Used in medicine for killing cancer cells.
  • X-Rays: Wavelengths around ~10 nm, frequency ~30 PHz. Used to view inside of bodies and objects.
  • UV Rays (Ultraviolet): Wavelengths around ~380 nm, frequency ~790 THz. Absorbed by the skin, used in fluorescent tubes.
  • Visible Light: Wavelengths from ~380 nm to ~750 nm, frequencies from ~400 THz to ~790 THz. Makes things able to be seen.
  • Infrared Rays: Wavelengths around ~1 mm, frequency ~300 GHz. Transmits heat from sun, fires, radiators.
  • Microwaves: Wavelengths around ~10 cm, frequency ~30 GHz. Used in cooking, radar, telephone and other signals.
  • Radio Waves: Longest wavelength (~100000 km), lowest frequency (~3 Hz). Used to broadcast radio and television.

Diagram: A visual representation of the electromagnetic spectrum showing the different types of waves (radio, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays) with their approximate wavelength/frequency ranges and common uses. It indicates a trend of increasing wavelength from gamma rays to radio waves.

details.summary: Comprehensive overview of the electromagnetic spectrum, detailing different types of EM waves, their relative wavelengths and frequencies, and practical applications.

subject: Chemistry
topic: Reaction of Metals and Non-Metals with Oxygen
text:
Metals and non-metals react differently with oxygen to form oxides with distinct chemical properties:

  • Metal + Oxygen → Metal oxide (basic form)
    • Most metal oxides are insoluble in water, but some dissolve to form alkalis (e.g., sodium oxide and potassium oxide).
  • Non-metal + Oxygen → Non-metal oxide (acidic form)
  • Amphoteric Oxides: Some metal oxides, such as aluminium oxide and zinc oxide, show both acidic and basic behavior. They react with both acids and bases to produce salt and water.
  • Reactivity with Oxygen:
    • Potassium (K) and Sodium (Na) react vigorously and catch fire in the open; hence, they are kept immersed in kerosene oil.
    • Iron does not burn on heating, but iron filings burn vigorously when sprinkled in a burner flame.
    • Copper does not burn, but hot copper becomes coated with a black layer of copper(II) oxide.
    • Silver and gold do not react with oxygen even at high temperatures.

details.summary: Explains the reactions of metals and non-metals with oxygen, the concept of amphoteric oxides (Al2O3, ZnO), and the varying reactivity of different metals (Na, K, Fe, Cu, Ag, Au) towards oxygen.

mcq.question: Which of the following metal oxides is amphoteric in nature?
mcq.explanation: Aluminium oxide reacts with both acids and bases to form salt and water, making it an amphoteric oxide.

content:
Metals and non-metals react differently with oxygen to form oxides with distinct chemical properties:

- **Metal + Oxygen → Metal oxide (basic form)**Most metal oxides are insoluble in water, but some dissolve to form alkalis (e.g., sodium oxide and potassium oxide).
- **Non-metal + Oxygen → Non-metal oxide (acidic form)**
- **Amphoteric Oxides:** Some metal oxides, such as aluminium oxide and zinc oxide, show both acidic and basic behavior. They react with both acids and bases to produce salt and water.
- **Reactivity with Oxygen:**Potassium (K) and Sodium (Na) react vigorously and catch fire in the open; hence, they are kept immersed in kerosene oil.
- Iron does not burn on heating, but iron filings burn vigorously when sprinkled in a burner flame.
- Copper does not burn, but hot copper becomes coated with a black layer of copper(II) oxide.
- Silver and gold do not react with oxygen even at high temperatures.

### Key Exam Facts
- **Summary:** Explains the reactions of metals and non-metals with oxygen, the concept of amphoteric oxides (Al2O3, ZnO), and the varying reactivity of different metals (Na, K, Fe, Cu, Ag, Au) towards oxygen.

Anodising is an electrochemical process of forming a thick, protective oxide layer on aluminium.

  • Aluminium naturally develops a thin oxide layer when exposed to air, which makes it resistant to further corrosion.
  • To make this protective layer thicker and stronger, a clean aluminium article is made the anode and electrolysed with dilute sulphuric acid.
  • The oxygen gas evolved at the anode reacts with the aluminium to form a thicker, highly protective oxide layer.
  • This oxide layer can be easily dyed to give aluminium articles an attractive, colorful finish.

details.summary: Anodising is the process of electrolytically coating aluminium with a thick oxide layer using dilute sulphuric acid as the electrolyte to enhance corrosion resistance and allow decorative dyeing.

mcq.question: During the anodising of aluminium, which acid is used as the electrolyte?
mcq.explanation: Dilute sulphuric acid is used as the electrolyte during the anodising process to form a thick protective oxide layer on the aluminium anode.

content:

- **Summary:** Anodising is the process of electrolytically coating aluminium with a thick oxide layer using dilute sulphuric acid as the electrolyte to enhance corrosion resistance and allow decorative dyeing.

R = mg

acc.(a) = g

R = mg + mg

R = m(g-g)

R = 0

text:
HYPERSONIC MISSILES

The Mach number (m) is a dimensionless quantity representing the ratio of the speed of an object to the speed of sound.

  • Formula: mach no = speed of object / speed of sound
  • Alternatively: speed of object = mach no x speed of sound

Classification of speeds based on Mach number (m):

  • If m < 1: Subsonic
  • If m = 1: Transonic
  • If m > 1: Supersonic
  • If m > 5: Hypersonic

Key characteristics of Hypersonic Missiles:

  • The term hypersonic refers to missiles capable of travelling at speeds exceeding Mach 5, i.e., more than five times the speed of sound.
  • They are extremely fast, making them difficult to intercept.
  • Example: Shaurya

Images related to Hypersonic Missiles:

  • Three fighter jets flying in the sky, illustrating high-speed aerial vehicles.
  • A large missile, identified as "SHAURYA", mounted on a military transport vehicle, ready for deployment.
  • A missile launching from the sea, with a prominent exhaust plume, visually representing missile launch and the concept of speed regimes.

PHYLLOTAXY: It is the arrangement of leaves on the stem or branch. This is usually of three types – alternate, opposite and whorled.

  • ALTERNATE:

    If more than two leaves arise at a node and form a whorl, it is called whorled, as in Alstonia.

details.summary: Phyllotaxy describes leaf arrangement on a stem: alternate (single leaf per node), opposite (pair of leaves per node), or whorled (more than two leaves per node).

subject: Physics
text:
A body performing circular motion is acted upon by a force which is always directed towards the centre of the circle. This is called centripetal force. Work done by centripetal force is always zero.

  • If a body of mass m is moving on a circular path of radius R with uniform velocity v, then the required centripetal force, F = mv²/R = mω²R.

  • Any of the forces found in nature such as frictional force, gravitational force, electrical force, magnetic force may act as a centripetal force.

  • Cyclist bends his body towards the centre on a turn while turning to obtain the required centripetal force.

  • Generally, in rain the scooter slips off the turning of a road because the friction between tyre and road is reduced. Due to this necessary centripetal force is not provided.

  • Vehicles can move on circular path safely, if friction force ≥ required centripetal force.

  • Roads are banked at turns to provide the required centripetal force for taking a turn.

  • Work done by Centripetal force is always zero.

details.summary: Definition, formula, and examples of centripetal force, including its applications and the fact that it does no work.

subject: Physics
text:
Work can be of following types

  1. Positive Work Done Positive work means that force is parallel to displacement.

    Examples

    • When a body falls freely under gravitational pull.

    • When a horse pulls a cart on a level road.

  2. Negative Work Done Negative work means that force is opposite to displacement.

    Examples

    • When a body is made to slide over a rough surface or when a positive charge is moved towards another positive charge.

  3. Zero Work Done If the force is perpendicular to the displacement and if either the force or the displacement is zero, work done will be zero.

    Examples

    • When a coolie travels on a platform with a load on his head.

    • When a body is moved along a circular path. When a person does not move from his position but he may be holding any amount of heavy load.

    • If the force is perpendicular to the displacement and if either the force or the displacement is zero, work done is zero.

subject: Biology
text:
Sexual reproduction in plants:

  • In sexual reproduction, two parents are involved. Hence two gametes are produced in these plants - male and female gametes.
  • The fusion of male and female gametes is called fertilization.
  • A Zygote is formed after fertilization.
  • The zygote develops into an embryo and finally into a new individual.

Flower Structure:

  • Flower is the sexual reproductive organ of a plant.
  • A typical angiospermic flower consists of four whorls of floral appendages:
    • Calyx: It is the outermost whorl of the flower. It is composed of leaflike green sepals. The sepals are essentially green in colour, but in some cases, they are coloured like petals.
    • Corolla: This is the second whorl of the flower and consists of a number of petals. Petals are generally brightly coloured and sometimes fragrant which make the flower to become attractive.
    • Androecium: It is the third whorl of the flower and is the male reproductive organ consisting of stamens. Each stamen is made of filament and anther. The filament supports the anther at its tip.
    • Gynoecium: This is the last and the fourth whorl of flower and is the female reproductive organ of the flower. It is composed of ovary, style and stigma.

details.summary: Details the process of sexual reproduction in plants and describes the four main whorls of a typical angiospermic flower: Calyx, Corolla, Androecium, and Gynoecium.

mcq.question: Which whorl of an angiospermic flower represents the female reproductive organ?
mcq.explanation: Gynoecium is the last and fourth whorl of the flower and is the female reproductive organ, composed of ovary, style, and stigma.

text:
Microsporogenesis:

  • It is a process of the formation and differentiation of microspores (pollen grains) from microspore mother cells (MMC).
  • As development occurs in the anther, the sporogenous cells undergo meiosis to form microspore tetrad.
  • Each cell of the sporogenous tissue has ability to give rise to a tetrad.
  • As anther matures, the microspores get detached from each other and forms pollen grain.

Macrosporogenesis (Megasporogenesis):

  • The process of formation of megaspore from the megaspore mother cell by meiotic division is known as megasporogenesis. This process takes place in ovule.
  • The megaspore mother cell is large and contains dense cytoplasm and a prominent nucleus. It undergoes meiosis to form 4 megaspores.
  • In most plants, only one megaspore functions and the other three degenerates.
  • The single functional megaspore develops into a female gametophyte.

details.summary: Explains the development of male gametophytes (microsporogenesis in the anther) and female gametophytes (macrosporogenesis/megasporogenesis in the ovule) through meiotic division.

mcq.question: During megasporogenesis, how many of the four produced megaspores typically remain functional in most plants?
mcq.explanation: In most plants, only one megaspore remains functional while the other three degenerate.

content:
**Microsporogenesis:**

- It is a process of the formation and differentiation of microspores (pollen grains) from microspore mother cells (MMC).
- As development occurs in the anther, the sporogenous cells undergo meiosis to form microspore tetrad.
- Each cell of the sporogenous tissue has ability to give rise to a tetrad.
- As anther matures, the microspores get detached from each other and forms pollen grain.

**Macrosporogenesis (Megasporogenesis):**

- The process of formation of megaspore from the megaspore mother cell by meiotic division is known as megasporogenesis. This process takes place in ovule.
- The megaspore mother cell is large and contains dense cytoplasm and a prominent nucleus. It undergoes meiosis to form 4 megaspores.
- In most plants, only one megaspore functions and the other three degenerates.
- The single functional megaspore develops into a female gametophyte.

### Key Exam Facts
- **Summary:** Explains the development of male gametophytes (microsporogenesis in the anther) and female gametophytes (macrosporogenesis/megasporogenesis in the ovule) through meiotic division.

The Harappan script and language remain undeciphered. The script is highly pictographic in nature, with the fish symbol being the most frequently represented pictograph.

  • Writing Style: Overlapping of letters indicates that it was written from right to left in the first line, and then left to right in the second line. This unique alternating style is known as boustrophedon.
  • Signboard Discovery: A major signboard inscription containing 10 large pictographs has been discovered at Dholavira in Gujarat.

content:

- **Summary:** The Indus Valley script is pictographic, undeciphered, written in boustrophedon style, and a famous 10-pictograph signboard was found at Dholavira.

text:
The history of the Vedic Age is reconstructed primarily from religious texts called the Vedas.

  • The Term 'Aryan': Derived from Arya, meaning 'favourably disposed towards newcomers' and later implying 'high birth'. It refers to a language group, not a race.
  • Origin Theories: The most accepted theory is that they originated in the great steppe land stretching from Poland to Central Asia. They were semi-nomadic pastoralists who migrated eastwards and southwards in the 2nd millennium BC.
  • Boghaz Koi Inscription (1400 BC): Found in Asia Minor (Turkey), this inscription records a peace treaty between the Hittites and Mittanis. It mentions Vedic deities: Indra, Mitra, Nasatya, and Varuna, supporting the Central Asian homeland theory.

subject: History
text:
The Rigvedic society and economy were pastoral and tribal in nature:

  • Economy:
    • Primarily semi-nomadic pastoralists, later turning to cultivation.
    • The cow was the most valued asset. The term Gauri (cow) is mentioned 176 times in the Rigveda.
    • Terms like Gavishti (search for cows) and Godhuli (measure of time) are derived from cow-related activities.
    • Cows were called Aghanya (not to be killed).
  • Society:
    • Based on kinship and organized as a tribe (Jana).
    • Patriarchal structure; the eldest male member of the family was known as the Kulapa.
    • The term Varna was used for colour (fair-complexioned Aryans vs. dark-complexioned indigenous people).
    • No rigid caste system existed. Members of the same family could pursue different occupations, as illustrated in a hymn of the 9th Mandala of the Rigveda.
    • Non-Aryans were referred to as Dasas or Shudras.

details.summary: Rigvedic society was patriarchal, kinship-based, and egalitarian with no rigid caste system. The economy was pastoral, centered heavily around cows (Aghanya).

mcq.question: In the Rigvedic society, what did the term 'Kulapa' denote?
options: The eldest male member and head of the family
The chief priest of the clan
The commander of the tribal army
mcq.explanation: The Kulapa was the eldest male member and head of the joint family unit in the patriarchal Rigvedic society.

content:
The Rigvedic society and economy were pastoral and tribal in nature:

- **Economy:** Primarily semi-nomadic pastoralists, later turning to cultivation.
- The cow was the most valued asset. The term *Gauri* (cow) is mentioned 176 times in the Rigveda.
- Terms like **Gavishti** (search for cows) and **Godhuli** (measure of time) are derived from cow-related activities.
- Cows were called Aghanya (not to be killed).
- **Society:** Based on kinship and organized as a tribe (Jana).
- Patriarchal structure; the eldest male member of the family was known as the Kulapa.
- The term **Varna** was used for colour (fair-complexioned Aryans vs. dark-complexioned indigenous people).
- No rigid caste system existed. Members of the same family could pursue different occupations, as illustrated in a hymn of the 9th Mandala of the Rigveda.
- Non-Aryans were referred to as *Dasas* or *Shudras*.

### Key Exam Facts
- **Summary:** Rigvedic society was patriarchal, kinship-based, and egalitarian with no rigid caste system. The economy was pastoral, centered heavily around cows (Aghanya).

subject: Mathematics
text:
To find the unit's place digit of a given expression, we analyze two main cases:

1. When Number is in the form of Product

To find the unit digit in the product of two or more numbers, we take the unit digit of every number and then multiply them. Then, the unit digit of the resultant product is the unit digit of the product of original numbers.

2. When Number is in the form of Index

Let the exponential number be of the form an where a is the base and n is the index (n ∈ I).

  • Case I: If a ends in 0, 1, 5, or 6, then the unit's place digit is 0, 1, 5, and 6, respectively, regardless of the power.
  • Case II: If a ends in 4 or 9:
    • If the power is odd, then the unit's place digit is 4 and 9, respectively.
    • If the power is even, then the unit's place digit is 6 and 1, respectively.
  • Case III: If a ends in 2, 3, 7, or 8, follow these steps:
    • Step I: First, divide the exponent of a by 4.
    • Step II: If any remainder comes on division, put it as the power of a and get the result.
    • Step III: If no remainder comes on division (i.e., remainder is 0), put 4 as the power of a and get the result.

details.summary: Rules to find the unit's digit of products and exponential numbers using cyclicity of 4.

mcq.question: What is the unit digit of 207 * 781 * 39 * 94?
mcq.explanation: Multiply the unit digits: 7 * 1 * 9 * 4 = 252. The unit digit is 2.

Let the exponential number be of the form **an** where *a* is the base and *n* is the index (n ∈ I).

- **Case I:** If *a* ends in 0, 1, 5, or 6, then the unit's place digit is **0, 1, 5, and 6**, respectively, regardless of the power.

Let a and b be two integers such that b ≠ 0. On dividing a by b, let q be the quotient and r be the remainder. The relationship between a, b, q and r is given by:

a = bq + r, where 0 ≤ r < b

In general terms:

Dividend = (Divisor × Quotient) + Remainder

mcq.question: When a positive integer n is divided by 5, the remainder is 2. What is the remainder when 3n is divided by 5?
mcq.explanation: Let n = 5q + 2. Then 3n = 3(5q + 2) = 15q + 6 = 5(3q + 1) + 1. Thus, the remainder is 1.

text:
Divisibility rules help determine if a number is divisible by another without performing full division:

DivisorCondition with Example
2If the unit place of a number is '0' or divisible by 2 (i.e., unit place is even).
e.g., 17980, 314782, 6148, 316
3If the sum of the digits of the given number is divisible by 3.
e.g., 24375: 2 + 4 + 3 + 7 + 5 = 21 (divisible by 3)
4If the last two digits of the number are divisible by 4.
e.g., 589372: 72 is divisible by 4
5If the digit at the unit place is 5 or 0.
e.g., 895, 700
6If the given number is divisible by both 2 and 3.
e.g., 759312: ends in 2 (divisible by 2) and sum of digits is 27 (divisible by 3)
7If twice the number at the units place is subtracted from the rest of the digits and the remainder is divisible by 7 (applicable for numbers > 99).
e.g., 875: 87 - 2(5) = 77 (divisible by 7)
8If the last three digits are divisible by 8.
e.g., 96432: 432 is divisible by 8
9If the sum of all the digits is divisible by 9.
e.g., 317349: 3 + 1 + 7 + 3 + 4 + 9 = 27 (divisible by 9)
10If the last digit of a number is '0'.
e.g., 130, 36980
11If the difference between the sum of digits at even places and the sum of digits at odd places is divisible by 11.
e.g., 10615: Sum of odd places = 1 + 6 + 5 = 12; Sum of even places = 0 + 1 = 1. Difference = 12 - 1 = 11 (divisible by 11)

mcq.explanation: For 10615, the difference between the sum of digits at odd places (1+6+5=12) and even places (0+1=1) is 11, which is divisible by 11.

text:
A Rhombus is a quadrilateral with all four sides equal. Key properties and formulas include:

  • Area of Rhombus: Area = 1/2 × d1 × d2, where d1 and d2 are the lengths of the diagonals.
  • Diagonals: The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles (90°).
  • Side-Diagonal Relationship: In the right-angled triangle formed by the half-diagonals, Side2 = (d1/2)2 + (d2/2)2.

details.summary: Formulae and properties of a rhombus, focusing on area calculation using diagonals and the right-angle bisection property.

mcq.question: If the area of a rhombus is 336 cm² and one of its diagonals is 48 cm, what is the perimeter of the rhombus?
mcq.explanation: Area = 1/2 * d1 * d2 => 336 = 1/2 * 48 * d2 => d2 = 14 cm. Half-diagonals are 24 cm and 7 cm. Side = sqrt(24^2 + 7^2) = 25 cm. Perimeter = 4 * side = 100 cm.

content:

text:
Key properties of determinants used to simplify complex matrix evaluations:

  • Scalar Multiplication: If any row or column is multiplied by a scalar k, the value of the determinant is multiplied by k.
  • Row/Column Swapping: Interchanging any two rows or columns changes the sign of the determinant.
  • Invariance under Transpose: The determinant remains unchanged if rows and columns are interchanged (i.e., |A| = |AT|).
  • Row/Column Operations: Operations of the form Ri → Ri + k Rj do not change the value of the determinant.

details.summary: Core properties of determinants including scalar multiplication, row/column swaps, transpose invariance, and elementary operations.

mcq.question: If the determinant of a 3x3 matrix A is 5, what is the determinant of the matrix obtained by swapping the first two rows of 2A?
mcq.explanation: Det(2A) = 2^3 * Det(A) = 8 * 5 = 40. Swapping two rows changes the sign, so the new determinant is -40.

content:
Key properties of determinants used to simplify complex matrix evaluations:

- **Scalar Multiplication:** If any row or column is multiplied by a scalar *k*, the value of the determinant is multiplied by *k*.
- **Row/Column Swapping:** Interchanging any two rows or columns changes the sign of the determinant.
- **Invariance under Transpose:** The determinant remains unchanged if rows and columns are interchanged (i.e., **|A| = |AT|**).
- **Row/Column Operations:** Operations of the form **Ri → Ri + k Rj** do not change the value of the determinant.

### Key Exam Facts
- **Summary:** Core properties of determinants including scalar multiplication, row/column swaps, transpose invariance, and elementary operations.

subject: Physics
topic: Key Concepts: Magnetism, Equilibrium, Buoyancy, and Vector Forces
text:
This section covers fundamental principles of physics frequently tested in defence examinations like NDA and CDS.

  • Properties of Magnetic Field Lines:
    • They form continuous closed loops (outside a magnet, they emerge from the North Pole and enter the South Pole; inside, they run from South to North).
    • They never intersect or cross each other because at any given point, the magnetic field can have only one unique direction.
    • The relative density of field lines represents the strength of the magnetic field (closer lines indicate a stronger field).
  • States of Equilibrium:
    • Stable Equilibrium: If a body is slightly displaced, it tends to return to its original position.
    • Unstable Equilibrium: If a body is slightly displaced, it moves further away from its original position (e.g., a rod balanced vertically on its tip).
    • Neutral Equilibrium: If displaced, the body remains in its new position without returning or moving further away.
  • Principle of Floatation:
    • The fraction of volume submerged ($f$) of a floating body is given by:
      f = V_sub / V_total = ρ_body / ρ_fluid
    • Since the acceleration due to gravity ($g$) cancels out from both sides of the equilibrium equation ($V_{sub} \cdot \rho_{fluid} \cdot g = V_{total} \cdot \rho_{body} \cdot g$), the fraction of volume submerged is independent of gravity. Thus, it remains identical on Earth and the Moon.

details.summary: A comprehensive summary of magnetic field line properties, mechanical equilibrium states, vector force resultants, and the gravity-independent nature of floating bodies.

mcq.question: Why do magnetic field lines never intersect each other?
options: Because they are always parallel to each other
Because at the point of intersection, the magnetic field would point in two different directions, which is impossible
Because they only exist outside the magnet
mcq.explanation: If magnetic field lines intersected, a compass needle placed at the intersection point would point in two directions simultaneously, which is physically impossible.

- The relative density of field lines represents the strength of the magnetic field (closer lines indicate a stronger field).

- Unstable Equilibrium: If a body is slightly displaced, it moves further away from its original position (e.g., a rod balanced vertically on its tip).

- **Principle of Floatation:**The fraction of volume submerged ($f$) of a floating body is given by:

subject: Indian Polity
text:
Powers and Functions of the President

The President of India is vested with various executive, legislative, financial, judicial, diplomatic, and military powers:

  • Executive Appointments: He appoints the Prime Minister (PM), Council of Ministers (COM), Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG), Chief Election Commissioner, Attorney General, Chairman of UPSC, and the Chairman and members of the Finance Commission.
  • Investigative Commissions: He can appoint a commission to investigate into the conditions of SCs, STs, and other backward classes.
  • Parliamentary Powers: He addresses the first session of parliament, and can summon, prorogue, or dissolve the Lok Sabha. He can also summon a joint sitting of both houses.
  • Assent to Bills: His assent is required for a bill to become law. He can give his assent, withhold it, or return the bill through his veto power. Note: The President does not have veto power in case of a Money Bill and Constitutional Amendment Bill.
  • Ordinance Making Power: He can promulgate ordinances when the parliament is not in session. The maximum duration within which it must be approved by parliament is 6 months and 6 weeks.
  • Financial Powers: Money bills can only be introduced in the Parliament with his prior recommendation.
  • Judicial Powers: He appoints judges of the Supreme Court, the Chief Justice, and High Court judges. He can seek advice from the Supreme Court on any matter, though this advice is not binding on him.
  • Pardoning Power: He can grant pardon, reprieve, respite, and remission of punishment, or suspend, remit, or commute the sentence of any person convicted of any offence.
  • Diplomatic Powers: He represents India on international forums and sends/receives diplomats like ambassadors and high commissioners.
  • Military Powers: He is the Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces. He can declare war or conclude peace, subject to the approval of Parliament.

Types of Veto

  • Absolute Veto: The power of the President to withhold his assent to a bill passed by the Parliament. The bill then ends and does not become an act.
  • Suspensive Veto: Exercised when the President returns a bill for reconsideration of the Parliament. However, if the bill is passed again, it is obligatory for the President to give his assent. The President does not possess this veto in case of a Money Bill.
  • Pocket Veto: The President neither ratifies, nor rejects, nor returns the bill, but simply keeps the bill pending for an indefinite period.

Pardoning Power of the President

PowerRelated To
1. PardonIt removes both the sentence and the conviction and completely absolves the convict from all sentences, punishments, and disqualifications.
2. CommutationIt denotes the substitution of one form of punishment for a lighter form.
3. RemissionIt implies reducing the period of sentence without changing its character.
4. RespiteIt denotes awarding a lesser sentence in place of one originally awarded due to some special fact, such as physical disability, etc.
5. ReprieveIt implies a stay of the execution of a sentence for a temporary period.

details.summary: Comprehensive overview of the executive, legislative, judicial, and emergency-related powers of the President of India, detailing veto types (Absolute, Suspensive, Pocket) and the five distinct forms of pardoning powers.

options: The President can exercise suspensive veto over Money Bills.

The maximum validity of an ordinance promulgated by the President is 6 weeks.

- **Absolute Veto:** The power of the President to withhold his assent to a bill passed by the Parliament. The bill then ends and does not become an act.
- **Suspensive Veto:** Exercised when the President returns a bill for reconsideration of the Parliament. However, if the bill is passed again, it is obligatory for the President to give his assent. The President does not possess this veto in case of a Money Bill.
- **Pocket Veto:** The President neither ratifies, nor rejects, nor returns the bill, but simply keeps the bill pending for an indefinite period.

### Pardoning Power of the President

PowerRelated To**1. Pardon**It removes both the sentence and the conviction and completely absolves the convict from all sentences, punishments, and disqualifications.**2. Commutation**It denotes the substitution of one form of punishment for a lighter form.**3. Remission**It implies reducing the period of sentence without changing its character.**4. Respite**It denotes awarding a lesser sentence in place of one originally awarded due to some special fact, such as physical disability, etc.**5. Reprieve**It implies a stay of the execution of a sentence for a temporary period.

### Key Exam Facts
- **Summary:** Comprehensive overview of the executive, legislative, judicial, and emergency-related powers of the President of India, detailing veto types (Absolute, Suspensive, Pocket) and the five distinct forms of pardoning powers.

Atmospheric Refraction is the bending of light as it passes through the Earth's atmosphere due to variation in air density and refractive index.

  • Advance Sunrise and Delayed Sunset: The Sun is visible to us about 2 minutes before the actual sunrise, and about 2 minutes after the actual sunset. This is due to atmospheric refraction.
  • Twinkling of Stars: This phenomenon occurs because starlight passes through a medium of gradually changing refractive index. The atmosphere bends starlight towards the normal, making the apparent position of the star slightly different from its actual position. Since the physical conditions of the Earth's atmosphere are not stationary, the apparent position and brightness of the star fluctuate, causing the twinkling effect.

The atmosphere bends starlight towards the normal, making the apparent position of the star slightly different from its actual position. The color of the clear sky is blue due to the scattering of light by molecules of air and other fine particles in the atmosphere.

  • Molecules of air are more effective in scattering light of shorter wavelengths (blue end) than light of longer wavelengths (red end).
  • Red light has a wavelength about 1.8 times greater than blue light.
  • When sunlight passes through the atmosphere, fine particles scatter the blue color more strongly than red.
  • Note: If the Earth had no atmosphere, there would not have been any scattering, and the sky would have looked dark.

details.summary: The blue color of the sky is due to the selective scattering of shorter wavelengths (blue) by atmospheric molecules. Without an atmosphere, the sky would appear dark.

mcq.question: If the Earth had no atmosphere, what color would the sky appear to an observer?
mcq.explanation: In the absence of an atmosphere, there would be no particles to scatter sunlight, making the sky appear completely dark.

text:
Ohm's Law states that the potential difference (V) across the ends of a given metallic wire in an electric circuit is directly proportional to the current (I) flowing through it, provided its temperature remains constant.

V ∝ I  or  V / I = constant = R  or  V = IR

  • Resistance (R): It is the property of a conductor to resist the flow of charges. Its SI unit is ohm (Ω).
  • 1 ohm = 1 volt / 1 ampere.
  • If the resistance is doubled, the current gets halved (since I = V/R).
  • Variable Resistance: A component used to regulate current without changing the voltage source.
  • Rheostat: A device used to change the resistance in an electric circuit.

details.summary: Ohm's Law (V = IR) relates voltage, current, and resistance. Resistance is measured in ohms, and a rheostat is used to vary resistance in a circuit.

mcq.question: If the resistance in a circuit is doubled while keeping the potential difference constant, what happens to the current?
mcq.explanation: According to Ohm's Law, I = V/R. If resistance (R) is doubled, the current (I) becomes half of its original value.

content:
**Ohm's Law** states that the potential difference (V) across the ends of a given metallic wire in an electric circuit is directly proportional to the current (I) flowing through it, provided its temperature remains constant.

Reactivity of Metals with Water

  • Potassium and Sodium react violently with cold water. In the case of sodium and potassium, the reaction is so violent and exothermic that the evolved hydrogen immediately catches fire.
  • Calcium with water is less violent. Calcium starts floating because the bubbles of hydrogen gas formed stick to the surface of the metal.
  • Magnesium does not react with cold water. It reacts with hot water. It also starts floating due to the bubbles of hydrogen gas sticking to its surface.
  • Aluminium, Iron and Zinc do not react either with cold or hot water. But they react with steam.
  • Lead, Copper, Silver and Gold do not react with water at all.

details.summary: Comparison of reactivity of various metals (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Fe, Zn, Pb, Cu, Ag, Au) with cold water, hot water, and steam.

- **Calcium** with water is less violent. Calcium starts floating because the bubbles of hydrogen gas formed stick to the surface of the metal.
- **Magnesium** does not react with cold water. It reacts with hot water. It also starts floating due to the bubbles of hydrogen gas sticking to its surface.
- **Aluminium, Iron and Zinc** do not react either with cold or hot water. But they react with steam.

text:
Reactivity of Metals with Acids

  • Hydrogen gas is not evolved when a metal reacts with nitric acid. It is because HNO3 is a strong oxidizing agent.
  • But Magnesium (Mg) and Manganese (Mn) react with very dilute HNO3 to evolve H2 gas.
  • The rate of formation of bubbles was the fastest in the case of magnesium. The reaction was also the most exothermic in this case.
  • The reactivity decreases in the order Mg > Al > Zn > Fe.
  • In the case of copper, no bubbles were seen. This shows that copper does not react with dilute HCl.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Steps Involved in the Extraction of Metals from Ores

The process begins with Ore and proceeds through Concentration of ore. The path then depends on the reactivity of the metal:

  • Metals of high reactivity (e.g., K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al):
    • Electrolysis of molten ore
    • Pure metal
  • Metals of medium reactivity (e.g., Zn, Fe, Pb, Cu):
    • Carbonate ore → Calcination
    • Sulphide ore → Roasting
    • Both lead to Oxide of metal
    • Reduction to metal (using carbon)
    • Purification of metal
  • Metals of low reactivity (e.g., Ag, Au):
    • Sulphide ores → Roasting
    • Metal
    • Refining

Note: Some metals are found in native state.

details.summary: Flowchart detailing the extraction methods (Electrolysis, Calcination, Roasting, Reduction) based on metal reactivity.

subject: Biology
text:
Pollination: Transfer of pollen grains from anther to stigma of same flower or between different flowers.

  • Self-pollination: Transfer of pollen grains from anthers to stigma of same flower or another flower of same plant.
  • Cross-pollination (Xenogamy): Transfer of pollen from flower of one plant to stigma of flower of another plant.

Fertilization: Fusion of male and female reproductive units.

  • After pollination, pollen grains attach.

Male Reproductive Organs:

  • Pair of testes (singular testis), two sperm ducts, penis.
  • Testis produces male gametes called sperms.
  • Millions of sperms produced.
  • Each sperm is a single cell with usual cell components.

Female Reproductive Organs:

  • Pair of ovaries, oviducts (fallopian tubes), uterus.
  • Ovary produces female gametes called ova (eggs).
  • Uterus is where development of baby takes place.

Fertilization Process:

  • When sperms contact egg, one sperm may fuse with egg.
  • Fusion of egg and sperm is fertilization.
  • Nuclei of sperm and egg fuse to form single nucleus → fertilized egg or zygote.
  • Internal fertilization: occurs inside female body (humans, cows, dogs, hens).
  • External fertilization: fusion outside female body, common in aquatic animals (fish, starfish).

Development of Embryo:

  • Fertilization forms zygote which develops into embryo.
  • Zygote divides repeatedly to form ball of cells.

details.summary: Overview of pollination, fertilization, male and female reproductive organs, and embryo development.

content:
**Pollination:** Transfer of pollen grains from anther to stigma of same flower or between different flowers.

- **Self-pollination:** Transfer of pollen grains from anthers to stigma of same flower or another flower of same plant.
- **Cross-pollination (Xenogamy):** Transfer of pollen from flower of one plant to stigma of flower of another plant.

**Fertilization:** Fusion of male and female reproductive units.

- After pollination, pollen grains attach.

**Male Reproductive Organs:**

- Pair of testes (singular testis), two sperm ducts, penis.
- Testis produces male gametes called sperms.
- Millions of sperms produced.
- Each sperm is a single cell with usual cell components.

**Female Reproductive Organs:**

- Pair of ovaries, oviducts (fallopian tubes), uterus.
- Ovary produces female gametes called ova (eggs).
- Uterus is where development of baby takes place.

**Fertilization Process:**

- When sperms contact egg, one sperm may fuse with egg.
- Fusion of egg and sperm is fertilization.
- Nuclei of sperm and egg fuse to form single nucleus → fertilized egg or zygote.
- Internal fertilization: occurs inside female body (humans, cows, dogs, hens).
- External fertilization: fusion outside female body, common in aquatic animals (fish, starfish).

**Development of Embryo:**

- Fertilization forms zygote which develops into embryo.
- Zygote divides repeatedly to form ball of cells.

### Key Exam Facts
- **Summary:** Overview of pollination, fertilization, male and female reproductive organs, and embryo development.

text:
The head of the tribe (Jana) was supreme and worked on the collective response of tribal assemblies.

  • Tribal assemblies: Sabha, Samiti, Gana, Vidhata (oldest).
  • These assemblies upheld social, military, religious activities.
  • Samiti comprised the whole clan; Sabha was a selected group of elderly people.
  • Vidhata engaged in redistributive functions.
  • Chief was called Gopati; women allowed in Sabha and Vidhata.
  • Vajrapati – officer of pasture (led by Kulapa and Gramini in war).
  • Senani – important functionary after Purohita.
  • Military functions performed by tribal units: rata, gana, grama.
  • Tax known as Bali was voluntary.

topic: Geographical Extent, Social Life, Purushasukta Theory, Political Organisation
text:
Geographical Extent: Aryans moved eastward and southward from Punjab to Delhi and upper Gangetic Doab; Satapatha Brahmana mentions Agni and Videha Madhava moving eastward.

Social Life:

  • Four‑fold division of society became clear: Brahmins (priests), Kshatriyas (warriors), Vaishyas (agriculturists, cattle‑rearers, traders), Sudras (servers of upper three).
  • Women enjoyed freedom and respect but status deteriorated compared to earlier period.
  • Institution of gotra appeared first time, signifying descent from common ancestors.
  • Concept of four Ashrams: Brahmacharya, Grihastha, Vanaprastha, Sanyas.
  • Chariot racing – main sport; gambling – main pastime.

Purushasukta Theory: Late hymn of 10th Mandala of Rigveda; four varnas originated from body of Purusha: Brahmana (mouth), Kshatriya (arms), Vaishya (thighs), Shudra (feet).

Political Organisation:

  • Tiny tribal settlements replaced by strong kingdoms; regular army maintained.
  • Powers of king (Samrat) increased; importance of assemblies declined; women no longer permitted to attend assemblies.
  • Term ‘rashtra’ (territory) first appeared.
  • References to priest (Purohita), Commander‑in‑chief (Senapati), Charioteer (Suta), Treasurer (Sangrahita), Tax collector (Bhagdugha), Chief queen (Mahisi), game companion (Aksavapa).

details.summary: Expansion, social stratification, Purushasukta, and political changes in Later Vedic Age.

**Political Organisation:**

subject: Physics
text:
Conservative and Non-conservative Forces

  • A force is said to be conservative, if the work done by the force in moving a body depends only upon the initial and final positions of the body and is independent of the path followed between the initial and final position, e.g. gravitational force, electrostatic force and magnetic force, etc.
  • A force is said to be non-conservative, if the work done by the force or against the force, in moving a body from one position to another, depends upon the path followed between the two positions. e.g. friction force, etc.

ENERGY

The energy of an object is its capacity for doing work. It is a scalar quantity and its unit is joule (J).

  • Energy can exist in different forms such as mechanical energy, heat energy, sound energy, light energy, chemical energy, etc.
  • Mechanical energy is of two types i.e. kinetic energy and potential energy.

1. Kinetic Energy

The energy possessed by a body by virtue of its motion is called its kinetic energy.

  • If a body of mass m is moving with velocity v, then kinetic energy = ½ mv² (or expressed as p²/2m).
  • When momentum is doubled kinetic energy becomes four times.
  • If a body is moving in horizontal circle then its kinetic energy is same at all points, but if it is moving in vertical circle, then the kinetic energy is different at different points.

Applications of kinetic energy are given below

  • (i) Kinetic energy of air is used to run wind mills.
  • (ii) Kinetic energy of running water is used to run the water mills.
  • (iii) A bullet fired from a gun can pierce a target due to its kinetic energy.

2. Potential Energy

It is the energy possessed by a body by virtue of its position.

  • Suppose a body is raised to a height h above the surface of the earth, then potential energy of body = mgh
  • Also, here potential energy = work done = mgh
  • When the body is projected upwards, then its kinetic energy goes on changing to potential energy and vice-versa.

Applications of potential energy are given below

  • (i) The potential energy of the wound spring of a clock is used to drive the hands of the clock.
  • (ii) Due to potential energy of the stretched bow, the arrow goes forward with a large velocity on releasing the bow.
  • (iii) The potential energy of water in dams is used to run turbines in order to produce electrical energy using the generators.

Principle of Conservation of Energy

According to the law of conservation of energy it can neither be created nor be destroyed but can only be transformed from one form to another.

  • The total amount of energy in the universe remains constant. e.g. when an object falls, its potential energy decreases but at the same time kinetic energy increases by an equal amount.

Transformation of Energy

  • In a heat engine, heat energy changes into mechanical energy. In the sun, mass changes into radiant energy.
  • In an electrical heater, the electric energy is converted into heat energy.
  • In an electric bulb, the electric energy is converted into light energy in burning coal, oil, etc. The chemical energy changes to heat energy.
  • When we rub our hands, heat is generated. Here, mechanical energy of muscles is converted into heat energy.
  • In an electromagnet the electric energy is converted into magnetic energy.

Einstein’s Mass-Energy Equivalence

In 1905, Einstein proved the relation between mass and energy. E = mc², where c is the velocity of light.

E = mc² leads to verification of the two laws, law of conservation of mass and law of conservation of energy.

POWER

The time rate of doing work is called power.

If W is work done in time t then power, P = W/t.

For a constant force F, the Power (P) = F·v = Fv cosθ where v = velocity of object, θ = angle between F and v.

  • Power is a scalar quantity with SI unit watt (W) or joule/s.
  • Some other units of power are 1 watt hour = 3600 J; 1 kilowatt hour = 3.6 × 10⁶ J; 1 HP (Horse Power) = 746 W.

subject: Biology
topic: Embryo Development and Types of Reproduction
text:
The cells then begin to form groups that develop into different tissues and organs of the body.

  • This developing structure is termed an embryo.
  • The embryo gradually develops the body parts such as hands, legs, head, eyes, ears, etc.
  • The stage of the embryo in which all the body parts can be identified is called a foetus.
  • When the development of the foetus is complete, the mother gives birth to the baby.
  • In animals which undergo external fertilization, development of the embryo takes place outside the female body. The embryos continue to grow within their egg coverings. After the embryos develop, the eggs hatch.
  • Viviparous animals – gives birth.
  • Oviparous animals – lays eggs.

Asexual Reproduction

  • In asexual reproduction, only one parent is involved
  • It mostly happens in primitive microscopic animals.
  • In hydra, reproduction occurs by budding. A bud is developed and detached which develops into a new organism.
  • Another type of asexual reproduction is found in unicellular amoeba called Binary Fission. The nucleus first divides into two, followed by the division of the body into two each part receiving a nucleus.

Musculoskeletal system:

  • The skeletal system includes the bones of the skeleton and the cartilages, ligaments, and other connective tissue that stabilize or connect the bones.

Bones:

  • There are 206 bones in the adult body.
  • Longest bone – Femur (thigh bone). And smallest bone – Stapes (in the ear).
  • The bones of the body perform five main functions:
    • provides support for the body
    • Stores minerals and lipids
    • Produce blood cells
    • Protect body organs
    • Provide leverage and movement
  • Each bone in the skeleton contains two forms of tissue: compact bone that is relatively solid and spongy bone. Compact bone is found on the external surface of the bone. Spongy bone is located inside the bone.
  • Joints - Connects two bones together.
  • Ligaments –They connect different bones.
  • Tendons – They connect tissue with bones. They are made of collagen.

subject: History
topic: Rise of Vishnu and Religious Developments
text:
CDS Pathfinder

Religion

Rise of Vishnu alongside Rudra new Gods (Vishnu, Rudra, Prajapati etc) came into prominence. Rig Vedic Gods (Indra, Varuna etc) lost prominence. Sacrifices became more elaborate. Increase in the prestige and importance of priestly class. Emergence of new philosophical concepts.

Sacrifices Performed in Later Vedic Period

  • Rajasuya Consecration Ceremony This conferred supreme power on the king. The Rajasuya sacrifice consists of five major ritual or ceremonies. Asvamedha horse sacrifice which was meant to establish kings supremacy over his neighbours. The Aitareya and Shatapatha Brahmana mention the names of some monarchs, who performed the sacrifice.
  • Ratnahanimasi Ceremony The king had to approach dignitaries who lived in permanent dwellings. Vajapeya chariot race which was meant to re-establish his supremacy over his own people within the kingdom.

Pottery

The later Vedic people used black and redware, black-strippedware, painted greyware pottery. Redware was most popular with them and has been found almost all over Western Uttar Pradesh. However, the most distinctive pottery of the period is known as Painted Greyware, which comprised bowls and dishes, used either for rituals or for eating by the upper classes.

Economic Life

  • The shift towards Gangetic valley with the use of iron and fire made possible the growth of agriculture. Pastoralism was no longer the main subsistence activity of the people, though cattle rearing was also practised.
  • Shatapatha Brahmana describes the various stages of agriculture such as ploughing, sowing, reaping and threshing. Both kharif and rabi crops were grown.
  • Rice (Vrihi) and wheat (Godhuma) become the chief crops of the later Vedic Aryans, though they continued to produce barley (Yava).

VEDIC LITERATURE

  • The word ‘Veda’ is derived from Sanskrit word vid, meaning to know, signifying knowledge par excellence. The Vedic text are shruti i.e. directly revealed to authors by God.
  • Smritis are remembered and collected parts of literature of later period. They are also called samhitas in the sense that they represent oral tradition of the time.
  • Four vedas and their Samhitas, the Brahmanas, the Aranyakas and the Upanishads form a class of literature known as shruti.

The Rig Veda

It is divided into 10 books or mandalas. Mandala II to VII are considered the oldest and known as family mandalas. Book I, VIII and X seem to be added later. It dated 1500 BC-1000 BC. It has 1028 hymns written by number of priestly families. The Rig Veda was written when Aryans were still in Punjab. Book II to VII are earliest and are attributed to Gritsamada, Vishvamitra, Vasudeva, Atri, Bhardwaj, Vashishtha, Kanva and Angiras. Rig Veda is recited by Hotri. Gayatri mantri is in 3rd mandal of Rig Veda.

The Yajur Veda

It is a ritualistic Veda. Written in prose, it deals with procedure for performance of sacrifices and contain rituals as well as hymns. It is divided into Shukla Yajur Veda (poetry) (including Vajasneyi samhita) and Krishna Yajur Veda (prose and poetry) (Katha, Matriyani and Taittiriya, Vapisthal samhita in which mantra and Brahamanas part are not separated). Yajur Veda is recited by Adhvaryu.

The Sama Veda

Word Sama derived from the root word saman means melody/music. It has 1603 verses, but except 99, all the rest of the hymns have been borrowed from the Rig Veda. It contains Dhrupada Raga. The Sama Veda shows that the Aryans loved music and were not merely puritans. Sama Veda is recited by udgatri.

The Atharva Veda

The Atharva Veda is entirely different from the other three Vedas and is the last of the four Vedas. The Satapatha Brahmana used the term trayi, i.e. the Rig Veda, Yajur Veda and Sama Veda. Atharva Veda mentions beliefs and practices of non-Aryans. It contains magical mantra etc. In it, the sabha and the Samiti are described as sisters and the two daughters of prajapati. This Veda is also known as Brahma Veda.

Smriti Literature

The Smriti literature contains following

The Brahamanas

These are the prose commentaries on various Vedic hymns. They explain the vedas in an orthodox way. They explain the hidden meanings behind the hymns of Brahamans. They are expressions of the cause (hetu). Shatapatha Brahamana is the largest Brahamana book. It has the story of Madhav.

The Aranyakas

The authors of the Aranyakas were sages dwelling in the forest and explained vedic texts for their pupils in the form of Aranyakas. So, these Aranyakas are known as forest books. They form the concluding part of Brahamanas.

details.summary: Notes on Vedic religion, sacrifices, pottery, economic life, and Vedic literature including the four Vedas, Brahmanas, Aranyakas, and Smriti.

Given diameter of hemisphere = 14 cm, therefore radius r = 7 cm.

Volume of cone = (1/3)πr^2 h, where h = 16 cm (from figure).

Volume of hemisphere = (2/3)πr^3.

Total volume = (1/3)πr^2 h + (2/3)πr^3 = (1/3)πr^2 (h + 2r).

Substituting r = 7 cm, h = 16 cm:

Total volume = (1/3) × (22/7) × 7^2 × (16 + 2×7) = (1/3) × (22/7) × 49 × (16+14) = (1/3) × (22/7) × 49 × 30 = (22 × 7 × 30) / 3 = (22 × 7 × 10) = 1540 cm^3.

Hence, the volume of the solid formed is 1540 cm^3.

Given volume of one cube = 343 cm^3 ⇒ side a = ∛343 = 7 cm.

When three cubes are joined end to end, dimensions of resulting cuboid: length = 3a = 21 cm, breadth = a = 7 cm, height = a = 7 cm.

Total surface area of cuboid = 2(lb + bh + hl) = 2[(21×7) + (7×7) + (21×7)] = 2[147 + 49 + 147] = 2×343 = 686 cm^2.

Hence, total surface area = 686 cm^2.

topic: Total Surface Area of Cube with Hemisphere
text:
Side of cube a = 14 cm, radius of hemisphere r = 7 cm.

Total surface area = Surface area of cube + Curved surface area of hemisphere - Base area of hemisphere.

Surface area of cube = 6a^2 = 6×14^2 = 6×196 = 1176 cm^2.

Curved surface area of hemisphere = 2πr^2 = 2×(22/7)×7^2 = 2×22×7 = 308 cm^2.

Base area of hemisphere = πr^2 = (22/7)×7^2 = 22×7 = 154 cm^2.

Total surface area = 1176 + 308 - 154 = 1330 cm^2.

Hence, total surface area = 1330 cm^2.

topic: Number of Coins to form a Cuboid
text:
Diameter of coin = 3.5 cm ⇒ radius r = 1.75 cm.

Thickness h = 4 mm = 0.4 cm.

Volume of one coin = πr^2 h = (22/7)×(1.75)^2×0.4.

Volume of cuboid = 21×11×7 = 1617 cm^3.

Number of coins n = Volume of cuboid / Volume of one coin = 1617 / [(22/7)×(1.75)^2×0.4] = 420.

Hence, 420 silver coins are required.

Slant height l = √[h^2 + (r2 - r1)^2] = √[16^2 + (105-42)^2] = √[256 + 63^2] = √[256 + 3969] = √4225 = 65 cm.

Hence, slant height = 65 cm.
