subject: Public Sector Enterprises
content:
# Mini-ratna Public Sector Enterprises

The government introduced the **Mini-ratna** category to grant limited autonomy to PSEs that meet certain profitability and net‑worth criteria.

## Category‑I Mini‑ratna
- **Eligibility**: Continuous profit for the last 3 years **or** a net profit of **₹30 crore or more** in any one of those 3 years.
- **Autonomy**: Can incur capital expenditure without government approval up to **₹500 crore** or **equal to their net worth**, whichever is lower.
- **Current Count**: 51 PSEs.

## Category‑II Mini‑ratna
- **Eligibility**: Continuous profit for the last 3 years **and** a positive net worth.
- **Autonomy**: Can incur capital expenditure without government approval up to **₹300 crore** or **50 % of their net worth**, whichever is lower.
- **Current Count**: 14 PSEs.

subject: Companies Act 2013
content:
# Dormant Company

Under the Companies Act 2013, a company is classified as **dormant** when:

- It is formed and registered for a future project or to hold an asset/intellectual property.
- It has **no significant accounting transaction** during its existence.

Dormant companies are exempt from certain compliance requirements such as filing annual returns.

subject: Companies Act 2013
content:
# NFRA

The Act mandates the constitution of the **National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA)**, which:

- Issues authoritative pronouncements on accounting and auditing standards.
- Regulates the audit profession and ensures audit quality.
- Has powers to investigate and sanction auditors and audit firms.

subject: Companies Act 2013
content:
# SFIO

The Companies Act 2013 grants **legal status** to the **Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO)**, enabling it to:

- Investigate serious frauds involving companies.
- Conduct investigations, gather evidence, and recommend prosecution.

subject: Companies Act 2013
content:
# CSR

The Act introduces a **CSR framework** requiring eligible companies to:

- Formulate a CSR policy.
- Spend **at least 2 % of the average net profit** of the preceding three financial years on CSR activities, or **2 % of net assets** if the profit is lower.
- Report CSR expenditures in the annual report.

subject: Competition Law
content:
# Competition Commission of India (CCI)

- **Established**: 2003 under the Competition Act, 2002.
- **Composition**: Chairperson + 6 members appointed by the Central Government.
- **Functions**:
  - Eliminate anti‑competitive practices.
  - Promote and sustain competition.
  - Protect consumer interests.
  - Ensure freedom of trade in Indian markets.

Accordingly, the industries were divided into four broad categories

  • i. Exclusive Government Monopoly This includes manufacture of arms and ammunition, production and control of atomic energy and the ownership and management of railway transport. These industries were the exclusive monopoly of the Central Government.
  • ii. Government Monopoly for New Units This category included coal, iron and steel, aircraft manufacture, ship building, manufacture of telephone, telegraphs and wireless apparatus (excluding radio receiving sets) and mineral oils. New undertakings in this category was to be undertaken only by the State.
  • iii. Regulation This category included industries of such basic importance like machine tools, chemicals, fertilizers, non-ferrous metals, rubber manufactures, cement, paper, newsprint, automobiles, electric engineering etc which the Central Government would feel necessary to plan and regulate.
  • iv. Unregulated Private Enterprise The industries in this category were left open to the private sector, individual as well as cooperative.

Industrial Policy Resolution, 1956

The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 classified the entire industrial sector in three schedules, which are as follows

  • Schedule A: In the first category, those industries were included whose future development was the exclusive responsibility of the State. 17 industries, were included in this category.
  • Schedule B: In this category, those industries were included which were progressively State-owned and in which the private enterprises would be expected only to supplement the efforts of the State. In this category, 12 industries were included.
  • Schedule C: All industries not listed in Schedule A or B were included in the third category. These industries were left open to the private sector.

The New Industrial Policy of 1991 was at the center of economic reforms that was launched during the early 1990s. This policy brought comprehensive changes in economic regulation in the country.

  • New industrial policy abolished all industrial licensing, irrespective of the level of investment, except for a short list of selected industries.
  • Government announced its intention to offer a part of government shareholding in the public sector enterprises to mutual funds, financial institutions, general public and the workers.
  • The 1956 Resolution had reserved 17 industries for the public sector. The 1991 industrial policy reduced this number to 8. As of now only 3 industries are reserved for government.

subject: Economics
content:
### Core Banking Solution
- Normal core banking functions include **transaction accounts, loans, mortgages and payments**.
- These services are delivered through multiple channels such as **ATMs, internet banking, mobile banking, etc.**
- The term *Core Banking Solution (CBS)* refers to the integrated system that enables banks to provide these services uniformly across all branches.

subject: Economics
content:
### Retail Banking
- When a bank executes transactions **directly with consumers** (individuals) rather than corporations or other banks, it is called **Retail Banking**.
- Services typically include savings & current accounts, personal loans, credit cards, mortgages, and debit/ATM cards.

subject: Economics
content:
### Narrow Banking
- A **restricted form of banking** where banks are required to take **calculated risk** only.
- A large portion of deposits is mobilised into **risk‑free assets** such as **government securities**.
- In India, banks **partially implement narrow banking**.

subject: Economics
content:
### Money – Definition & Types
- Money plays a **crucial role** in economic transactions.
- **Modern money** includes **paper notes and coins**.
- In India, the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** is authorised to issue currency notes on behalf of the Government of India.
- **Legal sanction**: Every Indian rupee is a **legal tender** – it cannot be refused for settlement of transactions.

#### Types of Money
1. **Legal Money** – Issued under legislation by the Government or RBI. The issuing authority undertakes to pay the holder an equal amount.
2. **Credit Money** – Represents a **promise of payment**, e.g., **cheques**.

subject: Economics
content:
### Money Stock Measures (India)
- Introduced by RBI from **1970‑71** based on the **Second Working Group on Money Supply**.

| Measure | Components (increasing order of liquidity) |
|---------|--------------------------------------------|
| **M1**   | • Currency notes & coins (money with the public)  
|         | • Demand deposits of banks (current & savings accounts) 
|         | • Other demand deposits with RBI |
| **M2**   | M1 **+** Savings bank deposits with **Post‑Offices** |
| **M3**   | M2 **+** Term deposits with banks (often called **Broad Money**) |
| **M4**   | M3 **+** All deposits of Post‑Offices |

- **Liquidity order**: M1 is the most liquid, followed by M2, M3, and M4 (least liquid).
- **M3** is the most important component and is commonly referred to as **Broad Money**.

subject: Economics
topic: Cheap Money vs. Dear Money Policy
content:
### Cheap Money Policy
- A monetary stance where **loans and advances are offered at low interest rates** and easy terms to industries, businessmen, and consumers.
- **Effect**: Increases **inflation**; used to combat **deflationary tendencies**.

### Dear Money Policy
- A monetary stance where **interest rates are raised** to **squeeze credit** in the economy.
- **Effect**: Helps **control inflation**.

content:
# Reserve Bank of India (RBI)

- **Establishment**: 
  - RBI Act, 1934 enacted in 1934.
  - Set up on the basis of the Hilton‑Young Commission recommendation (April 1935).
- **First Governor**: Sir Osborne Smith (British). 
- **Nationalisation**: 1949 – first Indian Governor was C.D. Deshmukh.
- **Current (22nd) Governor**: Urijit Patel (appointed September 2016).
- **Board of Directors**: 14 directors (including the Governor), 4 Deputy Governors, 1 government official.
- **Headquarters**: Mumbai.
- **Purpose**: Separate currency and credit from the Government of India (GOI).

subject: Banking & Finance
content:
# Key Functions of RBI

1. **Banker to the Government** – transacts banking business of the Union and State governments.
2. **Regulator of the Banking System** – provides broad parameters for the functioning of banks and the financial system.
3. **Custodian of Foreign Reserves** – manages investment and utilisation of foreign reserves.
4. **Credit Control** – uses monetary policy tools to control money supply and liquidity.
5. **Currency Management** – oversees the issuance and circulation of currency notes and coins (though printing is done by the Security Press).

subject: Monetary Policy
content:
# Monetary Policy Committee

- **Members**: 6 members in total.
  - 3 members from RBI (including the Governor) – each has a casting vote.
  - 3 external members appointed by the Government.
- **Finance Ministry Nominee**: Participates in deliberations but has no voting right.
- **Purpose**: Set policy interest rates and guide monetary policy.

subject: Credit Control
content:
# Quantitative (General) Credit Control Instruments

| Instrument | Description |
|------------|-------------|
| **Bank Rate** | Also called rediscount rate – rate at which RBI lends to commercial banks. |
| **Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)** | Proportion of net demand and time liabilities banks must keep with RBI. |
| **Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)** | Ratio of liquid assets (cash, gold, approved securities) banks must hold; capped at 40% of total deposits. |
| **Repo Rate** | Rate at which RBI lends short‑term money to banks against securities; injects liquidity. |
| **Reverse Repo Rate** | Rate at which banks park excess liquidity with RBI; withdraws liquidity. Always 100 basis points (1%) less than the Repo rate. |
| **Open Market Operations (OMOs)** | RBI sells or buys government securities to withdraw or inject liquidity, respectively. |

These tools control the volume of credit and indirectly influence inflationary/deflationary pressures.

subject: Credit Control
content:
# Qualitative (Selective/Direct) Credit Control

- **Definition**: Targeted measures to influence the composition of credit rather than its overall volume.
- **Typical Instruments** (not exhaustively listed in the source but commonly used):
  - **Credit Rating** of borrowers.
  - **Sector‑specific lending limits**.
  - **Priority sector lending** mandates.
  - **Credit‑rating based interest rate adjustments**.

These tools aim to direct credit to desired sectors or projects.

Insurance has been an important part of the Indian financial system. Until recently, insurance services were provided by the public sector i.e. life insurance by the Life Insurance Corporation of India and general insurance by the General Insurance Corporation and its four subsidiaries.

(i) General Insurance Corporation (GIC)

Established on 1st January, 1973, It has four subsidiary companies, which are as follows

  • i. National Insurance Company Limited, Kolkata.
  • ii. The New India Assurance Company Limited, Mumbai.
  • iii. The Oriental and Insurance Company Limited, New Delhi.
  • iv. United India Fire and General Insurance Company Limited, Chennai.

(ii) Life Insurance Corporation (LIC)

  • • Established on 1st September, 1956.
  • • Head office Mumbai, Zonal offices 7 (Mumbai, Kolkata, Delhi, Chennai, Kanpur, Hyderabad and Bhopal).

Reforms in Insurance Sector

The reforms in the insurance sector started with the enactment of Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority Act, 1999. The Act paved the way for the entry of private insurance companies into the insurance market and also Constitution of Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority. In 1993, Malhotra Committee was set-up to recommend reforms in insurance sector.

Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI)

  • • IRDAI was constituted on 19th April, 2000 to protect the interest of the holders of insurance policies and to regulate, promote and ensure orderly growth of the insurance industry. The authority consists of a Chairperson, three whole-time members and four part-time members.
  • • It provides for regulating the insurance sector, the authority has been issuing regulations covering almost the entire segment of insurance industry, namely; regulation on insurance agents, solvency margin, re-insurance, registration of insurers, obligation of insurers to rural and social sector, accounting procedure etc.

text:
TAX STRUCTURE

Tax is a compulsory payment by the citizens to the government to meet the public expenditure. It is legally imposed by the government on the taxpayer and in no case taxpayer can deny to pay taxes to the government. Tax can be direct or indirect, which are as follows

Direct Tax

A direct tax is that tax, which is borne by the person on whom it is levied. A direct tax cannot be shifted to other person.

Some of the direct taxes are as follows

  • i. Income Tax It is the tax levied directly on the income of the people by the Central Government.
  • ii. Corporate Tax It is levied on the profit of the companies or corporations. It is the largest source of revenue of the Central Government, covering about 18% of the total revenue.
  • iii. Wealth Tax This tax is levied on the net wealth of the individuals, Hindu undivided family and joint stock companies. It is a minor source of revenue of the government, primarily imposed to reduce concentration of wealth in the society.
  • iv. Gift Tax This tax is imposed by the Central Government on all donations and gifts over and above the prescribed limits to the family members. However, donation given by the charitable institutions and companies is not covered under gift tax. This tax is basically imposed to check the evasion of estate duty and wealth tax.
  • v. Interest Tax This tax is imposed on the interest income of the commercial banks on their gross loans and advances. Presently, it is not in force in India.

Indirect Tax

Indirect taxes are those taxes which have their primary burden or impact on one person, but that person succeeds in shifting his burden on to others.

TAX STRUCTURE

Tax is a compulsory payment by the citizens to the government to meet the public expenditure. It is legally imposed by the government on the taxpayer and in no case taxpayer can deny to pay taxes to the government. Tax can be direct or indirect, which are as follows

**Direct Tax**

A direct tax is that tax, which is borne by the person on whom it is levied. A direct tax cannot be shifted to other person.

Some of the direct taxes are as follows

- i. Income Tax It is the tax levied directly on the income of the people by the Central Government.
- ii. Corporate Tax It is levied on the profit of the companies or corporations. It is the largest source of revenue of the Central Government, covering about 18% of the total revenue.
- iii. Wealth Tax This tax is levied on the net wealth of the individuals, Hindu undivided family and joint stock companies. It is a minor source of revenue of the government, primarily imposed to reduce concentration of wealth in the society.
- iv. Gift Tax This tax is imposed by the Central Government on all donations and gifts over and above the prescribed limits to the family members. However, donation given by the charitable institutions and companies is not covered under gift tax. This tax is basically imposed to check the evasion of estate duty and wealth tax.
- v. Interest Tax This tax is imposed on the interest income of the commercial banks on their gross loans and advances. Presently, it is not in force in India.

**Indirect Tax**

Indirect taxes are those taxes which have their primary burden or impact on one person, but that person succeeds in shifting his burden on to others.

subject: GST
content:
# Goods and Services Tax (GST)

- **GST** is a *comprehensive indirect tax* levied on the manufacture, sale, and consumption of goods and services across India.
- It **replaces** a multitude of central and state taxes, thereby simplifying the tax structure.
- GST is collected **at every stage of the supply chain** using the *input tax credit* mechanism, ensuring that tax is paid only on the value added at each stage.

---

## Central Taxes Replaced by GST

| Central Tax | Replaced by GST |
|-------------|-----------------|
| Central Excise Duty | ✔ |
| Additional Duties of Excise | ✔ |
| Customs Duties (including SAD) | ✔ |
| Service Tax | ✔ |
| Cesses and Surcharges on Supply of Goods and Services | ✔ |

---

## State Taxes Subsumed in GST

| State Tax | Replaced by GST |
|-----------|-----------------|
| Value Added Tax (VAT) | ✔ |
| Central Sales Tax | ✔ |
| Purchase Tax | ✔ |
| Luxury Tax | ✔ |
| Entry Tax | ✔ |
| Entertainment Tax | ✔ |
| Taxes on Advertisements | ✔ |
| Lotteries, Betting, Gambling | ✔ |
| State Cesses and Surcharges | ✔ |

---

## Key Features

- **Uniformity**: Same tax rates across all states.
- **Simplification**: Single tax instead of multiple overlapping taxes.
- **Transparency**: Real‑time tax credit and compliance through GSTN portal.
- **Economic Growth**: Reduces cascading taxes, lowers cost of goods and services.

---

## Important Terms

- **Input Tax Credit (ITC)**: Credit for tax paid on inputs that can be offset against output tax liability.
- **GSTN**: Goods and Services Tax Network – the IT infrastructure for GST administration.
- **GST Council**: Inter‑governmental body that decides on rates, exemptions, and other GST parameters.

subject: Public Finance
chapter: Financial Relations between Centre and States
content:
# Articles 264 & 293

- **Article 264**: Provides the *financial relations* between the Union and State governments, outlining the distribution of revenue and the powers of the Centre.
- **Article 293**: Deals with *financial relations* between the Union and the Union Territories.

---

## Key Points

- **Centre’s Residuary Powers**: The Constitution reserves residual powers to the Centre, ensuring it can legislate on matters not explicitly assigned to the States.
- **Revenue Sharing**: States receive a share of certain Union taxes and are also entitled to revenue from taxes listed in the Union List that are levied by the States.
- **Transfer of Proceeds**: Some taxes are levied by the Central Government but the entire proceeds are transferred to the States.

---

## 7th Schedule Lists

- **List I**: Enumerates *Union taxes* (e.g., Income Tax, Customs Duty, Central Excise Duty).
- **List II**: Enumerates *State taxes* (e.g., VAT, State Excise Duty, State Cesses).
- **List III**: Enumerates *Concurrent taxes* that both Union and States can levy.

---

## Fiscal Devolution

- The Constitution provides for a *clear division of fiscal powers* between the Central and State governments, ensuring balanced development and autonomy.

subject: Finance Commission
content:
# 14th Finance Commission (Headed by YV Reddy)

## Key Recommendations

1. **Devolution of Taxes to States**: Increase the share of central taxes allocated to states from **32% to 42%**.
2. **Fiscal Deficit Target**: Aim for a fiscal deficit of **3% of Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP)** for the period 2015‑2020.
3. **GST Compensation Fund**: Establish an *autonomous* and *independent* GST compensation fund to facilitate compensation to states for 5 years.
4. **Amendments to FRBM Act**: Remove the definition of *effective revenue* to streamline fiscal calculations.

---

## Significance

- **Equitable Revenue Sharing**: Ensures states receive a fair share of national tax revenues.
- **Fiscal Discipline**: Sets clear deficit targets to promote responsible budgeting.
- **GST Transition**: Provides a structured mechanism for compensating states during the GST implementation phase.

subject: Union Budget
content:
# Union Budget

- **Definition**: The Union Budget is an *annual financial statement* presented by the Finance Minister in Parliament, detailing the government's revenue and expenditure for the upcoming fiscal year (1st April – 31st March).
- **Constitutional Basis**: Though the term *budget* is not used in the Constitution, Article 112 refers to the *Annual Financial Statement* comprising the *Revenue Capital Budget* and *Budget Estimates* for the next fiscal year.

---

## Components

1. **Revenue Budget**: Estimates of revenue receipts and expenditure.
2. **Capital Budget**: Estimates of capital receipts and expenditure.
3. **Budget Estimates**: Detailed estimates for each department and scheme.

---

## Purpose

- **Transparency**: Provides a clear picture of government finances.
- **Planning**: Guides fiscal policy and resource allocation.
- **Accountability**: Enables Parliament to scrutinize and approve the government's financial plans.

subject: General Studies
content:
# Types of Inflation

- **Cost‑Push Inflation**
  - Created and sustained by an increase in the cost of production.
  - Independent of the state of demand.
  - Example: Trade unions bargaining for higher wages, leading to higher production costs and consequently higher prices.

- **Stagflation**
  - Simultaneous rise in the general price level and fall in output and employment.
  - Entrepreneurs raise prices to maintain profit margins but only partially succeed, leading to declining output and investment.

- **Hyper‑Inflation**
  - Very rapid growth in the rate of inflation.
  - Money loses its value to the extent that alternative mediums of exchange (barter, foreign currency) become common.
  - Also known as *Galloping Inflation*.

subject: General Studies
content:
# Measurement of Inflation

- **General Price Index (GPI)**
  - Measures changes in average prices of goods and services.
  - A base year is selected and its index is set to 100.
  - Current year index > 100 indicates inflation; < 100 indicates deflation.

- **Wholesale Price Index (WPI)**
  - Measures changes in wholesale prices on a weekly basis.
  - Weekly indices are averaged to obtain the annual WPI.
  - Base year (average annual wholesale prices) is assumed as 100.

- **Consumer Price Index (CPI)**
  - Measures changes in price level of goods and services purchased by households.
  - Base year after 2015 revision: 2012.
  - CPI is compiled separately for urban and rural populations and also published as a combined CPI (Urban + Rural).

subject: General Studies
content:
# Deflation

- **Definition**: A state where the value of money rises and the price of goods and services falls.

- **Causes**:
  1. Government withdraws money from circulation.
  2. Heavy direct taxes or large public loans (voluntary or compulsory).
  3. Central Bank sells securities in the open market, reducing money supply.
  4. Central Bank increases the bank rate, curtailing credit.

- **Measures to Check Deflation**:
  1. Increase money supply.
  2. Promote credit creation by banks.
  3. Reduce taxes to increase purchasing power.
  4. Increase public expenditure and employment opportunities.
  5. Repay old public debts to increase money in circulation.
  6. Provide economic subsidies to the industrial sector.

subject: General Studies
content:
# Foreign Trade

- A characteristic feature of modern economies.
- India has a long history of international trade, with recent shifts in traditional areas and destinations of export/import.

subject: General Studies
content:
# Balance of Trade (BoT)

- **Definition**: Difference between a nation’s imports of goods and services and its exports.
- **Importance**: Most important element of the Balance of Payments.
- **Possibilities**:
  1. **Balanced BoT** – Exports = Imports.
  2. **Adverse BoT** – Exports < Imports.
  3. **Favourable BoT** – Exports > Imports.

subject: General Studies
content:
# Balance of Payment (BoP)

- **Definition**: Record of all economic transactions between residents of a country and the rest of the world over a specific period (usually a year).
- **Participants**: Individuals, firms, and government bodies.
- **Structure**: Divided into two main accounts:
  1. Current Account (trade in goods and services, income, current transfers).
  2. Capital and Financial Account (capital transfers, investment flows).

subject: Economics
content:
# Foreign Direct Investment (FDI)

- **FDI** is an investment in a foreign country through the acquisition of a local company or the establishment of an operation on a new greenfield site.
- It involves a **direct** investment that gives the investor a lasting interest in the foreign enterprise.
- FDI is distinguished from portfolio investment by the **control** and **long‑term commitment** it entails.

---

## Types of FDI

- **Greenfield Investment**: Setting up a new production facility or operation from scratch in the host country.
- **Brownfield Investment**: Purchasing or leasing existing production facilities to launch a new production activity.

---

## Key Points

- FDI is a major source of capital, technology, and managerial expertise for host economies.
- It often leads to job creation, export promotion, and integration into global value chains.
- Host countries may impose restrictions or incentives to attract FDI.

subject: Economics
content:
# Brownfield Investment

- **Brownfield** refers to the acquisition or lease of existing production facilities in a foreign country.
- The investor uses pre‑existing infrastructure, machinery, and workforce to start or expand operations.
- Advantages: faster time‑to‑market, lower initial capital outlay, and reduced risk compared to greenfield projects.
- Disadvantages: potential legacy issues, higher regulatory scrutiny, and limited flexibility in design.

subject: Economics
content:
# Consolidated FDI Policy (India, 2010)

- Effective from **1st April 2010**, India’s FDI regime was consolidated under a single policy framework.
- The policy is issued by the **Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion (DIPP)**.
- Objectives:
  - Clarify and streamline FDI rules.
  - Provide predictability for foreign investors and sectoral regulators.
  - Encourage investment in priority sectors.
- The policy covers all sectors, with sector‑specific guidelines and approval mechanisms.

subject: Economics
content:
# Foreign Institutional Investor (FII)

- An **FII** is a foreign entity registered outside the country in which it invests.
- In India, FIIs invest in the country’s financial markets (equities, bonds, etc.).
- **2013**: India adopted the international definition to distinguish FII from FDI.
  - **Stake < 10%**: Treated as **FII**.
  - **Stake > 10%**: Treated as **FDI**.
- FIIs can invest in both primary and secondary markets, including shares, debentures, and warrants of listed or unlisted companies.

subject: Economics
content:
# Participatory Notes

- Instruments issued by **registered foreign institutional investors**.
- Targeted at overseas investors who are **not registered with SEBI** but wish to invest in Indian stock markets.
- Provide a mechanism for foreign investors to gain exposure to Indian securities without direct registration.

subject: Economics
content:
# Foreign Trade Policy (FTP) 2015‑20

- A five‑year framework aimed at **increasing exports of goods and services**, generating employment, and adding value.
- Aligns with the **Make in India** vision.
- Focuses on both manufacturing and services sectors, with emphasis on improving the **ease of doing business**.
- **Key Features**:
  - Position India as a significant participant in world trade by 2020.
  - **Merchandise Exports from India Scheme (MEIS)** to promote specific services for targeted markets.
  - **Reduce export obligation by 25%** to boost domestic manufacturing.
  - Support for industrial products in major markets with rates ranging from **2% to 3%**.
  - Branding initiatives to promote exports in sectors where India has traditional strengths.

subject: International Relations
content:
# International Organisation

- A forum of **co‑operation among sovereign states** based on a multilateral international agreement.
- Comprises a relatively stable range of participants.
- Examples include the **United Nations**, **World Bank**, **IMF**, and **World Trade Organization**.

subject: Economics
topic: Structure and Role of the IMF
content:
# International Monetary Fund (IMF)

- **Founding**: Established in 1944 during the Bretton Woods Conference and became operational in 1945.
- **India’s Role**: India is a *founder member* of the IMF.
- **Governance**:
  - The **Board of Governors** is the highest decision‑making body.
  - The **Finance Minister of India** serves as the *ex‑officio Governor* on this board.
  - The **RBI Governor** acts as the *alternate Governor* for India.
- **Primary Purpose**: To ensure the stability of the *International Monetary System*—the global network of exchange rates and international payments that enables cross‑border transactions.
- **Key Functions**:
  - Surveillance of member economies.
  - Provision of financial assistance.
  - Technical assistance and capacity building.

> **Fact**: The IMF’s decision‑making body is the Board of Governors, not the Executive Board.

---

## World Trade Organization (WTO)

- **Origin**: Replaced the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) under the Marrakesh Agreement in 1995.
- **Purpose**: Sets global rules for trade between nations, facilitating producers, exporters, and importers.
- **Key Agreements**:
  - **TRIPS** (Trade‑Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights) negotiated during the Uruguay Round (1986‑94).
  - **MFN** (Most‑Favoured‑Nation) status is accorded among members.
- **TRIPS Highlights**:
  - Covers *product* and *process* patents.
  - Developed countries had to enact patent laws in 1995; developing countries had a 10‑year grace period.
  - Patent protection period: 20 years.
  - India enacted the Patents (Amendment) Act in 2005 to comply.

---

## International Labour Organization (ILO)

- **Establishment**: Created in 1919 as part of the League of Nations, post‑World War I.
- **Mission**: Promote social reform at an international level.
- **Key Achievements**:
  - Eight‑hour working day.
  - Maternity protection.
  - Child labour laws.
  - Workplace safety and peaceful industrial relations.
- **Facts**:
  - Headquarters: Geneva.
  - Membership: 187 member states.
  - Director‑General (2012‑17): Guy Ryder.
  - Nobel Peace Prize: 1969.

---

## Asian Development Bank (ADB)

- **Founded**: 1966, headquartered in Manila, Philippines.
- **Purpose**: Foster economic growth and cooperation in Asia‑Pacific; accelerate development of developing countries.
- **Structure**: International partnership of 67 member countries.
- **India**: Founder member.

---

## Asia‑Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC)

- **Nature**: Inter‑governmental forum for economic growth, trade, and investment in the Asia‑Pacific.
- **Unique Feature**: Operates on *non‑binding commitments*, open dialogue, and equal respect for all participants.

---

## Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC)

- **Headquarters**: Vienna, Austria.
- **Established**: 1960.
- **Members**: 12 (as of the text).
- **Significance**:
  - Holds ~2/3 of world oil reserves.
  - Accounts for 33.3% of global oil production.
- **Objective**: Stabilise oil prices and safeguard collective interests.

---

## BRICS

- **Acronym**: Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa.
- **Purpose**: Economic cooperation and coordination among emerging economies.
- **Key Themes**:
  - Trade and investment.
  - Development of financial institutions.
  - Political coordination on global issues.

---

## Summary

These institutions collectively shape global economic governance, trade rules, labour standards, development finance, and energy markets. Understanding their structures, mandates, and key facts is essential for competitive exams like NDA, CDS, and AFCAT.

subject: Indian Economy
content:
# Reserve Bank of India (RBI) – Core Functions

1. **Issuing Currency** – RBI is the sole issuer of bank‑notes and coins in India.
2. **Regulating Money Supply** – Through open‑market operations, repo/ reverse repo, and the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR).
3. **Banker‑to‑Banker** – Acts as the lender of last resort to commercial banks.
4. **Managing Foreign Exchange** – Maintains the foreign‑exchange reserves and regulates the foreign‑exchange market.
5. **Regulator of the Banking System** – Issues licences, supervises banks, and enforces prudential norms.
6. **Government’s Banker** – Holds the government’s deposits, manages the public debt, and facilitates government borrowing.

**Functions NOT performed by RBI**
- Directly stabilising the exchange rate of the rupee (it influences but does not set the rate).
- Directly forwarding short‑term or long‑term loans to the Government (the Treasury does that).

---

> **Key Takeaway**: RBI’s mandate is to maintain monetary stability, not to act as a commercial lender or a direct stabiliser of the exchange rate.

subject: Economics
topic: General Agreement on Trade in Services (GATS)
content: The **General Agreement on Trade in Services (GATS)** is a treaty under the World Trade Organization (WTO) that entered into force in **January 1995**. It provides a framework for the liberalisation of trade in services among WTO members. All WTO members are automatically parties to GATS, making it a universal agreement for service‑sector trade.

subject: Economics
content: The **Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)** is a requirement that banks maintain a certain proportion of their net demand‑and‑time liabilities in the form of liquid cash, gold, or other securities. It is expressed as a percentage of total assets and is prescribed by the central bank to ensure liquidity and control credit expansion.

subject: Social Welfare
content:
The **Mid‑Day Meal Scheme** aims to improve school children’s nutrition. The mandated norms are:
- Minimum **450 kcal** per meal.
- Minimum **12 g of protein** per meal.
- Adequate quantities of micronutrients such as **iron, folic acid, and Vitamin‑A**.
Provision of essential fatty acids and medicines for common cold/diarrhoea is **not** part of the core norms.

subject: Economics
content:
The **Balance of Payments (BoP)** of a country records all economic transactions with the rest of the world. The three broad elements taken into account are:
1. **Current Account** – trade in goods & services, primary income, secondary income.
2. **Changes in Foreign Exchange Reserves** – movements in the central bank’s reserve holdings.
3. **Errors and Omissions** – statistical discrepancies that balance the accounts.
All three are required for a complete BoP statement.

subject: Economics
content: **Frictional unemployment** (also called **search unemployment**) occurs when workers are temporarily between jobs, searching for or transitioning to a new position that better matches their skills. It is a normal part of a dynamic labour market.

subject: Economics
content:
FDI involves **direct control** over production or business operations in the host country. Common modes are:
- **Acquisition** – buying an existing company (or a majority stake) in the target country.
- **Greenfield Investment** – expanding operations or setting up new facilities.
Investing only in **shares/stocks** for financial returns without control is classified as **Portfolio Investment**, not FDI.

subject: International Relations
topic: Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi‑Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation
content: The **Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi‑Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation (BIMSTEC)** links **ASEAN** and **SAARC** economies, fostering regional cooperation in trade, technology, and development. It was originally signed as the **Bangkok Agreement** in 1997 before being renamed BIMSTEC.

subject: Economics
content:
A **devaluation** of a country’s currency typically:
- **Promotes export trade** by making domestic goods cheaper abroad.
- **Encourages import substitution** as imported goods become relatively more expensive.
It does **not** expand import trade; rather, it aims to reduce import volumes.

subject: Economics
content:
To curb a **current‑account deficit**, the government may:
1. **Devalue the domestic currency** – makes exports competitive and imports costlier.
2. **Attract greater FDI and FII inflows** – brings in foreign capital, improving the financial account and indirectly supporting the current account.
Reducing export subsidies would generally **worsen** the deficit, as it makes exports less competitive.

subject: Banking
content:
# Main Functions of Exim Bank

The Export‑Import Bank of India (Exim Bank) is a specialized financial institution that:

- **Promotes exports** by providing credit facilities, insurance, and guarantees to exporters.
- **Curtails imports** by offering import credit and financing to importers.
- **Facilitates foreign exchange** transactions for Indian exporters and importers.
- **Supports infrastructure development** related to trade and logistics.

**Key point:** The primary mandate is to *promote exports and curtail imports*.

---

> **Quiz:** What is the main function of Exim Bank?
> 
> *Answer:* Promote exports and curtail imports.

subject: General Studies
content:
### Companies Bill (Amended 2012) – Salient Features
- **CSR Preference** – For spending the amount earmarked for Corporate Social Responsibility, the company shall give preference to local areas where it operates.
- **Punishment for False Inducement** – Penalty for falsely inducing a person to enter into an agreement with a bank or financial institution to obtain credit facilities.
- **Independent Directors** – ‘Independent directors’ are **excluded** while computing the “one‑third of retiring directors”.
- **Auditor Appointment Limit** – **There is a limit** on the number of companies in which a person may be appointed as auditor (the Bill **does not** remove this limit).  
> **Not a feature:** *There is no limit in respect of companies in which a person may be appointed as auditor* (this statement is **incorrect**).

subject: General Studies
content:
### Institutions asked to provide official estimates of black (unaccounted) money held by Indians (both in India and abroad)
1. **National Institute of Public Finance and Policy (NIPFP)**
2. **National Council of Applied Economic Research (NCAER)**
3. **National Institute of Financial Management (NIFM)**
All three institutions were approached by the Government of India for this purpose.

subject: General Studies
content:
### Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan → Swachh Bharat Mission
- **Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan** was merged into the **Swachh Bharat Mission (SBM)** in 2014.
- The merger aimed to consolidate all sanitation and cleanliness initiatives under a single flagship programme.
- **Key point:** The statement *"The Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan is restructured into the Swachh Bharat Mission"* is **correct**.

subject: General Studies
content:
### Two Sub‑Missions of Swachh Bharat Mission
- **SBM‑U (Urban)** – focuses on cities and towns.
- **SBM‑G (Rural)** – focuses on villages and gram panchayats.
- **Note:** The mission is **not** divided into *Union Territories* and *States*; that statement is **incorrect**.

subject: General Studies
content:
### Objectives of the National AYUSH Mission (approved by the Union Cabinet)
1. **Improvement of AYUSH education** – increase the number of upgraded AYUSH educational institutions.
2. **Better access to AYUSH services** – expand AYUSH hospitals & dispensaries, ensure availability of drugs and trained manpower.
3. **Sustained availability of quality raw material** – secure raw material supply for AYUSH systems of medicine.
All three points are official objectives of the Mission.

subject: General Studies
content:
### Words used with “Growth” in the 12th Five Year Plan
- The official title was **“Faster, More Inclusive, Sustainable Growth.”**
- Keywords: **faster**, **more inclusive**, **sustainable**.
- Hence the correct combination is **2, 3 and 4** (faster, more inclusive, sustainable).

subject: Economics
content:
### What does *demand* mean?
- **Demand** = *quantity demanded at a certain price during a particular period of time*.
- It is not merely desire, need, or the quantity demanded alone; price and time are essential components.

subject: Economics
content:
### Exceptional (Perfectly Elastic) Demand Curve
- **Shape:** Horizontal line.
- **Interpretation:** Consumers are willing to purchase any quantity at a given price, but none at any higher price.
- This is the graphical representation of *perfectly elastic* demand.

subject: General Studies
content:
### Core Tenets of Socialism
- **Historical Materialism** – material conditions shape history.
- **Dialectical Materialism** – change occurs through contradictions and their resolution.
- **Alienation & Class Struggle** – focus on the exploitation of the working class.
- **Not a tenet:** *Individual Freedom* (this is more associated with liberalism).

INTERNATIONAL AWARDS AND HONOURS

Nobel Prize

  • The Nobel prizes are given under the will of Alfred Bernhard Nobel, who died in 1896.
  • Nobel prizes are given each year in the six fields. The Nobel prizes for Peace, Physics, Chemistry, Medicine and Literature were started in 1901. The Nobel Prize for Economics was started in 1968.
  • The awards are presented in Stockholm in an annual ceremony on 10th December, except the Peace Prize, which awarded in OSLO, Norway.
  • The prize is not awarded posthumously however, if a person is awarded a prize and dies before receiving it, the prize may still be presented.

text:
• Ramon Magsaysay Award is an annual award given in memory of former Philippine President Ramon Magsaysay. Basic objective of award is to perpetuate the former President exemplary integrity in governance, courageous service to the people and ideal decision-making in democratic society.
  • Award is given by Ramon Magsaysay Award foundation to only Asian individuals. Since its inception in 1958, award were given in six different categories viz Government service, public service, community leadership, journalism, literature and creative communication arts, peace and international understanding and emergent leadership. But, from 2009 onwards awards are given for emergent leadership or in uncategorised category.
  • Vinoba Bhave was first Indian to receive Magsaysay Award.

- **Ramon Magsaysay Award** is an annual award given in memory of former Philippine President Ramon Magsaysay. Basic objective of award is to perpetuate the former President exemplary integrity in governance, courageous service to the people and ideal decision-making in democratic society.
- Award is given by Ramon Magsaysay Award foundation to only Asian individuals. Since its inception in 1958, award were given in six different categories *viz* Government service, public service, community leadership, journalism, literature and creative communication arts, peace and international understanding and emergent leadership. But, from 2009 onwards awards are given for emergent leadership or in uncategorised category.
- **Vinoba Bhave** was first Indian to receive Magsaysay Award.

subject: Defence
text:
Valour Awards: Param Vir Chakra, Maha Vir Chakra, and Vir Chakra are awarded for the highest degree of valour or self-sacrifice in the presence of enemy. These are awarded by the Government of India. All these awards were established on 26th January, 1950.

  • Param Vir Chakra (PVC): It is India's highest military decoration, awarded for the highest degree of valour or self-sacrifice in the presence of the enemy. The medal is a circular bronze disc of 1.375 inches in diameter and is held by a purple ribbon. In the centre of the medal, the emblem of India is made on a crafted circle, and outside the circle is a replica of vajra in four directions. On the reverse side, 'Param Vir Chakra' is written in Hindi and English, separated by two lotus flowers. Major Somnath Sharma was the first army man to receive this honour.
  • Maha Vir Chakra (MVC): It is the second highest military decoration in India and is awarded for acts of conspicuous gallantry in the presence of the enemy, whether on land, at sea, or in the air. It may be awarded posthumously. The words 'Maha Vir Chakra' are embossed in Hindi and English on the reverse with two lotus flowers in the middle. The decoration is worn on the left chest with a half-white and half-orange ribbon about 3.2 cm in width, the orange being near the left shoulder. Lt Col Dewan Ranjit Rai was the first army man to win the Mahavir Chakra.
  • Vir Chakra: It is an Indian gallantry award presented for acts of bravery in the battlefield. It is third in precedence in the war time gallantry awards and comes after the Param Vir Chakra and Maha Vir Chakra.

details.summary: Covers wartime gallantry awards of India established on 26th January 1950: Param Vir Chakra (highest, first recipient Major Somnath Sharma), Maha Vir Chakra (second highest, first recipient Lt Col Dewan Ranjit Rai), and Vir Chakra (third in precedence).

subject: Defence
topic: Peace Time Gallantry Awards and Other Military Awards
text:
Peace Time Gallantry Awards: These awards include Ashoka Chakra, Kirti Chakra, and Shaurya Chakra. topic: National Bravery Award and Literary & Cultural Awards
text:
National Bravery Award:

  • It was started in 1957 by the Indian Council for Child Welfare (ICCW) to recognise and honour children who have performed outstanding deeds of bravery and self-sacrifice.
  • Awards are given to children below the age of 18 years.
  • Awards are announced on 14th November (Children's Day) and presented by the Prime Minister on the eve of Republic Day. The awardees receive a medal, certificate, and cash.

Literary and Cultural Awards:

  • Bharatiya Jnanpith Award: An Indian literary award presented annually by the Bharatiya Jnanpith Trust to an author for their outstanding contribution towards literature. Instituted in 1961, the award is bestowed only on Indian writers who have been writing in Indian languages included in the Eighth Schedule to the Constitution of India and in English. As of 2015, the cash prize has been revised to ₹11 lakh with a bronze replica of Saraswati. G. Sankara Kurup was the first recipient in 1965.
  • Sahitya Akademi Awards: Started in 1954. These awards are conferred by the government to the most outstanding literary work published in languages recognised by the Constitution, as well as English and Rajasthani.
  • Saraswati Samman Award: An annual award for outstanding prose or poetry literary works in any of the 22 Indian languages listed in Schedule Eight of the Constitution of India. Instituted in 1991 by the K.K. Birla Foundation. It consists of ₹10 lakh, a citation, and a plaque. The first recipient was Harivansh Rai Bachchan.
  • Moorti Devi Award: An annual literary award presented by the Bharatiya Jnanpith Trust/organisation for work that emphasises Indian philosophy and culture. The prize includes an amount of ₹4 lakh, a plaque/statue of Saraswati, and a shawl. C.K. Nagaraja Rao was the first recipient in 1983 for his Kannada language work Pattamahadevi Shantala Devi.

text:
Rajiv Gandhi Khel Ratna Award It is India's highest honour given for achievement in sports. It is awarded by Government of India, since 1991-92.

It recognises the spectacular and most outstanding performance by a sports person over a period of 4 years immediately preceding the year during which award is given.

First Khel Ratna award was given to Viswanathan Anand in 1991. In 2016, the award was given jointly to PV Sindhu, Sakshi Malik, Dipu Karmakar and Jitu Rai.

Arjuna Award Instituted in 1961. Carries a cash prize of ₹ 500000, a bronze statuette of Arjuna and a scroll. The Arjuna awards are given by the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports, Government of India to recognise outstanding achievement in National sports.

Dronacharya Award Dronacharya Award is an award presented by the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports, Government of India for excellence in sports coaching. The award comprises a bronze statuette of Dronacharya, a scroll of honour and a cash component of ₹ 700000 (seven lakhs). The award was instituted in 1985. BI Fernandez (Cuba) is the first foreign coach to be awarded Dronacharya Award.

Dhyanchand Award Instituted in 2002, in honour of famous hockey player, Major Dhyanchand. Carries a cash prize of ₹ 500000. Dhyanchand Award is India's highest award for lifetime achievement in sports and games, given by the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports.

Rashtriya Khel Protsahan Puruskar It was introduced in 2009 to promote involvement of corporates and institutional boards in sports.

Maulana Abul Kalam Azad (MAKA) Trophy Instituted in 1956-57. It is given to top performer of inter-state university tournament. It is a rolling trophy.

Film Awards

National Film Awards

Dada Saheb Phalke Award

Filmfare Awards

The filmfare awards are presented annually by the Times Group to honour both artistic and technical excellence of professionals in the Hindi language film industry of India. The filmfare ceremony is one of the oldest film events in India. The awards were first introduced in 1954. The 61st Filmfare awards were held on 15th January, 2016 at the Prince Ahuja Studio in Mumbai.

subject: Science & Technology
topic: Space Programme of India and Major Missions
text:
Genesis and Institutional Framework:

  • The Indian Space Programme was launched in 1962, when the Indian National Committee for Space Research (INCOSPAR) was formed.
  • The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) was established in 1969, followed by the establishment of the Space Commission and the Department of Space in 1972.
  • ISRO is responsible for the planning, execution, and management of space research activities and space application programmes. Headquarters of ISRO is located at Bengaluru.
  • India's first Satellite Communication Earth Station was established at Arvi near Pune.
  • The first Indian satellite, Aryabhatta, was launched on 19th April, 1975 from Baikonur (erstwhile USSR).
  • The first Indian Remote Sensing Satellite was launched on 17th March, 1988.
  • The first Indian Communication Satellite, APPLE, was launched on 19th June, 1981 from Kourou in French Guiana. It was the first Indian satellite placed in geostationary orbit.

Some of the Important Space Programmes of India:

  • Cartosat-2c: Earth observatory satellite launched by PSLV into Sun-synchronous orbit on 22nd June, 2016. Primary objective is to design and develop a highly agile satellite with a spatial resolution of 1.0 m in panchromatic band to meet user demand for cartographic application at cadastral level, urban planning, etc.
  • GSAT-15: Communication satellite launched on 10th November, 2015 from Kourou using Rocket Ariane into Geostationary orbit. It carried 24 Ku-band transponders (noted as 24 km bond) and 2 GAGAN navigational payloads.
  • Astrosat: Launched on 28th September, 2015 using PSLV-XL into equatorial orbit. It is a multiwavelength space observatory designed to study X-ray, visible, near UV, far UV, and hard X-ray radiations.
  • Indian Regional Navigational Satellite System (IRNSS) / NAVIC: Comprises a constellation of 7 satellites (IRNSS-1A to IRNSS-1G), all of which have been launched into Geo-stationary orbit and Geo-synchronous transfer orbit using Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV). It provides positioning services over India and up to 1500 km beyond its borders, offering Standard Positioning Service (SPS) for all users and Restricted Service (RS) for authorized users.
  • Mars Orbiter Mission (MOM) / Mangalyaan: Launched on 5th November, 2013 using PSLV-XL C25; entered Mars orbit on 24th September, 2014. Primary aims were technological demonstration of interplanetary mission capabilities and scientific study of Martian surface features, morphology, mineralogy, and atmosphere.
  • Chandrayaan-1: Launched in 2008 using PSLV-XL C11 to develop technology for lunar study, chemical mapping, and detection of water-ice on the Moon. (Chandrayaan-II planned for launch in 2017).
  • GAGAN (GPS Aided GEO Augmented Navigation): A regional Satellite-Based Augmentation System (SBAS) jointly developed to improve GNSS receiver accuracy through reference signals. Implemented by the Airports Authority of India (AAI) and ISRO, it comprises 15 Indian Reference Stations, 3 Indian Navigation Land Uplink Stations, and 3 Indian Mission Control Centers. Provides 3-meter positioning accuracy in Indian airspace, assisting navigation and difficult landings at airports such as Mangalore and Leh.

- **Cartosat-2c:** Earth observatory satellite launched by **PSLV** into Sun-synchronous orbit on **22nd June, 2016**. Primary objective is to design and develop a highly agile satellite with a spatial resolution of 1.0 m in panchromatic band to meet user demand for cartographic application at cadastral level, urban planning, etc.
- **GSAT-15:** Communication satellite launched on **10th November, 2015** from Kourou using Rocket Ariane into Geostationary orbit. It carried 24 Ku-band transponders (noted as 24 km bond) and 2 GAGAN navigational payloads.
- **Astrosat:** Launched on **28th September, 2015** using PSLV-XL into equatorial orbit. It is a multiwavelength space observatory designed to study X-ray, visible, near UV, far UV, and hard X-ray radiations.
- **Indian Regional Navigational Satellite System (IRNSS) / NAVIC:** Comprises a constellation of 7 satellites (IRNSS-1A to IRNSS-1G), all of which have been launched into Geo-stationary orbit and Geo-synchronous transfer orbit using Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV). It provides positioning services over India and up to 1500 km beyond its borders, offering Standard Positioning Service (SPS) for all users and Restricted Service (RS) for authorized users.
- **Mars Orbiter Mission (MOM) / Mangalyaan:** Launched on **5th November, 2013** using **PSLV-XL C25**; entered Mars orbit on **24th September, 2014**. Primary aims were technological demonstration of interplanetary mission capabilities and scientific study of Martian surface features, morphology, mineralogy, and atmosphere.
- **Chandrayaan-1:** Launched in **2008** using **PSLV-XL C11** to develop technology for lunar study, chemical mapping, and detection of water-ice on the Moon. (Chandrayaan-II planned for launch in 2017).
- **GAGAN (GPS Aided GEO Augmented Navigation):** A regional Satellite-Based Augmentation System (SBAS) jointly developed to improve GNSS receiver accuracy through reference signals. Implemented by the Airports Authority of India (AAI) and ISRO, it comprises 15 Indian Reference Stations, 3 Indian Navigation Land Uplink Stations, and 3 Indian Mission Control Centers. Provides 3-meter positioning accuracy in Indian airspace, assisting navigation and difficult landings at airports such as Mangalore and Leh.

### Key Exam Facts
- **Summary:** Overview of India's space journey beginning with INCOSPAR in 1962, the foundation of ISRO in 1969, landmark historical satellites (Aryabhatta, APPLE), and milestone missions including Cartosat-2c, GSAT-15, Astrosat, IRNSS (NAVIC), Mars Orbiter Mission, Chandrayaan-1, and GAGAN.

DivisionIt usually consists of 15000 combat troops and 8000 support elements. Each division is composed of several Brigades.
BrigadeA Brigade generally consists of around 3000 combat troops with supporting elements. An Infantry Brigade usually has 3 Infantry Battalions along with various Support Arms and Services.

National Cadet Corps (NCC)

It was established in 1948. Its main objective is to stimulate interest among the youth in the defence of the country in order to build up a reserve manpower to expand armed forces.

Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF)

It was set-up in 1939. Its main objective is to assist the State/Union Territory Police in maintenance of law and order. The 88th Battalion of CRPF, known as 'Mahila Battalion' paramilitary force comprising entirely of women.

Home Guard

It was established in 1946, to assist the police in maintaining security, to help defence forces and to help local authorities.

Coast Guard

It was set-up in 1978. Its objective is to protect the maritime and other national interests in the maritime zones of India.

Intelligence Bureau (IB)

It was set-up in 1920. Its objective is to collect secret information relating to country's security. It was originally set-up as Central Special Branch (CSB) in 1887 and renamed IB in 1920.

Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI)

It was established in 1953. Its objective is to investigate cases of misconduct by public servants, cases of cheating, embezzlement, fraud also work on International crime cases in collaboration with INTERPOL.

National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB)

It was established in 1986. Its objective is to collect crime statistics at the national level.

Rapid Action Force (RAF)

It was established in 1991, wing of CRPF. It deals with riot, crowd control, relief operation.

text:
Indian Missiles

Agni (I-VI) Agni series of missile is a ballistic missile having 6 missiles in it with a range varying from 700-10000 km. Agni I-V are in operational stage while VI is in testing and developmental stage.

Prithvi Prithvi is a tactical surface to surface Short-Range Ballistic Missile (SRBM). It has three versions - Prithvi I, II, III with range of 150-350 km.

Dhanush (SS-350) Dhanush is reportedly a naval version of Prithvi-III, which can be launched from ships. It can carry 500 kg of conventional or nuclear warhead.

Astra Astra is Beyond Visual Range (BVR) air to air missile. Astra is designed to be capable of engaging targets at varying range and altitudes allowing for both short-range targets (upto 20 km) and long range targets (upto 80 km) using alternative propulsion modes.

Akash Akash is a medium range surface to air missile. The missile can target aircraft upto 30 km away, at altitudes of 18000 m. Akash can be fired from both tracked and wheeled platforms. Akash is said to be capable of both conventional and nuclear warheads, with a reported payload of 60 kg.

**Prithvi** Prithvi is a tactical surface to surface Short-Range Ballistic Missile (SRBM). It has three versions - Prithvi I, II, III with range of 150-350 km.

**Dhanush (SS-350)** Dhanush is reportedly a naval version of Prithvi-III, which can be launched from ships. It can carry 500 kg of conventional or nuclear warhead.

**Astra** Astra is Beyond Visual Range (BVR) air to air missile. Astra is designed to be capable of engaging targets at varying range and altitudes allowing for both short-range targets (upto 20 km) and long range targets (upto 80 km) using alternative propulsion modes.

**Akash** Akash is a medium range surface to air missile. The missile can target aircraft upto 30 km away, at altitudes of 18000 m. Akash can be fired from both tracked and wheeled platforms. Akash is said to be capable of both conventional and nuclear warheads, with a reported payload of 60 kg.

subject: International Relations
text:
There are six principle organs of the United Nations, which are as follows

1. General Assembly

  • Headquarters of General Assembly is at New York. General Assembly consists of all member states of the UN. Each member nation can send five delegates, but each nation has only one vote.
  • The General Assembly meets at least once in a year and the session commences on the first Tuesday of September. It appoints the Secretary General of UN Secretariat on the recommendation of the Security Council.
  • The presidency of the Assembly rotates each year among the five geographical groups of the countries viz Asia, African, Latin America, East European and West European and other states.

- The General Assembly meets at least once in a year and the session commences on the first Tuesday of September. It appoints the Secretary General of UN Secretariat on the recommendation of the Security Council.
- The presidency of the Assembly rotates each year among the five geographical groups of the countries viz Asia, African, Latin America, East European and West European and other states.

subject: Indian Polity
text:
The main aim of Security Council is the maintenance of the international peace and security. The Security Council originally consisted of eleven members, but increases to fifteen in 1965.

Security Council comprises of five permanent members namely China, UK, Russia, France and USA and 10 non-permanent members, elected for a term of 2 years by a two-third majority of the General Assembly, five non-permanent members retire every year. Retiring members cannot be re-elected immediately.

Permanent member have veto power, which can be cast against any decision supported by the majority members. The headquarters of Security Council is at New York (US).

text:
The United Nations Trusteeship Council was established to help ensure that trust territories were administered in the best interests of their inhabitants and of international peace and security.

Trusteeship Council was formed in 1945. The headquarters of Trusteeship Council was at New York (US). The Trusteeship Council suspended operation on 1st November, 1994. With the independence of Palau, the last remaining United Nations trust territory, on 1st October, 1994.

subject: Indian Polity
text:
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) is the primary judicial organ of the United Nations. The ICJ was established in 1945. It consists of 15 judges. The judges of the court are elected by the General Assembly along with the Security Council for a 9 years term.

Its main functions are to settle legal disputes submitted to it by states and to provide advisory opinions on legal questions submitted to it by only authorised international organs, agencies and the UN General Assembly. The headquarters of ICJ is at Hague (Netherland).

subject: Indian Polity
text:
The United Nations Secretariat is one of the principle organs of the United Nations, an inter governmental organisation charged with aiding/helping states to collectively maintain international peace and security. It serves as a forum for member-states to discuss and resolve pressing issues in the international field through primarily diplomatic resources.

The Secretariat is composed of a Secretary General, assisted by a staff of international civil servants worldwide. The Secretary General is appointed by the General Assembly upon the recommendation of the Security Council.

The Secretary General of the UN is elected for 5 years and eligible for re-election, although, none so far has held office for more than two terms.

The present Secretary General of the UN is Antonio Guterres.

## Sentence Ordering Technique

- **Read all sentences first** to get the overall theme.
- **Identify the introductory sentence** (often labelled S1) – it sets the context.
- **Look for linking words** (e.g., *first*, *then*, *however*, *on the other hand*) that indicate sequence.
- **Group related ideas** – sentences that discuss the same sub‑topic usually stay together.
- **Check logical flow** – cause → effect, problem → solution, general → specific, etc.
- **Validate the final order** by rereading the paragraph to ensure it reads smoothly.

### Common Pitfalls
- Assuming the longest sentence is the conclusion.
- Ignoring pronoun references that tie sentences together.
- Over‑relying on alphabetical order of options.

### Example Application
The passages given in questions 44‑48 illustrate how the above steps lead to the correct sequences (e.g., **PSRQ** for the hormone paragraph).

subject: Biology
content:
## Hormonal Control of Blood Glucose

- **Insulin**
  - Secreted by β‑cells of the pancreas in response to a rapid rise in blood glucose.
  - Promotes uptake of glucose by muscle and adipose tissue.
  - Stimulates glycogen synthesis in liver and inhibits gluconeogenesis.
  - Lowers blood glucose level – a **homeostatic** function.

- **Glucagon**
  - Secreted by α‑cells of the pancreas when blood glucose falls.
  - Stimulates glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in the liver.
  - Raises blood glucose level.

- **Combined Action**
  - The two hormones work antagonistically to keep glucose within a narrow physiological range (≈70‑110 mg/dL).
  - This regulation exemplifies the endocrine system’s role in maintaining internal balance (homeostasis).

subject: Ecology
content:
## Interdependence in Terrestrial Ecosystems

- **Earthworms**
  - Create burrows that improve soil aeration and water infiltration.
  - Their casts enrich the soil with organic matter, enhancing plant growth.

- **Plants**
  - Benefit from improved soil structure and nutrients, leading to higher productivity.

- **Rabbits**
  - Feed on the vegetation; their population size is linked to plant availability.
  - Rabbits host fleas that can transmit *myxomatosis* virus, influencing rabbit mortality.

- **Food‑Web Cascade**
  - Changes in earthworm activity → soil quality → plant growth → rabbit food supply → rabbit population → flea‑borne disease dynamics.

- **Human Impact**
  - Over‑exploitation of resources can disrupt these links, leading to ecological imbalance.

subject: Ecology
content:
## Components of a Healthy Water Ecosystem

1. **Primary Sources** – Rain and snowfall provide ~99 % of freshwater.
2. **Catchment Areas** – Thick forests act as natural catchments, slowing runoff and allowing infiltration.
3. **Sub‑soil Recharge** – Trees transfer rainwater to deeper soil layers, sustaining water availability for months.
4. **Monsoon Dynamics** – 30‑35 intense downpours occur over four months; the challenge is to store this water for the remaining 365 days.
5. **Human Interference** – Deforestation and poor land‑use practices undermine the natural links, leading to water scarcity and flash floods.

**Key Takeaway:** Maintaining forest cover and protecting catchment zones are essential for long‑term water security.

subject: Political Science
content:
## Understanding Politics through Aristotle’s Lens

- **Politics as a Social Activity** – For Aristotle, politics is the collective pursuit of the *good society*.
- **Sources of Disagreement**
  - *How* decisions should be made.
  - *Who* should have a say.
  - *Distribution* of resources and power.
- **Contemporary Dimensions**
  - Conflict vs. cooperation.
  - Questions of justice, equity, and resource allocation.
- **Logical Flow of Ideas**
  1. People *disagree* (S1).
  2. Disagreements cover *decision‑making* and *resource distribution* (R & S).
  3. Collective discussion leads to *political activity* aimed at a *good society* (P).

**Implication:** Recognising the inherent disagreements helps in structuring democratic deliberations.

## How Regular Exercise Improves the Body

- **Strength & Flexibility** – Muscle conditioning enhances power; stretching improves joint range of motion, reducing injury risk.
- **Endurance** – Cardiovascular adaptations increase oxygen delivery, allowing prolonged activity.
- **Energy Expenditure** – Exercise burns calories, preventing excess fat accumulation.

  1. **Strength Training** – Increases muscle mass.
  2. **Aerobic Activities** – Boosts cardiovascular endurance.
  3. **Flexibility Work** – Enhances mobility.
- **Overall Impact** – Regular activity makes organ systems more efficient, supporting health and longevity.

This Writ is applicable to the public offices only and not to Private Offices.

Perfect competition is a market form in which there are a large number of firms, homogenous product, infinite elasticity of demand for an individual firm and no control over price rise. Perfect competition provides both allocative efficiency and productive efficiency.

In oligopoly, small group of large sellers (oligopolists) dominate the market. Monopolistic competition occurs when an industry has many firms offering products that are similar but not identical. topic: Individual Privileges of Member of Parliament
text:
Individual Privileges of Member of Parliament include:

  • Immunity from arrest during the session of Parliament. This privilege is available in civil case only.
  • A MP may refuse to appear in court or present any evidence, during a Parliamentary session.
  • No member is liable to any proceeding in any given court for anything said or any vote by him/her in the Parliament or its committees.

Privileges would not be fettered by the Article-191(a) of the Constitution. And it must be read subject to the Article 20-22 and Article-32 of the Constitution. Privileges does not cover freedom of speech in his/her private or personal capacity.

text:
The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 added words 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity' in the Preamble of the Constitution of India. This Amendment is termed as Mini Constitution. Other Provision of this Amendment:

  • Added Fundamental Duties by the citizens (new Part IV A).
  • Made the President bound by the advice of the cabinet.
  • Provided for administrative tribunals and tribunals for other matters (Added Part-XIV A).
  • Frozen the seats in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies on the basis of 1971 census till 2001-Population Controlling Measure.
  • Made the constitutional amendments beyond judicial scrutiny.
  • Curtailed the power of judicial review and writ jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and High Courts.
  • Raised the tenure of Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies from 5 to 6 years.

subject: History
content:
### Key Idea
- **Statement:** *No civilisation can arise without first passing through a stage of agriculture.*
- **Reasoning:** When agricultural productivity improves, a surplus of food is created. This surplus means **not everyone needs to be involved in food production**, freeing a portion of the population for other activities.
- **Implication:** The existence of a reliable food surplus is the **foundation** on which complex societies (cities, trade, specialised crafts, etc.) are built.

---
**Reference from passage:**
> "...no civilisation can become one without passing through the stage of agriculture. This is because at some stage in the development of agriculture, as productivity improves, not all people would need to be engaged in producing or procuring food."

subject: History
content:
### How surplus labour fuels new activities
1. **Surplus generation** – When agricultural output exceeds the basic subsistence needs, **extra food** can support additional people.
2. **Free time** – Those extra people have **time** that can be directed toward:
   - Construction of walls, monuments, and public infrastructure (e.g., irrigation canals)
   - Manufacture of tools, weapons, jewellery
   - Long‑distance trade and commerce
   - Artistic and cultural production
   - Invention and scientific inquiry
   - Record‑keeping and administration
3. **Feedback loop** – New infrastructure (like irrigation) can **further raise agricultural productivity**, creating an ever‑larger surplus.

---
**Reference from passage:**
> "A significant number of people could be freed up to pursue other activities such as building walls or monuments… creating new public infrastructure such as irrigation canals that further improve the productivity of agriculture…"

subject: History
subchapter: Societal mechanisms for channeling surplus labour
content:
### Why people were persuaded to take up non‑agricultural work
- **Ideologies** – Shared belief systems that gave meaning to new occupations (e.g., religious duties, civic pride).
- **Hierarchies** – Social stratification that assigned specific roles to different groups.
- **Power structures** – Rulers or elites who could **coerce** or **incentivise** large numbers of people to work on state‑directed projects, often with **little personal reward**.

---
**Reference from passage:**
> "In the ancient world, this often involved creating new ideologies and new hierarchies or power structures to coerce or otherwise convince large groups of people to devote their time to the new tasks for very little reward."

subject: Biology
text: Smallpox is not an epidemic disease. An epidemic is the rapid spread of an infectious disease to a large number of people in a given population within a short period of time, usually two weeks or less. Malaria and elephantiasis both are vector (Mosquito) borne diseases, thus during favourable conditions like flood or heavy rain, the sudden increase in numbers of mosquito will also cause outbreak of these diseases. Similarly, cholera is also an epidemic disease as it is water borne disease, thus presence of bacteria Vibrio cholerae in local water source like pond or well will cause outbreak of cholera in every member of locality in a short period of time. A pandemic is an epidemic of world-wide proportions.

details.summary: Explanation of epidemic diseases and examples.

content:
Smallpox is not an epidemic disease. An epidemic is the rapid spread of an infectious disease to a large number of people in a given population within a short period of time, usually two weeks or less. Malaria and elephantiasis both are vector (Mosquito) borne diseases, thus during favourable conditions like flood or heavy rain, the sudden increase in numbers of mosquito will also cause outbreak of these diseases. Similarly, cholera is also an epidemic disease as it is water borne disease, thus presence of bacteria Vibrio cholerae in local water source like pond or well will cause outbreak of cholera in every member of locality in a short period of time. A pandemic is an epidemic of world-wide proportions.

### Key Exam Facts

subject: Biology
content:
### Sequence of Organs in Urine Flow
1. **Kidney** – filtration of blood to form urine.
2. **Ureter** – two tubes (one per kidney) that convey urine to the bladder.
3. **Urinary Bladder** – stores urine until micturition.
4. **Urethra** – conduit through which urine is expelled from the body.

**Correct order**: Kidney → Ureter → Urinary Bladder → Urethra.

content:
### Pituitary Gland
- **Uniqueness**: The only major endocrine gland **not found in pairs** in humans.
- **Size & Appearance**: Roughly oval, reddish‑grey, about the size of a pea seed.
- **Location**: Sits in the **sella turcica**, a small bony cavity of the brain.
- **Function**: Known as the **master gland**; it directly or indirectly controls almost all other endocrine glands.
- **Other Paired Glands**: Adrenal glands, testes, ovaries.

subject: Biology
content:
### Mitochondrion
- **Semi‑autonomous organelle** that possesses its own DNA and ribosomes.
- **Discovery**: First observed by **Kölliker in 1850**.
- **Genetic Material**: Contains circular DNA, enabling it to synthesize some of its own proteins.
- **Reproduction**: New mitochondria arise by growth and division of pre‑existing mitochondria (no de‑novo synthesis).
- **Other Organelles**: Golgi apparatus, lysosome, endoplasmic reticulum – **do not contain DNA**.

text:
According to the tri-cellular model of atmospheric circulation, circulation takes place in three cells:

  • Hadley Cell: Air rises at the equator (0°) and descends near sub-tropical high-pressure zones (30° N and S).
  • Ferrel Cell: Air descends at sub-tropical high-pressure zones (30° N and S) and ascends at sub-polar low-pressure zones (60° N and S).
  • Polar Cell: Air rises in sub-polar low-pressure zones (60° N and S) and descends at the poles in both hemispheres.

details.summary: Detailed explanation of the three atmospheric circulation cells: Hadley, Ferrel, and Polar, including their rising and descending air locations.

content:
According to the tri-cellular model of atmospheric circulation, circulation takes place in three cells:

- **Hadley Cell:** Air rises at the equator (0°) and descends near sub-tropical high-pressure zones (30° N and S).
- **Ferrel Cell:** Air descends at sub-tropical high-pressure zones (30° N and S) and ascends at sub-polar low-pressure zones (60° N and S).
- **Polar Cell:** Air rises in sub-polar low-pressure zones (60° N and S) and descends at the poles in both hemispheres.

The technology of store tools. For instance, during palaeolithic age, tools were made of quartzite and sharpened by chipping technique. Mesolithic age was characterised by use of ‘microlith’ store tools; while during neolithic age tools were more specialised (like knife, dagger, etc.) and were completely or partially polished.

There was large regional variations in the type and technology of tools in different periods. For example, in the foothills of Himalayas, tools were majorly made up of pebbles, while in central India basaltic rocks were main type of stone used in making tools.

Stone Age in India did not evolve uniformly in a unilinear fashion over the sub-continent. For instance, stone tools in Shivalk hills date back to about 2 to 1.2 million years, while in Bori (Maharashtra) they data back to 1 million years back.

subject: Indian Polity
text:
108. The provisions of the Constitution of India pertaining to the institution of Panchayat do not apply to which one of the following States?

  • (a) Meghalaya
  • (b) Tripura
  • (c) Assam
  • (d) Goa

(a) Panchayati Raj is the basic unit of administration in a system of governance. The Constitutional (73rd Amendment) Act, 1992 came into force in India on 24th April, 1993 to provide constitutional status to the Panchayati Raj institutions. This act was extended to the Panchayats in the tribal areas of eight states, namely Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha and Rajasthan from 24th December, 1996. Currently, the Panchayati Raj system exists in all States of India except Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram and in all Union Territories except Delhi and Jammu and Kashmir.

  • (a) Volga
  • (b) Dnieper
  • (c) Don
  • (d) Danube

(a) Volga river does not drain into Black sea. Black sea is a body of water and marginal sea of the Atlantic Ocean between Eastern Europe, the Car casus and Western Asia. Many rivers drain into it such as the Danube, Dnieper, Southern Bug, Dniester, Don and the Rioni. The Volga river is the longest river in Europe. It is also Europe's largest river in terms of discharge and drainage basin. The Volga river flows through Central Russia and drains into Caspian sea.

text:
Perfect competition: Perfect competition is the situation prevailing in a market in which buyers and sellers are so numerous and well informed that all elements of monopoly are absent and the market price of a commodity is beyond the control of individual buyers and sellers.

Monopoly: A monopoly is a specific type of economic market structure. A monopoly exists when a specific person or enterprise is the only supplier of a particular good. As a result, monopolies are characterised by a lack of competition within the market producing a good or service.

Monopolistic competition: Monopolistic competition is a type of imperfect competition such that many producers sell products that are differentiated from one another (e.g., by branding or quality) and hence are not perfect substitutes.

Oligopoly: An oligopoly is a market form wherein a market or industry is dominated by a small number of large sellers.
