text:
Conversion: To convert speed of an object from m/s to km/h, multiply it by 18/5. e.g., 5 m/s = 5 * 18/5 km/h = 18 km/h.

Average Speed: Defined as total distance travelled divided by total time taken.

Relative Speed: The speed of an object with respect to other. If two bodies move with speeds x km/h and y km/h:

  • If moving in opposite directions: (x + y) km/h
  • If moving in same direction: (x - y) km/h

Important Rules:

  • Rule 1: If A travels with speed x km/h for t1 h and with speed y km/h for t2 h, then average speed = (x*t1 + y*t2) / (t1 + t2).
  • Rule 2: If a man/vehicle covers two equal distances with speed x km/h and y km/h respectively, average speed = 2xy / (x + y).
  • Rule 3: If a man changes his speed to (x/y) of his usual speed and gets late by t min, usual time = (t * x) / (y - x). If he reaches early by t min, usual time = (t * x) / (y - x).

text:
Definitions:

  • Still water: If the speed of water is zero, then water is considered to be still water.
  • Stream water: If the water of a river is moving at a certain speed, then it is called stream water.
  • Downstream motion: In water, the direction along the stream is called downstream.
  • Upstream motion: In water, the direction against the stream is called upstream.

Rules:

  • Rule 9: If the speed of a boat in still water = x km/h and speed of stream = y km/h, then:
    • (i) Speed of boat downstream = (x + y) km/h
    • (ii) Speed of boat upstream = (x - y) km/h
  • Rule 10: Let the speed of boat in downstream = u km/h and speed of boat in upstream = v km/h, then:
    • (i) Speed of boat in still water = 1/2(u + v) km/h
    • (ii) Speed of stream (current) = 1/2(u - v) km/h
formulas: Speed of boat downstream = x + y
Speed of boat upstream = x - y
Speed of boat in still water = 1/2(u + v)

Usually (2-4) questions have been asked from this chapter. Generally questions are asked on Man-hours formulae, total wages paid for a work, number of days to complete a certain work and pipes and cisterns.

In this chapter, we will study the relationship among the quantity of work given, wages given, stipulated time, number of persons etc.

IMPORTANT RULES AND FORMULAE

  • Rule 1: If a person can do a piece of work in 'n' days, then he will do 1/n of the work in one day and if a person can do 1/n th of work in one day, then he will complete the work in n days. e.g. If Raj can do a piece of work in 20 days, then he will do 1/20th of the work in one day.
  • Note: In the problems related to time and work it is always considered that a man/woman works at uniform rate.
  • Rule 2: A and B can do a piece of work in x days and y days, respectively. Then, time taken by (A + B) to complete the work is equal to reciprocal of (A + B)'s one day's work, i.e. xy / (x + y).
  • Rule 3: If A and B can complete a work in x days and A alone can finish that work in y days, then number of days required to complete the work by B = xy / (y - x) days.
  • Rule 4: If A and B can do a piece of work in x days, B and C can do same work in y days, C and A can do same work in z days. Then, they will complete the same work in 2xyz / (xy + yz + zx) days by working together.

details.summary: Introduction to Time and Work chapter covering basic definitions, uniform rate assumption, and four fundamental rules for calculating work completion time for individuals and groups.

text:
If A and B can do a piece of work in x days and y days, respectively and they received k as wages by working together, then share of A = (yk / (x+y)) and share of B = (xk / (x+y)). Wages are directly proportional to the work done and indirectly proportional to the time taken by the individual.

Some Other Formulae

  • If A and B can do a piece of work in x and y days, respectively. A and B started working together but A left the work t days before completing the work, then time taken to complete the work will be ((x+t)y / (x+y)) days.
  • If A and B do a piece of work in x and y days, respectively. Both begin together but after some days, A leaves the work and the remaining work is completed by B in x days. Then, the time after which A left is given by T = ((b-x)a / a+b).
  • If A and B can do a piece of work in x and y days, respectively. They start working together and after t days B leaves the work, then time taken to finish the whole work will be (x(y-t) / y) days.

Problems on pipes and cisterns are based on the basic concept of time and work. Pipes are connected to a tank or cistern and are used to fill or empty the tank or cistern.

Rule 9

If there are two pipes A and B takes 'a' and 'b' h respectively to fill a tanker, then the two pipes together fill (1/a + 1/b) part of the tank in 1h and time taken to fill the tank will be (ab / a+b) h. If a pipe fills a tank in 'a' h, then in 1 h only 1/a of the tank is filled.

Rule 10

(i) If a pipe can fill a tank in 'a' h and another can fill the tank in 'b' h but a third pipe empties the filled tank in 'c' h, then in one hour (1/a + 1/b - 1/c) part of the tank will be filled (when all the three pipes are open) and time taken to fill the tank will be (abc / bc + ac - ab) h.

(ii) If a pipe can fill a tank in a1 h and another pipe can empty the filled tank in a2 h, then in one hour (1/a1 - 1/a2) part of the tank will be filled. (when both pipes are open) and time taken to fill the tank will be (a1 a2 / a2 - a1) h.

Problems on pipes and cisterns are based on the basic concept of time and work. Pipes are connected to a tank or cistern and are used to fill or empty the tank or cistern.

### Rule 9

If there are two pipes A and B takes 'a' and 'b' h respectively to fill a tanker, then the two pipes together fill (1/a + 1/b) part of the tank in 1h and time taken to fill the tank will be (ab / a+b) h. If a pipe fills a tank in 'a' h, then in 1 h only 1/a of the tank is filled.

### Rule 10

(i) If a pipe can fill a tank in 'a' h and another can fill the tank in 'b' h but a third pipe empties the filled tank in 'c' h, then in one hour (1/a + 1/b - 1/c) part of the tank will be filled (when all the three pipes are open) and time taken to fill the tank will be (abc / bc + ac - ab) h.

(ii) If a pipe can fill a tank in a1 h and another pipe can empty the filled tank in a2 h, then in one hour (1/a1 - 1/a2) part of the tank will be filled. (when both pipes are open) and time taken to fill the tank will be (a1 a2 / a2 - a1) h.

### Key Formulas
- Time taken = (ab / (a+b))
- Part filled in 1h = (1/a + 1/b - 1/c)

- Part filled in 1h = (1/a1 - 1/a2)

### Rule for Doubling/Multiplying at Compound Interest
If a sum doubles in $t$ years at a certain compound interest rate, it will become $2^n$ times the original sum in $n \times t$ years.

**Example Logic:**
- If amount doubles in 15 years ($2^1$), it becomes $2^3 = 8$ times in $3 \times 15 = 45$ years.
- If amount doubles in 5 years, it becomes $2^4 = 16$ times in $4 \times 5 = 20$ years.

When a borrower makes annual payments against a compound interest loan:
1. Calculate the interest accrued on the outstanding principal for the year.
2. Add the interest to the principal to get the total amount due.
3. Subtract the annual payment from the total amount due to get the new outstanding principal for the next year.
4. Repeat for each year.

**Formula:**
$P_{new} = (P_{old} \times (1 + \frac{r}{100})) - \text{Payment}$

For any principal $P$, rate $r$, and time $t > 1$ year:
- **CI > SI**: Compound interest is always greater than simple interest for the same principal, rate, and time period (greater than 1 year).
- **Reason**: CI is calculated on the principal plus accumulated interest, whereas SI is calculated only on the original principal.

### Finding Rate from Difference between CI and SI
For 2 years, the difference between CI and SI is given by:
$$CI - SI = P \times (\frac{r}{100})^2$$

**Derivation:**
- $SI = P \times \frac{r}{100} \times 2 = \frac{2Pr}{100}$
- $CI = P(1 + \frac{r}{100})^2 - P = P(1 + \frac{2r}{100} + \frac{r^2}{10000}) - P = \frac{2Pr}{100} + \frac{Pr^2}{10000}$
- Difference $= \frac{Pr^2}{10000}$

If $SI$ and $CI$ are known, $P$ can be found from $SI$, and then $r$ can be calculated using the difference formula.

Cost Price (CP): The price, at which an article is bought is called its cost price. All the overhead expenses in the transaction like freight, damage etc., are added to the cost price.

Selling Price (SP): The price at which an article sold is called its selling price.

  • Profit (SP > CP): When an article is sold at a price more than its cost price, then profit is earned.
  • Loss (CP > SP): When an article is sold at a price lower than its cost price, then loss is incurred.

Note: Profit and loss percentage is always calculated as the percentage of CP unless otherwise specified.

List Price/Marked Price: The price of an article which is displayed on the price tag is known as marked price. It is the normal price of the thing/products without a discount. Sometimes the shopkeeper increases or decreases the cost price, then this price is taken as the list price of the article.

content:
**Cost Price (CP):** The price, at which an article is bought is called its cost price. All the overhead expenses in the transaction like freight, damage etc., are added to the cost price.

**Selling Price (SP):** The price at which an article sold is called its selling price.

- **Profit (SP > CP):** When an article is sold at a price more than its cost price, then profit is earned.
- **Loss (CP > SP):** When an article is sold at a price lower than its cost price, then loss is incurred.

**Note:** Profit and loss percentage is always calculated as the percentage of CP unless otherwise specified.

**List Price/Marked Price:** The price of an article which is displayed on the price tag is known as marked price. It is the normal price of the thing/products without a discount. Sometimes the shopkeeper increases or decreases the cost price, then this price is taken as the list price of the article.

### Key Formulas
- Profit = Selling price - Cost price
- Loss = Cost price - Selling price
- Profit % = (Profit / CP) * 100% = ((SP - CP) / CP) * 100%
- Loss % = (Loss / CP) * 100% = ((CP - SP) / CP) * 100%

Rule 1: If there is a profit of r%, then (i) SP = (100 + r) * CP / 100 (ii) CP = 100 * SP / (100 + r)

Rule 2: If there is a loss of r%, then (i) SP = (100 - r) * CP / 100 (ii) CP = 100 * SP / (100 - r)

Rule 3: When there are two successive profits or losses of x% and y%, then the resultant profit or loss percent is given by (±x ± y + (±x)(±y)/100)%.

  • Take positive for profit and negative for loss.
  • If the sign of result is positive, there is a total gain.
  • If the sign of result is negative, there is a total loss.

Rule 4: When two different articles are sold at the same selling price, getting gain/loss of x% on the first and gain/loss of y% on the second, then the overall % gain or % loss in the transaction is given by [100(x + y) + 2xy / (100 + x) + (100 + x)]%. The above expression represent overall gain or loss accordingly as its sign is positive or negative.

When two different articles are sold at the same selling price getting a gain of x% on the first and loss of x% on the second, then the overall % loss in the transaction is given by (x/10)^2 %.

Note: That in such questions there is always a loss.

text:
A ratio is the comparison of two or more quantities of the same type (or kind) by division. If a and b are two quantities of the same kind (or same unit), then the fraction a/b is called the ratio a to b and we write it as a : b.

  • Antecedent: a
  • Consequent: b

Example: If a fruit box contains 8 oranges and 7 lemons then the ratio of oranges to lemons is 8 to 7 or 8:7.

Note: If both terms a and b of a ratio are multiplied or divided by the same quantity, then ratio remains unchanged.

i.e., a : b is same as na : nb => a/b = na/nb and a : b is same as a/n : b/n => (a/n) / (b/n) = a/b.

details.summary: Introduction to the definition of ratio, its components (antecedent and consequent), and the property of equivalent ratios.

mcq.explanation: 1.5 m = 150 cm (units must be same). Ratio of 90 cm to 1.5 m = 90/150 = (90/30) / (150/30) = 3/5. As this ratio is same as 3 : x, then 3/x = 3/5 => 3x = 5 * 3 => x = 5.

A **ratio** is the comparison of two or more quantities of the same type (or kind) by division. If *a* and *b* are two quantities of the same kind (or same unit), then the fraction *a/b* is called the ratio *a* to *b* and we write it as *a : b*.

- **Antecedent:** *a*
- **Consequent:** *b*

**Example:** If a fruit box contains 8 oranges and 7 lemons then the ratio of oranges to lemons is 8 to 7 or 8:7.

**Note:** If both terms *a* and *b* of a ratio are multiplied or divided by the same quantity, then ratio remains unchanged.

i.e., *a : b* is same as *na : nb* => *a/b = na/nb* and *a : b* is same as *a/n : b/n* => *(a/n) / (b/n) = a/b*.

### Key Formulas
- a : b = a/b
- a : b = na : nb
- a : b = (a/n) : (b/n)

### Key Exam Facts
- **Summary:** Introduction to the definition of ratio, its components (antecedent and consequent), and the property of equivalent ratios.

text:
1. Compound Ratio: When two or more ratios are multiplied together, they are said to be compound ratio. If a/b, c/d and e/f are all ratios, then their compound ratio is ace/bdf.

2. Duplicate Ratio: When a ratio is compounded with itself, the resulting ratio is called the duplicate ratio. So, a^2 : b^2 is duplicate ratio of a : b.

3. Triplicate Ratio: If a ratio is compounded three times with itself, then resulting ratio is called triplicate ratio. So, a^3 : b^3 is the triplicate ratio of a : b.

4. Subduplicate Ratio: If two numbers are in ratio, then the ratio of their square roots is called subduplicate ratio. If a : b is ratio, then the subduplicate ratio is sqrt(a) : sqrt(b).

5. Subtriplicate Ratio: If two numbers are in ratio, then the ratio of their cube roots is called subtriplicate ratio. If a : b is ratio, then the subtriplicate ratio is cbrt(a) : cbrt(b).

6. Reciprocal Ratio: If a : b is a ratio, then 1/a : 1/b is its reciprocal ratio, i.e., b : a.

Important Points:

  • Usually, the ratio is expressed in its lowest terms.
  • Ratio exists only between quantities of the same kind.
  • Ratio is a fraction, so it has no units.
  • Ratio is taken only between positive quantities.

The equality of two ratios is called proportion. '::' is the sign of proportion. So, if a : b = c : d, we write it as a : b :: c : d and say that a, b, c and d are in proportion. The quantities a, b, c and d are called the first, second, third and fourth terms of proportion respectively. First and fourth terms are called extreme terms and second and third terms are called means or middle terms.

If quantities a, b, c and d are in proportion, then a/b = c/d => ad = bc, i.e., product of extreme terms = product of middle terms. This is also called cross-product rule.

Types of Proportion: 1. Continued Proportion: The non-zero quantities of same kind, a, b, c, d, e, f, ... are said to be continued proportion, if a/b = b/c = c/d = e/f = ...
formulas: Continued Proportion: a/b = b/c = c/d = e/f

text:
For four non-zero quantities a, b, c and d in proportion (a : b :: c : d), the following properties apply:

  • Invertendo: If a:b::c:d, then b:a::d:c (a/b = c/d => b/a = d/c)
  • Alternendo: If a:b::c:d, then a:c::b:d (a/b = c/d => a/c = b/d)
  • Componendo: If a:b::c:d, then (a+b):b :: (c+d):d
  • Dividendo: If a:b::c:d, then (a-b):b :: (c-d):d
  • Componendo and Dividendo: If a:b::c:d, then (a+b):(a-b) :: (c+d):(c-d)

details.summary: Fundamental algebraic properties of proportions.

content:
For four non-zero quantities *a, b, c* and *d* in proportion (*a : b :: c : d*), the following properties apply:

- **Invertendo:** If *a:b::c:d*, then *b:a::d:c* (a/b = c/d => b/a = d/c)
- **Alternendo:** If *a:b::c:d*, then *a:c::b:d* (a/b = c/d => a/c = b/d)
- **Componendo:** If *a:b::c:d*, then *(a+b):b :: (c+d):d*
- **Dividendo:** If *a:b::c:d*, then *(a-b):b :: (c-d):d*
- **Componendo and Dividendo:** If *a:b::c:d*, then *(a+b):(a-b) :: (c+d):(c-d)*

### Key Formulas
- a/b = c/d => b/a = d/c
- a/b = c/d => a/c = b/d
- (a+b)/b = (c+d)/d
- (a-b)/b = (c-d)/d
- (a+b)/(a-b) = (c+d)/(c-d)

### Key Exam Facts
- **Summary:** Fundamental algebraic properties of proportions.

Mixture or Alligation: If two or more quantities are mixed together in a certain ratio, then the product is called mixture.

Mean Price: Cost price of a unit quantity of the mixture is called the mean price.

Rule of Mixture or Alligation: It is the rule to find the ratio in which two or more ingredients are mixed or to be mixed. If two quantities are mixed in the ratio n1:n2, then n1/n2 = (P2 - Pm) / (Pm - P1), where P1, P2 and Pm are cheaper price, dearer price and mean price respectively.

text:
Variations: When a change in a certain quantity leads to a certain change in another quantity then it is called variations.

Direct Variation: If x varies directly with y, then as x increases (decreases) y also increases (decreases). i.e., x ∝ y => x = ky, where k is the constant of variation.

Inverse Variation: If x varies inversely with y, then an increase in the value of x causes a decrease in the value of y. i.e., x ∝ 1/y => x = k'/y, where k' is the constant of variation.

  • Rule 3: If m and n are positive rational numbers, then log_a(m^n) = n log_a(m)

- If 'a' is a positive real number and n is a positive rational number, then (i) log_a(n^x) = (x/y) log_a(n), (ii) a^(log_a(n)) = n, (iii) log_a(n) = log_a^2(n^2) = log_a^3(n^3) = log_a^m(n^m)

Logarithm can have any positive base other than 0. But there are two most important base which are generally used.

  1. Common Logarithm: Logarithm to the base '10' is called common logarithm. It is also called Brigg's logarithm. e.g. log 100 = log_10 100 = 2; log 1000 = log_10 1000 = 3
  2. Natural Logarithm: Logarithm to the base e is called natural logarithm. It is also called Napier logarithm. log_e(x) is usually denoted by ln x. e is irrational number between 2 and 3. ln x = y => e^y = x

ANTILOGARITHM

The positive number 'a' is called the antilogarithm of a number b, if log a = b. If 'a' is antilogarithm of b, it is written as a = antilog b. So, a = antilog b <=> log a = b

topic: Characteristic and Mantissa of a Logarithm
text:
The logarithm of a positive real number 'n' consists of two parts:

  • The integral part is known as the characteristic. It is always an integer (positive, negative or zero).
  • The decimal part is called the mantissa. The mantissa is never negative and is always less than one.

To Find the Characteristic:

  • Case I: The characteristic of the log of a number greater than 1 is positive and numerically one less than the number of digits to the left of the decimal part.
  • Case II: The characteristic of log of a number less than 1 is negative and numerically one more than the number of zeroes immediately after the decimal point. It is represented by a bar over the digit.

Rules for Inserting Decimal Point:

  • Rule 5: When the characteristic of the logarithm is positive, we insert the decimal point after the (n + 1)th digit, where n is the characteristic.
  • Rule 6: When the characteristic of the logarithm is negative, we insert the decimal point such that the first significant figures is at nth place, where n is the characteristic.

Some Important Points:

  • The base of a logarithm is never taken as zero and negative.
  • Log of negative integers are not defined and also log_e 0 is not defined.
  • Logarithmic function is positive as well as negative but exponential function is always positive.

text:
Linear polynomial: A polynomial of degree 1.

e.g., $9x+7$, $x-9$, $x+2$ etc.

Quadratic polynomial: A polynomial of degree 2.

The general form of quadratic polynomial in $x$ is $ax^2 + bx + c$, where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are real and $a eq 0$.

e.g., $x^2 - 7x + 12$, $5y^2 - 2z^2 - 4$ etc., are all quadratic polynomials.

Cubic polynomial: A polynomial of degree 3.

The general form of a cubic polynomial in $x$ is $ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d$, where $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ are real and $a eq 0$.

e.g., $3x^3 + 2x^2 + 7x - 1$, $8y^3 + 5y + 2$, $x^3 - 8$ etc., are all cubic polynomials.

Biquadratic polynomial: A polynomial of degree 4.

The general form of a biquadratic polynomial in $x$ is $ax^4 + bx^3 + cx^2 + dx + e$, where $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ and $e$ are real numbers and $a eq 0$.

e.g., $6x^4 + 3x^3 + 2x^2 + x + 2$, $x^4 - 8$ etc., are all biquadratic polynomials.

Based on Number of Terms:

(i) Monomial: A polynomial containing only one term is called a monomial. e.g. $6x^2$

(ii) Binomial: A polynomial containing two terms is called a binomial. e.g. $5x^3 + 7xy$

(iii) Trinomial: A polynomial containing three terms is called a trinomial. e.g. $7x^2 y + 5x + 6$

FACTORISATION

To express a polynomial as the product of other polynomials of degree less than that of the given polynomial is called factorisation.

e.g. $x^2 - 49 = x^2 - 7^2 = (x-7)(x+7)$

**Linear polynomial:** A polynomial of degree 1.

e.g., $x^2 - 7x + 12$, $5y^2 - 2z^2 - 4$ etc., are all quadratic polynomials.

**Cubic polynomial:** A polynomial of degree 3.

The general form of a cubic polynomial in $x$ is $ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d$, where $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ are real and $a \neq 0$.

e.g., $3x^3 + 2x^2 + 7x - 1$, $8y^3 + 5y + 2$, $x^3 - 8$ etc., are all cubic polynomials.

**Biquadratic polynomial:** A polynomial of degree 4.

The general form of a biquadratic polynomial in $x$ is $ax^4 + bx^3 + cx^2 + dx + e$, where $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ and $e$ are real numbers and $a \neq 0$.

e.g., $6x^4 + 3x^3 + 2x^2 + x + 2$, $x^4 - 8$ etc., are all biquadratic polynomials.

**Based on Number of Terms:**

**(i) Monomial:** A polynomial containing only one term is called a monomial. e.g. $6x^2$

**(ii) Binomial:** A polynomial containing two terms is called a binomial. e.g. $5x^3 + 7xy$

**(iii) Trinomial:** A polynomial containing three terms is called a trinomial. e.g. $7x^2 y + 5x + 6$

**FACTORISATION**

To express a polynomial as the product of other polynomials of degree less than that of the given polynomial is called factorisation.

e.g. $x^2 - 49 = x^2 - 7^2 = (x-7)(x+7)$

- (a^3 - b^3) = (a-b)(a^2 + b^2 + ab)

Methods of Factorisation

These methods are given below

Factorisation by Taking Out the Common Factor

If each term of an expression has a common factor, take out the common factors.

Factorisation by Grouping

Sometimes in a given polynomial, it is not possible to take out a common factor directly. However, on rearranging the terms of the polynomial and grouping them such that all the terms have a common factor, the polynomial can be easily factorised.

text:
To factorise the polynomial, follow the following steps

(i) Let $p(x)$ be a given polynomial.

(ii) Find all the possible factors of constant term in $p(x)$.

(iii) Take any one of the factors, say $(\alpha)$ and find $p(\alpha)$. If $p(\alpha)=0$ the $(x-\alpha)$ is a factor of $p(x)$.

(iv) Divide the polynomial $p(x)$ by $(x-\alpha)$ to find its all other factors.

To factor (a⁴b⁴ – 16c⁴):

  • Recognize as a difference of squares: [(a²b²)² – (4c²)²]
  • Apply the difference of squares formula (A² – B² = (A – B)(A + B)): [a²b² + 4c²] [a²b² – 4c²]
  • Apply the formula again to the second term: [a²b² + 4c²] [(ab)² – (2c)²]
  • Final factorization: [a²b² + 4c²] [(ab – 2c) (ab + 2c)]

Factor Theorem Example: To check if (x - 2) is a factor of a polynomial, substitute x = 2 into the polynomial. If the result is 0, then (x - 2) is a factor.

Example Calculation: For a polynomial (e.g., x4 - 6x3 + 12x2 - 24x + 32), substituting x = 2 gives:

  • 24 - 6(2)3 + 12(2)2 - 24(2) + 32
  • = 16 - 6(8) + 12(4) - 48 + 32
  • = 16 - 48 + 48 - 48 + 32
  • = 0

Since the result is 0, (x - 2) is a factor of the polynomial x4 - 6x3 + 12x2 - 24x + 32.

text:
To find the HCF of polynomials which cannot be factorised easily, we use successive division method.

  • Step I Arrange the given polynomials in descending order of powers of its variables.
  • Step II If any common factor is present in the terms of each polynomial, it should be taken out.
  • Step III Divide the polynomial of highest degree by the polynomial of lowest degree. Or If both the polynomials are of the same degree then any one of them can be taken as divisor or dividend.
  • Step IV After the first division take the remainder as the new divisor and first divisor as new dividend.
  • Step V Continue this process of dividing the last divisor by the last remainder until the remainder becomes zero.
  • Step VI The product of common factors obtained from step II and last divisor is the HCF of given polynomials.

Note

  • If the first term of a remainder is negative at any stage, the sign of all of its term must be changed.
  • If at any stage, the remainder contains common factor it should be taken out.

details.summary: Explains the step-by-step process of finding the Highest Common Factor (HCF) of polynomials using the successive division method, particularly useful when factorization is difficult. Includes important notes regarding handling negative remainders and common factors in remainders.

text:
EXAMPLE 6. The HCF of two polynomials is x + 3 and their LCM is x³ - 7x + 6. If one of the polynomials is x² + 2x - 3. Then, the other is

  • a. x² - x - 6
  • b. x² - x + 6
  • c. x² + x + 6
  • d. None of these

Sol. d. Here, HCF = x + 3 and LCM = x³ - 7x + 6

Also, one polynomial = x² + 2x - 3

As, LCM × HCF = Product of two polynomials

Other polynomial = LCM × HCF⁄One polynomial

= (x + 3)(x³ - 7x + 6)⁄x² + 2x - 3

= (x + 3)(x - 1)(x² + x - 6)⁄(x + 3)(x - 1)

= x² + x - 6

So, other polynomial is x² + x - 6.

content:
**EXAMPLE 6.** The HCF of two polynomials is *x* + 3 and their LCM is *x*³ - 7*x* + 6. If one of the polynomials is *x*² + 2*x* - 3. Then, the other is

- a. *x*² - *x* - 6
- b. *x*² - *x* + 6
- c. *x*² + *x* + 6
- d. None of these

**Sol. d.** Here, HCF = *x* + 3 and LCM = *x*³ - 7*x* + 6

Also, one polynomial = *x*² + 2*x* - 3

As, LCM × HCF = Product of two polynomials

Other polynomial = LCM × HCF⁄One polynomial

= (*x* + 3)(*x*³ - 7*x* + 6)⁄*x*² + 2*x* - 3

= (*x* + 3)(*x* - 1)(*x*² + *x* - 6)⁄(*x* + 3)(*x* - 1)

= *x*² + *x* - 6

So, other polynomial is *x*² + *x* - 6.

### Key Formulas
- HCF = x + 3
- LCM = x^3 - 7x + 6
- One polynomial = x^2 + 2x - 3
- LCM * HCF = Product of two polynomials
- Other polynomial = (LCM * HCF) / One polynomial
- (x + 3)(x^3 - 7x + 6) / (x^2 + 2x - 3)
- (x + 3)(x - 1)(x^2 + x - 6) / ((x + 3)(x - 1))
- x^2 + x - 6

text:
An expression in the form of p(x)/q(x), where p(x) and q(x) are polynomials and q(x)≠0 is called a rational expression.

In the rational expression p(x)/q(x), p(x) is called the numerator and q(x) is called the denominator of the rational expression.

Every polynomial is a rational expression. Since, p(x) can always be written as p(x)/1 and a constant function 1 is a polynomial of degree 0.

Every rational expression need not be a polynomial.

Every polynomial is a rational expression. Since, p(x) can always be written as **p(x)/1** and a constant function 1 is a polynomial of degree 0.

Working Rule to Reduce the Given Rational Expression in its Lowest Term

2. Elimination Method

In this method, one variable is eliminated from both equations to have an equation in one variable, so it is called elimination method.

Steps used in this method are given below.

Step I Make the coefficient of one variable (x or y) numerically equal by multiplying both equations by some suitable non zero constant.

Step II Now, add or subtract both equations, so that one variable is eliminated and the remaining equation is in one variable only.

Step III Solve the equation in one variable to get the value of this variable (x or y).

Step IV Substitute this value (x or y) in either of the given equations to get the value of other variable.

EXAMPLE 5. The solution of the given system of equations 2x + 5y = 11 and 3x + 4y = 13 is

Sol. b. Given equations are, 2x + 5y = 11 ...(i) and 3x + 4y = 13 ...(ii)

On multiplying Eq. (i) by 3 and Eq. (ii) by 2, we get

6x + 15y = 33 ...(iii)

6x + 8y = 26 ...(iv)

On subtracting Eq. (iv) from Eq. (iii), we get

(6 x + 15y) – (6x + 8y) = 33 – 26 => 7y = 7 => y = 1

Put y = 1 in Eq. (i), 2x + 5 × 1 = 11

=> 2x = 11 – 5 => 2x = 6 => x = 3

Hence, solution of system of equations is (3, 1).

3. Cross-multiplication Method

Let us consider a general system of two simultaneous linear equations

a1x + b1y + c1 = 0 ...(i)

a2x + b2y + c2 = 0 ...(ii)

where, $ rac{a_1}{a_2} eq rac{b_1}{b_2}$ then the solution of the system is given by,

$x = rac{b_1c_2 - b_2c_1}{a_1b_2 - a_2b_1}$ and $y = rac{c_1a_2 - c_2a_1}{a_1b_2 - a_2b_1}$

$ herefore rac{x}{b_1c_2 - b_2c_1} = rac{y}{c_1a_2 - c_2a_1} = rac{1}{a_1b_2 - a_2b_1}$

This method is called cross multiplication method.

Remembering Technique (Cross-multiplication)

The following diagram helps in remembering the above solution.

The arrows between the two numbers indicate that they are to be multiplied. The downward arrows indicate first product while upward arrows indicate the second product. The second product is to be subtracted from the first.

EXAMPLE 6. The system of equations ax - by = a2 - b2 and x + y = a + b has the solution.

Sol. a. Given, pairs of linear equations are

ax - by - (a2 - b2) = 0 ...(i)

x + y - (a + b) = 0 ...(ii)

On comparing Eqs. (i) and (ii) with a1x + b1y + c1 = 0 and a2x + b2y + c2 = 0, we get

a1 = a, b1 = -b, c1 = -(a2 - b2)

a2 = 1, b2 = 1, c2 = -(a + b)

By cross multiplication, we have

$\Rightarrow rac{x}{b(a+b) - (-b)(-(a^2-b^2))} = rac{y}{-(a^2-b^2)(1) - (-b)(-(a+b))} = rac{1}{a(1) - (-b)(1)}$

$\Rightarrow rac{x}{b(a+b) - b(a^2-b^2)} = rac{y}{-(a^2-b^2) - b(a+b)} = rac{1}{a+b}$

$\Rightarrow rac{x}{b(a+b) - b(a-b)(a+b)} = rac{y}{-(a-b)(a+b) - b(a+b)} = rac{1}{a+b}$

$\Rightarrow rac{x}{b(a+b)[1 - (a-b)]} = rac{y}{(a+b)[-(a-b) - b]} = rac{1}{a+b}$

$\Rightarrow rac{x}{b(a+b)(1-a+b)} = rac{y}{(a+b)(-a+b-b)} = rac{1}{a+b}$

$\Rightarrow rac{x}{b(a+b)(1-a+b)} = rac{y}{(a+b)(-a)} = rac{1}{a+b}$

So, $x = rac{b(a+b)(1-a+b)}{a+b} = b(1-a+b)$ and $y = rac{(a+b)(-a)}{a+b} = -a$. This is not matching the options. Let's recheck the calculation.

Let's re-evaluate the cross multiplication step:

$ rac{x}{(-b)(-(a+b)) - (1)(-(a^2-b^2))} = rac{y}{(-(a^2-b^2))(1) - (a)(-(a+b))} = rac{1}{(a)(1) - (1)(-b)}$

$\Rightarrow rac{x}{b(a+b) + (a^2-b^2)} = rac{y}{-(a^2-b^2) + a(a+b)} = rac{1}{a+b}$

$\Rightarrow rac{x}{ab+b^2 + a^2-b^2} = rac{y}{-a^2+b^2 + a^2+ab} = rac{1}{a+b}$

$\Rightarrow rac{x}{a^2+ab} = rac{y}{b^2+ab} = rac{1}{a+b}$

$\Rightarrow rac{x}{a(a+b)} = rac{y}{b(b+a)} = rac{1}{a+b}$

$\Rightarrow x = rac{a(a+b)}{a+b} = a$ and $y = rac{b(a+b)}{a+b} = b$. So, x = a and y = b is the required solution.

a1 = a, b1 = -b, c1 = -(a2 - b2)

a2 = 1, b2 = 1, c2 = -(a + b)

By cross multiplication, we have

$\Rightarrow  rac{x}{b(a+b) - (-b)(-(a^2-b^2))} =  rac{y}{-(a^2-b^2)(1) - (-b)(-(a+b))} =  rac{1}{a(1) - (-b)(1)}$

$\Rightarrow  rac{x}{b(a+b) - b(a^2-b^2)} =  rac{y}{-(a^2-b^2) - b(a+b)} =  rac{1}{a+b}$

$\Rightarrow  rac{x}{b(a+b) - b(a-b)(a+b)} =  rac{y}{-(a-b)(a+b) - b(a+b)} =  rac{1}{a+b}$

$\Rightarrow  rac{x}{b(a+b)[1 - (a-b)]} =  rac{y}{(a+b)[-(a-b) - b]} =  rac{1}{a+b}$

$\Rightarrow  rac{x}{b(a+b)(1-a+b)} =  rac{y}{(a+b)(-a+b-b)} =  rac{1}{a+b}$

$\Rightarrow  rac{x}{b(a+b)(1-a+b)} =  rac{y}{(a+b)(-a)} =  rac{1}{a+b}$

So, $x =  rac{b(a+b)(1-a+b)}{a+b} = b(1-a+b)$ and $y =  rac{(a+b)(-a)}{a+b} = -a$. This is not matching the options. Let's recheck the calculation.

Let's re-evaluate the cross multiplication step:

$ rac{x}{(-b)(-(a+b)) - (1)(-(a^2-b^2))} =  rac{y}{(-(a^2-b^2))(1) - (a)(-(a+b))} =  rac{1}{(a)(1) - (1)(-b)}$

$\Rightarrow  rac{x}{b(a+b) + (a^2-b^2)} =  rac{y}{-(a^2-b^2) + a(a+b)} =  rac{1}{a+b}$

$\Rightarrow  rac{x}{ab+b^2 + a^2-b^2} =  rac{y}{-a^2+b^2 + a^2+ab} =  rac{1}{a+b}$

$\Rightarrow  rac{x}{a^2+ab} =  rac{y}{b^2+ab} =  rac{1}{a+b}$

$\Rightarrow  rac{x}{a(a+b)} =  rac{y}{b(b+a)} =  rac{1}{a+b}$

$\Rightarrow x =  rac{a(a+b)}{a+b} = a$ and $y =  rac{b(a+b)}{a+b} = b$. So, x = a and y = b is the required solution.

### Key Formulas
- x = (b1c2 - b2c1) / (a1b2 - a2b1)
- y = (c1a2 - c2a1) / (a1b2 - a2b1)
- a1x + b1y + c1 = 0
- a2x + b2y + c2 = 0
- 2x + 5y = 11

- 6x + 15y = 33

- 2x + 5(1) = 11

- ax - by = a^2 - b^2
- x + y = a + b
- ax - by - (a^2 - b^2) = 0
- x + y - (a + b) = 0
- a1 = a, b1 = -b, c1 = -(a^2 - b^2)
- a2 = 1, b2 = 1, c2 = -(a + b)
- x / (b(a+b) + (a^2-b^2)) = y / (-(a^2-b^2) + a(a+b)) = 1 / (a+b)
- x / (a^2+ab) = y / (b^2+ab) = 1 / (a+b)
- x / (a(a+b)) = y / (b(a+b)) = 1 / (a+b)
- x = a
- y = b

topic: Solutions of Quadratic Equations - By Factorisation
text:
Solutions of quadratic equations can be determined by using any of the following two methods:

1. By Factorisation

In this method, the middle term of the quadratic equation is splitted and the given quadratic equation is converted into a product of two linear factors. Then, the roots of the equation are obtained by equating each factor equal to zero.

Let the quadratic equation be ax^2 + bx + c = 0 and its linear factors are (px + q) and (rx + s), then ax^2 + bx + c = (px + q)(rx + s).

Now, ax^2 + bx + c = 0 => (px + q)(rx + s) = 0 => px + q = 0 or rx + s = 0 => x = -q/p or x = -s/r.

Thus, -q/p and -s/r are the roots of the equation, ax^2 + bx + c = 0.

details.summary: Explanation of the factorisation method for solving quadratic equations.

Let D = b2 - 4ac be the discriminant of the quadratic equation, ax2 + bx + c = 0, where a ≠ 0. Then, the following cases arise:

  • (i) If D > 0, then the two roots are real and distinct.
  • (ii) If D = 0, then the two roots are real and equal and are given by α = β = -b / 2a.
  • (iii) If D < 0, then there are no real roots, i.e., given equation has imaginary roots.

IMPORTANT POINTS:

  • 1. If a, b, c ∈ Q and D is a perfect square, then equation has rational roots.
  • 2. If one root of quadratic equation is p + √q, then other root will be p - √q.

The equations which at the outset are not quadratic equations, but can be reduced to quadratic equations by suitable substitutions or simplifications are called equations reducible to quadratic equations.

  • Rule 1: ax^(2n) + bx^n + c = 0, where n ≥ 2. Use substitution x^n = y ⇒ x^(2n) = y^2 and equation reduces to ay^2 + by + c = 0.
  • Rule 2: Px + Q/x = R. Reduce the given equation to a quadratic equation by multiplying both sides by 'x'. So, Px^2 + Q = Rx or Px^2 - Rx + Q = 0.
  • Rule 3: sqrt(x + b) + x = c or sqrt(a - x^2) = bx + c. Square both sides to get a quadratic equation without the radical. Solve the equation by factorisation or by quadratic formula.
  • Rule 4: sqrt(ax + b) ± sqrt(cx + d) = e or sqrt(ax + b) ± sqrt(cx + d) ± sqrt(ex + f) = 0. To solve such type of equations, follow the steps: Square both sides once, so that only one term containing radical is obtained. Keep the term containing radical on one side and all other terms on the other side. Square again to get, the quadratic equation and solve it.

text:
Linear inequality in one variable: A linear inequality which has only one variable is called linear inequality in one variable. e.g., ax + b < 0, where a != (-b/a), 4x + 7 >= 0.

Linear inequality in two variables: A linear inequality which has two variables, is called linear inequality in two variables. e.g., 3x + 11y <= 0, 4t + 3y > 0.

General Rules to Solve Linear Inequalities:

  • Equal numbers may be added or subtracted from both sides of an inequality without changing the sign of inequality. e.g., If a > b, then for any number c, a + c > b + c or a - c > b - c.
  • If both sides of an inequality are multiplied or divided by the same positive number, then the sign of inequality remains the same. e.g., If a > b and c > 0, then a/c > b/c and ac > bc.
  • If both sides of an inequality are multiplied or divided by the same negative number, then the sign of inequality is reversed. e.g., If a > b and c < 0, then a/c < b/c and ac < bc.

Graphical Solution of Linear Inequalities in Two Variables:

Let the inequality be ax + by + c >= 0.

  • Step I: Consider it as ax + by + c = 0 by changing the inequality sign to equality sign. Draw the graph of this equation.
  • Step II: Choose any point not on the line, (usually (0, 0)). Find whether this point satisfy the inequality or not. If it does, then shade the half-plane containing that point. Otherwise shade the other half-plane.

Note:

  • (i) If the inequality is strict (> or <), graph a dashed line. If the inequality is not strict (>= or <=), graph a solid line.
  • (ii) In order to solve a system of two or more linear inequalities with the same variables, graph each inequality on the same set of axes. The intersection of the region of all the inequalities is the required solution set.

A well defined collection of objects is called a set. The objects in a set are called its members or elements.

  • Sets are usually denoted by capital letters A, B, C, X, Y and Z etc.
  • Elements of a set are denoted by small letters a, b, c etc.

  • If x is not an element of set A, we write x ∉ A.

Examples:

  • The collection of vowels in English alphabet is a set A containing five elements namely a, e, i, o and u, where a ∈ A but b ∉ A.
  • The collection of first four prime numbers is a set A containing the elements 2, 3, 5 and 7, where 3 ∈ A but 1 ∉ A.

text:
Sets are generally represented by two ways:

1. Roster or Tabular form or listing method: In this method, all the elements of a set are listed, within curly braces { } being separated by commas.

  • If A is a set of first eight prime numbers, then A = {2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19}
  • If B is a set of squares of first five natural numbers, then B = {1, 4, 9, 16, 25}
  • If A is a set of vowels of English alphabets, then A = {a, e, i, o, u}

Note: The order in which the elements are written in a set makes no difference and also the repeated elements are taken only once each.

2. Set Builder form or Rule method: In this method, instead of listing all the elements of a set, we write the set by some special property or properties satisfied by all its elements and write it as.

  • The set B of all even natural numbers can be written as B = {x : x is a natural number and x = 2n for n ∈ N} or B = {x : x ∈ N, x = 2n, n ∈ N} and reads it as 'B' is the set consisting of all elements x such that x has the property of even natural number. The symbol ':' or '|' stands or such that.
  • The set A = {3, 5, 7, 9, 11}, then it is represented as A = {x : x = 2n + 1 where n ∈ N, n < 6}

Types of Sets:

  • 1. Empty set: A set which does not contain any element is called an empty set or null set or void set. It is denoted by φ or { }. e.g., A = set of all odd numbers divisible by 2 and B = {x : x ∈ N and 5 < x < 6}. The sets which have atleast one element are called non void or non-empty set.
  • 2. Singleton set: A set consisting of a single element is called a singleton set. e.g., (i) The set {5} is a singleton set. (ii) {x | x ∈ W and x + 6 = 6} = {0} which is a singleton set.
  • 3. Finite set: A set which consists of a definite number of elements, is called a finite set. Empty set is also a finite set. e.g., (i) The set {1, 2, 3, 4} is a finite set, because it contains a definite number of elements i.e. only 4 elements. (ii) B = Set of vowels in English Alphabets = {a, e, i, o, u}. (iii) A = Set of even prime natural numbers => A = {2}. Note: The number of distinct elements contained in a set A is called the cardinal number of A and is denoted as n(A). If A = {a, e, i, o, u}, then n(A) = 5.
  • 4. Infinite set: A set which consists of infinite number of elements is called an infinite set. It is represented by writing a few elements of the set followed by e.g., (i) Set of square of natural numbers is an infinite set, because natural numbers are infinite and it can be represented as {1, 4, 9, 16, 25, ...}. (ii) Set of all points in a plane.
  • 5. Equal sets: Two sets A and B are said to be equal, if they have exactly the same elements and we write A = B. Otherwise, two sets are said to be unequal and we write A ≠ B. e.g., Let A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {4, 3, 1, 2}, then A = B because each element of A is in B and vice-versa.
  • 6. Equivalent sets: Two sets A and B are equivalent, if their cardinal numbers are same i.e. n(A) = n(B) and we write A ↔ B or A ~ B. e.g., Let A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {4, 5, 6}, then n(A) = n(B), A ↔ B or A ~ B.

(ii) Empty set is a subset of every set i.e. φ ⊆ A. e.g., Let A = {2, 4, 6} and B = {6, 4, 2, 8}. Then, A ⊆ B but B ⊄ A i.e. A is a subset of B but B is not a subset of A. Note: The total number of subsets of a finite set containing n elements is 2^n.
  • 8. Super set: If A is a subset of B, then we say that B is superset of A and we write B ⊇ A. e.g., If A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, then, B ⊇ A.
  • 9. Comparability of sets: Two sets A and B are said to be comparable, if either A ⊂ B or B ⊂ A or A = B, otherwise A and B are said to be incomparable. e.g., Let A = {1, 2, 3}, B = {1, 2, 4, 6} and C = {1, 2, 4}. Since, A ⊄ B and B ⊄ A. So, A and B are incomparable but C ⊂ B and so B and C are comparable sets.
  • 10. Proper subset: If A ⊆ B and A ≠ B, then A is called a proper subset of B and we write A ⊂ B. e.g., If A = {1, 2, 3, 4, ...} and B = {..., -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, ....}, then A ⊂ B. Note: The total number of proper subset of a finite set containing n elements is (2^n - 1).
  • 11. Universal set: If there are some sets under consideration, then there happens to be a set which is a superset of each one of the given sets. Such a set is known as the universal set and it is denoted by U. e.g., If A = {1, 2, 3}, B = {2, 3, 4, 5, 7} and C = {2, 4, 6, 8}, then U = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8} is a universal set for A, B and C. For the set of all integers, the universal set can be the set of rational numbers or the set of real numbers.
  • 12. Power set: The collection of all subsets of a set A, is called power set of A and it is denoted by P(A). In P(A), every element is a set. e.g., Let A = {1, 2, 3}. Then, P(A) = {φ, {1}, {2}, {3}, {1,2}, {2,3}, {3,1}, {1,2,3}}.

1. Union of Sets: Let A and B be any two sets. The union of A and B is the set of all the elements of A and all the elements of B, the common elements being taken only once. It is denoted by A U B and read as 'A union B'. Thus, A U B = {x : x is in A or x is in B}.

2. Intersection of sets: Let A and B be any two sets. The intersection of A and B is the set of all those elements which belongs to both A and B. It is denoted by A intersection B and read as 'A intersection B'. Thus, A intersection B = {x : x is in A and x is in B}.

3. Disjoint sets: Two sets A and B are said to be disjoint, if they have no common element i.e. A intersection B = phi.

4. Difference of sets: Let A and B be two sets. The difference of two sets is the set of all those elements of A which do not belong to B. It is denoted by A - B and read as A minus B. Thus, A - B = {x : x is in A and x is not in B}.

topic: Symmetric Difference, Complement, and Laws of Algebra of Sets
text:
Symmetric Difference of Two Sets: Let A and B be two sets. The symmetric difference of sets A and B is the set (A - B) U (B - A) and is denoted by A Δ B. It is a set consisting of all those members of A which are not in B or all those which are in B but not in A. Thus, A Δ B = {x : x ∈ A but x ∉ B} U {x : x ∈ B but x ∉ A}. A Δ B = (A - B) U (B - A).

Complement of a Set: Let U be the universal set and A be any set such that A ⊂ U. The complement of A with respect to U is the set of all those elements of U which are not in A. It is denoted by A' or A^c or U - A. Thus, A' = {x : x ∈ U and x ∉ A}.

Laws of Algebra of Sets:

  • Idempotent laws: (i) A U A = A, (ii) A ∩ A = A
  • Identity laws: (i) A U φ = A, (ii) A ∩ U = A
  • Commutative laws: (i) A U B = B U A, (ii) A ∩ B = B ∩ A
  • Associative laws: (i) (A U B) U C = A U (B U C), (ii) (A ∩ B) ∩ C = A ∩ (B ∩ C)
  • Distributive laws: (i) A U (B ∩ C) = (A U B) ∩ (A U C), (ii) A ∩ (B U C) = (A ∩ B) U (A ∩ C)
  • De-Morgan's laws: (i) (A U B)' = A' ∩ B', (ii) (A ∩ B)' = A' U B'

More Results on Operations on Sets:

  • A - (B ∩ C) = (A - B) U (A - C)
  • A - (B U C) = (A - B) ∩ (A - C)
  • A ∩ (B - C) = (A ∩ B) - (A ∩ C)
  • A ∩ (B Δ C) = (A ∩ B) Δ (A ∩ C)
  • (A - B) U (B - A) = (A U B) - (A ∩ B)

Cardinality Results:

  • n(A U B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A ∩ B)
  • n(A U B) = n(A) + n(B) if A, B are disjoint sets.
  • n(A - B) = n(A) - n(A ∩ B)
  • n(A Δ B) = n(A) + n(B) - 2n(A ∩ B)
  • n(A U B U C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) - n(A ∩ B) - n(B ∩ C) - n(A ∩ C) + n(A ∩ B ∩ C)

An ordered pair consists of two objects or elements in a given fixed order.

If A and B are two sets and a ∈ A, b ∈ B, then the ordered pair of elements a and b is denoted by (a, b).

The natural numbers and their squares can be represented by ordered pair in the following way: (1, 1), (2, 4), (3, 9), (4, 16), ....

Two ordered pairs (a, b) and (c, d) will be equal, if and only if a = c and b = d.

Note: {a, b} = {b, a} but (a, b) ≠ (b, a).

chapter: Measurements of Angles and Trigonometric Ratios
text:
Trigonometry is the branch of Mathematics which deals with the measurements of sides and angles of triangles and the problems based on these angles.

Angle

An angle is considered as the figure obtained by rotating a given ray about its endpoint. The original ray is called the initial side and the ray into which the initial side rotates is called terminal side. In figure, OA is initial side and OB is the terminal side of ∠AOB. The point O is called its vertex.

Quadrants

Let XOX' and YOY' be two lines at right angles in the plane of paper. These two perpendicular lines divide the plane of the paper into four equal parts, these four parts are known as four quadrants and lines XOX' and YOY' are known as X-axis and Y-axis, respectively.

The parts XOY, YOX', X'OY' and Y'OX are known as 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 4th quadrant, respectively.

Relation between Angles, Radius and Arc Length

If l is the length of a circle of radius r. And this arc subtends an angle θ radians at the centre of the circle, then l = rθ ⇒ θ = l/r.

**Trigonometry** is the branch of Mathematics which deals with the measurements of sides and angles of triangles and the problems based on these angles.

### Angle

An angle is considered as the figure obtained by rotating a given ray about its endpoint. The original ray is called the **initial side** and the ray into which the initial side rotates is called **terminal side**. In figure, *OA* is initial side and *OB* is the terminal side of ∠AOB. The point *O* is called its vertex.

### Quadrants

Let *XOX'* and *YOY'* be two lines at right angles in the plane of paper. These two perpendicular lines divide the plane of the paper into four equal parts, these four parts are known as four quadrants and lines *XOX'* and *YOY'* are known as *X*-axis and *Y*-axis, respectively.

The parts *XOY*, *YOX'*, *X'OY'* and *Y'OX* are known as 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 4th quadrant, respectively.

### Relation between Angles, Radius and Arc Length

If *l* is the length of a circle of radius *r*. And this arc subtends an angle *θ* radians at the centre of the circle, then *l = rθ* ⇒ *θ = l/r*.

### Key Formulas
- l = r * theta
- theta = l / r

The ratio of the sides of a right angled triangle with respect to its angle are called trigonometric ratios. The side opposite to the right angle is called the hypotenuse. Relative to the angle θ, the side opposite to angle θ is called the perpendicular side and the remaining side is called base.

(i) For angle θ, perpendicular = BC, base = AB and hypotenuse = AC

(ii) For angle α, perpendicular = AB, base = BC and hypotenuse = AC

Trigonometric ratios of θ in right angled ΔABC are defined below:

  • sin θ = Perpendicular/Hypotenuse = BC/AC = P/H
  • cos θ = Base/Hypotenuse = AB/AC = B/H
  • tan θ = Perpendicular/Base = BC/AB = P/B
  • sec θ = Hypotenuse/Base = AC/AB = H/B
  • cot θ = Base/Perpendicular = AB/BC = B/P
  • cosec θ = Hypotenuse/Perpendicular = AC/BC = H/P

text:
The sign of trigonometric ratios depends on the quadrant in which the angle theta lies:

  • I Quadrant (0 < theta < 90°): All trigonometric ratios are positive.
  • II Quadrant (90° < theta < 180°): sin theta and cosec theta are positive. All other trigonometric ratios are negative.
  • III Quadrant (180° < theta < 270°): tan theta and cot theta are positive. All other trigonometric ratios are negative.
  • IV Quadrant (270° < theta < 360°): cos theta and sec theta are positive. All other trigonometric ratios are negative.

text:
Cosine rule: In a triangle ABC, if a, b, c are the sides opposite to angles A, B and C respectively, then:

  • cos A = (b^2 + c^2 - a^2) / 2bc
  • cos B = (c^2 + a^2 - b^2) / 2ac
  • cos C = (a^2 + b^2 - c^2) / 2ab

Circumcircle of a triangle: The circle passing through the vertices of a triangle ABC is called circumcircle. Its radius R is called the circumradius and its centre is known as circumcentre. Here, R = a / (2sin A) = b / (2sin B) = c / (2sin C).

Sine rule: In a triangle ABC, if a, b, c are the three sides opposite to the angles A, B, C respectively, then: a / sin A = b / sin B = c / sin C.

topic: Basic Concepts and Angle of Elevation
text:
Height and Distance is an important application of trigonometry which helps us to find the height of any object and distance of that object from any point which are not directly measurable, provided the angle of elevation/depression from a point is known.

  • Line of sight: A line of sight is the line drawn from the eye of an observer to the point, where the object is viewed by the observer.
  • Horizontal Line: The line of sight which is parallel to ground level is known as horizontal line.
  • Angle of Elevation: Angle of elevation is defined as an angle formed by the line of sight with the horizontal line when an object is viewed in the upward direction. Let P be the position of the object above the horizontal line OA and O be the eye of the observer, then ∠AOP is called angle of elevation.

IMPORTANT POINTS:

  • If the observer moves towards the perpendicular line (tower/building), then angle of elevation increases and if the observer moves away from the perpendicular line (tower/building), then the angle of elevation decreases.
  • If the angle of elevation of Sun above a tower decreases, then the length of shadow of a tower increases.
  • If height of tower is doubled and the distance between the observer and foot of the tower is also doubled, then the angle of elevation remains same.

A horizontal dashed line AE is drawn from the observer's eye A to the tower at E, parallel to ground BC. A straight slanted line labeled 'Line of sight' connects eye A to the top of the tower D.

Angle of Elevation Diagram: Depicts an observer's eye at point O looking up at an object at point P. The horizontal line OA extends to the right from point O. The line of sight OP forms an acute angle theta (labeled 'Angle of elevation') with the horizontal baseline OA.

mcq.question: What happens to the angle of elevation of the top of a tower if both the height of the tower and the distance of the observer from its foot are doubled?
mcq.explanation: Since tan(theta) = Height / Distance, doubling both numerator and denominator keeps the ratio (2H)/(2D) = H/D unchanged, hence the angle of elevation remains constant.

text:
Angle of depression is defined as an angle formed by the line of sight with the horizontal line when an object is viewed in the downward direction.

Important Points:

  • The angle of depression of a point P as seen from a point O is numerically equal to the angle of elevation of O as seen from P.
  • Angle of elevation and angle of depression are always acute angle.
  • Unless mentioned, the height of the observer is not considered.

text:
Point: The figure of which length, breadth and height cannot be measured is called a point. It is infinitesind.

Line Segment: The straight path between two points P and Q is called a line segment. This can be represented as PQ (with bar over it).

  • P and Q are called the end points of the line segment.
  • The line segment has a definite length.
  • Distance between P and Q is called the length of the line segment PQ.

Line: A line segment extended endlessly on both sides, is called a line. It is denoted by PQ (with double arrow over it) or QP (with double arrow over it).

  • A line is a set of infinite number of points.
  • A line have no end points and no definite length.

Ray: A ray extends indefinitely in one direction. This is exhibited by an arrow i.e. PQ (with arrow over it).

  • P is called the initial point of the ray. The ray has no definite length.

Collinear Points: Three or more points are said to be collinear if a single straight line passes through them. Here, A, B and C are collinear.

Non-collinear Points: Three or more points not lying on a single straight line are called non-collinear points. Here, A, B and C are non-collinear.

Intersecting Lines: Two lines having a common point are called intersecting lines. This common point is the point of intersection i.e. O.

text:
Concurrent Lines: Three or more lines intersecting at the same point are said to be concurrent. This common point is the point of concurrence i.e. O.

Non Intersecting lines/Parallel Lines: If two lines lie in the same plane and do not intersect when produced on either side, then such lines are said to be parallel to each other. If l and m are two parallel lines, we write l || m and read it as l is parallel to m.

ANGLES: An angle is formed by two rays with a common initial point. Let 'O' is the initial point, then O is called the vertex. P is a point in the interior of angle AOB and R is a point in the exterior of angle AOB.

Types of Angle:

  • Acute angle: 0° < angle < 90°
  • Right angle: angle = 90°
  • Obtuse angle: 90° < angle < 180°
  • Straight angle: angle = 180°
  • Reflex angle: 180° < angle < 360°
  • Complete angle: angle = 360°

Pairs of Angle:

  • Complementary Angles: Two angles are said to be complementary, if the sum of their measure is 90°. Complement of x is (90° - x).
  • Supplementary Angles: Two angles are said to be supplementary, if the sum of their measures is 180°. Supplement of x is (180° - x).

Two angles are called a pair of vertically opposite angles, if their arms form two pairs of opposite rays.

text:
A plane (closed) figure bounded by three line segments is called a triangle. It is denoted by Δ.

ΔABC has:

  • three vertices, namely A, B and C.
  • three sides, namely AB, BC and CA.
  • three angles, namely ∠A, ∠B and ∠C.
  • Sum of three angles of a triangle is 180°. i.e., ∠A + ∠B + ∠C = 180°
  • Area of a triangle = 1/2 × base × height = 1/2 × BC × AD

text:
1. On the Basis of Angles

  • (i) Right Angled Triangle: A triangle in which one of the angle measures 90° is called a right angled triangle. The side opposite to the right angle is called its hypotenuse and the remaining two sides are called as perpendicular and base depending upon conditions. Here, ΔABC is a right angled triangle in which ∠B = 90° and AC is hypotenuse.
  • (ii) Acute Angled Triangle: A triangle in which every angle measure more than 0° but less than 90° is called an acute angled triangle. Here, ΔABC is an acute angled triangle.
  • (iii) Obtuse Angled Triangle: A triangle in which one of the angle measures more than 90° but less than 180° is called an obtuse angled triangle. Here, ΔABC is an obtuse angled triangle and ∠ABC is the obtuse angle.

topic: Classification of Triangles on the Basis of Sides
text:
Triangles are classified based on their sides:

  • Equilateral Triangle: A triangle having all sides equal. In triangle ABC, AB = BC = AC. All angles are equal and measure 60 degrees.
  • Isosceles Triangle: A triangle in which two sides are equal. In triangle ABC, AB = AC. The angles opposite to equal sides are equal, i.e., angle B = angle C.
  • Scalene Triangle: A triangle in which all sides are of different lengths. In triangle ABC, AB is not equal to BC is not equal to AC.

Note: The sum of the lengths of three sides of a triangle is called its perimeter. Perimeter of triangle ABC = AB + BC + AC.

Incentre and Angle Bisector: The point of intersection of all three angle bisectors of a triangle is called its incentre (denoted by I). The circle with centre I touching all sides is the incircle. Inradius (r) = 1/3 * Height = Side / (2 * sqrt(3)).

Perpendicular Bisector and Circumcentre: The point of intersection of perpendicular bisectors of the sides is the circumcentre (denoted by C). The circle passing through vertices A, B, and C is the circumcircle. Circumradius (R) = 2/3 * Height = Side / sqrt(3).

Altitudes and Orthocentre: The altitude is a line segment perpendicular from a vertex to the opposite side. The point of intersection of all three altitudes is the orthocentre (H).

Medians and Centroid: A line segment joining the mid-point of a side to the opposite vertex is a median. The point of intersection of all three medians is the centroid (G). Centroid divides the median in the ratio 2:1. A median bisects the area of the triangle.

topic: Some Important Results of a Triangle
text:
Some Important Results of a Triangle:

  • If two angles of a triangle are equal, then the sides opposite to them are also equal.
  • In a triangle, the side opposite to a greater angle is the longest side.
  • The sum of all the three interior angles of a triangle is 180°.
  • If a side of a triangle is produced, then the exterior angle so formed is equal to the sum of the two interior opposite angles.
  • An exterior angle of a triangle is greater than either of the interior opposite angles.
  • A triangle must have atleast two acute angles.
  • If a perpendicular is drawn from the vertex of a right angled triangle to the hypotenuse, then the triangles on both sides of the perpendicular are similar to the original triangle and also to each other.
  • In a right angle triangle ABC, angle B = 90° and AC is hypotenuse. The perpendicular BD is dropped on hypotenuse AC from right angle vertex B, then: (i) BD = (AB * BC) / AC, (ii) AD = AB^2 / AC, (iii) CD = BC^2 / AC, (iv) 1/BD^2 = 1/AB^2 + 1/BC^2.
  • The area of the equilateral triangle described on the side of a square is half the area of the equilateral triangle described on its diagonal.
  • In triangle ABC, if angle B > 90° and AD is perpendicular dropped on BC, then AC^2 = AB^2 + BC^2 + 2BC * BD.
  • In triangle ABC, if angle B < 90° and AD perpendicular to BC, then AC^2 = AB^2 + BC^2 - 2BC * BD.
  • In any triangle, the sum of the square of any two sides is equal to twice the square of half of the third side together with twice the square of the median which bisect the third side. Here, AD is median, so AB^2 + AC^2 = 2AD^2 + 2(1/2 BC)^2.
  • In a triangle ABC, three times the sum of the squares of the sides of a triangle is equal to four times the sum of the squares of the medians of the triangle. So, in triangle, if AD, BE, FC are the medians, then 3(AB^2 + BC^2 + AC^2) = 4(AD^2 + BE^2 + CF^2).
  • In an equilateral triangle ABC, the side BC is trisected at D. Then, 9 AD^2 = 7 AC^2.
  • When the bisector of one internal base angle and the bisector of external angle meet at a point then the formed angle is equal to one half of the vertical angle. Here, angle BEC = 1/2 angle BAC.

• The side BC of triangle ABC is produced to D. The bisector of angle A meets BC in L. Then angle ABC + angle ACD = 2 angle ALC.
  • In a triangle ABC, the bisector of angle B and angle C intersect each other at a point O. Then, angle BOC = 90 degrees + 1/2 angle A.
  • In a triangle ABC, the side AB and AC are produced to P and Q, respectively. The bisectors of angle PBC and angle QCB intersect at a point O. Then, angle BOC = 90 degrees - 1/2 angle A.
  • In a triangle ABC, angle B > angle C. If AN is the bisector of angle BAC and AM perpendicular to BC, then angle MAN = 1/2 (angle B - angle C).
  • The bisectors of the base angles of a triangle can never enclose a right angle.
  • A triangle is an isosceles if and only if any two altitudes are equal.
  • If the three sides of a triangle be produced in order, then the sum of all the exterior angles so formed is 360 degrees. So, angle DAB + angle EBC + angle ACF = 360 degrees.
  • Sum of any two sides of a triangle is greater than its third side. Here, in triangle ABC, AB + AC > BC; similarly, AB + BC > AC, BC + AC > AB.
  • The difference between any two sides of a triangle is less than its third side. Here, in triangle ABC, AC - AB < BC. Similarly, BC - AC < AB, BC - AB < AC.
  • If the bisector of the vertical angle of a triangle bisects the base, then that triangle is an isosceles.
  • If the altitude from one vertex of a triangle bisects the opposite side, then the triangle is an isosceles.

  • Medians of equilateral triangle are equal.

  • The sum of any two sides of a triangle is greater than twice the median drawn to the third side.
  • Perimeter of a triangle is greater than the sum of its three medians. So, AB + BC + AC > AD + BE + CF.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Congruent Figures: The geometrical figures having the same shape and size are known as congruent figures. e.g. Two circles of the same radii and two squares of the same sides are congruent.

Congruent Triangles: Two triangles are said to be congruent, if both are exactly of same size i.e. all angles and sides are equal to corresponding angles and sides of other.

  • Every triangle is congruent to itself: ΔABC ≅ ΔABC
  • If ΔABC ≅ ΔDEF, then ΔDEF ≅ ΔABC
  • If ΔABC ≅ ΔDEF and ΔDEF ≅ ΔPQR, then ΔABC ≅ ΔPQR

In congruent triangles, corresponding parts are equal and we write in short ‘CPCT’, i.e. corresponding part of congruent triangles.

Criteria for Congruence of Triangles:

  • Theorem 1 (SAS criteria): Two triangles are congruent if two sides and the included angle of one triangle are equal to the corresponding sides and the included angle of other triangle.
  • Theorem 2 (ASA criteria): Two triangles are congruent if two angles and the included side of one triangle are equal to the corresponding two angles and the included side of the other triangles.
  • Theorem 3 (SSS criteria): Two triangles are congruent if three sides of one triangle are equal to the corresponding three sides of the other triangle.
  • Theorem 4 (RHS criteria): Two triangles are congruent if the hypotenuse and other side of one triangle are equal to the hypotenuse and the corresponding side of the other triangle.
  • Theorem 5 (AAS criteria): Two triangles are congruent if two angles and a side other than the included side of one triangle are equal to the corresponding two angles and a side other than the included side of other triangle.

In congruent triangles, corresponding parts are equal and we write in short ‘CPCT’, i.e. corresponding part of congruent triangles.

**Criteria for Congruence of Triangles:**

- **Theorem 1 (SAS criteria):** Two triangles are congruent if two sides and the included angle of one triangle are equal to the corresponding sides and the included angle of other triangle.
- **Theorem 2 (ASA criteria):** Two triangles are congruent if two angles and the included side of one triangle are equal to the corresponding two angles and the included side of the other triangles.
- **Theorem 3 (SSS criteria):** Two triangles are congruent if three sides of one triangle are equal to the corresponding three sides of the other triangle.
- **Theorem 4 (RHS criteria):** Two triangles are congruent if the hypotenuse and other side of one triangle are equal to the hypotenuse and the corresponding side of the other triangle.
- **Theorem 5 (AAS criteria):** Two triangles are congruent if two angles and a side other than the included side of one triangle are equal to the corresponding two angles and a side other than the included side of other triangle.

### Key Formulas
- ∠BIC = 90° + 1/2 ∠A
- AB = sqrt(AD^2 + BD^2)
- BD = AB^2 / BC
- AB^2 = BD * BC

Theorem 2: The internal bisector of an angle of a triangle divides the opposite sides internally in the ratio of the sides containing the angle. If AD is internal bisector of angle A, then AB/AC = BD/DC.

Theorem 6: If two triangles are equiangular, then the ratio of their corresponding sides is the same as the ratio of the corresponding medians. BC/QR = AD/PS.

A quadrilateral, in which opposite sides are parallel is called a parallelogram.

  • Area = Base × Height = b × h
  • Perimeter = 2(a + b)

Properties of Parallelogram:

content: For a parallelogram with sides $a$ and $b$ and diagonals $d_1$ and $d_2$, the relationship is given by $d_1^2 + d_2^2 = 2(a^2 + b^2)$. Additionally, the length of a diagonal must satisfy the triangle inequality with the sides. If sides are 12 cm and 8 cm, and one diagonal is 10 cm, the other diagonal $d$ can be calculated or bounded. Using the formula: $10^2 + d^2 = 2(12^2 + 8^2) \Rightarrow 100 + d^2 = 2(144 + 64) = 416 \Rightarrow d^2 = 316 \Rightarrow d \approx 17.77$ cm. Thus, $d > 12$ cm.

Semi Circle: A diameter divides the circle into two equal parts. Each of the two is called a semi-circle.

Segment: The area enclosed by an arc and its corresponding chord is called a segment of the circle. The segment containing the minor arc is called minor segment. The segment containing the major arc is called major segment.

Sector: The area enclosed by any two radii and the arc determined by the end points of the radii is called a sector of the circle.

Circumference: The length of the complete circle is called its circumference.

Concentric Circles: Two or more circles having the same centre are called concentric circles.

Tangent: A tangent to a circle is a straight line that touches the circle at a single point. The distance between external point P from which tangent is drawn and the point of contact of the tangent is called length of tangent.

Properties of Tangent To a Circle:

  • Only two tangents can be drawn from a point outside the circle.
  • Only one tangent can be drawn through a point lying on the circle.
  • No tangent can be drawn from a point lying inside the circle.
  • A tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.

Relative Position of two Circles: Two circles will:

  • (i) be disjoint, when OO' > r1 + r2.
  • (ii) be touching externally, when OO' = r1 + r2.
  • (iii) be intersecting when OO' < r1 + r2.
  • (iv) be touching internally, when OO' = |r2 - r1|.
  • (v) one of the circle will lie inside the other, when OO' < |r2 - r1|.

text:
Theorem 1: If two arcs of a circle are congruent, then the corresponding chords are equal.

Theorem 2: Equal arcs (or chords) subtend equal angle at the centre. Here, if AB = PQ, then ∠AOB = ∠POQ.

Theorem 3: The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord. Here, if OD ⊥ AB, then AD = DB.

Theorem 4: The line joining the centre to the mid-point of a chord is perpendicular to the chord. Here, if AD = DB, then ∠ADO = ∠ODB = 90°.

Theorem 5: The perpendicular bisectors of two chords of a circle intersect at its centre. Here, AB, CD are the chords and l, m are perpendicular bisector of AB and CD. So, l and m meet at centre ‘O’.

Theorem 6: There is one and only one circle passing through three non-collinear points.

  • An infinite number of circles can be drawn to pass through a single point.
  • An infinite number of circles can be drawn to pass through two given points.
  • A unique circle can be drawn to pass through three given non-collinear points.

Theorem 7: Equal chords of congruent circles are equidistant from the corresponding centres. Here, if AB = CD, then OP = O’Q. Conversely if OP = O’Q, then AB = CD.

Theorem 8: Equal chords of a circle are equidistant from the centre. Here, if AB and CD are equal chords of circle, then OP = OQ. Conversely, if OP = OQ, then also AB = CD i.e. chords at equal distance from the centre are equal.

Cyclic Quadrilateral: A quadrilateral whose all vertices lie on a circle is called a cyclic quadrilateral.

text:
Locus: The path traced by a point moving under a given condition is called locus. e.g., The locus of points (in a plane) equidistant from a fixed point (in a plane) is a circle with the fixed point as centre. The plural of locus is loci.

  • The locus may be a line segment or lines, straight or curved.
  • Every point which satisfies the given geometrical condition(s) lies on the locus and vice-versa.

Basic Locus Theorem:

  1. The locus of points at a fixed distance d from point p is a circle with the given point p as its centre and d as its radius.
  2. The locus of points at a fixed distance d from a line m is a pair of parallel lines at a distance of d from line m and located on either side of m.
  3. The locus of points equidistant from two points A and B is the perpendicular bisector of the line segment joining the two points.
  4. The locus of points equidistant from two parallel lines m1 and m2, is a line parallel to both m1 and m2 and midway between them.
  5. The locus of points in the interior of an angle equidistant from the sides of an angle is the bisector of the angle.
  6. The locus of points equidistant from two intersecting lines l1 and l2, is a pair of bisectors that bisect the angles formed by l1 and l2.

Locus in Some Standard Cases:

  1. The loci of all points d units from a circle having a radius r units are two concentric circles with radii of r-d and r+d units respectively.
  2. The locus of all points equidistant from two concentric circles is a third circle whose radius is the average of the radii of the given circles.
  3. The locus of the mid-points of all parallel chords of a circle is the diameter of the circle, which is perpendicular to the given chords.

content:
This page contains solutions to geometry problems involving circles, chords, and triangles.

- **Angles in the same segment:** Angles subtended by the same arc at the circumference are equal.
- **Angle at the centre:** The angle subtended by an arc at the centre is double the angle subtended by it at any point on the remaining part of the circle.
- **Intersecting Chords Theorem:** If two chords AB and CD intersect at P, then AP * PB = CP * PD.
- **Pythagoras Theorem:** Used extensively in right-angled triangles formed by chords and radii.
- **Cyclic Quadrilateral:** Properties used to solve for angles in inscribed triangles.
- **In-radius of equilateral triangle:** r = a / (2 * sqrt(3)).

### Key Formulas
- OB^2 = OP^2 + BP^2
- (OA)^2 = (OP)^2 + (AP)^2
- AP * PB = CP * PD
- r = a / (2 * sqrt(3))

### Theorem
*In a cyclic quadrilateral (a quadrilateral whose vertices lie on a single circle), the sum of each pair of opposite angles is **180°** (supplementary).*  
Mathematically, if the quadrilateral is ABCD, then:
```
∠A + ∠C = 180°
∠B + ∠D = 180°
```

content:
### Central‑Angle Theorem
*The angle subtended by an arc at the centre of the circle is twice the angle subtended by the same arc at any point on the remaining part of the circle.*  
If an arc **AB** subtends **∠AOB** at the centre **O** and **∠APB** at a point **P** on the circle (but not on the arc), then:
```
∠AOB = 2 × ∠APB
```

content:
### Tangent‑From‑External‑Point Property
*From a point outside a circle, the two tangents drawn to the circle are equal in length.*  
If **P** is an external point and **PA** and **PB** are tangents touching the circle at **A** and **B** respectively, then:
```
PA = PB
```

chapter: Area and Perimeter of Plane Figures
text:
Definition: Area of a plane figure is the amount of surface enclosed by its boundary. It is measured in square units. The perimeter of a plane figure is the total length of the sides enclosing the figure. The unit of perimeter is the same as the unit of sides of a given figure.

Square Properties: Let each side of a square be a unit.

  • Perimeter of square = 4(Side) = 4a units
  • Diagonal of square = sqrt(2) * (Side) = a*sqrt(2) units
  • Area of square = Side * Side = (a)^2 sq units = 1/2 * (Diagonal)^2 = 1/2 * d^2 sq units

Isosceles Triangle: Let sides of an isosceles triangle be a, b, and b.

  • (i) Perimeter of isosceles triangle = a + b + b = a + 2b units
  • (ii) Area of isosceles triangle = (s - b) * sqrt(s - a) = 1/4 * a * sqrt(4b^2 - a^2) sq units, where a = Base and b = Equal sides and s = semi-perimeter
  • (iii) Area of a right isosceles triangle, in which equal sides from a right angle is given by Area = 1/2 * a^2 sq units
  • (iv) If theta is the angle between two equal sides of isosceles triangle, then Area of triangle = 1/2 * a^2 * sin(theta)

content: 1. **Heron's Formula**: The area of a triangle with sides $a, b, c$ is given by $\sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}$, where $s = \frac{a+b+c}{2}$.\n2. **Right-Angled Triangle Check**: A triangle with sides 7, 24, 25 is a right-angled triangle because $7^2 + 24^2 = 49 + 576 = 625 = 25^2$. The area can also be calculated as $\frac{1}{2} \times 7 \times 24 = 84 \text{ cm}^2$.\n3. **Area of Circle**: $A = \pi r^2$.

subject: Mathematics
content: 1. **Perpendicular Diameters**: If two diameters of a circle are mutually perpendicular, they form four right-angled isosceles triangles with the center as the vertex.\n2. **Area of Triangle formed by Radii**: For a triangle formed by two radii and a chord (where the angle between radii is $90^\circ$), the area is $\frac{1}{2} \times r \times r = \frac{r^2}{2}$.\n3. **Ratio Calculation**: The ratio of the area of the circle ($\pi r^2$) to the area of such a triangle ($\frac{r^2}{2}$) is $\frac{\pi r^2}{r^2/2} = 2\pi$.

subject: Mathematics
topic: Maximum Area Rectangle in a Circle
content: 1. **Inscribed Rectangle**: The rectangle of maximum area inscribed in a circle is a square.\n2. **Diagonal Relationship**: The diagonal of the inscribed square is equal to the diameter of the circle ($d$).\n3. **Area Calculation**: If the diameter is $d$, the side of the square $s$ satisfies $s^2 + s^2 = d^2 \Rightarrow 2s^2 = d^2 \Rightarrow s^2 = \frac{d^2}{2}$. Thus, the maximum area is $\frac{d^2}{2}$.

subject: Mathematics
content: 1. **Segment Area**: The area of a segment is the area of the corresponding sector minus the area of the triangle formed by the radii and the chord.\n2. **Major Segment**: Area = Total Area of Circle - Area of Minor Segment.\n3. **90 Degree Chord**: For a chord subtending $90^\circ$ at the center, the minor sector area is $\frac{90}{360}\pi r^2 = \frac{\pi r^2}{4}$. The triangle area is $\frac{1}{2}r^2$. The minor segment area is $\frac{\pi r^2}{4} - \frac{r^2}{2}$. The major segment area is $\pi r^2 - (\frac{\pi r^2}{4} - \frac{r^2}{2}) = \frac{3\pi r^2}{4} + \frac{r^2}{2}$.

subject: Mathematics
content: 1. **Midpoint Triangle**: Joining the midpoints of the sides of a triangle forms a new triangle whose sides are half the length of the original triangle's sides.\n2. **Perimeter Ratio**: The perimeter of the new triangle is half the perimeter of the previous triangle.\n3. **Infinite Series**: The sum of the perimeters of all such triangles formed is a geometric series: $P + \frac{P}{2} + \frac{P}{4} + \dots = \frac{P}{1 - 1/2} = 2P$, where $P$ is the perimeter of the first triangle.

subject: Mathematics
content: 1. **Semicircle Area**: Area of a semicircle with diameter $d$ is $\frac{1}{2}\pi (\frac{d}{2})^2 = \frac{\pi d^2}{8}$.\n2. **Right Triangle Property**: In a right-angled triangle with legs $a, b$ and hypotenuse $c$, $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$.\n3. **Area Relationship**: Let $x, y, z$ be the areas of semicircles on sides $a, b, c$ respectively. $x = \frac{\pi a^2}{8}$, $y = \frac{\pi b^2}{8}$, $z = \frac{\pi c^2}{8}$. Since $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$, it follows that $x + y = z$, or $x + y - z = 0$.

subject: Mathematics
content: 1. **Inscribed Square**: A square inscribed in a circle of diameter $2a$ (radius $a$) has a diagonal equal to $2a$. Its area is $\frac{d^2}{2} = \frac{(2a)^2}{2}

text:
Perimeter of a regular polygon: If a is the side of a regular polygon and r is the inradius, then a = 2r tan(pi/n). The perimeter p = na = 2nr tan(pi/n).

Area of a polygon: Area = nr^2 tan(pi/n) = pr/2.

Rolling rings: If a smaller ring of radius r1 rolls over a bigger ring of radius r, the number of revolutions is related to the ratio of the radii.

Wheel revolutions: The number of rounds n made by a wheel of diameter D in traversing a distance is given by n = distance / (pi * D).

chapter: Surface Area and Volume of Solids
text:
Solid Figures: The objects which occupy space (i.e. they have three dimensions) are called solid figures. The solid figures can be derived from the plane figures.

Surface Area of Solid Figure: Surface area of a solid body is the area of all of its surfaces together. It is always measured in square units. Surface area is also referred to as the total surface area. The area of four walls or the area excluding top and bottom is called curved surface area or lateral surface area.

Volume of Solid Figure: The measure of space occupied by a solid is called its volume. It is always measured in cubic units.

Cuboid: A figure which is surrounded by six rectangular surfaces, is called cuboid. It is also called rectangular parallelepiped.

  • A cuboid has 8 corners, 12 edges, 6 faces and 4 diagonals.

text:
A hollow cylinder is one which is empty from inside and has some difference between the internal and external radius. Let R and r be the external and internal radii of the hollow cylinder and h be its height. Then:

  • Volume of hollow cylinder: pi * (R^2 - r^2) * h cu units
  • Curved surface area: 2 * pi * R * h + 2 * pi * r * h = 2 * pi * (R + r) * h sq units
  • Total surface area: 2 * pi * R * h + 2 * pi * r * h + 2 * pi * (R^2 - r^2) = 2 * pi * (R + r) * (h + R - r) sq units

text:
If a right circular cone is cut-off by a plane parallel to the base of the cone, then the portion of the cone between the cutting plane and base of the cone is called the frustum of the cone. Let R, r be the radii of base and top (R > r) of the frustum of a cone. Let height of frustum of a cone be h and slant height be l, then:

  • (i) Slant height of frustum of right circular cone = sqrt(h^2 + (R-r)^2) units
  • (ii) Volume of frustum of right circular cone = (pi * h / 3) * (R^2 + r^2 + Rr) cu units
  • (iii) Curved (lateral) surface area of frustum of right circular cone = pi * l * (R + r) sq units
  • (iv) Total surface area of frustum of right circular cone = Area of base + Area of top + Lateral surface area = pi * [R^2 + r^2 + l(R + r)] sq units
  • (v) Total surface area of bucket = pi * [(R + r)l + r^2] sq units [it is open at the bigger end]

The set of all points in space, which are equidistant from a fixed point, is called a **sphere**. Let radius of sphere be *r*, then:

- (i) Volume of sphere = (4/3) * pi * r^3 cu units
- (ii) Surface area of sphere = 4 * pi * r^2 sq units
- (iii) Volume of a hollow sphere = (4/3) * pi * (R^3 - r^3) cu units, where r = Inner radius and R = Outer radius

### Key Formulas
- V = (4/3) * pi * r^3
- SA = 4 * pi * r^2
- V_hollow = (4/3) * pi * (R^3 - r^3)
