Spherical mirrors can be regarded as a part of a hollow reflecting spheres of glass. These are of two types: (i) Concave mirror, (ii) Convex mirror.

Concave mirror: The spherical mirror whose reflecting surface is inwardly leaned, called concave mirror. It is also called converging mirror.

Convex mirror: The spherical mirror whose reflecting surface is outwardly leaned, called convex mirror. It is also called diverging mirror.

Real Image:

  • Real images can be formed on a screen by the actual intersection of reflected (or refracted) light rays.
  • The image formed on a cinema screen is a real image.
  • A concave mirror forms real image, when an object is placed beyond its focus.

Image Formation by Concave Mirror:

The following are the positions and nature of the images formed in a concave mirror for different positions of the object:

  • (i) When the object is at infinity: Image is formed at F.
  • (ii) When the rays are parallel to the principal axis: The image is formed at F.
  • (iii) When the object is between infinity and C: The image formed is real, inverted and smaller in size and is formed between F and C.
  • (iv) When the object is at C: The image formed is inverted, real, equal in size and is formed at C itself.
  • (v) When the object is between F and C: The image is formed beyond C and is inverted, real and larger than the object.
  • (vi) When the object is at focus: The image is formed at infinity. The image is real, inverted and infinitely large in size.
  • (vii) When the object is between F and P: The images formed behind the pole. The image is virtual, erect and large.

Mirror Formula:

  • If v is the image distance, u is the object distance and f is the focal length of a mirror, then 1/v + 1/u = 1/f = 2/R
  • The linear magnification (m) produced by a mirror is equal to the ratio of the image distance to the object distance with negative sign, m = -v/u = f/(f-u) = (f-v)/f
  • If the magnification has positive sign, then the image is virtual and erect.
  • If the magnification has negative sign, then the image is real and inverted.

- If the magnification has positive sign, then the image is virtual and erect.
- If the magnification has negative sign, then the image is real and inverted.

### Key Formulas
- 1/v + 1/u = 1/f = 2/R
- m = -v/u = f/(f-u) = (f-v)/f

### Key Exam Facts
- **Summary:** Mathematical relations for spherical mirrors.

text:
When a ray of light passes from one medium to other, it bends from its path. This phenomenon of bending of light is called as refraction of light.

  • When light passes from rarer medium to a denser medium, it bends towards the normal at the point of incidence.
  • When light passes from a denser medium to a rarer medium, it bends away from the normal.
  • When a ray of light enters from one medium to other medium its frequency and phase do not change but wavelength and velocity change.

Laws of Refraction:

  • The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.
  • The ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is a constant for a given medium. sin i / sin r = μ [Snell's law]

where, μ is refractive index of the second medium with respect to first. μ = μ2 / μ1 = c/v2 / c/v1 = v1 / v2 or 1μ2 = v1 / v2

subject: Physics
text:
Some Illustrations of Refraction:

  • Twinkling of stars.
  • Oval shape of sun in the morning and evening.
  • Bending of a linear object when it is partially dipped in a liquid inclined to the surface of the liquid.
  • A fish in a pond when viewed from air appears to be at a smaller depth than actual depth.
  • A coin at the base of a vessel filled with water appears raised.

Total Internal Reflection:

In case of propagation of light from denser to rarer medium through a plane boundary. Critical angle is the angle of incidence for which angle of refraction is 90°. If light is propagating from denser medium towards the rarer medium and angle of incidence is more than critical angle, then the light incident on the boundary is reflected back in the denser medium, obeying the law of reflection. This phenomenon is called total internal reflection.

text:
A lens is a piece of transparent glass bounded by two spherical surfaces.

There are two types of lenses:

  • Convex lens (converging lens): A lens which is thicker at the centre and thinner at its ends.
  • Concave lens (diverging lens): A lens which is thinner at the centre and thicker at its ends.

Key Definitions:

  • The centre point of a lens is known as its optical centre.
  • The line joining the centres of the surfaces of the lens is called the principal axis of the lens.
  • The distance of the first focus from the optical centre of the lens is called the first focal length.
  • The distance of the second focus from the optical centre of the lens is called the second focal length.

If v is the image distance, u is the object distance and f is the focal length of a lens, then the lens formula applies. Magnification m is defined as the ratio of image size to object size.

  • If magnification m is positive, the image is virtual and erect.
  • If magnification m is negative, the image is real and inverted.
  • If m is the total magnification of two lenses in contact having magnification m1 and m2, then m = m1 x m2.
  • Power (P) of a lens is the reciprocal of focal length (f). SI unit is dioptre (D).
  • For combined lenses: P = P1 + P2 or 1/F = 1/f1 + 1/f2.
  • If two lenses of equal focal length but opposite nature are in contact, the combination behaves as a plane glass plate (f = infinity).

Note: When a lens is dipped in a liquid of higher refractive index, the focal length increases and convex lens behaves as concave lens and vice-versa. An air bubble in water appears as convex but behaves as concave lens.

text:
• Scattering of Light: When sunlight passes through the earth’s atmosphere, much of the light is absorbed by the fine dust particles and air molecules in the atmosphere which give out the absorbed light in some other direction. This is scattering of light.
  • The scattering of light by particle in its path is called Tyndall effect.
  • The blue coloured light present in white sunlight is scattered much more easily by air molecules causes the blue colour of the sky.
  • The sun and the surrounding sky appear red at sunrise and at sunset because at that time most of blue colour present in sunlight has been scattered out and away from our line of sight, leaving behind mainly red colour in the direct sunlight beam that reaches our eyes.
  • Dangers signals are of red colour because red colour of light scatter least and therefore signals can be seen from far.
  • If the earth had no atmosphere, there would have been no scattering of sunlight at all. In that case, no light from the sky would have entered our eyes and the sky would have looked dark and black to us.

text:
• Interference of Light: When two waves of exactly same frequency travels in a medium, in the same direction simultaneously, then due to their superposition at same points, intensity of light is maximum while at some other points intensity is minimum. This phenomenon is called interference of light.
  • Thin layer of oil on water surface and soap bubbles show various colours in white light due to interference of waves reflected from the two surfaces of the film.
  • Polarisation is the only phenomenon which proves that light is a transverse wave.
  • Diffraction of Light: If an opaque obstacle is kept between a source of light and a screen, a sufficiently distinct shadow is obtained on the screen. This shows that light which travels the obstacle is small. There is a departure from straight line propagation and so the light bends round the corners of obstacle and enters in the geometrical shadow. This bending of the light is called diffraction.

text:
• Human Eye: An optical instrument which forms real image of the objects.
  • The ability of an eye to focus the distant objects as well as the nearby objects on the retina by changing the focal length of its lens is called accommodation.
  • Least distance of distinct vision is 25 cm.
  • Far point of normal eye is at infinity.
  • Defects of Human Eye:
  • Myopia: A person suffering from myopia can see the near objects clearly while far objects are not clear; concave lens is used to remove it. Myopia is caused (i) due to high converging power of eye lens or (ii) due to eye ball being too long.
  • Hypermetropia: A person suffering from hypermetropia can see the distant objects clearly but not the near objects. Caused (i) due to low converging power of eye lens or (ii) due to eye ball being too short.
  • Presbyopia: In the old age, the power of accomodation of the eye is so much lost that a person can neither see the near objects distinctly nor the distant objects. To correct this defect bifocal lens is used.
  • Astigmatism: In this defect, a person cannot distantly see the horizontal and vertical lines, simultaneously at a normal distance. To correct this defect, cylindrical lens is used.
  • Cataract: In this defect, an opaque, white membrane is developed on cornea due to which a person loses power of vision partially or completely. This defect can be removed by removing this membrane through surgery.
  • Note: Colour blindness is a genetic disorder which occurs by inheritance. John Dalton was colour blind.

subject: Physics
text:
When two or more charged bodies come in contact, the total charge is conserved.

  • Conductors: Allow passage of electrical charges, very low resistance (e.g., copper, aluminium, gold, silver). Human body and earth are conductors; silver is the best.
  • Distribution: Charges are always distributed on the surface of a conductor.
  • Resistors: Offer high resistance (e.g., eureka, nichrome).
  • Insulators: Infinite resistance, do not allow passage of current (e.g., rubber, glass, ebonite).
  • Note: Presence of free electrons makes a substance a conductor.

text:
OHM'S LAW

If the physical circumstances of the conductor (length, temperature, etc) remains constant then the current flowing through the conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across its ends.

Resistance

The resistance of a conductor is directly proportional to its length and inversely proportional to its cross-sectional area. If l and A are respectively length and cross-sectional area of a conductor and R is its resistance, then R is proportional to l/A => R = rho * (l/A). Unit of resistance is ohm (Ω).

  • Where, rho is a constant of material of conductor is called specific resistance or resistivity. Its SI unit is ohm-metre.
  • On increasing the temperature of the metal, its resistance increases.
  • Those materials whose electrical conductivity lies in between that of insulators and conductors are called semiconductors. On increasing the temperature of semiconductor, its resistance decreases.

text:
• 1 kilowatt hour = 3600000 J = 3.6 x 10^6 J
  • 1 Horse power (HP) = 746 W
  • 1 Horse power (HP) = 550 foot-pound/second
  • Unit = (volt x ampere x hour) / 1000
  • Unit = (watt x hour) / 1000

Heating Effect of Electric Current

Heat is produced when electric current is passed through a conductor. This effect is called the heating effect of electric current.

Note: The filament of an electric bulb gets very hot and therefore easily oxidised. Thus, bulbs are sealed with inactive nitrogen and argon gases to prevent oxidation of the filament and increase its life. In electric bulb, tungsten is used for the construction of filament because it has high melting point.

Important Points Based on Heating Effect

  • In home appliances like electric iron, electric heater and heating rod, the heating element used is of a nichrome (an alloy of Ni and Cr) wire. Nichrome has high melting point and high resistivity. To avoid the risk of electric shock, the metal body of electrical appliances is earthed.
  • An electric fuse is generally prepared from tin-lead alloy (63% tin + 37% lead). It should have high resistance and low melting point. It is connected in the series.
  • Tubelight contains a long tube of glass which is linked internally with a fluorescent substance. It is filled with an inert gas like argon along with some mercury.

text:
Magnetic Effect of Current

When electricity passes through insulated copper wire, it develops a magnetic field around it. Larger the amount of electricity, stronger the magnetic field. And when we place compass needle in the radius of the magnetic field it diverts from its North-South position.

Magnets

Magnet is a piece of iron or other materials that can attract iron containing objects and the property of attracting the magnetic substance by a magnet is called magnetism.

  • The magnets which do not lose their magnetism with normal treatment are called permanent magnets.
  • The materials which retain their magnetism for a long time are called hard magnetic materials.
  • In bar, rod and horse-shoe magnets, North or South poles are either indicated by the letter N or S.
  • When poles of two magnets are brought close together, they exert force on each other. This force is called intersection between the poles.
  • If we cut a magnet in two parts, then each separate part will behave as a magnet.
  • Permanent magnets are usually made of alloys such as carbon steel, chromium steel, cobalt steel, tungsten steel and alnico (alloy of aluminium, nickel, cobalt and iron).
  • Such permanent magnets are used in microphones, loudspeakers, electric clocks, ammeters, voltmeters, speedometer and many other devices.
  • Note: The Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) technique which is used to scan inner human body parts in hospitals also uses magnets for its working.

Magnetic Field

The space in the surrounding of a magnet or a current carrying conductor in which its magnetic effect can be experience is called magnetic field.

  • Magnetic lines of force are imaginary lines in the magnetic field, which shows the direction of magnetic field continuously.
  • The magnetic field lines originate from the North pole of a magnet and end at its South pole.
  • The magnetic field lines do not intersect one another.

text:
Magnetic Materials

According to behaviour of magnetic substances, they are classified into three classes:

  • Diamagnetic substances: Substances when placed in an external magnetic field, acquire a very low magnetism in direction opposite to the field. e.g. copper, silver, bismuth, zinc, diamond, salt, water, mercury, etc. The permeability of diamagnetic substance is less than one.
  • Paramagnetic substances: Substances when placed in an external field, acquire a feeble magnetism in the direction of field. e.g. aluminium, sodium, potassium, oxygen, etc. The permeability of paramagnetic substance is slightly greater than one.
  • Ferromagnetic substances: Substances when placed in a magnetic field, acquire a strong magnetism in the direction of field. These substances when brought near the end of a strong magnet get radially attracted towards it. e.g. iron, nickel, cobalt, magnetite, etc. The permeability of ferromagnetic substance is much greater than one.

Electromagnet

An electromagnet is a solenoid coil that attains magnetism due to flow of current. It works on the principle of magnetic effect of current. It is used in electric bells, electric motors, telephone, diaphragms, loudspeakers etc.

Magnetic Flux: The magnetic flux linked with a surface is equal to the total number of magnetic lines of force passing through that surface normally. Its unit is weber.

Electromagnetic Induction: When a change occurs in the magnetic flux linked with the coil, an emf is induced in the coil. The phenomenon is called electromagnetic induction.

  • The phenomenon of production of induced emf in a circuit due to change in magnetic flux in its neighbouring circuit is called mutual induction.
  • When the electric current flowing through a circuit changes, the magnetic flux linked with circuit also change. As a result an induced emf is set up in the circuit. This phenomenon is called self-induction.
  • Microphone converts sound energy into electrical energy and works on the principle of electromagnetic induction.

text:
Electric Generator: It is a device which converts mechanical energy into electrical energy. An electric generator is based on the principle of electromagnetic induction. It is used to produce electric current by varying magnetic field through a coil.

  • A generator can produced both alternating current and direct current.
  • AC generator consists of slip rings, armature, magnet and brushes while DC generator consists of magnet commutator, armature and brushes.
  • Note: Electric motor is a rotating device which converts electrical energy into mechanical energy.

Transformer: Transformer is a device which converts low voltage AC into high voltage AC and high voltage AC into low voltage AC. It is based on mutual induction.

  • Core of a transformer is made up of soft iron.
  • Step-up transformer converts a low voltage of high current into a high voltage of low current.
  • Step-down transformer converts a high voltage of low current into a low voltage of high current.
  • The main energy losses in a transformer are given below: (a) Iron loss (b) Flux loss (c) Hysteresis loss (d) Humming loss
  • Transformer is used in voltage regulators, refrigerators, computer, air conditioner.
  • Step-down transformer is used for welding purpose.
  • Audio transformer allowed telephone circuits to carry on a two-way conversation over a single pair of wires.
  • Radio frequency transformers are used in radio communication.
  • Note: A mobile phone charger is one of the best example of step down transformer as it extracts the power from the home supply (AC 220V) and convert it to DC of required voltage.

Cathode Rays: If the gas pressure in a discharge tube is 10^-2 to 10^-3 mm of Hg and a potential difference of 10^4 V is applied between the electrode, then a beam of electrons emerges from the cathode which is called cathode rays.

  • Cathode rays are invisible and travel in a straight line.
  • These rays are deflected by electric and magnetic fields.
  • These rays can ionise gases.
  • They can produce chemical change and thus affect a photographic plate.
  • When they strike a target of heavy metal such as tungsten, they produce X-rays.

X-Rays: When cathode rays strike on a heavy metal of high melting points, then a very small fraction of its energy converts into a new type of waves, called X-rays.

  • X-rays are electromagnetic waves and these produce photoelectric effect.
  • X-rays were discovered by scientist Roentgen.
  • These produce illumination on falling the fluorescent substances and travel in a straight line with the speed of light.
  • X-rays penetrate through different depth into different substances.
  • Soft X-rays have greater wavelength and lower frequency and hard X-rays have lower wavelength and higher frequency.
  • X-rays ionise gases through which they pass.
  • X-rays are not deflected by electric and magnetic fields.
  • They show all the important properties of light rays like, reflection, refraction, interference, diffraction and polarisation, etc.
  • X-rays are used in surgery, radiotherapy, engineering department and searching.
  • Note: Barium and Iodine are some chemicals used as contrast mediums for X-ray based imaging method. i.e. they absorbs X-ray to highlight the targeted body part.

text:
Compact fluorescent lamp converts electrical energy into radiant energy.

  • It has two components:
    • A glass tube filled with argon and mercury vapour and coated with layer of fluorescent materials.
    • An electronic ballast circuit.
  • The ballast circuit (small circuit board with rectifiers, a filter capacitor and usually two switching transistors) takes a 220V input from external power source and sends a current into the fluorescent tube as output.
  • When power supply is given to the CFL, filament attached with the cathode heats up and emits electrons in the tube. This ionises the argon and mercury vapour particles, causing it, ultraviolet light emission.

Semiconductor: Materials whose electrical conductivity at room temperature lies in between that of insulator and conductor. A semiconductor in an extremely pure form is known as intrinsic semiconductor.

  • If a measured and small amount of chemical impurity is added to intrinsic semiconductor, it is called extrinsic semiconductor or doped semiconductor.
  • External semiconductors are of two types: (i) n-type semiconductor (ii) p-type semiconductor.
  • An extrinsic semiconductor in which electrons are majority charge carrier is called n-type semiconductor.
  • An extrinsic semiconductor in which holes are the majority charge carrier is called p-type semiconductor.

Special Purpose Diodes:

  • p-n junction diode: An arrangement consisting a p-type semiconductor brought into a close contact with n-type semiconductor.
  • Rectifier: A device which converts alternating current (AC) or voltage into direct current (DC).
  • LED: Specially designed diode made up of GaAsP, used in electronic gadgets as indicator light. It converts electrical energy into optical energy.
  • Zener diode: A highly doped p-n junction diode which is not damaged by high reverse current. It can be used as voltage regulator.
  • Photo diode: A special p-n junction diode fabricated with a transparent window to allow light to fall on the diode. It is used in reverse biasing.
  • Note: Diode valve acts as a rectifier and triode valve can be used as amplifier oscillator and detector.

The term communication refers to the transmitting receiving and processing of information by electronic means. A basic communication system consists of an information source, a transmitter, a link and a receiver.

  • Electromagnetic waves which are used in radio, television and other communication system are radiowaves and micro waves.
  • Ground wave propagation: The radio wave travel through atmosphere following the surface of the earth from transmitting antenna to receiving antenna. Useful for low range frequencies upto 1500 kHz.
  • Space wave propagation: Utilises electromagnetic waves of very high frequency band (30 MHz to 300 MHz), ultra high frequency band (300 MHz to 3000 MHz) and microwaves (100 GHz to 300 GHz).
  • Sky wave propagation: The radio waves from the transmitting antenna reach the receiving antenna after entering in ionosphere. The sky wave frequency lies between 2 MHz to 30 MHz.
  • Communication satellite: A space craft provided with microwave receiver and transmitter. Placed in orbit around the earth. Frequencies lie in UHF/microwave regions.
  • Remote sensing: Technique to obtain information about an object by observing it from a distance without contact.
  • Cables: Parallel wire lines (not for microwaves), Twisted pair wires (telephone), Coaxial cables (long distance high frequency, e.g., TV channel).
  • Note: Maser means 'Microwave Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation'.

content:
### Surface Tension
- **Definition**: Surface tension (γ) is the energy required to increase the surface area of a liquid by unit area, or equivalently the force acting along a line of unit length on the surface of a liquid.  
  \[ \gamma =  rac{F}{L} \]  
- **Units**: N m⁻¹ (or J m⁻²).
- **Molecular Origin**: Molecules at the surface experience a net inward cohesive force because they are not surrounded by similar molecules on all sides. This creates a contractile ‘film’ that minimizes surface area.
- **Temperature Effect**: As temperature rises, kinetic energy of molecules increases, weakening cohesive forces. Consequently, surface tension **decreases** with temperature.
- **Related Forces**:
  - **Cohesive force** – attraction between like molecules (e.g., water‑water).
  - **Adhesive force** – attraction between unlike molecules (e.g., water‑glass).
- **Angle of Contact (θ)**: The angle formed between the liquid surface and a solid at the point of contact.
  - Acute θ (< 90°) → strong adhesion (wetting).
  - Obtuse θ (> 90°) → weak adhesion (non‑wetting).
  - Water on clean glass: acute angle; mercury on glass: obtuse angle.
- **Applications**:
  - **Raincoat coating** – hydrophobic coating gives a high contact angle; water beads up and does not spread, making the fabric waterproof.
  - **Droplet shape** – small droplets become spherical because surface tension minimizes surface area.
  - **Camphor dancing & needle floating** – both phenomena are sustained by surface tension forces acting at the liquid‑air interface.

---
### Capillary Action
- **Definition**: The rise (or fall) of a liquid in a narrow tube due to the combined effect of surface tension and adhesive forces between the liquid and tube material.
- **Capillary Rise Formula**:
  \[ h =  rac{2\gamma \cos	heta}{ho g r}

content:
### Cathode Rays
- **Definition**: A stream of electrons emitted from the cathode in a discharge tube.
- **Nature**: Charged particles (negative charge).
- **Deflection**: Can be deflected by both electric and magnetic fields; the direction of deflection is opposite to that of positively charged particles.
- **Speed**: Travel at speeds **much less than the speed of light** (typically a few % of *c* depending on the accelerating voltage).
- **Key Properties**:
  - Produce fluorescence on certain phosphorescent screens.
  - Responsible for the operation of CRT displays and electron microscopes.
- **Historical Note**: Discovered by J.J. Thomson (1897) leading to the identification of the electron.

subject: Physics
content:
### X‑rays
- **Discovery**: Discovered by **Wilhelm Röntgen** in 1895.
- **Nature**: A form of electromagnetic radiation; therefore they travel at the speed of light (*c*) in vacuum.
- **Interaction with Matter**:
  - Can **pass through thin aluminium** and many other low‑Z materials.
  - Not deflected by electric or magnetic fields because they are uncharged photons.
- **Classification**:
  - **Soft X‑rays**: Lower frequency, lower energy, lower penetrating power.
  - **Hard X‑rays**: Higher frequency, higher energy, greater penetrating power.
- **Velocity**: All X‑rays, like all EM waves, have the same velocity in vacuum as ultraviolet, visible, and radio waves.
- **Attenuation**: The distance an X‑ray travels before being significantly absorbed is **minimum in dense, high‑Z materials** (e.g., iron) and maximum in gases like air.
- **Applications**: Medical imaging, crystallography, security scanning, industrial non‑destructive testing.

text:
Matter: Anything that has mass, occupies space and can be felt by our one or more sense organs is called matter. Matter is found in five physical states: solid, liquid, gas, plasma, and Bose-Einstein condensate. Out of which, three states, i.e., solid, liquid and gas are more common.

  • Solid: They have a fixed shape, volume and high density. The particles in solids are (closely) packed and held in rigid positions. They can be true or crystalline (i.e., having ordered arrangement of constituent particles to a larger distance) like metals or amorphous or pseudo solids (i.e., having short range arrangement of constituents particles) like non-metals, glass, most of the polymers, etc.
  • Liquid: They have a fixed volume but no fixed shape and have moderate to high densities. The particles in liquids are loosely packed and free to move. Their thermal conductivity decreases with rise in temperature with the exception of water.
  • Gas: They have neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume and have very low density. The particles in gas are widely spaced apart and uniformly distributed in the container.

Two More States of Matter:

  • Plasma: The state consists of super energetic and super excited particles which are in the form of ionised gases. Due to the presence of plasma, the sun and stars glow.
  • Bose-Einstein Condensate (BEC): They are formed by cooling a gas of extremely low density to super low temperatures.

chapter: Laws of Chemical Combination and Atomic Structure
text:
In chemical changes, the chemical composition as well as chemical properties of the matter changes and a new substance is formed. Burning of any substance, photosynthesis, ripening of fruits, etc., are examples of chemical change. Physical changes are reversible (i.e. can be reversed to obtain the original substance) while chemical changes are irreversible.

Laws of Chemical Combination

Combination of elements/atoms to form compounds is governed by following basic laws:

  • Law of Conservation of Mass: This law was put forth by Antoine Lavoisier in 1789. It states that, matter can neither be created nor destroyed but can be converted from one form to another. In a chemical reaction, total mass of reactants is equal to total mass of products. In terms of energy, it is called law of conservation of energy.
  • Law of Definite Proportions: A pure compound always contains same elements combined in same proportions by mass, whatever be its source. This is called law of definite proportions by weight and is given by Joseph Proust, e.g. water obtained from any source like tap water, well water, etc., always contain hydrogen and oxygen in 1:8 by mass.
  • Law of Multiple Proportions: This law was proposed by John Dalton in 1803. It states that when the fixed mass of an element combines with different masses of another element, then the masses of other elements (in two or more compounds) are in the ratio of small whole numbers. e.g. H2O (2g H : 16g O), H2O2 (2g H : 32g O) or 1g H : 32g O. Thus, ratio of O combining with same mass of H = 1:2.
  • Gay Lussac's Law of Gaseous Volumes: The volume of reactants and products in large number of chemical reactions are related to each other by small integers, provided the volumes are measured at same temperature and pressure. These statements are considered as the law of definite proportions by volume given by Gay-Lussac.

details.summary: Overview of fundamental laws governing chemical combinations including Conservation of Mass, Definite Proportions, Multiple Proportions, and Gaseous Volumes.

In a chemical reaction, total mass of reactants is equal to total mass of products. In terms of energy, it is called law of conservation of energy.
- **Law of Definite Proportions:** A pure compound always contains same elements combined in same proportions by mass, whatever be its source. This is called law of definite proportions by weight and is given by **Joseph Proust**, e.g. water obtained from any source like tap water, well water, etc., always contain hydrogen and oxygen in 1:8 by mass.
- **Law of Multiple Proportions:** This law was proposed by **John Dalton in 1803**. It states that when the fixed mass of an element combines with different masses of another element, then the masses of other elements (in two or more compounds) are in the ratio of small whole numbers. e.g. H2O (2g H : 16g O), H2O2 (2g H : 32g O) or 1g H : 32g O. Thus, ratio of O combining with same mass of H = 1:2.
- **Gay Lussac's Law of Gaseous Volumes:** The volume of reactants and products in large number of chemical reactions are related to each other by small integers, provided the volumes are measured at same temperature and pressure. These statements are considered as the law of definite proportions by volume given by Gay-Lussac.

### Key Formulas
- H2O: 2g H : 16g O
- H2O2: 2g H : 32g O
- Ratio of O = 1:2

### Key Exam Facts
- **Summary:** Overview of fundamental laws governing chemical combinations including Conservation of Mass, Definite Proportions, Multiple Proportions, and Gaseous Volumes.

text:
MOLECULES

The term molecule was given by Avogadro. It is the smallest particle of a compound which can exist in free state. All the properties of a compound depend on its constituent molecules. Molecules of a compound contain two or more different types of atoms in a fixed ratio. e.g. ammonia (NH3), water (H2O), etc.

  • Molecular mass: is the mass of a molecule. It is an additive property and is calculated by adding the atomic masses of total atoms present in a molecule. e.g. NH3 = 14 + (1)x3 = 17.
  • Equivalent weight: is obtained by dividing molecular or atomic mass by valency.

Mole Concept

The number of molecules present in 12 g of C-12 atom is called one mole. 1 mol = 6.022 x 10^23 = Avogadro's number.

  • Number of moles = Mass (in g) / Atomic or molecular mass (g mol^-1)
  • 1 mol of atom = 6.022 x 10^23 atoms
  • 1 mol of molecules = 6.022 x 10^23 molecules
  • Atomic mass: is the relative mass as compared with an atom of C-12 and is expressed in amu. (1 amu = 1.6 x 10^-24 g).
formulas: Equivalent weight = (Molecular mass or atomic mass) / Valency
Number of moles = Mass (in g) / Atomic or molecular mass (g mol^-1)

text:
ATOMIC STRUCTURE

Atoms are the basis of chemistry, even they are the basis for everything in the universe. Maharishi Kanad was one of the first person to propose that matter is made up of every small particles called parmanu. John Dalton called the particles by the name of atom.

DALTON'S ATOMIC THEORY

In 1808, John Dalton gave a theory, called atomic theory of matter which is based upon laws of chemical combination. According to this theory:

  • Atom is the smallest indivisible particle of an element, i.e. it can neither be created nor be destroyed.
  • Atoms of different elements differ in mass, size and chemical properties.
  • Atoms of same or different elements combine together to form compound or molecule. The 'number' and 'kinds' of atoms in a given molecule is fixed.
  • Atoms of the same elements can combine in more than one ratio to form different compounds.

Atom: The smallest particle of the element that can exist independently and retain all its capable of independent chemical reactions. Atoms are made up of subatomic particles like electrons, protons, neutrons, meson, positron, etc.

Molecule: The smallest particle of an element or a compound existence under ordinary conditions.

Properties of Atom:

  • Atomic Number (Z): Number of protons inside the nucleus of its atom. (In case of neutral atom, Z = number of protons = number of electrons).
  • Mass Number (A): Total number of protons and neutrons (nucleons) present in one atom of an element. (A = number of protons + number of neutrons = atomic number + number of neutrons = number of electrons + number of neutrons).

Properties of Subatomic Particles:

  • Neutron (0n1): Neutral particle. Discovered by Chadwick. Mass = 1.6 x 10-27kg.

Note: Hydrogen and protium is the only atom that does not possess neutrons.

Discovery of Subatomic Particles:

  • Cathode Rays: Travel in straight lines, cast shadows of metallic objects. In electrical/magnetic fields, behavior is similar to negatively charged electrons. First precise measurement of charge on electron made by Robert A. Millikan in 1909.

Different Atomic Species:

  • Isotopes: Atoms of the same element having the same atomic number (Z) but different mass number (A). Examples: 1H1, 1H2, 1H3; 6C12, 6C13, 6C14; 8O16, 8O17, 8O18; 10Ne20, 10Ne21, 10Ne22.
  • Isobars: Atoms of different elements having the same mass number (A) but different atomic number (Z). Examples: 1H3 and 2He3; 18Ar40, 19K40, 20Ca40; 52Te130, 56Ba130, 54Xe130.
  • Isoelectronic Species: Species having the same number of electrons but different nuclear charge. They have the same bond order. Example: Mg2+ and Na+ (both have 10 electrons).
  • Isotones: Atoms having the same number of neutrons. Example: 6C14, 7N15.

Bohr-Bury Scheme: Shows electron distribution in shells. A shell has a maximum of 2n2 electrons (n = shell number). K shell (n=1) = 2, L shell (n=2) = 8. Outermost shell cannot have more than 8 electrons.

Quantum Numbers: Four types: 1) Principal (n=1, 2, 3...), 2) Azimuthal (l=0 to n-1), 3) Magnetic (m = -1 to +1 including 0), 4) Spin (s = +1/2, -1/2).

The splitting of a heavy nucleus into two smaller of nearly comparable masses and release of about 200MeV of energy is called nuclear fission. Nuclear fission was discovered by 'Hahn' and 'Strassmann' in 1939.

  • Atom bomb is the result of uncontrolled nuclear fission.
  • The device in which controlled nuclear fission (chain reactions) is carried out is called nuclear reactor. The fission is controlled by absorbing neutrons by using cadmium or boron rods.
  • Heavy water (D2O, molecular weight 20) and graphite are used as moderator for slowing down the fast moving neutrons. U235 is used as a nuclear fuel.

The union of (two or more) lighter nuclei to form a heavier nucleus is called the nuclear fusion. It is also accompanied by release of energy because the total mass of products is lesser than the total mass of reactants.

  • Nuclear fusion occurs only at extremely high temperature (> 10^6 K), so it is also called thermonuclear reactions.
  • Hydrogen bomb (mixture of deuterium oxide and tritium dioxide) is the result of nuclear fusion.
  • Source of solar (sun) and stellar energy is nuclear fusion.
  • The source of emission of large amount of energy during nuclear fission or fusion processes is conversion of mass into energy. It is given by the relation, E = mc^2 and calculated in MeV.

text:
An ion is an electrically charged species. A positively charged ion is called cation, e.g. Na+, H+, Mg2+ while a negatively charged ion is called anion, e.g. Cl-, F-, I-.

  • A cation contains less electrons than a normal atom while an anion contains more electrons than a normal atom.
  • When an atom loses one electron, it carries one positive charge, i.e. converted into cation, and if it gains one electron, it carries one negative charge, i.e. converted into anion.
  • There is no change in atomic number or number of protons when an atom forms ion.

subject: Chemistry
text:
An electron of an atom, located in the outermost shell (valence shell) of the atom, that can be transferred to or shared with another atom is called valence electrons.

  • Elements having same number of valence electrons have similar chemical properties.
  • Elements having 1, 2 or 3 valence electrons in their atoms are metals and form cation while those having 4, 5, 6 or 7 are non-metals and form anion.
  • Elements with 8 valence electrons (except H and He which have 2 valence electrons) are inert, i.e. unreactive and exist as neutral atom.
  • If number of valence electrons = 1, 2 or 3, Valency = Number of valence electrons.
  • If number of valence electrons >= 4, Valency = 8 - number of valence electrons.

details.summary: Definition of valence electrons and rules for determining valency.

content:
An electron of an atom, located in the outermost shell (valence shell) of the atom, that can be transferred to or shared with another atom is called **valence electrons**.

- Elements having same number of valence electrons have similar chemical properties.
- Elements having 1, 2 or 3 valence electrons in their atoms are **metals** and form **cation** while those having 4, 5, 6 or 7 are non-metals and form **anion**.
- Elements with 8 valence electrons (except H and He which have 2 valence electrons) are inert, i.e. unreactive and exist as neutral atom.
- If number of valence electrons = 1, 2 or 3, Valency = Number of valence electrons.
- If number of valence electrons >= 4, Valency = 8 - number of valence electrons.

text:
The bond formed by the transfer of electrons from one atom (usually metal) to another (usually non-metal) is called electrovalent bond and the compound is called electrovalent or ionic compound. In other words, it is an intercoulombic forces of attraction between two oppositely charged species. The number of electrons transferred shows the electrovalency of the atom.

The properties of electrovalent compounds are as follow:

  • They are usually crystalline solids, i.e. have definite shape and are hard and brittle.
  • They have high melting and boiling points.
  • They conduct electricity when dissolved in water or in molten state due to the presence of free or mobile ions.
  • These are soluble in water and insoluble in organic solvents like alcohol, benzene, etc.
  • If the electronegativity difference of two atoms is 1.7, the bond between them is 50% ionic.

text:
The bond formed by the sharing of electrons between two atoms of same or different elements is called covalent bond and the compound is called covalent compound. When a non-metal combines with another non-metal, a covalent bond is formed. Covalent bond may be single, double or triple depending upon the number of sharing pairs of electrons. The number of electrons shared shows the covalency of the element.

The properties of covalent compounds are as follow:

  • Normal covalent compounds are gases or liquid under ordinary conditions of temperature and pressure.
  • These do not conduct electricity (due to the absence of free ions) and are insoluble in water but dissolve in organic solvents.
  • Graphite although is covalent but conducts electricity because of the presence of free electrons (electrical conduction).
  • These show stereoisomerism because covalent bond is directional in nature.

text:
Redox Reactions: The reactions which involve both oxidation and reduction as its two half reactions are called redox reactions. When the same one molecule is oxidised or reduced simultaneously, the reaction is called disproportionation reaction.

Oxidation: The process which involves gain of oxygen or any other electronegative element or loss of hydrogen or loss of one or more electrons (de-electronation) from an atom, ion or molecule is called oxidation. e.g. Mg -> Mg2+ + 2e-. The positive valency of an element increases by oxidation.

Reduction: The process which involves the gain of hydrogen or electropositive element or one or more electrons (electronation) or loss of oxygen by an atom, ion or molecule is called reduction. e.g. S + 2e- -> S2-. Reduction involves decrease in the positive valency of an element.

Oxidising Agent (Oxidant): It is a substance which accepts electron in the chemical reaction, i.e. electron acceptors are oxidising agent. All the positively charged species behave like oxidising agents. Oxidising agents are Lewis acids.

Reducing Agent (Reductant): The substance which donates electron in a chemical reaction is called reducing agent, i.e. electron donors are reducing agents. All the negatively charged species behave like reducing agents. Reducing agents are Lewis bases.

Oxidation State: It is the real or imaginary charge which an atom appears to have in its combined state. Oxidation state of an element may be positive, negative, zero or fractional.

Rules for Determining Oxidation State:

  • The oxidation state of an element in its free or uncombined state is zero. e.g. oxidation state of O in O2 and O3 is zero.
  • Oxidation state of hydrogen in most of its compounds is +1 but in metallic hydrides it is -1.
  • Oxidation state of oxygen in most of its compounds is -2. Except peroxides (-1), superoxides (-1/2) and oxygen fluorides (+2 or +1).

text:
Gases exhibit dependency on temperature, pressure, volume and mass. These interrelations can be analysed by gas laws. At STP/NTP, temperature (T) = 273.15 K, pressure (p) = 1 atm = 101.35 kPa, volume (V) = 22.4 L mol^-1.

Boyle's Law (Robert Boyle-1662)

At constant temperature, the volume of fixed mass of a gas is inversely proportional to its pressure.

Charles' Law (Jacques Charles-1787)

At constant pressure, volume of fixed mass of a gas is directly proportional to the absolute temperature.

Gay Lussac's Law (J.Gay Lussac-1802)

At constant volume, the pressure of fixed mass of a gas is directly proportional to its temperature.

Avogadro's Law (Amedeo Avogadro-1811)

At constant temperature and pressure, the volume of any gas is directly proportional to the number of moles of gas.

text:
Gas Equation

The three laws (Boyle's, Charle's and Avogadro's law) can be combined together in a single equation which is known as ideal gas equation.

Graham's Law of Diffusion (or Effusion)

The rate of diffusion (r) of a gas at constant temperature and pressure is inversely proportional to the square root of its molecular mass, M or density, d.

details.summary: Ideal gas equation derivation and Graham's law of diffusion.

content:
### Gas Equation

The three laws (Boyle's, Charle's and Avogadro's law) can be combined together in a single equation which is known as ideal gas equation.

### Graham's Law of Diffusion (or Effusion)

The rate of diffusion (r) of a gas at constant temperature and pressure is inversely proportional to the square root of its molecular mass, M or density, d.

### Key Formulas
- pV = nRT
- R = 0.0821 L atm mol^-1 K^-1 = 8.3143 J mol^-1 K^-1 = 5.189 x 10^19 eV mol^-1 K^-1 = 1.99 cal mol^-1 K^-1
- k = R/N = R / 6.022 x 10^23
- d = pM/RT
- n = Mass (m) / Molecular weight (M)
- r1/r2 = sqrt(M2/M1) = sqrt(d2/d1)

### Key Exam Facts
- **Summary:** Ideal gas equation derivation and Graham's law of diffusion.

A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more substances on molecular level is called true solution or solution. e.g. lemonade, soda water. The substance which is dissolved in a liquid to make a solution is called 'solute' and the liquid in which the solute is dissolved is called 'solvent'.

A true solution does not scatter light and its particles cannot be seen even by microscope. e.g. salt solution, sea water, sugar solution, copper sulphate solution, vinegar, etc.

Depending upon the amount of solute present, the solutions can be classified as:

  • A solution, in which more quantity of solute can be dissolved without raising its temperature is called unsaturated solution.
  • A solution, in which no more solute can be dissolved at that temperature is called saturated solution.

text:
The amount of a solute dissolved in unit weight or volume of solution is called strength (concentration) of a solution.

So, concentration of a solution = (Amount of solute (in g) / Weight of solution) = (Amount of solute (in g) / Volume of solution)

Different Terms to Express Concentration

  • Parts Per Million: It shows the parts of solute present per million parts of solution, i.e. ppm. = (Mass of solute (in g) * 10^6) / Volume of solution (in mL)
  • Molarity (M): The number of moles of solute dissolved in one litre of solution is called its molarity.
  • Molality (m): The number of moles of solute dissolved in 1000 g of a solvent is called its molality.
  • Normality (N): The number of gram equivalents of solute dissolved in one litre of solution is known as its normality.

Note: Normality and molarity are affected by temperature as these depend upon the volume whereas molality remains unaffected from temperature change.

m = (Weight of solute (in g) * 1000) / (Molecular weight * weight of solvent (in g))
N = (Weight of solute (in g) * 1000) / (Equivalent weight * volume of solution (in mL))

subject: Chemistry
text:
Osmosis

It is the process of movement of solvent molecules from the solution of low concentration to high concentration through semipermeable membrane.

  • If pressure greater than osmotic pressure (pressure require to stop osmosis) is applied on the solution of high concentration, reverse osmosis takes place. e.g. desalination of sea water.
  • Isotonic solutions have same concentration and osmotic pressure. e.g. 0.91% solution of pure NaCl is isotonic with human red blood cells (RBCs).

Diffusion

  • Diffusion is the process of spontaneous mixing of different gases and in this process, molecules of a substance move from higher concentration to lower concentration and goes on until a uniform mixture is formed. Its rate is highest for gases and lowest in solids. e.g. the smell of food being cooked, reaches us even from a considerable distance by the process of diffusion. Due to diffusion the scent spread all over the room if the lid is opened.

details.summary: Definitions and examples of Osmosis, Reverse Osmosis, and Diffusion.

content:
### Osmosis

It is the process of movement of solvent molecules from the solution of low concentration to high concentration through semipermeable membrane.

- If pressure greater than osmotic pressure (pressure require to stop osmosis) is applied on the solution of high concentration, **reverse osmosis** takes place. e.g. desalination of sea water.
- **Isotonic solutions** have same concentration and osmotic pressure. e.g. 0.91% solution of pure NaCl is isotonic with human red blood cells (RBCs).

### Diffusion

- Diffusion is the process of spontaneous mixing of different gases and in this process, molecules of a substance move from higher concentration to lower concentration and goes on until a uniform mixture is formed. Its rate is highest for gases and lowest in solids. e.g. the smell of food being cooked, reaches us even from a considerable distance by the process of diffusion. Due to diffusion the scent spread all over the room if the lid is opened.

subject: Chemistry
text:
The substances which have sour taste and turn blue litmus to red are called acids.

  • According to Arrhenius acids give hydrogen ion H+ in an aqueous solution. HCl (aq) -> H+(aq) + Cl-(aq)
  • According to Bronsted Lowry concept, acids donate proton (hydrogen ion). HCl + NH3 -> Cl- + NH4+
  • According to Lewis concept, acids have tendency to accept electrons, i.e. these behave as electrophiles. e.g. electron deficient species like BF3, AlCl3, positive ions like Na+, K+ and molecules having multiple bond between dissimilar atoms (e.g. CO2, SO2, etc).
  • Most of the acids contain hydrogen.
  • HCl, H2SO4, HNO3 are mineral acids and are much stronger than organic acids.
  • Aqua-regia is a mixture of concentrated hydrochloric acid and concentrated nitric acid in the ratio 3 : 1. It can dissolve inert materials like platinum, gold, etc.

Properties of Acids

  • Acids liberate hydrogen gas with more reactive metals. e.g. Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2
  • Acids evolve carbon dioxide (CO2) gas with metal carbonates and bicarbonates. e.g. MCO3 + H2SO4 -> MSO4 + H2O + CO2
  • In aqueous solution, they are conductor of electricity due to the presence of free H+ ions.

text:
These substances which have bitter taste and turn red litmus to blue are called bases.

  • According to Arrhenius, bases give hydroxyl ion (OH-) in aqueous solution. e.g. NaOH, KOH, CsOH, Mg(OH)2, etc. NaOH (aq) -> Na+(aq) + OH-(aq)
  • According to Bronsted Lowry concept, bases have a tendency to accept proton, e.g. NH3, H2O, etc. NH3 + H2O <-> NH4+ + OH-
  • According to Lewis concept, bases have a tendency to donate electron pair. e.g. simple anions like Cl-, F-, OH-, etc., molecules containing lone pairs like NH3, R-O-H, R-O-R, etc.

Properties of Bases

  • Base reacts with metal to form salt and liberates hydrogen gas. However, such reactions are not possible with all metals.
  • Water soluble bases are called alkali. Thus, all alkalis are bases but all the bases are not alkali.
  • In aqueous solution and molten state, they are good conductors of electricity.

subject: Chemistry
text:
pH Scale: SPL Sorensen suggested a scale to express the acidity or basicity of an aqueous solution in terms of hydrogen ion concentration. It is based on the ionic product of water.

  • pH is defined as the negative logarithm to the base 10 of the hydrogen ion concentration in moles per litre.
  • In pure water or neutral solution, [H+] = 10^-7, so pH = 7.
  • In an acidic solution, [H+] > 10^-7, so pH < 7.
  • In an alkaline solution, [H+] < 10^-7, so pH > 7.

Importance of pH in Everyday Life:

  • Bee/Ant sting: Contains formic acid; treated with mild base like baking soda or calamine.
  • Wasp sting: Contains base; treated with mild acid.
  • Tooth decay: Mouth pH below 5.5 leads to decay; toothpaste (basic) helps maintain pH.
  • Stomach acidity: Excess HCl is neutralised by antacids like milk of magnesia [Mg(OH)2] or aluminium hydroxide [Al(OH)3].
  • Soil pH: Crops grow in specific ranges (e.g., rice prefers slightly acidic soil, sugarcane prefers neutral, citrus prefers alkaline).

Note: Strong acids/bases are corrosive. Pickles are kept in glass jars because acids react with metal pots.

|---|---|
| Soft drinks | 2.0-4.0 |
| Tears | 7.4 |
| Lemon | 2.2-2.4 |
| Sea water | 8.5 |
| Human urine | 4.8-8.4 |
| Cow's milk, saliva | 6.5 |
| Rain water | 6.0 |
| Human blood | 7.36-7.42 |

text:
Thermodynamics deals with the study of heat and energy changes occurring during a physical and chemical processes.

  • Open system: Can exchange matter as well as energy with its surroundings, e.g., hot tea in a cup.
  • Closed system: Can exchange energy but not matter with its surroundings, e.g., hot water in a closed beaker.
  • Isolated system: Can exchange neither matter nor energy with its surroundings, e.g., thermos flask.

subject: Chemistry
text:
• Isothermal Process: The process in which temperature of the system remains constant, i.e., dT = 0. Maximum work done during the isothermal expansion of 'n' moles of an ideal gas is given as W_max = -2.303 nRT log(V2/V1).
  • Adiabatic Process: The process in which no heat enters or leaves the system during any step of process, i.e., dq = 0.
  • Isobaric Process: The process which takes place at constant pressure, i.e., dp = 0.
  • Isochoric Process: The process in which volume of system remains constant, i.e., dV = 0.
  • Cyclic Process: In a cyclic process, a system in a given state goes through a series of different processes but finally returns to its initial state, i.e., dE or dU = 0.
  • Spontaneous Process: A process, i.e., physical or chemical change, which can proceed by itself. It is also known as feasible and probable process. The process is spontaneous if free energy change, ΔG is negative.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Surface Chemistry deals with the phenomenon that occurs at the surface or interfaces.

Catalysis: The term catalyst is given by Berzelius. A catalyst is a substance which alters the rate of reaction without being consumed in it and the phenomenon is known as catalysis.

General Characteristics of Catalysts:

  • A catalyst remains unchanged in mass and chemical composition during a reaction.
  • Only a very small amount of catalyst is sufficient to catalyse a reaction. A catalyst does not initiate a reaction.
  • A catalyst does not change the equilibrium state of a reversible reaction as it increases the rate of forward as well as backward reaction to the same extent.
  • When a reversible reaction is performed in a closed container, a state is reached when the rate of forward and backward reactions become equal. This state is called chemical equilibrium or equilibrium state.
  • Free energy change (ΔG°) at equilibrium is zero.

Types of Catalyst:

  1. Positive and Negative Catalysts: Increases rate (positive) or decreases rate (negative).
  2. Induced Catalyst: The product of one reaction acts as catalyst for another reaction.
  3. Catalytic Promoters and Inhibitors: Promoters increase activity, inhibitors decrease activity.
  4. Catalytic Poisons: Destroy the activity of a catalyst completely.

Enzyme Catalysis: Known as biocatalysts. All enzymes are protein in nature, highly sensitive to temperature (optimum 25-37°C), and affected by pH change.

subject: Chemistry
content:
### Definition
A **colloidal solution** (or colloid) is a **heterogeneous system** in which one substance (the *dispersed phase*) is distributed as very fine particles throughout another substance (the *dispersion medium**).

### Size Range
- Particle size: **1 nm – 100 nm**
- Larger than particles in a true solution (<1 nm) but smaller than those in a suspension (>100 nm).

---

subject: Chemistry
content:
### Brownian Movement
- **Definition**: The rapid, random zig‑zag motion exhibited by colloidal particles when they are bombarded by molecules of the dispersion medium.
- **Significance**: Prevents settling of colloidal particles and contributes to the stability of the colloid.

---

subject: Chemistry
content:
### Tyndall Effect
- **Definition**: When a strong, converging beam of light passes through a colloidal solution, the light path becomes visible because the colloidal particles scatter the light.
- **Example**: The blue appearance of sea water.
- **Distinguishing Feature**: Unlike true solutions, colloids show this visible scattering of light.

---

subject: Chemistry
content:
### Electrophoresis
- **Definition**: Migration of charged colloidal particles under the influence of an external electric field toward the electrode of opposite charge.
- **Application**: Used for separation and analysis of colloidal particles (e.g., proteins, DNA).

---

subject: Chemistry
content:
### Dialysis
- **Definition**: A method of purifying colloidal solutions by allowing small soluble impurities to pass through a semi‑permeable membrane while retaining the larger colloidal particles.
- **Process**: The colloidal dispersion is placed in a dialysis bag; the bag is immersed in a large volume of pure solvent. Over time, the solvent diffuses in and out, carrying away low‑molecular‑weight contaminants.

---

subject: Chemistry
content:
### Emulsion
- **Definition**: A colloidal system consisting of **two immiscible liquids** where one liquid forms the dispersed phase and the other acts as the dispersion medium.
- **Common Example**: Milk (fat droplets dispersed in water).

---

subject: Chemistry
content:
### Types of Emulsions
| Type | Dispersed Phase | Continuous Phase | Example |
|------|----------------|------------------|---------|
| **Oil‑in‑Water (O/W)** | Oil droplets | Water | Milk, mayonnaise |
| **Water‑in‑Oil (W/O)** | Water droplets | Oil (lubricating oil) | Stiff greases |

---

subject: Chemistry
content:
### Emulsifying Agents
- Small amounts of substances added during emulsion preparation to **stabilise** the system.
- Common agents: **soap, gums, agar, proteins**.
- **Mechanism**: They adsorb at the oil‑water interface, reducing interfacial tension and forming a protective film around droplets, preventing coalescence.

---

subject: Chemistry
content:
### Gel
- **Definition**: A colloidal system where the **dispersed phase is liquid** and the **dispersion medium is solid**.
- **Examples**: Butter, cheese.
- **Syneresis (Weeping)**: Over time, a gel may expel the liquid dispersed phase; this phenomenon is called **syneresis** or **weeping**.

---

subject: Chemistry
content:
### Fog, Clouds, Mist
- **Classification**: Colloidal systems of **liquid particles dispersed in a gas** (air).
- **Differences**:
  - **Fog**: Visible water droplets near the ground.
  - **Clouds**: Water droplets or ice crystals suspended at higher altitudes.
  - **Mist**: Very fine droplets, often formed by rapid cooling of humid air.

---

subject: Physics
content:
## Secondary Batteries (Rechargeable)
- Function as **both galvanic and electrolytic cells**; they can be **re‑charged** and reused.
- Common examples: **Lead‑acid (lead storage) battery**, **Nickel‑Cadmium (Ni‑Cd) battery**.
- Unlike primary (non‑rechargeable) cells, the chemical reactions are **reversible**:
  - During discharge the cell operates as a **galvanic cell** producing electrical energy.
  - During charging an external voltage drives the reverse reaction, restoring the original chemical composition.
- Typical applications:
  - **Lead‑acid** – automobiles, inverters, UPS systems.
  - **Ni‑Cd** – torchlights, electric shavers, portable electronic devices.

subject: Physics
content:
## Important Batteries

| Battery Type | Anode (‑) | Cathode (+) | Electrolyte | Typical Uses |
|--------------|----------|------------|-------------|--------------|
| **Leclanche (Dry) cell** | Zinc | Carbon (graphite) rod | Paste of **NH₄Cl** and **ZnCl₂** | Transistors, clocks |
| **Mercury cell** | Zinc‑mercury amalgam | Paste of **HgO** and carbon | Paste of **KOH** and **ZnO** | Hearing aids, watches, camera |
| **Lead‑storage cell** | Lead | Lead dioxide (PbO₂) (packed with lead) | **38 % H₂SO₄** (sulphuric acid) | Automobiles, inverters |
| **Nickel‑Cadmium cell** | Cadmium | Nickel dioxide (NiO₂) | **KOH** solution | Torchlights, electric shavers |

**Key points**
- The **anode** is the site of oxidation; the **cathode** is the site of reduction.
- The **electrolyte** provides ionic conductivity and participates in the redox reactions.
- Choice of materials determines voltage, capacity, shelf‑life, and suitable applications.

subject: Physics
content:
## Fuel Cells

- **Definition**: A fuel cell is a **galvanic cell** that converts the chemical energy of a fuel (e.g., **H₂, CH₄, CH₃OH**) directly into electrical energy.
- **Typical reaction** (hydrogen‑oxygen fuel cell):
  ```
  2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O   (ΔE° ≈ 1.23 V)
  ```
- **Historical note**: First used in the **Apollo space programme**; water produced was condensed and used as drinking water for astronauts.

### Advantages
- **Higher efficiency** than conventional power stations or batteries because fewer energy‑conversion steps are involved.
- **Reduced losses**: Minimal waste heat, no moving mechanical parts → lower frictional losses.
- **Clean energy**: The only combustion product of a hydrogen‑oxygen fuel cell is **water**, making it a non‑polluting source.

### Disadvantages
- **Scale limitation**: Not yet viable for large‑scale power generation; fossil‑fuel or nuclear plants remain essential.
- **Hydrogen storage**: Hydrogen is a low‑density gas; storing it requires **large volumes** or **high‑pressure tanks**.
- **Safety concerns**: High‑pressure storage increases risk of leaks and accidents; hydrogen is highly flammable.

subject: General Science
content:
### Second Law of Electrolysis

- **Statement**: The masses of the elements liberated at the electrodes during electrolysis are directly proportional to their atomic masses when an appropriate integral divisor is applied.
- **Mathematical Form**:
  $$\frac{W_E}{W_E'} = \frac{M_E}{M_E'}$$
  where \(W_E\) and \(W_E'\) are the masses of two different elements produced, and \(M_E\) and \(M_E'\) are their respective atomic masses.
- **Implication**: This law allows calculation of the equivalent weight of an element and is the basis for determining the composition of compounds via electrolysis.

subject: General Science
content:
### Electrochemical Series (Reactivity Series)

- **Definition**: A list of metals (and hydrogen) arranged in order of increasing standard reduction electrode potential (E°). It is also called the *reactivity series* because reactivity follows the reverse order of the series.
- **Key Points**:
  - Lower (more negative) reduction potential → greater reducing power.
  - Metals higher in the series can displace metals lower in the series from their salt solutions.
  - Metals placed **before hydrogen** can liberate H₂ from dilute acids.
- **Typical Order (most reactive → least reactive)**:
  ```
  K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Ni > Sn > Pb > (H) > Cu > Ag > Au
  ```
- **Examples**:
  - No reaction: \(\text{Cu} + \text{FeSO}_4 \rightarrow \text{No reaction}\)
  - Displacement: \(\text{Fe} + \text{CuSO}_4 \rightarrow \text{FeSO}_4 + \text{Cu}\)
  - Acid reaction: \(\text{Zn} + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{ZnCl}_2 + \text{H}_2\)
- **Applications**:
  - Predicting feasibility of redox reactions.
  - Selecting appropriate metals for corrosion protection (e.g., using Zn as a sacrificial anode).

subject: General Science
content:
### Corrosion

- **Definition**: Oxidative deterioration of a metal surface caused by the environment, leading to unwanted corrosion products.
- **Common Forms**:
  - **Rusting of Iron**: \(4Fe + 3O₂ + 6H₂O \rightarrow 2Fe₂O₃·xH₂O\)
  - **Tarnishing of Silver**: Formation of silver sulfide (Ag₂S).
  - **Green Coating on Copper/Bronze**: Basic copper carbonate \(Cu(OH)₂·CuCO₃\).
- **Nature**: Primarily an electrochemical process involving anodic dissolution of metal and cathodic reduction of oxygen/hydrogen ions.
- **Accelerating Factors**:
  - Impurities in the metal.
  - Presence of acidic ions (H⁺), electrolytes (e.g., NaCl), and gases such as CO₂, SO₂, NO, NO₂.

### Prevention of Corrosion

1. **Barrier Protection** (coating):
   - Paints, greases, and plating with less reactive metals (Zn, Cu, Ni, Cr, Sn).
   - Adherent films like iron phosphate or magnetic oxide (Fe₃O₄).
2. **Alloying**: Adding suitable alloying elements to improve corrosion resistance (e.g., stainless steel with Cr and Ni).
3. **Cathodic Protection**:
   - **Sacrificial Anode**: Attaching a more reactive metal (e.g., Zn) that preferentially corrodes.
   - **Impressed Current**: Supplying external current to make the protected metal the cathode.

subject: Chemistry
content:
### Periodic Trends (Left → Right)
- **Electronegativity** increases.
- **Ionisation potential** (first ionisation energy) increases.
- **Electron affinity** increases.
- **Acidic nature of oxides** increases.
- **Non‑metallic nature** increases.

These trends arise because, moving across a period, the effective nuclear charge felt by the valence electrons increases while the shielding remains almost constant, pulling electrons closer to the nucleus.

---
### Periodic Trends (Top → Bottom)
- **Atomic radius** increases.
- **Electropositive / metallic nature** increases.
- **Reducing nature** increases.
- **Basic nature of oxides** increases.
- **Electronegativity**, **ionisation potential**, **electron affinity**, **acidic nature of oxides** and **non‑metallic nature** decrease.

The increase in principal quantum number (n) down a group adds electron shells, which outweighs the increase in nuclear charge, leading to the observed trends.

subject: Chemistry
topic: Common Features of Elements in a Group
content:
All elements belonging to the same **group** (vertical column) possess the same **number of valence electrons**. Consequently, they exhibit **similar chemical properties** such as:
- Valence‑electron driven reactivity
- Types of oxides formed (basic, amphoteric, acidic)
- Typical oxidation states

The systematic variation of physical properties (atomic radius, ionisation energy, etc.) within a group is described in the *Group Trends* section of the notes.

subject: Chemistry
content:
Hydrogen (Z = 1) has three isotopes:
| Isotope | Symbol | Neutrons | Nature |
|---------|--------|----------|--------|
| **Protium** | \(^1\)H | 0 | Stable, most abundant |
| **Deuterium** | \(^2\)H or D | 1 | Stable, "heavy" hydrogen |
| **Tritium** | \(^3\)H or T | 2 | Radioactive (β‑emitter, half‑life ≈ 12.3 years) |

These isotopes differ only in neutron count, which influences physical properties (e.g., boiling point) but not chemical behaviour under most conditions.

subject: Chemistry
content:
- **Atomic number:** 1
- **Mass number (most common):** 1 (\(^1\)H)
- **State at STP:** Colourless, odourless gas
- **Combustion:** Burns with a characteristic *pop* sound; forms water (H₂O).
- **Reactivity:** Highly inflammable; forms covalent bonds with most non‑metals and ionic bonds with highly electropositive metals.
- **Support for combustion:** Does **not** support combustion; it is a *fuel* rather than an oxidiser.

subject: Chemistry
content:
### Water – The Neutral Oxide of Hydrogen
- **Melting point:** 0 °C (273 K)
- **Boiling point:** 100 °C (373 K) – unusually high due to extensive **hydrogen‑bonding** between H₂O molecules.
- **Polarity:** Dipole moment = 1.85 D; leads to high dielectric constant (ε ≈ 81).
- **Universal solvent:** Ability to dissolve a wide range of ionic and polar substances stems from its polarity and hydrogen‑bonding capability.
- **Specific heat:** Very high (4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹), making water an excellent coolant.
- **Test for water:** Anhydrous CuSO₄ turns **blue** in the presence of water (hydrated CuSO₄·5H₂O).

### Soft vs. Hard Water
- **Soft water:** Forms lather readily with soap (no calcium/magnesium ions).
- **Hard water:** Contains Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ ions that react with soap to produce insoluble scum, reducing lather formation.

### Coinage (Currency) Metals – Group 11

- **Elements:** Cu (Copper), Ag (Silver), Au (Gold)
- **General Characteristics**
  - d‑block transition elements
  - Very hard, malleable and ductile
  - High density, high melting and boiling points
- **Important Compounds & Uses**
  - **CuSO₄ (Copper sulphate pentahydrate)** – blue vitriol; used as a mordant in dyeing and to test for water presence.
  - **Alloys:** Copper is alloyed with gold and silver for making ornaments.
  - **AgNO₃ (Silver nitrate)** – called *lunar caustic*; stored in dark brown bottles because it is photosensitive.
  - **Aqua‑regia dissolution:** Au, Ag, Pt and similar noble metals are resistant to most acids but dissolve in aqua‑regia (HCl : HNO₃ = 3 : 1).
- **Key Points**
  - These metals are economically important as currency and jewelry.
  - Their compounds find applications in textile dyeing, analytical chemistry, and metallurgy.

topic: Alkaline Earth Metals (Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba, Ra)
content:
### Alkaline Earth Metals – Group 2

- **Elements:** Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba, Ra (s‑block)
- **General Characteristics**
  - Soft, relatively low melting points compared to transition metals
  - Form divalent cations (M²⁺) and oxides that are basic
- **Notable Facts & Uses**
  - **Calcium (Ca):** Most abundant element in Earth’s crust.
  - **Magnesium (Mg):** Present in chlorophyll (green pigment of leaves).
  - **Beryllium (Be):** Shows diagonal relationship with aluminium (similar ionic radii & some chemical behaviour).
- **Important Compounds**
  - **Mg(OH)₂ – Milk of Magnesia:** Mild base, used as an antacid.
  - **MgSO₄ – Epsom salt:** Mordant in dyeing/tanning; also used as a purgative.
  - **CaO – Quicklime:** Hisses on contact with water; used in glass making, cement, mortar, bleaching powder, calcium carbide, drying agents for ammonia/alcohol, and iron extraction.
  - **Ca(OH)₂ – Slaked Lime:** Used in manufacturing bleaching powder, caustic soda, soda lime, and for softening hard water.
  - **CaCO₃ – Calcium carbonate:** When dipped in water releases CO₂ bubbles (acidic reaction).
  - **CaSO₄ – Gypsum:** Widely used in construction (plaster of Paris) and as a drying agent.
- **Key Points**
  - Alkaline earth metals are essential in biological systems (Mg in chlorophyll, Ca in bones).
  - Their oxides and hydroxides are important industrial bases and drying agents.

### IVA Group (Carbon Family)
- **Elements:** C, Si, Ge, Sn, Pb

- **Tetrahalide stability & volatility:**
  - Stability decreases with increasing molecular weight.
  - Volatility order: **CF₄ > CCl₄ > CBr₄ > CI₄**

*The trend is due to the increasing size and decreasing bond dissociation energy of the C–X bond as X becomes heavier.*

subject: Chemistry
content:
### Carbon
- Forms the **largest number of compounds** of any element (except hydrogen) because of:
  1. **Catenation power** – strong C–C bonds allow long chains and rings.
  2. **Tetravalency** – each carbon can form four covalent bonds.
- Exists in several **allotropic forms**; the two major crystalline allotropes are **diamond** and **graphite**.
- **Key properties:**
  - Atomic number: 6
  - Electron configuration: 1s² 2s² 2p²
  - Non‑metal, high electronegativity (2.55 Pauling)
  - Forms strong covalent bonds with many elements.

subject: Chemistry
content:
### Diamond
- **Structure:** 3‑dimensional tetrahedral network; each carbon atom is sp³‑hybridised and bonded to four other carbon atoms.
- **Physical properties:**
  - Hardest known natural material.
  - Bad conductor of electricity (insulator).
  - High thermal conductivity.
- **Uses:**
  - Jewellery (precious gemstone).
  - Abrasive for cutting/sharpening hard tools (rock‑drilling machines, glass cutting, etc.).
- **Key point:** The rigidity of the 3‑D network gives diamond its exceptional hardness.

subject: Chemistry
content:
### Graphite
- **Structure:** Layered 2‑dimensional hexagonal sheets; each carbon atom is sp²‑hybridised, bonded to three neighbours, with a delocalised π‑electron system above and below each sheet.
- **Preparation:** Large‑scale artificial production by the **Acheson process**.
- **Physical properties:**
  - Good conductor of electricity (due to delocalised electrons).
  - Soft, lubricating, and slippery.
- **Uses:**
  - Dry lubricant.
  - Moderator in nuclear reactors (slows down neutrons).
  - Pencil “lead” (mixed with clay).
- **Key point:** The weak van‑der‑Waals forces between layers allow them to slide over each other, giving graphite its lubricating property.

subject: Chemistry
content:
### Fullerenes
- A newer class of carbon allotropes beyond diamond and graphite.
- The first identified fullerene is **C₆₀**, shaped like a soccer ball (truncated icosahedron).
- Exhibit unique chemical and physical properties, useful in nanotechnology, materials science, and medicine.

subject: Chemistry
content:
### Coal
- **Nature:** Amorphous carbonaceous rock used primarily as a fuel.
- **Types (by carbon content):**
  1. **Peat** – ~60 % C
  2. **Lignite (brown coal)** – ~70 % C
  3. **Bituminous** – 78–83 % C (most common)
  4. **Anthracite** – ~90 % C

### Charcoal
- **Forms:** Animal charcoal, wood charcoal, sugar charcoal, activated charcoal.
- **Uses:**
  - Production of fuel gases:
    - **Water gas:** CO + H₂
    - **Producer gas:** N₂ + CO
    - **Semi‑water gas:** mixture of water gas and producer gas.
  - Fuel for heating and metallurgical processes.
  - **Deodorant** in water purification and **decolourising sugar**.
- **Note:** Charcoal is obtained by **pyrolysis** of organic material in limited oxygen.

content:
### VA Group (Group 15) – Elements
- **Elements**: N (7), P (15), As (33), Sb (51), Bi (83)
- **Abundance**: Phosphorus is the most abundant in the earth’s crust.
- **Key Properties & Uses**:
  - **Nitrogen (N)**: Essential component of explosives; used in chips packets and electric bulbs to increase life due to its inert nature.
  - **Ammonia (NH₃)**: Alkaline gas, highly soluble in water, dried over quicklime.
  - **Nitrogen Oxides**: When dissolved in water they form oxy‑acids (e.g., NO₂ → HNO₃). Nitric acid is a strong acid employed in fertilizer and explosive synthesis.
  - **Phosphorus (P)**:
    - *Red phosphorus*: Used in match industry and to make phosphor bronze (Cu‑Sn‑P alloy).
    - *Ignition temperature*: 543 K (higher than white phosphorus, 303 K) → less prone to spontaneous ignition.
  - **Arsenic, Antimony, Bismuth**: Not detailed in the excerpt but belong to the same group.

**Important Reactions**
- **Formation of nitric acid**: \(	ext{NO}_2 + H_2O ightarrow HNO_3\)
- **Ammonia preparation**: Typically via Haber‑Bosch process (not in text but related).

---
**Key Take‑aways**
1. The VA group elements show a trend of decreasing electronegativity and increasing metallic character down the group.
2. Nitrogen and its oxides are central to both agriculture (fertilizers) and defense (explosives).
3. Red phosphorus is safer to handle than white phosphorus due to its higher ignition temperature.

subject: Chemistry
topic: Elements, Oxidation States and Major Compounds
content:
### VIA Group (Group 16) – Elements (Chalcogens)
- **Elements**: O (8), S (16), Se (34), Te (52), Po (84)
- **Abundance**: Oxygen is the most abundant element of this family and of the whole crust.
- **Common Oxidation State**: –2 (except in peroxides, superoxides, and higher oxidation states).

#### Important Properties & Applications
- **Oxygen (O₂)**:
  - Gaseous form supports combustion.
  - **Ozone (O₃)**: Allotrope, diamagnetic gas, absorbs UV radiation in the stratosphere.
- **Sulphur (S)**:
  - **Sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄)** – *Oil of vitriol*; dibasic, strong dehydrating agent, used in making explosives.
  - **Sulphur dioxide (SO₂)** – Bleaching agent (temporary bleaching due to reduction).
  - **Sulphur oxides** (SO₂, SO₃) contribute to acid rain.
- **Selenium (Se) & Tellurium (Te)**: Not detailed but share similar chemistry.
- **Polonium (Po)**: Radioactive, limited practical uses.

#### Representative Reactions
- **Formation of Sulphuric Acid**: \(2\,SO_3 + H_2O ightarrow H_2SO_4\)
- **Ozone Formation**: \(3\,O_2 \xrightarrow{UV}\ O_3 + O_2\)

---
**Key Points**
1. The chalcogens exhibit a clear trend: non‑metallic character decreases down the group.
2. Oxygen’s –2 oxidation state dominates, but higher states (+1, +2, +4, +6) appear in peroxides, superoxides, and oxides of sulfur.
3. Sulphuric acid’s dehydrating power makes it indispensable in industrial chemistry.

content:
### Organic Compounds
- **Definition**: Chemistry of hydrocarbons and their derivatives is termed *organic chemistry*.
- **First laboratory‑synthesised organic compound**: **Urea** (NH₂‑CONH₂) – prepared by **Wöhler**.
- **First organic compound synthesised from its elements**: **Acetic acid** (CH₃COOH) – synthesised by **Kolbe**.
- **Major natural sources**: Plants, animals, coal, and petroleum.

subject: Organic Chemistry
content:
### Hydrocarbons
- **Definition**: Compounds containing **only carbon (C) and hydrogen (H)**.
- **Two broad classes**:
  1. **Saturated hydrocarbons** – *Paraffins* or **Alkanes** (contain only C–C single bonds).
  2. **Unsaturated hydrocarbons** – contain one or more multiple bonds (C=C or C≡C).

subject: Organic Chemistry
content:
### Alkanes (Paraffins)
- **General formula**: \(C_{n}H_{2n+2}\)  where \(n = 1, 2, 3, \dots\).
- **Hybridisation**: All carbon atoms are **sp³‑hybridised**.
- **Isomerism**: Exhibit **chain (structural) isomerism**.
- **First member**: **Methane (CH₄)**
  - *Source*: Wet, marshy lands; also present in animal exhaled air (from cellulose‑rich diet).
  - *Coal*: Cavities contain ~90 % methane, called **fire‑damp** (explosion hazard in mines).
  - *Uses*: Gaseous fuel, production of **carbon black**, precursor for many organic syntheses.

- **Typical structural representation**: \(R\!–\!CH=CH_{2}\) (where *R* is a hydrocarbon substituent).
- **Common name**: **Alkylene**
- **IUPAC name**: **Alkenes**
- **First member**: **Ethylene (Ethene, C₂H₄)**
  - *Industrial importance*: Manufacture of **plastics** (polyethylene), **artificial ripening** of fruits (banana, apple, orange), **anaesthetic** applications, etc.

content:
### Alcohols
- **General formula:** CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH (where *n* ≥ 1)
- **Common name:** Alkyl alcohol
- **IUPAC name:** Alkanol

---
### Classification
| Type | Structure | Example |
|------|-----------|---------|
| Primary | R‑CH₂OH | Methanol (CH₃OH) |
| Secondary | R₂CH‑OH | Isopropanol (CH₃CHOHCH₃) |
| Tertiary | R₃C‑OH | tert‑Butanol ( (CH₃)₃COH ) |

---
### Lucas Test
- **Reagent:** Conc. HCl + anhydrous ZnCl₂ (Lucas reagent).
- **Purpose:** Distinguish primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols based on rate of reaction (formation of alkyl chloride).

---
### Methanol (CH₃OH)
- **Also known as:** Wood spirit, methyl alcohol, carbinol.
- **Production:** Obtained by destructive distillation of wood.
- **Uses:** Solvent for paints & varnishes, manufacturing dyes, drugs, perfumes; also used as motor fuel mixed with petrol.
- **Destructive distillation of wood yields:**
  - Wood gas (gaseous)
  - Tar (liquid)
  - Charcoal (solid residue)
  - Methyl alcohol (liquid)
  - Acetic acid (vinegar)

---
### Coal Distillation Products
- Coal gas (mainly H₂, CH₄, CO)
- Ammoniacal liquor
- Coal tar
- Coke

---
### Ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH)
- **Also known as:** Ethyl alcohol, grain alcohol.
- **Denatured (methylated) spirit:** Ethanol rendered unfit for drinking by addition of methanol or pyridine.
- **Reactivity:** Changes colour of sodium or potassium metal (produces a characteristic orange‑red flame/solution).
