Diagram showing an electric dipole on an equatorial line with point Q at distance x from center O, forming a triangle with charges -q and +q.

**(i) At a Point on the Axial Line:** The electric field intensity is given by *E_p = (1 / 4*pi*epsilon_0) * (2px / (x^2 - l^2)^2)*. For a short dipole where *2l << x*, this simplifies to *E_p = (1 / 4*pi*epsilon_0) * (2p / x^3)*.

text:
Electric Flux: Defined as the total number of electric field lines crossing through an area. SI unit is Nm^2C^-1. Flux through a small area element delta_S is delta_Phi_E = E * delta_S * cos(theta).

Special Cases:

  • 0 < theta < 90 degrees: Flux is positive.
  • theta = 90 degrees: Flux is zero.
  • 90 < theta < 180 degrees: Flux is negative.

Gauss's Theorem: The electric flux over any closed surface is 1/epsilon_0 times the total charge enclosed by that surface. Phi_E = Sigma_q / epsilon_0. If total enclosed charge is zero, total electric flux is zero.

text:
Conductors: Materials through which electric charge can flow easily. Silver is the best conductor of electric charge.

Insulators: Materials like glass, rubber, wood, etc., through which electric charge cannot flow. These are also called dielectrics when an electric field is applied, as induced charges appear on the surface without conducting.

Dielectrics: In a dielectric, an external field induces a net dipole moment. Induced charges produce a field (E_in) opposing the external field (E_0), resulting in a reduced field inside the dielectric: E = |E_0| - |E_in|.

Dielectric Constant (K): The ratio of the strength of the external field to the reduced value of the electric field. Also known as relative permittivity or specific inductive capacity (denoted by K or epsilon_r). Note: The value of K is always greater than 1.

Polarisation (P): The induced dipole moment developed per unit volume in a dielectric slab. If p is the induced dipole moment and N is the number of atoms per unit volume, then P = Np.
image_descriptions: A diagram showing a rectangular dielectric slab placed in an external electric field E_0. The slab shows internal induced charges with an opposing internal electric field E_in pointing in the opposite direction to E_0. A vector sigma_p is shown at the bottom.

details.summary: Overview of electrical properties of materials including conductors, insulators, dielectrics, dielectric constant, and polarisation.

**Dielectrics:** In a dielectric, an external field induces a net dipole moment. Induced charges produce a field (E_in) opposing the external field (E_0), resulting in a reduced field inside the dielectric: E = |E_0| - |E_in|.

**Dielectric Constant (K):** The ratio of the strength of the external field to the reduced value of the electric field. Also known as relative permittivity or specific inductive capacity (denoted by K or epsilon_r). Note: The value of K is always greater than 1.

**Polarisation (P):** The induced dipole moment developed per unit volume in a dielectric slab. If p is the induced dipole moment and N is the number of atoms per unit volume, then P = Np.

### Key Formulas

Electrical Capacitance: The amount of charge needed to raise the potential of a conductor by unity. It is a scalar quantity. The SI unit is farad (1F = 1C/1V).

Capacitance of an isolated spherical conductor: C = 4 * pi * epsilon_0 * R = R / (9 * 10^9).

Capacitor: A device that stores electrostatic energy. Net charge on a capacitor is zero, but charge on either plate is finite.

Capacitance of Capacitor: Ratio of charge (q) and applied potential (V), i.e., C = q/V.

Spherical Capacitor Capacitance: Formulas provided for cases where external or internal spheres are connected to earth, in air or medium.

topic: Factors Affecting Capacitance of a Capacitor
text:
The capacitance of a capacitor is affected by the following factors:

  • Area (A): Capacitance is directly proportional to area (C ∝ A).
  • Distance (d): Capacitance is inversely proportional to the distance between the plates (C ∝ 1/d).
  • Dielectric Medium (K): Capacitance is directly proportional to the dielectric constant of the medium (C ∝ K).

details.summary: Factors influencing the capacitance of a capacitor include plate area, distance between plates, and the dielectric medium.

subject: Physics
text:
There are two common methods of grouping capacitors:

1. Series Grouping

In a series arrangement, the charge on each plate of each capacitor has the same magnitude, equal to the charge supplied by the battery. The potential difference is distributed inversely in the ratio of capacitors.

  • V = V1 + V2 + V3 + ...
  • V1 : V2 : V3 ... = 1/C1 : 1/C2 : 1/C3 ...

The equivalent capacitance Cs is given by:

1/Cs = 1/C1 + 1/C2 + 1/C3 + ... = sum(1/Ci)

2. Parallel Grouping

In a parallel arrangement, the potential across each capacitor is exactly the same. The charge is distributed in the ratio of capacitance:

  • Q = Q1 + Q2 + Q3 + ...
  • Q1 : Q2 : Q3 ... = C1 : C2 : C3 ...

The equivalent capacitance Cp is given by:

Cp = C1 + C2 + C3 + ... = sum(Ci)

Circuit diagram showing three capacitors C1, C2, and C3 connected in parallel with a battery V.

details.summary: Explanation of series and parallel grouping of capacitors and their equivalent capacitance formulas.

subject: Physics
text:
The energy of a charged capacitor is measured by the total work done in charging the capacitor to a given potential. For an additional small charge (dq) transferred from one plate to another, the work done is dW = V'dq = (q'/C)dq.

The total work done in transferring charge Q is:

W = integral(q'/C dq) from 0 to Q = Q^2 / 2C

This work is stored as electrostatic potential energy U:

U = Q^2 / 2C = (CV)^2 / 2C = 1/2 CV^2

The energy stored per unit volume is called energy density:

Energy density = 1/2 * epsilon_0 * E^2

Total energy stored in any combination is the sum of energies stored in individual capacitors: U = U1 + U2 + U3 + ...

details.summary: Derivation and formulas for electrostatic potential energy stored in a capacitor and energy density.

text:
Rate of flow of charge is called the electric current (i).

Current is a scalar quantity. Unit of electric current is ampere. The direction of flow of current is opposite to the direction of flow of electrons.

According to its magnitude and direction, electric current is of two types:

  • Direct Current (DC): An electric current whose magnitude and direction do not change with time. e.g., a cell, battery or DC dynamo are the sources of direct current.
  • Alternating Current (AC): An electric current whose magnitude changes continuously and direction changes periodically. e.g., AC dynamo is the source of alternating current.

text:
When an electric field is applied across the conductor, then the electric field gives a constant velocity to the free electrons along the length of the wire, this velocity is called drift velocity (v_d). It is of the order of 10^-4 m/s.

Current flowing in a wire is i = neAv_d, where n = number of free electrons in unit volume of wire and A = area of cross-section of the wire.

Constant R is called electric resistance of the circuit. Unit of electric resistance R is ohm (Ω). Inverse of electric resistance is called the electric conductance. Its unit is ohm-1 or mho.

Ohmic Conductor: The conductor which obey the Ohm's law is known as ohmic conductor. e.g. Metallic wire.

Non-ohmic Conductor: The conductor which not obey the Ohm's law is known as non-ohmic conductor. e.g. Diode valve, triode valve.

Electrical Resistance

Electrical resistance is defined as the ratio in the potential difference (V) across the ends of the conductor to the current (i) flowing through it, i.e. R = V/i. The SI unit of electrical resistance is Ω (ohm) and its dimension is [ML2T-3A-2].

Effect of Temperature on the Resistance

  • On increasing the temperature of the metal, its resistance increases.
  • On increasing the temperature of semiconductor its resistance decreases.
  • On increasing the temperature of alloy, their resistance increase but it is small compared to the pure metals.
  • On increasing the temperature of electrolytes, their resistance decreases.

Specific Resistance

Ratio of electric field and the current density at a point in the conductor is called the current density at a point in the conductor is called the specific resistance or resistivity. It is a constant for the material. ρ = E/J or ρ = RA/l. Its unit is ohm-metre.

Some factors affecting specific resistance are given below:

  • Resistivity increases on mixing of impurity and increase of mechanical stress.
  • The resistance of super conductor is zero.

Conductivity

Inverse of specific resistance is called conductivity (σ). Unit of conductivity is mho/metre.

Conductance

Inverse of resistance is called conductance. Unit of conductance is ohm-1 or siemen or mho.

Combination of Resistance

(i) Series combination: In this combination, resistances are joined end to end. In series combination, equivalent resistance is equal to sum of individual resistance. R = R1 + R2 + R3. In series combination, current through each resistance is same. i = i1 = i2 = i3. In series combination potential difference across each resistance is different. V = V1 + V2 + V3. Such that V1 : V2 : V3 = R1 : R2 : R3.

(ii) Parallel combination: In this combination, first ends of all the resistances is connected to one point and second ends of all the resistances is connected to other point. In parallel combination, equivalent resistance is given by 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3.

text:
Electric Cell: A device which maintains a continuous flow of charge (or electric current) in a circuit by a chemical reaction. It contains two rods of different metals called electrodes.

Types of Electric Cell:

  • Electrochemical cell: Chemical energy is converted into electric energy.
    • Primary cell: Used only for discharge. Current leaves the cell at the positive terminal, goes through the external circuit, and enters at the negative terminal. Examples: Daniell cell, Leclanche cell.
    • Secondary cell: Current passes in both directions. During discharge, current leaves at the positive terminal and enters at the negative terminal. Most commonly used is a lead accumulator.
  • Photo cell: Radiant energy is converted into electric energy.
  • Thermocouple cell: Thermal energy is converted into electric energy.

Electromotive Force (emf):

The energy given by the cell in the flow of unit charge in the whole circuit. Alternatively, the potential difference across the terminals of the cell when no current is being taken from the cell. Unit is volt. It is a constant for the cell.

Internal Resistance of a Cell (r):

The resistance offered by the electrolyte of the cell. If current i is taken, potential difference is V, then r = (E - V) / i or r = R(E/V - 1), where R is external resistance.

Factors affecting internal resistance:

  • Increases if distance between plates increases.
  • Decreases if area of electrodes increases.
  • Decreases if concentration of electrolyte increases.

Terminal Voltage:

Voltage across the terminals of a cell. It is not constant and depends on the current drawn (larger current = smaller terminal voltage). Relation: E = V + ir.

content:
**Electric Cell:** A device which maintains a continuous flow of charge (or electric current) in a circuit by a chemical reaction. It contains two rods of different metals called electrodes.

### Types of Electric Cell:

- **Electrochemical cell:** Chemical energy is converted into electric energy.**Primary cell:** Used only for discharge. Current leaves the cell at the positive terminal, goes through the external circuit, and enters at the negative terminal. Examples: Daniell cell, Leclanche cell.
- **Secondary cell:** Current passes in both directions. During discharge, current leaves at the positive terminal and enters at the negative terminal. Most commonly used is a lead accumulator.
- **Photo cell:** Radiant energy is converted into electric energy.
- **Thermocouple cell:** Thermal energy is converted into electric energy.

### Electromotive Force (emf):

The energy given by the cell in the flow of unit charge in the whole circuit. Alternatively, the potential difference across the terminals of the cell when no current is being taken from the cell. Unit is volt. It is a constant for the cell.

### Internal Resistance of a Cell (r):

The resistance offered by the electrolyte of the cell. If current *i* is taken, potential difference is *V*, then *r = (E - V) / i* or *r = R(E/V - 1)*, where *R* is external resistance.

### Factors affecting internal resistance:

- Increases if distance between plates increases.
- Decreases if area of electrodes increases.
- Decreases if concentration of electrolyte increases.

### Terminal Voltage:

Voltage across the terminals of a cell. It is not constant and depends on the current drawn (larger current = smaller terminal voltage). Relation: *E = V + ir*.

### Key Formulas
- i = i1 + i2 + i3
- i1 : i2 : i3 = 1/R1 : 1/R2 : 1/R3
- E = W/q
- r = (E - V) / i
- r = R(E/V - 1)
- E = V + ir

Combination of Cells:

  • In series: Negative end of each cell is connected to the positive end of the next. For n cells with emf E and internal resistance r: Total emf = nE, Total internal resistance = nr. Current i = nE / (nr + R).
    • If nr < R: Current is n times the current from one cell.
    • If nr >> R: No benefit in joining cells in series.
  • In parallel: Positive terminals connected to one point, negative to another. For n cells: Total emf = E, Total internal resistance = r/n.

text:
Combination of cells in parallel: Current taken from the combination is given by i = (nE) / (r + nR).

  • If (r/n) >> R, i.e., total internal resistance of cells is greater than external resistance, then current taken from the combination is n times that from one cell.
  • If (r/n) << R, i.e., total internal resistance of cells is less than external resistance, then current taken from the combination is equal to that from one cell. So, there is no benefit of connecting cells of low internal resistance in parallel.

Mixed grouping: In this combination, a certain number of cells are connected in various series and all such series are then connected in parallel. Number of cells = mn, emf of combination = nE, total internal resistance = (nr)/m. Current taken in external resistance, i = (mnE) / (nr + mR). For maximum current in the circuit, mR = nr.

If two cells oppose each other, then current taken from them is I = (E1 - E2) / (r1 + r2 + R). Similarly, if cells support each other, then I = (E1 + E2) / (r1 + r2 + R).

Charging current of a cell: i = (emf of charger - emf of cell) / (total resistance of the circuit). In a battery of N cells each of emf E, if n cells are wrongly connected, then net emf, E' = NE - 2nE.

topic: Rheostat, Kirchhoff's Laws, and Wheatstone's Bridge
text:
Rheostat: It is a variable resistor which is used to control current in the circuit. The construction is very similar to the construction of a potentiometer.

Kirchhoff's Laws:

  • Junction law: The algebraic sum of the current flowing into any junction is zero. Thus, ΣI_junction = 0.
  • Loop law: The algebraic sum of the potential difference in any closed loop is equal to zero. Thus, Σ_closed_loop ΔV = 0 => ΣE + RI = 0, ΔE = - ΣRI.

Wheat Stone's Bridge: It is an arrangement of four resistances making a closed circuit. The resistance of a given conductor can be determined with its help. When there is no deflection in the galvanometer, then P/Q = R/S. In this case, V_B = V_D and the bridge will be balanced.
image_descriptions: Symbol of a rheostat.
Circuit diagram of a Wheatstone bridge with four resistors P, Q, R, S arranged in a diamond shape with a galvanometer in the center.
content:
**Rheostat:** It is a variable resistor which is used to control current in the circuit. The construction is very similar to the construction of a potentiometer.

**Kirchhoff's Laws:**

- **Junction law:** The algebraic sum of the current flowing into any junction is zero. Thus, ΣI_junction = 0.
- **Loop law:** The algebraic sum of the potential difference in any closed loop is equal to zero. Thus, Σ_closed_loop ΔV = 0 => ΣE + RI = 0, ΔE = - ΣRI.

**Wheat Stone's Bridge:** It is an arrangement of four resistances making a closed circuit. The resistance of a given conductor can be determined with its help. When there is no deflection in the galvanometer, then P/Q = R/S. In this case, V_B = V_D and the bridge will be balanced.

### Key Formulas
- ΣI_junction = 0
- Σ_closed_loop ΔV = 0
- ΣE + RI = 0
- ΔE = - ΣRI
- P/Q = R/S

Different Measuring Devices:

  • Ammeter: A device used to measure electric current in a circuit. It is always connected in series with the current source and has very low resistance.
  • Voltmeter: A device used to measure the potential difference across the ends of a conductor. It is always connected in parallel and has very high resistance.
  • Galvanometer: A device used to detect the presence of the electric current in a circuit.

text:
To convert a galvanometer into an ammeter, a low resistance wire called a shunt is connected in parallel with the galvanometer.

  • Resistance of shunt, S = (i_g * G) / (i - i_g)
  • where, G = resistance of galvanometer, i = range of ammeter, and i_g = safe current for galvanometer coil.

To convert a galvanometer into a voltmeter, a high resistance (R) is connected in series with the galvanometer.

  • R = (V / i_g) - G
  • where, V = range of voltmeter.

details.summary: Methods for converting a galvanometer into an ammeter or voltmeter.

To convert a galvanometer into a voltmeter, a high resistance (R) is connected in series with the galvanometer.

Whenever electric current passes through a conductor, it becomes hot. This indicates electric energy is converted into heat energy, known as Joule heating effect.

  • H = (W / 4.2) = (VIt / 4.2) = (V^2t / 4.2R) = (I^2Rt / 4.2)

Electrical Power: The rate at which work is done by the source of emf in maintaining current in a circuit. P = VI = V^2/R = I^2R. SI unit is watt.

Electrical Energy: Total work done by the source of emf. SI unit is joule.

Kilowatt-hour (kWh): Known as Board of Trade Unit (BTO). 1 kWh = 1000 * 3600 = 3.6 * 10^6 Joule.

text:
The production of electricity with the help of heat is called thermoelectricity.

  • Seebeck Effect: Current flows in a couple of wires due to temperature difference at junctions without an external battery.
  • Peltier Effect: Absorption or evolution of heat at a junction of two dissimilar metals when current is passed. Peltier coefficient, pi = T * (dE/dtheta).
  • Thomson Effect: Absorption or evolution of heat along the length of a wire when current is passed through it while kept at different temperatures. Thomson coefficient, sigma = -T * (dS/dtheta).

text:
Electrolysis: The process where electric current passes through an electrolyte and decomposes it into constituents.

Faraday's Laws of Electrolysis:

  • (i) First law: Amount of substance deposited (m) is directly proportional to charge (q). m = zq or m = zit, where z = electrochemical equivalent.
  • (ii) Second law: If same current is passed through different electrolytes for same time, ratio of masses liberated is equal to ratio of their chemical equivalents. m1/m2 = E1/E2 or z1/z2 = E1/E2.

Faraday Constant (F): Quantity of charge required to liberate one gram equivalent of a substance. F = E/A = 96500 coulomb or F = Ne, where N = Avogadro's number and e = electronic charge.

Biot-Savart Law: According to this law, the magnetic field dB at the point P due to the small current element of length dl is given by:

dB = (μ₀ / 4π) * (i dl sinθ / r²)

In vector form: dB = (μ₀ / 4π) * (i dl x r) / r³

Where μ₀ is a constant called permeability of free space, and μ₀ = 4π x 10⁻⁷ Wb/A-m.

Rules to Find the Direction of Magnetic Field:

  • Right hand palm rule: If we spread our right hand in such a way that thumb is towards the direction of current and fingers are towards that point, where we have to find the direction of field, then the direction of field will be perpendicular to the palm.
  • Maxwell's right handed screw rule: If a right handed cork screw is rotated, so that its tip moves in the direction of flow of current through the conductor, then the rotation of the head of the screw gives the direction of magnetic lines of force.

1. Magnetic field due to straight wire of infinite length: B = (mu_0 * I) / (2 * pi * r)

2. Magnetic field due to conducting rod of radius R at a point at distance r:

  • If r < R: B = (mu_0 * I * r) / (2 * pi * R^2) (B proportional to r)
  • If r = R: B = (mu_0 * I) / (2 * pi * R)
  • If r > R: B = (mu_0 * I) / (2 * pi * r) (B proportional to 1/r)

3. Magnetic field due to hollow cylindrical pipe of radius R:

  • If r < R: B = 0
  • If r >= R: B = (mu_0 * I) / (2 * pi * r)

topic: Force on Current Carrying Conductors and Moving Charges
text:
Force between two Parallel Current Carrying Conductor: Two linear parallel conductor carrying currents in the same direction attract each other while in opposite direction they repel each other. Therefore, force between two current carrying parallel conductor per unit length is F = (μ₀ / 4π) * (2I₁I₂ / r²)

Magnetic Field of a Moving Point Charge: The magnetic field due to a charge q, moving with speed v at a point P at distance r from the charge is given by B = (μ₀ / 4π) * (q / r²) * (v x r)

Force on a Moving Charge in Magnetic Field: Force on a moving charge in the magnetic field is given by Fₘ = qvB sinθ = q(v x B). It is also called Lorentz force.

  • Electromagnetic and gravitational forces act on neutral and large bodies.
  • If the moving charge is moving perpendicular to the magnetic field, then its kinetic energy remains constant.
  • The force acting in the presence of electric and magnetic field simultaneously: F = q(E + v x B)

Rules to Find the Direction of Force:

  • Right hand palm rule: If a linear conductor is grasped in the palm of the right hand with thumb pointing along the direction of the current, then the finger tips will point in the direction of lines of force.
  • Fleming’s left hand rule: If we spread the forefinger, central finger and thumb of our left hand in such a way that these three are perpendicular to each other, then first forefinger is in the direction of magnetic field, second central finger is in the direction of current and thumb will represent the direction of force.

Motion of Charged Particle in a Magnetic Field: When a charged particle enters in a magnetic field perpendicularly, then it moves on a circular path. Radius of circular path, r = mv / Bq = sqrt(2mEₖ) / qB. Time period of particle, T = 2πm / Bq. Frequency of particle, n = Bq / 2πm.

  • If a charged particle is moving in the direction of magnetic field, then it experiences no force.
  • The velocity of proton moving in a magnetic field changes continuously.

Force on a Current Carrying Conductor in Magnetic Field: When a current carrying conductor is placed in magnetic field, then it experiences a force on it, this force is given by Fₘ = Bil sinθ = il x B. When θ = 90° or sinθ = 1, then F = ilB (Maximum). When θ = 0 or sinθ = 0, then F = ilB x 0 = 0.

Application of Current Carrying Conductor:

  • (i) Magnetic force acting on a current carrying conductor is not central force because F = BIdl sinθ expression does not depends upon r.
  • (ii) The force dF is always perpendicular to B and idL.

MAGNET: A naturally occurring black coloured substance called lodestone can attract pieces of iron kept nearby. In early days, the Greeks observed this property of loadstone an oxide called magnetite (Fe₃O₄). This type of substance is called magnet. Magnet is of two types: (i) Natural Magnet, (ii) Artificial Magnets.

text:
Important Facts Related to Magnet:

  • Artificial magnets have short life and natural magnets have long life.
  • Magnetism of earth has infinite time.
  • Unstable magnet is an induced magnet.
  • Magnets are used in electric bells, fans, washing machines, etc.

Pole Strength: The ability of a magnetic pole to attract magnetic material is known as pole strength. It is denoted by m. The pole strength of North and South pole is represented by +m and -m.

Magnetic Axis: The line joining north pole and the south pole of a magnet is called the magnetic axis.

Effective Length of Magnet: The distance between the north pole and the south pole of the magnet is called the effective length of the magnet.

Magnetic Dipole: Two equal and opposite poles separated by a distance 2l are said to constitute a dipole.

Magnetic Moment: The magnetic moment of a bar magnet is given by the product of its length and pole strength. It is represented by M.

Magnetic Field: The area surrounding the magnet in which, another magnet experiences a force on it is called magnetic field.

Magnetic Field Lines: The imaginary lines which represents the direction of magnetic field. Properties:

  • Magnetic lines of force always form closed curves.
  • They leave the north pole and enter the south pole externally.
  • They move from the south pole to the north pole within the magnet.
  • They tend to contract laterally.
  • The magnetic field lines never intersect each other.

**Pole Strength:** The ability of a magnetic pole to attract magnetic material is known as pole strength. It is denoted by *m*. The pole strength of North and South pole is represented by +*m* and -*m*.

**Magnetic Axis:** The line joining north pole and the south pole of a magnet is called the magnetic axis.

**Effective Length of Magnet:** The distance between the north pole and the south pole of the magnet is called the effective length of the magnet.

**Magnetic Dipole:** Two equal and opposite poles separated by a distance 2*l* are said to constitute a dipole.

**Magnetic Moment:** The magnetic moment of a bar magnet is given by the product of its length and pole strength. It is represented by *M*.

**Magnetic Field:** The area surrounding the magnet in which, another magnet experiences a force on it is called magnetic field.

**Magnetic Field Lines:** The imaginary lines which represents the direction of magnetic field. Properties:
- Magnetic lines of force always form closed curves.
- They leave the north pole and enter the south pole externally.
- They move from the south pole to the north pole within the magnet.
- They tend to contract laterally.
- The magnetic field lines never intersect each other.

### Key Formulas
- Pole strength (m) = Magnetic force / Magnetic induction = F/m
- M = (2l) * m
- I = M/V
- μ = B/H
- φ = I/H
- μ_r = 1 + φ
- μ_r = μ/μ_0
- μ = μ_0(1 + φ)
- τ = mBl sin θ + mBl sin θ = 2mBl sin θ = MB sin θ
- τ = M x B

topic: Work Done in Rotating a Dipole in a Magnetic Field
text:
The total work done in deflecting the dipole through an angle θ from 0° is:

  • W = MB(1 - cosθ)
  • If θ = 0°, then W = MB[1 - 1] = 0
  • If θ = 90°, then W = MB
  • If θ = 180°, then W = 2MB

where, M is magnetic dipole moment.

text: The earth is a natural source of magnetic field. It behaves as a magnet which causes a freely suspended magnet to point always in a north-south direction. The south pole of a earth's magnet is towards the earth's north pole (geographical north), while the north pole of earth's magnet is towards the earth's south pole (geographical south). The positions of the earth's magnetic poles are not well defined on the globe, they are spread over an area.

subject: Physics
text:
To have a complete knowledge of the earth's magnetism at a place, the following three elements must be known:

  • (i) Angle of declination: The angle between the magnetic meridian and geographical meridian at a place.
  • (ii) Angle of dip or inclination: The angle which the axis of needle makes with the horizontal.
  • (iii) Horizontal component of the earth's field: The direction of the earth's field at the magnetic poles is normal to the earth's surface and at magnetic equator it is parallel to the earth's surface.

The resultant earth's field can be resolved into two components:

  • BH = Be cosθ
  • BV = Be sinθ
  • BV / BH = tanθ
  • Be = sqrt(BH2 + BV2)

It illustrates the horizontal component (H) and vertical component (B) of the Earth's magnetic field, with angle of dip (theta) between the resultant field and the horizontal component.

content:
To have a complete knowledge of the earth's magnetism at a place, the following three elements must be known:

- **(i) Angle of declination:** The angle between the magnetic meridian and geographical meridian at a place.
- **(ii) Angle of dip or inclination:** The angle which the axis of needle makes with the horizontal.
- **(iii) Horizontal component of the earth's field:** The direction of the earth's field at the magnetic poles is normal to the earth's surface and at magnetic equator it is parallel to the earth's surface.

The resultant earth's field can be resolved into two components:

- BH = Be cosθ
- BV = Be sinθ
- BV / BH = tanθ
- Be = sqrt(BH2 + BV2)

### Key Formulas
- B_H = B_e cos(theta)
- B_V = B_e sin(theta)
- B_V / B_H = tan(theta)
- B_e = sqrt(B_H^2 + B_V^2)

It illustrates the horizontal component (H) and vertical component (B) of the Earth's magnetic field, with angle of dip (theta) between the resultant field and the horizontal component.

subject: Physics
text:
On the basis of magnetic properties, materials are classified into three categories:

  • Diamagnetic substance: These substances when placed in an external magnetic field, acquire feeble magnetism opposite to the direction of the magnetic field. Examples: Bi, Zn, Au, NaCl, H2O, etc.
  • Paramagnetic substance: These substances when placed in an external magnetic field, acquire feeble magnetism in the direction of the magnetic field. Examples: Al, Na, Pt, Mn, CuCl2, O2, etc.
  • Ferromagnetic substance: These substances when placed in an external magnetic field are strongly magnetised in the direction of the field. Examples: Fe, Ni, Co, Fe2O3, etc.

details.summary: Classification of magnetic materials based on their response to external magnetic fields.

- **Paramagnetic substance:** These substances when placed in an external magnetic field, acquire feeble magnetism in the direction of the magnetic field. Examples: Al, Na, Pt, Mn, CuCl2, O2, etc.

Electromagnetic Induction: Whenever the magnetic flux linked with a closed circuit changes, an induced emf is produced in the circuit. This emf lasts only, so long as the change in flux lasts. This phenomena is called electromagnetic induction.

Faraday's Laws:

  • First Law: Whenever the magnetic flux linked with a coil changes, an induced emf is induced in the circuit.
  • Second Law: Induced emf is equal to the negative rate of change of magnetic flux.

Induced Current and Induced Charge: If a circuit has a resistance (R):

  • Induced current, i = (1/R) * (dφ/dt)
  • Induced charge, q = (1/R) * Δφ

text:
Atomic species are of three types:

  • Isotopes: The atoms of same element which have same atomic number but different mass number are called isotopes. e.g., 17Cl35, 17Cl37, 1H1, 1H2, 1H3. The chemical properties of isotopes are same. Isotope used for treatment of blood cancer is Ag191.
  • Isobars: The atoms of different elements which has same mass number but different atomic number are called isobars. e.g., 18Ar40, 20Ca40.
  • Isotones or Isoneutronic: The atoms of different elements of which the nuclei have the same number of neutrons but different number of protons are called the isotones. e.g., (11Na23 and 12Mg24) and (19K39 and 20Ar40) are the isotones.

Mirror Nuclei: The nuclei, having the same mass number A but with the proton and neutron number interchanged, are called mirror nuclei.

topic: Einstein Mass-Energy Equivalence and Pair Production
text:
Einstein Mass-Energy Equivalence Principle: Einstein made the suggestion that energy mass are equivalent. He predicted that if the energy of a body changes by an amount E, then it's mass changes by an amount given by the equation: E = mc^2 (where c is the speed of light).

Pair Production: When an energetic gamma-ray photon falls on a heavy substance, it is absorbed by some nucleus of the substance and an electron and a positron are produced. This phenomenon is called 'pair production' and may be represented by the equation: hv -> +1B^0 + -1B^0

Pair Annihilation: The converse phenomenon of pair production is called pair annihilation. When an electron and a positron come very close to each other, they annihilate each other by combining together and two gamma-photons are produced. This phenomenon can be represented by the following equation: +1B^0 + -1B^0 -> hv + hv

details.summary: Einstein's mass-energy equivalence, pair production, and pair annihilation.

topic: Mass Defect and Nuclear Binding Energy
text:
Mass Defect: It is found that mass of the nucleus is less than the total mass of protons and neutrons, this mass difference is called mass defect. If mass defect is delta m, then: delta m = Zm_p + (A - Z)m_n - M. Where Z = atomic number, m_p = mass of proton, m_n = mass of neutron, and M = mass of nucleus.

Nuclear Binding Energy: The minimum energy required to separate the nucleons up to an infinite distance from the nucleus, is called nuclear binding energy. It is expressed as: delta E = delta m * c^2 = delta m * 931.5 MeV. Nuclear binding per nucleon = Nuclear binding energy (delta E) / Total number of nucleons (A). Packing fraction was introduced by Aston and is expressed by packing fraction, f = (delta m / A) * 10^4.
formulas: delta E = delta m * c^2 = delta m * 931.5 MeV
Nuclear binding per nucleon = delta E / A

text:
Nuclear Fission: The process of splitting of a heavy nucleus into two nuclei of nearly comparable masses with the liberation of energy is called nuclear fission. When U^235 is bombarded with fast moving neutrons, it splits: 92U^235 + 0n^1 -> 56Ba^141 + 36Kr^92 + 30n^1 + Energy. The reason for liberation of energy is that total mass of resultant nuclei is less than the mass of initial nucleus, this mass defect changes into energy. Nuclear fission was discovered by Otto han and Strassman.

  • Thermal neutrons have energy approx 0.25 eV.
  • The number of neutrons is produced is proportional to r^3 (r = size of fissionable material).

If the particle starting the nuclear fission reaction is produced as a product and further takes part in the nuclear fission reaction, then a chain of fission reaction started, which is called nuclear chain reaction.

Nuclear chain reactions are of two types:

  • Controlled Chain Reaction: A fission chain reaction which proceeds slowly and in balanced manner without any explosion and in which the energy released can be controlled.
  • Uncontrolled Chain Reaction: A nuclear chain reaction in which fission neutrons keep on increasing until the whole of the fissile substance is consumed. Atom bomb works on the principle of uncontrolled chain reaction.

Critical Size: The minimum size of piece of a radioactive element to continue the chain reaction is called critical size. The critical mass of uranium is 10 kg.

The spontaneous emission of some types of invisible rays from some substances is called radioactivity and these substances are called radioactive substances. The emitted rays are called radioactive rays.

For radioactive elements ratio of number of neutrons to number of protons is greater than 1.

1. Alpha-rays: Rays of relatively low penetrating power emitted by radium and other radioactive substances are known as alpha-rays. Alpha-rays consists of alpha-particles 2He^4. Alpha-particles have two unit positive charge and has a mass of four times that of a proton.

Some properties of alpha-rays:

  • Alpha-particles are deflected in electric and magnetic fields.
  • Velocity of alpha-particles is of the order 1/10th to that of light.
  • Alpha-particles ionise the gases through which they pass.
  • Alpha-particles have very less penetrating power. These are stopped by aluminium foil of thickness of a 0.1 mm.
  • Alpha-particles produce fluorescence in substances like zinc sulphide.
  • Alpha-particles get scattered while passing through metal foils.
  • On being stopped alpha-particles produce heating effect.
  • Alpha-particles can produce artificial radioactivity in certain elements.
  • The energies of alpha-particles emitted from a radioactive substance is not the same.

2. Beta-rays: A form of ionising radiation, emitted by radioactive substances, which consists of negatively charged electrons. Beta-rays are very fast moving electrons. Beta-particles carry 1 unit negative charge.

  • Beta-particles are deflected in electric and magnetic fields.

subject: Physics
text:
Half-Life (T_1/2): The time interval in which mass of a radioactive substance or the number of atoms reduced to half its initial value.

  • Half-life is constant for a radioactive element.
  • Half-life cannot be changed by physical or chemical changes.
  • C^14 is used to predict the age of archaeological findings.
  • Mean Life (tau): The sum of life times of all atoms divided by the number of atoms present initially.
  • Mean life is greater than half-life.
  • The percentage of atoms left one mean life time is equal to 37%.

details.summary: Definitions and formulas for half-life and mean life of radioactive substances.

content:
**Half-Life (T_1/2):** The time interval in which mass of a radioactive substance or the number of atoms reduced to half its initial value.

- Half-life is constant for a radioactive element.
- Half-life cannot be changed by physical or chemical changes.
- C^14 is used to predict the age of archaeological findings.
- **Mean Life (tau):** The sum of life times of all atoms divided by the number of atoms present initially.
- Mean life is greater than half-life.
- The percentage of atoms left one mean life time is equal to 37%.

### Key Formulas
- N = N_0 * (1/2)^n
- n = total time (T) / half-life period
- T_1/2 = 0.6931 / lambda
- Mean life tau = 1 / lambda
- 1 curie (1 Ci) = 3.7 * 10^10 decay/second
- 1 amu = 931.5 MeV

### Key Exam Facts
- **Summary:** Definitions and formulas for half-life and mean life of radioactive substances.

text:
Motion of Cathode Rays (Electrons) Parallel in Electric Field:

An electron have mass (m) and charge (e). It moves in electric field (E). Then,

  • force on electron, F = eE
  • when electron is projected in the direction of electric field or opposite direction, then its path is linear line.
  • electric field intensity, E = V/d = potential between plates / distance between plates
  • applied acceleration on electron, a = F/m = eE/m

Motion of Cathode Rays (Electron) Perpendicular to Electric Field:

An electron have mass (m) and charge (e). It enters into electric field perpendicularly. Then,

  • force on electron, F = eE.
  • with velocity v_x, the time required to pass length of electric field, t = l/v_x.
  • Acceleration produced in perpendicular direction of motion, a = F/m = eE/m

Matter Wave:

  • Light exhibits dual character (wave and particle).
  • Louis-de-Broglie in 1942 extended the idea of photons to material particles like electrons.

de-Broglie Relation:

  • According to quantum theory, E = hv (i).
  • According to Einstein, E = mc^2 (ii).
  • Equating (i) and (ii): hv = mc^2 => h(c/lambda) = mc^2 => lambda = h/mc.
  • General form: lambda = h/mv = h/sqrt(2mE).

Properties of Matter Wave:

  • lambda is inversely proportional to v.
  • If particle is at rest (v=0), wavelength is infinite (lambda = infinity).
  • Not electromagnetic in nature.
  • Defines a region of uncertainty.

Photoelectric Effect:

  • Emission of electrons from a metal surface by the action of light.
  • Based on the law of conservation of energy.
  • Photons completely disappear and transfer energy to photoelectrons.
  • Ratio of electrons emitted to photons incident is less than unity.

details.summary: Definition and principles of the photoelectric effect.

content:
**Photoelectric Effect:**

- Emission of electrons from a metal surface by the action of light.
- Based on the law of conservation of energy.
- Photons completely disappear and transfer energy to photoelectrons.
- Ratio of electrons emitted to photons incident is less than unity.

### Key Exam Facts
- **Summary:** Definition and principles of the photoelectric effect.

subject: Physics
text:
Laws of Photoelectric Effect

  • There is no time lag between emission of electrons and incidence of light.
  • The number of emitted electrons is directly proportional to the intensity of incident light.
  • The kinetic energy of emitted electrons does not depend upon the intensity of incident light.
  • The kinetic energy of emitted electrons is directly proportional to the frequency of incident light.
  • The number of emitted electrons does not depend on the frequency of incident light.
  • If the frequency of incident light is less than threshold frequency, then no electron will be ejected.
  • The photoelectric emission is an instantaneous process. The time lag between the incidence of radiations and emission of photoelectrons is very small or less than even 10^-9 second.

Threshold Frequency

The minimum frequency of light necessary to eject the electrons from metallic surface is called threshold frequency (v0). For a frequency lower than cut-off frequency, no photoelectric emission is possible even, if the intensity is large.

Work Function

The minimum energy required to eject the electrons from metal is called the work function of metal (W).

Einstein's Equation of Photoelectric Effect

Kinetic energy, Ek = h(v - v0) => 1/2 mv^2max = h(v - v0) or 1/2 mv^2max = hv - hv0 [since W = hv0] or 1/2 mv^2max = hv - W

where, Ek = maximum kinetic energy of photoelectron, v = frequency of incident light, v0 = threshold frequency, h = Planck's constant, W = work function.

- The kinetic energy of emitted electrons does not depend upon the intensity of incident light.
- The kinetic energy of emitted electrons is directly proportional to the frequency of incident light.
- The number of emitted electrons does not depend on the frequency of incident light.
- If the frequency of incident light is less than threshold frequency, then no electron will be ejected.
- The photoelectric emission is an instantaneous process. The time lag between the incidence of radiations and emission of photoelectrons is very small or less than even 10^-9 second.

### Threshold Frequency

The minimum frequency of light necessary to eject the electrons from metallic surface is called threshold frequency (v0). For a frequency lower than cut-off frequency, no photoelectric emission is possible even, if the intensity is large.

### Work Function

The minimum energy required to eject the electrons from metal is called the work function of metal (W).

### Einstein's Equation of Photoelectric Effect

Kinetic energy, Ek = h(v - v0) => 1/2 mv^2max = h(v - v0) or 1/2 mv^2max = hv - hv0 [since W = hv0] or 1/2 mv^2max = hv - W

where, Ek = maximum kinetic energy of photoelectron, v = frequency of incident light, v0 = threshold frequency, h = Planck's constant, W = work function.

### Key Formulas
- W = hv0
- Ek = h(v - v0)
- 1/2 mv^2max = hv - W

### Key Exam Facts
- **Summary:** Covers the fundamental laws of the photoelectric effect, definitions of threshold frequency and work function, and Einstein's photoelectric equation.

subject: Physics
text:
Relation between Stopping Potential and Threshold Frequency

If electron is retarded through a potential difference of V0, then all kinetic energy will be converted to potential energy. eV0 = Kmax = 1/2 mv^2max = hv - hv0 = hv - W [since W = hv0]. V0 is called stopping potential.

Photoelectric Cell

It is a device based on phenomena of photoelectric effect which converts light energy directly into electric energy. These are of three types: (i) Photoemissive cell, (ii) Photovoltaic cell, (iii) Photoconductive cell. Note: Saturation current in the photocell varies with distance as i proportional to 1/d^2.

Applications of Photoelectric Cells

  • In reproduction of sound in cinema, television and phototelegraphy.
  • In measuring the temperature of celestial bodies.
  • To control the temperature in furnace and in chemical process.
  • In automatic doors.
  • In photoelectric counters.
  • In automatic switches for street lights.
  • In photoelectric sorters.
  • In space for obtaining electrical energy from sunlight during space travel, v >= v0 or lambda <= lambda0.

X-RAYS

When fast moving cathode rays strike on a metal piece of high melting point and of high mass number, then some invisible rays produced. These rays are called X-rays. These rays were discovered by Roentgen. The device used to produce X-rays is called coolidge tube.

Properties of X-rays

  • These are electromagnetic in nature.
  • X-rays travel in straight line with speed of light.
  • These show reflection, refraction, interference, diffraction and polarisation.
  • Wavelength of X-rays is the order of 1 Angstrom.
  • These are not deflected by electric and magnetic fields.

When X-rays are scattered by loosely bound electrons in a target some of the scattered X-rays have a long wavelength, then the incident X-rays. This is called compton shift in wavelength. The phenomenon in which the wavelength of the incident X-rays increases and hence the energy decreases due to scattering from an atom is known as Compton effect.

Expressions for Compton Shift:

  • Kinetic energy of recoil electron: E_K = hc/lambda - hc/lambda'
  • Direction of recoil electron: tan theta = (lambda * sin phi) / (lambda' - lambda * cos phi)
  • Compton wavelength of electron: h / m_0 * c = 0.024 Angstrom

content:
### Bragg's Law and X-ray Diffraction

**Bragg's Law:**
The condition for constructive interference (diffraction) of X-rays from crystal planes is given by:
$$ n\lambda = 2d \sin	heta $$
Where:
- $n$ is an integer (order of diffraction),
- $\lambda$ is the wavelength of the X-rays,
- $d$ is the interplanar spacing (distance between atomic planes),
- $	heta$ is the glancing angle (angle between incident ray and the plane).

**Maximum Wavelength Limit:**
For X-rays to be usefully studied via diffraction, the wavelength $\lambda$ must be comparable to or smaller than the interatomic spacing $d$. The maximum possible wavelength occurs when $\sin	heta = 1$ (i.e., $	heta = 90^\circ$) and $n=1$.
$$ \lambda_{max} = 2d $$
Thus, the upper limit for the wavelength of X-rays that can be resolved by a crystal with interplanar spacing $d$ is $2d$.

### Moseley's Law

Moseley's law relates the frequency of characteristic X-rays emitted by an element to its atomic number $Z$.

**Formula:**
$$ \sqrt{
u} = a(Z - b) $$
Or in terms of wavelength $\lambda$ (since $
u = c/\lambda$):
$$  rac{1}{\lambda} \propto (Z - b)^2 $$
$$ \lambda \propto  rac{1}{(Z - b)^2} $$

For K-series radiation (like $K_\alpha$), the screening constant $b$ is approximately 1.
$$ \lambda \propto  rac{1}{(Z - 1)^2} $$

**Application:**
To find the wavelength for a different element, use the ratio:
$$  rac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2} = \left(  rac{Z_2 - 1}{Z_1 - 1} ight)^2 $$
Where $\lambda_1$ and $Z_1$ correspond to the first element, and $\lambda_2$ and $Z_2$ correspond to the second element.

content:
### Properties of Nuclear Radiation

1. **Gamma Rays ($\gamma$):**
   - Nature: Electromagnetic radiation (high frequency, short wavelength).
   - Origin: Emitted by an excited nucleus when it transitions to a lower energy state. They are **not** constituents of the nucleus (unlike protons and neutrons).
   - Penetrating Power: Highest among alpha, beta, and gamma rays.

2. **Beta Rays ($ eta$):**
   - Nature: High-speed electrons ($ eta^-$) or positrons ($ eta^+$).
   - Origin: Nuclear origin (result of neutron-proton conversion within the nucleus), but they do not revolve in orbits around the nucleus like orbital electrons.

3. **Neutron to Proton Ratio ($N/Z$):**
   - For light stable nuclei, $N/Z \approx 1$.
   - For heavier stable nuclei, $N/Z > 1$ (typically up to 1.5) to overcome electrostatic repulsion between protons.
   - Therefore, the statement "The neutron to proton ratio for stable nuclei is always less than one" is **false**.

subject: Physics
content:
### Factors Affecting X-ray Penetrating Power

The penetrating power of X-rays depends on their energy (or frequency/wavelength).

1. **Potential Difference ($V$):**
   - Increasing the potential difference between the cathode and anode increases the kinetic energy of the electrons striking the target.
   - This results in higher energy (shorter wavelength) X-rays.
   - **Higher energy X-rays have greater penetrating power.**
   - Therefore, increasing $V$ increases penetrating power.

2. **Filament Current ($I$):**
   - Increasing the filament current increases the number of electrons emitted per second.
   - This increases the **intensity** (number of X-ray photons) but does **not** significantly change the maximum energy (penetrating power) of the individual X-ray photons.
   - Thus, changing filament current primarily affects intensity, not penetrating power.

A physical change is a change in which the composition of a substance is not affected, i.e. no new substance is formed. e.g. Interconversion of states is a physical change because these changes occur without a change in composition and no change in the chemical nature of the substance.

When an ordinary piece of iron is magnetised in the presence of a strong magnetic field. Here the colour, density, mass and the composition remains the same. Hence, magnetisation is a physical change. The physical changes are reversible. Magnetisation can be reversed by heating the piece of iron.

Evaporation, distillation, sublimation, condensation and crystallisation are examples of physical changes.

The blue colour of copper sulphate crystal disappears when it is heated strongly because on heating water of crystallisation of crystal is lost. It regains its blue colour when moistened with a drop of water.

Some facts about the physical changes are:

  • Physical changes are temporary and reversible.
  • Composition of the constituent of matter remains same during physical change i.e. constituent particles of matter does not change.
  • Physical changes are due to the change in physical properties like density, volume, state temporarily.

Note:

  • Amount of space that a substance or object occupies is called volume of that substance.
  • Density is the degree of compactness of a substance. It is defined as mass per unit volume.

The complex food material gets converted into simple molecules of glucose which is oxidised in the body cells to release energy.

text:
Matter: Anything that occupies space and possesses mass is termed as matter. It is made up of small particles with intermolecular spaces between them.

Classification of Matter:

  • Physical classification: Matter may be classified into five states: Solids, liquids, gases, plasma, and Bose-Einstein condensate.
  • Chemical classification: Matter may be classified into (a) pure substances (elements and compounds) and (b) mixtures.

1. Solids:

  • Solids have a definite shape and a definite volume.
  • Intermolecular forces operating between the molecules are very strong, keeping positions fixed; molecules can only vibrate about their mean position.
  • Molecules are closely packed and associated with minimum energy.

Note:

  • The melting point of a solid is an indication of the strength of intermolecular forces of attraction.
  • Melting point of a solid ∝ strength of intermolecular forces.

Types of Solids:

  • Amorphous solids: Constituent particles do not possess orderly arrangement over long range. e.g., glass, rubber, plastic. Glass is a supercooled liquid.
  • Crystalline solids: Constituent particles are arranged in an orderly arrangement over long range. e.g., graphite, diamond, NaCl.

Classification of Crystalline Solids:

  • (a) Ionic solids: Constituent particles are ions, strong electrostatic forces of attraction. e.g., NaCl, BaCl2, ZnS.
  • (b) Metallic solids: Constituent particles are positively charged kernels and free electrons. Interparticle forces are metallic bonds. e.g., Fe, Cu, Al.
  • (c) Covalent solids: Constituent particles are atoms, strong covalent bonds. e.g., diamond, quartz, SiO2.
  • (d) Molecular solids: Constituent particles are molecules, hydrogen bonds or van der Waals’ forces. e.g., solid CO2, I2.

2. Liquids

Characteristics of liquids are as follows:

  • (i) Liquids have no definite shape but have a definite volume.
  • (ii) Intermolecular forces operating between the molecules are weak due to which they can slide over one another but cannot escape the boundary in normal conditions.
  • (iii) Molecules are closely packed and associated with intermediate energy due to motion.

3. Gases

Characteristics of gases are as follows:

  • (i) Gases have neither definite shape nor volume.
  • (ii) Intermolecular forces operating between the molecules are very weak due to which their positions are not fixed and thus, they can move freely.
  • (iii) Molecules are wide apart and are associated with maximum energy.
  • (iv) Gases exert pressure on the walls of the container due to collision of molecules with the walls of the container.

Note: Compressibility depends upon the intermolecular spaces between the particles of matter. Compressibility ∝ intermolecular spaces. Solid < liquid < gas

text:
CHANGE IN STATE AND LATENT HEAT

The conversion of a substance from one state to another state at a definite temperature is known as change in state. The state of substance can be changed by changing temperature or pressure.

e.g. Solid state <=> Liquid state <=> Gaseous state

During the change in state the temperature of the substance does not change but internal potential energy of molecules change (kinetic energy of molecules remain same).

The amount of heat energy required by a substance from one state to another state at atmospheric pressure is called latent heat of that substance.

Terms Related to Change of State

  • Melting point: The temperature at which a solid melts to become a liquid at the atmospheric pressure is called its melting point. When a solid melts, its temperature remains the same. Melting point of those substances which contract upon melting reduces on increasing pressure. On the other hand melting point of those substances which expand upon melting increases with increasing pressure.
  • Freezing point: The temperature at which a liquid becomes solid at the atmospheric pressure is called its freezing point.
  • Boiling point: The temperature at which a liquid starts boiling at the atmospheric pressure is called its boiling point. Boiling is a bulk phenomenon. **CHANGE IN STATE AND LATENT HEAT**

The conversion of a substance from one state to another state at a definite temperature is known as change in state. The state of substance can be changed by changing temperature or pressure.

e.g. Solid state <=> Liquid state <=> Gaseous state

During the change in state the temperature of the substance does not change but internal potential energy of molecules change (kinetic energy of molecules remain same).

The amount of heat energy required by a substance from one state to another state at atmospheric pressure is called latent heat of that substance.

**Terms Related to Change of State**

- **Melting point:** The temperature at which a solid melts to become a liquid at the atmospheric pressure is called its melting point. When a solid melts, its temperature remains the same. Melting point of those substances which contract upon melting reduces on increasing pressure. On the other hand melting point of those substances which expand upon melting increases with increasing pressure.
- **Freezing point:** The temperature at which a liquid becomes solid at the atmospheric pressure is called its freezing point.
- **Boiling point:** The temperature at which a liquid starts boiling at the atmospheric pressure is called its boiling point. Boiling is a bulk phenomenon. Boiling point of water increases in presence of impurities in the water. Boiling point increases on increasing pressure upon liquid that's why food cooks comparatively faster in pressure cooker.

PURE SUBSTANCES

These substances have fixed composition and non-variable properties. These can not be separated into simple substances by physical methods. Elements and compounds are pure substances.

1. Elements

An element is a substance which cannot be split up into two or more simpler substances by the usual chemical methods of applying heat, light or electric energy.

There are 118 elements known at present, out of which 92 elements occur in nature, while remaining 26 elements have been prepared artificially except one. Elements may be found in all the three forms as solid, liquid or gas.

  • Solid: Sodium (Na), carbon (C), aluminium (Al) etc.
  • Liquid: Mercury (Hg), bromine (Br) etc.
  • Gas: Oxygen (O2), hydrogen (H2) etc.

Elements are divided in the following forms:

  • (i) Metals: The elements which have a tendency to form positive ions by loss of electrons are called metals, e.g. silver, tin, zinc etc. Metals are the elements having lustre, ductility, malleability, conductivity etc. All metals except mercury exists as solids at room temperature. Oxides of metals are basic or amphoteric in nature. Aluminium is the most abundant metal in the earth's crust.
  • (ii) Non-metals: The elements which have a tendency to form negative ion by gain of electrons are called non-metals. e.g. hydrogen, oxygen, sulphur etc. They are in solid or gaseous form under normal conditions except bromine which exists as liquid. Oxides of non-metals are neutral (in low oxidation state) or acidic (in higher oxidation state) in nature.
  • (iii) Metalloids: They are the elements whose properties fall between those of metals and non-metals. e.g. boron (B), silicon (Si), germanium (Ge), arsenic (As), antimony (Sb), tellurium (Te) and polonium (Po) etc.

text:
Mixtures

A mixture is a substance which consists of two or more elements or compounds not chemically combined together. e.g. air, milk, ink, brine, lime water, glass, paints, soil, food, wood, kerosene etc.

There are two types of mixtures, which are as follows:

  1. Homogeneous Mixture or Solution: A homogeneous mixture has a same composition throughout its mass. It has no visible boundaries of separation between the various constituents, e.g. solution of sugar in water, alloy, solution of salt in water, a mixture of alcohol and water etc.
  2. Heterogeneous Mixture: A heterogeneous mixture does not have a uniform composition throughout its mass. It has visible boundaries of separation between the various components, e.g. solution of K2Cr2O7 in water, solution of CaCO3 in water, solution of oil in water, gun powder, soil, etc.

Note: A mixture which boils at a definite temperature and distils over without any change in composition is called azeotropic mixtures. e.g. ethanol-water, acetone-benzene, benzene-chloroform etc.

Properties of a Mixture

Following are the main properties of a mixture:

  • A mixture can be separated into its components by physical methods like, filtration, evaporation, sublimation, distillation, magnet etc.
  • A mixture shows the properties of all the constituents present in it. Energy is usually neither given out nor absorbed during the preparation of a mixture.
  • The composition of a mixture is variable, i.e. the constituents can be present in any proportion by weight.
  • A mixture does not have a definite melting point, boiling point etc. (except azeotropic mixture).

text:
Methods for Separation of Mixture

General methods used for the separation of a mixture are as follows:

  • (i) Crystallisation: This method is based on the difference in the solubility of the various compound dissolved in a common solvent. e.g. a mixture of KNO3 and NaCl can be separated by this process.
  • (ii) By separatory funnel: This method is used to separate a mixture of two immiscible liquids. e.g. mixture of oil and water, extraction of iron from its ore.
  • (iii) Sublimation: When a solid changes directly from solid to gaseous state on heating, the process is known as sublimation. This process is used to separate such mixtures that contain a sublimable volatile component from a non-sublimable impurity. This process is generally used for the separation of naphthalene, anthracene, benzoic acid, camphor, NH4Cl, iodine etc. Iodine (I2) is the only halogen which sublimes. NH4Cl sublimes due its decomposition.
  • (iv) Distillation: This method is used for the purification of liquids which boils without decomposition and contain non-volatile impurities. e.g. pure water can be obtained from sea water by distillation, mixture of ether and toluene, benzene and aniline, etc.
  • (v) Fractional distillation: This process is used to separate a mixture of two or more miscible liquids which possess their boiling points within the limit of 10 to 15 K. e.g. petrol, diesel, kerosene.
  • (vi) Distillation under reduced pressure: This process is used for those liquids which decomposes below their boiling point under reduced pressure, liquid boils at low temperature. Hence, the temperature for decomposition is not reached. Thus, this process is known as vacuum distillation, e.g. glycerol can be separated by this method. It is also used for the concentration of sugar cane juice in sugar industry.
  • (vii) Steam distillation: It is used for the separation and purification of liquids which are appreciably volatile in steam from non-volatile components of mixture, e.g. o-nitrophenol and p-nitrophenol are separated by this method. Aniline is also purified by this method.
  • (viii) Evaporation: It is the process by which soluble solids can be obtained from their solution by allowing the solvent to vaporise, e.g. salt can be obtained from salt solution by evaporation.

This law establishes the relationship between the masses of reactants and products during a chemical reaction. This law was postulated by A. Lavoisier in 1750.

This law states "During any physical or chemical change, the total mass of the products is equal to the total mass of the reactants."

Or

Example: C + O2 -> CO2 (12g + 32g -> 44g). 12 g carbon combines with 32 g oxygen to give 44 g carbon dioxide. This law may be explained with the help of Landolt's experiments.

text:
It is stated by modern research that mass can be converted into energy. There is some energy formed in each reaction, by which some mass has been lost. According to Einstein, mass and energy are related as E = mc2 where, m = the mass of substance, c = velocity of light (3 x 108 m/s) and E = energy.

But in chemical reactions energy released or absorbed is too less, hence, the change in mass (decrease or increase) taking place becomes negligible. These changes can be clearly seen in nuclear reactions.

This law was proposed by John Dalton. It states that, "An element may form more than one compound with another element. For a given mass of an element, the masses of other elements (in two or more compounds) come in the ratio of small integers."

e.g. in NH3, 14 g of nitrogen requires 3 g of hydrogen and in hydrazine (N2H4) 14 g of nitrogen requires 2 g of hydrogen. Hence, fixed mass of nitrogen required hydrogen in the ratio 3 : 2 in two different compounds (3 : 2 is a simple ratio). Thus, this is in agreement with "law of multiple proportions".

text:
This law was proposed by Richter in 1972. This law is known as the law of equivalent proportions or law of combining weights. This law states that "When two different elements combine separately with the same weight of a third element the ratio in which they do so will be the same or some simple multiple of the ratio in which they combine with each other."

e.g. carbon and sulphur react separately with oxygen (third element) to give carbon dioxide (CO2) and sulphur dioxide (SO2). They also react together to form carbon disulphide (CS2).

  • In carbon dioxide 12 parts by weight of carbon are combine with 32 parts by weight of oxygen and in sulphur dioxide (SO2) 32 parts by weight of sulphur combine with 32 parts by weight of oxygen.
  • Ratio of weight of carbon and sulphur which combine with fixed weight (32 parts) of oxygen is = 12 : 32 or 3 : 8 ...(i)
  • In carbon disulphide, 12 parts by weight of carbon reacts with 64 parts by weight of sulphur. Hence, ratio of weight of carbon and sulphur in which they combines to form CS2 is = 12 : 64 or 3 : 16 ...(ii)
  • Ratio (i) and (ii) are related to each other as follows: 3 : 8 and 3 : 16 or 3 : 3 and 8 : 16 and 1 : 2

Thus, this is an agreement with "law of reciprocal proportions."

text:
Gaseous state is the simple state of the matter. The behaviour of gases is governed by some general laws known as Gas laws. These laws are relationships between temperature, pressure, volume and mass.

Boyle's Law

According to Boyle's law, at constant temperature, pressure of a gas varies inversely with its volume.

Charles' Law

According to this law, at constant pressure the volume of a given mass of a gas varies directly with its temperature. Bursting of hydrogen balloon and making of chappati are the applications of Charles' law.

Gay-Lussac's Law

According to this law, "At a constant volume, the pressure of a given mass of a gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature."

Avogadro's Law

Under similar conditions of temperature and pressure, equal volume of all gases contain equal number of molecules. Or, at a given temperature and pressure, the volume of any gas is directly proportional to the number of moles of gas.

Dalton's Law of Partial Pressure

According to this law, if two or more gases, which do not react chemically, are enclosed in a vessel, the total pressure exerted by the gaseous mixture is the sum of partial pressures exerted by the constituent gases.

Ideal Gas

The gas which obeys gas laws at all conditions of temperature and pressure is known as ideal gas.

- P1V1/T1 = P2V2/T2
- PV/T = R
- PV = RT
- PV = nRT
- PV = (W/M)RT
- pM = dRT

It has been found that majority of the elements found to possess several isotopes. Isotopes are the different atoms of the same element possessing different atomic masses but same atomic number. The atomic mass of each isotope is determined separately and then combined according to the ratio of their proportion of occurrence.

If an element have three isotopes with atomic masses m1, m2 and m3 and these occur in the ratio of x, y and z respectively, then its average atomic mass is:

Gram Atomic Mass: The atomic mass of an element expressed in grams is the gram atomic mass or it is also called gram atom, e.g., the atomic mass of oxygen is 16 u, therefore gram atomic mass of oxygen is 16 g.

Molecular Mass: The sum of the atomic masses of all the atoms in a molecule of the substance is called molecular mass of the substance. It is expressed in atomic mass unit(u).

When the number of atoms of an element present on right hand side [RHS] of the equation becomes equal to that of present on left hand side [LHS] of the equation, the equation is said to be balanced. To balance a chemical equation, following steps are followed:

  • Check the number of atoms of each element present on RHS and LHS of a equation whether they are equivalent or not.
  • If not, multiply the element by a number to the corresponding element.
  • Continue multiplying until all numbers become equivalent to the corresponding element.

e.g., Na2O + HCl → NaCl + H2O

It is generally expressed in terms of molarity and normality.

  • (i) Molarity (M): It is the number of moles of solute present in 1L of the solution. It is denoted by M. Molarity (M) = Number of moles of solute / Volume of solution (in L). e.g., 0.25 mol L-1 (or 0.25 M) solution of NaOH means that 0.25 mol of NaOH is dissolved in 1 L of solution.
  • (ii) Formality (F): It is the number of gram formula weight of solute dissolved in 1 litre of solution when formula weight equals to the atomic weight, then formality equals to molarity. Formality (F) = Gram formula weight of solute / Volume in litre.
  • (iii) Normality (N): It is the number of gram equivalents of solute dissolved per litre of the solution. Normality (N) = Gram equivalent of solute / Volume of solution (L). e.g., 0.50 g equiv.L-1 (or 0.50 N) solution of H2SO4 means that 0.50 g equiv. of H2SO4 is dissolved in 1 litre of solution.
  • (iv) Molality (m): It is the number of moles of the solute dissolved in 1 kg of solvent. It is denoted by m. Molality (m) = Number of moles of solute / Mass of solute (in kg). e.g., 1.00 m kg-1 (or 1.00 m) solution of KCl means that 1 mol (74.5 g) KCl is dissolved in 1 kg of water.

Molality is independent of temperature whereas molarity, normality and formality change with temperature. This is because volume depends upon temperature and the mass do not.

subject: Chemistry
text:
The first definite theory about the structure of the matter was put forward by John Dalton in 1890.

Its main postulates are:

  • All matter is made up of very small particles known as atoms.
  • Atom neither be created nor be destroyed, it is the smallest particle that takes part in a chemical reaction.
  • All atoms of an element are alike and of different elements are different.
  • Atoms of different elements have different masses and chemical properties.
  • Atoms combine together in the ratio of small whole numbers.

Drawbacks of Dalton's Atomic Theory:

  • It does not explain why atoms of different elements differ in their mass, valencies etc.
  • It does not explain the existence of isotopes and isobars.
  • It does not explain how and why atoms of elements combine with each other to form molecules.

Constitution of Atom: Several phenomenon like radioactivity reveals that atoms are divisible and comprises of three fundamental particles namely electron, proton and neutron.

Electron (_-1 e^0): Electron was discovered by J.J. Thomson in 1897. When an electric charge at high voltage is passed through a gas at low pressure, (10^-6 atm) a stream of rays is emitted from the cathode surface. These are called as cathode rays.

  • Magnitude of charge on electron = -1.6 x 10^-19 C.
  • Mass of electron = 9.108 x 10^-28 g.

Properties of Cathode Rays:

  • Cathode rays always travel in straight line path away from the cathode and cast shadows of metallic objects placed in their path.
  • Cathode rays produce mechanical motion of a spin wheel placed in their path. Thus, they possess kinetic energy and must be material particles.
  • The beam of cathode rays are deflected towards the positively charged plate, hence the particles in the cathode rays carry negative charge.

Proton (1p^1 or 1H^1)

The existence of positively charged particles in an atom was shown by E. Goldstein in 1886. When high voltage is supplied across the electrodes a new kind of rays produced which passed through the perforated cathode and caused a glow on the wall opposite to the anode. These rays are also known as anode rays or canal rays.

  • The magnitude of charge on proton is 1.6 x 10^-19 C.
  • Mass of proton = 1.673 x 10^-27 kg.

Properties of Anode Rays

  • The anode rays travel in a straight line and cast shadow.
  • The anode rays are deflected by the magnetic and electric field and bent in the opposite direction of cathode rays.
  • The anode rays can also rotate the wheel placed in their path and also have heating effect.
  • The charge to mass ratio (e/m) for positive rays depends upon the nature of the gas taken in the tube and it is less than e/m of electron. e/m = 9.579 x 10^7 C kg^-1
  • The removal of electrons from neutral atoms or molecules of gas results in the formation of positively charged ions. These positively charged ions move towards perforated cathode and constitute beam of positive rays.

Neutron (0n^1)

The neutrons were discovered by James Chadwick. These particles are neutral having charge equals to zero. Their mass is approximate same as that of a hydrogen atom, i.e. 1.675 x 10^-27 kg.

ATOMIC MODELS

Various atomic models were proposed to show the arrangement and distribution of particle [electrons, protons and neutrons] within an atom.

Thomson's Atomic Model

The first simple model of an atom was proposed by J.J. Thomson. According to Thomson, an atom is a positively charged uniform sphere of radius 10^-8 cm in which electrons are embedded in such a way that negative charge equals to positive charge. This model also called plum-pudding model and watermelon model. This model was unable to explain the stability of an atom.

text:
Rutherford's Atomic Model (1912)

This model was based upon alpha-particle scattering experiment. The alpha-particles scattering experiments performed by Rutherford are concerned with the discovery of the nucleus.

The following conclusions were drawn from these experiments:

  • A major portion of the atom is empty space because most of alpha-particles passed straight through the atom.
  • The atom has a very small rigid, positively charged body called nucleus and the alpha-particles are repelled from the metal foil due to this positively charged nucleus.
  • The whole mass of the atom is concentrated in the nucleus, so it is very heavy and rigid.

Main postulates of this model are as follows:

  • An atom mainly consists of free space. Each atom contain a heavy positively charged body at its centre called the nucleus.

content:
**Rutherford's Atomic Model (1912)**

This model was based upon alpha-particle scattering experiment. The alpha-particles scattering experiments performed by Rutherford are concerned with the discovery of the nucleus.

The following conclusions were drawn from these experiments:

- A major portion of the atom is empty space because most of alpha-particles passed straight through the atom.
- The atom has a very small rigid, positively charged body called nucleus and the alpha-particles are repelled from the metal foil due to this positively charged nucleus.
- The whole mass of the atom is concentrated in the nucleus, so it is very heavy and rigid.

Main postulates of this model are as follows:

- An atom mainly consists of free space. Each atom contain a heavy positively charged body at its centre called the **nucleus**.
- The negatively charged electrons revolving around the nucleus are called planetary electrons.
- The size of the nucleus (r = 10^-15 m) is very small as compared to that of atom (r = 10^-10 m).
- All protons and neutrons are stablised in the nucleus by a strong interaction force.
- Rutherford atomic model failed because he could not explain the electronic structure of atom. In other words it does not tell about the distribution of electrons around the nucleus.

**Note:** During alpha-particle scattering experiment, alpha-particles were subjected to bombard a thin sheet of heavy metals like gold, platinum because their nuclei is large, thus provides good results.

### Key Formulas
- r(nucleus) = 10^-15 m
- r(atom) = 10^-10 m

text:
Neils Bohr proposed this atomic model which is based upon the Planck's quantum theory of radiations.

  • The electrons in an atom revolve around the nucleus only in certain selected circular paths called orbits. Each orbit have a definite amount of energy.
  • Electron in the particular orbit, does not lose or gain energy.
  • Only those orbits are permitted in which the angular momentum (mvr) of the electron is a whole number multiple of h/2π (h is a Planck's constant i.e. mvr = nh/2π) where n = 1, 2, 3...
  • The energy is emitted when an electron jumps from higher energy level to lower energy level and energy is absorbed when an electron jumps from lower energy level to higher energy level.

Failures of Bohr's Atomic Theory

  • He could not explain the splitting of spectral lines in the presence of magnetic field (Zeeman effect) and electric field (Stark effect).
  • He could not explain the line spectra of atoms containing more than one electron called multi-electron atoms.
  • He could not explain the three dimensional existence of atom.
  • Bohr's theory failed due to the dual nature of matter and uncertainty principle.

text:
3. Magnetic Quantum Number (m) (Lande): It determines direction of orientation of electrons in suborbit (subshell) because it gives the orientation or distribution of the electron cloud. It has all values from -l through zero to +l, with total of (2l + 1) values. It explains splitting of spectral lines under the influence of magnetic field (Zeeman effect).

4. Spin Quantum Number (s) (Uhlenbech and Goldschmidt): It determines the orientation of the spin of the electron. It has two values of spinning of electron about its own axis. The spin quantum number either equal to -1/2 (anti-clockwise) and +1/2 (clockwise) depending upon the spin of electron.

Electronic Configuration of Elements: The arrangement of electrons in various shells, subshells or orbitals of an atom is known as electronic configuration of the element. Filling of electrons in different orbitals is governed by the following rules:

  • Aufbau's Principle: Sub-shells are filled with electrons in the increasing order of their energies. Sub-shell of lower energy will be filled first with electrons followed by higher energy sub-shell.
  • (n+l) rule: The lower the value of (n+l) for an orbital the lower is its energy. If two orbitals have same value of (n+l), the orbital with lower value of n will be filled first.
  • Hund's Rule of Maximum Multiplicity: Pairing of electrons in a sub-shell starts after all the available atomic orbitals or the sub-shell are singly filled (half-filled).
  • Pauli's Exclusion Principle: No two electrons can have the same value of all the four quantum numbers.

Radioactivity: The spontaneous emission of electromagnetic radiations [alpha, beta and gamma-rays] due to the disintegration of unstable nucleus. Discovered by Prof. Henry Becquerel in 1896; term coined by Madam Curie. Activity is measured in becquerel (1 disintegration per second). 1 curie = 3.7 x 10^10 disintegrations s^-1.

Stability of Nucleus:

  • If neutron-proton ratio (n/p) > 1.5, nucleus is unstable. Maximum stability at n/p = 1.
  • Greater mass defect = lower energy level = more stability.
  • Activity measured by Geiger Muller counter.

Alpha Rays (alpha-rays): Deflected towards negative plate, doubly ionised helium atom, decreases atomic number by 2 and mass number by 4, maximum ionisation in gases, low penetration power.

Beta Rays (beta-rays): Deflected towards positive plate, electrons, increases atomic number by 1, lesser ionisation than alpha, strongest reducing agent.
