topic: Viceroys and Governor Generals of India
text:
Lord Elgin II (AD 1894-99)

  • Indian Council Act of 1892 was passed.
  • Setting up of Durand Commission in 1893 to define the Durand Line between India and Afghanistan (now between Pakistan and Afghanistan).
  • British officials assassinated by Chapekar brothers in 1897. Lyall commission appointed after famine of 1896-97.

Lord Curzon (AD 1899-1905)

  • Appointment of Police Commission in 1902 under Sir Andrew Frazer to review police administration.
  • Appointment of Universities Commission in 1902 and passing of Indian Universities Act in 1904.
  • Establishment of Department of Commerce and Industry. Passed the Indian Coinage and Paper Currency Act (1899) and put India on a gold standard.

Lord Minto II (AD 1905-10)

  • Establishment of Muslim League by Agha Khan in 1906. Split of Congress in annual session of 1907 in Surat.
  • The Indian Council Act of 1909 or the Morley-Minto Reforms was passed.
  • Popularization of anti-partition and Swadeshi Movement.

Lord Hardinge II (AD 1910-16)

  • Annie Besant announced the Home Rule Movement.
  • Coronation durbar of king George V held in Delhi in 1911.
  • Creation of Bengal Presidency (like Bombay and Madras) in 1911 or partition of Bengal was cancelled (1911).
  • Transfer of capital from Calcutta to Delhi in 1911.
  • Establishment of the Hindu Mahasabha in 1915 by Madan Mohan Malaviya.
  • Gandhiji came back to India from South Africa (1915).

Lord Chelmsford (AD 1916-1921)

  • Formation of Home Rule Leagues by Annie Besant and Tilak in 1916.
  • Lucknow Pact between the Congress and Muslim League in 1916.
  • Appointment of Saddler’s Commission in 1917 for reforms in educational policy.
  • Jallianwalla Bagh massacre of 1919.
  • Appointment of SP Sinha as governor of Bihar (the first Indian to become a governor).

Lord Reading (AD 1921-26)

  • Moplah rebellion in Kerala in 1921.
  • Communist Party was founded in 1920 by MN Roy.
  • Chauri Chaura incident on 5th February, 1922 and subsequent withdrawal of non-cooperation movement.
  • Vishwabharati University started in 1922 and Kakori train robbery of 1925.
  • Establishment of Swaraj Party by CR Das and Motilal Nehru in 1922.
  • Decision to hold simultaneous examinations for the ICS both in Delhi and London, with effect from 1923.

Lord Irwin (AD 1926-31)

  • Appointment of the Harcourt Butler Indian States Commission in 1927.
  • Visit of Simon Commission to India in 1928 and boycott of the Commission by the Indians.
  • An All-Parties Conference held at Lucknow in 1928 for suggestions for the (future) Constitution of India, the report of which was called the Nehru Report or the Nehru Constitution.
  • Murder of Saunders, the assistant superintendent of police of Lahore.
  • Bomb blast in the Assembly Hall of Delhi in 1929.

Lord Willingdon (AD 1931-36)

  • Second Round Table Conference in 1931 and failure of the conference, resumption of Civil Disobedience Movement.
  • Announcement of Communal Award in 1932 under which separate communal electorates were set-up.
  • 'Fast to death' by Gandhiji in Yervada prison, broken after the Poona Pact in 1932.
  • Third Round Table Conference in 1932 and the Government of India Act of 1935.
  • Establishment of All India Kisan Sabha in 1936. Burma separated from India in 1935.
  • Congress Socialist Party by Acharya Narendra Dev and Jaya Prakash Narayan in 1934.

Lord Linlithgow (AD 1936-44)

  • First general elections in 1936-37, Congress attained absolute majority in 5 states.
  • Escape of Subhash Chandra Bose from India in 1941 and organization of the Indian National Army.
  • Cripps Mission and Cripps plan to offer dominion status to India and setting up of a Constituent Assembly, its rejection by the Congress.
  • Passing of the 'Quit India Resolution' by the Congress in 1942. Outbreak of Indian 'August Revolution' or revolt of 1942 after the arrest of national leaders.

Lord Wavell (AD 1944-47)

  • Wavell Plan and the Simla Conference in 1945.
  • Rajagopalachari's CR formula in 1944, failure of Gandhi-Jinnah talks in 1944.
  • End of World War II in 1945.

text:
End of British Rule:

  • Proposals of the Cabinet Mission Plan in 1946 and its acceptance by the Congress.
  • Observance of ‘Direct Action Day’ in 16th August, 1946 by the Muslim League.
  • Announcement of the end of British Rule in India by Clement Atlee (Prime Minister of England) on 20th February, 1947.

Lord Mountbatten (AD March 1947-August 1947):

  • Last Governor-General of India and introduction of Indian Independence Bill in the House of Commons.
  • India Independence Act passed by the British Parliament on 4th July, 1947 by which India became independent on 15th August, 1947.

C Rajagopalachari (1948-1950):

  • The last Governor-General of free India. (The first being Mountbatten). The only Indian Governor-General, remained in office till January, 1950.

content:
**End of British Rule:**

- Proposals of the Cabinet Mission Plan in 1946 and its acceptance by the Congress.
- Observance of ‘Direct Action Day’ in 16th August, 1946 by the Muslim League.
- Announcement of the end of British Rule in India by Clement Atlee (Prime Minister of England) on 20th February, 1947.

**Lord Mountbatten (AD March 1947-August 1947):**

- Last Governor-General of India and introduction of Indian Independence Bill in the House of Commons.
- India Independence Act passed by the British Parliament on 4th July, 1947 by which India became independent on 15th August, 1947.

**C Rajagopalachari (1948-1950):**

- The last Governor-General of free India. (The first being Mountbatten). The only Indian Governor-General, remained in office till January, 1950.

### Key Exam Facts
- **Summary:** Covers the final stages of British rule in India, including the Cabinet Mission, Mountbatten's tenure, and the appointment of C. Rajagopalachari.

text:
Permanent Settlement:

  • Introduced in Bengal, Bihar-Odisha, districts of Banaras and Northern districts of Madras by Lord Cornwallis in 1793. Sir John Shore planned this settlement.
  • It declared Zamindars as the owners of the land. Hence, they could keep 1/11th of the revenue collected to themselves while the British got a fixed share of 10/11th of the revenue collected.
  • The Zamindars were free to fix the rate. Assured of their ownership, many Zamindars stayed in towns and exploited their tenants.
  • The system was introduced to ensure the revenue receipt of the British colonial power, where a Zamindar was declared the proprietor of land on condition of fixed revenue payments to the British regime.
  • The peasants were turned into tenant farmers and deprived of the land title including other rights and privileges enjoyed during the Mughal period.
  • The Zamindars collected the rents of land through different intermediate collectors.
  • The peasantry was subject to deprivation of his share in produce from land and relegated to abject poverty. This revenue system accounted for 57% of cultivated area in the country.
  • The Commission, inquiring the reasons of the Great Bengal Famine in 1943, recommended the abolition of intermediaries on land interest to the British Government.

Ryotwari Settlement:

  • It was introduced in Bombay, Madras and Asom. Munro and Charles Reed recommended it. In this system, the direct settlement was made between the Government and the Ryots.
  • The revenue was based on the basis of the quality of the soil and the nature of the crop.
  • The revenue was fixed for a period not exceeding 30 years.
  • It was based on the Scientific Rent Theory of Ricardo. The position of the cultivator became more secure.

Mahalwari System:

  • It was introduced in the area of Ganga valley, NWFP, parts of Central India and Punjab.
  • Revenue settlement was to be made by village or estates with landlords.
  • In this system, a settlement was made with the village which maintained a form of common ownership known as Bhai Chara or with Mahals, which were group of Villages. Revenue was periodically revised.

Taluqdari System:

  • In the district of Oudh, there existed another system known as Taluqdari system.
  • The government entered into an agreement with the Taluqdar for a period of 30 years.
  • The Taluqdar collected the stipulated revenues from different villages put under his charge and deposited them with the government, after deducting the cost of collection of the revenues and his own remuneration for the arduous work.
  • Unlike the Bengal Zamindars, the Oudh Taluqdars had no real rights over the lands under their charge. Moreover, they worked as revenue collectors for the fixed period of the settlement, and not in perpetuity.

text:
Revolt of 1857:

The mighty upsurge of 1857, swept over many parts of Northern and Central India like an avalanche. The British Empire in India was rattled to its foundation. It was the most significant movement of resistance against European colonial rule.

Causes of the Revolt:

Political:

  • Nana Sahib was refused pension as he was the adopted son of Peshwa Baji Rao-II.
  • Awadh (Lucknow) was annexed in 1856, on charge of mal administration and Jhansi was annexed owing to Doctrine of Lapse.

**Causes of the Revolt:**

**Political:**

- Nana Sahib was refused pension as he was the adopted son of Peshwa Baji Rao-II.
- Awadh (Lucknow) was annexed in 1856, on charge of mal administration and Jhansi was annexed owing to **Doctrine of Lapse**.

subject: History
topic: Causes and Outbreak of the Revolt of 1857
text:
Military Discrimination

Indian soldiers were paid low salaries, they could not rise above the rank of Subedar and were racially insulted.

Religious Discrimination

  • The social reforms by British was against the people's will (widow remarriage, abolition of sati, school for girls, Christian missionaries etc).
  • Soldiers were asked to use the Enfield Rifles with greased (by pork or beef) cartridges.

Economic Grievances

Heavy taxations, discriminatory tariff policy; destruction of traditional handicrafts that hit peasants, artisans and small zamindars.

Outbreak of the Revolt

  • Bengal Resentment in which 19 native infantry of Behrampur, refused to use the newly introduced Enfield Rifle.
  • Mangal Pandey of 34th native infantry fired at the sergeant major of his regiment. Known as a part of Mutiny of Barrackpur.
  • Where the rulers were loyal to the British, the soldiers revolted as in Gwalior and Indore. In some places, people revolted before the sepoys.
  • In the beginning, the rebels were successful. Europeans were killed, police stations and law courts were attacked and revenue records were destroyed. But, the revolt was soon suppressed.

Suppression of the Revolt

  • John Lawrence remarked, "Had a single leader of ability arisen among them we must have been lost beyond redemption."
  • Delhi was captured on 20th September, 1857 by John Nicholson and Bahadur Shah II was deported to Rangoon, where he died in 1862. His sons were shot dead in Delhi.
  • Jhansi was captured by Hugh Rose on 17th June, 1858. Rani Lakshmi Bai died in the battlefield.
  • Kanpur was recaptured on 6th December, 1857 by Colin Campbell. Lucknow was recaptured on 21st March, 1858 by Colin Campbell, Havelock and Outram.
  • Nana Sahib and Hazrat Mahal both escaped to Nepal. William Taylor and Edgre suppressed the revolt at Arrah.
  • Tantia Tope was betrayed by a friend. He was captured and executed on 15th April, 1859.

Causes Behind the Failure of the Revolt

  • Lack of unity and poor organisation of the revolt and lack of common motive for participating in the revolt.
  • All the classes of the society were not effected or participated in the revolt. The military equipment of rebels was inferior.
  • Some of the rulers like Scindhias, Nizam and Holkars helped Britishers in repressing the revolt.

subject: History
text:
Brahmo Samaj

  • Brahmo Samaj was founded by Raja Ram Mohan Roy in 1828 at Calcutta.
  • Roy believed in the modern scientific approach and principles of human dignity and social equality. He put his faith in monotheism.
  • He wrote the Gift to Monotheists (1809) and translated it into Bengali the Vedas and five Upanishads to prove his conviction to that ancient Hindu text.
  • In 1814, he set-up Atmiya Sabha in Calcutta to campaign against idolatry, caste rigidities, meaningless rituals and other social evils. Mirat-ul Akhbar was founded and edited by him.
  • In 1825, he established a Vedanta college where courses in both Indian learning and Western social and physical science were offered. He also opposed Jury Act of 1827.
  • Roy was a gifted linguist. He knew more than a dozen language including Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic, English, French, Latin, Greek and Hebrew. He opposed Sanskrit system of education, because he thought it would keep the country in darkness.
  • Keshub Chandra Sen was acharya of samaj. He later formed Bharmo Samaj of India in 1866. He lost much of his respect because he married his minor daughter to minor prince.

Prarthana Samaj

  • Mahadev Gobind Ranade along with Dr Atmaram Pandurang reorganised Paramhansa Sabha under the guidance of Keshab Chandra Sen and founded Prarthana Samaj in 1867. It was primarily a Social Reform and Social Work Movement.
  • A paper named Subodh Patrika was started in order to spread the teaching of the society. Night schools and reading rooms were opened for the benefit of working class. Orphanages were opened and schools for girls were started.

subject: History
text:
Prarthana Samaj

  • Prominent members included Ramkrishna Gopal Bhandarkar, Narayan Ganesh Chandarvarkar, and Gopal Ganesh Agarkar, KT Telang.

Arya Samaj

  • Founded by Dayanand Saraswati (Mulshankar) (1824-83).
  • First unit set up in Bombay (1875); headquarters later established in Lahore.
  • Views published in Satyarth Prakash (The True Exposition).
  • Slogan: Go Back to the Vedas.
  • Advocated widow remarriage; opposed idol worship, casteism, untouchability, and purdah.
  • Established Kanya Gurukuls and DAV (Dayanand Anglo-Vedic) Schools/Colleges.
  • Dayanand was the first to use the term Swaraj and recognize Hindi as the National Language of India.
  • Started the Shudhi movement.

Rama Krishna Mission

  • Founded by Swami Vivekananda at Baranagar in 1897.
  • Vivekananda attended the World Parliament of Religious Conferences at Chicago in 1893.
  • Revived Hindu Spiritualism.
  • Popularised by Irish woman Margaret Nobel (Sister Nivedita).

Young Bengal Movement

  • Led by Henry Vivian Derozio (1826-1831).
  • Derozio was the first nationalist poet of Modern India.
  • Edited Hesperus and Calcutta Literary Gazette.
  • Supported women's rights and education.

Satya Shodhak Samaj

  • Founded by Jyotiba Phule in 1873.
  • Objective: Powerful movement against upper caste domination and Brahminical supremacy.
  • Works: Sarvajanik Satyadharma and Gulam Giri.
  • Opened a girls' school at Poona with his wife; pioneer of widow remarriage movement in Maharashtra.
  • Founded by Kandukuri Veeresalingam Pantulu (widow remarriage movement).

Other Movements

  • Veda Samaj: Founded by Sridharalu Naidu in Madras (1864).
  • Deva Samaj: Founded by Shri Shiv Narain Agnihotri in Lahore (1887).
  • Dharma Sabha: Founded by Radhakant Deb (1830); defended status quo against reformers.
  • Radha Swami Movement: Founded by Tulsi Ram (Shri Dayal Saheb) in 1861.
  • Ahmadiya Movement: Founded by Mirza Ghulam Ahmed in 1889.
  • The Aligarh Movement: Founded by Sir Syed Ahmed Khan for modern Muslim education.
  • Faraizi Movement: Founded by Haji Shariatullah in 1818.

topic: The Surat Split or Surat Session of INC (1907)
text:
The Indian National Congress split in two groups, the moderate and extremist groups at the Surat session in 1907. Extremists were led by Lal Lajpat Rai, B G Tilak and Bipin Chandra Pal and the moderates by Gopal Krishna Gokhale.

  • The government launched a massive attack on the extremists (between 1907 and 1911) by suppressing their newspaper (Incitement to offences) and their leaders.

subject: History
text:
The Non-Cooperation Movement which was the first mass movement under the leadership of Mahatma Gandhi, was launched to press three main demands:

  • i. The Khilafat issue
  • ii. The redressal of the Punjab wrongs
  • iii. The attainment of Swaraj

The programme of the movement had two main aspects: Destructive and Constructive.

Under the first category came:

  • Surrender of titles and honorary offices and resignation from nominated seats in local bodies.
  • Refusal to attend official functions.
  • Gradual withdrawal of children from officially controlled schools and colleges.
  • Boycott of British Courts by lawyers and litigants.
  • Refusal on the part of the military, clerical and labour classes to offer themselves as recruits for service in Mesopotamia.
  • Boycott the elections to the Legislative Council.
  • Boycott of the foreign goods.

The Prince of Wales visited India during this period.

details.summary: Details regarding the Non-Cooperation Movement's demands and its destructive programme.

• In November 1927, the British Government appointed the Indian Statutory Commission known as the Simon Commission (after the name of Chairman).
  • John Simon, a British politician, was appointed as Chairman of the commission to review the situation in India with a view to introduce further reforms and extension of parliamentary democracy.

  • The agenda for the second round table conference held in London was to discuss the report of Simon Commission.

subject: History
text:
Hindustan Republic Association

  • In October 1924, a meeting of revolutionaries from all parts of India was called at Kanpur.
  • Attended by leaders like Sachindranath Sanyal, Jogesh Chandra Chatterjee, Ram Prasad Bismil, Bhagat Singh, Shiv Verma, Sukhdev, Bhagwati Charan Vohra, and Chandra Shekhar Azad.
  • Decided to set up the Hindustan Republican Association, later reorganized as the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA).
  • HSRA founded at Kanpur in October 1924.

Kakori Conspiracy Case

  • Dacoity in a running train on 9th August 1925 at Kakori on the Lucknow-Saharanpur section.
  • 29 arrested and tried. Ram Prasad Bismil, Ashfaqullah Khan, Roshan Lal, and Rajendra Lahiri were sentenced to death.

Saunders Murder

  • First revolutionary act of HSRA was the murder of Mr. Saunders, Assistant Superintendent of Police, Lahore, who ordered the lathi-charge that wounded Lala Lajpat Rai during the Anti-Simon Commission protest (28th October 1928).
  • Saunders killed at Lahore railway station on 30th October 1928 by Bhagat Singh, Chandra Shekhar Azad, and Rajguru.

Bomb at Legislative Assembly

  • Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt threw two crude bombs in Central Legislative Assembly on 8th April 1929, protesting the Public Safety Bill and Trade Disputes Bill.
  • Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev, and Rajguru were hanged on 23rd March 1931 at Lahore jail following the Central Assembly Bomb Case.

Chittagong Armoury Raid

  • Surya Sen (1930) masterminded the raid on Chittagong armoury. He was hanged in 1933.

Chandra Shekhar Azad

  • On 27th February 1931, surrounded by police at Alfred Park, Allahabad, he shot himself dead.

Lahore Session or Poorna Swaraj (1929)

  • 19th December 1929: Under Pandit JL Nehru, the Lahore Session passed a resolution declaring Poorna Swaraj (Complete Independence) as the Congress objective.
  • 31st December 1929: Tri-colour flag of freedom hoisted.
  • 26th January 1930: Fixed as the first Independence Day.

subject: History
text:
The Civil Disobedience Movement

  • Started by Gandhiji on 12th March 1930 with the Dandi March.

Dandi March

  • Launched 12th March 1930.
  • Gandhiji marched from Sabarmati Ashram (Ahmedabad) with 78 followers.
  • After 24 days, he symbolically broke the Salt Law at Dandi on 6th April 1930.
  • This inaugurated the Civil Disobedience Movement.
  • Sparked patriotism in the British Army; Garhwali soldiers refused to fire on people in Peshawar.

Gandhi-Irwin Pact

  • Signed in March 1931.
  • Congress agreed to suspend Civil Disobedience Movement and participate in the Second Round Table Conference.
  • Gandhi appointed as Congress representative.

Second Round Table Conference (1st September to 1st December 1931)

  • Opened in London. Gandhi represented the INC and met British PM Ramsay Macdonald.
  • In 1932, INC was declared an illegal organization.
  • British Government refused to concede the demand for dominion status.

details.summary: Details regarding the launch of the Civil Disobedience Movement, the Dandi March, the Gandhi-Irwin Pact, and the Second Round Table Conference.

content:
### The Civil Disobedience Movement

- Started by Gandhiji on 12th March 1930 with the Dandi March.

### Dandi March

- Launched 12th March 1930.
- Gandhiji marched from Sabarmati Ashram (Ahmedabad) with 78 followers.
- After 24 days, he symbolically broke the Salt Law at Dandi on 6th April 1930.
- This inaugurated the Civil Disobedience Movement.
- Sparked patriotism in the British Army; Garhwali soldiers refused to fire on people in Peshawar.

### Gandhi-Irwin Pact

- Signed in March 1931.
- Congress agreed to suspend Civil Disobedience Movement and participate in the Second Round Table Conference.
- Gandhi appointed as Congress representative.

### Second Round Table Conference (1st September to 1st December 1931)

- Opened in London. Gandhi represented the INC and met British PM Ramsay Macdonald.
- In 1932, INC was declared an illegal organization.
- British Government refused to concede the demand for dominion status.

### Key Exam Facts
- **Summary:** Details regarding the launch of the Civil Disobedience Movement, the Dandi March, the Gandhi-Irwin Pact, and the Second Round Table Conference.

subject: History
text:
Gandhiji started his fast unto death in Yeravada jail near Poona, on 25th September, 1932.

  • He wanted the Communal Award to be withdrawn.
  • Political leaders of different political persuasion, including Madan Mohan Malaviya, MC Raja and BR Ambedkar now became active.
  • The Poona Pact according to which the idea of separate electorates for the depressed classes was abandoned, but the seats reserved for them in the provincial legislatures were increased from 71 in the Award to 147 and in the Central Legislature to 18% of the total.
  • Poona Pact agreed upon to appoint electorate for upper and lower classes. Upliftment of harijan was now became Gandhi's main concern.
  • He started an All India Anti-Untouchability League in September, 1932 and the weekly Harijan in January, 1933 even before his release.
  • 8th January, 1933 was observed a 'Temple Entry Day'.
  • After the Poona Pact, Mahatma Gandhi lost interest in the Civil Disobedience Movement and fully engrossed in the Anti-Untouchability Movement, which led to the foundation of the Harijan Sevak Sangh.

subject: History
text:
The Government of India Act, 1935 had two main parts, dealing with Federation of India and Provincial Autonomy.

Some of its main features were:

  • It provided for the establishment of Federation of India consisting of governor's provinces and princely states.
  • Dyarchy was withdrawn from the provinces and implanted at the centre.
  • The proposed federal legislature was to be bicameral with Council of States with 250 members and a Federal Assembly of 375 members.
  • Three fold division of subjects was made i.e., federal, provincial and concurrent.
  • Provision was made for the establishment of a federal court with original appellate and advisory jurisdiction.
  • The most important thing of the act was Provincial Autonomy.
  • The act divided the British Indian Provinces into two categories: 11 governor's provinces (Madras, Bombay United Provinces, Punjab, Bihar Central Provinces and Berar, Assam, NWFP, Orissa and Sindh and five chief commissioner's provinces.

details.summary: Key provisions and features of the Government of India Act, 1935.

- Provision was made for the establishment of a federal court with original appellate and advisory jurisdiction.
- The most important thing of the act was Provincial Autonomy.
- The act divided the British Indian Provinces into two categories: 11 governor's provinces (Madras, Bombay United Provinces, Punjab, Bihar Central Provinces and Berar, Assam, NWFP, Orissa and Sindh and five chief commissioner's provinces.

### Key Exam Facts

subject: History
text:
The Quit India Movement (1942)

  • Quit India movement also known as proposal and leaderless revolt.
  • The Congress met at Bombay on 8th August, 1942 and passed the famous Quit India Resolution. Gandhiji gave the slogan 'Do or Die'.
  • The Quit India Movement became a powerful mass campaign galvanising people into vehemently demanding freedom from the British rule.
  • On 9th August, 1942, Gandhiji and other Congress leaders were arrested and the Congress party was declared illegal once again.
  • The violence that had broken out in different parts of the country. Many government offices were destroyed, telegraph wires were cut and communication paralysed.
  • Mahatma Gandhi disclaimed all responsibilities for the violence which was the consequence of repressive measure taken by the British.
  • The parallel government was set-up in Ballia in Eastern Uttar Pradesh, by Chittu Pandey.
  • Patel, Rajagopalachari and the communists opposed the movement. Usha Mehta ran an illegal radio station from Bombay.
  • The movement finally crushed. Span of the movement was short lived, but the importance of the movement lay in demonstrating the intensity of the nationalist feeling that people displayed and the extent to which people would go to make sacrifices in order to achieve freedom.
  • The Muslim League did not support the Quit India Movement.
  • Achyut Patwardhan, Ram Manohar Lohia, Jayaprakash Narayan and Aruna Asaf Ali were the movement's leaders.

text:
The Indian National Army (INA)

  • The Indian National Army led by Subhash Chandra Bose was in cooperation with the Japanese.
  • Subhash Chandra Bose, after founding the Forward Bloc, in January 1939, escaped from India and went to Berlin (Germany) via Moscow.
  • The Quit India Movement was in full swing in India, Subhash Chandra Bose, who had escaped from his confinement in Calcutta in 1941 formed the Indian National Army in 1943, in Singapore, along with Rasbehari Bose.
  • The Azad Hind Fauj as the INA was known aimed at a military campaign for the liberation of India.
  • The INA consisted mostly of Indian soldiers of the British Army who had taken prisoners by the Japanese after they had conquered the British colonies in South-East Asia.
  • INA had three fighting brigades named Gandhi, Azad and Nehru. Even women's regiment called the Rani Jhansi Regiment formed.
  • In July 1944, Subhash Chandra Bose asked for Gandhi's blessings for India's last war of independence.
  • Subhash Chandra Bose who was now called Netaji by the soldiers of the INA gave his followers the battle cry of 'Jai Hind'. Subhash Chandra Bose also gave the slogan 'Dilli Chalo'.
  • Rangoon and Singapore were the two INA headquarters.
  • 12th November, 1945 was celebrated as the INA Day.
  • The last echo of the INA Movement was heard when the INA prisoners were tried at the Red Fort in Delhi and were defended by a panel of lawyers which included Tej Bahadur Sapru, Bhulabhai Desai and Jawaharlal Nehru.

details.summary: The Indian National Army (Azad Hind Fauj) was revived and led by Subhash Chandra Bose in Singapore in 1943. It consisted of Indian POWs and organized brigades including the Rani Jhansi Regiment. The Red Fort trials of INA prisoners were defended by Bhulabhai Desai, Tej Bahadur Sapru, and Jawaharlal Nehru.

mcq.explanation: 12th November, 1945 was celebrated as the INA Day.

text:
Rajagopalachari Formula

  • C Rajagopalachari (CR), the veteran Congress leader, prepared a formula for Congress League Cooperation. It was acceptance of the league's demand for Pakistan.
  • The main points in CR plan were:
    • Muslim League to endorse Congress demand for independence.
    • League to cooperate with Congress in forming a provisional government at centre.
    • After the end of the war, the entire population and Muslim majority areas in the North-West and North-East of India decide by plebiscite.
    • In case of acceptance of Partition Agreement to be made jointly for safeguarding defence, commerce communication etc.
    • The above terms to be operative only if England transferred full powers to India.
  • Jinnah wanted the Congress to accept the Two Nation Theory. He wanted only the Muslim of North-West and North-East to vote in the plebiscite and not the entire population.
  • Hindu leaders led by Vir Savarkar condemned the CR Plan.

details.summary: The CR Formula was proposed by C. Rajagopalachari to resolve the political deadlock between the Indian National Congress and the All-India Muslim League. It suggested cooperation for provisional government and post-war plebiscites in Muslim-majority provinces.

mcq.explanation: Jinnah rejected the CR Plan because he wanted Congress to accept the Two-Nation Theory and insisted that only the Muslim population of the North-West and North-East vote in the plebiscite, rather than the entire population.

subject: History
text:
The Cabinet Mission Plan (1946)

  • The Atlee Government announced in February 1946, the decision to send a high-powered mission of three British Cabinet members: Pethick Lawrence—Secretary of State for India; Stafford Cripps—President of the Board of Trade and AV Alexander, First Lord of Admiralty to India to find out ways and means for a negotiated peaceful transfer of power of India.
  • Atlee recognised India’s right to complete independence.
  • The mission and Lord Wavell rejected the Muslim League’s demand for Pakistan. The mission proposed a Two-Tier Federal Plan, which was initially accepted by both the Congress and Muslim League.
  • The Muslim League eventually decided to keep away.
  • In September 1946, an interim cabinet headed by Jawaharlal Nehru was formed by the Congress.
  • The Muslim League joined the cabinet but decided to boycott the Constituent Assembly which started its work of framing the Constitution on December 1946.
  • The Muslim League on 6th June and the Congress on 24th June, 1946 accepted the long-term plan, put forward by the Cabinet Mission.
  • July 1946, Elections were held in provincial assemblies for the Constituent Assembly. The Congress got 209 of the total 273 seats.
  • Later Mountbatten devised a ‘Plan Balkan’ that seek transfer of power to separate provinces. The plan was quickly abandoned after Nehru reacted violently to it.
  • 29th July, 1946, the League withdrew its acceptance of the long-term in a reaction against Nehru’s statement and gave a call for ‘direct action’ from 16th August, 1946 to achieve Pakistan.

details.summary: The Cabinet Mission (1946) consisting of Pethick Lawrence, Stafford Cripps, and A.V. Alexander proposed a Two-Tier Federal Plan and rejection of Pakistan, leading to constituent assembly elections and eventual political friction.

mcq.explanation: The Cabinet Mission comprised three British Cabinet members: Pethick Lawrence (Secretary of State for India), Stafford Cripps (President of the Board of Trade), and A.V. Alexander (First Lord of Admiralty).

- Atlee recognised India’s right to complete independence.
- The mission and Lord Wavell rejected the Muslim League’s demand for Pakistan. The mission proposed a **Two-Tier Federal Plan**, which was initially accepted by both the Congress and Muslim League.
- The Muslim League eventually decided to keep away.
- In September 1946, an interim cabinet headed by Jawaharlal Nehru was formed by the Congress.
- The Muslim League joined the cabinet but decided to boycott the Constituent Assembly which started its work of framing the Constitution on December 1946.
- The Muslim League on 6th June and the Congress on 24th June, 1946 accepted the long-term plan, put forward by the Cabinet Mission.
- July 1946, Elections were held in provincial assemblies for the Constituent Assembly. The Congress got 209 of the total 273 seats.
- Later Mountbatten devised a **‘Plan Balkan’** that seek transfer of power to separate provinces. The plan was quickly abandoned after Nehru reacted violently to it.
- 29th July, 1946, the League withdrew its acceptance of the long-term in a reaction against Nehru’s statement and gave a call for *‘direct action’* from 16th August, 1946 to achieve Pakistan.

- **Summary:** The Cabinet Mission (1946) consisting of Pethick Lawrence, Stafford Cripps, and A.V. Alexander proposed a Two-Tier Federal Plan and rejection of Pakistan, leading to constituent assembly elections and eventual political friction.

text:
Mountbatten Plan (3rd June, 1947)

  • The freedom with partition formula was coming to be widely accepted well before Mountbatten came.
  • The important points of the plan were:
    • Punjab and Bengal Legislative Assemblies would meet in two groups: Hindus and Muslims to vote for partition.
    • In case of partition, two dominions and two Constituent Assemblies would be created.
    • Sindh would take its own decision.
    • Referendum in NWFP and Sylhet, district of Bengal would decide the fate of these areas.
    • Freedom would come on 15th August, 1947.
  • A Boundary Commission would be set-up if partition was to be effected.
  • On July, 1947 the British Parliament ratified the Mountbatten Plan was the ‘Independence of India’ Act, 1947. The act was implemented on 15th August, 1947.
  • Pakistan became independent on 14th August, 1947. MA Jinnah became the first Governor-General of Pakistan.
  • At midnight of 15th August, 1947 as the clock struck 12, India became free. Nehru proclaimed it to be the nation with his famous ‘tryst with destiny’ speech.
  • On the morning of 15th August, 1947, Lord Mountbatten was sworn-in as Governor-General and Jawaharlal Nehru as the first Prime Minister of free India.

subject: History
content:
### Key Peasant Movements

1. **Pagal Panthis Movement (1824-33)**
   - **Location**: Bengal
   - **Leaders**: Karam Shah, Tipu Shah (Hajong and Garo tribes)
   - **Cause**: Against the hike in rent in Bengal.

2. **Moplah Rebellion (1921)**
   - **Location**: Malabar region, Kerala
   - **Leaders**: Sayyad Ali, Sayyid Fazi
   - **Cause**: Against the oppression and exploitation of Muslim Moplah peasants by Hindu Zamindars and the British Government.

3. **Indigo Revolt (1860)**
   - **Location**: Nadia district of Bengal
   - **Leaders**: Digambar Biswas, Bishnu Biswas, Harish Chandra Mukherjee (Editor of *Hindu Patriot*)
   - **Cause**: Peasants were forced to grow Indigo in their fields by European factory owners.
   - **Literary Reference**: Dinbandhu Mitra wrote the play *Neel Darpan* about this revolt, which was translated into English by Madhusudan Datta.

4. **Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (1870)**
   - **Location**: Pune
   - **Leader**: M.G. Ranade
   - **Cause**: To popularise the legal rights of peasants.

5. **Eka Movement (1921)**
   - **Location**: Awadh
   - **Leader**: Madari Parsi
   - **Cause**: Higher extraction of rent.

6. **Champaran Satyagraha (1917)**
   - **Location**: Bihar
   - **Leaders**: Gandhiji and Dr. Rajendra Prasad
   - **Cause**: Against the *Tinkathia* system imposed by European Indigo planters.

7. **Kheda Satyagraha (1918)**
   - **Location**: Uttar Pradesh (Note: Historically Kheda is in Gujarat, but the source text lists UP)
   - **Leader**: Gandhiji
   - **Cause**: Against the ignored appeal for remission of land revenue in case of crop failure.

8. **UP Kisan Sabha (1918)**
   - **Location**: Uttar Pradesh
   - **Leaders**: Indira Narain Dwivedi, Madan Mohan Malviya
   - **Cause**: To organise peasants.

9. **Awadh Kisan Sabha (1920)**

# Militant Nationalism

Militant Nationalism refers to the more radical wing of the Indian freedom struggle that emerged in the early 20th century. It was characterized by:

- **Direct action** against British policies (boycotts, protests, and sometimes violent agitation).
- **Strong nationalist rhetoric** emphasizing *“Swaraj”* (self‑rule) and *“Swadeshi”* (self‑reliance).
- Leaders such as **Bal Gangadhar Tilak**, **Lala Lajpat Rai**, and **Bipin Chandra Pal**.
- The movement was a response to the **Partition of Bengal (1905)**, which was seen as a divide‑and‑rule tactic by the British.
- It laid the groundwork for later movements like the **Home Rule Movement** and the **Civil Disobedience Movement**.

Key facts:
- The first large‑scale expression of militant nationalism was against the **Partition of Bengal**.
- Militant leaders demanded *complete independence* and were willing to use *direct action*.

---

## Swadeshi Movement

The Swadeshi Movement (1905‑1908) was a direct response to the Partition of Bengal. Its main features were:

- **Boycott of British goods** and promotion of Indian‑made products.

- **Mass participation** from all sections of society.
- It was initiated by leaders like **Bal Gangadhar Tilak** and **Lala Lajpat Rai**.

Key facts:
- The movement was started because **Lord Curzon divided Bengal** in 1905.
- It aimed to weaken the British economy by cutting off revenue from Indian trade.

# Cripps Proposals (1942)

- **Purpose**: To secure Indian cooperation in World War II and lay groundwork for post‑war self‑government.
- **Key Provisions**:
  1. **Participation of Indian States** – Indian princely states were invited to join the Constitution‑making body.
  2. **British Commitment** – The British government promised to accept and implement the Constitution after the war.
  3. **Provincial Undertakings** – Only provinces that accepted the proposals were required to give an undertaking; it was *not* a blanket requirement for all provinces.
  4. **War Resources** – The proposals did **not** guarantee that no resources of British India would be used for the war; this was a point of contention.
- **Outcome**: The proposals were rejected by the Indian National Congress and the Muslim League, leading to the Quit India Movement in 1942.

> **Important**: The correct statements about the proposals are 1 and 2.

---

- **Key Terms**:
  - *Constitution‑making body*: A council to draft a post‑war constitution.
  - *Princely states*: Semi‑autonomous regions ruled by local monarchs under British suzerainty.

---

- **Why it matters**: Understanding the Cripps Proposals helps explain the political climate that led to India’s eventual independence in 1947.

- **Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov (Lenin)**: A key figure who sought to exploit the chaotic political situation in St. Petersburg (later Petrograd).
- **Background**: Lenin spent most of the early 20th century in Europe, traveling and campaigning. He lived in exile partly due to safety concerns as a known socialist and enemy of the Tsarist regime.

- **Machine Gun Regiment Incident**: When the Machine Gun Regiment refused to leave Petrograd for the frontline, Lenin attempted to maneuver them into a **putsch** (coup).
- **Kerensky's Role**: **Alexander Kerensky**, a member of both the Provisional Government and the Petrograd Soviet, was arguably the most important figure of the time. He adeptly thwarted Lenin's coup attempt.
- **Kornilov Affair**: Kerensky faced political setbacks and feared his Minister of War, **Kornilov**, was aiming for a military dictatorship. Kerensky appealed to the Bolsheviks for military aid against Kornilov.
- **Bolshevik Ascendancy**: By autumn 1917, the Bolsheviks gained the upper hand, winning majority votes in the **Petrograd and Moscow Soviets**.
- **Leon Trotsky**: Elected as the President of the Petrograd Soviet.

  - 1975: Fall of Saigon – North Vietnamese forces overrun South Vietnam, leading to reunification under communist rule.
- **Outcome**: Vietnam unified under a single communist government; U.S. involvement ended with significant political and social repercussions.

> **Fact**: In 1975, South Vietnam was overrun by North Vietnamese forces, and the country was united under Communist rule.

subject: History
content:
# Iran‑Iraq War (1980‑1990)

- **Trigger**: Began shortly after the Iranian Revolution of 1979.
- **Motivation**: Iraq sought control over oil‑rich Iranian border territory.

  - Heavy casualties on both sides; estimated 500,000–1,000,000 deaths.

> **Fact**: War began shortly after the Iranian Revolution of 1979. Iraq wanted control over oil‑rich Iranian border territory.

subject: History
content:
# Falkland War (1982)

- **Parties**: Great Britain vs. Argentina.
- **Cause**: Dispute over sovereignty of the Falkland Islands.
- **Outcome**: Britain won the war; Argentina withdrew.

> **Fact**: Military conflict between Great Britain and Argentina on the question of sovereignty over the Falkland Islands led to the war. Britain won the war.

subject: History
content:
# French Revolution (1789‑1799)

- **Causes**
  - **Social**: Estates system (First, Second, Third Estates) → inequality, tax burden on Third Estate.
  - **Economic**: National debt, poor harvests, bread shortages.
  - **Political**: Weak monarchy (Louis XVI), lack of representation, influence of Enlightenment ideas.
  - **Intellectual**: Enlightenment thinkers (Voltaire, Rousseau, Montesquieu) promoted liberty, equality, fraternity.

- **Key Ideals**
  - *Liberty*: Freedom from arbitrary rule.
  - *Equality*: Legal equality before the law.
  - *Fraternity*: National unity and solidarity.

- **Outcome**
  - Abolition of the monarchy and feudal privileges.
  - Rise of Napoleon Bonaparte and the Napoleonic Code.
  - Spread of revolutionary ideas across Europe, influencing subsequent revolutions (e.g., 1848).

- **Significance**
  - Shift from absolute monarchy to constitutional governance.
  - Birth of modern nation‑state concepts.
  - Catalyst for the decline of feudalism and the rise of bourgeois democracy.

subject: History
content:
• In 1917 the Bolsheviks, led by Vladimir Lenin, overthrew the Provisional Government in the October Revolution.
• The newly formed Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic (RSFSR) became the **first socialist state in the world**. This marks the beginning of the Soviet Union (established formally in 1922).

subject: History
content:

subject: History
content:

• Abundant **coal and iron ore** facilitated steam power and machinery; other minerals (lead, copper, tin) were also available, though not as plentiful as coal.
• The iron industry grew rapidly after the 1780s, but the **textile sector** (cotton, wool) is usually regarded as the symbolic industry of the early revolution.
• A network of navigable rivers and an indented coastline helped internal trade, but the **real breakthrough** in goods movement came from canals and later railways.

subject: History
content:
• Formed in **1889** in Paris, the **Second International** united socialist, labour, and trade‑union parties across Europe.
• It aimed to coordinate political action, share strategies, and support workers’ struggles internationally.
• It later split over issues such as World War I.

subject: History

subject: General Studies - History

The road started at **Ledo** in Assam, India, passed through **Myanmar (Burma)** and entered **China**. It **did not pass through Thailand**. The road was named after U.S. General Joseph Stilwell.

The new state was initially called the **Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic (RSFSR)** and later became the core of the **USSR** in 1922.

subject: Geography
content:
### Cosmology
- **Definition**: The scientific study of the universe as a whole – its origin, structure, evolution, and eventual fate.
- **Scope**: Encompasses all physical matter and energy, including planets, stars, galaxies, and the intergalactic medium.
- **Scale**: The universe contains **billions of galaxies**, each hosting billions of stars.
- **Historical Milestones**:
  - **AD 140 – Ptolemy**: Proposed a **geocentric model** – Earth at the centre, with the Sun and other celestial bodies revolving around it.
  - **1543 – Copernicus**: Introduced the **heliocentric model** – Sun at the centre of the *universe* (later refined to the solar system).
  - **Kepler**: Supported Copernicus but clarified that the Sun is the centre of the **solar system**, not the entire universe.

*These concepts form the foundation for modern astrophysics and are frequently referenced in the Geography section of the NDA exam.*

subject: Geography
topic: Evolution of the Universe – Main Theories
content:
### Major Theories on the Origin & Evolution of the Universe

1. **Big Bang Theory**
   - **Proponent**: Georges Lemaître (1927)
   - **Key Idea**: The universe began as a **singular, extremely hot and dense point** that exploded ~13.8 billion years ago.
   - **Consequences**: Rapid expansion leading to the formation of **galaxies, stars, and other heavenly bodies**.
   - **Evidence**: Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation, red‑shift of distant galaxies, abundance of light elements.

2. **Steady State Theory**
   - **Proponents**: Hermann Bondi, Thomas Gold, Fred Hoyle (1948)
   - **Key Idea**: Although the universe is expanding, **new matter is continuously created** to keep the overall density constant.
   - **Implication**: The universe has **no beginning or end** and looks the same at any epoch (the "perfect cosmological principle").
   - **Status**: Largely abandoned after observational evidence (e.g., CMB) favored the Big Bang.

3. **Pulsating (Oscillatory) Theory**
   - **Concept**: The universe undergoes **alternating phases of expansion and contraction** (a cosmic “heartbeat”).
   - **Current Understanding**: Observations indicate the universe is **currently expanding**, but the theory remains a historical alternative.

*These theories are often asked in the NDA/CDS/AFCAT Geography section to test conceptual understanding of the universe.*

subject: Geography
content:

*Understanding the exam pattern helps prioritize study time and improves accuracy in answering geography‑related MCQs.*

subject: General Studies
content:
- Galaxies are giant assemblies of stars, planets, gases, and dust held together by the force of gravity.
- Stars account for most of the mass of a galaxy.
- Stars occur in huge bunches or clusters.
- Due to their size, galaxies are sometimes called 'Islands Universe'.
- Examples: Milky Way and Andromeda.

subject: General Studies
content:
- Our own galaxy is called the Milky Way (or Akash Ganga).
- The Milky Way contains about 300 billion stars, one of which is our Sun.
- Andromeda is the nearest galaxy to the Milky Way.
- In 1924, Edwin Hubble first demonstrated the existence of galaxies beyond the Milky Way.

subject: General Studies
content:
Galaxies are structurally found in three forms:
1. **Spiral**: Have a central nucleus with great spiral arms. Examples: Milky Way and Andromeda.
2. **Elliptical**: Do not have spiral arms.
3. **Irregular**: Have no defined shape.

subject: General Studies
content:
- The solar system comprises the Sun, 8 planets (Pluto is not considered a planet), their moons, and other non-stellar objects.
- It is believed to have developed from the condensation of gases and other lesser bodies.
- The Sun is at the center, and all planets revolve around it in elliptical orbits.
- The Sun is the nearest star to the Earth.
- The size of the solar system is estimated to be about 10^5 AU.

subject: General Studies
content:
- The Sun accounts for more than 99% of the mass of the solar system.
- Its immense gravitational pull keeps planets rotating in definite elliptical orbits.
- **Composition**: Primarily Hydrogen (~72%) and Helium (~26%), with trace amounts of other gases and minerals.
- **Layers**: The light-radiating surface is called the **Photosphere**. Above the photosphere is the **Chromosphere**.
- **Fraunhofer Lines**: Hundreds of dark lines super-imposed on the Sun's white light. Each line indicates the presence of specific elements.

subject: General Science
content:
### Venus
- **Nicknames**: Earth’s twin, Morning Star, Evening Star.
- **Brightness**: Brightest heavenly body after the Sun and Moon due to **70% albedo**.
- **Temperature**: Hottest planet in the solar system due to **97% CO2** in its atmosphere.
- **Proximity**: Closest planet to Earth.
- **Size**: Slightly smaller than Earth (diameter is **500 km less**).
- **Rotation**:
  - Direction: Clockwise (East to West), unlike other planets.
  - Period: Slowest rotation period (**243 days**).
- **Orbit**: Orbital period around the Sun is **225 days**.
- **Atmosphere**: Thick, contains Carbon Dioxide and Nitrogen.
- **Moons/Rings**: No rings or moons.
- **Exploration**: Visited by European Space Agency’s *Venus Express* Spacecraft.

subject: General Science
content:
### Earth
- **Position**: Third nearest planet to the Sun.
- **Uniqueness**: Only planet with life.
- **Size**: 5th largest planet in the solar system; almost identical in size and makeup to Venus.
- **Appearance**: Appears blue-green from space due to water and landmasses (called the **Blue Planet**).
- **Composition**:
  - Water: **71%**
  - Landmass: **29%**
- **Orbital Speed**: Rotates around the Sun at **29.79 km/sec**.
- **Age**: Formed about **4.54 billion years ago** (based on radiometric dating).
- **Dimensions**:
  - Circumference at Pole: **40,008 km**
  - Circumference at Equator: **40,075 km**
  - Surface Area: Nearly **510 million sq km**
- **Moon**: Has only one moon, which is relatively large, terrestrial, and planet-like. Its diameter is about **one-quarter** of Earth’s.
- **Shape**:
  - **Oblate Spheroid**: Flattened along the axis from pole to pole with a bulge around the equator.
  - **Geoid**: Another term for the shape of Earth.
- **Gravity/Weight**: Weight is **less at the equator** and **more at the poles** due to the oblate shape and centrifugal force.

subject: General Science
content:
### Mars
- **Position**: Fourth terrestrial planet from the Sun.
- **Nickname**: **Red Planet** (appears as a reddish ball through a telescope).
- **Revolution Period**: **687 days**.
- **Rotation Period**: **24.6 hours**.

subject: General Studies
content:
### Key Facts About Planets
- **Biggest Planet**: Jupiter
- **Smallest Planet**: Mercury
- **Biggest Satellite**: Ganymede
- **Smallest Satellite**: Deimos
- **Blue Planet**: Earth
- **Green Planet**: Uranus
- **Brightest Planet**: Venus
- **Brightest Planet Outside Solar System**: Sirius (Dog Star)
- **Closest Star of Solar System**: Proxima Centauri
- **Coldest Planet**: Neptune
- **Evening Star**: Venus
- **Red Planet**: Mars
- **Slowest Revolution in Solar System**: Neptune
- **Slowest Rotation in Solar System**: Venus
- **Earth’s Twin**: Venus
- **Only Satellite with an Atmosphere like Earth**: Titan

subject: General Studies
content:
### Comets
- **Composition**: Contain dust, ice, carbon dioxide, ammonia, methane, and more.
- **Orbit**: Travel on an elliptical orbit around the Sun on a regular schedule.
- **Structure**: Has a head and a tail. The tail originates when the comet gets closer to the Sun.
- **Origin**: May have originated from the 'Oort cloud', a huge cloud thought to surround the solar system.
- **Brightest Part**: The head (coma).
- **Naming**: Named after their discoverer (e.g., Shoemaker-Levy, Halley’s comet).
- **Halley’s Comet**: Becomes visible to the naked eye every 76 years when it nears the Sun.

subject: General Studies
content:
### Asteroids
- **Location**: Circle in a broad belt between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter.
- **Nature**: Debris left over from the formation of inner planets.
- **Alternative Names**: 'Planetoids' or small planets.
- **Composition**: Chunks of rock covered in frozen gases.

subject: General Studies
content:
### Meteors, Meteoroids, and Meteorites
- **Meteor**: A meteoroid that has entered the Earth’s atmosphere, usually making a fiery trail as it falls. Also known as a 'shooting star' or 'falling star'.
- **Meteoroid**: Small bodies that travel through space. Smaller than asteroids; most are smaller than the size of a pebble.
- **Meteorite**: (Definition cut off in source, but generally defined as a meteoroid that survives passage through the atmosphere and lands on Earth's surface).

subject: Geography
content:
### Rotation of Earth
- The Earth spins on its imaginary axis from West to East.
- One complete rotation takes **23 h 56 min 40.91 s** (a sidereal day).
- At the equator, day and night are of equal length.
- **Implications of rotation**:
  - Causes day and night.
  - Influences the direction of winds and ocean currents.
  - Produces the rise and fall of tides every day.

subject: Geography
content:
### Revolution of Earth
- The Earth moves in an elliptical orbit around the Sun.
- One orbital period (a tropical year) is **365 days 5 h 48 min 45.51 s**.
- Every fourth year an extra day is added → **leap year**.
- **Consequences of revolution**:
  - Changes of seasons.
  - Variation in the length of day and night throughout the year.
  - Shifting of the major wind belts.
- The figure (not shown) typically illustrates how Earth’s position in its orbit determines the seasons and day‑length variations.

subject: Geography
content:
### Equinox
- An **equinox** occurs when day and night are of equal length.
- The Sun is directly overhead at the equator.
- Two equinoxes each year:
  - **21 March** – *Vernal (Spring) Equinox*.
  - **23 September** – *Autumnal (Fall) Equinox*.

subject: Geography
content:
### Summer Solstice
- After the March equinox, the Sun appears to move northward.
- On **21 June**, the Sun is vertically overhead at the **Tropic of Cancer**.
- **Northern Hemisphere**: longest day, shortest night.
- **Southern Hemisphere**: shortest day, longest night.

subject: Geography
content:
### Winter Solstice
- On **22 December**, the Sun is vertically overhead at the **Tropic of Capricorn**.
- **Southern Hemisphere**: longest day, shortest night.
- **Northern Hemisphere**: shortest day, longest night.

subject: Geography
content:
### Some Important Facts
| Phenomenon | Date | Hemisphere |
|------------|------|------------|
| Longest day (summer) | **21 June** | Northern Hemisphere |
| Shortest day (winter) | **22 December** | Northern Hemisphere |
| Equal day & night (equinox) | **21 March** & **23 September** | Both Hemispheres |
| Longest day (summer) | **22 December** | Southern Hemisphere |
| Shortest day (winter) | **21 June** | Southern Hemisphere |
| Equal day & night (equinox) | **21 March** & **23 September** | Both Hemispheres |

subject: Geography
content:
# Lunar Eclipse

- **Definition**: A lunar eclipse occurs when the Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon, casting its shadow on the Moon.
- **When it Happens**: It can only happen on a *full moon* day because the Sun, Earth, and Moon must be aligned.
- **Why It Doesn’t Occur Every Full Moon**:
  - The Moon’s orbit is inclined about 5° to the ecliptic plane.
  - For an eclipse to occur, the full moon must also be near one of the two *nodes* (points where the Moon’s orbit crosses the ecliptic).
  - If the full moon is far from a node, the Earth’s shadow misses the Moon.
- **Types of Lunar Eclipse**:
  - *Total* – the entire Moon passes through the Earth’s umbra.
  - *Partial* – only part of the Moon enters the umbra.
  - *Penumbral* – the Moon passes through the Earth’s penumbra, causing a subtle dimming.
- **Key Facts for Exams**:
  - Remember the alignment: Sun → Earth → Moon.
  - Full moon + node alignment = eclipse.
  - Only the *full* moon can produce a lunar eclipse.

---

**Quick Recap**: A lunar eclipse is a rare celestial event that requires the full moon to be near a node, allowing the Earth’s shadow to fall on the Moon. It can be total, partial, or penumbral.

subject: Geography
content:
# Volcanism

- **Definition**: Volcanism refers to all phenomena associated with the movement of heated material from the Earth’s interior toward its surface.
- **Key Components**:
  - **Magma**: Molten rock beneath the surface.
  - **Lava**: Magma that reaches the surface.
  - **Gases**: Water vapor, CO₂, SO₂, etc., released during eruptions.
- **Processes Leading to Eruption**:
  1. **Temperature Increase with Depth** – Heat from radioactive decay raises temperatures.
  2. **Pressure Reduction** – Tectonic plate movements create fractures, lowering overlying rock pressure.
  3. **Melting Point Reduction** – Lower pressure allows rocks to melt at lower temperatures, forming magma.
- **Eruption Dynamics**:
  - **Explosive**: High gas content and viscosity cause violent eruptions.
  - **Effusive**: Low viscosity allows lava to flow smoothly.
- **Important Terms**:
  - *Vent*: Opening through which magma and gases escape.
  - *Pluton*: Intrusive igneous body that solidifies underground.
  - *Caldera*: Large volcanic crater formed after a major eruption.

---

**Exam Tip**: Focus on the two main processes (temperature rise & pressure drop) that create magma, and remember the difference between explosive and effusive eruptions.

subject: General Studies
content:
### Universal Time (Standard Time) and Time Zones

*   **Standard Time Definition**: To avoid confusion from multiple local times within a single country, a specific meridian is chosen for the entire nation. The time based on this meridian is called Standard Time.
*   **Indian Standard Time (IST)**:
    *   Meridian: **82.5° East**.
    *   Offset: **5 hours 30 minutes ahead** of Greenwich Mean Time (GMT).
*   **Time Zone Calculation**:
    *   The Earth is divided into **24 longitudinal zones**.
    *   Each zone covers **15° of longitude** (360° / 24 hours = 15° per hour).
    *   Time difference: **1° of longitude = 4 minutes**.
*   **Multi-Time Zone Countries**:
    *   Large countries with significant East-West stretches adopt multiple time zones.
    *   **Russia**: Has **11 time zones**.
    *   **USA and Canada**: Have **5 time zones** each (Atlantic, Eastern, Central, Mountain, Pacific).

subject: General Studies
content:
### International Date Line

*   **Location**: The **180° meridian** running over the Pacific Ocean.
*   **Deviations**: It deviates at **Fiji, Samoa, and Gilbert Islands** to avoid cutting through land masses, ensuring convenience for travelers.
*   **Date Change Rules**:
    *   Crossing from **West to East**: **Repeat a day** (lose a day in terms of calendar progression, i.e., go back one day).
    *   Crossing from **East to West**: **Lose a day** (gain a day in terms of calendar progression, i.e., skip forward one day).
    *   *Note: The text states 'repeat a day' for West to East and 'lose a day' for East to West. Standard convention: West to East = subtract 1 day; East to West = add 1 day.*

subject: General Studies
content:

subject: General Studies
content:
### Lithosphere: Interior Structure of the Earth

*   **Structure**: The interior of the Earth is divided into three main parts.
*   **The Crust**:
    *   It is the **outermost** layer of the Earth.
    *   It is the **thinnest** layer of the Earth.
    *   It has the **least density** (text cuts off at 'least d', implying density).

subject: Geography
content:
### Density of Earth's Core
- The density of the Earth's core is **17.2 gm/cm³**.
- This is many times greater than the average density of the Earth, which is **5.53 gm/cm³**.

### Discontinuities
Discontinuities are transition zones separating the crust, mantle, and core, caused by differences in density between layers.

| Discontinuity | Location/Function |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Conrad** | Lies between the upper crust and lower crust. |
| **Mohorovicic (Moho)** | Separates the crust and the mantle. |
| **Repetti** | Lies between the upper mantle and lower mantle. |
| **Gutenberg** | Separates the core and the mantle. |
| **Lehman** | Separates the upper core and the lower core. |

subject: Geography
content:
### Formation and Composition
- The Earth formed from the same cloud of matter as the Sun, but planets acquired different compositions during the formation and evolution of the solar system.

### Elemental Composition
The Earth is composed mostly of:
- **Iron**: 32.1%
- **Oxygen**: 30.1%
- **Silicon**: 15.1%
- **Magnesium**: 13.9%
- **Sulfur**: 2.9%
- **Nickel**: 1.8%
- **Calcium**: 1.5%
- **Aluminium**: 1.4%
- **Trace elements**: 1.2%

subject: Geography
content:
### Continental Drift Theory
- **Proposed by**: Alfred Wegener in **1915**.
- **Purpose**: To explain the origin and evolution of continents and oceans.

### Key Points
- **Pangaea**: About **250 million years ago**, there was only one supercontinent named Pangaea (meaning 'All Earth').
- **Panthalass**: Pangaea was surrounded by one mass of water body named Panthalass.
- **Breakup**: The present shape of continents and oceans is due to the breakup of Pangaea, which started about **200 million years ago**.
- **Rifting**: The Northern rift cut Pangaea from East to West, creating:
  - **Laurasia** in the North.
  - **Gondwanaland** in the South.
- **Tethys Sea**: A shallow sea situated between Laurasia and Gondwanaland.

subject: Geography
content:
### Plate Tectonics Theory
- **Definition**: A scientific theory that describes the large-scale motions of Earth’s lithosphere.
- **Core Concept**: The lithosphere is divided into several rigid segments (plates).

subject: Geography
content:
### Classification of Igneous Rocks

**1. On the basis of mode of occurrence:**
*   **Intrusive Rocks:**
    *   Formed due to the solidification of rising magma **below** the surface of the Earth.
    *   Examples: Granite, Lapolith, Batholiths, Sills.
*   **Extrusive Rocks:**
    *   Formed due to the cooling and solidification of hot and molten magma **at** the Earth's surface.
    *   Examples: Basalt, Andesite.

**2. On the basis of silica content:**
*   **Acidic Rocks:**
    *   Have **more** silica content.
    *   Example: Granite.
*   **Basic Rocks:**
    *   Have **less** amount of silica content.
    *   Example: Gabbro.

subject: Geography
content:
### Sedimentary Rocks

*   **Formation:** Formed due to the aggregation and compaction of sediments derived from older rocks, plants, and animals. They often contain fossils of plants.
*   **Classification (based on nature of sediments):**
    1.  Mechanically formed rocks.
    2.  Chemically formed rocks.
    3.  Organically formed rocks.

subject: Geography
content:
### Metamorphic Rocks

*   **Definition:** Changed form of igneous and sedimentary rocks. They change in form or composition **without disintegration**.
*   **Process:** The process of changing already formed rocks is called **metamorphosis**.
*   **Agents of Metamorphism:**
    1.  Heat
    2.  Compression pressure
    3.  Solution

**Common Transformations (Original Rock -> Metamorphic Rock):**
*   Limestone -> Marble
*   Sandstone -> Quartzite
*   Shale/Clay -> Slate, Phyllite, Schist
*   Coal -> Diamond or Graphite
*   Granite -> Gneiss
*   Clay -> Slate

subject: Geography
content:
### Weathering

*   **Definition:** Disintegration and decay of rocks **in situ** (in place) under the influence of elements of weather (changes in temperature, moisture, and atmospheric gases).
*   **Chief Agents:**
    1.  Insolation
    2.  Frost
    3.  Rainwater
    4.  Atmospheric gases
    5.  Organisms

**Types of Weathering:**
1.  **Physical Weathering (or Mechanical Weathering):**
    *   Involves rock disintegration **without** any change in the chemical constituents of the rocks.
    *   Factors: Temperature changes (implied by 'temper' in text, typically thermal expansion/contraction).

subject: Geography
content:
### Zones where most earthquakes occur
- Young fold‑mountain zones
- Zones of folding and faulting
- Junction of continental and oceanic margins
- Zones of active volcanoes
- Along various plate boundaries

These regions correspond to areas of intense tectonic activity where stress accumulation and release generate seismic events.

subject: Geography
content:
### Traditional earthquake belts
- **Circum‑Pacific Belt** – also called the *Ring of Fire*; encircles the Pacific Ocean and hosts the majority of the world’s seismic and volcanic activity.
- **Mid‑Continental Belt** – interior continental regions where ancient cratonic blocks are re‑activated.
- **Mid‑Atlantic Belt** – follows the Mid‑Atlantic Ridge, a divergent plate boundary in the Atlantic Ocean.

These belts were identified before the modern plate‑tectonic theory but still accurately describe major seismic zones.

subject: Geography
content:
### What is a tsunami?
- A series of high sea waves generated when seismic waves from an earthquake travel through seawater and displace large volumes of water.
- Often mistakenly called **tidal waves**; the term arose because the wave’s appearance resembles an unusually high tide.
- **Frequency:** The Pacific Ocean, surrounded by the Ring of Fire, experiences at least **two tsunamis per year** on average.

**Key points**
- Tsunamis are not caused by tides; they are caused by sudden vertical displacement of the seafloor (earthquakes, landslides, volcanic eruptions, or meteorite impacts).
- Wave energy can travel across entire ocean basins with little loss of speed.

subject: Geography
content:
### Landform definition
- A **landform** is a natural feature of the Earth’s surface.
- Classification is based on physical attributes such as:
  - Elevation
  - Slope
  - Orientation
  - Stratification
  - Rock exposure
  - Soil type

### Topography
- The arrangement of landforms in a landscape is called **topography**.

### Common landforms
- **Mountains**
- **Plateaus**
- **Plains**
- **Islands**
- **Deserts**
- *(and many others such as valleys, dunes, fjords, etc.)*

subject: Geography
content:
### Mountain classification (by mode of formation)
1. **Fold Mountains**
   - Formed by compressive forces generated by endogenetic processes (e.g., tectonic collisions, earthquakes, landslides).
   - Classic examples: **Himalayas, Alps, Andes, Rockies, Atlas**.
2. **Block Mountains**
   - Created when large blocks of the Earth’s crust are uplifted or down‑dropped along parallel faults due to tectonic activity.
   - Often associated with **horsts** (uplifted blocks) and **grabens** (down‑dropped blocks).
3. *(The text hints at other types such as volcanic and residual mountains, but they are not detailed in the excerpt.)*

### Related terminology
- **Mountain ridge, range, chain, group, cordillera** – different scales and arrangements of mountain systems.

text:
A relatively low-lying and flat land surface with least difference between its highest and lowest points is called a plain. The plains are divided into structural, erosional, and depositional plains.

Forms of Plain:

  • Structural Plain: Formed due to the uplift of a part of the sea floor. e.g., the Great Plain of USA.
  • Erosional Plain: Formed when the elevated tract of land is worn down to a plain by the process of erosion. e.g., Plain of North Canada.
  • Depositional Plain: Formed by filling up of sediments into depressions along the foothills, lakes, and seas. e.g., Indo Ganga Plain.

topic: Deserts and Major Deserts of the World
text:
A desert is a barren area of land where little precipitation occurs and consequently living conditions are hostile for plant and animal life. About to one-third of land surface of the Earth is arid or semi-arid.

Formation and Characteristics:

  • Deserts are formed by weathering processes as large variations in temperature between day and night put strains on the rocks which consequently break in pieces.
  • Hot Deserts: Located on the western coasts of the continents between latitudes 15° and 30° North and South (S) because of the effects of off-shore trade winds. Examples: Sahara, Arabian, Great Australian Desert, etc.
  • Cold Deserts: Located in the interior of the continents such as Gobi, Takla Makan, etc. Some are found at some distance from the sea, such as Atacama. These deserts are dry due to the effect of orographic barrier.

subject: Geography
text:
An island is any piece of land that is surrounded by water. A grouping of geographically or geologically related islands is called an archipelago. The various types of islands are named according to the way they were formed.

Types of Island:

  • Continental Island: It is simply an island that rests on the continental shelf. Because of this, these islands are always quite close to a given continent. Also, the water level around a continental island is very shallow, typically less than 600 feet. Canadian island of Newfoundland is a continental island, as is Greenland. Great Britain is the largest continental island in Europe.
  • Volcanic Islands: Formed when volcanoes deep in the ocean rise above the water's surface.
  • Coral Island: An island that forms a ring and partially or totally encloses a shallow body of water or lagoon. Coral islands are large collections of coral atop rock (usually volcanic) in the ocean. Lakshadweep island in Indian ocean is the best example of coral islands.
  • Alluvial Islands: Formed by the outward flow of water depositing silt and gravel at the mouth of a river. New Moore island at the mouth of Ganga river in West Bengal is an alluvial island.
  • Barrier Islands: Formed by waves depositing sand on the shallow ocean bottom as they crash on the shoreline.
  • Tectonic Island: Formed by the result of tectonic activity. By tectonic movement, long island arcs (archipelagoes) are formed. Indonesia, Philippines, Japan groups of islands are the best examples of it.

details.summary: Categorizes islands into Continental, Volcanic, Coral, Alluvial, Barrier, and Tectonic islands, citing notable examples like Lakshadweep, New Moore Island, Newfoundland, and island arcs of Indonesia and Japan.

mcq.question: Which of the following is an example of an Alluvial Island?

subject: NDA/NA Pathfinder
content:
# Atmosphere

- **Definition**: A thick gaseous envelope surrounding the Earth, held by gravity.
- **Significance**:
  - Acts as a filter, absorbing unwanted radiation.
  - Provides essential gases for life.
  - Supports the biosphere.
- **Key Functions**:
  - Protects life by absorbing harmful UV radiation.
  - Regulates temperature and weather patterns.

subject: NDA/NA Pathfinder
content:
# Vertical Extent of the Atmosphere

- **Effective atmosphere**: ~97% of the atmosphere is confined within 29 km of the Earth’s surface.
- **Full vertical range**: 16 km to 29 000 km from sea level.
- **Non‑uniformity**: The atmosphere is neither uniform nor homogeneous; density and composition vary with altitude.

subject: NDA/NA Pathfinder
content:
# Composition of the Atmosphere

- **Major gases**: Nitrogen (≈78 %), Oxygen (≈21 %), Carbon Dioxide (≈0.04 %).
- **Trace gases**: Helium, Hydrogen, Ozone, Argon, etc.
- **Ozone**: Concentrated in the stratosphere; absorbs UV radiation, protecting life.
- **Particulates**: Dust, aerosols, and water vapour are present, especially in the troposphere.

subject: NDA/NA Pathfinder
content:
# Troposphere

- **Altitude**: Extends up to ~16 km from the surface.
- **Thickness variation**: 8 km at the poles, 16 km at the equator.
- **Normal Lapse Rate**: Temperature drops by 1 °C for every 165 m rise (≈6.4 °C per km).
- **Weather**: Contains almost all water vapour, dust particles, and CO₂; all weather phenomena (condensation, precipitation, storms) occur here.
- **Tropopause**: Boundary between troposphere and stratosphere.

subject: NDA/NA Pathfinder
content:
# Stratosphere

- **Altitude**: Extends up to ~50 km; bounded above by the stratopause.
- **Temperature Inversion**: Temperature increases with height, rising from ~‑60 °C at the tropopause to 0 °C at the stratopause.
- **Ozonosphere**: Region rich in ozone; absorbs harmful UV radiation.
- **Dust & Particulates**: Stratosphere is largely free of dust and aerosols.

subject: Geography
content:
- The distribution of pressure on the globe is highly uneven.
- This unevenness is partly a result of the variation in the distribution of temperature.
- There are **seven pressure belts** on the globe.

subject: Geography
content:
- **Location**: Located on either side of the geographical equator in a zone extending between **5°N and 5°S**.
- **Seasonal Drift**: The location is not stationary; it drifts Northward during summer solstice and Southward during winter solstice with the migration of the Sun.
- **Cause**: **Thermally induced** due to intense heating of the ground surface by almost vertical Sun rays.
- **Wind Convergence**: Represents the zone of convergence of North-East and South-East trade winds.
- **Characteristics**: Characterised by light and feeble winds and frequent calm conditions.
- **Alternative Name**: Also known as the **Belt of Calm** or **Doldrums**.

subject: Geography
content:
- **Location**: Extends between **30° to 35°** in both hemispheres.
- **Cause**: **Dynamically induced** (not thermally induced). It owes its origin to the rotation of the Earth and the sinking/settling down of winds.
- **Mechanism**: Convergence of winds at higher altitudes above this zone results in the subsidence (descent) of air. The descent concentrates the air volume, causing high pressure.
- **Alternative Name**: Also called **Horse Latitude**.

subject: Geography
content:
- **Location**: Extends between **60° to 65°** in both hemispheres.
- **Cause**: **Dynamically induced**. It is not thermally induced because low temperatures throughout the year would typically result in high pressure, not low pressure.
- **Hemispheric Difference**: More developed and regular in the **Southern Hemisphere** than in the Northern Hemisphere due to the over-dominance of water (ocean) in the Southern Hemisphere.

subject: Geography
content:
- **Location**: At the poles.
- **Cause**: High pressure persists throughout the year due to the prevalence of **very low temperatures**.

The strong and rapidly moving circumpolar westerly air circulation in a narrow belt of a few 100 km width in the upper limit of troposphere is called jet stream. Their circulation path is wavy and meandering.

The extent of the jet streams narrows down during the summer season because of their Northward shifting while these extend upto 20° North latitude during winter season.

subject: Geography
text:
Cyclone

Cyclones are the centres of low pressure surrounded by closed isobars having increasing pressure outward and closed air circulation from outside towards the central low pressure in such a way that air blows inward in anticlockwise direction in the Northern hemisphere. Air blows inward in clockwise direction in the Southern hemisphere.

Anti-cyclone

They are the wind system, which has the highest air pressure at the centre and lowest at the outer margins surrounded by circular isobars where wind blows from centre to outward in clockwise direction in Northern hemisphere from centre to outward in anticlockwise direction in Southern hemisphere.

They are high pressure system and common in sub-tropical belts and practically absent in the equator region. They are generally associated with rainless fair weather and that's why they are called as weatherless phenomena.

Thunderstorms

Thunderstorms are local storms characterised by swift upward movement of air and heavy rainfall with cloud thunder and lighting. Structurally, thunderstorms consist of several convective cells, which are characterised by strong updraft of air.

Tornado

Tornadoes are very strong tropical cyclones of smaller size. In the Mississippi valley (US), they are called twisters. They are more destructive than cyclones as the speed of winds is very high, exceeding 320 km per hour.

text: Humidity of air refers to the content of the water vapour present in the air at a particular time and place. Humidity is measured by an instrument called hygrometer. Another instrument used for the same purpose is sling psychrometer.

details.summary: Definition of humidity and the instruments used to measure it.

subject: Geography
text:
The atmospheric humidity is expressed in a number of ways:

  • Humidity Capacity: The capacity of air of certain volume at certain temperature to retain maximum amount of moisture content.
  • Absolute Humidity: The total weight of moisture content per volume of air at definite temperature.
  • Specific Humidity: The mass of the water vapour in grams contained in a kilogram of air.
  • Relative Humidity: The ratio of the amount of water vapour actually present in the air having definite volume and temperature to the maximum amount the air can hold.
  • Condensation: The change of physical state of matter from gaseous phase into liquid phase.
  • Dew Point: The temperature at which relative humidity reaches 100% and air is completely saturated.
  • Smog: Smoke + Fog, occurs in areas where air contains a large amount of smoke.
  • Fog: Droplets of water suspended in the lower layer of the atmosphere. Visibility less than 1 km.
  • Haze: Formed by water particles that have condensed in the atmosphere with visibility between 1 km to 2 km.
  • Frost: Moisture on the ground surface that condenses directly into ice when condensation occurs below freezing point.

Precipitation Types:

  • Convectional Precipitation: Occurs daily in the afternoon in equatorial regions. Short duration, heavy rainfall, thick cumulonimbus clouds, thunder and lightening.
  • Orographic Precipitation: Windward slope receives maximum rainfall, leeward slope receives less.
  • Cyclonic Precipitation: Associated with temperate cyclones when two extensive air masses of different physical properties converge. In tropical regions, air masses of similar properties converge to form tropical cyclones.

subject: Geography
content:
### Weather
- **Definition**: The sum total of atmospheric conditions (temperature, pressure, wind, moisture, cloudiness, precipitation, visibility) at a specific place and time.

### Climate
- **Definition**: The long‑term average of weather conditions over a period of at least 30 years for a given region.

Understanding the distinction is essential for interpreting climatic zones and their vegetation patterns.

subject: Geography
content:
### Climatic Zones (Latitude Bands)
| Zone | Latitude Range | Typical Climate | Representative Vegetation |
|------|----------------|----------------|---------------------------|
| **Equatorial Zone** | 10° N – 10° S | Hot, wet year‑round; rainfall throughout the year | Equatorial rain forest (e.g., selva) – ebony, mahogany, dye woods |
| **Hot Zone** | 30° N – 30° S | Generally warm; precipitation varies with sub‑type | (i) **Tropical Monsoon** – heavy summer rain; monsoonal forest (teak, sal, sisam, eucalyptus, acacia)\n(ii) **Tropical Marine** – summer rain; similar forest types\n(iii) **Sudan type** – savanna (tropical grassland) – grasses\n(iv) **Desert** – rain mainly in summer, little overall; desert vegetation & scrub (cacti) |
| **Warm Temperate Zone** | 30° N – 45° S | Moderate temperatures; precipitation pattern varies | (i) **Western Margin (Mediterranean type)** – winter rain; Mediterranean forests (oak, pine, fir, eucalyptus, giant sequoia, cedar)\n(ii) **Central Continental (Steppe type)** – light summer rain; steppe, temperate grasslands\n(iii) **Eastern Margin** – heavier summer rain; mixed forest‑grassland mosaics |

These zones illustrate how latitude, rainfall distribution, and temperature together dictate natural vegetation types.

An ocean current is a continuous, directed movement of ocean water.

- **Merging**: Joins the North Atlantic Drift.
- **Role**: Transports cold, nutrient‑rich water into the North Atlantic, affecting sea‑ice distribution and marine life.
