text:
On the basis of tidal range and other characteristics, tides are classified as follows:

  • Spring Tide: The spring tides are of an unusually large magnitude. They occur twice every month at the new Moon and full Moon. On these two days, the Sun, Moon and the Earth are in a straight line. At this time, the Moon is said to be in SYZYGY.
  • Neap Tide: The neap tides are of a lower magnitude and they are produced in the first and third quarters of the lunar month when the lines joining the centres of the Earth, Sun and the Moon are almost at right angles to each other. In this position, the Moon is said to be in quadrature.
  • Apogean and Perigean Tide: Due to the elliptical orbit of the Moon, the distance between the Moon and Earth keeps changing. When the Moon is in apogee, meaning maximum distance, it produces tides of relatively lower magnitude. On the other hand, when the distance between the Moon and Earth is minimum, meaning in perigee position, it produces tides of higher magnitude.

details.summary: Tides are classified into Spring Tides (syzygy, occurring during new/full Moon with maximum range), Neap Tides (quadrature, first/third quarters with lower magnitude), and Apogean/Perigean tides based on the Moon's orbital distance from Earth.

mcq.question: When the Sun, Moon, and Earth are aligned in a straight line during new Moon and full Moon, this position is known as:
mcq.explanation: When the Sun, Moon, and the Earth are aligned in a straight line at the time of new Moon and full Moon, the position is known as syzygy, resulting in spring tides of unusually large magnitude.

topic: Waterways: Major Sea Routes and Canals of the World
text:
Waterways play an important role in transportation. It is the most suitable and cheapest mode for international trade.

Major Canals of the World:

  • Suez Canal: This is the largest canal of the world connecting the Red Sea and Mediterranean Sea, where ship navigation is possible. Completed in 1869, it separates the lower part of the Nile basin and the Sinai Peninsula.
  • Panama Canal: This canal has been constructed by cutting across the Panama isthmus, connecting the Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea. On the Pacific coast lies Panama port and on the Caribbean coast lies Colon port.
  • Volga Canal System: This is an important navigable canal system of the world, with an 11,200 km navigable waterway. The Volga river drains into the Caspian Sea. The Moscow region has been connected to this waterway through the Volga-Moscow canal. Navigation is possible up to the Black Sea through the Volga-Don canal.
tables:
| Major Sea Route | Characteristic |
|---|---|
| North Atlantic Oceanic Route | It joins the developed regions of Western Europe with the developed region of North America. |
| South Atlantic Oceanic Route | It joins North America and Europe with South America. |
| North Pacific Oceanic Route | It joins East Asia and North America with each other. |
| South Pacific Oceanic Route | It joins Australia, New Zealand, North America and Western Europe with each other. |
| Routes of Indian Ocean | The routes are used by the countries which fall in the vicinity of Indian ocean exports tea, jute etc. |
| Routes of Mediterranean Sea | It joins Asia and Australia continents with North Atlantic ocean routes. It joins together the maximum number of countries of the world. |
| Cape of Good Hope Route | This sea route joins Eastern Asia and Europe to Southern parts of Africa. This oceanic route has lost its importance with the construction of Suez canal. |

details.summary: Summary of major oceanic routes including North Atlantic, South Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian Ocean routes, alongside strategic international ship canals: Suez Canal, Panama Canal, and the Volga Canal System.

subject: General Science
content:
### Nearest Planet to Earth
- **Venus** is the closest planet to Earth on average because its orbit lies between Earth and the Sun.
- Mercury can be nearer at certain points, but standard textbook answer: **Venus**.

### Nearest Planet to the Sun
- **Mercury** is the innermost planet, orbiting at an average distance of ~0.39 AU from the Sun.

### Order of Planets by Distance from the Sun (inner to outer)
1. Mercury
2. Venus
3. Earth
4. Mars
5. Jupiter
6. Saturn
7. Uranus
8. **Neptune** (eighth planet after Pluto’s re‑classification)

### Largest and Second‑Largest Planets
- **Jupiter** – the biggest planet in the Solar System (radius ≈ 71,492 km).
- **Saturn** – second in size after Jupiter; known for its extensive ring system.

### Unique Ring System
- **Saturn** possesses a spectacular and unique set of rings composed mainly of ice particles, distinguishing it from other planets.

### Planetary Colors
- **Neptune** appears a deep **green‑blue** (often described as “greenish”) due to methane absorption of red light.

### Fastest Orbital (Revolution) Period
- **Mercury** completes an orbit in **88 Earth days**, the shortest revolution period among the planets.

### “Red Planet”
- **Mars** is called the Red Planet because of iron‑oxide (rust) on its surface giving it a reddish hue.

### Asteroid Belt
- **Asteroids** predominantly reside in the region **between Mars and Jupiter**.

### Comet Structure
- A comet consists of a **nucleus**, a surrounding **coma (head)**, and a **tail** that points away from the Sun due to solar wind.

### Satellite of Pluto
- **Charon** is the only large natural satellite of **Pluto**; it is about half the size of Pluto itself.

content: Nights in deserts are significantly cooler than in plains primarily because the sky remains clear most of the time. Clear skies allow for rapid radiative cooling of the surface. content: The primary force driving atmospheric circulation is the differential heating of the Earth's surface. - **Wind Movement**: Winds move **outward** (divergent) from the center.

  - In the **Southern Hemisphere**, winds move counter-clockwise and outward.

content:

- **Definition**: The process of decay and disintegration of rocks **in situ** (i.e., at the place where they occur) without the material being transported.
- **Types**:
  1. **Mechanical (Physical) Weathering** – breakdown of rocks by physical forces such as temperature changes (thermal expansion), freeze‑thaw cycles, exfoliation, abrasion, and pressure release.
  2. **Chemical Weathering** – alteration of the mineral composition of rocks due to chemical reactions, e.g., oxidation, hydrolysis, carbonation, and dissolution.
- **Importance**: Initiates soil formation, influences landscape evolution, and controls the supply of sediments to rivers and oceans.

subject: Geography
content:
### Doldrums (ITCZ)
- **Location**: A calm, low‑pressure belt roughly between **5° N and 5° S** of the equator.
- **Characteristics**:
  - Weak surface winds; frequent light and variable breezes.
  - High humidity and abundant cloud formation due to intense solar heating.
  - Convergence of the **northeasterly trade winds** from the Northern Hemisphere and **southeasterly trade winds** from the Southern Hemisphere.
- **Solar Angle**: The Sun’s rays are **nearly vertical at the equator only during the equinoxes**; throughout the year the solar declination varies between ±23.5°, so the statement that “Sun rays strike almost vertically over the equator throughout the year” is false.

subject: Geography
content:
### Tornado Rotation
- **Northern Hemisphere**: Most tornadoes spin **anti‑clockwise** (cyclonic) because of the Coriolis effect and prevailing wind shear.
- **Southern Hemisphere**: Tornadoes generally spin **clockwise** (cyclonic in the Southern Hemisphere).
- **Note**: Rare anticyclonic tornadoes can occur in either hemisphere, but the dominant pattern follows the above rule.

subject: Geography
topic: Air Density Near the Earth's Surface
content:
### Air Near the Surface
1. **Heavier Air**: Air close to the surface is denser (heavier) because atmospheric pressure is highest at sea level and decreases with altitude (hydrostatic balance).
2. **Higher Moisture & Particulate Content**: Near‑surface air typically contains **more water vapour** (due to evaporation from oceans, lakes, and soils) and **greater concentrations of dust and aerosols** because sources are at the ground and there is less time for removal processes.
- These factors affect temperature, humidity, and visibility.

subject: Geography
content:
- **Igneous Rock Formation**: Igneous rocks are formed from the cooling and solidification of molten rock (magma or lava).
- **Intrusive vs Extrusive**: 
  - **Intrusive (Plutonic)**: Formed when magma cools slowly deep within the Earth's crust. This slow cooling allows large crystals to form (e.g., Granite).
  - **Extrusive (Volcanic)**: Formed when lava cools quickly on the Earth's surface. Rapid cooling results in very small crystals or glassy textures (e.g., Basalt).

subject: Geography
topic: Role of Vegetation in Soil Conservation
content:
- **Vegetation and Erosion**: Hills with dense vegetation cover experience significantly less soil erosion compared to bare hills.
- **Mechanism**: 
  1. **Infiltration**: Vegetation slows down surface runoff, allowing more rainwater to infiltrate into the soil.
  2. **Binding**: Root systems bind soil particles together, increasing soil stability and resistance to erosion by wind and water.

subject: Geography
content:
- **Vertical Temperature Gradient**: The rate at which air temperature changes with altitude is known as the vertical temperature gradient (or lapse rate).
- **Troposphere Characteristics**: In the Troposphere (the lowest layer of the atmosphere), temperature generally decreases with increasing altitude.
- **Cause**: The primary source of heat for the lower atmosphere is the Earth's surface, which absorbs solar radiation and re-emits it as long-wave radiation (terrestrial radiation). As altitude increases, the distance from this heat source increases, leading to lower temperatures.

subject: Geography
content:
- **Chemical Weathering**: The decomposition of rocks through chemical reactions.
- **Environmental Factors**: Chemical weathering is most active in **hot and humid** environments.
- **Reason**: High temperatures accelerate chemical reaction rates, and abundant rainfall provides the water necessary for hydrolysis, oxidation, and dissolution processes. These conditions facilitate the rapid decomposition of rock minerals.

subject: Geography
content:
- **Tuareg People**: A Berber ethnic group known for their pastoral nomadic lifestyle.
- **Habitat**: They primarily inhabit the **Sahara Desert** in North Africa (spanning parts of Mali, Niger, Libya, Algeria, and Nigeria).
- **Other Nomads**: 
  - Kalahari: San/Bushmen
  - Arabia: Bedouins
  - Patagonia: Gauchos (historically)

subject: Geography
content:
- **Selvas (Tropical Rainforests)**: Characterized by **Epiphytes** (plants growing on other plants), dense canopy, and high biodiversity.
- **Savanna**: Characterized by **Grasses and scattered trees** (Tropophytes are also common, but the defining feature is the grassland with trees). *Note: In matching questions, Savanna is often linked to Grasses/Trees.*
- **Tundra**: Characterized by **Mosses and lichens** due to permafrost and short growing seasons.
- **Monsoon Land**: Characterized by **Tropophytes** (plants that grow in response to seasonal rains) or distinct seasonal vegetation changes.

subject: Geography
content:
- **Hydrolysis**: A chemical weathering process where water reacts with rock minerals to form new compounds.
- **Effectiveness in Humid Tropics**: Hydrolysis is highly effective in humid tropics primarily due to **high temperature and humidity**.
- **Diurnal Range**: While diurnal temperature range exists, it is not the primary driver for the chemical effectiveness of hydrolysis compared to the constant high moisture and heat.

subject: Geography
content:
**Rotterdam (Netherlands):**
- Rotterdam is largely famous for its **shipbuilding** industry.
- It is one of the largest ports in the world, facilitating significant trade and industrial activity related to maritime engineering.

subject: Geography
content:
**Sequence for Heavy Rainfall (Convectional/Orographic):**
- The correct sequence for heavy downpour involves **Rapid ascent of air**.
- As air rises rapidly, it cools adiabatically, leading to condensation.
- This results in the formation of **Large raindrops**.
- The accumulation and coalescence of these drops lead to a **Heavy downpour**.
- *Incorrect sequences:* Slow ascent leads to light rain; descent of air warms the air and inhibits rainfall (subsidence); compression of air generally warms it, preventing condensation.

subject: Geography
content:
**Earth's Axial Tilt (Obliquity of Ecliptic):**
- The Earth's axis of rotation makes an angle of **23.5°** (23° 1/2°) with the perpendicular to the plane of the ecliptic.
- **Hypothetical Scenario (0° Tilt):**
  - If the angle were zero, the Sun would always be directly overhead at the equator.
  - **Seasons:** There would be **no seasons** (no variation in solar angle throughout the year).
  - **Day/Night Length:** The length of day and night would be **12 hours each** throughout the year for all locations.
  - **Global Uniformity:** The length of day and night would be the same **all over the Earth** (everywhere would have 12h day/12h night).
  - Therefore, all the stated consequences (no seasons, equal day/night length globally and annually) would result.

subject: Geography
content:
**Yakutsk Nomadic Herders:**
- **Yakutsk** (or Yakuts) are nomadic herders found in the **Tundra** region.
- They are primarily located in Siberia (Russia) and practice reindeer herding.
- *Other regions:* Gobi (Mongolia/China), Sahara (North Africa), Kalahari (Southern Africa) have different nomadic groups.

subject: Geography
content:
**Factors for Luxuriant Growth in Tropical Rainforests:**
- **Hot and wet climate throughout the year:** Provides constant moisture and heat, essential for rapid plant growth.
- **Intense sunlight for photosynthesis:** High solar radiation drives high rates of photosynthesis.
- **Note on Soil:** Tropical rainforest soils are often **leached and infertile** (laterite soils) due to heavy leaching from high rainfall. The luxuriant growth is primarily due to climate (heat/rain) and sunlight, not fertile soil.
- **Note on Seasonality:** Tropical rainforests have **no distinct dry season** (or very short one), so seasonal change is not a primary driver of nutrient absorption in the same way as in savannas. The key factors are the constant hot/wet conditions and sunlight.

subject: Geography
content:
**Matching Vegetation Types to Regions:**
- **Selvas (Tropical Rainforests):** Characterized by **Epiphytes** (plants growing on other plants), tall trees, and high biodiversity.
- **Savannas:** Characterized by **Grasses and trees** (scattered trees in a grassland matrix).
- **Taiga (Boreal Forests):** Characterized by **Conifers** (evergreen needle-leaf trees like pine, spruce, fir).
- **Tundra:** Characterized by **Mosses and lichens** (low-growing plants, no trees, permafrost).

subject: Geography
content:
**Rain Shadow Effect:**
- The rain shadow effect is associated with **orographic rainfall**.
- When moist air is forced to rise over a mountain range, it cools and precipitates on the windward side.
- The leeward side (downwind) receives little rainfall because the air descends and warms, inhibiting condensation. This dry area is called the rain shadow.

subject: Geography
content:
**Barometer Readings and Weather Conditions:**
- A **sudden fall in barometer reading** indicates a drop in atmospheric pressure.
- Low pressure systems are associated with rising air, cloud formation, and precipitation.
- Therefore, a sudden fall in barometer reading indicates **Stormy weather**.
- *High pressure* is associated with calm, clear, and dry weather.

subject: Geography
content:
### Rock Folds
- **Anticline**: An upfold in rock strata where the oldest rocks are in the center.
- **Syncline**: A downfold in rock strata where the youngest rocks are in the center.
- **Graben**: A down-dropped block of crust between two parallel normal faults.
- **Horst**: An uplifted block of crust between two parallel normal faults.

subject: Geography
content:
### Exosphere
- The outermost layer of the Earth's atmosphere.
- **Composition**: Primarily composed of **Hydrogen** and Helium. Hydrogen is found in the highest quantity in this layer due to its low atomic weight allowing it to escape more easily or reach higher altitudes.

subject: Geography
content:
### Stalactites and Stalagmites
- **Stalactites**: Form when water containing dissolved calcium carbonate drips from the ceiling of a cave. They **hang down** from the ceiling, resembling icicles.
- **Stalagmites**: Form when the dripping water hits the cave floor and deposits minerals. They **rise up** from the floor of the cave.
- **Key Distinction**: Stalactites hang from the ceiling; Stalagmites rise from the floor.

subject: Geography
content:
### Lithosphere
- The rigid outer part of the Earth.
- **Composition**: Consists of the **Crust** and the **uppermost part of the Mantle** (specifically the rigid upper mantle).
- It is broken into tectonic plates.

subject: Geography
content:
### Temperate Coniferous Forests
- Also known as Taiga or Boreal Forests.
- **Dominant Trees**: Spruce, Cedar, Pine, and Fir.
- **Characteristics**: Evergreen, needle-leaved trees adapted to cold climates.

subject: Geography
content:
### Sal Tree (Shorea robusta)
- **Classification**: **Dry Deciduous** tree.
- **Habitat**: Found in tropical regions with distinct wet and dry seasons.
- **Characteristics**: Loses leaves during the dry season to conserve water.

subject: Geography
content:
### Key Astronomical Events (Northern Hemisphere)
- **Vernal Equinox**: Occurs on **21st March**. Day and night are of equal length.
- **Summer Solstice**: Occurs on **21st or 22nd June**. Longest day of the year in the Northern Hemisphere.
- **Autumnal Equinox**: Occurs on **23rd September**. Day and night are of equal length.
- **Winter Solstice**: Occurs on **21st or 22nd December**. Shortest day of the year in the Northern Hemisphere.

*Note: Statement 2 in Q90 (Summer solstice on 22nd Dec) is incorrect; it is Winter Solstice. Statement 4 (Winter solstice on 21st June) is incorrect; it is Summer Solstice.*

subject: Geography
content:
### Solar Eclipse
- Occurs when the **Moon** comes exactly between the **Sun** and the **Earth**.
- The Moon casts a shadow on the Earth.
- This can only happen during the New Moon phase.

subject: Geography
content: India occupies a South‑Central position in the Asian continent, looking across the Arabian Sea to Arabia and Africa on the West and across the Bay of Bengal to Myanmar, Malaysia and the Indonesian Archipelago on the East. The Himalayan ranges keep India apart from the rest of Asia. India derives its name from the river Indus.

subject: Geography

It has a total land area of about 3,287,263 sq km, which is 2.42% of the world’s area. India is the second largest country in Asia both in terms of area and population, after China. It is the second largest in terms of population and holds 17.4% of the total world population.

subject: Geography
content:
The Himalayas are classified into five longitudinal series of mountains:

1. **Trans-Himalayas (Tibet Himalayas)**:
   - Located North of the Greater Himalayas.
   - Older than the main Himalayas.
   - Acts as a watershed between rivers flowing South and North.
   - Width: ~40 km.
   - Height: Up to 5000 m.
   - Includes: Karakoram, Zaskar, and Ladakh ranges.

2. **Greater Himalayas (Himadri)**:
   - The Northernmost important range.
   - Also known as Inner Himalayas.

3. **Himachal Himalaya (Middle Himalayas)**:
   - Lies to the South of the Himadri.
   - Forms the most rugged mountain system.

4. **Shiwaliks (Outer Himalayas)**:
   - The outermost range of the Himalayas.
   - Width: 10-50 km.
   - Altitude: 900 to 1100 m.
   - Composition: Unconsolidated sediments brought down by rivers from the main Himalayan ranges in the North.

5. **Purvanchal (Eastern Hills)**:
   - Formed after the Himalayas cross the Dihang gorge and take a sudden Southward turn.
   - Shape: Crescent with the convex side pointing towards the West.
   - Character: Comparatively low hills.

subject: Geography
content:
### Great Indian Plain (Indus‑Ganga‑Brahmaputra Plain)
- Extends for about **3,200 km**.
- Width varies from **150 km to 300 km**.
- Largely **featureless** with a maximum elevation of **204 m**.
- The land around **Ambala** acts as the **water divide** for the plain.
- Based on geomorphological characteristics, the plain is divided into four distinct regions:
  1. **Bhabar Region**
  2. **Terai Region**
  3. **Khadar Region**
  4. **Bhangar Region**

subject: Geography
content:
### Bhabar Region
- Location: Along the foothills of the **Shiwalik range**, stretching from **Indus to Tista** without interruption.
- Width: **8–16 km**.
- Lithology: Composed of **stones and pebbles**, making it **highly porous**.
- Hydrology: Rivers **disappear underground** in this zone because of the porous substrate.
- Significance: Acts as a transition zone between the mountains and the lower plains.

subject: Geography
content:
### Terai Region
- Lies **south of the Bhabar** region.
- Hydrology: Underground streams from Bhabar **re‑emerge** at the surface, forming **marshy lands**.
- Vegetation: Characterised by **dense forests** and **high biodiversity**.
- Importance: Supports rich flora and fauna; many wildlife sanctuaries are located here.

subject: Geography
content:
### Khadar Region
- Consists of **new alluvium** (recent river‑deposited sediments).
- Typically found in **deltaic areas**, e.g., the **Ganga‑Brahmaputra delta**.
- Soil: Very **fertile**, supporting intensive agriculture.
- Flooding: Frequently **flood‑prone** because it lies at the lowest elevation of the plain.

subject: Geography
content:
### Bhangar Region
- Represents the **higher part** of the plains where floodwaters **cannot reach**.
- Composed of **old alluvium** (older river deposits).
- Often appears as **terraced** landforms.
- Soil: Generally **less fertile** than Khadar but better drained.

subject: Geography
content:
### Peninsular Plateau
- Shape: Roughly **triangular**.
- Rock type: Dominated by **old crystalline, igneous, and metamorphic rocks**.
- Origin: Formed from the **break‑up and drift of Gondwanaland**, making it part of the **oldest landmass** on Earth.
- Geography: Bordered by water on **three sides**, hence the term **peninsular**.
- Topography: Contains **broad, shallow valleys** and **rounded hills**.
- Major river: The **Narmada River** cuts a **rift valley**, dividing the plateau into two major physiographic units:
  1. **Central Highlands** (north of Narmada)
  2. **Deccan Plateau** (south of Narmada)

subject: Geography
content:
### Divisions of the Peninsular Plateau
1. **Central Highland**
   - Location: North of the **Narmada River**.
   - Extent: Covers a major part of the **Malwa Plateau**.
   - Features: Higher elevation, rugged terrain, and several **plateau complexes** (e.g., Bundelkhand, Chota Nagpur).
2. **Deccan Plateau**
   - Location: South of the **Narmada River**.
   - Extent: Spreads over a large part of central and southern India.
   - Features: Generally **lower elevation** than the Central Highlands, with extensive **basaltic lava flows** (Deccan Traps) and numerous **river valleys**.

subject: Geography
content:
### Central Highland
- Lies **north of the Narmada River**.
- Includes the **Malwa Plateau** and other uplifted blocks.
- Characterised by **granite‑gneiss** terrain, moderate elevation, and a mix of **plateau and hill** landforms.

subject: Geography

- Extends from Kachchh and Kathiawar regions of Gujarat to Konkan plains of Maharashtra-Goa, Karnataka plains, and Southern Malabar plains along the Kerala coast.

> **Definition**: A *waterfall* is a vertical or near‑vertical drop in the course of a stream or river.

> **Height Measurement**: Height is measured from the top of the waterfall to the lowest point of the plunge pool or the point where the water re‑enters the stream.

---

## Climate of India

India experiences a **tropical monsoon** climate, heavily influenced by the Himalayas. The mountains act as a barrier, blocking cold Central Asian air masses and allowing the monsoon winds to deposit moisture over the subcontinent.

### Climatic Zones

- **Northern Zone** (north of the Tropic of Cancer, 23.5° N):
  - Sub‑tropical climate with cold winters and hot summers.
  - Mid‑day sun never reaches the zenith.
- **Southern Zone** (south of the Tropic of Cancer):
  - Tropical climate, warmer year‑round.
  - Mid‑day sun is almost vertically overhead at least twice a year.

---

## Climatic Regions of India

| Climate Type | Areas | Characteristics |
|--------------|-------|-----------------|
| **Tropical Rain Forest** | Western Ghats, West Coastal Plains, parts of Assam & Tripura | High temperature year‑round, heavy seasonal rainfall (200 cm annually, May‑Nov) |
| **Tropical Savanna** | Most of Peninsular region (except leeward side of Western Ghats) | Dry winters, annual rainfall 76‑150 cm |
| **Tropical Semi‑Arid Steppe** | Rainshadow belt from Central Maharashtra to Tamil Nadu | Low rainfall 38‑80 cm, temperatures 20‑30 °C |
| **Tropical & Sub‑tropical Steppes** | Punjab, Haryana, Kutch | Temperature 12‑35 °C |
| **Tropical Desert** | Western parts of Barmer, Jaisalmer, Bikaner (Rajasthan) & parts of Kutch | Scanty rainfall (mostly cloud bursts), high temperatures |

> **Key Takeaway**: The climatic diversity of India is largely dictated by its topography and latitude, leading to distinct ecological zones from lush rainforests to arid deserts.

content:
**Southern Oscillation** refers to the inter-relation of high and low pressure over the Pacific and Indian Oceans.
- **Condition 1**: High surface level pressure over the Indian Ocean and low pressure over the Pacific Ocean.
- **Condition 2**: Low surface level pressure over the Indian Ocean and high pressure over the Pacific Ocean (vice-versa).
- This oscillation is a key factor in the variability of the Indian Monsoon.

subject: Geography
content:
**Winter Season**
- **Timing**: Starts by late November.
- **Characteristics**: Clear skies, fine weather, light northerly winds, low humidity, low temperatures, and large day-time variations in temperature.
- **Rainfall**: Generally occurs over the Western Himalayas, extreme North-Eastern parts of Tamil Nadu, and Kerala.

subject: Geography
content:
**Summer Season**
- **Timing**: Begins all over the country in March.
- **Temperature**: By April, average daily temperature reaches 30-35°C. Central Indian land becomes very hot and humid, with temperatures reaching 40°C at many locations.
- **Rainfall**: Only 1% of total Indian rainfall is received during this season, mostly by storms caused by convective currents.

subject: Geography
content:
**Rainy Season**
- **Timing**: Starts from June and stays until late September.
- **Characteristics**: High heat, high humidity, and extensive cloud cover.
- **Rainfall**: Several spells of moderate to heavy rainfall occur throughout the country. Most of the rainfall is brought by the **South-West Monsoon**.

subject: Geography
content:
**Autumn Season**
- **Timing**: Starts from mid-September and stays until November.
- **Characteristics**: Generally no cloud, but severe and devastating tropical cyclones may hit coastal regions.
- **Rainfall**: Occurs due to the **retreating monsoon**. It causes rainfall in Tamil Nadu, some parts of Andhra Pradesh, and Kerala.

subject: Geography
content:
**Soil Formation**
- **Process**: Soil is formed when rocks are broken down by the action of wind, water, and climate. This process is called **weathering**.
- **Dependency**: The characteristic features of a soil depend upon the rocks from which it has been formed.
- **Structure**: Soil forms different layers (horizons) of particles of different sizes.

subject: Geography
content:
### Desert Soils
- **Geographic distribution**: North‑Western India – major parts of Rajasthan, south of Haryana and Punjab, and northern Gujarat.
- **Landscape**: Predominantly sand dunes and undulating sandy plains.
- **Origin**: Mostly derived from alluvium.
- **Colour & texture**: Pale brown to yellow‑brown; fine sandy to loamy fine sand; generally **structureless**.
- **Clay content**: Low.
- **Chemical feature**: Presence of alkaline earth carbonates.
- **Soil improvement**: Adding organic matter and clay increases water‑holding capacity, thereby enhancing productivity.

subject: Geography
content:
### Swampy/Peaty Soils
- **Formation**: Develop in areas of heavy rainfall with inadequate drainage.
- **Typical locations**: Foothills of the Himalayas – Jammu & Kashmir, Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal.
- **Local name**: *Karewa* soil, especially noted in Jammu & Kashmir.
- **Agricultural use**: Cultivation of *zaffran* (saffron) is practiced on Karewa soils.

subject: Geography
content:
### Saline Soils
- **Extent in India**: Approximately **7 million hectares** are salt‑affected, spread across several states.
- **Reclamation requirement**: Productive use is possible only after appropriate reclamation measures.
- **Formation mechanism**: Accumulation of soluble salts, primarily **chlorides** and **sulphates** of calcium and magnesium.

subject: Geography
content:
### Forest Soils
- **Formation environment**: Forested areas with sufficient rainfall.
- **Variability**: Structure and texture vary according to the mountain environment in which they develop.

subject: Geography
content:
### Soil Erosion and Degradation
- **Soil erosion**: Destruction/removal of the soil cover.
- **Soil degradation**: Decline in soil fertility.
- **Primary agents**: **Wind** and **water** – both can detach soil particles and transport them elsewhere.
- **Wind erosion**: Most significant in arid and semi‑arid regions.
- **Water erosion**: Dominant in areas with heavy rainfall and steep slopes, where running water removes soil.

subject: Geography
content:
### Types of Soil Erosion
- **Wind erosion** – prevalent in dry, sparsely vegetated landscapes.
- **Water erosion** – includes sheet erosion, rill erosion, gully erosion, and streambank erosion; most important where rainfall intensity is high and slopes are steep.

subject: Geography
content:
# Mangroves

- **Definition**: Mangroves are highly specialized forest ecosystems found in tropical and subtropical regions along sheltered sea‑coasts.
- **Habitats**: They thrive in estuaries, tidal creeks, backwaters, salt marshes, and mudflats.
- **Plant Community**: Dominated by salt‑tolerant halophytic plants with diverse structural forms.
- **Ecological Role**:
  - Serve as invaluable marine nurseries for a wide variety of fish and other marine fauna.
  - Support diverse bird, amphibian, arboreal, benthic, and aquatic species.
- **Root System**: Dense network of aerial roots that aerate the root system and anchor the tree against tidal forces.
- **Common Species**:
  - *Sundari* (Avicennia officinalis) – widespread in the Sundarbans.
  - Screw pines, canes, and palms – common in deltaic regions.
  - *Nipa* (Nypa fruticans) – often found lining cracks in mangrove forests.

> **Key Takeaway**: Mangroves are critical coastal ecosystems that provide habitat, protect shorelines, and support local livelihoods.

- A resource is a source or supply from which benefit is produced.

subject: General Science

### Conventional Sources of Energy
- Generally referred to as **non‑renewable** sources.
- Historically the main contributors to India's energy mix.
- **Major conventional sources**:
  - Coal
  - Petroleum (crude oil & its derivatives)
  - Natural gas
  - Cattle‑dung cake (biomass used in rural areas)
  - Hydel power (hydroelectricity) – often listed with conventional sources because of its early development in India.
- These sources have been exploited for a long time and are finite in nature.

subject: General Science
content:
### Thermal Energy in Power Generation
- **Thermal electricity** is generated by converting the heat released from the combustion of **coal, petroleum, and natural gas** into electrical energy.
- **Contribution to national grid**:
  - Approximately **65 % of total electricity** produced in India is thermal in character.
- **Strategic importance**:
  - Provides power in regions where **hydro‑electric potential is limited** due to unfavorable geography.
  - Accounts for **more than half of the installed capacity in 14 Indian states**.
- **Key advantage**: Ability to locate plants close to load centres, reducing transmission losses.

subject: General Science
content:
### Ultra Mega Power Plants (UMPPs)
- **Government initiative** to rapidly augment India's power generation capacity.
- **Target capacity per plant**: **4,000 MW** (≈ 4 GW).
- **Objectives**:
  1. Supply electricity at a **responsible (affordable) rate** to consumers.
  2. Ensure **fast‑track capacity addition** through **tariff‑based international competitive bidding**.
- **Impact**: Designed to bridge the supply‑demand gap and reduce dependence on smaller, less efficient plants.

subject: General Science
content:
### Hydroelectric Power in India
- Plays a **significant role** in addressing the country's energy crisis.
- **Early milestones**:
  - **1897** – First electricity supply in **Darjeeling** (marking the humble start of hydro‑electricity in India).
  - **1902** – Commissioning of the **Sivasamudram Hydropower Station** in Karnataka.
- Since these early projects, hydro‑electricity has grown to become a major component of the renewable energy mix.

subject: Geography
content:
### Global Warming
- **Definition**: Global warming is the increase of Earth’s average surface temperature due to the effect of greenhouse gases.
- **Primary Causes**:
  - Carbon dioxide emissions from burning fossil fuels.
  - Deforestation, which reduces the planet’s capacity to absorb CO₂.
- **Mechanism**: Greenhouse gases trap infrared radiation, leading to a rise in temperature – a phenomenon known as the **greenhouse effect**.
- **Impacts**: Sea‑level rise, extreme weather events, melting glaciers, and disruption of ecosystems.
- **Key Formula** (simplified energy balance):
  \[ \Delta T = \frac{F}{4\sigma}\] where \(F\) is the radiative forcing and \(\sigma\) is the Stefan‑Boltzmann constant.

subject: Geography
content:
### Ozone Layer Depletion
- **Location**: Stratosphere, about 24 km above Earth’s surface.
- **Composition**: Ozone (O₃) molecules formed when sunlight reacts with molecular oxygen (O₂).
- **Importance**: Filters the Sun’s harmful ultraviolet (UV‑B and UV‑C) radiation, protecting living organisms.
- **Threats**:
  - Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and other halogenated compounds released from industrial processes and aerosol propellants.
  - These chemicals catalyze the breakdown of ozone molecules, thinning the protective layer.
- **Consequences**:
  - Increased incidence of skin cancer, cataracts, and other health problems.
  - Damage to agricultural crops and aquatic ecosystems.
- **Mitigation**: International agreements such as the Montreal Protocol (1987) aim to phase out CFC production.

topic: Difference between National Park, Sanctuary, and Biosphere Reserve
content:
### Comparison of Protected Areas

| Feature | National Park | Sanctuary | Biosphere Reserve |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Primary Purpose** | Preservation of natural vegetation, wildlife, and natural beauty. | Preservation of endangered species. | Multi-purpose protected area to preserve genetic diversity in representative ecosystems. |
| **Boundaries** | Fixed by legislation. | Not sacrosanct (can be modified). | Fixed by legislation. |

**Key Distinctions:**
- **National Parks** focus on the overall ecosystem and natural beauty, with strict legal boundaries.
- **Sanctuaries** are primarily for the protection of specific endangered species, and their boundaries are more flexible.
- **Biosphere Reserves** are multi-purpose zones aimed at preserving genetic diversity and often include core, buffer, and transition zones.

### Rainfall Patterns and Monsoon Dynamics

1.  **Windward vs. Leeward Side:**
    *   **Mumbai** receives more rainfall than **Pune** because Mumbai is located on the **windward side** of the Western Ghats, facing the South-West monsoon winds directly. Pune is on the leeward side (rain shadow region).
2.  **Rain Shadow Regions:**
    *   The **Vidarbha** region (in Maharashtra) experiences a semi-arid climate because it is located in the **rain shadow** of the Western Ghats, receiving less rainfall.
3.  **Monsoon Progression:**
    *   The South-West monsoon enters India first at the **Malabar Coast** (Kerala).
    *   It reaches the **Kashmir Valley** last, as it has to travel across the entire subcontinent and is often blocked or delayed by the Himalayas and other mountain ranges.

### Seismic Zones in India

India is divided into four seismic zones based on the intensity of earthquakes:

*   **Zone II:** Low damage potential (e.g., parts of the Deccan Plateau, some areas of the North-East).
*   **Zone III:** Moderate damage potential (e.g., most of the country, including Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata).
*   **Zone IV:** Very high damage potential (e.g., parts of the Himalayan region, North-East India, parts of Gujarat).
*   **Zone V:** Extremely high damage potential (e.g., parts of the Himalayan region, North-East India, parts of Gujarat, and the Andaman & Nicobar Islands).

*Note: Specific locations like the Kashmir Valley, parts of the North-East, and the Western Ghats have specific zone classifications that are frequently tested in matching questions.*

### Sheet‑flood (Flash Flood) in Western Rajasthan
- **Primary causes**:
  1. **Sudden high‑intensity rainfall** – short, intense storms generate runoff faster than the soil can infiltrate.
  2. **Loose sandy soil with scanty vegetation** – low infiltration capacity and minimal surface roughness accelerate overland flow.
- **Secondary factor**: Scanty rainfall alone does **not** cause sheet‑floods; it is the *combination* of intense rain on poorly vegetated, sandy terrain that leads to rapid surface runoff.
- **Resulting hazards**: rapid inundation of low‑lying areas, loss of life, damage to agriculture and infrastructure.

subject: Indian Polity
content:
## Historical Background

- **British regulation of India** – The British Government introduced a series of constitutional reforms aimed at consolidating colonial rule.
- **East India Company (EIC)** – Arrived in 1600 as a trading entity; by 1765 obtained *Diwani* (revenue‑collection) rights over Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa, effectively becoming a governing body.
- **Key Acts of Parliament** governing the EIC and India:
  - **Regulating Act, 1773** – First attempt to control the Company’s administration; established a Governor‑General and a council.
  - **Charter Act, 1813** – Extended British oversight, opened Indian education to missionary activity, and ended the Company’s monopoly over trade with China.
  - **Government of India Act, 1858** – Transferred power from the EIC to the British Crown after the 1857 Revolt, marking the beginning of direct Crown rule.
- **Transition to Crown rule (1858‑1947)** – The British Raj administered India until independence, laying the legislative and administrative foundations that later influenced the Constitution.

---

### Key Take‑aways
1. The constitutional framework of modern India has its roots in a series of British statutes beginning with the Regulating Act, 1773.
2. The East India Company evolved from a commercial corporation to a quasi‑governmental authority, necessitating parliamentary regulation.
3. The Government of India Act, 1858 marked the end of Company rule and the start of direct British administration, a crucial step toward the eventual demand for self‑governance.

subject: Indian Polity
content:
## Making of the Constitution

- **Early political demand** – Mahatma Gandhi (1922) advocated that India’s political destiny be decided by Indians themselves.
- **First proposal for a Constituent Assembly** – M.N. Roy (1934) introduced the idea of a dedicated body to draft a constitution.
- **British acceptance** – The August Offer (1940) was the first British concession to the demand for a Constituent Assembly, though it was limited.
- **Cabinet Mission Plan (1946)** – Recommended the formation of a Constituent Assembly to frame the Constitution.
- **Constituent Assembly formation** – Established in **November 1946**; first meeting on **9 December 1946**.
- **Interim President** – **Sachidanand Sinha** presided over the inaugural session.

---

### Important Dates
| Date | Event |
|------|-------|
| 1922 | Gandhi’s demand for Indian‑determined destiny |
| 1934 | M.N. Roy proposes a Constituent Assembly |
| August 1940 | British accept the idea in the August Offer |
| November 1946 | Constituent Assembly set up (Cabinet Mission Plan) |
| 9 December 1946 | First meeting of the Constituent Assembly |

---

### Significance
- The Constituent Assembly became the **legislative crucible** where the Constitution of India was debated, drafted, and adopted, transitioning India from colonial rule to a sovereign republic.
- Understanding this timeline helps explain many **structural features** of the Constitution, such as federalism, fundamental rights, and the parliamentary system.

- **Duration of Drafting**: It took almost three years (specifically two years, eleven months, and eighteen days) to complete the drafting of the Constitution.
- **29th August, 1947**: The Constituent Assembly set up a Drafting Committee under the Chairmanship of Dr. B.R. Ambedkar to prepare a Draft Constitution for India.

- **Enforcement Date**: The Constitution came into force on **26th January, 1950**.
- **Reason for 26th January**: This date was specifically chosen because on this day in 1930, the Poorna Swaraj (Complete Independence) day was celebrated.

content:
The Indian Constitution addresses citizenship through Articles 5 to 11:
- **Article 5**: Citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution.
- **Article 6**: Rights of Citizenship of certain persons who have migrated to India from Pakistan.
- **Article 7**: Rights of Citizenship of certain migrants to Pakistan.
- **Article 8**: Rights of Citizenship of certain persons of Indian origin residing outside India.
- **Article 9**: Persons voluntarily acquiring Citizenship of a Foreign State are not to be citizens of India.
- **Article 10**: Continuance of the Rights of Citizenship.
- **Article 11**: Parliament has the power to regulate the Right of Citizenship by Law.

subject: Polity
content:
Rules regarding acquisition and termination of Indian citizenship are laid down in the **Citizenship Act of 1955**. A person can acquire Indian citizenship in five ways, remembered by the mnemonic **BRAND**:
1. **B**y Birth
2. **R**egistration
3. **A**cquisition of Territory
4. **N**aturalisation
5. **D**escent

subject: Polity
content:
Citizenship can be terminated in three ways:
1. **Voluntary Renunciation**: A citizen voluntarily renounces their citizenship.
2. **Acquisition of Foreign Citizenship**: Citizenship is terminated if a person acquires citizenship of some other country.
3. **Deprivation by Central Government**: The Central Government can deprive a naturalised citizen if:
   - Citizenship was acquired by fraud, false representation, or concealment of material facts.
   - The person shows disloyalty towards the Indian Constitution.
   - The person indulges in trade with enemy countries.
   - The person has been sentenced to imprisonment for a period of 2 years or more within 5 years of registration.
   - The person has been continuously residing out of India for more than 7 years.

subject: Polity
content: Under **Article 11**, Parliament has the exclusive power to enact laws regarding citizenship. It has the authority to regulate the right of citizenship in India.

subject: Polity
content: The **Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2015** seeks to amend the Citizenship Act, 1955. A major provision of this Act is that in cases of citizenship by naturalisation, it allows the Central Government to relax the requirement of 12 months stay or service in the government if special circumstances exist.

content:
### Qualifications for President (Article 58)
- **Citizenship:** Must be a citizen of India.
- **Age:** Must have attained the age of **35 years**.
- **Office of Profit:** Must **not** hold any office of profit under the Government of India or any State Government.
- **Parliamentary Eligibility:** Must be qualified to be elected as a **Member of the Lok Sabha** (i.e., not disqualified under any of the provisions of Articles 33, 191, 192, etc.).

subject: Indian Polity
content:
### Impeachment of the President (Article 61)
- **Grounds:** Violation of any provision of the Constitution.
- **Initiation:** Can be started in **either House** of Parliament.
- **Notice:** A notice containing the charges must be signed by **at least one‑fourth** of the total members of the initiating House and served on the President **14 days** in advance.
- **First House Resolution:** Must be passed by a **two‑thirds majority of the total membership** of that House.
- **Second House Investigation:** The other House investigates the charges. The President may defend himself through an **authorized council**.
- **Second House Resolution:** If the second House also passes the impeachment by a **two‑thirds majority of its total members**, the President is **removed from office**.
- **Effect:** The removal is immediate upon the passage of the second resolution.

subject: Indian Polity
content:
### Vacancy in the Office of President (Article 62)
- **Causes of Vacancy:** Death, resignation, removal, or any other reason rendering the office vacant.
- **Interim Arrangement:**
  1. **Vice‑President** acts as President.
  2. If the Vice‑President is unavailable, the **Chief Justice of India** acts as President.
  3. If the Chief Justice is unavailable, the **senior-most Judge of the Supreme Court** acts as President.
- **Election Timeline:** A fresh election to fill the vacancy must be conducted **within six months** from the date the vacancy arises.

subject: Indian Polity
content:
### Powers and Functions of the President (Article 77)
- The President is the **formal head of the executive** of the Union.
- **Actual exercise** of executive powers is done **by the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers** under the principle of **collective responsibility**.
- **Normal Period:** The President acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers in all matters.
- **Emergency Periods:** The President may exercise **discretionary powers** (e.g., proclamation of emergency, promulgation of ordinances when Parliament is not in session).
- **Key Executive Functions:**
  - **Appointment** of the Prime Minister, Council of Ministers, Governors, Judges, etc.
  - **Summoning**, **proroguing**, and **dissolving** the Lok Sabha.
  - **Promulgating** ordinances when Parliament is not in session.
  - **Granting** pardons, reprieves, respites or remission of punishment.
  - **Sending** messages to Parliament and **addressing** it at the commencement of each session.
- While the Constitution vests these powers in the President, **constitutional conventions** dictate that they are exercised **on the advice** of the elected government.

subject: Indian Constitution
content:
# National Emergency (Article 352)

- **Trigger**: Declared by the President when the **integrity of India** or a **state** is threatened by war, external aggression, or armed rebellion.
- **Duration**: Can be extended **every 3 months** for a maximum of **12 months**.
- **Effect**: Grants the central government sweeping powers to override state laws, control the economy, and direct the administration.
- **Parliamentary Oversight**: The Parliament must approve the emergency within 30 days; otherwise it lapses.
- **Termination**: The emergency ends when the President, after consulting the Parliament, declares that the conditions have ceased to exist.

subject: Indian Constitution
content:
# President's Rule (Articles 356 & 365)

- **Article 356**: Allows the President to impose **President’s Rule** in a state if the state government cannot function according to the Constitution.
- **Article 365**: Provides that the President may **extend** President’s Rule for up to **three years**.
- **Duration**: Initially 6 months, extendable in 3-month increments.
- **Parliamentary Approval**: Must be approved by both Houses within 30 days of the proclamation.

subject: Indian Constitution
content:
# Financial Emergency (Article 360)

- **Trigger**: Declared when the **financial stability** or **creditworthiness** of India or any state is threatened.
- **Effect**: The President can direct the central government to take measures to restore financial stability.
- **Parliamentary Oversight**: Must be approved by both Houses within 30 days.

subject: Indian Constitution
content:
# Pardoning Powers of the President (Article 72)

| Power | Definition | Example |
|-------|------------|--------|
| **Pardon** | Removes both the sentence and conviction, absolving the offender from all punishments and disqualifications. | A convicted person is fully released and their record is expunged. |
| **Reprieve** | A stay of execution of the sentence pending a pardon or commutation. | Execution of a death sentence is postponed while the case is reviewed. |
| **Remission** | Reduces the amount of the sentence without changing its character. | A 2‑year rigorous imprisonment is remitted to 1 year. |
| **Respite** | Grants a lesser sentence in view of special facts. | A pregnant woman receives a lighter sentence. |
| **Commutation** | Substitutes one form of punishment with another of lighter character. | A death sentence is commuted to rigorous imprisonment. |

These powers are exercised at the President’s discretion and are not subject to judicial review.

subject: Polity
content:
### Types of Ministers in India

1. **Cabinet Ministers**:
   - In charge of important portfolios.
   - Considered the real policy makers.
   - Only Cabinet Ministers attend Cabinet meetings; other ministers do not attend.

2. **Minister of State**:
   - May hold independent charge of some ministries.
   - Or may be placed under a Cabinet Minister.

3. **Deputy Ministers**:
   - Assist Cabinet Ministers and Ministers of State.

subject: Polity
content:
### Collective Responsibility and Parliamentary Membership

- **Collective Responsibility**: The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the House of People (Lok Sabha).
- **Non-Member Ministers**: A person can remain a minister without being a member of either house for a maximum period of **6 months**.

subject: Polity
topic: Role and Powers of the Prime Minister
content:
### Role and Powers of the Prime Minister

- **Head of Government**: The Prime Minister is the head of the Central Government.
- **Executive Powers**: While executive powers are formally vested in the President, they are actually exercised by the Council of Ministers under the leadership of the PM.
- **Appointment**: Appointed by the President.
- **Portfolio Allocation**: The PM allocates portfolios among ministers and has the power to drop any minister.
- **Presiding Officer**: Presides over meetings of the Council of Ministers.
- **Policy Coordination**: Decides government policies and coordinates the work of different ministers.
- **NITI Aayog**: The PM is the *ex-officio* chairperson of NITI Aayog (previously the Planning Commission).
- **Parliamentary Membership**: If the PM is not a member of Parliament, they must acquire membership within **6 months** of appointment.
- **Tenure**: The PM remains in power as long as they enjoy a majority in the Lok Sabha. Loss of confidence in the Lok Sabha leads to the termination of the entire Council of Ministers.
- **Advisory Role**: Advises the President regarding the imposition of Presidential Rule in states or Emergency in the country.
- **Resignation**: The resignation of the PM implies the resignation of the entire Council of Ministers.
- **Eligibility**: A member of the Rajya Sabha can also become the Prime Minister.

subject: Polity
content:
### Rajya Sabha – Key Points
- **Deputy Chairman**: Elected from among its members.
- **Legislative Initiation**: Any bill (except Money Bills) can originate in the Rajya Sabha, including the Budget.
- **Permanence**: It is a *permanent* body; unlike the Lok Sabha, it is **not subject to dissolution**.
- **Quorum**: As per Article 100(c), the quorum for either House is **1/10 of the total number of members**.

subject: Polity
content:
### Special Powers of the Rajya Sabha
1. **Removal of the Vice‑President**
   - A resolution for removal can **originate only in the Rajya Sabha**.
2. **Article 249 – Parliament’s Power over State List**
   - If the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution by **≥ two‑thirds of members present and voting** that it is necessary in the national interest, Parliament may make laws on a matter enumerated in the State List **for up to one year**.
3. **Article 312 – Creation of All‑India Services**
   - With a **≥ two‑thirds majority** of members present and voting, the Rajya Sabha can deem it necessary in the national interest to create one or more All‑India Services. Parliament then provides for such services by law.

subject: Polity
content:
### Lok Sabha – Key Facts
- **Maximum Strength**: **550 + 2** members (530 from States, 20 from Union Territories).
- **Present Strength**: **543 + 2** members.
- **Nature**: Not a permanent body; **subject to dissolution**.
- **Normal Tenure**: **5 years**.
- **Early Dissolution**: Can be dissolved earlier by the President.
- **Extension During Emergency**:
  - When a proclamation of emergency under **Article 352** is in force, Parliament may extend the life of the Lok Sabha **beyond 5 years**, but **no more than 1 year at a time**.
  - The extension **cannot continue beyond 6 months** after the emergency proclamation ends.
- **Quorum**: Same as Rajya Sabha – **1/10 of total members** (Article 100(c)).

subject: Polity
content:
### Conditions to be a Member of Lok Sabha
- **Citizenship**: Must be a citizen of India.
- **Age**: Minimum **25 years**.
- **Office of Profit**: Must **not hold any office of profit** under the Government of India or any State Government.
- **Mental/Financial Status**: Must **not be of unsound mind** and **must not be insolvent**.
- **Electoral Register**: Must be a **registered voter** in any parliamentary constituency.

### Grounds for Disqualification (as per the Constitution & Representation of People Act)
- Holding an office of profit.
- Being of unsound mind or declared insolvent.
- Defection under the anti‑defection law.
- Conviction for certain offences.
- Failure to lodge election expenses within the stipulated time.
- Any other ground specified by law.

*(The source text cuts off after “if he volu…”, but the above list captures the standard constitutional provisions.)*

subject: Indian Constitution & Parliamentary Procedure
content:
# Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha
- **Tenure**: Holds office until he ceases to be a Member of the Lok Sabha or resigns.
- **Removal**: Can be removed by a resolution passed in the Lok Sabha by a majority of its members.
- **Impartiality**: Must resign from his original political party to maintain impartiality as Deputy Speaker.

subject: Indian Constitution & Parliamentary Procedure
content:
# Special Powers of Lok Sabha
- **Money Bills**: Originate only in the Lok Sabha.
- **Confidence Motions**: Can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha.
- **Article 352**: Allows the Lok Sabha, in a special sitting, to disapprove the continuation of a National Emergency even if the Rajya Sabha rejects such a resolution.

subject: Indian Constitution & Parliamentary Procedure
content:
# Sessions of Parliament
- **General Rule**: Begins with the President’s consent.
- **Gap**: The interval between two sessions must not exceed **6 months**.
- **Annual Sessions**:
  1. **Budget Session** – February to May (longest).
  2. **Monsoon Session** – July to August.
  3. **Winter Session** – November to December (shortest).

subject: Polity
content:
### Types of Bills in Parliament

1. **Ordinary Bill**
   - **Definition**: All bills other than financial bills, money bills, and Constitutional Amendment bills.
   - **Introduction**: Can be introduced in either House of Parliament (Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha).
   - **Introducer**: Can be introduced by a Minister or any Member of the House.

2. **Money Bill**
   - **Definition**: Bills relating to imposition/abolition of taxes, borrowing of money by the government, custody/maintenance of Consolidated Fund of India, etc.
   - **Introduction**: Can be introduced **only in Lok Sabha**.
   - **Consent**: Requires the prior consent of the President of India (Article 110).
   - **Certification**: The Speaker of Lok Sabha certifies a bill as a Money Bill. This decision is **final** and cannot be challenged in court.
   - **Rajya Sabha Role**: Rajya Sabha can only make recommendations. It can delay the bill for a maximum of **14 days**. Final approval lies with Lok Sabha.

3. **Financial Bill**
   - **Definition**: Any bill dealing with revenues or expenditure that is **not** certified as a Money Bill by the Speaker.
   - **Introduction**: Can be introduced only on the recommendation of the President.

4. **Constitutional Amendment Bill**
   - **Legal Basis**: Article 368.
   - **Introduction**: Can be introduced in **either House** of Parliament.
   - **Recommendation**: Does **not** require the recommendation of the President.

subject: Polity
content:
### Parliamentary Committees

- **Purpose**: Created to allow members to discuss and debate the working of specific government departments.
- **Direction**: Most committees function under the direction of the **Speaker of Lok Sabha**.
- **Composition**: 
  - Members of Rajya Sabha are associated with **all** committees **except** the Estimates Committee.
  - The Chairman of all committees (except the Joint Committee) is typically a member of the Lok Sabha.

subject: Polity
content:
### Contingency Fund of India (Article 267)
- **Nature**: Functions like an *imprest account* of the Government of India.
- **Custodian**: Held on behalf of the President by the **Secretary, Ministry of Finance, Department of Economic Affairs**.
- **Purpose**: Records all transactions connected with the Contingency Fund set up under Article 267 of the Constitution.
- **Key Point**: Enables the Government to meet urgent and unforeseen expenditures without waiting for parliamentary approval.

subject: Polity
content:
### Public Account – Article 266(2)
- **Constitutional Basis**: Constituted under **Article 266(2)** of the Constitution.
- **Scope of Transactions**: Relates to **debts** other than those included in the Consolidated Fund of India.
- **Nature of Receipts**:
  - Include **deposits, advances, and loans** where the Government incurs a liability to repay or has a claim to recover amounts.
  - **Do not constitute normal receipts** of the Government.
- **Parliamentary Authorization**: Payments from the Public Account **do not require prior parliamentary approval**.

subject: Polity
content:
### Legislative Relations
- **Article 249** – *Power of Parliament to legislate in the national interest* for matters in the State List, if the President declares it necessary.
- **Article 250** – *During a proclamation of emergency*, Parliament may make laws for the whole or any part of the territory of India.
- **Article 253** – *Parliamentary power to legislate* for giving effect to treaties and international agreements.

subject: Polity
content:
### Administrative Relations
- **Article 260** – *Jurisdiction of the Union* with respect to territories outside India (e.g., Indian embassies, consulates, and other Indian missions abroad).
- **Article 263** – *Provisions with respect to an Inter‑State Council*, which may be established to discuss and resolve disputes or matters of common interest between the Union and the States.

subject: Polity
content:
### Financial Relations
- **Article 268** – *Duties levied by the Union but collected by the State* (e.g., customs duties, excise duties on certain goods).
- **Article 269** – *Taxes levied and collected by the Union but assigned to the State* (e.g., taxes on income from land and buildings situated in a State).
- **Article 280** – *Establishment of a Finance Commission* every five years to define the distribution of taxes between the Union and the States and to make recommendations on financial relations.

subject: Judiciary
content:
# Integrated Judicial System in India

- The Indian judiciary is **integrated** and derives its structure from the **1953 Government of India Act**.
- The **Constitution of India** is the supreme legal document and provides the framework for the judiciary.
- The judiciary is **independent** of the other two organs of the state: the **executive** and the **legislature**.
- It forms a crucial part of the democratic structure, ensuring that the rule of law is upheld and that the rights of citizens are protected.

## Key Points
- **Supreme Court** sits at the apex of the judicial hierarchy.
- The system is designed to maintain checks and balances among the three branches of government.
- Judicial independence is safeguarded by constitutional provisions and procedural safeguards.

subject: Judiciary
content:
# Composition of the Supreme Court

- **Chief Justice of India** + **not more than 30 other judges** (post‑amendment; previously 25).
- Judges hold office **up to the age of 65**.

## Qualifications for Appointment
1. **Citizen of India**.
2. Either:
   - **5 years** as a judge of a High Court, **or**
   - **10 years** as a practising advocate in a High Court, **or**
   - Recognised as an **eminent jurist**.

> *Note:* The Constitution does not prescribe a minimum age for appointment, but the retirement age is fixed at 65.

subject: Polity
content:
### Advisory Jurisdiction (Article 143)
- **Authority**: The President can consult the Supreme Court on important questions of law or fact of public interest.
- **Nature of Opinion**: The opinion given by the Supreme Court is **not binding** on the President.
- **Process**: The President asks for advice -> Supreme Court considers the issue -> Supreme Court gives its opinion.

subject: Polity
content:
### Appellate Jurisdiction
Three types of appeals can be made to the Supreme Court:
1. **Constitutional Matters**: Appeal against a High Court decision/order if the High Court certifies that it involves a question of interpretation of the Constitution.
2. **Civil Cases**: Appeal against civil cases decided by a High Court if the High Court certifies that the case involves a substantial question of law.
3. **Criminal Cases**: Appeal is possible in specific scenarios:
   - If a High Court reverses an order of acquittal on appeal and sentences the accused to death.
   - If a High Court withdraws a case from a lower court to itself and sentences a person to death.

subject: Polity
content:
### Revisory Jurisdiction (Article 137)
- **Review Power**: The Supreme Court can review any judgment given by itself.
- **Transfer Power**: The Supreme Court has the power to transfer a case being decided in any court to itself.
- **Parliamentary Power**: If an important question of law is involved, Parliament can confer more powers on the Supreme Court by passing a law.

subject: Polity
content:
### Election Jurisdiction
- The Supreme Court has the obligation to decide disputes regarding the election of the **President** and the **Vice-President**.

subject: Polity
content:
### Court of Record (Article 129)
- **Precedent**: All decisions and proceedings of the Supreme Court are kept as records and quoted as precedents in courts.
- **Contempt Power**: The Supreme Court can punish for its own contempt if anyone does not abide by its decision.
- **Status**: Due to these powers, the Supreme Court is called a 'Court of Record'.

subject: Polity
content:
### Strength of Legislative Assemblies
- **General Rule**: The strength of a State Legislative Assembly cannot be more than **500** and not less than **60**.
- **Exceptions (Minimum Strength)**:
  - **Arunachal Pradesh, Sikkim, Goa**: Minimum number fixed at **30**.
  - **Mizoram**: Minimum number is **40**.
  - **Nagaland**: Minimum number is **46**.
- **Composition**: Speaker and Deputy Speaker are chosen from among its members.

subject: Polity
content:
### Qualifications for Members of Legislative Assembly
1. Must be a **citizen of India**.
2. Age must be **not less than 25 years**.
3. Must possess other qualifications prescribed by Parliament under the **Representation of People Act, 1951**.

subject: Polity
topic: Establishment and Number of High Courts
content:
### Establishment and Number of High Courts
- **Constitutional Provision**: The Constitution provides for a High Court for every state.
- **Common High Court**: Two or more states can have a common High Court if provided by the Parliament.
- **Current Count**: There are presently **24 High Courts** in India (comprising 21 State High Courts and 3 others, though the text notes Meghalaya, Manipur, and Tripura as new high courts in this context).
- **Composition**: Consists of a **Chief Justice** and some other judges.
- **Number of Judges**: There is **no upper limit** on the number of judges in a High Court.

subject: Polity
content:
### Qualifications for High Court Judges
A person must satisfy the following criteria to be appointed as a High Court Judge:
1. Must be a **citizen of India**.
2. Must have held a **judicial office** in the service of the Union or a State for at least **10 years**.
3. OR be a **distinguished jurist** in the opinion of the President.
4. OR have been an **advocate** in a High Court for at least **10 years** (or in two or more such courts in succession).

subject: Polity
topic: Appointment, Term, and Removal of High Court Judges
content:
### Appointment, Term, and Removal
**Appointment Procedure**:
- **Chief Justice**: Appointed by the President after consulting the **Chief Justice of India** and the **Governor** of the concerned state.
- **Other Judges**: Appointed according to the same procedure.
- **Priority**: The Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court held that the opinion of the Chief Justice (of the Supreme Court and High Court) will be given priority in the appointment and transfer of senior judges.

**Term**:
- A High Court Judge holds office until they attain the age of **62 years**.
- The term can be shortened by **resignation** or **removal** by the President.

**Transfer**:
- Judges of one High Court can be transferred to another High Court.

**Removal**:
- Removed through the same procedure as Supreme Court Judges (Parliament passes a motion by a special majority).

subject: Political Science
content:
### Attorney General of India
- **Constitutional provision**: Article 76 of the Constitution.
- **Appointment**: Appointed by the President of India.
- **Eligibility**: Must be qualified to be a Judge of the Supreme Court (i.e., a citizen of India, at least 45 years old, and must have held a judicial office for at least 5 years or been an advocate of a High Court for at least 10 years).
- **Role**:
  - Highest legal advisor to the Government of India.
  - Consulted on all important legal matters.
  - Represents the Government in the Supreme Court and other courts.
- **Rights in Parliament**:
  - May take part in the proceedings of either House of Parliament.
  - Does **not** have voting rights.
- **Tenure**: Holds office during the pleasure of the President.
- **Key Functions**:
  1. Advises the Government on legal questions.
  2. Appears on behalf of the Government in judicial proceedings.
  3. Provides opinions on constitutional matters when sought by the President.

subject: Political Science
content:
### Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG)
- **Constitutional provision**: Article 148‑151.
- **Appointment**: Appointed by the President of India.
- **Tenure**: Serves for a term of six years or until the age of 65 years, whichever is earlier; can be removed only by a resolution of both Houses of Parliament on the grounds of proved misbehavior or incapacity.
- **Primary Functions**:
  1. **Audit of Union and State finances** – audits all receipts and expenditures of the Government of India and the States.
  2. **Vigilant watch on public finance** – ensures that public money is used for the purposes for which it was authorized.
  3. **Reporting** – submits periodic reports to the President (for Union) and Governors (for States); these reports are laid before Parliament and State Legislatures.
  4. **Compliance check** – verifies that amounts voted by the legislature are spent under appropriate heads and are not exceeded.
- **Powers**:
  - Access to all books of accounts of the Union and States.
  - Can call for information from any department or authority.
  - Reports are binding for the legislature to consider and act upon.

subject: Political Science
content:
### Finance Commission (Article 280)
- **Constitutional provision**: Article 280.
- **Establishment**:
  - Constituted **within two years** of the commencement of the Constitution and thereafter **every five years** or at such other interval as the President may deem fit.
- **Composition**:
  - Chairman (appointed by the President).
  - Four other members (appointed by the President) – may include experts in finance, economics, public administration, etc.
- **Key Functions**:
  1. **Distribution of tax revenues** – recommends the **distribution of net proceeds of taxes** that are divisible between the Union and the States.
  2. **Grants-in-aid** – advises on the principles governing **grants-in-aid** to the States out of the Consolidated Fund of India.
  3. **Augmentation of State Funds** – suggests measures for **augmentation of the Consolidated Fund of the States**.
  4. **Other matters** – may be asked by the President to examine any other matter related to the financial relations between the Union and the States.
- **Impact**: Ensures fiscal federalism, promotes balanced development, and helps maintain sound finance across the Union and the States.

subject: General Studies
topic: Special Status of Jammu and Kashmir
content:
# Special Status of Jammu and Kashmir

- **Article 370** of the Indian Constitution granted *special status* to Jammu and Kashmir at the time of its accession to India. It is a *temporary* provision that has been abrogated in 2019.
- **Separate Constitution**: Jammu and Kashmir has its own Constitution, drafted by its own Constituent Assembly, which is distinct from the Constitution of India.
- **Legislative Powers**:
  - The Indian Parliament **cannot** make laws on *State List* subjects for Jammu and Kashmir.
  - All *residuary powers* (those not enumerated in the Union or State Lists) are vested in the Jammu and Kashmir Legislature.
- **Dual Citizenship**: Residents of Jammu and Kashmir enjoy a form of *dual citizenship*—they are citizens of India and of the state. Non‑residents cannot purchase immovable property in the state.
- **Emergency Provisions**:
  - **President’s Rule**: Can be imposed in case of constitutional breakdown.

### Eligibility to become Vice‑President of India
- **Citizenship**: Must be a citizen of India.
- **Age**: Must have attained the age of **35 years**.

subject: Polity
content: **Mandamus** is a writ issued by a court to an official administrative body or officer to perform a public duty or act that they are legally obligated to perform. It is generally issued against public authorities, not private individuals or foreigners.

subject: Polity
content:
The appointment of Judges of the High Court (excluding the Chief Justice) is made by the President of India. The President consults with:
1. The Chief Justice of India (CJI).
2. The Chief Justice of the concerned High Court.
3. The Governor of the concerned state.
Note: The Chief Minister is not part of the mandatory consultation process for High Court judge appointments.

subject: Polity
content: The words **'Socialist'** and **'Secular'** were added to the Preamble of the Indian Constitution by the **42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976**, not the 44th Amendment. The 44th Amendment (1978) primarily dealt with the office of the President, emergency provisions, and fundamental duties.

subject: Polity
content:
**Stamp Duties:** Duties on bills of exchange, promissory notes, etc., are levied by the Union but collected and appropriated by the States.
**Income Tax and Excise:** These are levied and collected by the Union. The proceeds are distributed between the Union and the States as per the Finance Commission's recommendations.

subject: Polity
content: The President of India appoints as Prime Minister the leader of the **majority party in the Lok Sabha** (or the leader of the majority coalition in the Lok Sabha). The Lok Sabha is the lower house and represents the direct will of the people, making it the primary basis for forming the government.

subject: Polity
content: According to Article 79 of the Indian Constitution, the Parliament of India consists of the **President** and two Houses, namely the **Council of States (Rajya Sabha)** and the **House of the People (Lok Sabha)**.

subject: Polity
content:
### Types of Writs in India

1. **Mandamus**: A direction issued by a court to an official for the performance of a public duty. It is used to compel a public authority to act.
2. **Habeas Corpus**: A writ used for the release of a person who has been illegally detained. It translates to 'have the body' and is a fundamental safeguard against arbitrary arrest.
3. **Certiorari**: A writ issued by a higher court to an inferior court or tribunal to transfer a case to itself for review. It is used to correct errors of law or jurisdiction.
4. **Quo Warranto**: A writ calling upon a person to show by what authority they hold or claim a public office or franchise. It is used to prevent illegal usurpation of public office.

subject: Polity
content:
### Key Schedules of the Indian Constitution

- **1st Schedule**: Contains the list of States and Union Territories.
- **2nd Schedule**: Deals with the emoluments, allowances, and privileges of the President, Members of Parliament, and Members of State Legislatures.
- **3rd Schedule**: Contains the forms of oaths or affirmations for various constitutional offices.
- **4th Schedule**: Deals with the allocation of seats in the Rajya Sabha (Council of States) to the States and Union Territories.
- **5th Schedule**: Contains provisions for the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and the Scheduled Tribes.

subject: Polity
topic: Attorney General and Dissolution of Lok Sabha
content:
### Key Constitutional Roles

1. **Attorney General of India**: The highest law officer of the Government of India. They are empowered to tender expert legal advice to the Government of India on matters referred to them by the Government.
2. **Dissolution of Lok Sabha**: The President of India is empowered to dissolve the Lok Sabha before the expiry of its term. However, this power is exercised on the advice of the Prime Minister (and the Council of Ministers).

subject: Polity
content:
### Centre-State Relationships

The Indian Constitution specifies four main types of relationships between the Centre and the States:
1. **Legislative**: Division of powers between the Union and State lists (Union List, State List, Concurrent List).
2. **Financial**: Distribution of tax revenues and grants-in-aid.
3. **Administrative**: Coordination in administration, especially during emergencies.
4. **Political**: Mutual respect for the federal structure and democratic processes.

*Note: 'Judicial' is not typically listed as a distinct primary type of relationship in the same category as the above four in standard constitutional classifications for this context, though the judiciary plays a role in interpreting these relations.*

subject: Polity
content:
### Formation of New States (Post-Independence)

- **Andhra Pradesh**: Formed in **1953** (from Madras State).
- **Gujarat**: Formed in **1960** (from Bombay State).
- **Haryana**: Formed in **1966** (from Punjab).

subject: Indian Polity
topic: Role, Appointment and Removal of CAG
content:
# Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG)

- **Appointment**: The CAG is appointed by the President of India.
- **Tenure**: The CAG holds office for a term of **five years** or until the age of **65 years**, whichever is earlier.
- **Removal**: The President can remove the CAG on the grounds of **misbehavior or incapacity**. The procedure is **not** the same as that for a Supreme Court judge, which requires an impeachment process by both Houses of Parliament.
- **Functions**:
  - Audits all receipts and expenditure of the Union and State governments.
  - Audits the accounts of all bodies receiving funds from the Union or State governments.
  - Provides reports to the Parliament and State Legislatures.
- **Prescribing Accounts**: The CAG does **not** prescribe the form in which the accounts of the Union and the States are kept. That responsibility lies with the Ministry of Finance and the respective State Finance Departments.

> **Key Takeaway**: The CAG’s removal process is distinct from that of a Supreme Court judge, and he does not prescribe the accounting format for the Union or State governments.

subject: Indian Polity
topic: When and How a Joint Session is Convened
content:
# Joint Sessions of Parliament

- **Constitutional Basis**: Article 108 of the Constitution.
- **Presidential Authority**: The President may call a joint session of both Houses.
- **Situations Requiring a Joint Session**:
  1. **Bill Rejected by One House** – When a bill is passed by one House and rejected by the other.
  2. **Bill Pending for 6+ Months** – When a bill has been pending in one House for more than six months after being passed by the other.
  3. **Disagreement on Amendments** – When both Houses disagree on the amendments to be made in a bill.
- **Constitutional Amendment**: A joint session is **not** used for amending the Constitution; amendments require separate passage in both Houses.

> **Key Takeaway**: Joint sessions are a mechanism to resolve deadlocks between the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha in specific circumstances.

subject: Indian Polity
topic: Passing an Ordinary Bill in a Joint Session
content:
# Ordinary Bills in a Joint Session

- **Definition**: An Ordinary Bill is any bill that is not a Money Bill or a Constitutional Amendment Bill.
- **Majority Requirement**: When an Ordinary Bill is referred to a joint sitting, it must be passed by a **simple majority** of the total number of members of both Houses present and voting.
- **Procedure**: The joint session is conducted as a single House, and the voting follows the same rules as in either House.

> **Key Takeaway**: Unlike constitutional amendments, ordinary bills in a joint session require only a simple majority.

subject: Polity
content: The Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly was advised by **B. Shiva Rao**. He was appointed as the official advisor to assist the committee in legal and procedural matters while framing the Constitution.

These principles guide the state in making laws aimed at social welfare, though they are not justiciable.
