subject: Biology
text:
Monosaccharides: A carbohydrate that cannot be hydrolysed further to give simpler unit ketone is called a monosaccharide. About 20 monosaccharides are known to occur in nature. Some common examples are glucose, fructose, ribose, etc.

Oligosaccharides: Carbohydrates that yield two to ten monosaccharide units, on hydrolysis, are called oligosaccharides. They are further classified as disaccharides, trisaccharides, tetrasaccharides. Amongst these the most common are disaccharides.

Polysaccharides: Carbohydrates which yield a large number of monosaccharide units on hydrolysis are called polysaccharides. Some common examples are starch, cellulose, glycogen, gums, etc. Polysaccharides are not sweet in taste, hence they are also called non-sugars.

  • Glucose occurs freely in nature as well as in the combined form. It is present in sweet fruits and honey. Ripe grapes also contain glucose in large amounts.
  • Starch is the main storage polysaccharide of plants. High content of starch is found in cereals, roots, tubers and some vegetables. It consists of two components— Amylose and Amylopectin. Amylose is water soluble component which constitutes about 15-20% of starch. Amylopectin is insoluble in water and constitutes about 80- 85% of starch.
  • Glycogen: The carbohydrates are stored in animal body as glycogen. It is also known as animal starch. It is present in liver, muscles and brain. When the body needs glucose, enzymes break the glycogen down to glucose. Glycogen is also found in yeast and fungi.

subject: Biology
text:
Proteins:

  • Proteins are the most abundant biomolecules of the living system.
  • The amino acids, which can be synthesised in the body, are known as nonessential amino acids. On the other hand, those which cannot be synthesised in the body and must be obtained through diet, are known as essential amino acids.
  • Amino acids are usually colourless, crystalline solids. These are water-soluble, high melting solids and behave like salts. This behaviour is due to the presence of both acidic (carboxyl group) and basic (amino group) groups in the same molecule.
  • In aqueous solution, the carboxyl group can lose a proton and amino group can accept a proton, giving rise to a dipolar ion known as zwitter ion. In zwitter ionic form, amino acids show amphoteric behaviour as they react both with acids and bases.
  • Proteins can be classified into two types on the basis of their molecular shape:
  • Fibrous proteins: examples are keratin (present in hair, wool, silk) and myosin (present in muscles), etc.
  • Globular proteins: Insulin and albumins are the common examples of globular proteins.

subject: Biology
text:
Chemical Nature of Hormones:

  • Steroids: e.g., estrogens and androgens.
  • Polypeptides: e.g., insulin and endorphins.
  • Amino acid derivatives: e.g., epinephrine and norepinephrine.

Key Hormones and Functions:

  • Insulin: Regulates blood glucose levels; released in response to rapid rise in blood glucose.
  • Glucagon: Increases blood glucose levels.
  • Epinephrine and Norepinephrine: Mediate responses to external stimuli.
  • Thyroxine: Produced in the thyroid gland. Low levels lead to hypothyroidism (lethargy, obesity); high levels lead to hyperthyroidism. Low dietary iodine can cause hypothyroidism and thyroid enlargement.
  • Adrenal Cortex Hormones: Glucocorticoids (carbohydrate metabolism, inflammatory reactions, stress response) and Mineralocorticoids (water and salt excretion).
  • Addison's Disease: Caused by improper adrenal cortex function; characterized by hypoglycemia, weakness, and increased susceptibility to stress.
  • Testosterone: Major male hormone; develops secondary male characteristics (deep voice, facial hair, physical constitution).
  • Estradiol: Main female hormone; develops secondary female characteristics and controls menstrual cycle.
  • Progesterone: Prepares the uterus for implantation of the fertilised egg.

Gland Classification:

  • Endocrine Glands: Ductless glands that secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream to target organs. Examples: pancreas, pituitary, thyroid, adrenal glands.
  • Exocrine Glands: Secrete substances through ducts. Examples: sweat glands, salivary glands, lacrimal glands (tear glands), mammary glands.

subject: Biology
text:
• Hypothalamus: Located in the lower central region of the brain. It controls metabolism, body temperature, and feelings of fullness.
  • Pituitary Gland: Known as the master gland, it controls the secretions of all other endocrine glands. It is situated at the base of the brain and also works as a growth hormone. Deficiency leads to dwarfism.
  • Pineal Gland: Present in the centre of the brain, beneath the corpus callosum. It generates melatonin, which helps the body recognize when it is time to sleep.

subject: Biology
text:
• Thyroid Gland: Located in the neck, below the larynx. It secretes the hormone 'Thyroxine', which regulates carbohydrate, protein, and fat metabolism for growth. Iodine is essential for the synthesis of thyroxine; deficiency leads to goitre.
  • Parathyroid Glands: Two pairs of tiny glands implanted on the thyroid gland's surface. They discharge parathyroid hormone, which affects blood calcium levels and bone metabolism.

subject: Biology
text:
• Adrenal Glands: Located on top of each kidney. They help the body respond to stress and maintain metabolism. They release Adrenaline (fight-or-flight response) and Cortisol (regulates stress and metabolism).
  • Pancreas (Mixed Gland): Situated behind the stomach. It secretes glucagon (raises blood sugar) and insulin (lowers blood sugar). It also secretes digestive enzymes.
  • Thymus: Located in the chest, behind the sternum. It plays a key role in immune system development during early life and produces Thymosin, which promotes the development of T-cells.

subject: Biology
text:
• Testes (in males): Located in the scrotum. Releases Testosterone, which regulates sperm production and secondary sexual characteristics.
  • Ovary (in females): Situated below the opening of the fallopian tubes on both sides of the uterus. Generates oestrogen and progesterone. Oestrogen regulates the menstrual cycle, and Progesterone prepares the uterus for pregnancy.

subject: Biology
text:
The nervous system of all animals is composed of highly specialised cells called neurons which can detect, receive and transmit different kinds of stimuli. The neural organisation is very simple in lower invertebrates. For example, in Hydra it is composed of a network of neurons. The neural organisation is better organised in insects, where a brain is present along with a number of ganglia and neural tissues. The vertebrates have a more developed neural system.

Human Nervous System

The human nervous system is divided into two parts: (i) the central neural system (CNS) and (ii) the peripheral neural system (PNS).

  • CNS: Includes the brain and the spinal cord; site of information processing and control.
  • PNS: Comprises all the nerves of the body associated with the CNS. It is divided into the somatic neural system (relays impulses from CNS to skeletal muscles) and the autonomic neural system (transmits impulses from CNS to involuntary organs and smooth muscles).
image_descriptions: Illustration of the human brain and neural pathways.

details.summary: Classification and function of the human nervous system.

subject: Biology
text:
A neuron is a microscopic structure composed of three major parts: cell body, dendrites, and axon.

  • Cell body: Contains cytoplasm with typical cell organelles and granular bodies called Nissl's granules.
  • Dendrites: Short fibres projecting out of the cell body containing Nissl's granules; transmit impulses towards the cell body.
  • Axon: A long fibre, the distal end of which is branched. Each branch terminates as a bulb-like structure called a synaptic knob, which possesses synaptic vesicles containing chemicals called neurotransmitters. Axons transmit nerve impulses away from the cell body to a synapse.
  • Classification: Based on the number of axon and dendrites, neurons are divided into: Multipolar (one axon, two or more dendrites), Bipolar (one axon, one dendrite; found in retina), and Unipolar (cell body with one axon; usually in embryonic stage).
  • Myelination: Axons are either myelinated or nonmyelinated. The gaps between two adjacent myelin sheaths are called nodes of Ranvier.

details.summary: Detailed structural and functional description of a neuron.

subject: Biology
text:
The human brain is well protected by the skull. Inside the skull, the brain is covered by cranial meninges consisting of an outer layer called dura mater, a very thin middle layer called arachnoid and an inner layer called pia mater. The brain can be divided into three major parts: (i) forebrain, (ii) midbrain, (iii) hindbrain.

FOREBRAIN

The forebrain consists of cerebrum, thalamus and hypothalamus.

  • Cerebrum: Forms the major part of the human brain.
  • Thalamus: The cerebrum wraps around a structure called thalamus, which is a major coordinating centre for sensory and motor signaling.
  • Hypothalamus: Lies at the base of the thalamus. It contains a number of centres which control body temperature, urge for eating and drinking. It also contains several groups of neurosecretory cells, which secrete hormones called hypothalamic hormones.

MIDBRAIN

  • Located between the thalamus/hypothalamus of the forebrain and pons of the hindbrain.
  • A canal called the cerebral aqueduct passes through the midbrain.

HINDBRAIN

Comprises pons, cerebellum and medulla (also called the medulla oblongata).

  • Pons: Consists of fibre tracts that interconnect different regions of the brain.
  • Cerebellum: Has very convoluted surface in order to provide the additional space for many more neurons.
  • Medulla: Connected to the spinal cord. Contains centres which control respiration, cardiovascular reflexes and gastric secretions.
  • Brain stem: Formed by midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata. It forms the connections between the brain and spinal cord.

Additional Functions:

  • The fore-brain is the main thinking part of the brain. It has regions which receive sensory impulses from various receptors. Separate areas of the fore-brain are specialised for hearing, smell, sight and so on. The sensation of feeling full is because of a centre associated with hunger, which is in a separate part of the fore-brain.
  • Many involuntary actions are controlled by the mid-brain and hind-brain.
  • All involuntary actions including blood pressure, salivation and vomiting are controlled by the medulla in the hind-brain.
  • Activities like walking in a straight line, riding a bicycle, picking up a pencil are possible due to a part of the hind-brain called the cerebellum. It is responsible for precision of voluntary actions and maintaining the posture and balance of the body.

subject: Chemistry
text:
ARTIFICIAL SWEETENING AGENTS

  • Natural sweeteners (e.g., sucrose): Add to calorie intake, therefore many people prefer to use artificial sweeteners.
  • Saccharin (Ortho-sulphobenzimide): The first popular artificial sweetening agent. It is excreted from the body in urine unchanged. It appears to be entirely inert and harmless when taken. Its use is of great value to diabetic persons.
  • Aspartame: The most successful and widely used artificial sweetener. Use is limited to cold foods and soft drinks because it is unstable at cooking temperature.
  • Alitame: High potency sweetener, although it is more stable than aspartame, the control of sweetness of food is difficult while using it.
  • Sucralose: Trichloro derivative of sucrose. Its appearance and taste are like sugar. It is stable at cooking temperature. It does not provide calories.

subject: Biology
text:
A wide range of organisms belonging to bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoans, helminths, etc., could cause diseases in man. Such disease causing organisms are called pathogens.

  • Salmonella typhi: A pathogenic bacterium which causes typhoid fever in human beings.
  • Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae: Bacteria responsible for pneumonia in humans, which infects the alveoli (air-filled sacs) of the lungs. As a result of the infection, the alveoli get filled with fluid leading to severe problems in respiration.
  • Rhino viruses: A group of viruses which cause the common cold. They infect the nose and respiratory passage but not the lungs.
  • Plasmodium: A tiny protozoan responsible for malaria disease. Plasmodium enters the human body as sporozoites (infectious form).
  • Entamoeba histolytica: A protozoan parasite in the large intestine of humans which causes amoebiasis (amoebic dysentery). Symptoms include constipation, abdominal pain and cramps, stools with excess mucous and blood clots.
  • Ascaris: The common round worm. An intestinal parasite that causes ascariasis. Symptoms include internal bleeding, muscular pain, fever, anemia and blockage of the intestinal passage.
  • Wuchereria: The filarial worm. Causes elephantiasis or filariasis. The genital organs are also often affected, resulting in gross deformities.
  • Trichophyton and Epidermophyton: Responsible for ringworms, one of the most common infectious diseases in man.

subject: Biology
text:
Active and Passive Immunity

  • Active Immunity: When a host is exposed to antigens, which may be in the form of living or dead microbes or other proteins, antibodies are produced in the host body.
  • Passive Immunity: When ready-made antibodies are directly given to protect the body against foreign agents.
  • Examples of Passive Immunity:
    • The yellowish fluid colostrum secreted by the mother during the initial days of lactation has abundant antibodies (IgA) to protect the infant.
    • The foetus receives some antibodies from their mother through the placenta during pregnancy.

text:
Tamil Nadu Coast Rainfall: The coast remains dry during the Southwest monsoon due to:

  • It is situated parallel to the Bay of Bengal branch of the SW monsoon.
  • It lies in the rain shadow area of the Arabian Sea branch of the SW monsoon.
  • It receives rainfall primarily from the 'Northeast or retreating' monsoon.

October Heat: During the retreating monsoon, skies are generally clear. A rise in temperature combined with high humidity makes the weather oppressive, known as 'October Heat'.

subject: Geography
text:
El Nino: Means 'Child Christ'. It is a complex weather system involving oceanic and atmospheric phenomena characterized by the appearance of warm currents off the coast of Peru.

Results of El-Nino:

  • Distortion of equatorial atmospheric circulation.
  • Irregularities in the evaporation of sea water.
  • Reduction in the number of planktons, which further reduces the number of fish in the sea.

topic: Local Storms of Hot Weather Season
text:
• Mango Shower: Pre-monsoon showers in Kerala and Karnataka that help in the early ripening of mangoes.
  • Blossom Shower: Showers that cause coffee flowers to blossom in Kerala.
  • Nor Westers: Dreaded evening thunderstorms in Bengal and Assam. Useful for the cultivation of tea, jute, and rice. In Assam, these are known as 'Bardoli Chheerha'.
  • Loo: Hot, dry, and oppressing winds blowing in the northern plains from Punjab to Bihar.

subject: Geography
text:
Mechanism: Spring tides occur when the Sun, Moon, and Earth lie in a straight line, a position called syzygy. In this alignment, the gravitational forces of the Sun and the Moon combine and act in the same direction.

Condition: These tides take place during the Full Moon and New Moon phases, when the Moon and the Sun reinforce each other's gravitational pull on the Earth's oceans.

Effect: The combined gravitational pull produces very high high tides and very low low tides. This results in the maximum tidal range observed during a lunar month.
image_descriptions: Conceptual explanation of the alignment of celestial bodies during Spring Tides.

details.summary: Mechanism, conditions, and effects of Spring Tides.

subject: Geography
text:
Neap Tides

  • Mechanism: Neap tides occur when the Sun and the Moon form a right angle (90°) with the Earth. In this position, their gravitational forces act against each other, reducing the total tidal force.
  • Condition: These tides occur during the First Quarter and Third Quarter phases of the Moon, when the pulls of the Sun and the Moon partially counteract each other.
  • Effect: Because the forces oppose each other, the high tides are lower than usual and the low tides are higher than normal. This produces the minimum tidal range.

Interval Between Spring & Neap Tides: The time interval between a spring tide and the following neap tide is about 7 days, as the Moon takes roughly one week to move from one alignment to the other.

Diagram showing Neap Tide alignment: Sun and Earth in a horizontal line, with the Moon positioned at a 90-degree angle relative to the Earth.

subject: Geography
text:
TROPOSPHERE: Its height is 8 Km near the poles and 18 Km near the equator. This layer contains dust particles and water vapor. The zone separating the troposphere from stratosphere is k/a 'tropopause'.

STRATOSPHERE: Its height extends up to 50 Km and one of the important features is it contains 'Ozone'. Also, the Aeroplanes also fly in this layer.

MESOSPHERE: Its height extends up to 80 Km and in this layer, temperature starts decreasing with height therefore it is the coldest layer. Also, meteors burn in this layer.

THERMOSPHERE: Radio wave communication occurs in this layer. Also, temperature start increasing with height. Also, k/a ionosphere due to presence of ions in this layer.

details.summary: Overview of the four primary layers of the atmosphere: Troposphere, Stratosphere, Mesosphere, and Thermosphere.

subject: Geography
text:
The atmosphere is divided into several layers based on altitude and temperature characteristics:

  • Troposphere: 0 to 10 miles, 62°F to -60°F. Contains the ozone layer.
  • Stratosphere: 11 to 31 miles, -60°F to 5°F.
  • Mesosphere: 32 to 85 miles, 5°F to -148°F.
  • Thermosphere: 86 to 372 miles, 930°F to 3600°F. Contains the Kármán line (start of outer space) and Aurora.
  • Exosphere: 310-620 miles and above. It is the last layer which further extends into space. Close to absolute zero.

Note: Dust and salt particles act as 'Hygroscopic' nuclei around which water vapor condenses to produce clouds.

subject: Geography
text:
An earthquake is the shaking of the earth caused by the release of energy, which generates waves that travel in all directions.

  • Focus (Hypocentre): The point where energy is released.
  • Epicentre: The point on the surface nearest to the focus; the first to experience waves.
  • Seismograph: Instrument used to record waves reaching the surface.
  • Types of Waves:
    • Body Waves: Generated at the focus, travel through the body of the earth.
      • P waves (Primary): Faster, similar to sound waves, travel through gaseous, liquid, and solid materials. Vibrate parallel to the direction of the wave.
      • S waves (Secondary): Arrive later, travel only through solid materials.
    • Surface Waves: Generated by interaction of body waves with surface rocks. They are the last to be recorded and are the most destructive.

Measurement Scales:

  • Richter Scale: Measures the magnitude of an earthquake.
  • Mercalli Scale: Measures the intensity of an earthquake.

Important Note: 'Tsunami' waves are generated by tremors in the ocean, not the earthquake itself.
image_descriptions: Iconographic representation of an earthquake focus and epicentre, and a seismograph wave pattern.

details.summary: Definition, terminology, wave types, and measurement scales related to earthquakes.

subject: Geography
text:
Types of Earthquakes

  • Tectonic Earthquake: Generated due to sliding of rocks along a fault plane.
  • Volcanic Earthquake: Occur at areas of active volcanoes.
  • Collapse Earthquake: Occur in area of intense mining where the roofs of underground mines collapse causing minor tremors.
  • Explosion Earthquakes: Occur due to the explosion of chemical or nuclear devices.
  • Reservoir Induced Earthquakes: Occur in areas of large reservoirs.

details.summary: Classification of earthquakes based on their origin.

subject: Geography
text:
Volcano

A volcano is a place where gases, ashes and/ or molten rock material – lava – escape to the ground.

  • The mantle contains a weaker zone called 'asthenosphere'.
  • The material in upper mantle is called as 'magma' and once it reaches the surface it is called as 'lava'.
  • The material that reaches the ground contains lava, pyroclastic debris, dust and gases such as nitrogen compounds, Sulphur compounds and minor amounts of chlorine, hydrogen and argon.

Stylized illustration of an erupting volcano with smoke and lava flow.

details.summary: Definition and composition of volcanoes and volcanic material.

subject: Geography
text:
Types of Volcanoes

  • Shield Volcano: Largest of all, made up of basalt, very fluid in nature, become explosive when water gets into the vent.
  • Composite Volcano: Explosive eruptions, have layers, eruption of cooler and more viscous lava than basalt.
image_descriptions: Comparison list of Shield Volcano and Composite Volcano characteristics.

details.summary: Classification of volcanoes into Shield and Composite types.

subject: Geography
text:
Volcanic Landforms:

  • CALDERA: Most explosive, collapse on themselves, collapsed depression is c/a caldera.
  • FLOOD BASALT: highly fluid lava that flows for long distance, e.g. Deccan trap.
  • MID OCEAN RIDGE: They occur in the oceanic areas.

SOME TERMINOLOGY:

  • BATHOLITHS: A large body of magmatic material that cools and form large domes. These are granitic bodies.
  • LACOLITHS: Dome shaped intrusive bodies with a level base and connected by a pipe like conduit from below.
  • LAPOLITHS: They are saucer shaped, concave to the sky body.
  • SILL: Horizontal bodies of intrusive igneous rocks are called sill or sheet depending on thickness. The thinner ones are called sheet and thick ones are called sills.
  • DYKES: Wall like structure that solidifies perpendicular to the ground.

text:
MAJOR OCEAN CURRENTS:

Factors influencing ocean currents:

  1. Primary forces that initiate the movement of water these are heating by solar energy, wind, gravity, Coriolis force.
  2. Secondary forces that influence the currents to flow.

subject: Geography
text:
Ocean Currents:

  • Due to Coriolis force, the current in northern hemisphere move in right direction and in southern hemisphere move in left direction.
  • The speed of current is k/a 'Drift' and is measured in knots.
  • Cold water is denser than warm water therefore it sinks whereas warm water stays on surface.
  • The mixing of warm and cold currents helps to replenish oxygen and favour the growth of planktons, the primary food for fish population.

Landforms:

Landforms are classified based on the agent of erosion and deposition (Running Water, Ground Water, Glaciers, Waves and Currents, and Winds).

| 5. WINDS | PEDIMENTS, PEDIPLAINS, INSELBERG, PLAYAS, DEFLATION HOLLOWS, CAVES | SAND DUNES, BARCHANS, SEIF |

text:
THUNDERSTORM – A thunderstorm is a well grown cumulonimbus cloud producing thunder and lightning. They are caused by intense convection on moist hot days.

TORNADO – Sometimes during severe thunderstorm a spiraling wind descends like the trunk of elephant with great force, with very low pressure at center, causing massive destruction on its way is called as tornado. The tornado over sea is called as Water spouts.

  • Tropical Cyclones are violent storms that originate over oceans.
  • The place where cyclone crosses coast is c/a Landfall of cyclone.
  • The Eye is a region of calm with subsiding air.
  • Torrential rains occur here.
  • Tropical cyclone moves in clockwise direction in southern hemisphere and anticlockwise direction in northern hemisphere.
  • They have high wind velocity and are more destructive in nature.

CONDITIONS REQUIRED FOR TROPICAL CYCLONE

  1. Large sea surface with temperature higher than 27 C.
  2. Presence of Coriolis force
  3. Small variations in the vertical wind speed.
  4. A pre-existing weak low-pressure area or low-level cyclonic circulation.
  5. Upper divergence above the sea level system.

EXTRA TROPICAL CYCLONE: Extra Tropical Cyclone forms due to clear frontal system and they can originate over both land and sea. Also, they rotate in the opposite direction as tropical cyclone.

text:
Clouds are a mass of minute water droplets or tiny crystals of ice formed by condensation of water vapour in free air at considerable elevations. They are grouped into four categories based on height, expanse, density, and transparency:

  • Cirrus: Formed at high altitudes (8000-12000 m). Thin and detached clouds with a feathery appearance. Always white in color.
  • Cumulus: Look like cotton wool. Formed at a height of 4000-7000 m. Exist in patches and have a flat base.
  • Stratus: Layered clouds covering large portions of the sky. Formed due to loss of heat or mixing of air masses with different temperatures.
  • Nimbus: Black or dark gray in color. Form at middle level or very near to the surface. Extremely dense and opaque to rays of the sun.

Common Phenomena:

  • Dew: Moisture deposited as water droplets on cooler surfaces of solid objects (grass blades, stones). Ideal conditions: clear sky, calm air, high relative humidity, cold and long nights. Dew point is above freezing point.
  • Frost: Forms on cold surfaces when condensation takes place below freezing point. Air temperature must be at or below freezing point.
  • Fog: A cloud with its base very near to the ground.
  • Smog: Fog mixed with smoke.
  • Sleet: Frozen raindrops and refrozen melted snow/water.

subject: Geography
text:
Climate Zones of the World

  • Equatorial Type: Both temperature and rainfall are extreme. Evergreen vegetation found (e.g., ebony, mahogany, rosewood). Example: Amazon forest.
  • Monsoon Type: Called 'seasonal reversal of winds'. Deciduous vegetation found (e.g., teak, sandalwood, neem, banyan, acacia). Examples: India, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Vietnam, China.
  • Desert Type: Called 'Xerophytes'. Lies majorly on the western side of continents. Examples: Sahara Desert, Great Australian desert, Atacama Desert.
  • Mediterranean Type: Called 'Sclerophytes'. Winters are wet and summers are dry. Majorly citrus fruit and olive vegetation. Examples: West California, France, Spain.
  • Tundra Type: Mosses and lichens are present. Softwood trees are present (e.g., Fir, Juniper, Spruces, Larch). Examples: Canada, US, Russia.

subject: Geography
text:
Petrology is science of rocks and pedology is study of soil.

Types of Rocks

  1. IGNEOUS ROCKS – Solidified from magma and lava.
  2. SEDIMENTARY ROCKS – Result of deposition of fragments of rocks by exogenous processes.
  3. METAMORPHIC ROCKS – Formed out of existing rocks undergoing recrystallisation.

IGNEOUS ROCKS

  • Also known as primary rocks.
  • Formed when magma cools and solidifies.
  • E.g. Granite, Gabbro, Pegmatite, Basalt, Volcanic breccia and tuff.

SEDIMENTARY ROCKS

  • They deposit through compaction turn into rocks.
  • Form due to process of Lithification.
  • E.g. Sandstone, Limestone, Conglomerate, Shale, Loess, Geyserite, Chalk, Coal, Chert, Halite, Potash.
  • Fossils are also found in these rocks only.

METAMORPHIC ROCKS

  • They form under the action of pressure, volume and temperature.
  • An arrangement of minerals or grains in metamorphic rocks is called foliation or lineation.
  • Also called as banded rocks.
  • E.g. Gneissoid, slate, schist, marble, quartzite, syenite.

subject: Geography
text:
Weathering refers to the breakdown of rocks and minerals at or near the Earth's surface through physical, chemical, or biological processes.

1. Physical Weathering

This involves breakdown of rocks without changing their chemical composition.

  • Frost Wedging: When water seeps into cracks, freezes, expands and wedges the rocks apart.
  • Thermal Expansion and Contraction: Repeated heating and cooling of rocks causes them to expand and contract thereby leading to its breakage.
  • Salt Crystallization: Salt crystals grow in cracks and pores, exerting pressure on the rock.
  • Abrasion: The grinding away of rock surfaces by friction, such as rocks are carried by wind, water or ice leading to its weathering.

2. Chemical Weathering

It involves alteration of chemical composition of rocks due to action of wind, water or acids.

  • Dissolution: In these minerals in rocks dissolve in water especially when the water is slightly acidic.
  • Oxidation: Certain minerals react with oxygen causing them to weaken and crumble.
  • Hydrolysis: Water reacts with minerals breaking them down and forming new minerals.

3. Biological Weathering

It involves breaking of rocks by the action of living organisms.

  • Root Wedging: Plant roots grow into cracks and exert pressure as they grow, widening the crack thereby resulting in breakage.
  • Burrowing Animals: Animals that burrow into rocks can weaken and expose them to break.
  • Lichens and Mosses: These organisms secrete various toxins and acids that dissolve rock and physically attach to surface of rock thereby resulting in weathering of rock.

|---|---|

| Biological Weathering | Breaking of rocks by the action of living organisms |

  • Tea: Ideal for areas with rainfall above 200cm and sloping hills; requires large amount of rainfall and no standing water.
  • Legumes: Best for biological nitrogen fixation of the soil.
  • Cash Crops: Crops grown for sale in the market.

text:
The Yokohama Strategy and Plan of Action for a Safer World was adopted at the World Conference on Natural Disaster Reduction in Yokohama (May 23rd-27th, 1994). It acknowledges the rising impact of natural disasters on human and economic life, particularly affecting vulnerable groups in developing countries.

  • Key Resolutions:
  • (i) Sovereign responsibility of each country to protect its citizens.
  • (ii) Priority to developing countries, especially least developed, land-locked, and small-island nations.
  • (iii) Development of national capacities and legislation for disaster prevention.
  • (iv) Promotion of sub-regional, regional, and international cooperation in human/institutional capacity-building, technology sharing, and resource mobilization.

The decade 1990-2000 was declared the International Decade for Natural Disaster Reduction (IDNDR).

topic: The Four Pillars of Human Development
text: Just as any building is supported by pillars, the idea of human development is supported by the concepts of equity, sustainability, productivity and empowerment.
tables:
| Approach | Description |
|---|---|
| Income Approach | This is one of the oldest approaches to human development. Human development is seen as being linked to income. The idea is that the level of income reflects the level of freedom an individual enjoys. Higher the level of income, the higher is the level of human development. |
| Welfare Approach | This approach looks at human beings as beneficiaries or targets of all development activities. The approach argues for higher government expenditure on education, health, social secondary and amenities. People are not participants in development but only passive recipients. The government is responsible for increasing levels of human development by maximising expenditure on welfare. |
| Basic Needs Approach | This approach was initially proposed by the International Labour Organisation (ILO). Six basic needs i.e.: health, education, food, water supply, sanitation, and housing were identified. The question of human choices is ignored and the emphasis is on the provision of basic needs of defined sections. |
| Capability Approach | This approach is associated with Prof. Amartya Sen. Building human capabilities in the areas of health, education and access to resources is the key to increasing human development. |

text:
• Growth of Population: Change of population in particular area between two points of time.
  • Growth Rate of Population: The change of population expressed in percentage.
  • Natural Growth of Population: The population increased by difference between births and deaths in a particular region between two points of time.
  • Actual Growth of Population: Births - Deaths + In Migration - Out Migration.
  • Positive Growth of Population: Happens when the birth rate is more than the death rate between two points of time or when people from other countries migrate permanently to a region.
  • Negative Growth of Population: If the population decreases between two points of time.
formulas: Actual Growth of Population = Births - Deaths + In Migration - Out Migration

subject: Economics
text:
Dumping: The practice of selling a commodity in two countries at a price that differs for reasons not related to costs is called dumping.

Outsourcing: Outsourcing or contracting out is giving work to an outside agency to improve efficiency and reduce costs. When outsourcing involves transferring work to overseas locations, it is described by the term off-shoring, although both off-shoring and outsourcing are used together. Business activities that are outsourced include information technology (IT), human resources, customer support and call centre services and at times also manufacturing and engineering.

Data processing is an IT related service easily carried out in Asian, East European and African countries. In these countries IT skilled staff with good English language skills are available at lower wages than those in the developed countries. Thus a company in Hyderabad or Manila does work on a project based on GIS techniques for a country like U.S.A or Japan. Overhead costs are also much lower making it profitable to get job-work carried out overseas, whether it is in India, China or even a less populous country like Botswana in Africa.

subject: Geography
text:
• Antarctica is the world's southernmost continent, located around the South Pole.
  • It is the fifth-largest continent, covering an area of 14.2 million square kilometers (5.5 million square miles).
  • It is the coldest, windiest, and driest continent, with average temperatures ranging from -30°C in summer to below -80°C in winter in the interior.
  • It is considered a polar desert because it receives very little precipitation, with only around 10cm (3.9 inches) of precipitation annually.
  • Eighteen countries operate year-round scientific research stations in Antarctica.
  • Ozone Hole: Antarctica is known for the Antarctic ozone hole, which forms annually during the Southern Hemisphere's spring (September to November).
  • Mount Erebus: Antarctica is home to Mount Erebus, the southernmost active volcano on Earth.
  • Highest Peak: Mount Vinson, located in the Sentinel Range of the Ellsworth Mountains, with an elevation of 4,892 meters (16,050 feet) above sea level.
  • Elevation: Antarctica is the highest continent on Earth: average elevation is 8,200ft (2500m). The elevation at the South Pole is 9,300ft (2835m). The highest point on the icecap is in Australian Antarctic Territory at 13,451ft (4100m).

text:
OPERATION SINDOOR was to eliminate terror nurseries which Pakistan had nurtured for years, and provide justice to the innocent families who lost their loved ones in cross-border attacks.

Weapons used in Operation Sindoor:

  1. SCALP MISSILE: Stands for 'Systeme de Croisiere Autonome a Longue Portee'. Origin: France. Air launched long range stealth cruise missile. Range: up to 450 Km. Used for deep penetration strikes on terror command centres and key infrastructure in PoK and Pakistan.
  2. HAMMER MISSILE: Stands for 'Highly agile modular munition extended range'. Origin: France. Air to Ground Precision Guided Munition. Range: up to 70 Km. Integrated with Rafale jets. Capable of hitting targets in all weather conditions, resistant to jamming, effective at low altitude and rough terrain, and capable of autonomous targeting.
  3. METEOR MISSILE: Beyond Visual Range Air to Air Missile (BVRAAM). Manufactured by MBDA, a European company. Range: up to 100 Km. Ensures air dominance by neutralizing aerial threats.
  4. BRAHMOS MISSILE: Developed jointly by DRDO and NPOM (Russia). Speed: 2.8 to 3 Mach. Range: 450 to 500 Km. Features fire and forget abilities and terminal altitude as low as 10 metres.

AKASH MISSILE SYSTEM:

A medium range, surface to air missile system developed by DRDO India, deployed by both the Indian Army and Indian Airforce.

  • The system is known for its mobility, ability to engage multiple targets, and features like built-in Electronic Counter-Counter Measures (ECCM).

subject: Defence
text:
The S-400 Missile system, also known as Sudarshana Chakra, is one of the world's most advanced long-range surface-to-air missile (SAM) systems, developed by Russia's Almaz-Antey.

  • Range: 400 Km.
  • Altitude: Intercepts targets from 10 meters to 30 kilometers.
  • Engagement: Can engage up to 36 multiple targets at the same time.
  • Speed: Can intercept targets traveling at speeds up to 4.8 kilometers per second.
  • Features: Locates targets at 600 km, engages all types of aerial targets (aircraft, UAVs, missiles).
  • Integration: Multifunction radar, anti-aircraft missile systems, launchers, autonomous detection and targeting systems, command and control centre.

text:
This section covers recent developments and testing of various missile systems.

  • RudraM-II: Indigenous, air-to-surface missile flight-tested by DRDO and the IAF. Designed for high-precision strikes against surface targets, tested at the Integrated Test Range (ITR), Chandipur.
  • Multi-layered Ballistic Missile Defence (BMD) System: Successfully flight-tested three consecutive times by DRDO.
  • Naval Anti-Ship Missile-Medium Range (NASM-MR): Successfully flight-tested by DRDO, marking a milestone in defense against long-range ballistic missile threats.
  • BrahMos Supersonic Cruise Missile: Air-launched version integrated onto 40 Sukhoi Su-30MKI fighter jets. Offers a strike range of approximately 450 km and travels at Mach 3 (jointly developed by India and Russia).
  • MPATGM (Man Portable Anti-Tank Guided Missile): A Third-generation, fire-and-forget missile with top attack capability. Flight-tested successfully against a moving target in KK Ranges, Ahilya Nagar, Maharashtra.
  • Project Kusha (Extended Range Air Defence System): An indigenous, long-range surface-to-air missile system developed by DRDO featuring three interceptor variants: M1 (~150 km range), M2 (~250 km range), M3 (~350-400 km range).
  • Poseidon ('Doomsday Missile'): An underwater nuclear-capable drone/missile carried by Russia's newest nuclear submarine 'Khabarovsk'.
  • ASRAAM (Advanced Short Range Air-to Air Missile): An air-to-air missile designed for targeting enemy aircraft using advanced infrared heat-seeking technology. Successfully integrated onto MiG-29 fighters.
  • RS-28 Sarmat: Liquid-fueled intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) successfully tested by Russia, designed to replace the Soviet-era RS-20 Voevoda systems.
  • ULPGM-V3 Precision-Guided Missile: An Indigenous precision-guided missile that completed final trials in both air-to-ground and air-to-air modes. Integrated with UAV platforms.
  • Suryastra Universal Rocket Launcher / Rocket System: A 300-km range rocket system flagged off in Shirdi, Maharashtra.
  • Agni-1: An indigenous short-range ballistic missile developed under the IGMDP, which underwent a successful test-launch from Chandipur, Odisha.

subject: English
topic: Identifying the Correct Order of Sentences
content:
### Sentence Rearrangement Strategy

1. **Identify the Start (S1) and End (S6):**
   - **S1** usually introduces the topic, a person, or a general statement.
   - **S6** often provides a conclusion, a result, or a summary.

2. **Analyze Logical Flow:**
   - Look for cause-and-effect relationships.
   - Identify chronological markers (e.g., "first," "then," "finally," "during the course of").
   - Track pronouns and references (e.g., "this," "these," "it") to link sentences.

3. **Group Related Ideas:**
   - Sentences describing the same event or argument should be kept together.
   - Contrast words (e.g., "however," "but") indicate a shift in perspective that must follow the initial statement.

4. **Eliminate Incorrect Options:**
   - Use the identified start and end sentences to eliminate options that do not begin with S1 or end with S6 (if S6 is a distinct concluding sentence in the options, though in this format S1 and S6 are fixed anchors).
   - Check for logical inconsistencies in the remaining options.

subject: English
content:
Sentence Rearrangement questions require arranging jumbled parts (P, Q, R, S) to form a coherent and grammatically correct sentence. Key strategies include:
1. **Identify the Subject and Verb**: Find the main subject and its corresponding verb to establish the core structure.
2. **Look for Connectors**: Words like 'while', 'if', 'then', 'but', 'and' often indicate the flow of logic.
3. **Check for Collocations**: Certain words naturally go together (e.g., 'do the difficult things', 'lay a firm foundation').
4. **Eliminate Incorrect Options**: Use the identified core structure to rule out options that break grammatical rules or logical flow.

**Key Examples from Practice:**
- *Biotechnology Context*: 'A Selection Committee meeting (R) for guest teachers (P) in the Department of Biotechnology (S) was also held (Q).' -> Sequence: SPRQ.
- *Cultural Centres Context*: 'Applications (R) from Indian Nationals for deployment (S) for contractual assignment at Cultural Centres abroad (Q) as Teacher of Indian Culture for two years (P) are invited in a prescribed format.' -> Sequence: RSQP.
- *Motivational Quote*: 'Do the difficult things (S) while they are easy (R) and do the great things (Q) while they are small (P).' -> Sequence: SRQP.
- *Relationship Quote*: 'If you can't (Q) handle me at my worst (S) then you sure (P) don't deserve me at my best (R).' -> Sequence: QSPR.
- *Regret Quote*: 'You will be more disappointed (S) by the things you didn't do (P) than by the ones you did do (R) twenty years from now (Q).' -> Sequence: SPRQ.
- *Success Quote*: 'A successful (R) man is one who can lay (P) a firm foundation with the bricks (Q) others have thrown at him (S).' -> Sequence: RPQS.
- *Knowledge Quote*: 'We know what we are (R) but not what we may be (S) we not know (Q) [Note: Original text implies 'We know what we are but not what we may be']' -> Sequence: RSQP.
- *Risk Quote*: 'If you are (R) the unusual (Q) you will have to settle (S) for the ordinary not willing to risk (P).' -> Sequence: RQSP.

subject: English
content:
### Rule
When a **superlative adjective** (e.g., *largest, best, most important*) is used, it must be preceded by the definite article **the**.

**Correct:** *The largest cotton centre in the country.*

**Incorrect:** *Largest cotton centre in the country.*

**Why?** The superlative denotes a unique entity within a set, and **the** signals that uniqueness.

subject: English
content:
### Rule
If the subject of a clause is **singular**, the verb must also be in its **singular form**.

**Correct:** *While every care **has** been taken…*

**Incorrect:** *While every care **have** been taken…*

**Why?** *Every care* is a singular collective noun; therefore the auxiliary verb should be *has* (singular) rather than *have* (plural).

subject: English
content:
### Rule
Use **subject pronouns** (I, you, he, she, we, they) when the pronoun functions as the **subject** of a clause.

**Correct:** *My sister and **I** are planning a trip…*

**Incorrect:** *My sister and **me** are planning a trip…*

**Why?** *Me* is an object pronoun; it cannot serve as the subject of a sentence.

subject: English
content:
### Rule
Use the **indefinite article** **a/an** before a **non‑specific, singular count noun**.

**Correct:** *Despite the thrill of winning **a** lottery last week…*

**Incorrect:** *Despite the thrill of winning **the** lottery last week…*

**Why?** The lottery mentioned is not a particular, previously identified lottery; it is an indefinite instance, so *a* is appropriate.

subject: English
topic: Identifying sentences with no grammatical error
content:
### Note
Not every sentence contains an error. When a sentence follows all grammatical rules—correct subject‑verb agreement, proper article usage, appropriate pronoun case, etc.—the correct answer in an error‑detection item is **No error**.

**Example:** *Children are not allowed to use the swimming pool unless they are with an adult.*

All components are grammatically sound; therefore the answer is **No error**.

subject: History
text:
Humanity's evolution is described through distinct stages:

  • Hunting and Fishing Stage: Characterized by the absence of economic, political, and social systems. Labour problems did not exist.
  • Pastoral Stage: Marked by economic activity, nomadic and migratory nature, and the movement of herds. Conflicts occurred among herd-owners; nominal property ownership was unknown.
  • Agricultural Stage: The class system began to develop, including a small artisan class, landed proprietors (Zamindars), and slaves.
  • Handicrafts Stage: Marked by the beginning of the labour problem and a drastic change in the self-sufficient village economy. A community of traders and merchants emerged.

details.summary: Overview of the transition from primitive hunting stages to the emergence of complex social and economic structures like the handicraft stage.

subject: Economics
text:
Post-independence land reforms aimed at equity and agricultural investment. Key points include:

  • Implementation: Slow progress due to resilient power structures.
  • Land Ceiling Laws: Enacted in the late 1950s and 1960s; amended in the 1970s to plug loopholes.
  • Surplus Land: Approximately 3 million hectares declared surplus (only 2% of net sown area in India), much of which is caught in litigation.
  • Issues: Benami transactions, illegal possession, and allotment of inferior/barren land to the landless.
  • Current Status: 83% of farmers operate holdings of less than 2 hectares; average holding size is 1.23 hectares.

details.summary: Analysis of the effectiveness of land reform policies in India and the resulting socio-economic challenges for the rural poor.

subject: History
text:
Cornwallis Code (1793): A body of legislation enacted by the East India Company to improve the governance of its territories in India.

Vernacular Press Act (1878): Enacted by the British to curtail the freedom of the Indian press and prevent criticism towards British policies.

First Factory Act (Lord Ripon's time): Adopted in 1881 to improve service conditions of factory workers. It banned the appointment of children below the age of seven and reduced working hours for children.

Morley-Minto Reforms (1909): Brought about a limited increase in the involvement of Indians in the governance of British India.

subject: Indian Polity
text:
Article 371A: Provides special privileges to the state of Nagaland to preserve their tribal culture.

Article 371: Confers special privileges to Assam, Meghalaya, Sikkim, Manipur, and Arunachal Pradesh. It empowers the President to establish separate development boards for Vidarbha, Marathwada, and the rest of Maharashtra, and the rest of Gujarat. Special provisions for Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, and Goa are covered under Articles 371D, 371E, 371J, and 371I respectively.

Zonal Councils: Advisory bodies set up under Part III of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, to foster cooperation among states grouped into five zones. The composition includes Northern, Central, Eastern, Western, and Southern Zonal Councils. North Eastern states are under another statutory body, the North Eastern Council.

subject: Indian Polity
text:
Article 53: Executive power of the Union is vested in the President, exercised directly or through subordinate officers.

Article 74: Provides for a Council of Ministers to aid and advise the President.

Article 361: Provides that the President or the Governor of a State shall not be answerable to any court for the exercise and performance of the powers and duties of their office.

Article 363: Bars the jurisdiction of courts in disputes arising out of treaties or agreements entered into before the commencement of the Constitution by any ruler of an Indian state.

Article 348: Prescribes that proceedings in the Supreme Court and High Courts, and authoritative texts of all bills, shall be in English.

### Fifth Schedule of the Constitution
- **Scope**: Deals with the administration and control of scheduled areas and Scheduled Tribes in any State **except** the four North-Eastern States: Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram.
- **Tribal Advisory Councils**: Constituted to give advice under the Fifth Schedule.

  - Empowered to make regulations to **prohibit or restrict** the transfer of land by or among members of the Scheduled Tribes.
  - Must submit reports to the President regarding the administration of scheduled areas in the state.

subject: Polity
content:
### Article 3: Formation of New States and Alteration of Boundaries
- **Parliament's Power**: Parliament has the exclusive power to enact legislation for the formation of new states.
- **State's Role**: A state has **no say** over the formation of new states beyond communicating its views to Parliament.
- **Ways Parliament can create new states**:
  1. Separating territory from any state.
  2. Uniting two or more states.
  3. Uniting part of states.
  4. Uniting any territory to a part of any state.
- **Alterations**: Parliament may increase or diminish the area of any state, alter boundaries, and alter the name of any state.

subject: Geography
text:
Soil Impoverishment relates to soil getting very deficient in plant nutrients. It occurs due to reasons like over-grazing, mono-cropping, leaching, erosion, and land use change.

An impoverished soil leads to an increase in input cost of crop cultivation in the form of fertilizers, pesticides, etc. Soil erosion refers to the removal of top fertile layers of the soil, caused by natural reasons (river erosion, glacial erosion) or anthropogenic factors (mining, urbanisation). Soil erosion leads to soil impoverishment.

details.summary: Definition and causes of soil impoverishment and soil erosion.

subject: Geography
text:
The successional development of a vegetation community in a habitat follows a specific sequence:

  • Nudation: The beginning of an area being bare.
  • Migration: Arrival of people/species to that area.
  • Reaction: People reacting to changing environmental conditions.
  • Stabilisation: The community tries to stabilise in a given area with a certain set of climatic conditions.

Therefore, the correct sequence is: Nudation -> Migration -> Reaction -> Stabilisation.

details.summary: Sequential phases of vegetation community development.

text:
Ballistic Missiles are rocket-propelled, self-guided weapons designed to deliver warheads (nuclear, conventional, etc.) to a predetermined target using a ballistic trajectory.

They are categorized by their range, from short-range (SRBMs) to intercontinental (ICBMs).

Types of Ballistic Missile on the basis of Range

  • Short Range Ballistic Missile: Range up to 1000 km
  • Medium Range Ballistic Missile: Range 1000 to 3000 km
  • Intermediate Range Ballistic Missile: Range 3000 to 5500 km
  • Intercontinental Ballistic Missile: Range exceeding 5500 km

Types of Ballistic Missile on the basis of Launch

  • Air Launched Ballistic Missile: Launched from Aircraft
  • Submarine Launched Ballistic Missile: Launched from submarine

Examples of Ballistic Missiles of India

Agni Series:

  • Agni I: Short range, 700 Km.
  • Agni II: Intermediate range, 2000 Km.
  • Agni III: Intermediate range, 3000 Km.
  • Agni IV: Intermediate range, 4000 Km.
  • Agni V: Intercontinental, over 5000 Km.

Prithvi Series:

  • Prithvi I: Short range, 150 Km.
  • Prithvi II: Short range, 250 to 300 Km.
  • Prithvi III (Dhanush): Short range, 350 to 600 Km.

Other Notable Missiles:

  • Shaurya: Surface to surface, 750 to 1900 Km.
  • Prahaar: Surface to surface, 150 Km.
  • Pralay: Tactical ballistic missile.
  • K 15 Sagarika: Submarine launched ballistic missile.

text:
A cruise missile follows a relatively low, sustained flight path using jet propulsion, while a ballistic missile follows a high, arcing trajectory powered by rockets, primarily during the initial launch phase, before falling under gravity.

  • Cruise missiles fly within the Earth's atmosphere, often at low altitudes to avoid radar detection.
  • Cruise missiles are guided throughout their flight, using a combination of navigation systems like GPS, inertial guidance, and terrain mapping.

Devices of Parliamentary Proceedings

  • Question Hour: The first hour of every parliamentary sitting. Members ask questions and ministers provide answers. Types: Starred, Unstarred, and Short Notice.
  • Zero Hour: Informal device not mentioned in Rules of Procedure. Used to raise matters of urgent public importance.
  • No Confidence Motion: Lok Sabha can remove the ministry. Requires support of 50 members to be admitted.
  • Adjournment Motion: Introduced to draw attention of the House to a definite matter of urgent public importance.
  • Calling Attention Motion: Introduced by a member to call the attention of a minister to a matter of urgent public importance and seek an authoritative statement.

Types of Voting Systems

1. First Past the Post (FPTP)

  • Also called Simple Majority System.
  • Candidate with the highest number of votes wins, even if less than 50%.
  • No need for absolute majority.
  • Used for: Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assembly elections.

2. Proportional Representation (PR)

  • Seats allocated in proportion to votes received.
  • Used in India for: Rajya Sabha, President, and Vice-President elections.
  • Uses Single Transferable Vote (STV).
Types of PR:
  • List System: Parties present a list; seats allotted based on vote percentage.
  • Single Transferable Vote (STV): Voters rank candidates in order of preference.

Money Bills

Article 110 defines money bills. A bill is a money bill if it contains:

  • Imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of any tax.
  • Regulation of borrowing of money by the Union government.
  • Custody of Consolidated Fund or Contingency fund, payment or withdrawal of money.
  • Appropriation of money out of the Consolidated Fund of India.

Budget

Mentioned in Article 112 as 'Annual Financial Statement'. The word 'budget' is not in the Constitution.

Stages in Enactment:

  1. Presentation of budget
  2. General discussion
  3. Scrutiny by departmental committees
  4. Voting on demands for grants
  5. Passing of appropriation bill
  6. Passing of finance bill

subject: Indian Polity
text:
Under Article 105:

  • 1. Freedom of Speech in Parliament: MPs can speak freely in Parliament. No court can question what they say inside the House. Subject to rules of the House.
  • 2. Immunity from Court Proceedings: No legal action for anything said in Parliament or any vote given.
  • 3. Immunity from Arrest (Civil Cases): Cannot be arrested in civil cases: 40 days before session, during session, and 40 days after session. Does NOT apply to criminal cases.
  • 4. Right to Exclude Strangers: Parliament can hold secret sittings and remove outsiders.
  • 5. Right to Punish for Contempt: Can punish members or outsiders for breach of privilege. Includes reprimand, suspension, imprisonment.
  • 6. Freedom from Jury Service: MPs are exempt from jury duty.

Classification:

  • Individual Privileges: Freedom of speech, Immunity from arrest (civil cases).
  • Collective Privileges: Control over internal proceedings, Power to punish for contempt, Right to regulate business.

chapter: Seventh Schedule of the Indian Constitution
topic: The Three Lists: Union, State, and Concurrent
text:
The Seventh Schedule of the Indian Constitution divides legislative powers between the Union and the States through three lists:

  • Union List (List I): Parliament has exclusive power to make laws. Currently contains around 100 subjects of national importance. Key items include Defence, Armed Forces, War & Peace, Foreign Affairs, Citizenship, Railways, Airways, Banking, Currency & Coinage, RBI, Atomic Energy, Interstate trade & commerce, Insurance, Supreme Court, CAG, and All India Services.
  • State List (List II): State Legislature has exclusive power. Currently contains around 61 subjects (reduced after 42nd Amendment) of local or regional importance. Key items include Police, Public Order, Public Health & Hospitals, Agriculture, Irrigation, Land, Local Government, Fisheries, Markets & Fairs, State Public Services, and State Judiciary (except High Court structure).
  • Concurrent List (List III): Both Parliament and State Legislatures can make laws. Currently contains around 52 subjects. If there is a conflict, the Union law prevails (Article 254). Key items include Education, Forests, Trade Unions, Marriage & Divorce, Adoption & Succession, Criminal Law, Civil Procedure, Electricity, and Economic & Social Planning.

Important Provisions:

  • Residuary Powers lie with the Parliament (Article 248).
  • During National Emergency, Parliament can legislate on State List subjects.
  • Rajya Sabha (Article 249) can allow Parliament to legislate on State List subjects in the national interest.
  • State List subjects can shift to the Concurrent List (e.g., Education via 42nd Amendment).

subject: Physics
topic: Momentum and Second Law of Motion
text:
Momentum has both direction and magnitude.

  • Its direction is the same as that of velocity, v.
  • Direction is the same as that of velocity, v.
  • The SI unit of momentum is kilogram-metre per second (kg m s-1).
  • Since the application of an unbalanced force brings a change in the velocity of the object, it is therefore clear that a force also produces a change of momentum.
  • The second law of motion states that the rate of change of momentum of an object is proportional to the applied unbalanced force in the direction of force.
  • The initial and final momentum of the object will be, p1 = mu and p2 = mv respectively.
  • While catching a fast moving cricket ball, a fielder in the ground gradually pulls his hand backwards with the moving ball.
  • The fielder increases the time during which the high velocity of the moving ball decreases to zero.
  • Thus, the acceleration of the ball is decreased and therefore the impact of catching the fast moving ball is also reduced.
  • That is, when F = 0, v = u for whatever time, t is taken. This means that the object will continue moving with uniform velocity, u throughout the time, t. If u is zero then v will also be zero. That is, the object will remain at rest.
formulas: Rate of change of momentum: m(v - u) / t
Applied force: F = m(v - u) / t
image_descriptions: A diagram illustrating the concept of force and momentum transfer on a carrom board, showing a hand holding a cue stick, a striker, and carrom coins. A pencil with a cap is also depicted, pointing towards the formulas related to momentum and force.

details.summary: This section defines momentum, its direction, and SI unit. It explains Newton's Second Law of Motion, stating that force is proportional to the rate of change of momentum. An example of catching a cricket ball illustrates the concept of increasing time to reduce impact. It also describes the state of an object when no net force acts on it.

subject: Physics
text:
THIRD LAW OF MOTION

  • The third law of motion states that when one object exerts a force on another object, the second object instantaneously exerts a force back on the first. These two forces are always equal in magnitude but opposite in direction.
  • Even though the action and reaction forces are always equal in magnitude, these forces may not produce accelerations of equal magnitudes. This is because each force acts on a different object that may have a different mass.
  • When a gun is fired, it exerts a forward force on the bullet. The bullet exerts an equal and opposite force on the gun. This results in the recoil of the gun. Since the gun has a much greater mass than the bullet, the acceleration of the gun is much less than the acceleration of the bullet.
image_descriptions: A stick figure drawing of a person reading a book, accompanied by question marks and an exclamation mark, possibly symbolizing the process of understanding or questioning a concept.

details.summary: This section explains Newton's Third Law of Motion, which describes action-reaction pairs. It clarifies that while forces are equal and opposite, accelerations may differ due to varying masses of the interacting objects, using the example of a gun recoiling after firing a bullet.

subject: Physics
text:
UNIVERSAL LAW OF GRAVITATION

  • Every object in the universe attracts every other object with a force which is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. The force is along the line joining the centres of two objects.
  • G is the constant of proportionality and is called the universal gravitation constant
  • The SI unit of G is N m2 kg-2.
  • Value of G is 6.673 × 10-11 N m2 kg-2.
image_descriptions: A diagram illustrating the Universal Law of Gravitation, showing two spherical objects, A and B, with masses M and m respectively, separated by a distance d. An arrow indicates the attractive force F between them, and the formula F = G * (Mm / d^2) is displayed. An icon of an open book with a magnifying glass is also present.

details.summary: This section defines the Universal Law of Gravitation, stating that every object attracts every other object with a force proportional to their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. It also specifies the universal gravitational constant (G), its SI unit, and its numerical value.

subject: Physics
topic: Importance of the Universal Law of Gravitation
text:
IMPORTANCE OF THE UNIVERSAL LAW OF GRAVITATION

The universal law of gravitation successfully explained several phenomena which were believed to be unconnected:

  1. the force that binds us to the earth;
  2. the motion of the moon around the earth;
  3. the motion of planets around the Sun
  4. the tides due to the moon and the Sun.

details.summary: This section highlights the significance of the Universal Law of Gravitation by listing the phenomena it successfully explained, including the force binding us to Earth, the motion of celestial bodies like the Moon and planets, and the occurrence of tides.

subject: Physics
text:
Weight

  • The law is universal; applicable to all bodies, whether big or small, celestial or terrestrial.
  • Inverse-square: If F is inversely proportional to the square of d, if d increases by a factor of 6, F becomes 1/36 times smaller.
  • Weight depends on mass (m) and acceleration due to gravity (g).
  • Weight is the force with which an object is attracted towards the earth.
  • Formula: W = m x g.
  • SI unit is Newton (N). It has both magnitude and direction.

Free Fall

  • Objects falling towards the earth under this force alone are in 'free fall'.
  • No change in direction of motion, but magnitude of velocity changes.
  • Acceleration due to gravity is denoted by g.
  • Unit of g is m s^-2.
  • g = 9.8 ms^-2.
  • Formula: F = mg; mg = G(M x m)/d^2; g = G(M/d^2).

Mass

  • Greater mass = greater inertia.
  • Mass is constant regardless of location (earth, moon, space).

Weight of Body in Lift

  • Stationary/Uniform speed: Apparent weight = True weight.
  • Going up with acceleration: Apparent weight > True weight.
  • Going down with acceleration: Apparent weight < True weight.
  • Free fall: Weight = 0 (Weightlessness).
  • Going down with acceleration > g: Body raises towards the ceiling.

details.summary: Overview of gravitational concepts including weight, free fall, mass properties, and the effect of lift acceleration on apparent weight.

subject: Physics
text:
The apparent weight of an object in a lift depends on the acceleration of the lift:

  • Lift moving upward or downward with constant velocity: a=0, R-mg=0, R=mg (Apparent weight = Actual weight).
  • Lift accelerating upward at rate 'a': R-mg=ma, R=m(g+a) (Apparent weight > Actual weight).
  • Lift accelerating upward at rate 'g': R-mg=mg, R=2mg (Apparent weight = 2 x Actual weight).
  • Lift accelerating downward at rate 'a': mg-R=ma, R=m(g-a) (Apparent weight < Actual weight).
image_descriptions: Four diagrams showing a person in a lift with a spring balance, indicating forces (R, mg) and acceleration (a) for different motion states.

details.summary: Analysis of apparent weight variations in a lift under different acceleration conditions.

subject: Physics
text:
Buoyancy is the upward force exerted by a fluid on an immersed object.

  • Water feels heavier when a bucket is out of the water.
  • Ships float because the upward force (buoyancy) is greater than the weight of the displaced water.
  • An object floats if its density is less than the density of the fluid.
  • Density is defined as mass per unit volume.

details.summary: Explanation of buoyancy, floating, and density principles.

subject: Physics
text:
Thrust: The force acting perpendicular to the surface.

Pressure: The thrust on unit area. SI unit is N/m^2 or Pascal.

subject: Physics
text: Relative density is the ratio of the density of a substance to the density of water. It has no unit.
formulas: Relative density = Density of a substance / Density of water

details.summary: Definition and formula for relative density.

subject: Physics
text:
Work: Work done = force x displacement (W = F.s). It is a scalar quantity. Unit is Joule (J) or Newton metre (Nm).

  • Work is positive if force is in the direction of displacement.
  • Work is negative if force is in the opposite direction (angle 180 degrees).

Energy: Capacity to do work. Measured in Joules. 1 kJ = 1000 J.

details.summary: Definitions and units for work and energy.

subject: Physics
text:
Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by an object due to its motion.

  • Examples: A falling coconut, a speeding car, a rolling stone, a flying aircraft, flowing water, blowing wind, a running athlete etc.
  • The Kinetic Energy of an object increases with its speed.
  • Kinetic energy possessed by an object of mass, m and moving with a uniform velocity, v is:
image_descriptions: Formula for Kinetic Energy: Ek = 1/2 * m * v^2

details.summary: Definition and formula for kinetic energy.

subject: Physics
text:
The potential energy possessed by the object is the energy present in it by virtue of its position or configuration.

  • An object increases its energy when raised through a height.
  • This is because work is done on it against gravity while it is being raised.
  • The energy present in such an object is the gravitational potential energy.
  • This is the potential energy (EP) of the object, Ep = mgh.
  • It is useful to note that the work done by gravity depends on the difference in vertical heights of the initial and final positions of the object and not on the path along which the object is moved.

details.summary: Definition and formula for gravitational potential energy.

subject: Physics
text:
Energy of a system during or after the process, whenever energy gets transformed, the total energy remains unchanged. This is the law of conservation of energy.

  • According to this law, energy can only be converted from one form to another.
  • An object of mass, m be made to fall freely from a height, h.
  • At the start, the potential energy is mgh and kinetic energy is zero.
  • As it falls, its potential energy will change into kinetic energy.
  • As the fall of the object continues, the potential energy would decrease while the kinetic energy would increase.
  • When the object is about to reach the ground, h = 0 and v will be the highest.
  • Therefore, the kinetic energy would be the largest and potential energy the least.
  • The sum of the potential energy and kinetic energy of the object would be the same at all points.
  • During the free fall of the object, the decrease in potential energy, at any point in its path, appears as an equal amount of increase in kinetic energy.
image_descriptions: Equation showing the sum of potential and kinetic energy is constant.

details.summary: Explanation of the Law of Conservation of Energy using free fall as an example.

subject: Physics
text:
Power is defined as the rate of doing work or the rate of transfer of energy.

  • Power = work/time
  • The unit of power is watt.
  • 1 watt = 1 joule/second or 1 W = 1 Js^-1.
  • 1 kilowatt = 1000 watts = 1000 W = 1000 J s^-1.
image_descriptions: Diagram of power formula P = W/t with an atom icon.

details.summary: Definition, formula, and units of power.

subject: Physics
text:
1 kW h is the energy used in one hour at the rate of 1000 J s^-1 (or 1 kW).

  • 1 kW h = 1 kW * 1 h = 1000 W * 3600 s = 3600000 J = 3.6 * 10^6 J.
  • The energy used in households, industries and commercial establishments are usually expressed in kilowatt hour.
  • For example, electrical energy used during a month is expressed in terms of 'units'. Here, 1 'unit' means 1 kilowatt hour.
image_descriptions: Table showing temperature conversion formulas between Celsius, Fahrenheit, and Kelvin.

details.summary: Explanation of commercial energy units and temperature conversion table.

subject: Physics
text:
• Sound is produced by vibrating objects.
  • The particles do not travel all the way from the vibrating object to the ear.
  • Sound waves are characterised by the motion of particles in the medium and are called mechanical waves.
  • Air is the most common medium through which sound travels.
  • When a vibrating object moves forward, it pushes and compresses the air in front of it creating a region of high pressure.
  • When the vibrating object moves backwards, it creates a region of low pressure called rarefaction (R).
  • More density of the particles in the medium gives more pressure.
image_descriptions: A small diagram showing a tuning fork vibrating, creating compressions and rarefactions in the air.

details.summary: Covers the basic mechanism of sound production and propagation through a medium.

subject: Physics
text:
• Sound is a mechanical wave and needs a material medium like air, water, steel etc.
  • It cannot travel through vacuum.
  • Compressions are the regions where particles are crowded together. Thus, compressions are regions where density as well as pressure is high.
  • Rarefactions are the regions of low pressure.
  • A peak is called the crest and a valley is called the trough of a wave.
  • The distance between two consecutive compressions (C) or two consecutive rarefactions (R) is called the wavelength.
  • The wavelength is usually represented by λ (Greek letter lambda).
  • Its SI unit is metre (m).
image_descriptions: A wave diagram showing density/pressure on the y-axis and distance on the x-axis, labeling crest, trough, and wavelength (λ).
Two wave diagrams comparing 'Soft sound' (low amplitude) and 'Louder sound' (high amplitude) with wave disturbance on the y-axis and time on the x-axis.

details.summary: Defines key wave terminology including compressions, rarefactions, crests, troughs, and wavelength.

subject: Physics
text:
• The SI unit of frequency was named as hertz.
  • The time taken by two consecutive compressions or rarefactions to cross a fixed point is called the time period of the wave.
  • A violin and a flute may both be played at the same time in an orchestra. Both sounds travel through the same medium. But the sounds we receive are different. This is due to the different characteristics associated with the sound. Pitch is one of the characteristics.
  • The faster the vibration of the source, the higher is the frequency and the higher is the pitch.
  • The magnitude of the maximum disturbance in the medium on either side of the mean value is called the amplitude.
  • The loudness or softness of a sound is determined basically by its amplitude.

details.summary: Explains frequency, pitch, time period, and amplitude as determinants of sound characteristics.

subject: Physics
text:
• Reverberation: A sound created in a big hall will persist by repeated reflection. The repeated reflection that results in this persistence of sound is called reverberation.
  • To reduce reverberation, the roof and walls of the auditorium are generally covered with sound-absorbent materials like compressed fibreboard, rough plaster or draperies.
  • Generally the ceilings of concert halls, conference halls and cinema halls are curved so that sound after reflection reaches all corners of the hall.
  • Ultrasound: Ultrasound is generally used to clean parts located in hard-to-reach places, for example, spiral tube, odd shaped parts, electronic components etc.
  • Ultrasounds can be used to detect cracks and flaws in metal blocks.

details.summary: Discusses the phenomenon of reverberation, methods to control it, and the industrial applications of ultrasound.

subject: Physics
text:
Applications of Ultrasound

  • Ultra sound is generally used to clean parts located in hard-to-reach places, for ex: spiral tube, odd shaped parts, electronic components etc...
  • Ultra sound can be used to detect crack and flaws in metal blocks.
  • Ultrasonic waves are made to reflect from various part of the heart and form the image of the heart.

Sonar

  • Sound navigation and ranging (SONAR) is a device that uses ultrasonic waves to measure the distance, direction and speed of underwater objects.
  • The sonar technique is used to determine the depth of the sea and to locate underwater hills, valleys, submarine, icebergs, sunken ship etc.

subject: Physics
text:
1. Streamline Flow / Steady Flow

It is the flow in which velocity at every point in the fluid will remain constant.

2. Turbulent Flow

In this flow, the fluid does not maintain constancy of the velocity.

Bernoulli's Theorem

When an incompressible and non-viscous liquid flows in a streamlined motion from one place to another, then at every point of its path the total energy per unit volume (Pressure energy + Kinetic energy + Potential energy) is constant.

Applications: Venturi meter, pitot tube, Bunsen's burner, atomizer are based on Bernoulli's theorem.
