chapter: Area and Perimeter of Plane Figures
text:
Area of the plane figure is the amount of surface enclosed by its boundary. It is measured in square units. The perimeter of plane figure is total length of the sides enclosing the figure. Unit of Perimeter is same as the unit of sides of a given figure.

SQUARE

Let each side of a square be a unit.

  • Perimeter of square = 4(Side) = 4a units
  • Diagonal of square = sqrt(2) * (Side) = a*sqrt(2) units
  • Area of square = Side * Side = (a)^2 sq units = 1/2 * (Diagonal)^2 = 1/2 * d^2 sq units

subject: Mathematics
text:
Let l and b be the length and breadth of a rectangle respectively, then:

  • Area of rectangle = Length × Breadth = l × b
  • Perimeter of rectangle = 2 (Length + Breadth) = 2(l + b) units
  • Diagonal of rectangle = sqrt(Length^2 + Breadth^2) = sqrt(l^2 + b^2) units
  • Area of track (Shaded region) = (l1b1 - l2b2) sq units

text:
(i) Let ABCD be a quadrilateral in which DM = h1 and BN = h2 are perpendiculars on diagonal AC from other two vertices B and D, then Area of the quadrilateral = 1/2 × Diagonal × (h1 + h2) = 1/2 × AC × (DM + BN) sq units.

(ii) Let d1 and d2 are two diagonals and θ is angle between them, then area of quadrilateral = 1/2 * d1 * d2 * sin(θ)

chapter: Area and Perimeter of Plane Figures
text:
Let adjacent sides of a parallelogram be b and a respectively and h is the corresponding altitude (height) of side a, then:

  • (i) Area of the parallelogram = (Base × Height) = a × h sq units
  • (ii) Perimeter of a parallelogram = 2(Sum of adjacent side) = 2(a + b) units

Note: Each diagonal of a parallelogram divides it into two triangles of equal area.

subject: Mathematics
chapter: Area and Perimeter of Plane Figures
text:
Let the length of each sides of a rhombus be a and length of both diagonals are d1 and d2, then:

  • (i) Area of rhombus = 1/2 * d1 * d2 sq units
  • (ii) Side of rhombus = 1/2 * sqrt(d1^2 + d2^2) units => 4a^2 = d1^2 + d2^2
  • (iii) Perimeter of rhombus = 4 * (Side) units

Note: Diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles.
image_descriptions: Diagram of a rhombus ABCD with diagonals d1 and d2 intersecting at point O at right angles, and side length 'a'.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Let the length of parallel sides of a trapezium be a and b and distance between them is h, then:

Area of trapezium = 1/2 * (Sum of parallel sides) * (Distance between them)

= 1/2 * (AB + CD) * h = 1/2 * (a + b) * h sq units
image_descriptions: A diagram of a trapezium with parallel sides labeled 'a' and 'b', and height 'h' indicated by perpendicular lines from the top vertices to the base.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Let the sides of a triangle be a, b, c and h be the corresponding altitude to side a, then:

  • (i) Perimeter of scalene triangle, 2s = (a + b + c) units
  • (ii) Semi-perimeter of scalene triangle, s = (a + b + c) / 2 units
  • (iii) Area of triangle = sqrt(s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)) sq units [Heron's formula]
  • or area of triangle = 1/2 * a * h sq units
  • (iv) The radius of incircle = (2 * Area) / Perimeter
  • (v) The radius of circumcircle = (abc) / (4 * Area)
image_descriptions: A triangle with sides labeled a, b, c and an altitude labeled h.

subject: Mathematics
text:
A figure bounded by three straight lines is called a triangle. Let perpendicular, base and hypotenuse of a right angled triangle (ΔABC) be p, b and h, respectively, then:

  • (i) Perimeter of right angled triangle = AB + BC + CA = (b + p + h) units
  • (ii) Area of right angled triangle = 1/2 * Base * Altitude = 1/2 * b * p sq units

text:
Isosceles Triangle Properties:

  • Let sides be a, b, and b.
  • Perimeter: a + b + b = a + 2b units.
  • Area (ii): (s - b) * sqrt(s - a) = (1/4) * a * sqrt(4b^2 - a^2) sq units, where a is the base, b are equal sides, and s is the semi-perimeter.
  • Area of a right isosceles triangle: (1/2) * a^2 sq units.
  • Area using angle: If θ is the angle between two equal sides, Area = (1/2) * a^2 * sin(θ).

text:
Equilateral Triangle Properties:

  • Let a be the side of an equilateral triangle.
  • Height (altitude): (sqrt(3) / 2) * a
  • Area: (sqrt(3) / 4) * a^2
  • Perimeter: 3 * Side = 3a
  • Radius of incircle: a / (2 * sqrt(3))

subject: Mathematics
text:
Circle Properties:

  • Circumference of circle = 2πr = πD units (where D is diameter, D = 2r)
  • Area of circle = πr^2 sq units
  • Distance covered by a wheel in one revolution = Circumference of the wheel

Circular Ring:

If 'R' and 'r' be outer and inner radii of a ring, then the area of ring = π(R^2 - r^2) sq units.

Semi-circle:

A diameter divides a circle into two equal parts. Each of these two arcs is called a semi-circle. If r is the radius of a circle, then:

  • Area of semi-circle = 1/2 πr^2 sq units
  • Perimeter of semi-circle = (πr + 2r) = (πr + D) units

  • (i) The perimeter of the quadrant = (Circumference of a circle)/4 + 2r = (π/2 + 2)r units

If θ be the angle at the centre of a circle of radius r, then:

  • (i) Length of the arc PQ = (2πrθ)/360 = (πrθ)/180
  • (ii) Area of sector OPRQO = (πr^2θ)/360
  • (iii) Area of segment PRQP = (Area of sector OPRQO) - (Area of ΔOPQ) = (πr^2θ)/360 - 1/2 r^2 sin θ
  • (iv) Area of major segment QPSQ = (Area of circle) - (Area of minor segment PRQP)

A polygon that has all sides equal and all interior angles equal are regular polygon. Let n = number of sides, a = length of side, r = radius of inscribed circle (inradius), R = radius of circumcircle.

  • Area of polygon = 1/4 na^2 cot(180/n) = nr^2 tan(180/n) = 1/2 nR^2 sin(360/n)
  • Perimeter of polygon = n * a = 2nr sin(π/n)
  • Inradius of polygon, r = 1/2 a cot(180/n)
  • Circumradius of polygon, R = 1/2 a cosec(180/n)
  • (i) Area of regular pentagon = 1/4 sqrt(5(5+2sqrt(5))) a^2 sq units
  • (ii) Area of regular hexagon = (3sqrt(3)a^2)/2 sq units
  • (iii) Area of regular octagon = 2(sqrt(2)+1) a^2 sq units

Key geometric properties for problem-solving:

  • If a room of dimensions (l x b) m is to be paved with square tiles, then:
    • (i) The side of the largest square tile = HCF of l and b
    • (ii) The least number of tiles required = (l x b) / (HCF of l and b)^2

  • The side of a square inscribed in a circle of radius r is sqrt(2)r.
  • The area of the largest triangle inscribed in a semi-circle of radius r is r^2.

This section provides step-by-step solutions for various geometric problems involving rectangles, squares, circles, and triangles.

  • Rectangle: Area = l x b, Perimeter = 2(l + b).
  • Equilateral Triangle: Area = (sqrt(3)/4) * a^2, Perimeter = 3a.
  • Circle: Area of sector = (theta/360) * pi * r^2.
  • Pythagoras Theorem: AB^2 + AD^2 = BD^2.

subject: Mathematics
chapter: Surface Area and Volume of Solids
text:
Solid Figures: The objects which occupy space (i.e. they have three dimensions) are called solid figures. The solid figures can be derived from the plane figures. A solid figure has surface area and volume.

Surface Area of Solid Figure: Surface area of a solid body is the area of all of its surfaces together. It is always measured in square units. Surface area is also referred to as the total surface area. The area of four walls or the area excluding top and bottom is called curved surface area or lateral surface area.

Volume of Solid Figure: The measure of space occupied by a solid is called its volume. It is always measured in cubic units.

Cuboid: A figure which is surrounded by six rectangular surfaces, is called cuboid. It is also called rectangular parallelopiped.

  • A cuboid has 8 corners, 12 edges, 6 faces and 4 diagonals.

details.summary: Introduction to solid geometry, defining surface area, volume, and the properties of a cuboid.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Cuboid Properties:

  • Volume of cuboid = Area of base × height = l × b × h
  • Total surface area of cuboid = 2(lb + bh + lh)
  • Diagonal of the cuboid = sqrt(l^2 + b^2 + h^2)
  • Lateral surface area or Area of four walls = 2(l + b)h
image_descriptions: Diagram of a cuboid with vertices labeled A, B, C, D showing length, breadth, and height.
Diagram showing a rectangular sheet of 48x36 with 8x8 squares cut from corners to form an open box.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Cube Properties:

A cuboid whose length, breadth and height are same is called a cube.

  • A cube has 6 surfaces, 12 edges, 8 corners and 4 diagonals.
  • Cube is a special case of cuboid which has 6 square faces.
  • Volume of a cube = (side)^3
  • Total surface area of a cube = 6 × (side)^2
  • Diagonal of a cube = sqrt(3) × edge
  • Lateral surface area or area of four walls = 4 × (side)^2
image_descriptions: Diagram of a cube with vertices labeled A, B, C, D.

details.summary: Definitions and formulas for cube geometry.

subject: Mathematics
text:
A right circular cylinder is a solid figure obtained by revolving the rectangle, say ABCD about its one side, say BC. Let base radius of right circular cylinder be r and its height be h. Then,

  • (i) Volume of the cylinder = (Area of base) x Height = pi * r^2 * h cu units
  • (ii) Curved surface area = Circumference of the base x Height = 2 * pi * r * h sq units
  • (iii) Total surface area = Curved surface + Area of two ends = 2 * pi * r * h + 2 * pi * r^2 = 2 * pi * r(h + r) sq units
formulas: Curved surface area = 2 * pi * r * h
Total surface area = 2 * pi * r(h + r)
image_descriptions: A diagram of a right circular cylinder with height labeled as h, and the base circle labeled with points D and C, and top circle with points A and B.

details.summary: Definitions and formulas for the volume and surface area of a right circular cylinder.

subject: Mathematics
text:
• Volume of prism = Area of base x height
  • Lateral surface area of prism = Perimeter of base x height
  • Volume of pyramid = 1/3 x Area of base x height
  • Lateral surface area = 1/2 x Perimeter of base x slant height
formulas: Volume of prism = Area of base * height
Lateral surface area of prism = Perimeter of base * height
Volume of pyramid = 1/3 * Area of base * height
Lateral surface area = 1/2 * Perimeter of base * slant height

details.summary: General formulas for prisms and pyramids.

subject: Mathematics
text:
A right circular cone is a solid, generated by the revolution of a right angled triangle about one of its sides containing the right angle. Let height of a right circular cone be h, slant height be l and its radius be r.

  • The slant height of the cone, l = AC = sqrt(r^2 + h^2) units
  • Volume of cone = 1/3 * pi * r^2 * h cu units
  • Curved surface area = pi * r * l sq units
  • Total surface area of a cone = Curved surface area + Base area = pi * r * (l + r) sq units
formulas: Curved Surface Area = pi * r * l
Total Surface Area = pi * r * (l + r)
image_descriptions: A diagram of a right circular cone showing height (h), slant height (l), and radius (r) with vertices labeled A, B, C and center O.

subject: Mathematics
text:
A hollow cylinder is one which is empty from inside and has some difference between the internal and external radius. Let R and r be the external and internal radii of the hollow cylinder and h be its height.

  • Volume of hollow cylinder = pi * (R^2 - r^2) * h cu units
  • Curved surface area = 2 * pi * R * h + 2 * pi * r * h = 2 * pi * (R + r) * h sq units
  • Total surface area = 2 * pi * R * h + 2 * pi * r * h + 2 * pi * (R^2 - r^2) = 2 * pi * (R + r) * (h + R - r) sq units
formulas: Curved Surface Area = 2 * pi * (R + r) * h
Total Surface Area = 2 * pi * (R + r) * (h + R - r)
image_descriptions: A diagram of a hollow cylinder showing external radius (R), internal radius (r), and height (h).

subject: Mathematics
text:
If a right circular cone is cut-off by a plane parallel to the base of the cone, then the portion of the cone between the cutting plane and base of the cone is called the frustum of the cone. Let R, r be the radii of base and top (R > r) of the frustum of a cone. Let height of frustum of a cone be h and slant height be l, then:

  • (i) Slant height of frustum of right circular cone = BC = sqrt(h^2 + (R-r)^2) units
  • (ii) Volume of frustum of right circular cone = (pi * h / 3) * [R^2 + r^2 + Rr] cu units
  • (iii) Curved (lateral) surface area of frustum of right circular cone = pi * l * (R + r) sq units
  • (iv) Total surface area of frustum of right circular cone = Area of base + Area of top + Lateral surface area = pi * [R^2 + r^2 + l(R + r)] sq units
  • (v) Total surface area of bucket = pi * [(R + r)l + r^2] sq unit [it is open at the bigger end]
image_descriptions: Diagram of a frustum of a cone showing height h, top radius r, and base radius R.
Diagram of a bucket-shaped frustum with height 24 cm, top radius 5 cm, and base radius 15 cm.

subject: Mathematics
text:
The set of all points in space, which are equidistant from a fixed point, is called a sphere. Let radius of sphere be r, then:

  • (i) Volume of sphere = (4/3) * pi * r^3 cu units
  • (ii) Surface area of sphere = 4 * pi * r^2 sq units
  • (iii) Volume of a hollow sphere = (4/3) * pi * (R^3 - r^3) cu units, where r = Inner radius and R = Outer radius
image_descriptions: Diagram of a sphere with radius r marked from the center O.

subject: Mathematics
text:
A plane passing through the centre cuts the sphere in two equal parts, each part is called a hemisphere.

Let the radius of hemisphere be r, then:

  • Volume of hemisphere = 2/3 * pi * r^3 cu units
  • Curved surface area of hemisphere = 2 * pi * r^2 sq units
  • Total surface area = 2 * pi * r^2 + pi * r^2 = 3 * pi * r^2 sq units
  • Volume of hemispherical shell = 2/3 * pi * (R^3 - r^3), where R = outer radius, r = inner radius
formulas: Volume of hemispherical shell = 2/3 * pi * (R^3 - r^3)
image_descriptions: A diagram showing a hemisphere with radius r marked from the center to the curved surface.

details.summary: Definitions and formulas for hemisphere volume and surface area.

text:
• If the side of a cube is increased by x%, then its volume is increased by [(1 + x/100)^3 - 1] * 100%.
  • If the length, breadth and height of cuboid are made x, y and z times respectively, then its volume is increased by (xyz - 1) * 100%.
  • If the length, breadth and height of a cuboid are increased by x%, y% and z% respectively, then its volume is increased by [x + y + z + (xy + yz + zx)/100 + xyz/(100)^2]%.
  • If the sides and diagonal of a cuboid are given, then the total surface area in terms of diagonal and sides is given by Total surface area = (Sum of the sides)^2 - (Diagonal)^2.
  • If the side of a cube is increased by x%, then the surface area is increased by [2x + x^2/100]%.
formulas: Volume increase (percentage) = [x + y + z + (xy + yz + zx)/100 + xyz/(100)^2]%
Total surface area = (Sum of the sides)^2 - (Diagonal)^2

subject: Mathematics
text: Statistics is the branch of Mathematics which deals with the collection, analysis and interpretation of numerical data. In this chapter, we shall study measures of central tendency i.e. mean, median and mode of ungrouped data and grouped data. Concept of cumulative frequency, the cumulative frequency distribution how to draw cumulative frequency curves (ogive) and graphical representation of data will also be discussed.

details.summary: Introduction to the scope of statistics including central tendency and graphical representation.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Collection of data is the first step in statistics towards achieving the goal or conclusion. On the basis of collection, data are of two types:

  • Primary data: The data collected actually in the process of investigation by the investigator is called primary data. It is original and first hand information.
  • Secondary data: The data collected by someone and used by any other person known as secondary data.

details.summary: Definition and classification of data collection methods.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Raw or Ungrouped data: When the data presented is random and is not prepared according to some order, it is known as raw or ungrouped data. It does not give us a clear picture of the class.

Grouped data: When the data is arranged in any manner like ascending or descending order etc., it is called grouped data. It can also be presented in the form of a table called frequency distribution table.

details.summary: Distinction between raw/ungrouped data and grouped data.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Class Intervals: Class intervals are the groups in which all the observations are divided. Each class is bounded by two figures (numbers) which are called class limits. The figure on the left side of a class, is called its lower limit and that on the right side of a class, is called its upper limit.

Class mark: It is the mid-point of the class interval.

Range or a class size: Difference between the upper limit and the lower limit of a class is called its class size.

Frequency of an observation: The number of times an observation occurs is called its frequency.
formulas: Class mark = (Lower class limit + Upper class limit) / 2

details.summary: Definitions of key statistical terminology used in frequency distributions.

subject: Mathematics
text: The tabular arrangement of data, showing the frequency of each observation is called a frequency distribution. It is a method of presenting the data in a summarized form. Frequency distribution is also known as frequency table.

details.summary: Definition of frequency distribution.

subject: Mathematics
text:
1. Discrete frequency distribution: A frequency distribution is called a discrete frequency distribution, if data are presented in a way such that exact measurements of the units are clearly shown.

2. Continuous frequency distribution:

  • Exclusive form: A frequency distribution in which upper limit of each class is excluded and lower limit is included. e.g., In the class 0-10, a student who has obtained 10 marks is not included in this class; it will be counted in the next class i.e., 10-20.
  • Inclusive method: The classes are so formed that the upper limit of a class is included in that class. e.g., In class 1000-1099, we include workers having wages between 1000 and 1099. If the income is exactly 1100, it will be included in the next class 1100-1199.

To convert inclusive to continuous, subtract 1/2 from the lower limit and add 1/2 to the upper limit of each class.

Cumulative frequency: If the frequency of first class interval is added to the frequency of second class and this sum is added to third class and so on, then frequencies so obtained are known as cumulative frequency.
formulas: Class size = Upper limit - Lower limit
tables:
| Marks | Number of students (frequency) |
|---|---|
| 40 | 7 |
| 60 | 3 |
| 80 | 3 |
| 100 | 2 |
| Total | 15 |

details.summary: Explanation of discrete and continuous frequency distributions, inclusive vs exclusive methods, and cumulative frequency calculation.

subject: Mathematics
text:
An average or central value of a statistical series is the value of the variable which describes the characteristic of the entire distribution. The following are the five measures of central tendency:

  • (i) Arithmetic mean or mean
  • (ii) Geometric mean
  • (iii) Harmonic mean
  • (iv) Median
  • (v) Mode

Out of these measures of central tendency, Arithmetic mean, median and mode are sometimes known as measures of location.

details.summary: Introduction to measures of central tendency.

subject: Mathematics
text:
The mean (or average) of number of observations is the sum of the values of all the observations divided by the total number of observations.

Mean = Sum of observations / Number of observation

Arithmetic mean of ungrouped or individual observations: If x1, x2, ..., xn are n observations, then:

  • (i) Mean (x̄) = (x1 + x2 + ... + xn) / n = (1/n) * Σ(xi) (Direct method)
  • (ii) Mean (x̄) = A + (1/n) * Σ(di) (Shortcut method), where A = Assumed mean and di = xi - A.

Properties of Arithmetic Mean:

  1. If every observation is increased by a constant, then the mean of the observations, so obtained also increases by the same constant.
  2. If every observation is decreased by a constant, then the mean of the observation, so obtained also decreases by the same constant.
  3. If each observation is multiplied by a constant, then the mean of the resulting observations can be obtained by multiplying the mean by the same constant.
  4. If each observation is divided by a constant, then the mean of the resulting observation can be obtained by dividing the mean by the same constant.
  5. The average of natural numbers from 1 to n is (n+1)/2.
  6. The average of odd numbers from 1 to n is [(Last odd number + 1) / 2] and the average of even numbers from 1 to n is [(Last even number + 2) / 2].
formulas: Average of natural numbers from 1 to n = (n+1)/2

details.summary: Definition, formulas, and properties of Arithmetic Mean.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Shortcut Method: New mean = Previous mean × Constant multiplied to each term = 18 × 3 = 54

Mean of grouped or continuous observations: If x1, x2, ..., xn are n observations whose corresponding frequencies are f1, f2, ..., fn, then:

  • (i) Direct Method: Mean x̄ = (x1f1 + x2f2 + ... + xnfn) / (f1 + f2 + ... + fn) = Σ(fixi) / Σfi
  • (ii) Assumed Mean Method: Mean x̄ = A + Σ(fidi) / Σfi, where A = Assumed mean and di = xi - A.
  • (iii) Step Deviation Method: Mean x̄ = A + (Σ(fiui) / Σfi) × h, where h = Difference between two consecutive class marks.

Weighted Arithmetic Mean: If corresponding weight of x1, x2, ..., xn are w1, w2, ..., wn respectively, then Weighted arithmetic mean = (w1x1 + w2x2 + ... + wnxn) / (w1 + w2 + ... + wn) = Σ(wixi) / Σwi

details.summary: Covers methods for calculating the mean of grouped data including direct, assumed mean, step deviation, and weighted arithmetic mean.

subject: Mathematics
text:
If two sets of observations are given, then the combined mean of both the sets can be calculated by the following formula:

x̄ = (n₁x̄₁ + n₂x̄₂) / (n₁ + n₂)

where, x̄ = Mean of sets of observations, x̄₁ = Mean of first set of observations, n₁ = Number of observations in first set, x̄₂ = Mean of second set of observations, n₂ = Number of observations in second set.

details.summary: Formula for calculating the combined arithmetic mean of two sets of observations.

subject: Mathematics
text:
If a, G and b are in GP, then the geometric mean between a and b is, G = √ab.

The harmonic mean of n positive numbers a₁, a₂, ..., aₙ is 1/H = 1/n * (1/a₁ + 1/a₂ + ... + 1/aₙ), where H denotes the harmonic mean.

details.summary: Definitions and formulas for Geometric Mean and Harmonic Mean.

subject: Mathematics
text:
After arranging the given data in ascending or descending order of magnitude, the value of the middle most observation is called the median of the data.

  • Median of an individual series: If n is an odd number, Median = Value of the (n+1)/2 th observation. If n is an even number, Median = [Value of the (n/2)th observation + Value of the (n/2 + 1)th observation] / 2.
  • Median of a discrete frequency series: First arrange the data in ascending or descending order and find cumulative frequency. Now, find N/2, where N = Σfᵢ. See the cumulative frequency just greater than N/2. The corresponding value of x is median.
  • Median of a continuous series: In this case, the class corresponding to the cumulative frequency just greater than N/2 is called the median class and the value of median is obtained by the following formula: Median = l + [(N/2 - c) / f] * h, where l = Lower limit of median class.

details.summary: Methods to calculate the median for individual, discrete, and continuous series.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Median:

  • f = Frequency of median class
  • h = Size of median class
  • c = Cumulative frequency of class before median class

Mode:

The data value which occurs maximum number of times in a data distribution is called mode.

  • Mode of individual series: The value which is repeated maximum number of times is called mode of the series.
  • Mode of a discrete frequency series: In this case, mode is the value of the variate corresponding to the maximum frequency.
  • Mode of a continuous series: The class which has maximum frequency is called modal class or group. The mode is given by the formula:

Mode = l + ((f1 - f0) / (2f1 - f0 - f2)) * h

where, l = Lower limit of modal class, h = Size of class interval, f1 = Frequency of modal class, f0 = Frequency of the class preceding the modal class, f2 = Frequency of the class succeeding the modal class.

details.summary: Definitions and formulas for calculating Median and Mode for individual, discrete, and continuous series.

subject: Mathematics
topic: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Relation between Mean, Median and Mode: The empirical relationship between the three measures of central tendency is given by: Mode = 3 (Median) - 2 (Mean). In case, mean = median = mode, then distribution is said to be symmetric distribution.

Some Useful Formulae:

  • Mean deviation for individual series: Σ|d_i| / n
  • Mean deviation for discrete series: Σf_i|d_i| / Σf_i
  • Standard deviation (σ) for ungrouped data: σ = sqrt(Σ|d_i|^2 / n)
  • Standard deviation (σ) for grouped data: σ = sqrt(Σf_i|d_i|^2 / n)
  • Variance = σ^2
  • Coefficient of variation = (Standard deviation / Mean) * 100
  • Coefficient of mean deviation = (Mean deviation / Mean) * 100
formulas: Coefficient of mean deviation = (Mean deviation / Mean) * 100

details.summary: Covers the empirical relationship between mean, median, and mode, along with standard statistical formulas for deviation, variance, and coefficients.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Graphical Representation of Data: There are many ways of picturing a frequency distribution of continuous type.

1. Bar Graph: Bars of uniform width are drawn with various heights representing the frequency of observation.

2. Histogram: Graphical representation of a frequency distribution in the form of rectangles with class intervals as bases and frequencies as height. No gap between consecutive rectangles.

Points to be remembered:

  • A histogram consists of a set of adjacent rectangles, whose bases are equal to class sizes and height are equal to class frequencies.
  • Total area of the histogram = Sum of areas of all rectangles = NK, where K = Size of a class and N = Sum of frequencies of all classes.
  • If frequency distribution is discontinuous (inclusive), change it to continuous (exclusive) and then construct a histogram.

3. Frequency polygon: Drawn by joining the mid-points of the respective tops of the rectangles of a histogram in case of equal class intervals.

details.summary: Explains graphical methods for data representation including Bar Graphs, Histograms, and Frequency Polygons.

subject: Mathematics
text:
A frequency polygon for a grouped data can also be drawn independently by plotting the mid-points of the all classes along X-axis and frequencies along Y-axis and joining the plotted points by straight line.

4. Ogive (Cumulative Frequency Curve)

When we plot the upper or lower class limits along X-axis and cumulative frequencies along Y-axis, And on joining them we get a curve called an ogive.

We have two types of ogive curves:

  • (a) less than ogive (i.e. the rising curve): It is the graph between upper limits and cumulative frequencies of a distribution.
  • (b) more than ogive (i.e. a falling curve): It is the graph between lower limits and cumulative frequencies of a distribution.

Note:

  • If we have both ogive (i.e. less than type and more than type), then these two ogives intersect each other at a point.
  • From this point, draw a perpendicular on X-axis, the point at which it cuts the X-axis gives the median. i.e. the x-coordinate of intersection point gives the median.

A pie chart showing expenditure distribution: A (30%), B (25%), C (20%), D (15%), E (10%).

details.summary: Explanation of frequency polygons, ogives (less than and more than types), and how to find the median using the intersection of two ogives.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Pie-Diagram (or Pie chart)

A type of graph in which a circle is divided into sectors such that each sector represents a proportion of the whole.

Thus, in a pie chart:

  • Data is represented by sectors of a circle.
  • Each part of data makes a certain central angle.
  • Sum of all the angles of sector is 360°.

  • Frequency Polygon: Can be drawn by joining the mid-points of the respective tops in a histogram.
  • Ogive: Used to determine the median.

subject: Mathematics
text:
A histogram is an equivalent graphical representation of the frequency distribution and is suitable for continuous random variables where the total frequency of an interval is evenly distributed over the interval.

A discrete frequency distribution is a distribution in which data are presented in a way that exact measurements of the units are clearly shown. Clearly, weights of a set of a students is continuous, while other three are discrete.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Key Statistical Concepts:

  • Median Formula: Median = l + ((N/2 - c)/f) * h
  • Mode Formula: Mode = l + ((f1 - f0)/(2*f1 - f0 - f2)) * h
  • Empirical Relationship: Mode = 3(median) - 2(mean)
  • Histogram Property: In a histogram, the width of the bars is proportional to the class interval.
  • Data Types: Primary data is collected by the investigator; secondary data is collected by other persons.
  • Pie Diagrams: All items are converted into angles.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Frequency Polygon: Can be drawn by joining the mid-points of the respective tops of the rectangle of a histogram in the case of equal class intervals.

Frequency Distribution: A comprehensive way to classify raw data of a quantitative variable. It shows how different values of a variable are distributed in different classes along with their corresponding class frequencies. It is an equivalent representation of original data.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Median Calculation: For even number of observations n, Median = (Value of (n/2)th term + Value of (n/2 + 1)th term) / 2.

Mode: The value with the maximum frequency of occurrence.

Geometric Mean: If X is the geometric mean of (x1, x2, ..., xn) and Y is the geometric mean of (y1, y2, ..., yn), then the geometric mean of (x1/y1, x2/y2, ..., xn/yn) is X/Y.

Properties: Arithmetic mean uses all data and is uniquely defined. Median uses only one or two numbers and may not be unique.

Histogram: When class intervals are on the X-axis and frequencies on the Y-axis, the resulting graph is a histogram.
formulas: Median = (Value of (n/2)th term + Value of (n/2 + 1)th term) / 2

subject: English
text:
Generally, 15 to 20 questions based on spotting the errors are asked in CDS exam. In these type of questions, the given sentences are divided into three parts with each part marked as (a), (b) and (c). We have to choose that part as our answer which has error. If there is no error in any part, then we have to choose option (d) as the answer.

'Spotting the errors' or 'Syntax' is that part of English language, where the grammatical skills of the candidates are comprehensively tested. It is an integrated grammar exercise, so it covers all the grammatical parts. This includes:

  • Parts of speech
  • Number, gender, cases and degrees
  • Confusing words
  • Uses of tenses
  • Non-finites
  • Determiners and articles

All these areas are to be studied thoroughly to score high in the CDS examination.

subject: English
text:
A word that refers to a person, place, thing, event, substance or quality is called a Noun. e.g. Ram, Delhi, Book, Lion, Street, etc.

Kinds of Noun

  • Common Noun: It is a name given to every person or thing of the same class or kind. e.g. - Boy, girl, fan, chair, etc.
  • Proper Noun: Details of a common noun are signified by proper noun. e.g. - Amit, Amita, Polar fan, Supreme chair, etc.
  • Material Noun: It refers to a material or substance from which things are made such as silver, gold, iron, cotton, diamond and plastic.
  • Collective Noun: Some nouns refer to groups of people (e.g. audience, team, committee, government etc). These are called as Collective Nouns.
  • Abstract Noun: It is the name of a feeling, quality or a state. e.g. - Feeling Love, fear, hate, anger, respect, pleasure, etc.; Quality Strength, pitch, innocence, gluttony, judgement, obedience, beauty, etc.; State Weariness, mercy, birth, death, etc.

details.summary: Definition and classification of nouns into Common, Proper, Material, Collective, and Abstract types.

subject: English
text:
There are two kinds of nouns of number: Singular Noun (refers to one person or thing, e.g., boy, girl, table, man) and Plural Noun (refers to more than one person or thing, e.g., boys, girls, tables, men).

  • Sometimes plurals are made by changing the inside vowel.
  • Sometimes plurals are made by adding 's' to the principal word of a compound noun.

subject: English
text:
Rules of Noun

  • Rule 1: Articles are not used before material nouns. e.g. - The leather is used in making shoes (X), Leather is used in making shoes (✓).
  • Rule 2: Material nouns and abstract nouns are not used in plural. e.g. - Cares of the old is necessary (X), Care of the old is necessary (✓).
  • Rule 3: Proper nouns are sometimes used as common nouns. e.g. - Samudragupta is the Napoleon of India. Kalidas is the Shakespeare of India.
  • Rule 4: Collective nouns usually take a singular verb and are substituted by a singular pronoun. e.g. - The jury has given its verdict. The team has performed to its potential.
  • Rule 5: Collective nouns takes a plural verb and are substituted by a plural pronoun when the group members do not behave as a whole but take different directions. e.g. - The jury are divided in their decision. The Ministry are much divided in their opinion regarding the foreign policy.
  • Rule 6: Collective nouns, even when they denote living beings, are considered to be of neuter gender. e.g. - India has a big army and it is divided into three major divisions.
  • Rule 7: Young children and animals are also referred to as neuter gender. e.g. - The baby started crying when it was hungry. The lizard lost its tail when it was frightened.

subject: English
text:
8. Personification and Gender: When objects without life are personified, they are considered either masculine or feminine gender.

  • Masculine Gender: Used for strength, violence, anger, and vengeance. Used with Sun, Death, Summer, and Winter. e.g., Nature has taken his vengeance by claiming lives of 100 persons.
  • Feminine Gender: Used for beauty, gentleness, and gracefulness. Used with Earth, Moon, Spring, Nature, and even Sun. e.g., Nature offers her lap to those who seek it.

9. Units of Counting: Units like pair, dozen, score, hundred, thousand, etc., retain their singular form when used after numbers. e.g., Ten pair, Five dozen, Two score, Six hundred, Three thousand, One lakh, Ten crore, Eight million, Ten billion. If the quantity is not mentioned before the unit, the plural form is used. e.g., My friend bought dozens of eggs from the market.

10. Compound Nouns: A compound word is not used in plural if a noun does the work of an adjective. e.g., He is pursuing a two year diploma course. He is a fifteen year old boy. I have got a hundred rupee note. He ran a five mile race. They went on a fifteen day tour.

11. Nouns used only in plural:

  • Instruments with two parts: scissors, spectacles, glasses, tongs, etc. (Use 'pair' to make singular).
  • Articles of dress: trousers, shorts, jeans, etc.
  • Collective nouns: Police, cattle, gentry, peasantry, clergy, people, poultry, majority, artillery, infantry, etc.
  • Other nouns: thanks, assets, premises, alms, proceeds, contents, refreshments, orders, repairs, requirements, rations, statistics (collection of data), credentials, etc.

12. Plural forms used in singular: Nouns like Mathematics, Statistics, Physics, Economics (all subjects), Gymnastics, News, Innings, Series, Measles, Rabies, Mumps, Rickets, Summons, Names of Books, etc.

13. Uncountable Nouns: Used in singular form only. Indefinite article (a, an) is not used before them, nor are they used with plural verbs. 'Much' is used in place of 'Many' for denoting plurality. Examples include: Advice, information, hair, luggage, business, work, word (promise), mischief, bread, scenery, abuse, vacation, evidence, employment, alphabet, poetry, furniture, baggage, trouble, fuel, wheat, rice, stationary, etc.

subject: English
text:
Cases of Noun

There are three types of cases of noun:

1. Nominative Case

A noun or pronoun is in the nominative case if it is used as the subject of a verb. e.g., Sachin Tendulkar scored a century.

Clue: Put Who in active sentence and What in passive sentence before the verb to get nominative case.

2. Objective Case

A noun or pronoun is in the objective case if it is used as the object of a verb. e.g., Sachin Tendulkar scored a century (Active). A century was scored by Sachin Tendulkar (Passive).

Clue: Put What in active sentence and Whom in the passive sentence after the subject and the verb to get the objective case.

3. Possessive Case

A noun is said to be in the possessive case if it denotes possession, authorship, origin, kind, etc. e.g., Amit's house is at the back-side.

How is Possessive Case Formed
  • i. By adding 's to a singular noun. e.g., Amit's, Donald's.
  • ii. By adding 's to plural nouns not ending in s. e.g., Children's school, Men's club.
  • iii. By adding only an apostrophe to a plural noun ending in s. e.g., Boys', victims', pilgrims'.
  • iv. By adding only an apostrophe to a singular noun when there are hissing sounds. e.g., Jesus' blessings, for peace' sake, for conscience' sake.
Rules of Possessive Case
  • i. In case of a compound noun, the possessive sign is attached only to the last word. e.g., My brother-in-law's marriage. The Queen-of-England's residence.
  • ii. When two or more nouns show joint possession, the apostrophe sign is put with the latter only. e.g., Dharmendra is Sunny and Bobby's father.
  • iii. The words his, hers, its, theirs, yours, ours are possessive and they are not written with the possessive sign. e.g., Neither did his efforts succeed nor your's / yours.
  • iv. The adverb 'else' combined with indefinite pronouns (somebody, anybody, etc) is expressed in possessive case as 'somebody else's' in place of 'somebody's else'. e.g., Is it your house? I thought it is somebody's else-/somebody else's?
  • v. The words church, house, school, shop are often omitted after a possessive case. e.g., Yesterday I met my friend at St John's.
  • vi. The possessive case is chiefly used with the names of living things.
  • vii. The possessive case is also used with nouns denoting time, space or weight. e.g., Stone's throw away distance, A minute's time, A day's journey.

subject: English
text:
Words used in place of nouns are called pronouns. They are used to avoid the repetition of nouns in a sentence.

Kinds of Pronoun

Personal Pronouns

This pronoun refers to or is related to the words which are used in place of nouns referring to person.

  • 1st Person: The one(s) speaking (I, me, my, mine, we, us, our, ours).
  • 2nd Person: The one(s) spoken to (you, your, yours).
  • 3rd Person: The one(s) spoken about (he, him, his, she, her, hers, it, its, they, their, theirs).

Rules of Personal Pronouns

  1. A personal pronoun must be of the same number, gender and person as the noun for which it stands, i.e. antecedent should agree with the noun.
  2. The component of the verb to be (is, am, are, was, were, will, shall), when it is expressed by a pronoun, should be in the nominative case.
  3. If a pronoun is used as the object of the verb or of a preposition, it should be in the objective case.
  4. Objective case is used after the following words: let, like, but, etc.
  5. Words such as as good as, as well as, as soon as, as beautiful as, as intelligent as, etc. are followed by nominative case.
  6. 2, 3, 1 Rule: The second person should come before the third and the third person before the first. This case applies to singular pronouns only.
  7. 1, 2, 3 Rule: 2, 3, 1 becomes 1, 2, 3 when we are talking about plural pronouns. Exception: When it comes to confessing something or committing a crime, 2, 3, 1 gets changed to 1, 2, 3 for all types of pronouns.
  8. When a pronoun stands for a collective noun, it must be in the neuter gender. But if the collective noun denotes separation or division, the pronoun used is plural.
  9. When two or more nouns are joined by 'and', the pronoun used would be plural.

subject: English
text:
Case II: Same person, the pronoun used for them must be singular.

Hint: If a single Article is used before the nouns, the verb and the pronoun are both singular, because the reference is to a singular person only.

  • The Comptroller and Auditor General has submitted his report.
  • The Chairman and the Managing Director has submitted his report.

10. When two or more singular nouns are joined by or, either-or or neither-nor, the pronoun and the verb should be singular. e.g., Either Raj or Amar is doing his duty.

11. Whenever one singular and one plural noun are used with either-or or neither-nor, the plural noun always comes second. In this case, the verb and the pronoun both become plural. e.g., Neither Amit nor his friends were present in their house.

12. While writing question tag, the subject and verb must be according to the main sentence. e.g., Our minister is intelligent, isn't he?; The boys are not enjoying themselves, are they?; They went to Delhi yesterday, didn't they?

subject: English
text:
Reflexive pronouns are pronouns that refer back to the subject of the sentence. They end in '-self', as in singular form, or '-selves' in plural form. e.g., Myself, themselves, yourself, ourselves etc.

Rules of Reflexive Pronouns:

  • 1. The reflexive pronoun is used with the following words: absent, avail, apply, enjoy, pride, resign, acquit, revenge, exert, adapt, adjust, etc. e.g., He absented himself from the class. He acquitted himself admirably in the meeting.
  • 2. With the following words, reflexive pronouns are not used: bathe, break, feed, hide, turn, move, rest, qualify, stop, etc. e.g., We bathed in the river. We fed at the motel.
  • 3. A reflexive pronoun cannot be used as a substitute for the subject. e.g., Amit and I / myself were present on the site. I / Myself will see to it that you do not get the job.

details.summary: Definition and usage rules for reflexive pronouns.

subject: English
text:
The pronouns that are used to point out the objects to which they refer are called demonstrative pronouns like these, that, those, such, it, this, etc. e.g., That is the book I was looking for.

Rules of Demonstrative Pronouns:

  • 1. Do not commit the error of omission by forgetting to use 'that' (for plural use 'those'). e.g., The Mumbai Film Studio is bigger than that of Noida.
  • 2. Pronoun 'it' comes before the phrase or clause to which it refers, whereas 'this' follows the phrase or clause it refers to. e.g., It is true that India has won the match.

details.summary: Definition and usage rules for demonstrative pronouns.

subject: English
text:
When a pronoun refers to a person or a thing in a general way, but not to any person or thing in particular, it is called indefinite pronoun like any, anyone, none, someone, everyone, everybody, one, etc.

Rules of Indefinite Pronouns:

  • 1. One, if used in a sentence, always repeats itself. e.g., One must respect one's country for one's sake.
  • 2. When we are not talking specifically about females, only masculine gender is used. e.g., Everyone was getting ready for his show.
  • 3. 'Either' is replaced by 'anyone' when we are talking about more than two persons or things. Same is the case with 'none' or 'neither'. e.g., I couldn't contact anyone of the three.
  • 4. 'Each other' should be used in speaking of two persons or things, 'one another' in speaking of more than two persons or things. e.g., We should love one another.

details.summary: Definition and usage rules for indefinite pronouns.

subject: English
text:
This pronoun refers or relates to some noun which comes after this pronoun. Besides, it acts as a conjunction also because it connects two sentences. e.g., Who, whom, which, where, etc. He is the boy who has topped the class.

Rules of Relative Pronouns:

  • 1. 'Who' is used for subject and 'Whom' for object. e.g., Who are you? Whom were you talking to? She is the girl whom I met in the train.

details.summary: Definition and usage rules for relative pronouns.

subject: English
text:
Rules for Relative Pronouns:

  • 'That' is preferred to 'who' or 'which' in the following cases:
    • Case I: After adjectives in the superlative degree. e.g., It is the best movie that I have ever seen.
    • Case II: After words like 'all', 'same', 'any', 'only', 'nothing', 'the only'. e.g., All that glitters is not gold.
    • Case III: After interrogative pronouns 'who' and 'what'. e.g., Who is the girl that comes in your dreams?
    • Case IV: After two antecedents, one denoting a person and the other an animal or a thing. e.g., The man and his dog that had entered the school were turned out.
  • The relative pronoun should be placed as near as possible to its antecedent.
  • 'What' is used without any antecedent.
  • 'Whose' is used to refer to persons only; 'of which' is used while referring to lifeless objects.

Interrogative Pronouns:

  • Used for making queries. Includes 'who', 'what', and 'which'.
  • Rules:
    • 'What' is used in a broad sense; 'Which' is used in a specific sense.
    • 'Which' is used in place of 'who' and 'what' when referring to a choice between two or among more than two things or persons.

details.summary: Rules governing the usage of relative pronouns (that, which, who, what, whose) and interrogative pronouns in English grammar.

subject: English
text:
A verb is a word (such as jump, think, happen or exist) that is usually one of the main parts of a sentence and that expresses an action, an occurrence, or a state of being.

1. Main Verbs

Main verbs have meanings related to actions, events and states. Most verbs in English are main verbs. e.g. go, show, exist, etc.

Main verbs can be divided into two categories; transitive and intransitive:

  • (i) Transitive Verbs: A transitive verb is a verb that can take a direct object. e.g. She played the piano.
  • (ii) Intransitive Verbs: An Intransitive verb has two characteristics. First, it is an action verb expressing a double activity like arrive, go, lie, sneeze, sit, die, etc. Second, unlike a transitive verb, it will not have a direct object receiving the action. Intransitive verbs have the pattern N + V (Noun + Verb). The clause is complete without anything else. e.g. John smiled. Nothing happened.

Linking Verbs

Some main verbs are called Linking Verbs. These verbs are not followed by objects. Instead they are followed by phrases which give extra information about the subject. Linking verbs include appear, feel, look, seem sound, smell, taste, become, etc. e.g. A face appeared at the window.

2. Auxiliary Verbs

Auxiliary verbs can be divided into two categories; primary and modal auxiliary verbs:

  • (i) Primary Auxiliary Verbs: Can be divided as:
    • Verbs 'to be': is, am, are, was, were, will be, shall be
    • Verbs 'to have': have, has, had
    • Verbs 'to do': do, does, did
  • (ii) Modal Auxiliary Verbs: Denote the mood/mode of the subject. They are can, could, may, might, should, used to, need, dare, etc.

subject: English
text:
Tenses

There are three basic tenses: Present, Past and Future. These can further be divided into the following segments:

  1. Simple: The action is mentioned simply. Nothing is said about whether the action is complete or not.
  2. Continuous: The action is incomplete or is going on at the time of speaking.
  3. Perfect: The action is finished or complete with respect to a certain point of time.
  4. Perfect Continuous: The action is going on continuously over a long period of time and is yet to be finished.

Simple Present

(He, She, It, Single name — V1 + s, es)

(They, you, I, Plurals — V1)

  • To express a habitual action. e.g. He goes for a walk in the morning. It rains in winter in Tamil Nadu. He often gets late for dinner.
  • To express universal truths. e.g. The sun rises in the East. Two and two make four.
  • In exclamatory sentences beginning with ‘here’ and ‘there’, to express what is actually taking place in the present. e.g. Here he comes! There goes the train!
  • To indicate a future event that is part of a plan or an arrangement. e.g. PM comes to the town next month. The Indian team goes to England this month.
  • To introduce quotations. e.g. Gita says, “Give your best and do not worry for the results”. Pope says, “A little knowledge is a dangerous thing”.

Present Continuous

(Is / Am / Are + V1 + ing)

  • To express an action going on at the time of speaking. e.g. I am studying in the class.
formulas: Simple Present (He, She, It, Single name) = V1 + s, es
Simple Present (They, you, I, Plurals) = V1
Present Continuous = Is / Am / Are + V1 + ing

details.summary: Explanation of basic tenses and detailed usage rules for Simple Present and Present Continuous tenses.

subject: English
text:
Present Continuous Usage:

  • To express a temporary action which may not be actually happening at the time of speaking. e.g. - I am preparing for the competition. I am working on a project.
  • It also represents future action or a definite arrangement in the near future. e.g. - I am going to Mumbai tomorrow. I am coming tonight.
  • When the reference is to a particular obstinate habit, the present continuous is used instead of present simple. An adverb, like always, constantly, etc, is also used. e.g. - It is no use scolding him, he is always doing what is forbidden.

Verbs normally used in Present Simple instead of Present Continuous:

  • (a) Verbs of Appearance: Look, appear, seem.
  • (b) Verbs of Emotion: Want, wish, desire, feel, like, love, hate, hope, prefer, etc.
  • (c) Verbs of Perception: See, hear, smell, taste, notice, recognise, etc.
  • (d) Verbs of Possession: Belong to, consist of, contain, own, etc.
  • (e) Verbs of Thinking: Agree, believe, consider, forget, imagine, know, mind, remember, etc.

Present Perfect (Has/Have + V3):

  • Used to indicate completed activities in the immediate past. It is a mixture of present and past. It always implies a strong connection of past with the present. e.g. - He has just gone out.
  • Used with past actions whose time is not given and not definite.
  • Used with adverbs like ever, just, recently, already, yet, so far, of late, lately, by the time, for, etc.
  • It can never be used with words like last, ago, yesterday, before, back, formerly, fixed time, etc.

details.summary: Covers rules for Present Continuous, verbs restricted from continuous tense, and usage of Present Perfect tense.

subject: English
topic: Present Perfect Continuous and Simple Past
text:
Present Perfect Continuous (Have been/Has been + V1 + ing):

  • To express an action which began at sometime in the past and is still continuing. e.g. - He has been playing since 8 o'clock. They have been writing since morning.

Simple Past (V2):

  • To indicate an action completed in the past at a definite time. e.g. - I did this. I did this yesterday.
  • Denoted by last, ago, yesterday, back, before, formerly, any fixed time, etc.
  • To indicate past habits, indicated generally by the words like often, seldom, never, normally, generally, always, frequently, rarely, daily, used to, etc. e.g. - As a kid, I often went to school on foot.
  • After 'it is time'. e.g. - It is time Indian cricket team started winning test matches.

Important Note: The conjunction since denotes present time dating back to some event. It is therefore, followed by a Simple Past Tense and preceded by some form of Present Perfect Tense. e.g. Many things have happened since I left the school.

Past Continuous (Was/Were + V1 + ing):

  • To denote an action going on at some time in the past. e.g. - When I went to his house, he was playing.
  • For persistent habits in the past. e.g. - He was always mooching around.
formulas: Present Perfect Continuous: Have been/Has been + V1 + ing

details.summary: Covers rules for Present Perfect Continuous, Simple Past, and Past Continuous tenses, including the specific usage of 'since'.

subject: English
text:
Past Perfect (Had + V3)

  • To describe an action completed before a certain moment in the past.
  • Used when one action got completed before the other started.

Past Perfect Continuous (Had been + V1 + ing)

  • To express an action that began before a certain point of time in the past and continued upto that time.
  • If there is Past tense in the Principal clause, it must be followed by a Past tense in the Dependent clause.
  • In Indirect narration, the Simple Past in the Dependent clause is changed to Past Perfect, if the Principal clause is in the Past tense.
  • Exception: If some universal, habitual or generally recognised fact is mentioned in the Dependent clause, the Present tense must be retained in all conditions.

Simple Future (Shall / Will + V1)

  • To express an action that is still to take place.

Future Continuous (Shall be / Will be + V1 + ing)

  • To express an action as going on at some time in the future.

Future Perfect (Shall have / Will have + V3)

  • To indicate the completion of an action by a certain future time.

Future Perfect Continuous (Will have been / Shall have been + V1 + ing)

  • To indicate an action which is in progress over a period of time and will be in progress at a certain time in future.

Subject-Verb Agreement

  1. If two subjects together express one idea, the verb is singular.
  2. When the plural noun denotes some specific quantity, distance, time or amount considered as a whole, the verb is generally singular.
  3. Two or more singular subjects connected by 'either-or', 'neither-nor', take a verb in singular.
  4. When the subjects joined by 'or' or 'nor' are of different numbers, the verb must be plural and the plural subject must be placed next to the verb.
formulas: Past Perfect Continuous: Had been + V1 + ing
Future Continuous: Shall be / Will be + V1 + ing
Future Perfect: Shall have / Will have + V3
Future Perfect Continuous: Will have been / Shall have been + V1 + ing

details.summary: This page covers advanced rules for English Tenses (Past and Future) and specific guidelines for Subject-Verb Agreement in the context of spotting errors.

subject: English
text:
• Rule 5: Any noun qualified by 'each' or 'every' is followed by a singular verb. Even if two nouns so qualified are connected by 'and', the verb must still be singular. e.g., Each one of these boys has the potential to get selected; Every man and woman was filled with joy; Every day and each hour teaches us something.
  • Rule 6: Verb is according to the first subject when they are connected with 'and not', 'as well as', 'in addition to', 'along with', 'besides', 'like', 'together', etc. e.g., Rahul and not his friend was absent; Amit, like his friends, is always late; He as well as you is a good boy.
  • Rule 7: When two nouns or pronouns are joined by 'not only...but also', the verb agrees with the second noun or pronoun. e.g., Not only the officer but also the soldiers were awarded.
  • Rule 8: If the subject is 'The number of', the singular verb is used and the noun is plural. e.g., The number of one-dayers played these days has led to the deterioration of the game.
  • Rule 9: A 'great many' is always followed by plural verb and a plural noun. e.g., A great many students have passed this year; A great many fish are there in the pond.
  • Rule 10: 'Many a' is always followed by a singular verb and a singular noun. e.g., Many a soldier has got medal this year; Many a student has passed this year with flying colours.
  • Rule 11: A singular or a plural verb is used with words as pains, a lot of, means, variety, plenty, rest, wages, according to the sense in which they are used. e.g., A large number of girls were absent on account of bad weather; The number of admissions has gradually fallen off; A variety of books on the subject are available.
  • Rule 12: A verb should agree with its subject and not with the complement. But in the case of sentence beginning with 'The', the verb is according to the predicate/complement. e.g., Our only guide was the stars; The stars were our only guide.
  • Rule 13: In a compound sentence, both auxiliary verbs and principal verbs should be mentioned separately if they differ in number, form or voice. In such cases, one verb cannot act for both the clauses. e.g., He has not and will not marry in near future (X); He has not married and will not marry in near future (✓); She is intelligent but her sisters dull (X); She is intelligent but her sisters are dull (✓).
  • Rule 14: Use of 'shall' and 'will'. To express simple future action 'shall' is used in the first person, and 'will' in the second and third person. e.g., I shall come; You will come; He will come. 'Shall' is used in the second and third persons to express Command, Promise, Threat, Determination. 'Will' is used in the first person to express Willingness, Promise, Threat, Determination. e.g., You shall not steal (Command); You shall have a holiday tomorrow (Promise); You shall be punished for this (Threat); You shall do it for your country (Determination); I will send you my book (Willingness); I will try to do better next time (Promise); I will punish you if you do that again (Threat); I will succeed or die in this attempt (Determination). In asking questions 'shall' is used in the first person and 'will' in the third person. In the second person, 'shall' and 'will' are used according to the answer expected. e.g., Shall we go?; We shall go; Will he come tomorrow?; He will come tomorrow; Will you do this for me?; I will do it for you.

subject: English
text:
UNREAL PAST/SUBJUNCTIVE MOOD

A wish, desire, purpose, supposition contrary to fact or condition is expressed in subjunctive mood. In subjunctive mood, 'were' and 'had' are used as the case may be. The sentence basically goes in the past tense.

Examples:

  • I wish I had a car.
  • I wish I had not met him.

There are three types of conditional clauses:

  • i. Present likely condition: e.g., I shall go for the preparation when I get the call letter. You will pass if you work hard.
  • ii. Present unlikely condition: e.g., If I had a house, I would not have rented yours. If I were there, I would not have let them go.
  • iii. Past condition: e.g., If she had studied, she would have got the call letter last year itself. If she had brought money, she could have bought the jewellery.

After, 'as if/as though':

  • He behaves as if he were the owner of this place.
  • He came in looking as though he had seen a ghost.

details.summary: Explanation of the Unreal Past/Subjunctive Mood and its application in conditional clauses.

subject: English
text:
THE INFINITIVE (To + V1)

Rules of Infinitive:

  1. In negative sentences, 'dare not' and 'need not' are used without 'to'. (e.g., You dare not leave India.)
  2. Prepositions 'but' and 'except' take the infinitive without 'to'. (e.g., He did nothing but cry.)
  3. Expressions like would rather, had rather, rather than, had better, as soon as, etc are followed by infinitive without 'to'. (e.g., I would rather go for picnic.)
  4. The infinitive without 'to' is used after Auxiliary verbs such as shall, will, can, may, did, should; but ought is an exception. (e.g., I should go. I ought to go.)
  5. The to of one infinitive can be made to do duty for to of another infinitive in the sentence, provided that the verbs in the two infinitives are synonymous. If two separate ideas are better expressed by two infinitives, to of the latter infinitive should be omitted. (e.g., It lies in my power to succeed or to fail.)
  6. Do not forget to use the preposition whenever the infinitive 'to' is made to qualify a noun. (e.g., I have no pen to write with.)

details.summary: Rules governing the usage of the Infinitive (To + V1) in English grammar.

subject: English
text:
THE GERUND (V1 + ing)

A verb which does the action of a noun. (e.g., Running tap makes a lot of noise. Smoking isn't a good habit.)

Rules of Gerund:

  1. The following words are followed by gerund: Avoid, dislike, enjoy, help (in the sense of avoid), mind, prevent, risk, stop, etc. (e.g., I cannot help looking at you.)
  2. The following phrases are followed by a gerund: Accustomed to, fed-up with, habitual to, addicted to, is no good, is used to, looking forward to, tired of, is worth, with a view to, owing to, object to, given to, taken to, etc. (e.g., I am accustomed to talking for hours.)
  3. A gerund, and not an infinitive is used after such verbs and participles as are followed by their appropriate prepositions: (e.g., desirous of, refrain from, debar from, restrain from, dissuade from, intent on, keen on, confident of, persist in, fond of, justified in, a hope of, disqualify from, prevent from, desist from, prohibit from, abstain from, bent on, aim at, insist on, succeed in, successful in, hesitate in, fortunate in.)
  4. The noun or pronoun governing a gerund must be in the possessive case. (e.g., Please excuse my being late. I remember his winning the race. I like my friend's coming on time.)

details.summary: Rules and usage of the Gerund (V1 + ing) in English grammar.

subject: English
text:
An adjective is a word used with a noun or a pronoun to add something to its meaning.

Kinds of Adjective

1. Proper Adjectives: Derived from proper nouns.

Proper NounsProper Adjectives
IndiaIndian
ChinaChinese
TurkeyTurkish
AmericaAmerican
ShakespeareShakespearian

2. Possessive Adjectives: My, our, your, his, their, her, its.

3. Adjectives of Quality: Shows traits of a person or thing. e.g., Fresh flowers were plucked.

4. Adjectives of Quantity: Shows how much of a thing is meant (Any, some, little, etc.).

5. Adjectives of Number: Shows how many persons or things are meant or in what order.

  • Definite Numeral Adjective: Denotes exact number or order (e.g., The first three benches).
  • Indefinite Numeral Adjective: Few, many, less, more, some, any, etc.
  • Distributive Numeral Adjective: Each and Every. 'Each' is used for two or more things; 'Every' is used for more than two things.

6. Exclamatory Adjectives: Used to express surprise (e.g., What an idea!).

7. Interrogative Adjectives: Used to ask questions (e.g., Which picture do you like the most?).

8. Demonstrative Adjectives: Points out which person or thing is meant (e.g., This boy is intelligent). Note: The plural forms 'these' and 'those' are often wrongly used with singular nouns 'kind of' and 'sort of'.

subject: English
text:
Comparison of Adjectives

  • Positive Degree: When only one case is there. e.g., Meerut is a big city.
  • Comparative Degree: When two cases are there. e.g., Meerut is bigger than Ghaziabad; She is better than anybody else in the school.
  • Superlative Degree: When more than two cases are there. e.g., Meerut is the biggest city of West Uttar Pradesh; He is the most corrupt politician of all in the country.

| Elder/ Eldest | For blood relations only. | I am his elder brother. |
| Old/ Older/ Oldest | For both persons and things. | My friend is older than me. |

| Further | Besides (in addition to) | I would like to add further meaning to the studies. (v) |
| Nearest | It shows distance | The nearest post-office is next to the college. |
| Next | It shows position | The nearest post-office is next to the college. |

details.summary: Covers degrees of comparison and usage of confusing adjective pairs.

subject: English
text:
Rules of Degrees

  1. Double comparative and double superlative are not used together. e.g., She is the most prettiest girl (X); She is the prettiest girl (v); This boy is more sweeter than that boy (X); This boy is sweeter than that boy (v).
  2. The Adjective ending in -er (e.g. wiser) should be used as 'more wise' while comparing two qualities of the same person or thing. e.g., He is wiser/more wise than strong; He is more wise/wiser than his brother.
  3. In comparative cases, 'other' is used with than. e.g., He is more intelligent than his classmates (X); He is more intelligent than his other classmates (v).
  4. In superlative cases, 'other' is not used. e.g., Samudragupta was the most powerful of all kings of his time.
  5. Adjectives expressing qualities, that do not have different degrees, cannot be compared. (e.g., Perfect, complete, circular, finish, square, empty, impossible, enough, full, unique, wonderful, marvelous, excellent, ultimate).
  6. Similar things should be compared when we compare two things. e.g., The climate of Dehradun is better than Meerut (X); The climate of Dehradun is better than that of Meerut (v).
  7. The comparative degree is generally followed by 'than', but the following comparative adjectives are followed by the preposition 'to'. (Superior, inferior, junior, senior, prefer, preferable, elder, younger, prior, etc.)
  8. If there is a gradual increase, it is expressed with two comparatives and not with positives. e.g., Indian fielding is getting better and better day-by-day.

details.summary: Rules governing the correct usage of comparative and superlative degrees in English grammar.

subject: English
text:
Rule 9: When two adjectives qualify the same noun, both adjectives should be represented in the same degree.

  • e.g., Taj Mahal is the most beautiful and the most sought-after place in India.
  • e.g., He is the best and honest minister of our time. (X)
  • e.g., He is the best and the most honest minister of our time. (✓)

Rule 10: The adjectives 'little' and 'few' are not made to qualify the nouns, 'quantity' and 'number'. Instead 'small' should be used to qualify these nouns.

  • e.g., Would you please lend me a small number of books for a month?
  • e.g., I asked him not to waste even a small quantity of food.

Rule 11: Do not say 'two first' for 'first two'.

  • e.g., I saw only the two first episodes of the serial. (X)
  • e.g., I saw only the first two episodes of the serial. (✓)

Rule 12: When two adjectives in different degrees of comparison are used in the same sentence, each should be complete in itself.

  • e.g., He is as good if not better than his brother. (X)
  • e.g., He is as good as if not better than his brother. (✓)

Rule 13: Worth + V1 + ing is placed after the same noun it qualifies.

  • e.g., Taj Mahal is a monument worth visiting.
  • e.g., Computer is a commodity worth buying.

subject: English
text:
Articles are the members of the determiners family. 'A', 'An' and 'The' are articles. Articles are used before nouns.

  • e.g. - My brother is a businessman.
  • e.g. - An apple a day keeps the doctor away.

Here, 'a' is an article which is used before the noun (businessman) and 'an' is an article which is used before the noun 'apple'.

details.summary: Definition and basic usage of articles A, An, and The.

subject: English
text:
Indefinite Articles

  • Indefinite article 'A' is used before the words starting with the consonants.
  • Indefinite article 'An' is used with the words starting with the vowel sound. (a, e, i, o, u)

Examples:

  • An umbrella is kept there.
  • A European lives in our colony.
  • Meerut has a university.
  • An honest and hardworking person always succeeds in life.
  • An hour is left.
  • An MA, An SP, An LLB

details.summary: Rules for using Indefinite Articles 'A' and 'An'.

subject: English
text:
Use of Indefinite Articles

(a) Before a common noun in singular to suggest the sense of one. e.g. - Twelve inches make a foot. There is a fan in the room. A man is standing on the road.

(b) Before a common noun in singular to suggest the vague sense of a certain or any. e.g. - A book is kept there.

(c) To make a common noun of a proper noun. In this case, both definite and/or indefinite article can be used according to the case. e.g. - Ajay is a Sherlok Holmes of our class. Samudragupta was the Napoleon of India.

(d) In the sense of each, every or per. e.g. - The doctor advised the patient to take the medicine twice a day. He studies for two hours a day.

(e) In exclamations before singular countable nouns. e.g. - What a shot! What a beautiful girl!

details.summary: Specific usage rules for Indefinite Articles.

subject: English
text:
Definite Article

Use of Definite Article 'The'

(a) When we speak of a particular person or thing or one already referred to. e.g. - The book is kept there. The CD of that movie is available in the market. The book you mentioned is available in the store. The pleasant weather is inviting us outside.

(b) Before the names of physical features in Geography. e.g. - The Himalayas, The Gangas, The Indian Ocean, etc.

  • However, if the reference is to a Single Island or a Single Mountain, 'the' is not used. e.g. - The Kanchenjunga is the highest peak of (X) the Himalayas in India. Kanchenjunga is the highest peak of the Himalayas in India. (✓) The North Andaman is a part of the (X) Andaman group of islands. North Andaman is a part of the Andaman group of islands. (✓)

(c) Before common nouns which are names of things unique or of their kind. e.g. - The Sun, The Moon, The Earth, The Sky.

(d) Before the names of countries which show federation. e.g. - The United States of America, The United Kingdom, The Republic of Korea, The Republic of South Africa, etc. Exception: The Netherlands, The Hague

(e) Before the names of religious and mythological books, newspapers, magazines, journals, etc. e.g. - The Bible, The India Today, The Times of India, etc

(f) Before Superlatives. e.g. - I am the best. He is the cleverest.

(g) As an adverb with a comparative. e.g. - The more, the merrier. The sooner, the better. The higher you go, the colder it is.

(h) Before terms denoting Nationality, Community and Castes. e.g. - The Australians, The Indians, The Hindus, etc

(i) Before historic events. e.g. - The Ist Battle of Panipat, The Revolt of 1857, The Quit India Movement, The Gulf War, etc.

(j) Before musical instruments. e.g. - I can play the flute very well. Ustad Amjad Ali Khan plays the sarod.

details.summary: Comprehensive rules for the usage of the Definite Article 'The'.

subject: English
text:
Usage of Articles:

  • (k) Before an adjective representing a class of people: The rich should help the poor.
  • (l) Before a unit of measurement: Cloth is sold by the metre.
  • (m) Before a common noun to give the force of superlative: He is the man.
  • (n) Before adjectives 'same' and 'whole' and after 'all' and 'both': He is the same person... The whole class... All the boys... Both the friends...
  • (o) Before a common noun to give the meaning of an abstract noun: The moralist in Gandhi...
  • (p) Before various Cups and Trophies: Sri Lanka has won the Asia Cup.
  • (q) Before comparative degree in case of a choice: He is the stronger of the two friends.

Omission of Articles:

  • (a) Before proper nouns: The New Delhi is the capital of India (Incorrect).
  • (b) Before material and abstract nouns used in general sense: The building is made up of the brick and the stone (Incorrect). Note: If specific, use article: The stone of Kota is of good quality.
  • (c) Before a noun in its widest sense: The science is a subject based on facts (Incorrect).
  • (d) Before noun following 'kind of': What kind of a person you are (Incorrect).
  • (e) Before uncountable nouns: He gave me advice.
  • (f) Before school, college, home, church, temple, sea, work, bed, table, hospital, market, prison, court when purpose is primary: I go to church every Sunday.
  • (g) Before names of diseases: AIDS can be prevented...
  • (h) Before regular meals except when preceded by an Adjective: I usually take breakfast at 9 o'clock.
  • (i) Before modes of travel: He will go by air.
  • (j) Before names of relations like uncle, mother, father: Uncle will come tomorrow.
  • (k) Before adjectives used as nouns signifying language or colours: He knows English.
  • (l) When two or more descriptive adjectives qualifying the same noun are connected by 'and', the Article is used before the first adjective only: It is a Hindi and English Dictionary.
  • (m) When two or more adjectives qualify different nouns, the Article is used before each adjective: The inner and the outer wall were both strongly defended.

details.summary: Detailed rules on the correct usage and omission of definite and indefinite articles in English grammar.

subject: English
text:
An adverb tells more about a verb, an adjective or another adverb.

e.g. - He is running fast. Here 'fast' is the adverb which tells how he is running.

Kinds of Adverb

  • Adverb of Time: Answers the question when, for how long or how often a certain thing happens. e.g. - I shall meet you tomorrow. We were late by two hours. The newspaper arrives daily.
  • Adverb of Place: Answers the question where. e.g. - I shall meet you in the market. I shall meet you there. We were studying in the institute.
  • Adverb of Manner: Answers the question how. e.g. - He is sitting quietly. He is dancing like Hritik Roshan.
  • Adverb of Frequency: It tells us how often an action takes place. e.g. - Delhi Police is with you, always.
  • Adverb of Degree or Quantity: These tell us how much or in what degree or to what extent. e.g. - We have studied enough. There is something fishy out here. There is little doubt of his success.

details.summary: Definition of Adverb and classification into five types: Time, Place, Manner, Frequency, and Degree/Quantity.

subject: English
text:
Rules of Adverbs

  • So and Too: They should not be used without their co-relatives 'that' and 'to'.
  • Difference between very and much: (a) 'Very' is used in positive degree and 'much' is used in comparative degree. (b) 'Very' is used with V1 + ing. 'Much' is used with V3.
  • Forms: Some words retain their form when they become adverbs: Fast, first, next, back, ill, better, best, etc.
  • Comparative: Adverbs ending in -ly form the comparative by adding 'more' and superlative by adding 'most'.
  • MPT RULE: If adverbs of manner, place and time are used in a single sentence, then the sequence followed is that of MPT.
  • Adjective Modification: When an adverb modifies an adjective or another adverb, the adverb comes before it.
  • Frequency: Adverbs of frequency such as always, ever, never, seldom, frequently, etc, are always placed before the verb they modify.
  • Enough: 'Enough' is both an Adjective and an Adverb. As an adverb, it is always placed after the adjective it modifies. As an adjective it is placed before the noun.
  • Only and Even: Should be placed immediately before the word intended to modify.
  • Beginning of sentence: An adverb can be placed at the beginning of a sentence, when it is intended to qualify, not any word in particular, but sentence as a whole.
  • Ever/Never usage: 'Ever' is sometimes misused for 'never'. 'Seldom or never' and 'seldom if ever' are both correct, but 'seldom or ever' is incorrect. In the same manner, 'little if anything' is correct, but 'little or anything' is wrong.

details.summary: Comprehensive list of 12 grammatical rules governing the usage and placement of adverbs in English sentences.

subject: English
text:
• Rule 13: 'Else' should be followed by 'but', and not by 'than'. e.g., 'It is nothing else but his carelessness which has led to his failure.', 'Aishwarya Rai is nothing else but a statue of beauty.'
  • Rule 14: 'Rather' and 'Fairly' can mean moderately. 'Fairly' is used with favourable adjectives and adverbs while 'rather' is used with unfavourable adjectives and adverbs. e.g., 'She is fairly intelligent but my sister is rather stupid.', 'He did fairly well in her exams but his sister did rather badly.', 'He grew up in rather unusual circumstances.'
  • Rule 15: 'Rather' can also be used when we are correcting something that we have just said. e.g., 'The process is not a circle but rather a spiral.'
  • Rule 16: 'Rather' is used in case of preference—would rather, had rather, rather than are used to express preference. e.g., 'I would rather study than sleep.', 'I prefer getting up early rather than sleeping late.'
  • Rule 17: We use 'rather' before verbs that introduce our thoughts and feelings, in order to express our opinion politely, especially when a different opinion has been expressed. e.g., 'I rather think that he was telling the truth.', 'I rather like the decorative effect.'
  • Rule 18: Adverb 'as' should be used to introduce predicative of the verbs such as regard, describe, define, treat, view, know. e.g., 'I regard him as my elder brother.', 'The newspapers described the situation as horrible.', 'Biology is defined as the study of nature.'
  • Rule 19: Adverb 'as' should not be used to introduce predicative of the verbs such as name, elect, think, consider, call, appoint, make, choose. e.g., 'He was considered the best dancer of his time.', 'He was appointed Governor by the President.', 'Saurav Ganguly was chosen the captain.', 'He was called dynamic by his mates.'
  • Rule 20: Negative Adverbs should not be used with words that are already negative in sense. Two negatives in the same sentence should be avoided. Seldom, nowhere, never, nothing, hardly, scarcely, neither, barely, rarely are some of the Adverbs. Verbs like 'deny', 'forbid', and conjunctions like 'unless', 'until', 'lest', 'both' are in this category. e.g., 'No one scarcely practises all the exercises.' (X), 'Scarcely anyone practises all the exercises.' (✓). Also: 'I rarely went to meet anybody in my childhood.', 'She hardly knows anything about me.', 'He does nothing without ever consulting me.', 'He has denied that he was going there.', 'Walk steadily, lest you should fall.', 'Both of them are not coming.' (X), 'Neither of them is coming.' (✓).
  • Rule 21: (a) 'Coward', 'miser', 'niggard', 'rogue' are Nouns. 'Cowardly', 'miserly', 'niggardly', 'roguish' are Adjectives. e.g., 'An officer is trained never to fight in a cowardly manner.', 'Although he seems brave, he is actually a coward.', 'It was a sheer cowardly act of violence.' (b) 'Fast' retains its form in both Adjective and Adverb. e.g., 'He is fast' (Adjective), 'He is running fast' (Adverb). (c) 'Direct' and 'Directly' are adverbs. Direct means straight and Directly means at once. e.g., 'Don't stop anywhere, return home direct.', 'Don't stop now, return home directly.' (d) 'Manly', 'masterly', 'slovenly', 'monthly', 'weekly', 'sickly', 'friendly' are Adjectives and should not be confused with Adverbs. e.g., 'He is earning fifty thousand rupees monthly / a month.', 'He is a friendly old man.'
  • Rule 22: The use of 'never' for 'not' is incorrect, because 'never' means not ever. e.g., 'I never remember having met him.' (X), 'I do not remember ever having met him.' (✓), 'We met the other day, but he never referred to the matter.' (X), 'We met the other day, but he did not refer to the matter.' (✓).
  • Rule 23: No sentence should begin with 'Due to'. It must be used after some form of the verb 'to be'. e.g., 'Due to bad weather, the match was abandoned.' (X), 'It was due to bad weather, the match was abandoned.' (✓).
  • Rule 24: 'Cent-per cent' It should be 'hundred per cent'.
  • Rule 25: 'Do the needful' It should be 'do what is necessary'.
