subject: English
text:
A conjunction is a part of speech that connects words, phrases, clauses or sentences. e.g. - and, but, while, though, although, lest etc.

Rules of Conjunctions

  • 1. 'Scarcely' and 'Hardly' should be followed by when and not by than. e.g. - Scarcely had I started for the institute, when the rain started. Hardly had he arrived, when he had to leave again.
  • 2. 'No sooner' is followed by than and not by when. e.g. - No sooner had I left, than the rain started. No sooner did he arrive, than he had to leave.
  • 3. 'Seldom or never' and 'seldom if ever' are both correct, but 'seldom or ever' is incorrect. e.g. - He seldom or never goes to see movies in a theatre.
  • 4. 'Either-or', 'Neither-nor', 'not only-but also', 'both-and', 'whether-or' etc., should be followed by the same parts of speech or of the same function.
  • 5. The conjunctions 'though' (or although) and 'but' do the work of setting one statement against another by way of oppositions or contrast and therefore, the correlative of 'though' is 'yet' or a comma (,). e.g. - Though he worked hard yet he could not top the class.
  • 6. After the adjective 'other' (which is regarded as a kind of comparative), the only word that can be correctly used for contrasting one thing with another is 'than'. The prepositions from, but, except in such a connection are wrong. e.g. - He had no other option than to fight.
  • 7. Conjunction 'that' is not used in the following cases: (a) Direct narration. (b) Indirect speech, if the sentence is interrogative.
  • 8. In a 'not only......but also' sentence, the verb should agree with the noun or pronoun mentioned second, because this is the part being emphasised.
  • 9. 'Such as' is used to denote a category, whereas 'such that' emphasises the degree of something by mentioning its consequences.
  • 10. 'Both' is followed by and not by as well as. Besides, both has positive sense and cannot be used in negative sentences.
  • 11. 'Unless' means if not and therefore, it should not be used in a sentence or clause which is already negative.
  • 12. 'Lest' expresses a negative sense and therefore cannot be used with not. 'Should' is always used with 'lest'.
  • 13. When 'suppose' is used in the beginning of a sentence to denote a command or a request, it is not followed by if.
  • 14. Avoid the error of using 'than' for 'from' after the adjective different.
  • 15. 'Nothing else' should be followed by but, not by than.
  • 16. The use of Present tense after as if and as though should be avoided. [Subjunctive Mood].

subject: English
text:
Preposition is a word that connects a noun, pronoun to another word, especially to a verb, another noun or an adjective.

  • In: Used for bigger places (towns, cities, countries) while 'at' is used for smaller places. e.g., I live at Shastri Nagar in Meerut.
  • In / Into: 'In' is used in speaking of things at rest. 'Into' is used in speaking of things in motion. e.g., He is shopping in the market; He jumped into the well; He is falling in love; He is in the office; The snake crawled into the hole; The cup broke-off into a hundred pieces.
  • On / Upon: 'On' denotes position, 'upon' denotes movement. e.g., The cat is on the table; The cat pounced upon the mouse.
  • With / By: 'With' denotes the 'instrument' and 'by' denotes the 'agent'. e.g., The letter was written by him with his pen; The music was generated by/with a guitar; The murder was committed by him with a pistol; The ball was hit by the batsman with his bat.
  • Ago / Before: 'Ago' refers to past time while 'before' denotes precedence between two events. e.g., Long ago, there was a king named Rama; Ram existed before Mahabharata was fought; He came before me; The train arrived before the scheduled time; India achieved independence 69 years ago.
  • Above / Below / Over / Under: 'Above' and 'below' merely denote position while 'over' and 'under' also carry a sense of covering or movement. e.g., We live below the roof; Sky is above us; Train is running under the bridge; The train is standing below the bridge; The bird is flying over the pond; A wire is passing above the building; I was wearing two sweaters under the jacket.
  • Under: Used before a noun to indicate that a person or thing is being affected by something or is going through a particular process. e.g., I'm rarely under pressure and my co-workers are always nice to me. Can also mean junior in ranks, e.g., He is under me. If something happens 'under' a particular person or government, it happens when that person or government is in power. e.g., There will be no new taxes under his leadership.

subject: English
text:
Rules for correct usage of prepositions and verbs:

  • Under vs Beneath: 'Under' is used for a particular name. 'Beneath' is used for abstract meanings.
  • Time Expressions: 'On time' (right time), 'In time' (not late), 'In good time' (comfortable margin).
  • Beginning/End: 'At the beginning/end' refers to literal points. 'In the beginning' implies early stage/change. 'In the end' implies eventually.
  • Verb Constraints: No preposition is used after verbs like: Order, request, reach, attack, resemble, emphasise, accompany, discuss, investigate, comprise, enter, flee, join, affect, board.
  • Verbs of Communication: Omit 'to' after advise, tell, ask, beg, command, encourage, request, inform, order.
  • Till vs Until: 'Till' is for time, 'until' for indefinite time. 'Until' is used at the start of a sentence.
  • Prepositional Pairs: Do not use the same preposition for two words if they require different ones (e.g., 'different from' and 'inferior to').
  • Since vs From: 'Since' is used for a point of time (perfect tense), 'from' is used for other tenses.
  • Time Phrases: Use 'in' for morning, afternoon, evening. Use 'at' for dawn, daybreak, noon, midday, midnight. No preposition is used if qualified by 'last' or 'next'.
  • Across vs Through: 'Across' a road, 'through' a tunnel.

details.summary: Grammar rules focusing on common prepositional errors and verb usage in English.

subject: English
text:
17. Between/Among: 'Between' is used while referring to two persons/things whereas 'Among' is used for more than two.

  • e.g. - Between the two of you, who is stronger?
  • e.g. - The sweets are to be distributed among ten friends.

18. Beside/Besides: 'Beside' means by the side of, whereas 'Besides' means in addition to.

  • e.g. - Besides eating, he is also watching T.V.
  • e.g. - You were sitting beside him.

19. From/Between: 'From' is normally used with to/till, whereas 'Between' is used with and.

  • e.g. - He works from nine to six (or nine till six).
  • e.g. - The meeting was scheduled to be held between 2 pm and 3 pm.

20. Within/In: 'Within' means before the end of time, whereas 'In' means at the end of time.

  • e.g. - He will return in five minutes.
  • e.g. - He will return within five minutes.

subject: English
text:
This section provides explanations for common errors in English grammar based on CDS exam patterns.

  • One of the: Takes a plural noun (e.g., 'bad habits').
  • Scenery/Furniture/Luggage: These words are always used in a singular form.
  • Mob: Refers to a group of people with one common thought of criminal consequence.
  • Collective Nouns: 'Bouquet' is used for flowers, 'bunch' for grapes.
  • Pluralization: 'Brother-in-law' becomes 'brothers-in-law'.
  • Pronoun Agreement: Ensure pronouns match the number and gender of the antecedent (e.g., 'One of them' takes 'his', not 'their').

subject: English
text:
This page provides explanations for spotting errors in English sentences. Key grammatical corrections include:

  • Tense usage: Use of past perfect for prior events (e.g., 99, 107, 116).
  • Subject-Verb Agreement: Singular verbs for collective nouns like 'news' (109) and plural verbs after 'one of' (125).
  • Prepositions: Correct usage of 'adhere to' (128), 'sympathise with' (132), and 'cope with' (110).
  • Superfluous words: Removing redundant words like 'not' with 'lest' (104) and 'even' (117).
  • Idiomatic usage: 'On foot' instead of 'by foot' (91), 'hundred rupee notes' (92).

subject: English
text:
Grammar Correction Rules:

  • 141: 'Sceneries' is incorrect; 'scenery' is always used in the singular.
  • 142: Use 'Utmost' instead of 'primary' when referring to importance.
  • 144: Use 'we had driven for miles' instead of 'we were driving for miles'.
  • 145: Use 'but' instead of 'and' for contradictory statements.
  • 146: Use 'and' instead of 'or' when combining actions that happen together.
  • 147: Use 'for' instead of 'since' when defining a specific time period.
  • 148: Use 'besides' instead of 'beside' (beside means 'next to', besides means 'except for' or 'in addition to').
  • 149: Use 'the better' instead of 'the best' when comparing two objects.
  • 150: Use 'is' instead of 'are' when connecting two subjects with 'either or', as the verb depends on the nearer subject.
  • 151: Use 'those who accept it' instead of 'Whomever must accept it'; 'must' indicates compulsion.
  • 152: Use 'you' for being more organised; comparative degree is required.
  • 153: Use 'hard' instead of 'hardly' to convey the correct meaning.
  • 154: Use 'who' instead of 'whom'; 'who' is nominative case, 'whom' is objective.
  • 155: Use 'looked after' instead of 'looked after for'.
  • 156: Use 'would' instead of 'will' in past tense sentences.
  • 157: 'All' should precede 'their'.
  • 158: Remove 'The' before 'temper' as it is an abstract noun.
  • 159: Use 'To that of his house' (Case of Attribute) when not followed by a preposition.
  • 160: Remove 'Of' after 'despite'.
  • 161: Use 'would' instead of 'will' when the reporting verb is in past tense.
  • 162: Remove 'Shall' when the condition is in present and the result is in future.
  • 163: Use 'Supports' instead of 'support' for the subjective case (singular).
  • 164: Use article 'a' before 'school teacher' as a countable noun.
  • 165: Use 'smoking' (gerund) instead of 'to smoke' (infinitive).
  • 166: Remove 'It' from the sentence.
  • 167: Use 'agree' instead of 'Agreeing'.

subject: English
text:
Vocabulary comprises one of the most scoring sections in the CDS exam. A sound vocabulary is essential for cracking questions based on synonyms and antonyms.

Steps to enrich vocabulary:

  • Step I: Identify the Word - Look up the meaning of new words encountered in textbooks, newspapers, or magazines using a dictionary. Example: 'Antique' means 'old and often valuable'.
  • Step II: Identify the Antonyms of that Word - Consider words with opposite meanings. Example: The opposite of 'Antique' is 'modern'.
  • Step III: Identify the Synonyms of that Word - Learn words similar or closer in meaning to enhance language proficiency. Example: 'Antique' can be replaced by 'Traditional' or 'Ancient'.
  • Step IV: Form a Proper Sentence - Use words in sentences to stimulate memory and ensure clarity. Example: 'People love to purchase antique items.'

details.summary: This section introduces the importance of vocabulary for the CDS examination and outlines a four-step methodology for building vocabulary skills: identifying words, finding antonyms, finding synonyms, and forming sentences.

subject: English
text:
• Aback: Taken by surprise. Synonyms: Surprised, thrown off guard. Antonyms: Relax, Contended. Example: Everyone was taken aback by Sachin's decision to quit.
  • Abandon: To leave something and never return to it. Synonyms: Desert, Leave. Antonyms: Continue, Carry on. Example: Railways has abandoned their outer signal.
  • Abase: To humiliate. Synonyms: Degrade, Disregard, Dishonour. Antonyms: Regard, Honour, Respect. Example: Abasing someone is immoral.
  • Abashed: Make someone feel embarrassed or ashamed. Synonyms: Embarrass, Humiliate. Antonyms: Unabashed, Undaunted. Example: He is abashed of his own mistakes.
  • Abate: To make or become less strong. Synonyms: Weaken, Lessen. Antonyms: Strengthen, Intensify. Example: We waited for the wind to abate.
  • Abbreviate: To shorten. Synonyms: To abridge, To curtail. Antonyms: Lengthen, Enhance. Example: The voluminous book was abbreviated for the convenience of the students.
  • Abdicate: To give up power. Synonyms: Relinquish, Renounce. Antonyms: Accept. Example: The old king abdicated the throne.
  • Aberrant: straying from the right or normal way. Synonyms: Deviant, atypical. Antonyms: Normal, Usual. Example: Aberrant behaviour can be a sign of rabies in an animal.
  • Abet: To encourage someone to do wrong. Synonyms: Assist, Incite, Encourage. Antonyms: Demotivate, Prevent. Example: She abetted the thief in the robbery.
  • Abeyance: A state of not happening or being used at present. Synonyms: Abandon, Suspension, Discontinuation. Antonyms: Continuation, Resumption. Example: The old generator has been in abeyance for six months.
  • Abhor: To feel hatred or dislike. Synonyms: Detest, Loathe. Antonyms: Like, Admire. Example: The world would be like heaven if all the people abhor none.
  • Abide: To accept something in accordance with. Synonyms: Obey, follow. Antonyms: Flout, Reject. Example: Citizens have to abide by the rules.
  • Abnegate: To give-up; renunciation. Synonyms: Discard, Reject. Antonym: Accept. Example: Abnegating superstitions is advantageous.
  • Abound: To exist in large numbers or amounts. Synonyms: Plenty, Suffice. Antonyms: Scarce, Scanty. Example: Kiwis abound in New Zealand.
  • Abrasive: Showing little concern for feeling of others. Synonyms: Rude, Annoying, Unfriendly. Antonyms: Pleasant, Friendly. Example: Abrasive behaviour of employees may prove harmful to a firm.
  • Abrogate: To end a law, agreement or custom formally. Synonyms: Abandon, Abort. Antonyms: Institute, Introduce. Example: Our country should abrogate outdated laws.
  • Abstain: Withhold or Refrain. Synonyms: Avoid, Cease. Antonyms: Do, Continue. Example: It is worth while to abstain from intoxicants.
  • Abstruse: Difficult to understand, obscure. Synonyms: Esoteric, Perplexing. Antonyms: Clear, Obvious. Example: You are not the only one who finds Enstein's theory abstruse.
  • Absurd: Ridiculous, Unreasonable. Synonyms: Foolish, Ridiculous. Antonyms: Reasonable, Genuine. Example: Political parties indulge in absurd arguments before the election.
  • Abut: To border upon. Synonyms: Adjoin, Lie next to, Adjacent. Antonyms: Far, Opposite. Example: Our land abuts a nature preserve.
  • Abysmal: extremely poor or bad. Synonyms: Awful, Terrible. Antonyms: Good, Pleasant. Example: The quality of her work is abysmal.
  • Accede: To agree. Synonyms: Consent, Acceptance. Antonyms: Disagree, Refusal, Denial. Example: The business contract between the two parties was acceded successfully.
  • Accentuate: To emphasise or to make noticeable. Synonyms: Highlight, Hype. Antonyms: Shadowed, Downtrodden. Example: People often shout to accentuate their opinion.
  • Accessible: Easy to obtain, approachable. Synonyms: Achievable, Acquiresome. Antonyms: Remote, Distant. Example: Everything is accessible with the Internet.
  • Accessory: A thing which can be added to something else in order to make it more useful, versatile or attractive. Synonyms: Adornment, Retrofit. Antonym: Subsidiary. Example: Cellular phones are incomplete without the accessories.
  • Acclaim: Public approval and praise. Synonyms: Praise, Applaud, Cheer. Antonyms: Criticise. Example: Sardar Patel was an acclaimed leader.
  • Accolade: An award or an expression of praise. Synonyms: Appreciation, Honour, Award. Antonym: Criticism. Example: Getting success is a great accolade.

details.summary: A comprehensive list of vocabulary words starting with the letter 'A', including synonyms, antonyms, and usage examples for each.

subject: English
text:
• Accord: Be harmonious or consistent. Synonyms: Concord, Agreement. Antonyms: Disagree, Contrast. Example: The board of directors could not reach an accord in the annual meeting.
  • Accost: Approach and address angrily or aggressively. Synonyms: Annoy, Confront. Antonyms: Aid, Help. Example: On the mistake of the son, father accosted him.
  • Accrue: To increase in number or amount. Synonyms: To collect, To accumulate. Antonyms: Disperse, Dwindle. Example: Crossing for a single run accrued the score of the team.
  • Adept: Skilful. Synonyms: Expert, Efficient. Antonyms: Unskilled, Inapt. Example: It seems that he is adept in computers.
  • Adjourn: Temporary breaking-off. Synonyms: Suspend, Interrupt. Antonyms: Carry out, Advance. Example: He has adjourned his journey. The court is adjourned for the day.
  • Adjunct: Something joined or added to another thing but is not an essential part of it. Synonyms: Supplement, Addition. Antonyms: Subtraction, Lessening. Example: The witness of the case has adjuncted a new twist in it.
  • Adjure: To urge solemnly. Synonym: Request. Antonym: Answer. Example: On the continuous adjuring of students, a picnic was arranged.
  • Admonish: To warn. Synonyms: Scold, Reprove. Antonyms: Allow, Compliment. Example: The teacher admonished the student for his insolent behaviour.
  • Adorn: Make more beautiful or attractive. Synonyms: To embellish, To decorate. Antonyms: Malign, Deface. Example: The temple is adorned with flowers.
  • Adroit: Very skilful. Synonyms: Expert, Proficient. Antonyms: Unskilled, Incompetent. Example: The showroom needs an adroit mechanic.
  • Afflict: Affect adversely. Synonyms: Suffer, Bother. Antonyms: Comfort, Aid. Example: The flood has greatly afflicted the crops in this village.
  • Affluence: Having a lot of money. Synonyms: Wealth, Prosperity. Antonyms: Scarcity, Poverty. Example: Generally, affluent fathers have spoilt kids.
  • Affront: An action or remark that causes outrage or offence. Synonyms: Insult, Offence. Antonyms: Honour, Compliment. Example: Poor dressing sense often causes affront.
  • Aggrandize: Increase power, status or wealth of. Synonyms: Exalt, Boost. Antonyms: Abase, Degrade. Example: Its a movie that aggrandizes the bad guys.
  • Aggravate: To make a problem worse. Synonyms: Worsen, Compound. Antonyms: Soothe, Calm. Example: The symptoms were aggravated by drinking alcohol.
  • Agog: very eager or curious to hear or see something. Synonyms: Eager, Impatient. Antonyms: Reluctant, Uninterested. Example: He was all agog on hearing the news of his promotion.
  • Altercation: A noisy argument or disagreement, especially in public. Synonyms: Quarrel, Bickering. Antonyms: Agreement, Harmony. Example: A general political talk should not lead to an altercation.
  • Altruism: Disinterested and selfless concern for the well-being of others. Synonyms: Benevolence, Humanitarianism. Antonyms: Greediness, Meanness. Example: Mother Teresa is known for her altruism.
  • Amalgamate: To combine to form a larger group. Synonyms: To merge, Combine. Antonyms: Separate, Disjoin. Example: Hutchison and Essar group amalgamated to form Hutchison-Essar.
  • Ambiguous: Open to more than one interpretation, not having one obvious meaning. Synonyms: Unclear, Confusing. Antonyms: Clear, Obvious. Example: Ambiguous answers must be removed.
  • Ameliorate: Making a situation better, less painful. Synonyms: Mitigate, Improve. Antonyms: Worsen, Aggravate. Example: Government grant is ameliorating the situation in the territory.
  • Amenable: Open and responsive to suggestions. Synonyms: Compliant, Manageable, Persuadable. Antonyms: Stubborn, Rigid, Non-compliant. Example: A better way to resolve the problems is being amenable.
  • Amicable: Friendly behaviour of a person. Synonyms: Friendly, Good-natured. Antonyms: Unfriendly, Hostile. Example: Noble people are always amicable.
  • Annul: To make something legally void. Synonyms: Cancel, Abolish, Invalidate. Antonyms: Accept, Validate. Example: The contract was annulled by the second party.
  • Anomaly: Deviation from the standard. Synonyms: Oddity, Peculiarity. Antonyms: Conformity, Normality. Example: We do not publish cheap quality books as it is an anomaly to our policy.

details.summary: A comprehensive list of English vocabulary words starting with 'A', including definitions, synonyms, antonyms, and usage examples.

subject: English
text:
• Antagonism: A strong feeling of dislike or hatred. Synonyms: Hate, Prejudice. Antonyms: Love, Affection. Example: Man cannot be an antagonist as he has to live in the society.
  • Antipathy: A strong feeling of dislike. Synonyms: Aversion, Dislike. Antonyms: Affinity, Cordiality. Example: Pakistan's antipathy is open to India.
  • Antithesis: The direct or exact opposite. Synonyms: Counterpart, Converse. Antonyms: Same. Example: It seems that he has decided to be in antithesis of my opinion.
  • Aphorism: A short, wise and true statement. Synonyms: Adage, Maxim. Antonyms: Nonsense, Absurdity. Example: Honesty is the best policy is a very practical aphorism.
  • Aplomb: Confidence and style. Synonyms: Assurance, Poise. Antonyms: Gaucheness, Discomposure. Example: Continuous failure had a great effect on his aplomb.
  • Apocryphal: Well-known but probably not true. Synonyms: Fictitious, Made-up. Antonyms: Authentic, Real. Example: Existence of God is an apocryphal fact to the people world wide.
  • Apogee: Most successful part of something. Synonyms: The top, Apex. Antonyms: Bottom, Base. Example: Romance is the apogee of a relationship.
  • Appease: to make someone pleased or less angry by giving or saying something they desire. Synonyms: To pacify, Placate. Antonyms: Annoy, Irritate. Example: His appeasing behaviour is always appreciated.
  • Append: To add something to the end of a writing. Synonyms: Add, Attach. Antonyms: Disjoin, Detach. Example: It is always advisable to append the hints to a mathematical problem.
  • Apportion: To divide something among people. Synonyms: Distribute, Allocate. Antonyms: Keep, Withhold. Example: The property of the deceased man was apportioned between his two sons.
  • Babble: To talk or say something in a quick, confused, excited or silly way. Synonyms: Chatter, Bumble. Antonyms: Quiet, Sense. Example: He seems to be babbling.
  • Badger: To try to make someone do something by asking them many times. Synonyms: Pester, Bother, Torment. Antonyms: Aid, Delight. Example: The peon had to be badgered to get the form signed by the principal.
  • Baleful: Full of evil intentions, menacing. Synonyms: Destructive, Malignant. Antonyms: Good, Helping, Promising. Example: His baleful behaviour was strange.
  • Banal: Trite; something boring; ordinary and not original. Synonyms: Common place, Trite, Boring, Dull. Antonyms: Entertaining, Original. Example: I hate the places that seem banal.
  • Bane: A cause of great distress or annoyance. Synonyms: Ruin, Destruction. Antonyms: Blessing, Boon, Advantage. Example: Traffic congestion and air pollution are major banes for Delhi and Delhiites.
  • Bashful: Tending to feel uncomfortable with other people and be embarrassed easily; shy. Synonyms: Diffident, Modest, Meek, Coy, Nervous. Antonyms: Open, Confident. Example: She feels bashful in my company.
  • Berate: To criticize or scold severely. Synonyms: Lash out, Tear into, Abuse. Antonyms: Praise, Compliment. Example: Father berated his son for his mistakes.
  • Bereavement: The situation you are in when a close friend or a family member has just died. Synonyms: Death, Loss. Antonyms: Happiness. Example: Bereavement caused by my father's death is immeasurable.
  • Bestow: To give or confer honour to someone. Synonyms: Award, Give, Grant, Present. Antonyms: Deprive, Refuse, Take. Example: A lot of awards are bestowed upon him.
  • Bigotry: Intolerance towards those who hold different opinion from oneself. Synonyms: Fanaticism, Prejudice. Antonyms: Tolerance, Impartiality. Example: A deeply ingrained bigotry prevented her from even considering the arguments.
  • Bizarre: Strange and difficult to explain. Synonyms: Strange, Weird. Antonyms: Explainable, Normal. Example: The bizarre events taking place in the deserted house led the people to assume that it was haunted.
  • Blabber: Talk foolishly. Synonyms: Chatter, Babble. Antonyms: Sense. Example: Blabbering is what one can expect from fools.
  • Bohemian: A socially unconventional person, especially an artist or a writer. Synonyms: Non-conformist. Antonyms: Conformist. Example: The Bohemian attitude is considered rebellious.
  • Bolster: To support or strengthen. Synonyms: Strengthen, Reinforce. Antonyms: Discourage, Undermine. Example: More money is needed to bolster the industry.
  • Boor: A person who is rude and does not consider other people's feelings. Synonyms: Lout, Rogue. Antonyms: Civilised, Decent, Modest. Example: Terrorists are nothing but boors.

subject: English
text:
• Bovine: Relating to or affecting cattle, looking or acting like a cow. Synonyms: Cow-like, Cattle-like. Antonym: Individual. Example: She stared at us with a stupid bovine expression.
  • Brag: To speak proudly of what you have done or what you own. Synonyms: Swagger, Boast. Antonym: Be modest. Example: He was bragging about his success.
  • Brash: Showing too much confidence and too little respect. Synonyms: Arrogant, Brazen. Antonyms: Diffident, Meek. Example: A brash man has less friends.
  • Bumble: To speak or move in a confused way. Synonyms: Lurch, Stumble. Antonyms: Efficient, Expert. Example: Bumbling persons create a doubt to security.
  • Bungle: To do something badly or unsuccessfully. Synonyms: Mishandle, Mismanage. Antonym: Succeed. Example: He has bungled the whole work.
  • Buoyant: Happy and confident. Synonyms: Happy, Joyous. Antonyms: Unhappy, Sad. Example: He was very buoyant about the visit to Agra.
  • Burgeon: To grow or develop quickly. Synonyms: Expand, Swell. Antonyms: Shrink, Contract. Example: Terrorism is burgeoning across the border.
  • Burly: A large and strong person. Synonyms: Tawny, Gigantic. Antonyms: Lean, Thin. Example: There must be a burly man for the role of a demon.
  • Bustling: If a place is bustling, it is full of busy activity. Synonyms: Dashing, Scurrying. Antonyms: Quiet, Inactive, Dormant. Example: The house, usually bustling with activity, was strangely silent.
  • Cabal: A group of people who secretly work together. Synonyms: Clique, Faction. Antonym: Individual. Example: He was assassinated by a cabal of aides.
  • Cache: A hidden store of provision, weapons, treasure; to hide weapons or other things. Synonyms: Hoard, Store. Antonyms: Discard, Remove. Example: People must create a cache of medicines for emergency.
  • Cajole: To persuade someone to do something by coaxing or flattery. Synonyms: Persuade, Coax. Antonyms: Dissuade, Discourage. Example: He knows how to cajole people into doing what he wants.
  • Calamity: An event that brings terrible loss, lasting distress or severe affliction. Synonyms: Tragedy, Catastrophe. Antonyms: Blessing, Godsend. Example: The great calamity was brought to rest.
  • Callous: Showing or having an insensitive and cruel disregard for others. Synonyms: Insensitive, Unsympathetic. Antonyms: Sensitive, Sympathetic. Example: People often think that doctors are callous.
  • Calumny: A false accusation. Synonyms: Defamation, Slander. Antonyms: Eulogy, Praise. Example: He is a victim of calumny.
  • Camouflage: To disguise. Synonyms: Hide, Conceal. Antonyms: Reveal, Show. Example: The camouflaged players arrived at the airport.
  • Canard: A false, report or story. Synonyms: Tale, Story. Antonym: Truth. Example: The newspaper was sued for publishing a canard about a celebrity.
  • Canny: Very clever and able to make intelligent decisions. Synonyms: Clever, Shrewd. Antonyms: Uncooperative. Example: Rohan is a canny card player.
  • Cantankerous: Bad tempered, argumentative and uncooperative. Synonyms: Bad tempered, Uncooperative. Antonyms: Affable, Good-natured. Example: Children are by nature cantankerous.
  • Capacious: Having a lot of space. Synonyms: Spacious, Open. Antonyms: Small, Cramped. Example: A bunglow is a capacious house to live-in.
  • Cardinal: Of the greatest importance, fundamental. Synonyms: Significant, Fundamental. Antonym: Unimportant. Example: Cardinal facts of the case are hidden.
  • Careen: To go forward quickly while moving from side to side. Synonyms: Lurch, Rock. Antonyms: Crawl, Creep. Example: I saw the duck careening through the ponds.
  • Castigate: To criticise severely. Synonyms: Rebuke, Chide, Scold. Antonyms: Admire, Praise. Example: Odd behaviour of a person is a matter of castigation.
  • Catalyst: Stimulus; a person who causes change by his presence. Synonyms: Impetus, Incentive. Antonyms: Inhibitor, Preventer. Example: Birbal was a catalyst in the court of Akbar.
  • Catapult: To suddenly put someone into an important position; to propel. Synonyms: Excel, Marshal. Antonyms: To recede, Decline. Example: Someone cannot be catapulted to be the chief straight way.
  • Charismatic: Possessing spiritual grace; inspiring. Synonyms: Charming, Fascinating. Antonyms: Offensive, Frightening. Example: Modi is a charismatic leader.

subject: English
text:
• Chaste: Morally pure or decent. Synonyms: Decent, Pure. Antonyms: Impure, Indecent. Example: The chaste conduct of the austere person commands respect.
  • Cherubic: Good natured. Synonyms: Innocent, Angelic. Antonyms: Demonic, Devilish. Example: His behaviour reveals his approach to be cherubic.
  • Chide: To express mild disapproval of someone, to scold someone gently. Synonyms: Rebuke, Scold. Antonyms: Admire, Praise. Example: Mother chided the son for his rude behaviour with the guests.
  • Chronic: Happening or existing frequently or most of the time. Synonyms: Persistent, Long standing. Antonyms: Temporary, Mild. Example: She suffers from chronic pain in her knees.
  • Churlish: Rude, unfriendly and unpleasant. Synonyms: Arrogant, ill-mannered. Antonyms: Gracious, Polite. Example: Churlish behaviour is his trademark.
  • Clout: Power and influence. Synonyms: Sway, Power. Antonym: Powerless. Example: Hitler was a man of great clout.
  • Coalesce: To grow together or unite into one; to fuse. Synonyms: Fuse, Join. Antonyms: Split, Breakup. Example: The ice-masses coalesced into a glacier over time.
  • Cogent: Very clear and easy for the mind to accept and believe. Synonyms: Convincing, Compelling. Antonyms: Vague, Unconvincing. Example: His ideas were cogent and sound.
  • Conciliate: To end a disagreement or someone's anger by acting in a friendly way or to slightly change your opinion. Synonyms: Appease, Placate. Antonym: Provoke. Example: The nagging child was conciliated by the toys.
  • Concomitant: Naturally accompanying or associated with something. Synonyms: Linked, Associated. Antonyms: Disassociated, Unlinked. Example: Loss of memory is a concomitant of old age.
  • Concussion: Temporary unconsciousness or confusion caused by a blow on the head. Synonym: Violent shaking. Antonym: Consciousness. Example: The accident caused the man a severe concussion.
  • Condone: To accept behaviour that is morally wrong. Synonyms: Accept, Allow. Antonyms: Condemn, Punish. Example: Parents always condone the fault of children.
  • Contentious: Causing or likely to cause disagreement. Synonyms: Controversial, Argumentative. Antonym: Agreeable. Example: The contentious issue may obstruct the development.
  • Contort: To twist or bend out of normal shape. Synonyms: Distort, Twist. Antonyms: Straighten, Smooth. Example: He contorted the instrument by rough handling.
  • Contrive: To invent or make something in a clever or unusual way. Synonyms: Create, Manufacture. Antonyms: Destroy, Ruin. Example: The Defence Ministry contrived a plan to tackle cross border terrorism.
  • Conundrum: A confusing and difficult question or problem. Synonyms: Dilemma, Quandary. Antonym: Easy-way. Example: Competitive exams make you face conundrums.
  • Convene: To call together for a meeting or activity. Synonyms: Summon, Call. Antonyms: Disperse, Leave. Example: We convened at the hotel for a seminar.
  • Convivial: (Of an event or atmosphere) Friendly, lively and enjoyable. Synonyms: Jovial, Pleasant. Antonyms: Sad, Unhappy. Example: The President of the club arranged a convivial cocktail party.
  • Copious: Ample, producing much. Synonyms: Plentiful, Abudant. Antonyms: Scarce, Meager. Example: The storm produced a copious amount of rain.
  • Dabble: Take part in an activity in a casual way. Synonyms: Tinker, Dally, Trifle. Antonym: Take seriously. Example: Rita dabbled in many things before she got married.
  • Dainty: Small and graceful. Synonyms: Elegant, Petite. Antonyms: Crude, Ugly. Example: The house looks dainty and beautiful.
  • Dank: Unpleasantly moist and cold. Synonyms: Wet, Damp. Antonyms: Arid, Dry. Example: He shivered as he entered the dank room.
  • Deadlock: A situation involving opposing parties, in which no progress can be made; stalemate. Synonyms: Gridlock, Dilemma. Antonyms: Solution, Agreement. Example: The mediator will help the opposing parties end the deadlock so the contract can be signed.
  • Debacle: A complete failure; a crushing defeat. Synonyms: Fiasco, Failure. Antonyms: Success, Accomplishment. Example: He faced a debacle in yesterday's game.
  • Debase: To adulterate, to make poor in quality or of less value. Synonyms: Degrade, Devalue. Antonyms: Upgrade, Enhance. Example: Debased commodities are sold in the market.

subject: English
text:
• Debauch: To destroy or damage something so that it is no longer considered good or moral. Synonyms: Abase, Corrupt. Antonyms: Ennoble, Uplift. Example: Western culture has debauched the moral fabric of our society.
  • Debilitate: To make someone very weak and infirm. Synonyms: Cripple, Disable. Antonyms: Strengthen, Enable. Example: The virus debilitates the body's immune system.
  • Decadence: Having low moral standards and behaviour. Synonyms: Corruption, Debauchery. Antonyms: Ascent, Decency. Example: Decadent people are not valued.
  • Decimate: To kill a large number of (something) or to reduce very heavily. Synonyms: Annihilate, Exterminate. Antonyms: Bear, Build, Create. Example: Population of endangered animals have been decimated.
  • Decrepit: Worn out or ruined because of age or neglect. Synonyms: Dilapidated, Battered. Antonyms: Firm, Healthy. Example: The building was a decrepit sample of bricks now.
  • Defalcate: To steal or misuse funds entrusted to one. Synonyms: Embezzle, Loot, Filch. Antonyms: Appropriate, Receive. Example: Public funds are defalcated by leaders.
  • Demure: (of a woman or her behaviour) Modest; shy; reserved. Synonyms: Meek, Bashful. Antonyms: Brazen, Shameless. Example: Her demure nature gets everybody's attention.
  • Deplore: To feel or express strong condemnation of something. Synonyms: Abhor, Denounce. Antonyms: Praise, Commend. Example: Public deplored the casual steps taken by the administration for the safety of women.
  • Depravity: The state of being morally bad, or an action that is morally bad. Synonyms: Perversion, Criminality. Antonyms: Goodness, Uprightness. Example: People were shocked by the depravity of her actions.
  • Deprecate: To criticise or express disapproval of something. Synonyms: Belittle, Detract. Antonyms: Approve, Commend. Example: Everybody deprecated the death of the charitable man.
  • Deride: To laugh at someone or something in a way that shows you think they are stupid or are of no value. Synonyms: Ridicule, Mock, Disdain. Antonyms: Admire, Approve. Example: He was derided at for his strange ways.
  • Desperado: A desperate or reckless person, especially a criminal. Synonyms: Bandit, Villain. Antonym: Civilised. Example: Law must punish the desperado.
  • Despot: A ruler who has total power and often uses it in cruel and unfair ways. Synonyms: Tyrant, Oppressor. Antonym: Democrat. Example: Hitler was one of the biggest despots.
  • Desultory: Lacking a plan, purpose or enthusiasm. Synonyms: Aimless, Chaotic. Antonyms: Organised, Systematic. Example: He wandered around, cleaning up in a desultory way.
  • Detract: Dimish the worth or value of something. Synonyms: Belittle, Decrease. Antonyms: Commend, Compliment. Example: Numerous errors in the book detracted the reader's attention.
  • Devious: Showing a skilful use of underhand tactics to achieve goals. Synonyms: Unfair, Fraudulent. Antonyms: Honest, Fair. Example: The minister was a devious politician.
  • Devolve: 1. Transfer of power to a lower level. 2. Pass into a worse state; degenerate. Synonyms: Delegate, Pass on. Antonyms: Centralize, Improve. Example: In a democratic system, power is devolved to the local level.
  • Diabolic: Extremely evil. Synonyms: Cruel, Atrocious. Antonyms: Kind, Moral. Example: The police quickly mobilised to track down the diabolical serial killer.
  • Diffident: Modest or shy because of a lack of self-confidence. Synonyms: Bashful, Meek. Antonyms: Bold, Confident. Example: He is too diffident to work in a company.
  • Disapprobation: Strong disapproval, typically on moral grounds. Synonyms: Deprecation, Disapproval. Antonyms: Approval, Approbation. Example: Sherry was used to constant disapprobation of critics.
  • Disconcert: To make someone upset; unsettle. Synonyms: Perplex, Baffle, Bewilder. Antonyms: Assist, Calm. Example: The whole experience had disconcerted him.
  • Earmark: Designate funds or resources for a particular purpose, procure. Synonyms: Attribute, Designate. Antonym: Disallow. Example: The government earmarked a huge package for agriculture.
  • Ebullient: Very happy and enthusiastic; exuberant. Synonyms: Cheerful, Exuberant. Antonyms: Unhappy, Depressed. Example: The man seems to be ebullient on his success.
  • Edifice: A large impressive building; a system that has been established for a long time. Synonyms: Monument, Building. Example: The glass edifice is an architectural wonder.

subject: English
text:
• Effeminate: Womanish; Feminine, Unmanly. Synonyms: Effete, Unmanly. Antonyms: Masculine, Manly. Example: He had a high and somewhat effeminate voice.
  • Effete: Weak and Powerless. Synonyms: Unmanly, Effeminate. Antonyms: Manly, Powerful. Example: His effete body looks pale.
  • Effusive: Expressing gratitude, approval or pleasure in a way that shows very strong feeling. Synonyms: Gushing, Unrestrained. Antonyms: Restrained, Reserved. Example: The coach was effusive in praising Tendulkar.
  • Emaciated: Very thin and weak, usually because of illness or extreme hunger. Synonyms: Thin, Skeletal. Antonyms: Chubby, Fat. Example: Chronic diseases make one emaciated.
  • Embodiment: someone or something that represents a quality or an idea exactly. Synonyms: Personification, Incarnation. Antonym: Exclusion. Example: Mother Teresa was often regarded as the embodiment of selfless devotion to others.
  • Enervate: to make someone feel weak and without energy. Synonyms: Debilitate, Devitalise. Antonyms: Strengthen, Energise. Example: We were enervated by the lengthy discussion.
  • Enjoin: To instruct or urge someone to do something or behave in a particular way. Synonyms: Urge, Command, Insist. Antonyms: Obey, follow. Example: The boss enjoined the workers to do the best.
  • Ensconce: To make yourself very comfortable or safe in a place or position. Synonyms: Settle, Install. Antonyms: Unsettle, Exhibit. Example: He ensconced in his new abode there.
  • Entree: Admittance; the right to enter something. Synonyms: Entry, Ingress. Antonyms: Exit, Refusal. Example: Entree to the country club is through sponsorship.
  • Entropy: Lack of order or predictability, gradual decline into disorder. Synonyms: Break up, Collapse. Antonyms: Improvement, Order. Example: The mishandling of the situation led to entropy.
  • Ephemeral: Existing only for a short time. Synonyms: Fleeting, Transient. Antonyms: Enduring, Lasting. Example: Fame in the show business is ephemeral.
  • Epoch: A long period of time, especially one in which there are new advances and great changes. Synonyms: Era, Span, Age. Example: The development of the steam engine marked an important epoch in the history of industry.
  • Equitable: Treating everyone fairly and in the same way. Synonyms: Unbiased, Reasonable. Antonyms: Partial, Biased. Example: He is fighting for a more equitable distribution of funds.
  • Excruciating: Intensely painful. Synonyms: Acute, Agonising. Antonyms: Painless, Calm, Easy. Example: The Uttrakhand disaster was an excruciating experience for the victims.
  • Expatiate: Speak or write in detail. Synonyms: Expound, Lecture. Antonyms: Compress, Abridge. Example: It is useless to expatiate upon the beauty of nature to one who is blind.
  • Facade: The principal front of a building that faces on to a street or open space. Synonyms: Front, Elevation, Frontage. Antonyms: Rear, Back. Example: The gallery's 18th century facade attracted the visitors.
  • Facetious: Treating serious issues deliberately with inappropriate humour. Synonyms: Flippant, Frivolous. Antonyms: Serious, Formal. Example: The facetious boy was chided.
  • Facile: 1. Ignoring the true complexities of an issue; superficial. 2. A success which is easily achieved. Synonyms: Superficial, Hasty. Antonyms: Thorough, Profound. Example: This problem needs more than just a facile solution.
  • Factitious: Artificial, not natural. Synonyms: Fake, Bogus. Antonyms: Natural, Real. Example: His explanations were all factitious.
  • Fallacious: Based on a mistaken belief; misleading. Synonyms: Erroneous, False. Antonyms: Genuine, True. Example: Someone is spreading fallacious information.
  • Fastidious: Very attentive to and concerned about accuracy and details; very concerned about matters of cleanliness. Synonyms: Painstaking, Meticulous. Antonyms: Careless, Sloppy. Example: His culinary skills are fastidious.
  • Fatuous: Stupid, not correct or not carefully thought about. Synonyms: Silly, Foolish. Antonyms: Sensible, Intelligent. Example: All his reasons appeared fatuous to me.
  • Feckless: Lacking initiative or strength of character; irresponsible. Synonyms: Useless, Worthless. Antonyms: Responsible, Competent. Example: Country does not need feckless people.
  • Fecund: Very fertile. Synonyms: Fertile, Fruitful. Antonyms: Unproductive, Infertile. Example: The soil of the plains is fecund.
  • Feisty: Having or showing exuberance, strong determination and lack of fear. Synonyms: Courageous, Gutsy. Antonyms: Cowardly, Dull. Example: Mountaineering needs feisty people.

subject: English
topic: Words starting with F and G
text:
• Felicity: 1. Intense happiness 2. The ability to find appropriate expressions for one's thoughts. Synonyms: Bliss, Delight, Eloquence. Antonyms: Sorrow, Unhappiness. Example: Felicity is a bliss to be enjoyed.
  • Fester: (of a problem or negative feeling) become worse or more intense, especially through long term neglect or indifference. Synonyms: Smoulder, Aggravate. Antonyms: Flourish, Grow. Example: It is better to express your anger than let it fester inside you.
  • Fetid: Smelling extremely bad, Foul. Synonyms: Smelly, Putrid. Antonyms: Aromatic, Perfumed. Example: The carcass of the dog has made the surroundings fetid.
  • Fidelity: Honest or lasting support, Loyalty, Faithfulness. Synonyms: Loyalty, Constancy. Antonyms: Dishonesty, Infidelity. Example: Friendship survives on fidelity.
  • Fiend: 1. Cruel, inhuman 2. An enthusiast or devotee of a particular thing. Synonyms: Barbarian, Ogre. Antonyms: Angel, God. Example: His hands were trembling as if he was some sort of fiend.
  • Flack: Strong criticism or opposition. Synonyms: Criticism, Censure. Antonyms: Appraisal, Praise. Example: Dowry should be a matter of flack.
  • Flagrant: Too bad to be ignored. Synonyms: Heinous, Shameless. Antonyms: Magnificent, Wonderful. Example: The killing of innocent villagers is an example of flagrant ways of Maoists.
  • Foment: To cause trouble to develop. Synonyms: Incite, Instigate. Antonyms: Deter, Discourage. Example: He was accused of fomenting violence.
  • Fortitude: Courage in pain or adversity. Synonyms: Courage, Bravery. Antonyms: Cowardice, Fear. Example: Fortitude makes you a winner.
  • Frenzied: Madly excited or uncontrolled. Synonyms: Wild, Frantic. Antonyms: Controlled, Calm. Example: The office was a scene of frenzied activity this morning.
  • Gainsay: To deny or contradict a fact or statement. Synonyms: Dispute, Oppose. Antonyms: Accept, Confirm. Example: There is no gainsaying the fact that they have built a great building.
  • Gall: Bold and impudent behaviour. Synonyms: Impudence, Insolence. Antonyms: Cordiality, Politeness. Example: After borrowing my car, he had the gall to complain about its seats.
  • Gallant: 1. Brave; heroic 2. (of a man) polite and kind towards woman. Synonyms: Valiant, Unafraid. Antonyms: Timid, Rude. Example: Although she lost, she made a gallant effort.
  • Garble: To make words or messages unclear and difficult to understand. Synonyms: Muddle, Jumble. Antonyms: Obvious, Clear. Example: The terrified child gave a garbled account of the incident to the police.
  • Garish: Too bright or colourful. Synonyms: Gaudy; Bright. Antonyms: Dull, Unflashy. Example: The decoration looked garish.
  • Gauche: Awkward and uncomfortable with other people, specially because young and lacking in experience. Synonyms: Awkward, Gawky. Antonyms: Elegant, Sophisticated. Example: She had grown from a gauche teenager to a self assured young woman.
  • Genial: Friendly and cheerful. Synonyms: Affable, Cordial. Antonyms: Hostile, Unfriendly. Example: His genial outpour surprised me.
  • Ghastly: Unpleasant and shocking. Synonyms: Terrible, Horrible. Antonyms: Pleasant, Charming. Example: The scene of the crime looks ghastly.
  • Giddy: Having a sensation of whirling and a tendency to fall or stagger. Synonyms: Dizzy, Light-headed. Antonyms: Steady, Sensible. Example: He was walking giddily.
  • Gingerly: In a careful or cautious manner. Synonyms: Warily, Cautiously. Antonyms: Carelessly, Rashly. Example: He did the work gingerly.
  • Gratify: To please someone or to satisfy a wish or need. Synonyms: Please, Gladden. Antonyms: Dissatisfy, Displease. Example: I am gratified by his words.
  • Grimace: To make an expression of pain, strong dislike, etc in which the face twists in an ugly way. Synonyms: Scowl, Frown. Antonyms: Smile. Example: After falling down, he started to stand up grimacing with pain.
  • Grisly: Causing horror or disgust. Synonyms: Gruesome, Ghastly. Antonyms: Pleasant, Attractive. Example: The grisly figure made the child cry.
  • Grubby: Covered with dirt. Synonyms: Filthy, Mucky, Grimy. Antonyms: Clean, Tidy. Example: One must clean off grubby hands before eating.
  • Gruff: (person's voice) Low and unfriendly. Synonyms: Rough, Hoarse. Antonyms: Soft, Mellow. Example: He speaks in a gruff way, but is really kind.

subject: English
topic: Words starting with H and I
text:
• Habituated: Used to something, especially something unpleasant. Synonyms: Accustom, Adapt. Antonyms: Avoid, Shun. Example: Bears can become habituated to people easily.
  • Haggard: Looking exhausted or unwell, especially from fatigue, worry or suffering. Synonyms: Drained, Tired. Antonyms: Fresh, Healthy. Example: The athletes looked haggard after the race.
  • Haggle: Dispute or bargain persistently. Synonyms: Barter, Negotiate. Antonyms: Concur, Comply. Example: Customers often haggle with the seller.
  • Hallowed: Very respected and praised because of great importance or great age. Synonyms: Holy, Sacred. Antonyms: Cursed, Unholy. Example: The site of the ancient temple is a hallowed ground.
  • Hapless: Having no luck; very unfortunate. Synonyms: Unlucky, Ill-fated. Antonyms: Fortunate, Lucky. Example: She plays the hapless heroine who is unlucky in love.
  • Harrowing: Extremely upsetting because connected with suffering. Synonyms: Tortuous, Painful. Antonyms: Calming, Comforting. Example: The harrowing news reached the village.
  • Headstrong: Very determined to do what one wants without listening to others. Synonyms: Wilful, Strong-willed. Antonyms: Undetermined, Tractable. Example: Being headstrong by nature, he did not listen to his wife's advice.
  • Heady: Having a strong exhilarating effect. Synonyms: Exciting, Thrilling. Antonyms: Boring, Dull. Example: The party seems heady today.
  • Hector: Talk to someone in a bullying way. Synonyms: Intimidate, Badger. Antonyms: Please, Assist. Example: The senior guy was hectoring the junior.
  • Heedless: Not giving attention to a risk or possible difficulty. Synonyms: Inattentive, Oblivious. Antonyms: Needful, Attentive. Example: He was driving heedlessly.
  • Heinous: Outrageously evil; horrifying. Synonyms: Wicked, Atrocious. Antonyms: Admirable, Delightful. Example: The man is facing charges over his heinous act.
  • Herald: To be a sign of something that is going to come or happen soon. Synonyms: Indicator, Sign. Antonyms: Aforeseen. Example: The early flowers are heralds of spring.
  • Horrendous: Shocking; horrible. Synonyms: Dreadful, Alarming. Antonyms: Pleasing, Wonderful. Example: Conditions in the refugee camps were horrendous.
  • Humane: Having or showing compassion. Synonyms: Compassionate, Kind. Antonyms: Unkind, Inhumane. Example: It is not humane to treat animals cruelly.
  • Hypothetical: Based on a situation that is not real, but that might happen. Synonyms: Imaginary, Theoretical. Antonyms: Real, Actual. Example: She described a hypothetical case to clarify her point.
  • Idolatry: Very great admiration or respect for someone, often too great. Synonyms: Reverence, Adoration. Antonyms: Vilification, Condemnation. Example: Newton was revered to the point of idolatry.
  • Impertinent: Rude and not showing respect towards someone older or in a higher position than you. Synonyms: Disrespectful, Rude. Antonyms: Polite, Mannered. Example: Its impertinent to ask strangers about their private lives.
  • Implausible: Not believable or realistic. Synonyms: Unbelievable, Doubtful. Antonyms: Reasonable, Convincing. Example: She's been making implausible claims.
  • Impolitic: Unwise words or actions that are likely to cause offence or problems. Synonyms: Unwise, Imprudent. Antonyms: Wise, Prudent. Example: I thought it impolitic to ask any question about her ex.
  • Improvident: Not giving thought to the future. Synonyms: Heedless, Inconsiderate. Antonyms: Provident, Farsighted. Example: He is improvident about his career.
  • Inalienable: Not subject to being taken away or given by the possessor. Synonyms: Absolute, Inviolable. Antonyms: Changeable, Alienable. Example: The group of women wanted equal inalienable rights as men.
  • Incorrigible: Beyond correction or change. Synonyms: Hardened, Hopeless. Antonyms: Correctable, Changeable. Example: She is an incorrigible chatterbox.
  • Incredulous: Not able or willing to believe something. Synonyms: Mistrustful, Doubtful. Antonyms: Believing, Credulous. Example: Everyone laughed the incredulous stories of the old man.
  • Indigent: Very poor. Synonyms: Penniless, Destitute. Antonyms: Rich, Affluent. Example: The heavy losses he incurred in business rendered him indigent.

subject: English
text:
• Infallible: Incapable of making mistakes or being wrong. Synonyms: Unerring, Flawless. Antonyms: Fallible, Erring. Example: I never claimed to be infallible.
  • Inimical: Harmful or limiting. Synonyms: Injurious, Harmful. Antonyms: Helpful, Advantageous. Example: A person with inimical behaviour is dangerous.
  • Iniquitous: Very unfair or evil. Synonyms: Wicked, Sinful. Antonyms: Good, Virtuous. Example: This decision seems iniquitous.
  • Innate: (of a quality) which you are born with or which is present naturally. Synonyms: Inborn, Ingrained. Antonyms: Acquired, Extrinsic. Example: He is a person with innate wisdom.
  • Insipid: Lacking flavour; weak or tasteless. Synonyms: Bland, Tasteless. Antonyms: Tasty, Delicious. Example: The dinner was insipid.
  • Jabber: Talk in a rapid, excited and often incomprehensible way. Synonyms: Prattle, Babble. Antonyms: Be silent, Speak clearly. Example: The train was full of people jabbering into their mobile phones.
  • Jaded: Not having interest or losing interest as you have experienced something too many times. Synonyms: Bored, Tired. Antonyms: Fresh, Activated. Example: Flying is exciting the first time you do it, but you soon become jaded.
  • Jaunty: Lively in manner or appearance. Synonyms: Merry, Cheerful. Antonyms: Unhappy, Depressed. Example: Success makes a person jaunty.
  • Jinx: Bad luck or a person or thing that brings bad luck. Synonyms: Misfortune, Curse. Antonyms: Good luck, Boon. Example: His luck has been so bad he feels jinxed.
  • Jocular: Funny or intended to make someone laugh. Synonyms: Funny, Humorous. Antonyms: Serious, Depressed. Example: Someone made a jocular remark to entertain the gathering.
  • Kaput: Broken; not working properly. Synonyms: Faulty, Broken. Antonyms: Operational. Example: My fridge has gone kaput.
  • Ken: A person's range of knowledge or understanding. Synonyms: Knowledge, Awareness. Antonyms: Ignorance. Example: Politics are beyond my ken.
  • Kernel: The central or most important part of something. Synonyms: Essence, Core. Antonyms: Exterior, Periphery. Example: We are to write the kernel of the story.
  • Kindle: Arouse or inspire (an emotion or feeling). Synonyms: Arouse, Rouse, Wake. Antonyms: Douse, Put out. Example: The trip kindled an interest in travel.
  • Knave: A dishonest man. Synonyms: Fraud, Cheat. Antonyms: Honest. Example: A knave cheated me on the bus.
  • Labile: Changing often or easily. Synonyms: Adaptable, Reactive. Antonyms: Balanced, Unreactive. Example: Our culture is the most labile of all.
  • Laborious: Tedious; needing a lot of time and effort. Synonyms: Tough, Arduous. Antonyms: Simple, Easy. Example: The project needs laborious people.
  • Lackadaisical: Lacking enthusiasm and determination. Synonyms: Lazy, Unenthusiastic. Antonyms: Enthusiastic, Excited. Example: Efforts from the man seem lackadaisical.
  • Laggard: A person who makes slow progress and lags behind others. Synonyms: Loiterer, Lingerer. Antonym: Leader. Example: A laggard can't win the race of life.
  • Lambaste: To criticise severely. Synonyms: Chastise, Castigate. Antonyms: Praise, Compliment. Example: His work was lambasted by everyone.
  • Languid: Showing or having very little strength, energy or activity. Synonyms: Enervated, Unenergetic. Antonyms: Energetic, Active. Example: He looked languid after a sleepless night.
  • Lassitude: A state of physical or mental weariness. Synonyms: Fatigue, Lethargy. Antonyms: Freshness, Vigour, Energy. Example: Symptoms of the disease include paleness and lassitude.
  • Leery: Cautious or wary due to realistic suspicions. Synonym: Careful. Antonym: Careless. Example: They were leery of their neighbours.
  • Leviathan: Extremely large and powerful. Synonyms: Titan, Huge. Antonyms: Powerless, Tiny. Example: Shakespeare is the leviathan of English literature.
  • Limber: (of a person or body part) Able to bend and move easily and smoothly. Synonyms: Flexible, Nimble. Antonyms: Rigid, Stiff. Example: His whole body is a limber of muscles.
  • Limpid: Clearly expressed and easily understood. Synonyms: Lucid, Clear. Antonyms: Unclear, Unintelligible. Example: The situation is a limpid one to get through.

subject: English
text:
• Livid: Extremely angry. Synonyms: Infuriated, Irate. Antonyms: Calm, Peaceful. Example: The boss was livid when yet another deadline was missed.
  • Macabre: Horrible, because concerned with death. Synonyms: Shocking, Gruesome. Antonyms: Pleasant, Pleasing. Example: Even the police were horrified at the macabre nature of the killings.
  • Magnanimous: Generous or forgiving. Synonyms: Benevolent, Charitable. Antonyms: Selfish, Mean-spirited. Example: The king was magnanimous towards his subjects.
  • Magnate: Successful businessman; tycoon. Synonyms: Tycoon, Mogul. Antonyms: Pawn, Nobody. Example: Ratan Tata is a business magnate.
  • Maladroit: Awkward in movement or unskilled in behaviour or action. Synonyms: Bumbling, Awkward. Antonyms: Adroit, Skilful. Example: She can be a little maladroit in social situations.
  • Malodorous: Stinking; foul-smelling. Synonyms: Noxious, Fetid. Antonyms: Aromatic, Fragrant. Example: The malodorous drain is a problem for the locality.
  • Maverick: An unorthodox or independent minded person. Synonyms: Non-conformist, Dissenter. Antonyms: Orthodox, Conformist. Example: He was considered as something of a maverick in the publishing word.
  • Mellifluous: Pleasingly smooth and musical to hear. Synonyms: Harmonious, Mellow. Antonyms: Noisy, Cacophonous. Example: She has a rich and mellifluous voice.
  • Mendacious: Not truthful; lying. Synonyms: Deceitful, Dishonest. Antonyms: Truthful, Honest. Example: All his statements are mendacious.
  • Miffed: Annoyed at someone's behaviour towards you. Synonyms: Irritated, Angry. Antonyms: Pleased. Example: The miffed employees called up a strike.
  • Minatory: Expressing or conveying a threat. Synonyms: Aggressive, Threatening. Antonyms: Unthreatening. Example: The minatory situation is under control.
  • Minuscule: Extremely small. Synonyms: Tiny, Minute. Antonyms: Huge, Vast. Example: The minuscule insects are hidden there in the bush.
  • Modicum: A small amount, especially of something good. Synonyms: Particle, Speck. Antonyms: Lot, Entirety. Example: Only a modicum of skill is necessary to put the pieces together.
  • Modish: Fashionable. Synonym: Stylish. Antonym: Traditional. Example: The showroom contains a lot of modish clothes.
  • Mollify: To make someone less angry. Synonyms: Appease, Placate. Antonyms: Enrage, Agitate. Example: All attempts to mollify the extremists have failed.
  • Moor: Wasteland. Synonyms: Upland. Antonyms: Cropland. Example: Government has decided to gentrify the moor.
  • Nadir: The worst or lowest point of something. Synonyms: Rock-bottom, Base. Antonyms: Zenith, Apex. Example: He is at the nadir on this matter.
  • Nebulous: (especially of ideas) not clear and having no form. Synonyms: Ambiguous, Vague. Antonyms: Clear, Certain. Example: These philosophical concepts can be nebulous.
  • Nefarious: (especially of activities) morally bad. Synonyms: Heinous, Odious. Antonyms: Delightful, Gentle. Example: The man was found to be involved in nefarious activities.
  • Nettle: To annoy or irritate someone. Synonyms: Irritate, Irk. Antonyms: To please, Calm. Example: His continuous questions nettled him.
  • Niggardly: ungenerous with money, time etc; mean. Synonyms: Mean, Miserly. Antonyms: Generous, Abundant. Example: Rita is a niggardly woman, so don't expect a handout from her.
  • Nihilism: The belief that traditional morals, ideas, beliefs have no worth or value. Synonyms: Negativity, Cynicism. Antonyms: Allowance, Approval. Example: Young generation shows a great deal of nihilistic traditions.
  • Non-plussed: So surprised and confused that one is unsure how to react. Synonyms: Astonish, Astound. Antonyms: Calm, Comfort. Example: I can't say why he was non-plussed at my arrival.
  • Obdurate: Not willing to change your opinion or the way you do something. Synonyms: Adamant, Hardened. Antonyms: Amenable, Submissive. Example: He is known for his obdurate determination.
  • Obfuscate: To make something more difficult to understand. Synonyms: Obscure, Confuse. Antonyms: Clarify, Enlighten. Example: This explanation has obfuscated everybody.

subject: English
text:
• Obliterate: To destroy completely; To remove a thought, feeling or memory from someone's mind. Synonyms: Demolish, Annihilate. Antonyms: Create, Establish. Example: An explosion obliterated the new building.
  • Obnoxious: Very unpleasant or rude. Synonyms: Repulsive, Offensive, Disgusting. Antonyms: Agreeable, Decent. Example: When she's in a bad mood she is obnoxious to everyone.
  • Obstinate: Unreasonably determined; stubborn. Synonyms: Adamant, Inflexible. Antonyms: Flexible, Amenable. Example: He can be very obstinate at times.
  • Obstreperous: Difficult to deal with and noisy. Synonyms: Unruly, Boisterous. Antonyms: Pacified, Tractable. Example: The executive refused to help the obstreperous clientele.
  • Obverse: Opposite or counterpart of a fact or truth. Synonyms: Complement, Counterpart. Antonyms: Reverse, Rear. Example: The two brothers are of obverse nature.
  • Obviate: Remove (a need or difficulty); avoid or prevent something undesirable. Synonyms: Remove, Prevent. Antonyms: Support, Allow. Example: A parachute can be used to obviate disaster.
  • Occult: Relating to magical powers and activities. Synonyms: Psychic, Magical. Antonyms: Natural, Obvious. Example: Some books in the library were on occult subjects.
  • Offbeat: Unusual and strange therefore surprising or noticeable. Synonyms: Bizzare, Unconventional. Antonyms: Ordinary, Conventional. Example: She decided to choose an offbeat career in fine arts and was successful.
  • Onerous: Difficult to do or needing a lot of effort. Synonyms: Arduous, Demanding. Antonyms: Effortless, Easy. Example: She found the duties of motherhood onerous.
  • Overweening: Too proud or confident in yourself. Synonyms: Brash, Haughty. Antonyms: Modest, Unassuming. Example: Nobody wants to be friendly with overweening people.
  • Overwrought: In a state of being upset, nervous and worried. Synonyms: Frantic, Agitated and Worried. Antonyms: Calm, Collected. Example: He was in an overwrought state for weeks after the accident.
  • Palliate: To reduce the bad effects of something; To reduce pain without curing its cause. Synonyms: Alleviate, Soothe. Antonyms: Aggravate, Agitate. Example: The medicine palliated the pain of the patient.
  • Pallid: 1. Very pale, in a way that looks unhealthy and not attractive. 2. Showing no enthusiasm or excitement. Synonyms: Anemic, Feeble, Uninspired. Antonyms: Enthusiastic, Hearty, Strong. Example: His pallid face reveals the tension.
  • Pandemonium: Wild and noisy disorder or confusion. Synonyms: Disorder, Chaos. Antonyms: Calm, Order. Example: Pandemonium reigned in the hall as the election results were announced.
  • Parched: Dried out because of too much heat. Synonyms: Arid, Scorched. Antonyms: Wet, Damp. Example: It was the height of summer and the land was parched and brown.
  • Parlous: Very bad, dangerous or uncertain. Synonyms: Bad, Dreadful. Antonyms: Good, Comfortable. Example: Relationship between the two countries have been in a parlous state for some time.
  • Parsimonious: Very unwilling to spend money or give something; stingy. Synonyms: Niggardly, Miserly. Antonyms: Extravagant, Generous. Example: Even the parsimonious Deepu went to the cafe.
  • Paucity: The fact that there is too little of something. Synonyms: Shortage, Dearth. Antonyms: Abundance, Sufficiency. Example: Wastage of water can cause its paucity.
  • Pejorative: Expressing disapproval or suggesting that something is not good or is of no importance. Synonyms: Disparaging, Deprecatory. Antonyms: Complimentary, Praising. Example: Make sure students realise that 'fat' is a pejorative word.
  • Pellucid: Very clear in meaning and easy to understand. Synonyms: Comprehensible, Understandable. Antonyms: Complex, Unclear. Example: The pellucid language of the book catches the attention of everyone.
  • Perky: Cheerful and lively. Synonyms: Bubbly, Lively. Antonyms: Depressed, Gloomy. Example: His perky face looks elegant to me.
  • Pesky: Causing trouble; Annoying. Synonyms: Nettlesome, Troublesome. Antonyms: Pleasing, Untroubling. Example: I've been trying to get rid of this pesky cold.
  • Plaudits: Enthusiastic approval; praise. Synonyms: Accolade, Acclaim. Antonyms: Blame, Censure. Example: She has received plaudits for her work with homeless people.

subject: English
text:
• Plenary: 1. Complete; full. 2. (of a meeting) To be attended by all participants, who otherwise meet in smaller groups. Synonyms: Absolute, Complete. Antonyms: Incomplete, Limited. Example: A plenary session of the UN Security Council was held this month.
  • Predicament: A difficult, unpleasant or embarrassing situation. Synonyms: Crisis, Deadlock. Antonyms: Advantage, Solution. Example: I have taken a loan to get out of my financial predicament.
  • Prevaricate: To avoid telling the truth or saying exactly what you think about something. Synonyms: Distort, Dodge. Antonyms: Confront, Face. Example: The convict prevaricated before the court.
  • Proclivity: A strong natural liking for something or tendency to do something that is usually bad. Synonyms: Predilection, Predisposition. Antonyms: Antipathy, Disinclination. Example: Gambling is his main proclivity.
  • Profligate: Wasteful with money and resources. Synonyms: Extravagant, Wasteful. Antonyms: Thrifty, Frugal. Example: She is well-known for her profligate spending habits.
  • Quagmire: 1. An area of soft wet ground which one sinks into if one tries and walks on it. 2. An awkward, complex or hazardous situation. Synonyms: Dilemma, Entanglement. Antonyms: Solution, Agreement. Example: The quagmire he is in seems unavoidable.
  • Quail: Feel or show fear or apprehension. Synonyms: Blanch, Cringe. Antonyms: Calm, Steady. Example: Students were quailing before the principal.
  • Quaint: Attractive because of being unusual and especially old-fashioned. Synonyms: Bizarre. Antonyms: Common. Example: The writer talked about the quaint customs of the natives.
  • Quandary: A state of not being able to decide what to do about a situation in which you are involved. Synonyms: Impasse, Difficulty. Antonyms: Solution, Certainty. Example: The unexpected results of the test have created a quandary for the researchers.
  • Querulous: Complaining in an annoyed way. Synonyms: Petulant, Bemoaning. Antonyms: Cheerful, Easy-going. Example: He is becoming a querulous person day by day.
  • Quibble: To argue or complain about small, unimportant things. Synonyms: Protest, Argument. Antonyms: Approval, Agreement. Example: There is no point quibbling over a couple of dollars.
  • Quip: A humorous and clever remark. Synonyms: Gag, Gibe. Antonyms: Seriousness, Praise. Example: They traded quips over a beer.
  • Quisling: A person who helps an enemy who has taken over his country. Synonyms: Collaborator, Betrayer. Antonyms: Supporter, Loyalist. Example: The ruler warned all the quislings.
  • Quixotic: Having ideas or intentions that are impressive but not practical. Synonyms: Impractical, Idealistic. Antonyms: Practical, Pragmatic. Example: They had quixotic dreams about future.
  • Rabid: Having a very extreme opinion about or interest in something. Synonyms: Crazed, Fanatical. Antonyms: Moderate, Liberal. Example: Amit is a rabid cricket fan.
  • Rankle: To make someone annoyed or angry for a long time. Synonyms: Anger, Embitter. Antonyms: Calm, Comfort. Example: It still rankles me that she got promoted and I didn't.
  • Raspy: Unpleasantly rough. Synonyms: Gruff, Hoarse. Antonyms: Soothing, Soft. Example: Her voice was raspy due to yelling so much.
  • Ratify: To make a treaty, agreement etc official by signing it or voting for it. Synonyms: Sanction, Approve. Antonyms: Disapprove, Deny. Example: Project was ratified by the officials.
  • Ravishing: Very beautiful. Synonyms: Gorgeous, Stunning. Antonyms: Ugly, Hideous. Example: She looked ravishing in her wedding dress.
  • Recondite: (of a subject or knowledge) Not known by many people and difficult to understand. Synonyms: Obscure, Esoteric. Antonyms: Obvious, Simple. Example: Geochemistry is a recondite subject.
  • Recoup: To get back money that one has spent or lost. Synonyms: Retrieve, Regain. Antonyms: Forefeit, Lose. Example: The gambler recouped his losses in the next game.
  • Rectitude: The quality of being honest and morally correct. Synonyms: Righteousness, Goodness. Antonyms: Infamy, Dishonesty. Example: Gandhiji was a man of unquestioned moral rectitude.
  • Redolent: Strongly reminiscent or suggestive of; fragrant; odorous; suggestive of an odour. Synonyms: Evocative, Suggestive. Antonyms: Bland, Unsavoury. Example: Rashi's house seemed to be redolent with the aroma of flowers.
  • Reek: (v/n) To smell strongly and unpleasantly; stink. Synonyms: Stink, Smell. Antonyms: Sweetness, Fragrance. Example: Her breath reeked of garlic.

subject: English
text:
• Renunciation: The formal rejection of something, typically a belief, claim or course of action. Synonyms: Repudiation, Abandonment. Antonyms: Agreement, Allowance. Example: The company renunciated the agreement made by them.
  • Repartee: Conversation or speech characterised by quick, witty comments or replies. Synonyms: Banter, Pleasantry. Antonyms: Seriousness, Question. Example: The two comedians engaged in witty repartee.
  • Replete: Filled or well supplied with something. Synonyms: Filled, Loaded. Antonyms: Lacking, Empty. Example: The book is replete with photographs.
  • Reprieve: To cancel or postpone a punishment. Synonyms: Abatement, Absolution. Antonyms: Charge, Punish. Example: He was sentenced to death but was granted a last minute reprieve.
  • Reproach: To criticise someone, especially for not being successful or not doing what is expected. Synonyms: Disgrace, Rebuke. Antonyms: Approval, Commendation. Example: His mother reproached him for not eating his dinner.
  • Repugnant: Causing a strong feeling of dislike or disgust. Synonyms: Repulsive, Abhorrent. Antonyms: Pleasant, Delightful. Example: The idea of cheating in an exam is morally repugnant to me.
  • Scintillate: Emit flashes of light, sparkle. Synonyms: Shine, Gleam. Antonyms: Dull. Example: Her scintillating performance on stage won her accolades.
  • Scoff: To laugh and speak about a person or idea in a way that shows you think they are silly or stupid. Synonyms: Belittle, Deride. Antonyms: Approve, Compliment. Example: The critics scoffed at his paintings.
  • Sententious: Trying to appear wise, clever and important in a way that is annoying. Synonyms: Moralistic, Self-righteous. Antonyms: Unimportant. Example: Due to his sententious and pompous way of speaking, he respected by none.
  • Servitude: The state of being under the control of someone else and of having no freedom; slavery. Synonyms: Bondage, Enslavement. Antonyms: Freedom, Mastery. Example: In the past, the majority of women were confined to a lifetime of servitude and poverty.
  • Sever: To put an end to (a connection or relationship); break off. Synonyms: Detach, Disconnect. Antonyms: Unite, Connect. Example: I severed myself from my double-faced friends.
  • Sham: Someone or something that is not what it pretends to be; pretence. Synonyms: Fake, Pretend. Antonyms: Real, Genuine. Example: They claimed that the election had been fair, but really it was a sham.
  • Skullduggery: Secret and dishonest behaviour. Synonyms: Trickery, Fraudulence. Antonyms: Honesty. Example: Skullduggery is never appreciated.
  • Sleaze: Activities especially business or political, of a low moral standard. Synonyms: Corrupt, Immoral. Antonyms: Moral, Principled. Example: Molestation is an obvious sleaze.
  • Slipshod: Characterised by a lack of care, thought or organisation; shabby. Synonyms: Careless, Disorganised. Antonyms: Careful, Meticulous. Example: She complained that the carpenter's work had been slipshod.
  • Slovenly: 1. Untidy and dirty 2. (of a person or action) careless; excessively casual. Synonyms: Messy, Scruffy. Antonyms: Tidy, Neat. Example: Change your slovenly habits right now.
  • Stalwart: 1. Loyal, reliable and hardworking. Synonyms: Staunch, Dependable. Antonyms: Non-reliable, Undependable. Example: I have a bunch of stalwart friends.
  • Stodgy: Dull and uninspired; lacking originality or excitement. Synonyms: Boring, Dull. Antonyms: Interesting, Lively. Example: The company did not succeed in shedding its stodgy image.
  • Stouthearted: Brave and determined. Synonyms: Fearless, Courageous. Antonyms: Timid, Cowardly. Example: The stouthearted soldiers won the battle.
  • Stupor: A state of near-unconsciousness or insensibility. Synonyms: Coma, Trance. Antonyms: Consciousness, Wakefulness. Example: He was lying under a table in a drunken stupor.
  • Taint: To damage something, especially by adding something harmful or undesirable to it. Synonyms: Contaminate, Pollute. Antonyms: Clean, Improve. Example: A leaky pipe can taint the entire water supply.
  • Tangible: Real or not imaginary; able to be shown, touched or experienced. Synonyms: Palpable, Touchable. Antonyms: Intangible, Abstract. Example: There is no tangible evidence to support her claim.
  • Thrifty: Using money and other resources carefully and not wastefully. Synonyms: Frugal, Prudent. Antonyms: Extravagant, Generous. Example: He is being thrifty in deciding his budget.

subject: English
text:
• Throttle: To attack or kill someone by choking or strangling; strangle. Synonyms: Gag, Smother. Antonyms: Release, Let go. Example: A leader was throttled by the Maoists.
  • Tirade: A long, angry speech of criticism or accusation. Synonyms: Diatribe, Invective. Antonyms: Compliment, Praise. Example: The coach directed a tirade at the team after the loss.
  • Titanic: Extremely powerful, strong, important or large. Synonyms: Colossal, Gigantic. Antonyms: Small, Puny. Example: A titanic wave let the Titanic sink in.
  • Titter: To give a short, half-suppressed laugh; giggle. Synonyms: Giggle, Snigger. Antonym: Cry. Example: He was tittering on his joke.
  • Toothsome: (Especially of food) attractive or pleasant. Synonyms: Tasty, Delicious. Antonyms: Unpleasant, Unsavoury. Example: Pizza is a toothsome food for this generation.
  • Torpid: Having or showing very little energy or movement; not active. Synonyms: Lethargic, Inactive. Antonyms: Energetic, Active. Example: The torpid boy is becoming obese day-by-day.
  • Tout: 1. To publicise; praise excessively. 2. To sell tickets unofficially, usually at a much higher rate than the official price. Synonyms: Laud, Praise. Antonyms: Criticise, Blame. Example: A local car dealership was touting its wares on the radio.
  • Ubiquitous: Existing everywhere; omnipresent. Synonyms: Universal, Pervasive. Antonyms: Rare, Scarce. Example: Reliance Jio's advertisements are ubiquitous.
  • Umbrage: A feeling of being offended by what someone had said or done. Synonyms: Annoyance, Chagrin. Antonyms: Calmness, Comfort. Example: Will she take umbrage if she isn't invited to the party?
  • Unabashed: Without any worry about possible criticism or embarrassment. Synonyms: Brazen, Unashamed. Antonyms: Ashamed, Sheepish. Example: He is an unabashed capitalist.
  • Unassuaged: Not soothed or relieved. Synonyms: Annoyed, Complaining. Antonyms: Contented, Pleased. Example: The customer is unassuaged with the services.
  • Unbridled: Not controlled or limited. Synonyms: Unrestricted, Unrestrained. Antonyms: Controlled, Restrained. Example: The unbridled riot caused a lot of damage.
  • Undiscerning: Lacking judgement, insight or taste. Synonyms: Obtuse, Indiscriminate. Antonyms: Insightful, Perceptive. Example: The situation showed undiscerning character of the lady.
  • Unequivocal: Leaving no doubt; unambiguous. Synonyms: Unambiguous, Absolute. Antonyms: Ambiguous, Doubtful. Example: The church is unequivocal in its condemnation of the violence.
  • Unexpurgated: (of a text) Complete and containing all the original material; uncensored. Synonyms: Exhaustive, Entire. Antonyms: Censored, Abridged. Example: Unexpurgated material has been sent for proof-reading now.
  • Vanity: 1. Excessive pride in or admiration of one's own appearance or achievements. 2. The quality of being worthless or futile. Synonyms: Egotism, Conceit. Antonyms: Modesty, Humility. Example: Vanity of a person thwarts his path of progress.
  • Vanquish: To defeat thoroughly. Synonyms: Conquer, Trounce. Antonyms: Surrender, Yield. Example: The school team was vanquished in the match.
  • Vaunt: Boast about or praise something, especially excessively. Synonyms: Boast, Brag. Antonyms: Deprecate, Condemn. Example: Even the noblest of fellows have been known to vaunt a bit.
  • Vehement: Expressing strong feelings; forceful, passionate or intense. Synonyms: Forceful, Passionate. Antonyms: Mild, Apathetic. Example: The proposal has faced vehement opposition from many people.
  • Venal: Willing to do dishonest things in return for money. Synonyms: Corrupt, Crooked. Antonyms: Honest, Ethical. Example: The country wants to get rid of venal leaders.
  • Venerable: Valued and respected because of old age, long use etc. Synonyms: Revered, Esteemed. Antonyms: Dishonourable, Disreputable. Example: The Hindu is a venerable newspaper.
  • Venerate: To honour or greatly respect a person or thing. Synonyms: Respect, Exalt. Antonyms: Denounce, Condemn. Example: The Ganges is a venerated river in India.

subject: English
text:
• Verve: Great energy and enthusiasm. Synonyms: Vigour, Enthusiasm. Antonyms: Lethargy, Inactivity. Example: She delivered her speech with tremendous verve.
  • Vindicate: To clear someone of blame or suspicion, to prove to be right or reasonable, to justify. Synonyms: Justify, Acquit. Antonyms: Blame, Charge. Example: The investigation vindicated her complaint about the newspaper.
  • Virulent: 1. (of a disease or poison) Extremely severe or harmful in its effects. 2. Full of hate and violent opposition. Synonyms: Fatal, Malicious. Antonyms: Harmless, Amicable. Example: There is a virulent relation between India and Pakistan these days.
  • Vitiate: To spoil or impair the quality or efficiency of something. Synonyms: Annihilate, Spoil. Antonyms: Fix, Mend. Example: Mishandling has vitiated the quality of machines.
  • Voracious: Insatiable appetite for food, facts/knowledge. Synonyms: Insatiable, Uncontrollable. Antonyms: Satiable, Controllable. Example: As a child, I had a voracious appetite for books.
  • Wallop: To strike or hit very hard. Synonyms: Bash, Batter. Example: The peon was walloping the bell continuously.
  • Whimper: To make a series of low, feeble sounds expressive of fear, pain or discontent. Synonyms: Sob, Whine. Antonyms: Laugh, Chuckle. Example: The dog that met with the accident was whimpering in front of the office.
  • Whisk: To take or move someone or something somewhere suddenly and quickly. Synonyms: Dart, Dash. Antonyms: Drag, Slow. Example: The sacks of grain were whisked to the godown for fear of rain.
  • Whit: A very small part or amount. Synonyms: Scrap, Bit. Antonyms: Lot, Whole. Example: The child accepted only a whit of the chocolate.
  • Wistful: Sad and thinking about something that is impossible or past. Synonyms: Contemplative, Nostalgic. Antonyms: Cheerful, Happy. Example: I thought about my childhood days and grew wistful.
  • Xenophobic: Extreme dislike or fear of foreigners, their customs, their religions etc. Synonyms: Animosity, Chauvinism. Antonyms: Tolerance, Impartiality. Example: Tourist guides cannot be xenophobic.
  • Yank: To pull something with a quick movement. Synonyms: Jerk, Tug. Antonym: Push. Example: The man yanked at the zip of the bag.
  • Zany: Strange, surprising or uncontrolled in an amusing way. Synonyms: Bizzare, Eccentric. Antonyms: Familiar, Sensible. Example: His zany behaviour is beyond explanation.
  • Zest: Enthusiasm, eagerness, energy and interest. Synonyms: Enthusiasm, Gutso. Antonyms: Apathy, Indifference. Example: His humour added zest to the performance.
