details.summary: This section covers the properties of virtual images and the specific image formation characteristics of concave mirrors based on object placement relative to the center of curvature (C), focus (F), and pole (P).

subject: Physics
text:
Image Formation by Convex Mirror

  • When the object is at infinity: The image is formed at focus.
  • When the object is between infinity and pole: The image is formed between pole and focus.
image_descriptions: Diagram showing light rays from an object at infinity hitting a convex mirror and converging at the focus F to form an image A'B'.
Diagram showing an object AB placed between infinity and the pole P of a convex mirror, with the image A'B' formed between the pole and focus F.

details.summary: Covers image formation characteristics for convex mirrors at different object positions.

subject: Physics
text:
Mirror Formula

  • If v is the image distance, u is the object distance and f is the focal length of a mirror, then 1/v + 1/u = 1/f = 2/R
  • The linear magnification (m) produced by a mirror is equal to the ratio of the image distance to the object distance with negative sign, m = -v/u = f/(f-u) = (f-v)/f
  • If the magnification has positive sign, then the image is virtual and erect.
  • If the magnification has negative sign, then the image is real and inverted.

details.summary: Mathematical relationships for spherical mirrors including magnification and sign conventions.

subject: Physics
text:
Uses of Spherical Mirrors

Concave Mirrors:

  • These are used as reflectors in automobiles (car, buses, etc.), head light, search light, hand torches and table lamps.
  • These are used as shaving mirrors.
  • These are used by doctors for focussing intense light to examine inside of eye, ears, etc.
  • Large concave mirrors are used in the application of solar energy, to focus the sun's rays for heating solar furnaces etc.

Convex Mirrors:

  • These are used as rear-view mirrors in automobiles as they give large view of the traffic.
  • Big convex mirrors are used as shop security mirrors.
  • These are used wherever we want to see erect images.

Note: We cannot use a concave mirror as a rear-view mirror in motor vehicles.

details.summary: Practical applications of concave and convex mirrors.

subject: Physics
text:
Refraction of Light

When a ray of light passes from one medium to other, it bends from its path. This phenomenon of bending of light is called as refraction of light.

  • When light passes from rarer medium to a denser medium, it bends towards the normal at the point of incidence.
  • When light passes from a denser medium to a rarer medium, it bends away from the normal.
  • When a ray of light enters from one medium to other medium its frequency and phase do not change but wavelength and velocity change.

Laws of Refraction

  • The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.
  • The ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is a constant for a given medium. sin i / sin r = μ [Snell's law]

where, μ is refractive index of the second medium with respect to first. μ = μ2/μ1 = c/v2 / c/v1 = v1/v2 or 1μ2 = v1/v2

Some Illustrations of Refraction

  • Twinkling of stars.
  • Oval shape of sun in the morning and evening.
  • Bending of a linear object when it is partially dipped in a liquid inclined to the surface of the liquid.
  • A fish in a pond when viewed from air appears to be at a smaller depth than actual depth.
  • A coin at the base of a vessel filled with water appears raised.

details.summary: Principles, laws, and natural phenomena related to the refraction of light.

subject: Physics
text:
Total Internal Reflection

In case of propagation of light from denser to rarer medium through a plane boundary. Critical angle is the angle of incidence for which angle of refraction is 90°.

  • If light is propagating from denser medium towards the rarer medium and angle of incidence is more than critical angle, then the light incident on the boundary is reflected back in the denser medium, obeying the law of reflection. This phenomenon is called total internal reflection.

details.summary: Definition and conditions for Total Internal Reflection.

subject: Physics
topic: Total Internal Reflection and Spherical Lenses
text:
Conditions of Total Internal Reflection:

  • Light must be propagating from denser to rarer medium.
  • Angle of incidence must exceeds the critical angle.

Sparkling of diamond, mirage and looming, shinning of air bubble in water and optical fibre are the examples of total internal reflection.

Note: Optical fibre is used for the transmitting and receiving the electrical signals after converting it into the light signal.

Spherical Lenses: A lens is a piece of transparent glass bounded by two spherical surfaces. There are two types of lenses:

  • Convex lens (converging lens): A lens which is thicker at the centre and thinner at its ends.
  • Concave lens (diverging lens): A lens which is thinner at the centre and thicker at its ends.

Key Definitions:

  • The centre point of a lens is known as its optical centre.
  • The line joining the centres of the surfaces of the lens is called the principal axis of the lens.
  • The distance of the first focus from the optical centre of the lens is called the first focal length.
  • The distance of the second focus from the optical centre of the lens is called the second focal length.
tables:
| Position of object | Position of image | Size of image | Nature of image |
|---|---|---|---|
| At infinity | At F2 | Highly diminished | Real and inverted |
| Beyond 2F1 | Between F2 and 2F2 | Diminished | -do- |
| At 2F1 | At 2F2 | Same size | -do- |
| Between 2F1 and F1 | Beyond 2F2 | Enlarged | -do- |
| At F1 | At infinity | Highly enlarged | -do- |
| Between F1 and lens | Behind the object, on the same side of the object | Enlarged | Virtual and erect |
image_descriptions: Diagram showing a convex lens with optical centre, principal axis, first focus (F1), and second focus (F2).
Diagram showing a concave lens with optical centre, principal axis, first focus (F1), and second focus (F2).

details.summary: Overview of Total Internal Reflection conditions and basic definitions/types of spherical lenses.

subject: Physics
topic: Image Formation by a Convex Lens
text:
Image Formation by a Convex Lens:

  • (i) Object at infinity: The image formed is at second focus, real, inverted and highly diminished.
  • (ii) Object beyond 2F1: The image formed is between F2 and 2F2 on the right side of the lens, real, inverted and diminished.
  • (iii) Object at 2F1: The image formed is at 2F2, real, inverted and of same size as that of the object.
  • (iv) Object between F1 and 2F1: The image formed is beyond 2F2, real, inverted and magnified.
tables:
| Position of object | Position of image | Size of image | Nature of image |
|---|---|---|---|
| At infinity | At F2 | Diminished | Erect and virtual |
| Between infinity and lens | Between F2 and lens | Diminished | Erect and virtual |
image_descriptions: Ray diagram for object at infinity showing parallel rays converging at F2.
Ray diagram for object beyond 2F1 showing image formed between F2 and 2F2.
Ray diagram for object at 2F1 showing image formed at 2F2.
Ray diagram for object between F1 and 2F1 showing image formed beyond 2F2.

details.summary: Detailed breakdown of image formation characteristics for convex lenses based on object position.

subject: Physics
text:
Image Formation by Convex Lens:

  • (v) Object at F1: The image formed is real, inverted, and highly enlarged at infinity.
  • (vi) Object between F1 and O: The image formed is behind the object, virtual, erect and enlarged.

Image Formation by a Concave Lens:

  • (i) Object at infinity: The image formed is at F2, erect, virtual and diminished.
  • (ii) Object anywhere between infinity and lens: The image formed is between F2 and lens, erect, virtual and diminished.

Lens Formula:

  • If v is the image distance, u is the object distance and f is the focal length of a lens, then 1/f = 1/v - 1/u.
  • Magnification, m = v/u = I/O = Size of image / Size of object.
  • If the magnification m has a positive value, the image is virtual and erect. If the magnification m has a negative value the image is real and inverted.
  • If m is the total magnification of two lenses in contact having magnification m1 and m2, then m = m1 x m2.
  • Power (P) of a lens is the reciprocal of focal length of lens i.e., P = 1/f. SI unit of power is dioptre (D).
  • If two or more lenses are combined, then there is an increase in the magnification of image, the final image is erect, and the spherical aberration is reduced.
  • If P is power of two lenses in contact having powers P1 and P2, then P = P1 + P2 or 1/F = 1/f1 + 1/f2.
  • If two lenses of equal focal length but of opposite nature are in contact, then combination will behaves as a plane glass plate and f = infinity.
  • Note: When lens is dipped in a liquid of higher refractive index the focal length increases and convex lens behaves as concave lens and vice-versa. An air bubble trapped in water or glass appears as convex but behaves as concave lens.
image_descriptions: Ray diagram showing object at F1 for a convex lens resulting in image at infinity.
Ray diagram showing object between F1 and O for a convex lens resulting in a virtual, erect, and enlarged image behind the object.
Ray diagram showing object at infinity for a concave lens resulting in a virtual, erect, and diminished image at F2.
Ray diagram showing object between infinity and lens for a concave lens resulting in a virtual, erect, and diminished image between F2 and lens.

details.summary: Covers image formation rules for convex and concave lenses, lens formula, magnification, power of lenses, and lens combinations.

subject: Physics
text:
Dispersion of Light:

  • Sir Isaac Newton observed that when a narrow beam of light is incident on a prism, the emergent beam is not only deviated but at the same time splits up into a coloured band of seven colours. This phenomenon is called dispersion of light.
  • The seven colours of band are Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange and Red (can be memorised as VIBGYOR).
  • The colour of an object is determined by the colour of the light reflected by it.
  • Violet colour deviates through maximum angle and red colour deviates through the minimum angle.
  • Rainbow is formed due to the dispersion of light suffering refractions and total internal reflection in the droplets present in the atmosphere.

Primary Colours:

  • Red, green and blue are called primary colours or basic colours.

Mixing of Colours:

  • Red + Green + Blue = White
  • Red + Blue = Magenta
  • Blue + Green = Peacock blue (or Cyan)
  • Red + Green = Yellow

details.summary: Explains the dispersion of light through a prism, the VIBGYOR spectrum, primary colours, and colour mixing rules.

subject: Physics
text:
Colour Properties: Magenta, Cyan and Yellow are secondary colours. A rose appears red because it absorbs all constituent colours of white light except red. If all colours are reflected, the object appears white; if all are absorbed, it appears black. The natural colour of transparent objects is due to selective transmission.

Scattering of Light: Sunlight passing through the atmosphere is scattered by air molecules and dust. Scattering by particles is called the Tyndall effect. Blue light is scattered more easily, causing the blue sky. At sunrise/sunset, red light reaches our eyes as blue is scattered away. Danger signals are red as they scatter least. Without an atmosphere, there would be no scattering, and the sky would appear black.

Interference and Diffraction: Interference occurs when two waves of the same frequency travel in the same direction; intensity is maximum at some points and minimum at others (e.g., oil films, soap bubbles). Polarisation proves light is a transverse wave. Diffraction is the bending of light around corners of an opaque obstacle.

Human Eye: An optical instrument forming real images on the retina. Least distance of distinct vision is 25 cm; far point is at infinity.

Defects of Vision:

  • Myopia: Cannot see far objects. Corrected by concave lens. Caused by high converging power or long eyeball.
  • Hypermetropia: Cannot see near objects. Corrected by convex lens. Caused by low converging power or short eyeball.
  • Presbyopia: Old age loss of accommodation. Corrected by bifocal lens.
  • Astigmatism: Cannot see horizontal and vertical lines simultaneously. Corrected by cylindrical lens.
  • Cataract: Opaque membrane on cornea, removed by surgery.

Note: Colour blindness is a genetic disorder (John Dalton was colour blind).

Optical Instruments: A simple microscope uses a convex lens of small focal length to see small objects.

details.summary: Covers light phenomena (scattering, interference, diffraction), human eye anatomy, vision defects, and basic microscopy.

subject: Physics
text:
Telescope is an optical instrument used for observing distinct images of heavenly bodies like stars, planets, etc., when the final image is formed at infinity.

  • Types:
    • Astronomical telescope (invented by Kepler in 1611)
    • Galilean telescope (invented by Galileo in 1609)
  • Construction:
    • In an astronomical telescope, the objective lens is a convex lens of large focal length but eye-piece is a convex lens of short focal length.
    • In a Galilean telescope, the objective lens is a convex lens of large focal length but the eye-piece is a concave lens of short focal length.
  • Periscope: Consists of two plane mirrors inclined at an angle of 45°. The principle of working of periscope is based upon reflection and refraction.

details.summary: Overview of telescope types, construction, and periscope principles.

subject: Physics
text:
Charge is the basic property associated with matter due to which it produces and experiences electrical and magnetic effects. The SI unit of electric charge is Coulomb.

  • Positively charged particles called protons (charge 1.6 x 10^-19 C).
  • Negatively charged particles called electrons (charge -1.6 x 10^-19 C).
  • Similar charges repel each other and opposite charges attract each other.

details.summary: Definition and properties of electric charge.

subject: Physics
text:
When two or more charged bodies come in contact, then total charge on all the bodies are conserved.

  • Conductors: Allow passage of electrical charges, have very low electrical resistance (e.g., copper, aluminium, gold, silver). Human body and earth act like a conductor. Silver is the best conductor.
  • Resistors: Offer high resistance to the flow of current (e.g., eureka, nichrome).
  • Insulators: Have infinite resistance and do not allow the passage of current (e.g., rubber, glass, ebonite).
  • Note: The presence of free electrons in a substance makes it a conductor.

details.summary: Conservation of charge and classification of materials based on conductivity.

subject: Physics
text: The force of attraction or the force of repulsion acting between the two point charges is proportional to the product of the magnitudes of the two charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.

details.summary: Mathematical representation of Coulomb's Law.

subject: Physics
text:
Electric Field: The region around an electric charge in which its effect can be experienced.

Electric Potential: The work done in bringing a unit positive charge from infinity to that point. Its SI unit is volt (V).

  • Potential difference (V_A - V_B) between two points A and B is the work done in bringing a unit charge from point B to point A.
  • Potential difference is a scalar quantity and is measured by means of voltmeter.
  • The electric potential inside a spherical surface is same at each point and is equal to the potential on the surface.
  • Electric potential on earth is considered to be zero.
  • A voltmeter connected in parallel with conductor measures potential difference.

details.summary: Definitions and properties of electric field and electric potential.

subject: Physics
text:
The rate of flow of electric charges through any cross-section of conductor is called electric current. The direction of positive charges is same as direction of conventional current.

  • The SI unit of electric current is ampere.
  • Current is measured by an instrument called ammeter.
  • An ammeter is connected in series with the conductor to measure the current passing through it.
formulas: Current = Charge / Time => I = Q / t

details.summary: Definition, measurement, and units of electric current.

subject: Physics
text:
There are two types of electric current: (i) Alternating current (AC) and (ii) Direct current (DC).

  • Alternating current is used in houses and factories and its frequency is 50 Hz.
  • Ordinary DC ammeter and DC voltmeter cannot measure alternating current/voltages. They record zero reading, when used in AC circuits, because average value of alternating current/voltage over a full cycle is zero.

Galvanometer: It is a device used to detect and measure electric current in a circuit. It can measure current up to 10^-6 A. A galvanometer can be converted into a voltmeter by connecting a very high resistance in its series.

Note: Conventionally the direction of electric current is opposite to that of electrons. Since, electrons flow from negative terminal of a cell to its positive terminal, electric current flows from positive terminal to negative terminal.

details.summary: Overview of AC/DC current, galvanometer function, and conventional current direction.

subject: Physics
text:
A capacitor or condenser is a device over which a large amount of charge can be stored.

  • Capacitance of capacitor (C) = Charge (Q) / Potential (V)
  • Its unit is coulomb/volt or farad.
  • A capacitor is used in several electrical devices having an electric motor and in several electronic circuits.

details.summary: Definition and usage of a capacitor.

subject: Physics
text:
Ohm's Law: If the physical circumstances of the conductor (length, temperature, etc) remains constant then the current flowing through the conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across its ends. i.e., I ∝ V or V = IR, where R is resistance.

Resistance: The resistance of a conductor is directly proportional to its length and inversely proportional to its cross-sectional area. If l and A are respectively length and cross-sectional area of a conductor and R is its resistance, then R ∝ l/A => R = ρ(l/A). Unit of resistance is ohm (Ω), where ρ is a constant of material of conductor is called specific resistance or resistivity. Its SI unit is ohm-metre.

  • On increasing the temperature of the metal, its resistance increases.
  • Those materials whose electrical conductivity lies in between that of insulators and conductors are called semiconductors. On increasing the temperature of semiconductor, its resistance decreases.
  • The reciprocal of resistance of a conductor is called the electrical conductance of the conductor. Conductance = 1 / Resistance. Unit of conductance is mho or siemen.
  • The specific resistance of the material depends only on the material of conductor and its temperature.
  • Resistivity increases with temperature.
  • Resistivity of a conductor change with impurity.
  • Resistivity of an alloy is greater than the resistivity of its constituents and remains unchanged with temperature.
  • If a wire is stretched or doubled on itself, its resistance will change, but its specific resistance will remains unaffected.
  • The reciprocal of resistivity of a conductor is called its conductivity. Its SI unit is mho m^-1 or siemen/metre (Sm^-1).

details.summary: Detailed explanation of Ohm's Law, resistance, resistivity, and conductance properties.

subject: Physics
text:
There are two combinations given below:

(i) Series combination: R = R1 + R2 + R3 and here current flows through each conductor is same. The total resistance in the series combination is more than the greatest resistance in the circuit.

(ii) Parallel combination: 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3 and here potential across each conductor is same. The total resistance in parallel combination is less than the least resistance of the circuit.
image_descriptions: Circuit diagram showing three resistors R1, R2, R3 in series connected to a battery E.
Circuit diagram showing three resistors R1, R2, R3 in parallel connected to a battery E.

details.summary: Comparison of series and parallel resistor combinations.

subject: Physics
text:
Electrical power is the electrical work done per unit time.

P = W / t or P = V x I

or P = I^2R (since V = IR)

or P = V^2 / R

Its SI unit is watt (W).

details.summary: Definition and formulas for calculating electric power.

subject: Physics
text:
Heat is produced when electric current is passed through a conductor. This effect is called the heating effect of electric current.

Important Points Based on Heating Effect:

  • In home appliances like electric iron, electric heater, and heating rod, the heating element used is of a nichrome (an alloy of Ni and Cr) wire. Nichrome has a high melting point and high resistivity. To avoid the risk of electric shock, the metal body of electrical appliances is earthed.
  • An electric fuse is generally prepared from a tin-lead alloy (63% tin + 37% lead). It should have high resistance and low melting point. It is connected in the series.
  • Tubelight contains a long tube of glass which is linked internally with a fluorescent substance. It is filled with an inert gas like argon along with some mercury.
  • The filament of an electric bulb gets very hot and therefore easily oxidised. Thus, bulbs are sealed with inactive nitrogen and argon gases to prevent oxidation of the filament and increase its life. In electric bulb, tungsten is used for the construction of filament because it has a high melting point.

details.summary: Covers the heating effect of electric current, practical applications like fuses and bulbs, and the properties of materials used in heating elements.

subject: Physics
text:
Magnets: A magnet is a piece of iron or other materials that can attract iron-containing objects, and the property of attracting magnetic substances is called magnetism.

  • Magnets which do not lose their magnetism with normal treatment are called permanent magnets.
  • Materials which retain their magnetism for a long time are called hard magnetic materials.
  • In bar, rod, and horse-shoe magnets, North or South poles are indicated by the letter N or S.
  • When poles of two magnets are brought close together, they exert force on each other. This force is called intersection between the poles.
  • If we cut a magnet in two parts, then each separate part will behave as a magnet.
  • Permanent magnets are usually made of alloys such as carbon steel, chromium steel, cobalt steel, tungsten steel, and alnico (alloy of aluminium, nickel, cobalt, and iron).
  • Such permanent magnets are used in microphones, loudspeakers, electric clocks, ammeters, voltmeters, speedometer, and many other devices.
  • Note: The Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) technique which is used to scan inner human body parts in hospitals also uses magnets for its working.

Magnetic Field: The space in the surrounding of a magnet or a current-carrying conductor in which its magnetic effect can be experienced is called magnetic field.

  • Magnetic lines of force are imaginary lines in the magnetic field, which shows the direction of magnetic field continuously.
  • The magnetic field lines originate from the North pole of a magnet and end at its South pole.
  • The magnetic field lines do not intersect one another.

details.summary: Definitions and properties of magnets, magnetic fields, and magnetic lines of force.

subject: Physics
text:
Magnetic Materials: According to the behaviour of magnetic substances, they are classified into three classes:

  • Diamagnetic substances: When placed in an external magnetic field, acquire a very low magnetism in the direction opposite to the field. e.g., copper, silver, bismuth, zinc, diamond, salt, water, mercury, etc. The permeability of diamagnetic substance is less than one.
  • Paramagnetic substances: When placed in an external field, acquire a feeble magnetism in the direction of the field. e.g., aluminium, sodium, potassium, oxygen, etc. The permeability of paramagnetic substance is slightly greater than one.
  • Ferromagnetic substances: When placed in a magnetic field, acquire a strong magnetism in the direction of the field. e.g., iron, nickel, cobalt, magnetite, etc. The permeability of ferromagnetic substance is much greater than one.

Electromagnet: An electromagnet is a solenoid coil that attains magnetism due to the flow of current. It works on the principle of magnetic effect of current. It is used in electric bells, electric motors, telephone, diaphragms, loudspeakers, etc.

details.summary: Classification of magnetic materials (diamagnetic, paramagnetic, ferromagnetic) and definition of an electromagnet.

subject: Physics
text: The magnetic flux linked with a surface is equal to the total number of magnetic lines of force passing through that surface normally. Its unit is weber.

details.summary: Definition and unit of magnetic flux.

subject: Physics
text:
When a change occurs in the magnetic flux linked with the coil, an emf is induced in the coil. The phenomenon is called electromagnetic induction.

  • The phenomenon of production of induced emf in a circuit due to change in magnetic flux in its neighbouring circuit is called mutual induction.
  • When the electric current flowing through a circuit changes, the magnetic flux linked with circuit also change. As a result an induced emf is set up in the circuit. This phenomenon is called self-induction.
  • Microphone converts sound energy into electrical energy and works on the principle of electromagnetic induction.

details.summary: Explanation of electromagnetic induction, mutual induction, and self-induction.

subject: Physics
text:
It is a device which converts mechanical energy into electrical energy. An electric generator is based on the principle of electromagnetic induction. It is used to produce electric current by varying magnetic field through a coil.

  • A generator can produced both alternating current and direct current.
  • AC generator consists of slip rings, armature, magnet and brushes while DC generator consists of magnet commutator, armature and brushes.
  • Note: Electric motor is a rotating device which converts electrical energy into mechanical energy.

details.summary: Working principle and components of electric generators.

subject: Physics
text:
Transformer is a device which converts low voltage AC into high voltage AC and high voltage AC into low voltage AC. It is based on mutual induction.

  • Core of a transformer is made up of soft iron.
  • Step-up transformer converts a low voltage of high current into a high voltage of low current.
  • Step-down transformer converts a high voltage of low current into a low voltage of high current.
  • The main energy losses in a transformer are given below: (a) Iron loss (b) Flux loss (c) Hysteresis loss (d) Humming loss
  • Transformer is used in voltage regulators, refrigerators, computer, air conditioner.
  • Step-down transformer is used for welding purpose.
  • Audio transformer allowed telephone circuits to carry on a two-way conversation over a single pair of wires.
  • Radio frequency transformers are used in radio communication.
  • Note: A mobile phone charger is one of the best example of step down transformer as it extracts the power from the home supply (AC 220V) and convert it to DC of required voltage.

details.summary: Types, applications, and energy losses in transformers.

subject: Physics
text:
If the gas pressure in a discharge tube is 10^-2 to 10^-3 mm of Hg and a potential difference of 10^4 V is applied between the electrode, then a beam of electrons emerges from the cathode which is called cathode rays.

  • Cathode rays are invisible and travel in a straight line.
  • These rays are deflected by electric and magnetic fields.
  • These rays can ionise gases.
  • They can produce chemical change and thus affect a photographic plate.
  • When they strike a target of heavy metal such as tungsten, they produce X-rays.

details.summary: Properties and production of cathode rays.

subject: Physics
text:
When cathode rays strike on a heavy metal of high melting points, then a very small fraction of its energy converts into a new type of waves, called X-rays.

  • X-rays are electromagnetic waves and these produce photoelectric effect.
  • X-rays were discovered by scientist Roentgen.
  • These produce illumination on falling the fluorescent substances and travel in a straight line with the speed of light.
  • X-rays penetrate through different depth into different substances.
  • Soft X-rays have greater wavelength and lower frequency and hard X-rays have lower wavelength and higher frequency.
  • X-rays ionise gases through which they pass.
  • X-rays are not deflected by electric and magnetic fields.
  • They show all the important properties of light rays like, reflection, refraction, interference, diffraction and polarisation, etc.
  • X-rays are used in surgery, radiotherapy, engineering department and searching.
  • Note: Barium and Iodine are some chemicals used as contrast mediums for X-ray based imaging method. i.e. they absorbs X-ray to highlight the targeted body part.

details.summary: Properties, types, and applications of X-rays.

subject: Physics
text:
These rays are positively charged particles and are called positive rays or canal rays. These rays were discovered by Goldstein.

  • These rays can affect the photographic plates.
  • These rays are capable of producing physical and chemical changes.
  • These rays are deflected by electric and magnetic fields.
  • These rays can produce fluorescence and phosphorescence.

details.summary: Properties and discovery of positive/canal rays.

subject: Physics
text:
Fluorescence: Some substances absorb the light of higher frequency or shorter wavelength and emits a light having lower frequency or higher wavelength in the presence of light source. This phenomenon of emission of light is called fluorescence. Such substances are called fluorescence substances.

  • Fluoresphor, petrol, uranium oxide and barium platino cyanide are examples of fluorescence substances.
  • Barium platino cyanide is used in search of X-rays.

Phosphorescence: Some substances after being kept in sunlight for sometime emit light even after the light source is removed. This phenomenon is called phosphorescence. Zinc sulphide, calcium sulphide and barium sulphide are examples of phosphorescence.

details.summary: Definitions and examples of fluorescence and phosphorescence.

subject: Physics
text:
Compact fluorescent lamp converts electrical energy into radiant energy.

  • It has two components:
    • A glass tube filled with argon and mercury vapour and coated with layer of fluorescent materials.
    • An electronic ballast circuit.
  • The ballast circuit (small circuit board with rectifiers, a filter capacitor and usually two switching transistors), takes a 220V input from external power source and sends a current into the fluorescent tube as output.
  • When power supply is given to the CFL, filament attached with the cathode heats up and emits electrons in the tube. This ionises the argon and mercury vapour particles, causing it, ultraviolet light emission.

details.summary: Working principle and components of a CFL.

subject: Physics
text:
When the ultraviolet rays (or the visible light of low wavelength or any other kind of electromagnetic radiation) are made incident on a metal, the electrons are emitted from it. This phenomenon is called the photoelectric emission or photoelectric effect.

Photoelectric cell is based on photoelectric effect. It is a device by which light energy is converted into the electrical energy.

Applications of photoelectric effect:

  • In reproduction of sound in cinema, television and photo telegraphy.
  • In automatic switches for street lights.
  • In photoelectric sorters.
  • To control the temperature in furnace and in chemical process.
  • In industries for locating minor flows or holes in metallic sheets.

details.summary: Definition and applications of the photoelectric effect.

subject: Physics
text:
Semiconductors are those materials whose electrical conductivity at room temperature lies in between that of insulator and conductor. A semiconductor in an extremely pure form is known as intrinsic semiconductor.

  • If a measured and small amount of chemical impurity is added to intrinsic semiconductor, it is called extrinsic semiconductor or doped semiconductor.
  • External semiconductors are of two types:
    • n-type semiconductor
    • p-type semiconductor
  • An extrinsic semiconductor in which electrons are majority charge carrier is called n-type semiconductor.
  • An extrinsic semiconductor in which holes are the majority charge carrier is called p-type semiconductor.

details.summary: Classification and types of semiconductors.

subject: Physics
text:
An arrangement consisting a p-type semiconductor brought into a close contact with n-type semiconductor is called a p-n junction or p-n junction diode.

  • A device which converts alternating current (AC) or voltage into direct current (DC) or voltage is known as rectifier. DC can be converted into AC with the help of an inverter.
  • LED's are specially designed diode made up of GaAsP, GaP and are used in electronic gadgets as indicator light. It is used as a rectifier which converts an alternating current into direct current.
  • LED's light up very quickly. A typical red indicator LED will achieve full brightness in microseconds.
  • LED or semiconductor laser is used to convert electrical energy into optical energy.
  • Zener diode is a highly doped p-n junction diode which is not damaged by high reverse current. It can be used as voltage regulator.
  • Photo diode is a special p-n junction diode fabricated with a transparent window to allow light to fall on the diode. It is used in reverse biasing.
  • Note: Diode valve acts as a rectifier and triode valve can be used as amplifier oscillator and detector.

details.summary: Types and functions of special purpose diodes.

subject: Physics
text:
Solar cell is a p-n junction device which converts solar energy into electrical energy. It is consist of a silicon or gallium arsenide p-n junction.

Uses of Solar Cell:

  • Solar cells are used as solar cooker.
  • Solar cells are used in wrist watches, calculators and light meters.
  • Solar cells are also used in artificial satellite to provide power inside the satellite.
  • Solar cells are used for charging storage batteries.

details.summary: Definition and applications of solar cells.

subject: Physics
text:
An IC can be defined generally as an arrangement of multifunction semiconductor devices. It consists of a single crystal chip of silicon, nearly 1.5 mm^2 in cross-section.

TV remote control is an electronic device containing an IC and few other components. If a key on a remote control is pressed, it emits infrared signals which are received by the electronic circuit of the TV receiver, etc.

details.summary: Definition of Integrated Circuits and example of TV remote control.

subject: Physics
text:
The word LASER is the short form of Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation. It is an optical device, which produces an intensive beam highly coherent, monochromatic light.

Applications of laser rays:

  • Laser rays are used in treatment of detached retina, treatment of skin cancer and surgery of brain.
  • Laser beams are used in signals and radio communications.
  • The property of high intensity is used to cut hard metals.
  • The weather informations are collected with the help of radar, an instrument based on the properties of laser.
  • The laser rays are parallel and do not spread. This property of laser rays is used in the measurement of long distance.

details.summary: Definition and applications of LASER.

subject: Physics
text:
The term communication refers to the transmitting receiving and processing of information by electronic means. A basic communication system consists of an information source, a transmitter, a link and a receiver.

  • Electromagnetic waves which are used in radio, television and other communication system are radiowaves and micro waves.
  • Ground wave propagation: The radio wave travel through atmosphere following the surface of the earth from transmitting antenna to receiving antenna. Useful for low range frequencies upto 1500 kHz. Generally used for local broadcasting.
  • Space wave propagation: The radio wave from the transmitting antenna reach the receiving antenna either directly or after reflection from the ground or from troposphere. Utilises the electromagnetic waves of very high frequency band (between 30 MHz to 300 MHz), ultra high frequency band (between 300 MHz to 3000 MHz) and microwaves having frequencies range 100 GHz to 300 GHz.
  • Sky wave propagation: The radio waves from the transmitting antenna reach the receiving antenna after entering in ionosphere. The sky wave frequency lies between 2 MHz to 30 MHz.
  • Communication satellite: A space craft, provided with microwave receiver and transmitter. It is placed in an orbit around the earth. The frequencies used in satellite communication lies in UHF/microwave regions. These waves can cross the ionosphere and reach the satellite.
  • Satellite communication is used effectively in mobile communication, metrology and weather forecasting.
  • Remote sensing is the technique to obtain information about an object by observing it from a distance and without coming to actual contact with it.
  • Parallel wire line is used to connect an antenna with TV receiver. Parallel wire lines are never used for transmission of microwaves.
  • Twisted pair wires are used to connect telephone system.
  • Coaxial cables are used for long distance high frequency transmission. e.g. TV channel transmission.

Note: Maser is a device working on the same principle as a laser. Maser means 'Microwave Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation'. It is used to produce very high magnetic field and in radio astronomy and communications.

details.summary: Overview of communication systems, propagation modes, and transmission media.

subject: Physics
text:
It is a better communication system for large number of channels and higher bandwidth transmission. Now-a-days optical fibres of very small diameters (~ 10^-5 m) are used in optical communication.

Advantages of optical communication over the conventional two wires or coaxial cable systems:

  • In optical fibres energy losses are less.
  • Secret information like banking, defence, etc., is more secure because optical signal is confined to the inside of fibre and cannot be tampered easily.
  • It can be used at high frequencies (~ 10^14 Hz).

Phenomenon of total internal reflection is the principle behind optical fibres. Light can be transmitted along it with almost no loss because of total internal reflection. Important applications of optical fibres are in telecommunications and medicine.

details.summary: Principles and advantages of optical communication.

subject: Physics
text: This section covers fundamental concepts related to rotational motion and gravitational forces, including torque, angular momentum, and the laws of gravitation.

details.summary: A collection of practice questions covering rotational motion, gravitation, and free fall.

subject: Physics
text:
Fluid Dynamics: After rising a short distance, the smooth column of smoke from a cigarette breaks up into an irregular and random pattern. Similarly, a stream of fluid flowing fast past an obstacle breaks up into eddies and vortices, which give the flow irregular velocity components transverse to the flow direction. These examples are the results of turbulent flow.

Surface Tension: Dirty cloths containing grease and oil stains are cleaned by adding detergents to water. Stains are removed because detergent reduces drastically the surface tension between water and oil.

details.summary: Notes on fluid dynamics (turbulent flow) and the role of detergents in reducing surface tension for cleaning.

subject: Physics
text: Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM): The force acting on a particle executing simple harmonic motion is directly proportional to the displacement and is directed towards the mean position.

details.summary: Definition of force in SHM.

subject: Physics
text:
Optics Notes:

  • Rear view mirrors in vehicles: Convex mirrors are used.
  • Viewfinders in automobiles: Convex mirrors are used to locate the position of vehicles behind.
  • Concave mirrors: Used as reflectors in automobiles and hand torches; used in the field of solar energy to focus sun's rays for heating solar furnaces.
  • Refraction phenomena: Twinkling of stars, oval shape of sun in morning and evening, sparking of diamond, mirage and looming.
  • Optical fibre: Efficient working is dependent on total internal reflection.
  • Total Internal Reflection (TIR) conditions: 1. Light must be propagating from denser to rarer medium. 2. The angle of incidence must exceed the critical angle.

details.summary: Key optical principles and applications including mirror types and refraction phenomena.

subject: Physics
text:
Calculations for Sound Waves:

  • Given velocity (v) = 330 m/s, frequency (f) = 550 Hz.
  • Using formula v = f * lambda, lambda = 330 / 550 = 0.6 m.
  • Sound Level: For I = 100 I0, beta = 10 log10(I/I0) = 10 log10(100) = 20 dB. Total noise level = 20 dB + 20 dB = 40 dB.
  • Simple Pendulum: Time period T = 2 * pi * sqrt(l/g). Time period does not depend on mass.
  • Echo/Distance: Distance = (speed * time) / 2. For speed 340 m/s and time 0.3s, distance = 51 m.

details.summary: Physics problem solutions covering wave motion, sound intensity, pendulum mechanics, and echo calculations.

subject: Physics
text:
Lens and Mirror Calculations:

  • Lens Formula: 1/v - 1/u = 1/f.
  • Power of Lens: P = 1/f(m) = 100/f(cm).
  • Myopia: Defect where far-off objects cannot be seen clearly. Remedy: Concave lens.
  • Plane Mirror: Distance between person and image = 2 * distance from mirror.
image_descriptions: Diagram showing a person standing 60 cm from a plane mirror with their image appearing 60 cm behind the mirror.
Ray diagram showing light rays passing through a concave lens, resulting in a virtual diminished image at focus.

details.summary: Optics solutions including lens power, focal length, myopia correction, and plane mirror reflection properties.

subject: Physics
text:
Resistance and Heating Effect:

  • Power of bulb: P = V^2 / R.
  • Effective Resistance (Parallel): 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3.
  • Heating Effect: Heat produced H = i^2 * R * t.
  • Resistance of wire: R = rho * (l/A). Thinner wire has higher resistance, producing more heat.

details.summary: Electricity calculations involving resistance in parallel circuits, power consumption, and Joule's law of heating.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Anything that has mass, occupies space and can be felt by our one or more sense organs is called matter. Matter is found in five physical states: solid, liquid, gas, plasma and Bose-Einstein condensate.

  • Solid: They have a fixed shape, volume and high density. The particles in solids are (closely) packed and held in rigid positions. They can be true or crystalline (i.e. having ordered arrangement of constituent particles to a larger distance) like metals or amorphous or pseudo solids (i.e. having short range arrangement of constituents particles) like non-metals, glass, most of the polymers, etc.
  • Liquid: They have a fixed volume but no fixed shape and have moderate to high densities. The particles in liquids are loosely packed and free to move. Their thermal conductivity decreases with rise in temperature with the exception of water.
  • Gas: They have neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume and have very low density. The particles in gas are widely spaced apart and uniformly distributed in the container.
  • Plasma: The state consists of super energetic and super excited particles which are in the form of ionised gases. Due to the presence of plasma, the sun and stars glow.
  • Bose-Einstein Condensate (BEC): They are formed by cooling a gas of extremely low density to super low temperatures.

details.summary: Overview of the five states of matter: Solid, Liquid, Gas, Plasma, and Bose-Einstein Condensate.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Properties of Matter:

  • Density: Measure of relative heaviness of objects having constant volume, defined as mass per unit volume. At 4°C, density of water is maximum while its specific volume is minimum. Gases possess very low density.
  • Compression: Gases are more compressible due to large intermolecular spaces; solids are least compressible. Liquids lie in between.
  • Thermal Expansion: Minimum in solids, maximum in gases due to intermolecular force of attraction.

details.summary: Covers density, compression, and thermal expansion properties of matter.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Change of States of Matter:

  • Boiling Point: Conversion of liquid to vapour. Increases with impurities. Decreases at high altitude due to low atmospheric pressure.
  • Melting Point: Conversion of solid to liquid by heating.
  • Sublimation: Solid directly to gas (e.g., naphthalene, camphor).
  • Freezing: Liquid to solid.
  • Evaporation: Liquid to vapour at any temperature; causes cooling.
  • Latent Heat: Heat supplied to change state without changing temperature.
formulas: Latent heat (L) = Quantity of heat (Q) / Mass (m)

details.summary: Definitions of phase changes and latent heat.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Classification of Matter:

  • Elements: Simplest form of matter. Term used by Robert Boyle in 1661. 118 elements known (98 natural).
  • Compounds: Two or more elements in a fixed ratio. Cannot be separated by physical methods. Homogeneous (e.g., water, sugar).
  • Mixtures: Two or more elements/compounds in any ratio.
    • Homogeneous: Uniformly distributed (e.g., salt solution).
    • Heterogeneous: Non-uniform, may exhibit Tyndall effect (e.g., colloidal solutions).

details.summary: Classification into elements, compounds, and mixtures.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Physical and Chemical Changes:

  • Physical Changes: Only physical properties (colour, hardness, density) change; chemical composition remains the same. Examples: Crystallisation, boiling, dissolution of salt/sugar, vaporisation, melting of ice.

details.summary: Distinction between physical and chemical changes.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Combination of elements/atoms to form compounds is governed by following basic laws:

  • Law of Conservation of Mass: Put forth by Antoine Lavoisier in 1789. It states that matter can neither be created nor destroyed but can be converted from one form to another. In a chemical reaction, total mass of reactants is equal to total mass of products.
  • Law of Definite Proportions: A pure compound always contains same elements combined in same proportions by mass, whatever be its source. Given by Joseph Proust, e.g., water obtained from any source like tap water, well water, etc., always contain hydrogen and oxygen in 1:8 mass.
  • Law of Multiple Proportions: Proposed by John Dalton in 1803. It states that when the fixed mass of an element combines with different masses of another element, then the masses of other elements (in two or more compounds) are in the ratio of small whole numbers. e.g., H2O (2g H : 16g O), H2O2 (2g H : 32g O). Thus, ratio of O combining with same mass of H = 1:2.
  • Gay Lussac’s Law of Gaseous Volumes: The volume of reactants and products in large number of chemical reactions are related to each other by small integers, provided the volumes are measured at same temperature and pressure.

details.summary: Overview of fundamental laws governing chemical combinations including Conservation of Mass, Definite Proportions, Multiple Proportions, and Gay Lussac's Law.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Molecules: The term molecule was given by Avogadro. It is the smallest particle of a compound which can exist in free state. All the properties of a compound depend on its constituent molecules. Molecules of a compound contain two or more different types of atoms e.g. ammonia (NH3), water (H2O), etc.

  • Molecular mass: Additive property calculated by adding atomic masses of total atoms in a molecule. e.g., NH3 = 14 + (1)x3 = 17.
  • Equivalent weight: Obtained by dividing molecular or atomic mass by valency.

Mole Concept: The number of molecules present in 12 g of C-12 atom is called one mole. 1 mol = 6.022 x 10^23 = Avogadro’s number.

  • Number of moles = Mass (in g) / Atomic or molecular mass (g mol^-1)
  • 1 mol of atom = 6.022 x 10^23 atoms
  • 1 mol of molecules = 6.022 x 10^23 molecules
  • Atomic mass is the relative mass as compared with an atom of C-12 and is expressed in amu. (1 amu = 1.6 x 10^-24 g).
formulas: Equivalent weight = Molecular mass or atomic mass / Valency
Number of moles = Mass (in g) / Atomic or molecular mass (g mol^-1)

details.summary: Definitions and calculations related to molecules, equivalent weight, and the mole concept.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Atoms are the basis of chemistry. Maharishi Kanad was one of the first to propose that matter is made up of small particles called parmanu. John Dalton called the particles by the name of atom.

Dalton’s Atomic Theory (1808): Based on laws of chemical combination. According to this theory:

  • Atom is the smallest indivisible particle of an element, i.e. it can neither be created nor be destroyed.
  • Atoms of different elements differ in mass, size and chemical properties.
  • Atoms of same or different elements combine together to form compound or molecule. The ‘number’ and ‘kinds’ of atoms in a given molecule is fixed.
  • Atoms of the same elements can combine in more than one ratio to form different compounds.

details.summary: Historical context of atomic theory and the core postulates of Dalton's Atomic Theory.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Atom: The smallest particle of the element that can exist independently and retain all its capable of independent chemical reactions. Atoms are made up of subatomic particles like electrons, protons, neutrons, meson, positron, etc.

Molecule: The smallest particle of an element or a compound existence under ordinary conditions.

Properties of Atom:

  • Atomic Number (Z): Number of protons present inside the nucleus of its atom. Atomic number (Z) = number of protons = number of electrons (in case of neutral atom).
  • Mass Number (A): Total number of protons and neutrons (i.e. nucleons) present in one atom of an element. Mass number (A) = number of protons + number of neutrons = atomic number + number of neutrons = number of electrons + number of neutrons.
formulas: Atomic number (Z) = number of protons = number of electrons
Mass number (A) = number of protons + number of neutrons = atomic number + number of neutrons = number of electrons + number of neutrons
image_descriptions: Diagram showing the representation of an atom with symbol X, atomic number at the bottom left, and mass number at the top right.

details.summary: Definitions and properties of atoms, molecules, atomic number, and mass number.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Properties of subatomic particles:

  • Electron (-1e0): Negatively charged particle, discovered by J.J. Thomson in 1897. Charge = -1.6 x 10-19C, Mass = 9.1 x 10-31g.
  • Proton (1H1): Positively charged particle, discovered by E. Goldstein. Charge = 1.6 x 10-19C, Mass = 1.6 x 10-27kg.
  • Neutron (0n1): Neutral particle, discovered by Chadwick. Mass = 1.6 x 10-27kg.

Note: Hydrogen and protium is the only atom that does not possess neutrons.

details.summary: Properties and discovery details of subatomic particles.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Cathode Rays: Travel in straight line and cast shadows of metallic object. Behaviour similar to negatively charged electrons. First precise measurement of charge on electron made by Robert A. Millikan in 1909.

Anode Rays: Discovered by Engen Goldstein in 1886. Also called canal rays. Travel in straight line and produce mechanical effects. Made up of protons.

details.summary: Discovery of cathode and anode rays.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Nucleus: Heavy and positively charged part at the centre of an atom (dia = 10-14m). Discovered by Rutherford by alpha-particle scattering experiment. Negatively charged electrons revolve around the nucleus in well defined orbits.

Planck's Quantum Theory: Radiant energy emitted or absorbed discontinuously in the form of small discrete packets of energy known as quantum. In case of light, the quantum of energy is called photon.

details.summary: Description of the nucleus and Planck's quantum theory.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Different Atomic Species:

  • Isotopes: Atoms of the same element having the same atomic number (Z) but different mass number (A). Examples: 1H1, 1H2, 1H3; 6C12, 6C13, 6C14; 8O16, 8O17, 8O18; 10Ne20, 10Ne21, 10Ne22.
  • Isobars: Atoms of different elements having the same mass number (A) but different atomic number (Z). Examples: 1H3 and 2He3; 18Ar40, 19K40, 20Ca40; 52Te130, 56Ba130, 54Xe130.
  • Isoelectronic Species: Species having the same number of electrons but different nuclear charge. They have the same bond order. Example: Mg2+ and Na+ both have 10 electrons.
  • Isotones: Atoms having the same number of neutrons. Example: 6C14, 7N15.

Bohr-Bury Scheme:

Describes electron distribution in shells. Maximum electrons in a shell = 2n2 (where n = shell number). K shell (n=1) = 2, L shell (n=2) = 8. Outermost shell cannot have more than 8 electrons.

Quantum Numbers:

  • Principal (n): 1, 2, 3, 4...
  • Azimuthal (l): 0 to n-1.
  • Magnetic (m or ml): -1 to +1 including 0.
  • Spin (s or ms): +1/2, -1/2.
formulas: E = N_0 * h * v = N_0 * h * c / lambda

details.summary: Overview of atomic species (isotopes, isobars, isoelectronic, isotones), Bohr-Bury electron distribution rules, and the four quantum numbers.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Radioactivity: Discovered by Henri Becquerel (1896). Term given by Marie Curie. It is the spontaneous emission of radiations by disintegration of heavy elements.

Types of Radiations:

  • Alpha (α) particles: 2He4. +2 unit charge, mass 4 units. High ionising power. Deflected towards negative plate. Equation: ZXA -> Z-2YA-4 + α
  • Beta (β) particles: Electrons. -1 charge, zero mass. Deflected towards positive plate. Equation: ZXA -> Z+1YA + β
image_descriptions: Nuclear decay equations showing the transformation of parent nucleus X to daughter nucleus Y via alpha and beta emission.

details.summary: Definition of radioactivity, historical discovery, and properties of alpha and beta decay particles.

subject: Chemistry
topic: Gamma Rays and Group Displacement Law
text:
Gamma (γ) rays (no charge and no mass) are not deflected from their path in the electric or magnetic field. These are electromagnetic radiations and have very high penetrating power. Emission of γ-rays is the secondary effect of radioactive charge.

  • Note:
  • 1. Stable nuclei are those for which number of neutrons and protons are equal.
  • 2. The time taken by half of the atoms of a radioactive element to disintegrate is called half-life. Its unit is time^-1.
  • 3. X-rays were discovered by Roentgen in 1896. These are electromagnetic waves of very short wavelength and are used to detect cracks in fractured bones.
  • 4. If the energies of α, β and γ-particles is same, then penetrating power α < β < γ.

Group Displacement Law: This law was put forward by Soddy, Fajan and Russel on the basis of following fact:

  • (i) When a radioactive element emits an α-particle, the atomic number of the resulting nuclide decreases by 4 units e.g., 238/92 U -> 234/90 Th + 4/2 He
  • (ii) When a radioactive element emits a β-particle, the atomic number of the resulting nuclide increases by one unit but the atomic mass remains unchanged e.g., 238/92 U -> 238/93 Np + 0/-1 e

details.summary: Covers properties of Gamma rays, half-life definition, and the Group Displacement Law for alpha and beta decay.

subject: Chemistry
text:
NUCLEAR REACTIONS are of following two types:

Nuclear Fission: The splitting of a heavy nucleus into two smaller of nearly comparable masses and release of about 200MeV of energy is called nuclear fission. Nuclear fission was discovered by ‘Hahn’ and ‘Strassmann’ in 1939.

  • Atom bomb is the result of uncontrolled nuclear fission.
  • The device in which controlled nuclear fission (chain reactions) is carried out is called nuclear reactor. The fission is controlled by absorbing neutrons by using cadmium or boron rods.
  • Heavy water (D2O, molecular weight 20) and graphite are used as moderator for slowing down the fast moving neutrons. U235 is used as a nuclear fuel.

Nuclear Fusion: The union of (two or more) lighter nuclei to form a heavier nucleus is called the nuclear fusion. It is also accompanied by release of energy because the total mass of products is lesser than the total mass of reactants.

  • Nuclear fusion occurs only at extremely high temperature (> 10^6 K), so it is also called thermonuclear reactions.
  • Hydrogen bomb (mixture of deuterium oxide and tritium dioxide) is the result of nuclear fusion.
  • Source of solar (sun) and stellar energy is nuclear fusion.
  • The source of emission of large amount of energy during nuclear fission or fusion processes is conversion of mass into energy. It is given by the relation, E = mc^2 and calculated in MeV.

details.summary: Explains the mechanisms of nuclear fission and fusion, including applications like nuclear reactors, atom bombs, and hydrogen bombs.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Isotopes of all the known elements with Z > 83 are radioactive and are called radioisotopes. These are used for various purposes, e.g. radiocarbon dating is used to determine the age of dead specimen with C^14 content by comparing it with C-12 content.

N = N0 (1/2)^n

where, n = total time(T)/t1/2

N0 = ratio of C^14/C^12 in green plant

N = ratio of C^14/C^12 in wood

Rock dating or uranium dating is used to determine the age of rocks or earth. It is based on 82Pb^206 and 92U^238 ratio.

subject: Chemistry
text:
The forces of attraction like interatomic, intermolecular or interionic forces which holds two or more constituents (atoms, molecules or ions) together are called chemical bonding.

In general, it is believed that atoms combine in order to complete their octet, i.e. 8 electrons in their outermost shell (with the exception of hydrogen and helium in case of which outermost shell can have a maximum of two electrons).

details.summary: Definition of chemical bonding and the octet rule.

subject: Chemistry
text:
An ion is an electrically charged species. A positively charged ion is called cation, e.g. Na+, H+, Mg2+ while a negatively charged ion is called anion, e.g. Cl-, F-, I-.

  • A cation contains less electrons than a normal atom while an anion contains more electrons than a normal atom.
  • When an atom loses one electron, it carries one positive charge, i.e. converted into cation, and if it gains one electron, it carries one negative charge, i.e. converted into anion.
  • There is no change in atomic number or number of protons when an atom forms ion.

details.summary: Definition and properties of cations and anions.

subject: Chemistry
text:
An electron of an atom, located in the outermost shell (valence shell) of the atom, that can be transferred to or shared with another atom is called valence electrons.

  • Elements having same number of valence electrons have similar chemical properties.
  • Elements having 1, 2 or 3 valence electrons in their atoms are metals and form cation while those having 4, 5, 6 or 7 are non-metals and form anion.
  • Elements with 8 valence electrons (except H and He which have 2 valence electrons) are inert, i.e. unreactive and exist as neutral atom.
  • If number of valence electrons = 1, 2 or 3, Valency = Number of valence electrons.
  • If number of valence electrons >= 4, Valency = 8 - number of valence electrons.

details.summary: Definition of valence electrons and rules for determining valency.

subject: Chemistry
text:
The bond formed by the transfer of electrons from one atom (usually metal) to another (usually non-metal) is called electrovalent or ionic compound. In other words, it is an intercoulombic forces of attraction between two oppositely charged species. The number of electrons transferred shows the electrovalency of the atom.

The properties of electrovalent compounds are as follow:

  • They are usually crystalline solids, i.e. have definite shape and are hard and brittle.
  • They have high melting and boiling points.
  • They conduct electricity when dissolved in water or in molten state due to the presence of free or mobile ions.
  • These are soluble in water and insoluble in organic solvents like alcohol, benzene, etc.
  • If the electronegativity difference of two atoms is 1.7, the bond between them is 50% ionic.

subject: Chemistry
text:
The bond formed by the sharing of electrons between two atoms of same or different elements is called covalent bond and the compound is called covalent compound. When a non-metal combines with another non-metal, a covalent bond is formed. Covalent bond may be single, double or triple depending upon the number of sharing pairs of electrons. The number of electrons shared shows the covalency of the element.

The properties of covalent compounds are as follow:

  • Normal covalent compounds are gases or liquid under ordinary conditions of temperature and pressure.
  • These do not conduct electricity (due to the absence of free ions) and are insoluble in water but dissolve in organic solvents.
  • Graphite although is covalent but conducts electricity because of the presence of free electrons (electrical conduction).
  • These show stereoisomerism because covalent bond is directional in nature.

text:
This bond is formed due to the electrostatic force of attraction between hydrogen atom and highly electronegative atom (N, O or F) present in the same or different molecules.

  • Intermolecular H-bonding: Occurs between different molecules of a compound (e.g., H2O, HF, NH3).
  • Intramolecular H-bonding: Occurs in different parts of the same molecule (e.g., o-nitrophenol).

Molecules having O—H, N—H or H—F bond show abnormal properties due to H—bond formation.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Redox Reactions: Reactions involving both oxidation and reduction.

Oxidation: Process involving gain of oxygen or electronegative element or loss of hydrogen or electropositive element or loss of electrons (de-electronation). The positive valency of an element increases by oxidation. e.g., Mg -> Mg2+ + 2e-.

Reduction: Process involving gain of hydrogen or electropositive element or loss of oxygen (electronation) or gain of electrons. Reduction involves decrease in the positive valency of an element. e.g., S + 2e- -> S2-.

Oxidising Agent (Oxidant): Substance which accepts electrons (electron acceptors). Positively charged species behave like oxidising agents. Oxidising agents are Lewis acids.

Reducing Agent (Reductant): Substance which donates electrons (electron donors). Negatively charged species behave like reducing agents. Reducing agents are Lewis bases.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Oxidation State: The real or imaginary charge which an atom appears to have in its combined state. It may be positive, negative, zero or fractional.

Rules for Determining Oxidation State:

  • The oxidation state of an element in its free or uncombined state is zero (e.g., O in O2 and O3 is zero).
  • Oxidation state of hydrogen in most of its compounds is +1 but in metallic hydrides it is -1.
  • Oxidation state of oxygen in most of its compounds is -2. Except peroxides (-1), superoxides (-1/2) and oxygen fluorides (+2 or +1).

details.summary: Rules for determining oxidation states of elements.

subject: Chemistry
text: RANCIDITY: The oils or fats containing materials get oxidised in the presence of oxygen or air and produce foul odour and taste. This process is called rancidity. It is the source of destructive free radicals. A sliced apple turns brown if kept open for sometimes due to oxidation of iron present in the apple. The chips packets are filled with inert gas nitrogen to protect them from being oxidised (or rancid).

• Oxidation state of elements of IA, IIA and IIIA subgroups in their compounds are +1, +2 and +3, respectively.
  • Oxidation state of any ion is equal to its charge present on it.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Gases exhibit dependency on temperature, pressure, volume and mass. These interrelations can be analysed by gas laws. At STP/NTP, temperature (T) = 273.15 K, pressure (p) = 1 atm = 101.35 kPa, volume (V) = 22.4 L mol^-1.

Boyle's Law (Robert Boyle-1662)

At constant temperature, the volume of fixed mass of a gas is inversely proportional to its pressure.

  • V proportional to 1/p [at constant temperature and moles (n)]
  • p1V1 = p2V2

Charles' Law (Jacques Charles-1787)

At constant pressure, volume of fixed mass of a gas is directly proportional to the absolute temperature.

  • V proportional to T [at constant pressure and moles]
  • V1/T1 = V2/T2

Gay Lussac's Law (J.Gay Lussac-1802)

At constant volume, the pressure of fixed mass of a gas is directly proportional to its temperature.

  • p proportional to T
  • p1/T1 = p2/T2 [at constant volume and moles]

Avogadro's Law (Amedeo Avogadro-1811)

At constant temperature and pressure, the volume of any gas is directly proportional to the number of moles of gas.

  • V proportional to n
  • V1/n1 = V2/n2 [at constant T and P]

details.summary: Fundamental gas laws describing relationships between pressure, volume, temperature, and moles.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Gas Equation

The three laws (Boyle's, Charle's and Avogadro's law) can be combined together in a single equation which is known as ideal gas equation.

  • V proportional to 1/p (Boyle's law)
  • V proportional to T (Charles' law)
  • V proportional to n (Avogadro's law)
  • On combining, V proportional to nT/p or V = R(nT/P) or pV = nRT (where, R = gas constant)
  • For 1 mole, pV = RT
  • Value of gas constant, R depends upon the units of measurements. R = 0.0821 L atm mol^-1 K^-1 = 8.3143 J mol^-1 K^-1 = 5.189 x 10^19 eV mol^-1 K^-1 = 1.99 cal mol^-1 K^-1
  • Gas constant, R for a single molecule is called Boltzmann constant (k) or k = R/N = R / 6.022 x 10^23
  • Density of a gas is directly proportional to pressure and inversely related to temperature, i.e. d = pM/RT [where n = Mass (m) / Molecular weight (M)]

Graham's Law of Diffusion (or Effusion)

The rate of diffusion (r) of a gas at constant temperature and pressure is inversely proportional to the square root of its molecular mass, M or density, d.

  • r1/r2 = sqrt(M2/M1) = sqrt(d2/d1)

details.summary: Derivation of the Ideal Gas Equation and Graham's Law of Diffusion.

text: Maxwell and Boltzmann proposed that gas molecules are always in rapid random motion colliding with each other and with the walls of container because of which their velocity changes. On increasing temperature, the velocity or molecular motion increases because of which the rate of reaction increases.

subject: Chemistry
text:
A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more substances on molecular level is called true solution or solution. e.g. lemonade, soda water. The substance which is dissolved in a liquid to make a solution is called 'solute' and the liquid in which the solute is dissolved is called 'solvent'.

A true solution does not scatter light and its particles cannot be seen even by microscope. e.g. salt solution, sea water, sugar solution, copper sulphate solution, vinegar, etc.

Depending upon the amount of solute present, the solutions can be classified as:

  • A solution, in which more quantity of solute can be dissolved without raising its temperature is called an unsaturated solution.
  • A solution, in which no more solute can be dissolved at that temperature is called a saturated solution.

details.summary: Definition and classification of solutions.

subject: Chemistry
text:
The amount of a solute dissolved in unit weight or volume of solution is called strength (concentration) of a solution.

So, concentration of a solution = Amount of solute (in g) / Weight of solution = Amount of solute (in g) / Volume of solution

Different Terms to Express Concentration

  • Parts Per Million: It shows the parts of solute present per million parts of solution, i.e. ppm.
  • Molarity (M): The number of moles of solute dissolved in one litre of solution is called its molarity.
  • Molality (m): The number of moles of solute dissolved in 1000 g of a solvent is called its molality.
  • Normality (N): The number of gram equivalents of solute dissolved in one litre of solution is known as its normality.

Note: Normality and molarity are affected by temperature as these depend upon the volume whereas molality remains unaffected from temperature change.
formulas: Concentration = Amount of solute (in g) / Weight of solution = Amount of solute (in g) / Volume of solution
ppm = Amount of solute (in g) * 10^6 / Volume of solution (in mL)
M = Weight of solute (in g) * 1000 / Molecular weight * volume of solution (in mL)
m = Weight of solute (in g) * 1000 / Molecular weight * weight of solvent (in g)
N = Weight of solute (in g) * 1000 / Equivalent weight * volume of solution (in mL)

details.summary: Formulas and definitions for expressing solution concentration.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Henry's Law

According to this law, 'at particular temperature, the solubility of a gas in a liquid is directly proportional to the pressure of the gas above the solvent.

Its main applications are as follow:

  • Soft drinks and soda water bottles are sealed under high pressure in order to increase the solubility of CO2 in them.
  • To minimise the painful effects (bends) accompanying the decompression of deep sea divers, oxygen diluted with less soluble helium gas is used as breathing gas.
  • Oxygen diluted with nitrogen cannot be used for this purpose due to high solubility of N2 in blood.

Osmosis

It is the process of movement of solvent molecules from the solution of low concentration to high concentration through semipermeable membrane.

  • If pressure greater than osmotic pressure (pressure require to stop osmosis) is applied on the solution of high concentration, reverse osmosis takes place. e.g. desalination of sea water.
  • Isotonic solutions have same concentration and osmotic pressure. e.g. 0.91% solution of pure NaCl is isotonic with human red blood cells (RBCs).

Diffusion

Diffusion is the process of spontaneous mixing of different gases and in this process, molecules of a substance move from higher concentration to lower concentration and goes on until a uniform mixture is formed. Its rate is highest for gases and lowest in solids. e.g. the smell of food being cooked, reaches us even from a considerable distance by the process of diffusion. Due to diffusion the scent spread all over the room if the lid is opened.

details.summary: Definitions and applications of Henry's Law, Osmosis, and Diffusion.

subject: Chemistry
text:
The substances which have sour taste and turn blue litmus to red are called acids.

  • According to Arrhenius acids give hydrogen ion H+ in an aqueous solution. HCl (aq) -> H+(aq) + Cl-(aq)
  • According to Bronsted Lowry concept, acids donate proton (hydrogen ion). HCl + NH3 -> Cl- + NH4+
  • According to Lewis concept, acids have tendency to accept electrons, i.e. these behave as electrophiles. e.g. electron deficient species like BF3, AlCl3, positive ions like Na+, K+ and molecules having multiple bond between dissimilar atoms (e.g. CO2, SO2, etc).
  • Most of the acids contain hydrogen.
  • HCl, H2SO4, HNO3 are mineral acids and are much stronger than organic acids.
  • Aqua-regia is a mixture of concentrated hydrochloric acid and concentrated nitric acid in the ratio 3 : 1. It can dissolve inert materials like platinum, gold, etc.

Properties of Acids

  • Acids liberate hydrogen gas with more reactive metals. e.g. Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2
  • Acids evolve carbon dioxide (CO2) gas with metal carbonates and bicarbonates. e.g. MCO3 + H2SO4 -> MSO4 + H2O + CO2
  • In aqueous solution, they are conductor of electricity due to the presence of free H+ ions.

subject: Chemistry
text:
These substances which have bitter taste and turn red litmus to blue are called bases.

  • According to Arrhenius, bases give hydroxyl ion (OH-) in aqueous solution. e.g. NaOH, KOH, CSOH, Mg(OH)2, etc. NaOH (aq) -> Na+(aq) + OH-(aq)
  • According to Bronsted Lowry concept, bases have a tendency to accept proton, e.g. NH3, H2O, etc. NH3 + H2O <-> NH4+ + OH-
  • According to Lewis concept, bases have a tendency to donate electron pair. e.g. simple anions like Cl-, F-, OH-, etc., molecules containing lone pairs like NH3, R-O-H, R-O-R, etc.

Properties of Bases

  • Base reacts with metal to form salt and liberates hydrogen gas. However, such reactions are not possible with all metals.
  • Water soluble bases are called alkali. Thus, all alkalis are bases but all the bases are not alkali.
  • In aqueous solution and molten state, they are good conductors of electricity.

Acid and Base in a Reaction

  • CH3COOH + H2O -> H3O + CH3COO-
  • Paraldehyde (a carbonyl compound) is used as a hypnotic.
  • Clove oil can be used as indicator.

subject: Chemistry
text:
When acid and base react together, they form salt and water. This reaction is known as neutralisation reaction, e.g. HNO3 + KOH -> KNO3 + H2O

  • When acid and base both are strong, 13.7 kcal energy is released. However, if either the acid or the base is weak, energy released is less than 13.7 kcal because some part of energy is utilised to ionise weak acid or base.

details.summary: Covers neutralisation reaction and energy release characteristics.

subject: Chemistry
text:
KNO3, K2SO4, NaNO3, KCl, NaCl, KNO3 are salts of strong acids and strong bases, so they cannot be hydrolysed and their aqueous solution is neutral.

Solutions of salts of Cl-, SO42-, NO3- with metals other than Na+ and K+ are acidic. e.g. NH4Cl.

Solutions of salts of Na+ and K+ with anions (except SO42-, NO3-, Cl-) are basic, e.g. CH3COONa.

pH SCALE

SPL Sorensen suggested a scale to express the acidity or basicity of an aqueous solution in terms of hydrogen ion concentration known as pH scale.

  • pH = -log[H+]
  • pH = log(1/[H+])
  • [H+] = 10-pH
  • In pure water, [H+] = 10-7, pH = 7
  • In acidic solution, [H+] > 10-7, pH < 7
  • In alkaline solution, [H+] < 10-7, pH > 7

Importance of pH in Everyday Life

  • Bee/Ant sting: Formic acid; remedy is mild base like baking soda or calamine.
  • Wasp sting: Basic; remedy is mild acid.
  • Tooth decay: pH of mouth below 5.5 leads to decay.
  • Acidity: Excess HCl in stomach neutralized by antacids like milk of magnesia [Mg(OH)2] or aluminium hydroxide [Al(OH)3].
  • Agriculture: Crops grow in specific pH ranges (e.g., rice prefers acidic soil, sugarcane prefers neutral, citrus prefers alkaline).

Note: Pickles are kept in glass jars because acid reacts with metal pots to produce poisonous substances.

subject: Chemistry
topic: pOH Scale and Common Ion Effect
text:
pOH Scale

The pOH value of an aqueous solution is defined as the negative logarithm of the hydroxide ion concentration. i.e., pOH = -log[OH-] and pH + pOH = 14.

Common Ion Effect

Addition of a strong electrolyte in the solution of weak acids or bases decreases the ionisation of acid or base due to the presence of common ion. e.g.

H2S (Weak acid) <-> 2H+ + S2-

HCl (Strong acid) -> H+ + Cl-

The reaction goes in the reverse direction due to the common ion effect.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Thermodynamics deals with the study of heat and energy changes occurring during a physical and chemical processes.

  • Open system: Can exchange matter as well as energy with its surroundings (e.g., hot tea in a cup).
  • Closed system: Can exchange energy but not matter with its surroundings (e.g., hot water in a closed beaker).
  • Isolated system: Can exchange neither matter nor energy with its surroundings (e.g., thermos flask).

Thermodynamic Processes:

  • Isothermal Process: Temperature remains constant (dT = 0).
  • Adiabatic Process: No heat enters or leaves the system (dq = 0).
  • Isobaric Process: Constant pressure (dp = 0).
  • Isochoric Process: Constant volume (dV = 0).
  • Cyclic Process: System goes through a series of processes but returns to its initial state (dE or dU = 0).
  • Spontaneous Process: A process that can proceed by itself. It is also known as feasible or probable process. The process is spontaneous if free energy change, ΔG is negative.

details.summary: Overview of thermodynamic systems and types of thermodynamic processes.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Surface Chemistry deals with the phenomenon that occurs at the surface or interfaces.

Catalysis: The term catalyst was given by Berzelius. A catalyst is a substance which alters the rate of reaction without being consumed in it.

General Characteristics of Catalysts:

  • A catalyst remains unchanged in mass and chemical composition during a reaction.
  • Only a small amount of catalyst is sufficient to catalyse a reaction.
  • A catalyst does not initiate a reaction.
  • A catalyst does not change the equilibrium state of a reversible reaction.
  • Free energy change (ΔG°) at equilibrium is zero.

Types of Catalyst:

  1. Positive and Negative Catalysts: Positive catalyst increases the rate of reaction; negative catalyst decreases it.
  2. Induced Catalyst: The product of one reaction acts as catalyst for another reaction.
  3. Catalytic Promoters and Inhibitors: Promoters increase activity, inhibitors decrease activity.
  4. Catalytic Poisons: Destroy the activity of a catalyst completely.

Enzyme Catalysis: Known as biocatalysts. All enzymes are protein in nature and highly sensitive to temperature (optimum 25-37°C).

text: In a colloid, the size of solute particles is bigger than that of true solution but smaller than that of suspension, i.e. lies between 1 to 100 nm. A colloidal solution is a heterogeneous system in which one substance is dispersed as very fine particles in another substance, called dispersion medium.

subject: Chemistry
text: The rapid zig-zag movement executed by colloidal particle is termed as Brownian movement.
