subject: Chemistry
text: It is the branch of chemistry which deals with inter-conversion of chemical energies and electrical energies. It can be converted into electrical energy by means of an electrochemical cell (electrolysis).

subject: Chemistry
text:
• Chemical changes involving production or consumption of electricity are called electrochemical changes.
  • The substance, which allow the electricity to pass through them are called electrolytes. e.g. common salt (NaCl), water (H2O) etc.
  • The substance which do not allow the electricity to pass through them are called non-electrolytes. e.g. sugar, wax, naphthalene etc.
  • A number of metals such as Na, Mg, Ca and Al and a number of chemicals such as NaOH, Cl2, Fe etc. are commercially produced by electrochemical methods.

subject: Chemistry
text: There are two types of emulsions

subject: Chemistry
text:
• Oil in water type e.g. milk in which tiny droplets of liquid fat are dispersed in water.
  • Water in oil type e.g. stiff greases, in which water being dispersed in lubricating oil.

subject: Chemistry
text: During the preparation of emulsion, a small amount of some substances such as soap, gum, agar and protein etc are added to stabilise the emulsion. These substances are known as emulsifying agents.

subject: Chemistry
text:
• Gel is a colloidal system in which dispersed phase is liquid and dispersion medium is solid. e.g. butter, cheese. When a gel is allowed to stand for some time, it loses the dispersed phase (liquid), this phenomenon is called syneresis or weeping of the gel.
  • Fog, clouds, mist are the colloidal systems of liquid in gas.
  • Smoke is a colloidal system of carbon (solid) in air (gas).
  • Foams are the colloidal systems in which a gas is dispersed in liquid. e.g. alcohol, castor oil, shaving cream etc.
  • Digestion of fats in intestine is aided by emulsification.
  • Coagulation is the process of precipitation of colloid when it is shaken with some electrolyte. Its applications are

subject: Chemistry
text:
1. Purification of muddy water by alum.
  2. Ferric chloride and alum are applied on wound to stop bleeding.

subject: Chemistry

Note

  1. Blue colour of sky is due to the scattering of light by dust particles present in air.
  2. The order of energy is 1 calorie > 1 joule > 1 erg.
  3. Milk is a natural emulsion while paint is an artificial emulsion.

subject: Chemistry
text:
It is a device, that produces an electric current from energy released by a spontaneous redox reaction (in short, which converts chemical energy into electrical energy).

This kind of cell includes the galvanic cell or voltaic cell. It has two conductive electrodes, i.e. anode or negative electrode (at which oxidation occurs) and cathode or positive electrode (at which reduction occurs). Electrolyte is filled in between the electrodes and contains freely moving ions.

subject: Chemistry
text:
An arrangement of one or more cells connected in a series, is called a battery. It is basically a galvanic cell.

Batteries are of two types :

subject: Chemistry
text: 1. Primary Batteries (non-rechargeable) These batteries act as galvanic cell and used only once. e.g. dry cell, mercury cell etc.

subject: Chemistry
text: Secondary Batteries (rechargeable): These act as galvanic as well as electrolytic cell and can be reused. e.g. lead storage battery, nickel-cadmium battery.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Fuel Cells: These are galvanic cells, which use energy of combustion of fuels like hydrogen (H2), methane (CH4), methanol (CH3OH) etc., as the source to produce electrical energy. e.g. hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell. This cell was used for the first time in Apollo space programme. The byproduct of this cell, i.e. water vapours, were condensed and used by the astronauts for drinking.

Advantages:

  • Fuel cells are more efficient than conventional power stations or batteries etc.
  • With a fuel cell there are fewer stages in producing the useful energy, so there is less opportunity to lose potentially useful energy, e.g. waste heat, friction from moving parts etc.
  • A hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell is a non-polluting clean fuel since, the only combustion product is water.

Disadvantages:

  • Fuel cells cannot be used for large scale energy production, so conventional fossil fuels or nuclear power stations still have an important future.
  • Hydrogen is a gas and requires a much larger storage volume as compared to fossil fuels like petrol.
  • Safe storage is also an issue, especially as it would be stored under high pressure to decrease the storage space required. This immediately makes leaks and, accidents more likely to happen because hydrogen is a highly flammable explosive gas, too easily ignited.
  • Efficient large scale technology is not yet developed to produce hydrogen on large scale, e.g. from electrolysis using solar power electricity, photovoltaic power system, wind turbines or hydroelectric power.
  • Although water is cheap and plentiful, it requires expensive electrical energy to electrolyse water to split it into hydrogen and oxygen.

details.summary: Detailed explanation of fuel cells, their advantages, and disadvantages.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Electrolysis: The process, in which a non-spontaneous reaction is carried out by using electrical energy is called electrolysis and the instrument or container, in which the process of electrolysis is done, is called electrolytic cell.

Electrolysis of brine (the water saturated or nearly saturated with salt, usually sodium chloride) gives hydrogen and chlorine. The products are gaseous.

Reactions:

  • NaCl -> Na+ + Cl-
  • H2O -> H+ + OH-
  • At anode: 2Cl- -> Cl2 + 2e- (Oxidation)
  • At cathode: 2H+ + 2e- -> H2 (Reduction)
  • Na+ + OH- -> NaOH
  • Net reaction: NaCl + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2 + Cl2

Note: During electrolysis, electrolytes get decomposed at the electrodes.

Uses:

  • In the production of oxygen for spacecraft and nuclear submarines.
  • In layering metals to fortify them.
  • In production of hydrogen for fuel.
  • In electrolytic etching of metal surfaces like tools or knives with a permanent mark or logo.
  • In electroplating, electrorefining, electroprinting, electro-metallurgy and industrial preparation.

subject: Chemistry
text:
When metals are arranged in the increasing order of their standard reduction electrode potential, a series is obtained, which is called electrochemical series. It is also called reactivity series (as reactivity follows the reverse order). Lower is the value of reduction potential, greater would be its reducing power.

Depending upon the reactivity, the occurrence of metals in the reactivity series may be represented as shown in the figure. Thus, gold is the least reactive metal and hence, found in native state. The more reactive metals of the series can displace the less reactive metals from their salt solutions.

e.g., Cu + FeSO4 → No reaction; but Fe + CuSO4 → FeSO4 + Cu. Moreover, metal placed before H can evolve H2 from dilute acids. e.g., Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + H2. The metals placed above are good reducing agent and reduces the metal oxides of the metal placed below them.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Corrosion is the process of oxidative deterioration of a metal surface by the action of environment to form unwanted corrosive products. e.g. conversion of iron into rust (Fe2O3 · xH2O). Corrosion of iron is called rusting. Tarnishing of silver (due to the formation of Ag2S), development of green coating [of Cu(OH)2 · CuCO3 (basic copper carbonate)] on copper and bronze. It is basically an electrochemical process. It is accelerated by the presence of impurities, H+, electrolytes such as NaCl and gases such as CO2, SO2, NO, NO2 etc.

Prevention of Corrosion:

  • By coating with a suitable material (barrier protection viz paint, grease, metals like Zn, Cu, Ni, Cr, Sn), adherent film of iron phosphate, adherent coating of magnetic oxide (Fe3O4).
  • By alloying with suitable metals.
  • By cathodic protection—the metal is made cathode by application of external circuit.
  • By using artificial anode (sacrificial protection), more anodic metal (like Zn, Mg, Al etc.,) is connected to iron article by a wire. In such cases, current flows towards more reactive metal and prevents iron from corrosion.
  • By galvanisation (covering of iron article with zinc).

subject: Chemistry
text:
Classification of Elements:

  • In 1896, Mendeleev gave a periodic law. According to which “the properties of elements are the periodic function of their atomic masses”.
  • There were seven periods (horizontal rows) and eight groups (vertical columns) in the periodic table of Mendeleev having 63 known elements at that time.
  • Moseley modified Mendeleev’s periodic law and proposed modern periodic law. According to modern periodic law, “the properties of elements are periodic function of their atomic numbers.”
  • There are eighteen vertical columns, known as groups and seven horizontal rows, known as periods, in the long form of periodic table.
  • Periodic Properties: The properties which are repeated at regular intervals are known as periodic properties. Atomic and ionic size, electron affinity, ionisation potential, electronegativity, electropositive character, acidic or basic character, metallic nature, etc., are some important periodic properties.

Characteristics of Periods:

  • The number of valence electrons in elements increases from 1 to 8 on moving from left to right in a period.
  • The elements in a period have consecutive atomic numbers.
  • The valency of the element increases from 1 to 4 and then decreases to 0 (zero) on moving from left to right in a period, with respect to hydrogen.
  • Atomic size, electropositive character, metallic character, reducing nature of elements and basic nature of oxides all decrease from left to right in a period.

details.summary: Historical development of the periodic table from Mendeleev to Modern Periodic Law, and trends within periods.

subject: Chemistry
text:
All the elements of a group of the periodic table have the same number of valence electrons and hence, have almost similar chemical properties.

  • Atomic radius, electropositive nature, metallic nature, reducing nature of elements and the basic nature of oxides increase from top to bottom in a group.
  • Electronegative nature, ionisation potential, electron affinity, electronegativity, non-metallic nature and acidic nature of oxides decrease down a group with increasing atomic number.

details.summary: Periodic trends within groups of the periodic table.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Hydrogen:

  • Hydrogen is the first element in the periodic table with atomic number 1 and mass number 1.
  • Hydrogen has three isotopes-protium or ordinary hydrogen (1H1), deuterium or heavy hydrogen (1H2 or 1D2), tritium (1H3 or 1T3). Tritium is the radioactive isotope of hydrogen.
  • Hydrogen is a non-supporter of combustion and burns with 'pop' sound. It is an inflammable gas.

Water:

  • Water is the neutral oxide of hydrogen. Pure water freezes at 0°C and boils at 100°C. This abnormal high boiling point is due to the association of H2O molecules through hydrogen bonding.
  • Water is a polar compound (dipole moment 1.85 D) and possesses a high dielectric constant, i.e. 81. Its presence is tested by using anhydrous copper sulphate which turns blue in the presence of water.
  • Water is a universal solvent because of its tendency to form H-bond and polar nature.
  • Water has very high specific heat and thus, widely used as a coolant.
  • Water which form lather with soap is called soft and which does not form lather is called hard water as the ions present in it form scum (precipitate) with the soap.

details.summary: Properties of Hydrogen, its isotopes, and water.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Hardness of Water:

  • Hardness of water may be due to the presence of bicarbonates of calcium or magnesium (temporary hardness) or due to the presence of chlorides or sulphates of Ca or Mg (permanent hardness).

Removal of Hardness of Water:

  • Temporary hardness is removed by boiling or by adding lime water (Clark's process).
  • Permanent hardness is removed by adding sodium carbonate (washing soda, Na2CO3) or calgon (sodium hexa metaphosphate, Na6P6O18 or zeolite which is also called permutit (hydrated sodium aluminium silicate, Na2Al2Si2O8·xH2O).
  • From sea water, pure water is obtained by a process, called reverse osmosis, i.e. by applying pressure higher than the osmotic pressure towards the solution side. This process is also called desalination of sea water.
  • Boiling, chlorination and treatment with UV irradiation all kill the microorganisms present in water.

details.summary: Types of water hardness and methods for removal.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Heavy Water:

  • Heavy water (D2O, molecular weight = 20) is the oxide of heavy hydrogen. It is used as a moderator in nuclear reactors.
  • In hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) oxygen is in -1 oxidation state, which is the intermediate oxidation state of oxygen. H2O2 behaves as an oxidising, reducing and bleaching agent.
  • Lead painting becomes blacken in air due to the formation of PbS by the action of H2S present in air, H2O2 is used to wash it. H2O2 oxidises PbS to PbSO4.

Aquifers:

  • An aquifer is an underground layer of water bearing permeable rock, i.e. they have opening through which only liquids and gases can pass.
  • Clay layers although are poor aquifers. This is because clay minerals are dense impermeable materials. They act as aquiferal, i.e. a layer of material that is almost impenetrable to water.

details.summary: Properties of heavy water, hydrogen peroxide, and definition of aquifers.

subject: Chemistry
text:
It is the process of extraction of metals from their ores is called metallurgy.

  • Metals occur in the form of minerals in nature.
  • Gangue or matrix are the impurities associated with ore.
  • Roasting is the process of heating ore (mainly sulphide ore) in the excess of air whereas calcination is heating the ore (carbonate or hydroxide ore) in the absence or limited supply of air.
  • Flux is added to gangue to convert it into slag.
  • Ores are the minerals from which metal is extracted conveniently and beneficially.

subject: Chemistry
text:
• Lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium and caesium are alkali metals and are s-block elements.
  • These metals are soft and can be cut with knife.
  • Lithium is the lightest metal.
  • Alkali metals are stored under kerosene or paraffins to protect them from the action of air.
  • Lithium shows diagonal relationship with magnesium.
  • In Castner's process, metallic sodium is prepared by electrolysis of molten NaOH.
  • Sodium is used in yellow light lamps.
  • Sodium chloride (NaCl) or common salt or table salt is used in our daily diet, as a preservative for pickles, meat and fish. It is also used in the manufacture of NaOH, Cl2 gas and soap.
  • Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) or caustic soda is used in the soap, dyes and artificial silk industries and in the refining of bauxite mineral.
  • Sodium bicarbonate is used in the kitchen for making food tasty and crispy. Sodium bicarbonate (sodium hydrogen carbonate or baking soda) is used for making baking powder, which is a mixture of baking soda and a mild edible acid such as tartaric acid. It is also an ingredient of antacids. Being alkaline, it neutralises excess acid in the stomach and provides relief. It is also used in soda acid fire extinguishers.
  • Sodium carbonate decahydrate (Na2CO3·10 H2O) or washing soda is used in the manufacture of glass, soap, washing powder and for softening hard water.
  • Sodium sulphate (Na2SO4·10H2O) is Glauber's salt. It is used as purgative.
  • Sodium thiosulphate (Na2S2O3·5H2O) is also known as hypo. It is used in photography as a fixing agent because it removes the undecomposed AgBr as soluble silver thiosulphate salt.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Elements of IB Group: 29Cu, 47Ag, 79Au are the elements of I B group. These elements are called coinage or currency metals. Their important properties are as follow:

  • They are d-block, transition elements.
  • These are very hard, malleable and ductile metals.
  • They have high density and high melting and boiling points.
  • CuSO4 is used as a mordant in dyeing. Copper sulphate pentahydrate is blue in colour and is called blue vitriol. CuSO4 is used to test the presence of water.
  • Copper is alloyed with gold and silver for making ornaments.
  • AgNO3 is called lunar caustic. It is stored in dark brown bottles because it is photosensitive.
  • Au, Ag, Pt, etc., metals which remain unaffected by the action of other strong acids dissolve in aqua-regia (which is a mixture of HCl and HNO3 in 3 : 1).

subject: Chemistry
topic: Elements of IIA Group (Alkaline Earth Metals)
text:
Elements of IIA Group (Alkaline Earth Metals):

  • II A subgroup elements are Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba and Ra. They are called alkaline earth metals and are s-block elements.
  • Calcium of this family is most abundant element in the earth's crust while magnesium is present in chlorophyll, the green pigment of the leaf.
  • Beryllium shows diagonal relationship with aluminium.
  • Mg(OH)2 is called milk of magnesia. Being a mild base, it is used as an antacid to neutralise the excess acid present in the stomach.
  • MgSO4 is used as a mordant in dyeing and tanning industry. It is also used as a purgative.
  • Calcium oxide (CaO), also called quicklime, gives hissing sound when dissolved in water. It is used in the manufacture of glass, calcium chloride, cement, mortar, bleaching powder, calcium carbide, slaked lime, etc. It is also used in the extraction of iron and as a drying agent for ammonia and alcohol.
  • Calcium hydroxide (slaked lime) [Ca(OH)2], is used in the manufacturing of bleaching powder, caustic soda and soda lime and for softening of hard water.
  • When CaCO3 is dipped in water, the bubbles evolve due to the evolution of carbon dioxide.
  • Calcium sulphate is gypsum (CaSO4 · 2H2O). It loses a 2/3rd part of its water of crystallisation when heated at 120°C to form (CaSO4)2 · H2O which is known as Plaster of Paris.
  • Gypsum is used in the preparation of building's plaster and anhydrous, CaSO4.
  • Anhydrous CaSO4 is a dehydrating agent and is used for the manufacture of ammonium sulphate (Sindri fertiliser) and sulphuric acid.
  • Plaster of Paris is a white powder, which sets into hard mass called gypsum on hydration with water, so it is used in making casting for statues, toys, for plastering fractured bones, etc.
  • Cement has the following composition: Calcium oxide (CaO, 50-60%), alumina (Al2O3, 5-10%) and magnesium oxide (MgO, 2-3%). Raw materials used for its preparation are limestone and clay. When cement mixed with water, the setting of cement takes place to give a hard mass. This is due to the hydration of the molecules of the constituents and their rearrangement. Adding gypsum is only to slow down the process of setting time of the cement.
  • Portland cement is a mixture of silicates and aluminates of calcium with small amount of gypsum. The chemical composition of portland are CaO, SiO2, Al2O3, SO3MgO, Fe2O3, silica SiO2 imparts strength to the cement due to the formation of dicalcium and tricalcium silicates.
  • Alumina (Al2O3) imparts quick setting property to the cement. It acts as a flux and lowers the clinkering temperature.

Elements of IIB Group:

Elements of III A Group (Boron Family):

  • Elements are 5B, 13Al, 31Ga, 49In and 81Tl.
  • Boron is a semi-metal. Rest of elements are metals.
  • Aluminium is the most abundant metal (and third most abundant element) in the earth's crust.
  • Boron halides are Lewis acids. The order of acidity is BBr3 > BCl3 > BF3.
  • Being lighter, all alloys are used in making aeroplanes.
  • Aluminium sulphate is used as a mordant in dyeing.

  • All are p-block elements.
  • The stability and volatility of tetrahalide of carbon decrease with increasing molecular weight of the tetrahalide e.g. CF4 > CCl4 > CBr4 > CI4.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Carbon forms the highest number of compounds due to its catenation power and tetravalency. It has two crystalline allotropes: Diamond and graphite.

Diamond

  • Purest form of carbon with a rigid three-dimensional network structure; each carbon atom is bonded to four other carbon atoms in tetrahedral fashion.
  • Hardest substance and a bad conductor of electricity.
  • Used in jewellery and as an abrasive for sharpening hard tools (rock drilling, glass cutting).

Graphite

  • Layered two-dimensional hexagonal structure.
  • Prepared artificially by Acheson process.
  • Good conductor of electricity.
  • Used as dry lubricant and in nuclear reactor as a moderator.

Note: Fullerenes form another class of carbon allotropes. The first one to be identified was C-60 which has carbon atoms arranged in the shape of football.

details.summary: Properties and uses of Diamond, Graphite, and Fullerenes.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Coal is the amorphous variety of carbon used as fuel. Types:

  • (a) Peat (60% carbon).
  • (b) Lignite or brown coal (70% carbon).
  • (c) Bituminous (78-83% carbon).
  • (d) Anthracite (90% carbon).

Charcoal can be animal charcoal, wood charcoal, sugar charcoal and activated charcoal. Used in manufacture of fuel gases like water gas (CO + H2), producer gas (N2 + CO) and as a deodorant/purifier.

details.summary: Classification of coal and types/uses of charcoal.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Air contains 0.03%-0.05% CO2. Solid CO2 is known as dry ice. It produces very low temperature (-100°C) with ether, used as a freezing mixture. It is a non-supporter of combustion, used as fire extinguisher.

When passed through lime water, it turns milky due to formation of calcium carbonate. In excess, the precipitate dissolves due to formation of soluble calcium bicarbonate.

subject: Chemistry
text:
• Organic Compounds: Chemistry of hydrocarbons and their derivatives. Urea (NH2CONH2) was the first organic compound prepared in laboratory by Wohler. Acetic acid (CH3COOH) was the first organic compound synthesised from its elements by Kolbe. Main sources are plants, animals, coal and petroleum.
  • Saturated Hydrocarbons (Alkanes): Contain C—C bond. General formula CnH2n+2 (n=1, 2, 3...). Carbon atoms are sp3-hybridised. Methane (CH4) is the first member, found in marshy land and coal mines (fire-damp).
  • Unsaturated Hydrocarbons: Contain C=C or C≡C bonds. Alkenes (Olefins): General formula CnH2n. First member C2H4 (ethylene). Alkynes (Acetylenes): General formula CnH2n-2. First member C2H2 (acetylene).
  • Aromatic Hydrocarbons: General formula CnH2n-6. Contain benzene ring. Benzene (C6H6) first synthesised by Berthelot.
  • Haloalkanes: General formula CnH2n+1X (X = Cl, Br, I).

subject: Chemistry
text:
Tertiary alkyl halide structure: R1-C(R2)(R3)-X

  • Common name: Alkyl halide; IUPAC name: Haloalkane.
  • Haloforms: Trihalo methane are called haloforms, e.g., chloroform (CHCl3), iodoform (CHI3).
  • Chloroform: Oxidises to COCl2 (carbonyl chloride or phosgene gas) in the presence of air and light. Kept in closed dark coloured bottles and mixed with ethyl alcohol as a negative catalyst. Used as a general anaesthetic.
  • Chloropicrin (CCl3NO2): Used as an insecticide and tear gas.
  • Carbon tetrachloride (CCl4): Used for extinguishing fire under the name pyrene.
  • Ethylene dibromide: Added to petrol in place of tetraethyl lead to save the environment from lead pollution.
  • Chlorofluorocarbons (freons or CFC): Used as refrigerants. Contain carbon, chlorine, hydrogen and fluorine; destroy the ozone layer.

2. Alcohols

  • General formula: CnH2n+1OH
  • Common name: Alkyl alcohol; IUPAC name: Alkanol.
  • Classification: Primary (R-CH2OH), secondary (R2CH-OH), tertiary (R3C-OH).
  • Lucas reagent: Conc. HCl + anhydrous ZnCl2; used to distinguish between primary, sec and tert-alcohols.
  • Methanol (CH3OH): Produced by destructive distillation of wood (wood spirit). Used as solvent for paints, varnishes, dyes, drugs, perfumes, and as motor fuel with petrol.
  • Destructive distillation of wood: Yields wood gas, tar, charcoal, methyl alcohol, and acetic acid.
  • Destructive distillation of coal: Yields coal gas (H2 + CH4 + CO), ammoniacal liquor, coal tar and coke.
  • Ethanol (CH3CH2OH): Ethyl alcohol or grain alcohol. Unfit for drinking when mixed with methanol or pyridine (methylated spirit or denatured alcohol).
  • Ethanol properties: Changes colour of sodium or potassium dichromate from orange to green. Used in manufacture of paints, varnishes, transparent soap, chloroform, and as fuel in internal combustion engines.

text:
• 3. Ethers: General formula CnH2n+2O. Common name: Dialkyl ether; IUPAC name: Alkoxy alkane. Behave like Lewis bases. Diethyl ether (C2H5OC2H5) is an industrial solvent and anaesthetic.
  • 4. Aldehydes: General formula CnH2n+1CHO or CnH2nO; IUPAC name: Alkanal. 40% formaldehyde is formalin (preservation of dead animals). Benzaldehyde is almond extract. Paraldehyde is a hypnotic. Eugenol is active component of clove oil.
  • 5. Ketones: General formula CnH2nO or (CnH2n+1)2O; IUPAC name: Alkanone. Ketones with -COCH3 (methyl ketonic group) give yellow colour in iodoform test. Acetone (CH3COCH3) is the first member, used as nail polish remover. Methyl Ethyl Ketone (MEK) is a paint stripper. Aldehydes and ketones with alpha-hydrogen atom give aldol condensation.
  • 6. Carboxylic Acids: General formula CnH2n+1COOH or CnH2nO2; IUPAC name: Alkanoic acid. First member is formic acid (HCOOH) present in ant/bee sting. HCOOH is the strongest carboxylic acid. CH3COOH is ethanoic or acetic acid (vinegar). Vinegar contains 6-10% acetic acid. Acetic acid is used in rubber manufacture from latex and casein from milk. Lactic acid is alpha-hydroxy propanoic acid, present in milk.

subject: Chemistry
text:
SOAPS

Soaps are the sodium or potassium salts of long chain carboxylic (fatty) acids (RCOONa) e.g. sodium palmitate (C15H31COONa), sodium stearate (C17H35COONa) and sodium oleate (C17H33COONa) etc. Animal fat or vegetable oil, sodium hydroxide, sodium chloride act as the raw materials for the manufacture of ordinary soap. The process of making soap is called saponification.

  • Soaps do not form lather with hard water due to the formation of scum.
  • When the medium is acidic, soaps form insoluble long chain fatty acids and hence, lost their cleansing action.

DETERGENTS

  • These are also called "soap-less" soaps as they do not contain any soap.
  • These are the long chain benzene sulphonic acid or the sodium salt of the long chain alkyl hydrogen sulphate.
  • Long chain hydrocarbons, sulphuric acid and sodium hydroxide are the raw materials for the manufacturing of detergents.
  • These are non-biodegradable and cause water pollution. However, straight chain detergents are biodegradable.
  • They form lather with soft as well as hard water.

details.summary: Comparison of soaps and detergents, their chemical composition, and properties.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Polymers

A polymer is a compound of high molecular weight formed by the union of a large number of molecules of one or two types of low molecular weight (known as monomers) and the process involving the formation of a polymer is called polymerisation.

Types of Polymers

On the basis of their origin, the polymers are classified in the following manner:

  1. Natural Polymers: These are found in nature, e.g. cellulose, starch, rubber, silk etc.
  2. Synthetic Polymers: These are prepared in the laboratory by synthetic means, e.g. polythene, nylon, orlon, dacron, etc.
  3. Semi-synthetic Polymers: These are synthesised by man from natural substances, e.g. rayon (a polymer of cellulose nitrate) is also called artificial silk due to its silk like appearance.

On the basis of intermolecular forces, these are classified as:

  1. Elastomers: In these polymers, the polymer chains are held together by weak van der Waals' forces, e.g. vulcanised rubber.
  2. Fibres: In this type, polymer chains are attached with one another through H-bonds, e.g. nylon-6,6.
  3. Thermoplastics: In these, the intermediate of elastomers and fibres. These are soften on heating and become hard on cooling, e.g. polystyrene, polythene, PVC, etc.
  4. Thermosetting: These are highly cross-linked, hard, non-fusible and insoluble polymers. These can only be moulded to desired shape on heating once. e.g. bakelite (phenol-formaldehyde resin), melamine, etc.

Some Important Synthetic Polymers

  • Polyethylene (polythene): The monomer units are ethylene molecules. It is frequently used in making coats, milk cartons and electrical insulation.
  • Polystyrene: The monomer units are styrene molecules. It is a white thermoplastic material and is used for making toys, combs, lining material for refrigerators and TV cabinets.
  • Teflon (Polytetrafluoroethylene): The monomer unit is tetrafluoroethylene molecule. It is very tough material. It is a bad conductor of electricity and is used in coating utensils, making seals, baskets, pipes, flooring, etc.
  • Polyvinyl Chloride (PVC): The monomer units are vinyl chloride molecules. PVC is a hard, horny material. It is resistant to chemicals as well as heat. It is used for making raincoats, hand bags, electrical insulators and floor covering.
  • Nylon or Nylon-6, 6: It was first fully synthetic fibre and has good elasticity, low water absorption and wrinkle resistant. It has also high tensile strength. It is used in making fishing nets, tyre cord, parachute fabrics, ropes, etc.

details.summary: Classification of polymers by origin and intermolecular forces, plus descriptions of common synthetic polymers.

subject: Chemistry
text:
• Phenol-formaldehyde Resins (Bakelite): Made by the reaction of phenol and formaldehyde in the basic medium. It is a cross-linked thermosetting polymer used for making combs, fountain pen barrels, electrical goods, and handles of crockery. Sulphonated bakelites are used as ion-exchange resins for softening hard water.
  • Rubber: A polymer of isoprene (2-methyl buta-1, 3-diene). It is insoluble in water, dilute acids, and alkalis, absorbs a large amount of water, and has low tensile strength and elasticity.
  • Neoprene: A synthetic rubber resembling natural rubber. Obtained by the polymerisation of chloroprene (2-chlorobuta-1, 3-diene). It is superior to natural rubber in stability and used for making hoses, shoe heels, stoppers, etc.
  • Buna-S: A copolymer of 1, 3-butadiene and styrene. Also known as SBR (Styrene-Butadiene Rubber). It has slightly less tensile strength than natural rubber and is used in the manufacturing of automobile tyres and rubber soles.
  • Terylene or dacron or phthalate: A polymer of ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid. It is a polyester used for making wash and wear fabrics, tyre cords, safety belts, and tents.
  • Vulcanisation of Rubber: The process of heating rubber with sulphur to make it hard, strong, and more elastic.
  • Kevlar: A polymer of terephthalic acid and 1,4-diaminobenzene; it is a polyamide used for making bulletproof vests.
  • Lexan or polycarbonate: A polymer of diethyl carbonate and bi-phenol. Used in making bulletproof windows and safety helmets.
  • Polyurethanes: A polymer of toluene diisocyanate and ethylene glycol. Used for making washable and long-lasting mattresses, cushions, and pillows.
  • Lucite: A polymer of methyl methacrylate. Used for making contact lenses. Also known as Plexiglass, acrylite, or perspex.
  • Orlon or Acrilon Polyvinyl Cyanide: A polymer of vinyl cyanide or acrylonitrile. Used as a substitute for wool in making synthetic blankets (acrylic fibres).

details.summary: Overview of various synthetic polymers, their chemical composition, and industrial applications.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Repeated cultivation of crops makes the soil deficient in elements, mainly nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. Substances added to the soil to make up for this loss are called fertilisers.

  • Basic Calcium Nitrate (Nitrate of lime) [CaO·Ca(NO3)2]: A good nitrogenous fertiliser used in acidic soil.
  • Ammonium Sulphate [(NH4)2SO4]: Contains 21.2% nitrogen. Repeated use makes soil acidic and unfit for seed germination; addition of lime becomes necessary.
  • Calcium Cynamide [CaCN2] (Nitrolim): Black in colour due to carbon; contains 19% nitrogen.
  • Urea [NH2CONH2] (Carbamide): Contains 46.6% nitrogen. It is the best nitrogenous fertiliser as it leaves only carbon dioxide after assimilation by plants; does not change soil pH.
  • Superphosphate of Lime [Ca(H2PO4)2·2CaSO4·H2O]: A phosphatic fertiliser.
  • Vermicompost: Process of composting using worms (red wigglers, white worms, earthworms) to create a mixture of decomposing vegetables or food, bedding material, and water-soluble nutrients.
  • Macronutrients: Magnesium, manganese, and sulphur are provided by inorganic fertilisers.

details.summary: Classification and characteristics of various nitrogenous and phosphatic fertilisers and the process of vermicomposting.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Substances which produce energy in the form of heat upon combustion are called fuels (e.g., coal, wood, kerosene, petrol, diesel, cooking gas). Fuel efficiency is expressed in terms of calorific value (kJg^-1).

  • Sulphur compound (ethyl mercaptan or thioethanol): Added to odourless LPG to impart a detectable smell.
  • LPG: Contains mainly butane and some propane.
  • CNG (Compressed Natural Gas): Contains mainly methane; used in vehicles as it produces less pollutants than petrol or diesel.
  • Petrol vs Diesel: Petrol is used for cars and aeroplanes; diesel is used for trucks, buses, trains, and ships.
  • Quality Metrics: Petrol quality is expressed in octane number; diesel quality is expressed in cetane number.
  • Propellants: Synthetic rubber, liquid ammonia, and liquid hydrogen.
  • Acetylene: Used in gas welding to weld/cut metals at 300°C flame temperature.

details.summary: Definitions and properties of various fuels, including LPG, CNG, and quality metrics like octane and cetane numbers.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Renewable and Non-renewable Resources

  • Natural resources such as coal, petroleum and natural gas take thousands of years to from naturally and cannot be replaced as fast as they are being consumed. It is a non-renewable resource.
  • Natural resources such as solar energy, water and fisheries are renewable resources.

details.summary: Distinction between renewable and non-renewable natural resources.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Petroleum

It is dark oily liquid also called rock oil, mineral oil, crude oil or black gold. On fractional distillation, it gives different substances at different temperatures.

details.summary: Definition and properties of petroleum.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Biogas or Gobar Gas

The gaseous mixture obtained by the degradation of animal and plant wastes by anaerobic microorganisms in the presence of water is called biogas. It is a convenient fuel for domestic use. It is used for street lighting.

  • Constituents of biogas are methane (45-70%), carbon dioxide, hydrogen, hydrogen sulphide.
  • Gobar gas is produced by the fermentation of cow dung. It contains CH4 (main component), CO2 and H2.
  • Note: Bagasse is the fibrous matter remains after sugarcane stacks are crushed to extract their juice. It is used as a biofuel and as a substitute for wood in many tropical and subtropical countries for the production of pulp, paper, board, etc.

details.summary: Composition and production of biogas and gobar gas, including a note on bagasse.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Flame

A flame is a region where combustion of gaseous substances take place. Innermost region of flame is black because of the presence of unburned carbon particles. Middle region is yellow luminous due to partial combustion. Outermost region is blue due to complete combustion of fuel which is the hottest part of the flame.

details.summary: Structure and characteristics of a flame.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Paint

It is a mixture of four ingredients, viz, binder, solvent, pigment and additives (like driers, plasticisers, emulsifiers, corrosion inhibitors, etc).

  • Binders are polymers (resins) forming a continuous film on the surface of the substrate. These are responsible for good adhesion. Resins, chlorinated rubber, latex (PVA) are the examples of binders.
  • Solvent (water or organic solvents like toluene, ketone, alcohol, etc.) is a medium where all other ingredients of paint are dispersed in molecular form (true solutions) or as colloidal dispersion (emulsions).
  • Pigments are responsible for imparting colour to the paint. It may also protect the substrate from UV light.
  • Ultramarine blue is the natural pigment made up of semiprecious mineral lapis lazuli. It is resistant towards fading.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Air

  • Composition of air is nitrogen (78.084%), oxygen (20.946%), argon (0.934%), carbon dioxide (0.033%) and small amount of other gases. Region of air present around the earth is called atmosphere.
  • Main layers from the surface of earth towards upward: (a) Troposphere (b) Stratosphere (c) Mesosphere (d) Thermosphere
  • Most of the atmospheric air is present in troposphere.
  • Ozone layer present in the stratosphere region (at a height of about 20 to 40 km) protects the living beings from the harmful UV radiations coming from the sun. Due to high concentration of ozone, this region is also known as ozonosphere.
  • In 1775, French scientist Lavoisier performed experiments on composition of air.

details.summary: Composition of air, atmospheric layers, and the ozone layer.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Air Pollution

It is due to the presence of foreign undesirable substances in air. The substance which causes pollution is known as pollutant. Main air pollutants are SO2, CO, nitrogen oxides, particulates, etc.

Carbon monoxide CO combines with the haemoglobin of the blood about 300 times more readily as compared to oxygen and forms a stable carboxyhaemoglobin complex due to which supply of oxygen is restricted which results in headache, nervousness, asphyxia and even death in some cases.

Major gaseous air pollutants: (a) Oxides of carbon (b) Oxides of nitrogen (c) Oxides of sulphur (d) Hydrocarbon (esp CH4)

details.summary: Definition of air pollution, effects of carbon monoxide, and major gaseous pollutants.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Methyl isocyanate (CH3NC) is responsible for the Bhopal gas tragedy (in 1984). In which thousands of people were killed. It was a case of serious air pollution in which MIC (Methyl Isocyanate) gas released from a pesticide manufacturing plant of union carbide.

Smog: The word smog is derived from smoke and fog. It is of two types:

  • Classical Smog: It is also called London smog. It is formed in cool humid climate and is reducing in nature.
  • Photochemical Smog: It is also called Los Angeles smog. It is formed in warm, dry and sunny climate and is oxidising in nature.

Particulates: These are minute solid particles and liquid droplets dispersed in air such as mists, dusts, smoke, etc.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Greenhouse effect: It is the heating up of earth and its objects due to trapping of infrared radiations (IR) by greenhouse gases present in atmosphere like CO2, CH4, NO, O3, chlorofluorocarbon and water vapours.

Global Warming: It is due to increased concentration of greenhouse gases due to melting of ice caps and glaciers, spreading of several infectious diseases like malaria, sleeping sickness, etc.

Acid Rain: The pH of normal rain water is 5.6-6.5 due to the dissolution of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. When the pH of rain water is below 5, it is called acid rain (by Robert Augus). The main cause of acid rain is oxides of sulphur and nitrogen (H2SO4 and HNO3).

Ozone Layer Depletion: Thinning of ozone layer because of its reaction with chlorine free radicals usually generated by chlorofluorocarbons is called ozone layer depletion.

details.summary: Explanation of greenhouse effect, global warming, acid rain mechanisms, and ozone layer depletion chemistry.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Water pollution is due to the presence of foreign substances, i.e water pollutants in water.

  • Cholera, dysentery, typhoid, etc., are water-borne diseases caused by bacteria.
  • Mercury causes minimata disease, chromium and arsenic causes cancer and cadmium causes itai-itai disease.
  • Presence of excessive fluoride leads to dental fluorosis, i.e. developmental disturbance of dental enamel.
  • The usual effect of agricultural run off due to the excessive increase of nutrients such as nitrogen, phosphorus etc., in an ecosystem like ponds or results in excessive algal growth in affected water bodies. It is called eutrophication.
  • For clean water, DO (Dissolved Oxygen) is 5-6 ppm and BOD (Biochemical Oxygen Demand) is less than 5 ppm.
  • Recycling, sewage treatment, incineration are some strategy to control water pollution.
  • Presbycusis is gradual hearing loss in both ears that commonly occurs in aged people but noise pollution also lead to it.

details.summary: Overview of water pollutants, associated diseases, eutrophication, and water quality parameters (DO and BOD).

subject: Chemistry
text:
Atomic Structure

  • Neutrons are present in all atoms except Hydrogen (H).
  • Positive rays in a discharge tube with perforated cathode travel parallel to the anode.
  • The increasing order (lowest first) for the value of e/m (charge/mass) is e, p, n, alpha.
  • The atomic number of an element is the number of protons.
  • Mass number is the sum of protons and neutrons.
  • Isotopes have the same number of protons but different number of neutrons.
  • Cathode rays travel in straight lines.
  • Electrons are the fundamental particles of an atom.

details.summary: Basic concepts of atomic structure including subatomic particles, isotopes, and properties of cathode/anode rays.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Chemical Bonding and Redox Reactions

  • Cation: A positively charged ion formed when an atom loses electrons, resulting in more protons than electrons.
  • Valency: The combining capacity of an element.
  • Ionic Bond: Formed by the transfer of electrons between atoms.
  • Covalent Bond: Formed by the sharing of electrons between atoms.
  • Hydrogen Bonding: A type of dipole-dipole attraction between molecules, not a true chemical bond.
  • Molten NaCl: Conducts electricity due to the presence of free ions.

details.summary: Brief overview of concepts related to atomic structure, bonding types, and electrical conductivity in ionic compounds.

Acids: An acid is a substance which:

  • donates a proton
  • accepts an electron pair
  • gives H+ in water

subject: Chemistry
text:
Chemical Thermodynamics and Surface Chemistry

  • A system which can exchange energy with the surroundings but no matter is called a closed system.
  • When a gas is subjected to adiabatic expansion, it gets cooled due to energy spent in doing work.
  • If a refrigerator's door is kept open, the room will be heated.
  • When ammonium chloride is dissolved in water, the solution becomes cold (endothermic).
  • 1 calorie > 1 joule > 1 erg.
  • In a jet engine, exchange of energy and matter takes place.
  • When a strong beam of light is passed through a colloidal solution, the light is scattered (Tyndall effect).
  • Colloidal solution commonly used in the treatment of eye disease is colloidal antimony.
  • Colloidal solution commonly used as a germ killer is colloidal silver.
  • Fog is an example of a colloidal system of liquid in a gas.
  • An emulsion consists of two liquids.
  • Artificial rain is caused by spraying neutral charged colloidal dust over a cloud.
  • The bleeding of a wound is stopped by the application of ferric chloride because blood reacts and a solid is formed which seals the blood vessels.
  • Dialysis can separate glucose from human blood.
  • The path of light becomes visible in a cinema hall (Tyndall effect) observed in all except sugar solution.

**Quicklime (calcium oxide) reacts with water**

When quicklime (CaO) is dissolved in water it reacts vigorously, releasing heat and producing a characteristic hissing sound due to rapid gas evolution.

> Reaction: CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂  (exothermic)

subject: Chemistry

**Elements of a group share similar chemical properties**

All elements belonging to the same vertical group in the periodic table exhibit comparable chemical behaviour because they have the same valence‑electron configuration.

subject: Chemistry

**Carbon dioxide turns lime water milky**

When CO₂ is bubbled through calcium hydroxide solution (lime water), it forms insoluble calcium carbonate, giving the solution a milky appearance.

> Reaction: Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃↓ + H₂O

subject: Chemistry
content:
**Hard water hinders soap lather**

Hard water contains high concentrations of calcium (Ca²⁺) and magnesium (Mg²⁺) ions. These cations react with the fatty‑acid salts of soap to form insoluble precipitates (scum), preventing the formation of a stable lather.

subject: Chemistry
content:
**Magnesium produces brilliant white light in fireworks**

When magnesium metal burns, it emits an intense white flame due to the excitation of Mg atoms. This property makes it a preferred component for white‑light pyrotechnic effects.

subject: Chemistry
content:
**Diamond is the three‑dimensional allotrope of carbon**

In diamond, each carbon atom is tetrahedrally bonded to four other carbon atoms, creating a rigid, three‑dimensional network that gives diamond its exceptional hardness.

subject: Chemistry
content:
**Mercury and bromine are liquids at 25 °C and 1 atm**

Among the elements, only mercury (Hg) and bromine (Br₂) are liquids under standard ambient conditions. (Chlorine is a gas, and helium is a noble gas.)

subject: Chemistry
content:
**Carbon forms the greatest number of compounds**

Carbon’s ability to catenate (form long chains) and to bond with many other elements results in an enormous variety of organic and inorganic compounds, more than any other element.

subject: Chemistry

**Calcium chloride is a white solid that readily absorbs water vapour**

CaCl₂ is highly hygroscopic; it deliquesces on exposure to atmospheric moisture, making it useful as a drying agent and in moisture‑control applications.

subject: Chemistry

**Granite is mainly composed of silica (SiO₂) and aluminium‑bearing minerals**

The primary constituents of granite are quartz (silica) and feldspar minerals, which are rich in aluminium silicates.

subject: Biology
text:
Biology is the branch of science concerned with the study of living organisms. The term 'biology' is coined by Lamarck and Treviranus. The study of plants is called Botany, while study of animals is called Zoology.

THE CELL: Cell is the basic structural and functional unit of all the living organisms. The word 'cell' comes from the Latin word cellula which means a 'small room'.

  • Living organisms may consist of one or more cells, according to this there are two types of organisms, i.e. unicellular (composed of single cell) and multicellular (composed of many cells).

'Non-living parts of cell' branches into 'Cell wall', 'Vacuoles', 'Fat droplets', 'Granules', and 'Waste materials'.

text:
Types of Cells:

On the basis of the organisation, complexity and variety, all cells can be grouped into two types:

  • (i) Prokaryotic cell: It is a simpler cell, lacking a true nucleus, i.e. nuclear membrane is absent in these cells, e.g. bacteria, mycoplasma, etc.
  • (ii) Eukaryotic cell: It is a complex cell with double membrane bound nucleus, e.g. plant and animal cells. Eukaryotic organisation is seen in all the protists, plants, fungi and animals.

Bacteria: Microscopic prokaryotic organisms whose single cell have neither a membrane enclosed nucleus nor other membrane enclosed organelles like mitochondria and chloroplasts.

  • The bacterial cell wall is strong and rigid.
  • Murein or peptidoglycan or mucopeptide is present in the cell wall.
  • Bacteria are mainly of two types: (i) Archaebacteria (obligate anaerobes), (ii) Eubacteria (true bacteria).
  • Examples: Staphylococcus aureus (causes boils, pneumonia, food poisoning), Staphylococcus thermophilus (yoghurt flavour), S. lactis (milk production).

subject: Biology
text:
Cell Wall

A rigid and solid covering that gives shape and strong structural support to the cell. It is a non-living structure.

  • Middle lamella: Composed of calcium pectate (chief component) and magnesium pectate.
  • Primary cell wall: Composed of cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin. Rigidity is due to lignin.
  • Secondary cell wall: Composed of cellulose and hemicellulose.
  • Tertiary cell wall: Present in tracheids of gymnosperms.
  • Bacterial cell wall: Composed of peptidoglycan or murein.
  • Fungal cell wall: Composed of chitin.

Functions of Cell Wall: Prevents cell from bursting or collapsing, allows material passage, and wards off pathogens.

Cell Membrane or Plasmalemma: Innermost layer of cell envelope, semipermeable. Consists of protein (52%), lipid (40%) and carbohydrate (5-10%). The 'fluid mosaic model' was given by Singer and Nicolson. Includes Pinocytosis (cell drinking) and Phagocytosis (cell eating).

subject: Biology
text:
Cell cycle is an orderly sequence of events or stages by which a cell duplicates its genome, synthesises the other constituents of the cell and eventually divides into two daughter cells. It is a cyclic process, which involves cell growth and cell division.

Cell division is an essential process in all living organisms. The mode of cell division is fundamentally similar in all organisms. During cell division, the processes like DNA replication and cell growth must take place in a sequential manner to ensure the correct division and formation of progeny cells with intact genome. Cell cycle involves two phases, i.e. interphase followed by M-phase.

1. Interphase

It is the period between the end of one cell division to the beginning of the next cell division (i.e. between true successive M-phase). Interphase is further divided into following three substages on the basis of various synthetic activity:

  • (i) G1-phase (Gap 1): It corresponds to the duration between the mitosis (M-phase) and initiation of replication of DNA. Cell grows, becomes metabolically active, but does not undergo DNA replication. Some time after G1-phase cell may enter S-phase and continue the cell cycle or it may enter into G0-phase. In G0-phase the cells leave cell cycle.
  • (ii) S-phase (Synthesis): It is known to be the phase, in which actual synthesis or replication of DNA takes place. In case of animal cell, during S-phase DNA replication begins inside the nucleus, while the duplication of centrioles takes place in the cytoplasm.
  • (iii) G2-phase (Gap 2): This phase is also called post-synthetic or pre-mitotic phase. During this stage, the synthesis of DNA stops and proteins required for M-phase are being synthesised, while the growth of the cell continues. It prepares the cell to undergo divisions.

2. M-phase

M-phase is the actual phase of cell division. It may occur in two way depending upon the type of cell, it is taking place in, i.e. mitosis (vegetative cell) or meiosis (generative cell).

details.summary: Detailed explanation of the cell cycle, including interphase (G1, S, G2 phases) and M-phase.

subject: Biology
text:
Mitosis is a type of cell division in which chromosomes replicate themselves and get equally distributed into daughter nuclei, i.e., the chromosome number in the parental and the progeny becomes same.

The four phases of mitosis are:

  • Prophase: Chromosome deviation in chromatids starts and nuclear membrane and nucleolus disappear.
  • Metaphase: Chromosomes line up in the middle and spindle fibres from centriole connect to each chromatid (half of chromosome).
  • Anaphase: Chromatids are pulled apart to separate poles and the membrane begins to pinch off in the middle.
  • Telophase: Complete division of cytoplasm (cytokinesis) and two cells are formed. Two daughter cells, which are formed by mitosis have same/equal number of chromosomes. It results in formation of somatic cells.

details.summary: Overview of Mitosis process and its four phases.

subject: Biology
text:
Meiosis is a type of cell division that results in the formation of four daughter cells each with half the chromosome number of the parent cell.

In the process of meiosis, there are two main stages:

Meiosis-I

It is further divided into four phases:

  • Prophase-I: The longest phase of meiosis-I. It is composed of five substages:
    • Leptotene: Chromatins condense to form chromosome.
    • Zygotene: Pairing of homologous chromosomes called synapsis, in this phase, synaptonemal complex is formed.
    • Pachytene: Crossing over between non-sister chromatids.
    • Diplotene: Longest duration phase, in which chiasmata formation takes place.
    • Diakinesis: It involves slipping of chiasmata called terminalisation.
  • Metaphase-I: Lining of chromosomes in the middle. Formation of spindle apparatus takes place and each centromere is joined by chromosomal fibres.
  • Anaphase-I: Separation of homologous chromosomes (disjunction) to form two cells with haploid number of the chromosomes.
  • Telophase-I: This is the last stage of meiosis-I, two cells with n number of chromosomes are formed.

Meiosis-II

It is very similar to mitosis.

  • Prophase-II: The shortening and thickening of the chromatids.
  • Metaphase-II: Lining of chromosomes in the middle.
  • Anaphase-II: Separation of chromosomes into chromatids.
  • Telophase-II: Uncoiling and lengthening of the chromosomes, four daughter cells with haploid set of chromosomes are formed.
tables:
| Mitosis | Meiosis |
|---|---|
| Found in somatic cells. | Found in diploid reproductive cells. |
| Forms two identical diploid cells. | Forms four haploid cells. |
| Every chromosome behaves independently. | Homologous chromosomes show pairing. |
| Chromosome number remains constant. | Chromosome number becomes half. |
| Crossing over does not occur. | Crossing over occurs. |

details.summary: Detailed breakdown of Meiosis-I and Meiosis-II phases and comparison with Mitosis.

subject: Biology
text:
Taxonomy is the branch of science that deals with the principles and procedures of biological classification. Classification means the ordering of organisms into groups. The classification results in an organised system, which is essential for the naming and cataloging of future specimens and reflects inter-relationships between living organisms. Biologists use method of classification to understand the evolutionary history and it provides an organised way of studying characteristics of living organisms.

Carolus Linnaeus is the Father of Taxonomy. 'Systema Naturae' and 'Species Plantarum' books are written by Carolus Linnaeus.

details.summary: Definition of taxonomy and historical context regarding Carolus Linnaeus.

subject: Biology
text:
Nomenclature means providing distinct and proper names to organisms. Two codes are:

  • ICBN: International Code of Botanical Nomenclature
  • ICZN: International Code of Zoological Nomenclature

Binomial nomenclature was given by Linnaeus. It uses two terms: genus and species (e.g., Mangifera indica).

  • Categories: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.
  • Genus and species terms proposed by John Ray.
  • Smallest unit: species.

Classification Systems:

  • Linnaeus (1758): Two kingdom classification (Plantae and Animalia).
  • Copeland (1956): Four kingdom classification.
  • Whittaker (1969): Five kingdom classification.

subject: Biology
text:
Classification of Plants: Plant Kingdom is divided into Cryptogamae and Phanerogamae. Cryptogamae includes Thallophyta, Bryophyta, and Pteridophyta.

(i) Thallophyta: Simplest, primitive plants. Body is an undifferentiated mass called thallus. Lack vascular tissues. Includes algae and lichens.

(a) Algae: Photosynthetic, aquatic, chlorophyll-containing thallophytes. Lack vascular tissue.

  • Chlorella: Sewage oxidation tanks.
  • Chlorella: Source of antibiotic chlorellin.
  • Laminaria: Source of iodine.
  • Gelidium and Gracilaria: Source of agar.
  • Spirogyra: Pond silk.

(b) Fungi: Non-vascular, heterotrophic, spore-forming eukaryotic organisms. Store food as glycogen. Cell wall of chitin or fungal cellulose.

  • Albugo candida: White rust of crucifers.
  • Puccinia graminis tritici: Black rust of wheat.
  • Rhizopus stolonifer: Fumatic acid.
  • Aspergillus: Aflatoxin.
  • Agaricus: Mushroom (filamentous structure called hyphae).

(c) Lichens: Symbiotic relationship between algae and fungi. Indicators of water pollution.

subject: Biology
text:
(ii) Bryophyta: Called amphibians of plant kingdom.

  • Lack vascular tissue.
  • Roots generally absent.
  • Examples: Riccia, Marchantia, Funaria.
  • Zoopsis: Smallest bryophyte.
  • Dawsonia: Largest moss.
  • Sphagnum: Used for dressing of wounds.

(iii) Pteridophyta: Name from Greek Pteris (fern) and phyton (plant).

  • Seedless vascular plants with body differentiated into true roots, stems, and leaves.
  • Secondary growth absent.
  • Examples: Selaginella, Equisetum, Dryopteris (male shield fern), Azolla, Marsilea, Salvinia (aquatic ferns), Adiantum (maiden hair fern), Cyathium (tree fern).

details.summary: Characteristics and examples of Bryophyta and Pteridophyta.

subject: Biology
text:
Phanerogamae are also known as spermatophytes. They include those plants which produce seeds. They are divided into two major types:

  • Gymnosperms: The term comes from Greek word Gymno (naked) and sperma (seed). These are vascular plants (possess xylem and phloem). Seeds are naked (no outer covering). Pollination is anemophily (by wind). Examples: Cycas (most primitive), Pinus (resin/turpentine), Ginkgo (living fossil), Ephedra (ephedrine), Sequoia gigantia (tallest), Rhynia (most primitive).
  • Angiosperms: Seed bearing, flowering vascular plants. Seeds are enclosed within fruits. Double fertilisation takes place. Examples: mustard plant (Brassica campestris). Divided into:
    • Monocots: Single cotyledon (e.g., maize, rice, grass).
    • Dicots: Two cotyledons (e.g., pea, rose, cotton, sunflower).

details.summary: Overview of Phanerogamae classification into Gymnosperms and Angiosperms.

subject: Biology
text:
Animals are classified to study relationships in animal groups. Storer and Usinger classified animals into phyla:

  • Phylum-Protozoa: Unicellular eukaryotic organisms. Metabolic activities (digestion, respiration, excretion, reproduction) occur in the unicellular body. Respiration/excretion via diffusion (e.g., Amoeba, Paramecium, Plasmodium).
  • Phylum-Porifera: Multicellular, marine, porous body. Pores are called ostia. Skeleton made of minute calcareous or silicon spicules (e.g., Sycon, sponge).
  • Phylum-Coelenterata: Aquatic, possess thread-like tentacles for holding food. Specialized cnidoblast cells for catching food. Hydra has regeneration capacity (e.g., Hydra, jellyfish, sea anemone).
  • Phylum-Platyhelminthes: Flatworms. Excretion via flame cells. No skeleton, respiratory, or circulatory system. Hermaphrodite. Internal parasites (e.g., Planaria, liver fluke, tapeworm).
  • Phylum-Aschelminthes: Nematoda or round worms. Long, cylindrical, unsegmented, unisexual. Complete alimentary canal. No circulatory/respiratory system. Excretion via protonephridia. Parasitic or free-living (e.g., Ascaris, threadworm).

details.summary: Classification of animals into various phyla including Protozoa, Porifera, Coelenterata, Platyhelminthes, and Aschelminthes.

subject: Biology
text:
• Wuchereria bancrofti (filaria) is a human parasitic roundworm causing elephantiasis (filariasis), spread by the Culex mosquito.
  • Phylum Annelida: Segmented worms with long, thin, soft bodies.
  • Alimentary canal is well-developed; nervous system is normal; blood is red.
  • Respiration occurs through skin; excretion via nephridia.
  • Movement via setae made of chitin (e.g., earthworm, Neries, leech).
  • Earthworms are hermaphrodites with four pairs of hearts; body is sensitive to acidic conditions, basic temperature, and humidity.

details.summary: Characteristics of Phylum Annelida and parasitic roundworms.

subject: Biology
text:
• Phylum Arthropoda: The largest phylum of Animalia.
  • Main feature: Jointed legs. Body divided into head, thorax, and abdomen, covered by a chitinous exoskeleton.
  • Circulatory system is open type.
  • Cockroach heart has 13 chambers; respiration via spiracles, trachea, or book lungs.
  • Insects have six feet and four wings (e.g., cockroach, prawn, crab, bug, housefly, mosquito).
  • Arachnids possess 8 legs (e.g., spider).
  • Ants and termites are social animals living in colonies.
  • Insect bites release formic acid, causing itching, swelling, and redness.

details.summary: Characteristics of Phylum Arthropoda.

subject: Biology
text:
• Phylum Mollusca: Soft, unsegmented bodies divided into head, muscular foot, and visceral hump, covered by a hard calcareous shell.
  • Alimentary canal is well-developed; respiration via gills or ctenidia.
  • Blood is blue due to haemocyanin; excretion via kidneys (e.g., Pila, Aplysia, Doris, Octopus, Sepia).
  • Phylum Echinodermata: All marine animals with a water vascular system.
  • Brain is not developed; special capacity for regeneration (e.g., starfish, sea urchin, sea cucumber).

details.summary: Characteristics of Phylum Mollusca and Echinodermata.

subject: Biology
text:
• Phylum Hemichordata: Formerly a sub-phylum of Chordata, now a separate phylum under non-chordata.
  • Phylum Chordata: Possess a notochord and dorsal hollow tubular nerve cord with paired pharyngeal gill slits.
  • Subdivided into Protochordata and Vertebrata.
  • Group Pisces: Aquatic, cold-blooded animals. Heart has two chambers and pumps impure blood.
  • Includes Cyclostomata (jawless fishes like lampreys), Chondrichthyes (cartilaginous fishes like Indian shark), and Osteichthyes (bony fishes like sea-horse).
  • Group Tetrapoda: Classified into four classes.
  • Amphibia: Cold-blooded, live on land and water. Respiration via gills, skin, and lungs (e.g., frog, Necturus, Ichthyophis, salamander). Water frogs respire through lungs on land.
  • Reptilia: Cold-blooded, crawling animals with flexible skeletons and two pairs of limbs. Eggs covered in calcium carbonate shells (e.g., lizard, snake, tortoise, crocodile, turtle, Sphendon).
  • Cobra is the only snake that makes nests. Sea snake (Hydrophis) is the world's most poisonous snake. Heloderma is the only poisonous lizard.

details.summary: Classification and characteristics of Chordata, Pisces, and Tetrapoda.

subject: Biology
text:
Aves

  • The animals of this group are warm-blooded (endothermic), tetrapod vertebrates with flight adaptation and show the property of Homeothermy.
  • Homeothermy is the thermoregulation that maintains internal body temperature regardless of external influence.
  • They respire through lungs.
  • Birds have no teeth, beak helps in feeding, e.g. crow, peacock, parrot, etc.
  • Flightless birds are kiwi and emu. Largest alive bird is Ostrich.
  • Smallest bird is humming bird.
  • Largest zoo in India is Alipur (Kolkata) and the largest zoo of the world is ‘Cruiser National Park’ in South Africa.

details.summary: Characteristics and facts about the class Aves.

subject: Biology
text:
Mammalia

  • They are heterotrophs, mostly omnivorous organisms.
  • These are warm-blooded or endothermic animals.
  • Tooth comes twice in these animals (diphyodont).
  • There is no nucleus in its red blood cells (except in camel and llama). Skin of mammals have hairs. External ear is present, e.g. human, whale, platypus, kangaroo, etc.
  • Mammals are divided into three subclasses:
    • Prototheria: It lays eggs, e.g. Echidna.
    • Metatheria: It bears the immature child, e.g. kangaroo.
    • Eutheria: It bears the well-developed child, e.g. humans, cow, etc.
  • Mammals give birth to young ones but Echidna and duck-billed platypus are the only egg laying mammals.
  • Bats have poor vision, but can fly in dark due to the production of ultrasonic waves by them.
  • Cheetah is the fastest mammal.
  • Blue whale is the largest mammal.
  • Spiny anteater is the most primitive mammal.
  • Gorilla is largest ape.
  • Panthera tigris is the largest animal of cat family.
  • Dolphin is the national aquatic animal of India.
  • Homo sapiens is the commonest mammal.
image_descriptions: A hierarchical flowchart titled 'Classification of animals' showing the division into Invertebrates (animals without backbone) and Vertebrates (animals with backbone). Invertebrates include: Protozoans (single-celled, microscopic), Flatworms (soft-bodied), Annelid worms (segmented), Echinoderms (spines), Coelenterates (soft-bodied, stinging cells), Molluscs (soft-bodied), Arthropods (hard external skeleton, jointed limbs), Arachnids (eight legs, two body parts), Crustaceans (hard exoskeleton, segmented body), Insects (wing, six-legged), Myriapodes (many legs, single pair of antennae). Vertebrates include: Fishes (scales, gills, cold-blooded), Reptiles (dry scaly skin, lay eggs on dry land, cold-blooded), Mammals (fur/hairs, warm-blooded), Amphibians (moist slimy skin, lay eggs in water, cold-blooded), Birds (feathers, wings, beaks, lay eggs, warm-blooded).

details.summary: Characteristics, classification, and notable facts about the class Mammalia.

subject: Biology
chapter: Genetics and Molecular Biology and Evolution of Life
text:
Gregor Johann Mendel is known as the Father of Genetics. The term 'Genetics' was first used by William Bateson in 1905.

  • Genetics is the process of transfer of character (traits) from one generation to next generation through genes.
  • A gene is known as the molecular unit of heredity of a living organism.
  • Dr. Hargovind Khorana (1968) discovered the genetic code and its function in protein synthesis.

Mendel's Experiments

GJ Mendel for the first time conducted experiments to understand the pattern of inheritance of variation in living organisms.

  • He conducted hybridisation (crossing) experiments on garden pea (Pisum sativum) for seven years and proposed the laws of inheritance in living organisms.
  • Mendel conducted artificial pollination/cross-pollination experiments using several true-breeding lines of pea.
  • A true-breeding line refers to one that have undergone continuous self-pollination and expressed stable traits for several generations.
  • Mendel selected 14 true-breeding pea plant varieties, which were similar except for one character with contrasting traits.

In 1900, Mendel's work was 'rediscovered' by three European scientists, Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns and Erich von Tschermak.
tables:
| Characters | Contrasting traits (Dominant) | Contrasting traits (Recessive) |
|---|---|---|
| Stem height | Tall | Dwarf |
| Flower colour | Violet | White |
| Flower position | Axial | Terminal |
| Pod shape | Inflated | Constricted |
| Pod colour | Green | Yellow |
| Seed shape | Round | Wrinkled |
| Seed colour | Yellow | Green |

details.summary: Overview of the history of genetics, Gregor Mendel's contributions, and the experimental setup using Pisum sativum.

subject: Biology
chapter: Genetics and Molecular Biology and Evolution of Life
text:
Mendel's laws of inheritance are based on his observations on monohybrid and dihybrid crosses. He summarised his findings into following three laws:

Law of Dominance

  • (a) Law of dominance states that, when two alternative forms of a trait or character (genes) are present in an organism, only one factor expresses itself in F1 progeny and is called dominant, while the other whose expression remain masked is called recessive.
  • (b) This shows that crossing between pure organisms for two contrasting characters produce only one character in F1-generation and both in F2-generation.

Law of Segregation

  • (a) This law states that, though, F1 hybrid, alleles for dominant and recessive characters remain together, but these alleles do not show any blending and both the characters are recovered as such in the F2-generation.
  • (b) These two co-existing alleles of an individual for contrasting trait segregate (separate) during gamete formation, so that each gamete receive only one of the two alleles.
  • (c) Alleles again unite during fertilisation of gametes.

Law of Independent Assortment

  • (a) It is also known as inheritance law and it states that alleles for one character assort independently of alleles for another character during gamete formation.
  • (b) When two pairs of traits are combined in a hybrid, segregation of one pair of character is independent of the other pair of characters during gamete formation.

Note: Back cross is performed between F1 hybrid and one of its parent whether dominant or recessive, while test cross is a cross between F1 hybrid and recessive parent only.

Exceptions to Principle of Dominance and Principle of Paired Factors

  • Incomplete dominance is the phenomenon, in which phenotype of the F1 hybrid offspring does not resemble any of the parent, but it is an intermediate between the expression of two alleles in their homozygous state. Red and white flowering true breeding lines of Mirabilis jalapa when crossed, they shows F1 hybrid having pink flowers, i.e. incomplete dominance (exception to dominance law).
  • Codominance is the phenomenon, in which two alleles of a hybrid express themselves independently. In this, offsprings show resemblance to both the parents. ABO blood group system in humans is the well-known example of codominance.

details.summary: Detailed explanation of Mendel's three laws of inheritance and exceptions including incomplete dominance and codominance.

subject: Biology
text:
The ABO blood group system was discovered by the Austrian scientist Karl Landsteiner. ABO blood grouping is controlled by the gene I. The plasma membrane of the Red Blood Cells (RBCs) has sugar polymers that protude from its surface. These gene controls the kind of sugar protruding from RBC. The gene I has three alleles, IA, IB and i. The alleles IA and IB produce a slightly different form of sugar, while allele i does not produce any sugar.

On the basis of the presence or the absence of the antigen A or B, four types of blood groups are present, which are A, B, AB and O.

  • For transfusion purpose the Rhesus factor and ABO grouping are the two most important compatibility factors to consider.
  • An individual may be Rh+ or Rh--factor. In simpler term, if an individual's blood type is A and positive for the Rhesus factor, then he or she is deemed to be 'A+'.

| Allele from parent 1 | Allele from parent 2 | Genotype of offsprings | Blood types of offsprings |
|---|---|---|---|
| I^A | I^A | I^A I^A | A |
| I^A | I^B | I^A I^B | AB |
| I^A | i | I^A i | A |
| I^B | I^A | I^A I^B | AB |
| I^B | I^B | I^B I^B | B |
| I^B | i | I^B i | B |
| i | i | i i | O |
