    • (iv) Distal Convoluted Tubule (DCT).

Bowman's Capsule

  • It is a double-walled cup and is lined by thin flat cells called podocytes.
  • It contains group of capillaries called glomerulus.
  • Glomerulus in the kidney acts as a dialysing bag.

Proximal Convoluted Tubule (PCT)

  • It is a highly coiled (convoluted) tubular structure.
  • It is about 12-24 mm in length.
  • Almost whole of vitamins, glucose, amino acids, sodium and potassium, etc., is reabsorbed here, mainly by active transport.

Henle's Loop

  • It is a U-shaped segment of nephron located in renal medulla.
  • Loop of Henle is long in mammals and birds, which secrete hypertonic urine, but short in other vertebrates like reptiles, etc.

Distal Convoluted Tubule (DCT)

  • It is similar to PCT region, i.e. greatly curved twisted.
  • It is connected to the collecting duct.
  • Active reabsorption of some Na+ takes place here.
  • It is impermeable to H2O.
  • Renal tubules along with large intestine accounts for most of the absorption of water in body.

Urine

  • Urine is formed after glomerular filtration, reabsorption and secretion. It is pale-yellow coloured transparent fluid due to the presence of urochrome pigment. It is acidic in nature and is slightly heavier than water.
  • It has a faint aromatic odour due to urinod.
  • Daily urine output in normal adult is 1.5-1.8 L.
  • Chemical composition of urine, i.e. water is 95-96%, urea is 2% and some other substances like uric acid, creatinine, etc., are 2-3%.
image_descriptions: Diagram of the human excretory system showing the inferior vena cava, aorta, left kidney, right kidney, renal artery, renal vein, ureter, urinary bladder, and urethra.

details.summary: Overview of the human excretory system components (ureters, bladder, urethra), nephron structure, and urine composition.

subject: Biology
text:
Skeleton System

The human skeleton consists of both fused and individual bones supported and supplemented by ligaments, tendons, muscles and cartilage, ligaments and tendons are connective tissue made up of collagen fibres. It is divided into two parts:

(i) Axial Skeleton (80 Bones)

  • It includes skull, vertebral column and bones of chest.
  • Vertebral column is responsible for the upright position of the human body.
  • Most of the body weight is located in back of the spinal column.
  • It provides flexibility to the neck and protection to spinal cord.
  • The total number of bones of head is 29.
  • The total number of bones in vertebral column is initially 33 and after development is 26.
  • The total number of bones of ribs is 24.

details.summary: Introduction to the human skeleton system and specific details regarding the axial skeleton.

subject: Biology
text:
(ii) Appendicular Skeleton (126 Bones)

  • It consists of pelvic and pectoral girdles.
  • Girdles are the structures, which connect the limb bones with the vertebral column.
  • Their functions are to make locomotion possible and to protect the major organs of locomotion, digestion, excretion and reproduction.
  • Calcium and phosphorous are two minerals that helps in giving strength to bones. Deficiency of these may cause we opening of bones.

details.summary: Details about the appendicular skeleton, including its components, functions, and important minerals for bone strength.

subject: Biology
text:
NERVOUS SYSTEM

The nervous system provides the fastest means of communication within the body, so that suitable response to stimuli can be made at once.

Nervous system is found only in animals and absent in plants. It is made up of nervous tissue. Nervous system controls the body by using a series of tissues throughout the body formed by a network of electrically conducting cells called neurons or nerve cells.

details.summary: Introduction to the nervous system, its function as a communication means, its presence in animals, and its composition of neurons.

subject: Biology
text:
Neuron

It is the structural and functional unit of nervous system.

Neurons are of three types:

(i) Motor Conducts messages from central nervous system to effector organs.

(ii) Sensory Conducts information from sensory organ to central nervous system.

(iii) Mixed Works both as sensory and motor neuron.

details.summary: Definition of a neuron as the structural and functional unit of the nervous system, and its three types: motor, sensory, and mixed.

subject: Biology
text:
Structure of Neuron

A neuron is a microscopic structure composed of three major parts, i.e. cell body, dendrites and axon.

  • Dendrites Cytoplasmic processes from cell body. They carry impulses towards cell body.
  • Cell body Also called cyton or soma. It contains cytoplasm and certain granular bodies called Nissl's granules.
  • Axon Single long extension of cell body that protected by membrane neurolemma.
  • Synapse It is the junction between the dendrites of one neuron with axon terminal knobs of other neuron.

details.summary: Detailed description of the structure of a neuron, including dendrites, cell body (cyton/soma), axon, and synapse.

subject: Biology
text:
Classification of Neuron/Nerve Cell

Neurons are of two types:

  1. Myelinated Axon is composed of Schwann cell coated by myelin sheath. The gap between adjacent myelin sheath is called nodes of Ranvier.
  2. Non-myelinated Axon is composed of Schwann cells not enclosed by myelin sheath.
image_descriptions: Diagram showing classification of neurons based on the number of axon and dendrites. It illustrates three types: Unipolar (with one axon), Bipolar (with one axon and one dendrite), and Multipolar (with one axon and two or more dendrites).

details.summary: Classification of neurons into myelinated and non-myelinated types, with a description of nodes of Ranvier. Also includes a diagrammatic classification based on axon and dendrite count.

subject: Biology
text:
Types of Nervous System

Main parts of nervous system are as follow:
image_descriptions: Flowchart illustrating the main parts of the vertebrate nervous system. It branches into Central Nervous System (CNS) and Peripheral Nervous System (PNS). CNS further branches into Brain and Spinal Cord. PNS further branches into Somatic Nervous System and Autonomic Nervous System. Autonomic Nervous System further branches into Parasympathetic Nervous System and Sympathetic Nervous System.

details.summary: Overview of the main parts of the vertebrate nervous system, presented as a hierarchical flowchart.

subject: Biology
text:
Central Nervous System (CNS)

The CNS is the site of information processing and control. It consists of brain and spinal cord.

  • Grey matter is made up of cell bodies of neuron and white matter has only nerve fibres.
  • Brain lies in the cranial cavity of skull. Brain and spinal cord are covered by two meninges in frog and three meninges in mammals.
  • Cerebrospinal fluid is present in and around brain and spinal cord.

details.summary: Description of the Central Nervous System (CNS), its components (brain and spinal cord), composition of grey and white matter, protective meninges, and the presence of cerebrospinal fluid.

subject: Biology
text:
Human Brain

Brain is soft, whitish in colour and somewhat a flattened organ.

  • It is the only thing in the universe, which is attempting to understand itself.
  • It is mainly divided into three main parts:
image_descriptions: Flowchart illustrating the main divisions of the Brain. It branches into Forebrain, Midbrain, and Hindbrain. Forebrain further branches into Cerebrum, Olfactory lobes, and Thalamus (Hypothalamus). Midbrain further branches into Corpora quadrigemina and Corpora diencephalon. Hindbrain further branches into Cerebellum, Medulla oblongata, and Pons.

details.summary: General description of the human brain, its unique characteristic, and its main divisions (Forebrain, Midbrain, Hindbrain) with their sub-parts.

subject: Biology
text:
Forebrain

It forms the greatest part of brain. It consists of following types:

  • Cerebrum It is the largest part of the brain covered by cerebral hemispheres. The roof of cerebrum is cerebral cortex. Cerebrum leads to consciousness, storage of memory of information.
  • Olfactory lobes These are pair of small sized structure, completely covered by cerebrum. These are the centre of skull.
  • Thalamus It is for integrity of sensory impulses sent from sense organs like eyes, ears and skin. It deals with pain, pressure and temperature.

details.summary: Detailed description of the Forebrain, its components (Cerebrum, Olfactory lobes, Thalamus), and their respective functions.

subject: Biology
topic: Parts of Brain: Forebrain Areas, Midbrain, and Hindbrain
text:
Forebrain Functional Areas:

  • Broca’s area: It is present in brain and is related with speech, while Wernick’s area of brain is related with understanding speech.
  • Hypothalamus: It deals with water balance in body, behavioural patterns of sex, sleep, stress, emotions, etc. It also regulates pituitary hormones and metabolism of fat, carbohydrate and water.

Midbrain:

It is located between hypothalamus and pons of the hindbrain.

  • It consists of two pairs of rounded swelling lobes called corpora quadrigemina (solid structures).
  • It deals with visual analysis, auditory, etc.
  • Midbrain of rabbit consists of four optic lobes.

Hindbrain:

It consists of cerebellum, pons varolii and medulla oblongata.

  • Cerebellum: It is in the bottom part of the head and back of it. It controls the coordination of accurate movements and balancing. It is considered as small brain.
  • Medulla oblongata: It is the lowermost part of brain, which is connected to spinal cord. It deals with control of heartbeats, blood vessels, breathing, salivary secretion and most of reflex and involuntary (uncontrolled) movements.
  • Pons Varolii: It is an oral mass that lies above medulla oblongata. It interconnects two cerebellar hemispheres and also joins the medulla with higher brain centres.

details.summary: Detailed anatomical overview of functional brain regions including speech centres (Broca's and Wernick's areas), the Hypothalamus, Midbrain (corpora quadrigemina), and Hindbrain structures (Cerebellum, Medulla oblongata, and Pons Varolii).

mcq.question: Which part of the human brain is considered as the 'small brain' and is responsible for coordinating accurate movements and body balancing?
mcq.explanation: The cerebellum, located at the bottom and back of the head, is considered as the 'small brain' and controls the coordination of accurate movements and body balancing.

subject: Biology
text:
Spinal Cord:

It is a long cord-like structure present at the back, centrally located and well-protected by bony vertebral column.

  • It gives out 31 pairs of spinal nerves in man.
  • It conducts impulses to and from the brain.
  • It is the centre for reflex actions and provides means of communication between spinal nerves and the brain.

Reflex Action:

It is unconditional, inborn and unlearned reflex to a stimulus.

Examples: Blinking of the eye when an object comes near to our eyes suddenly, rapid withdrawal of hand when burned, sneezing, coughing, yawning, knee-jerk reflex, etc.

Acquired Reflex Action:

It is also called as conditioned reflex and dependent on past experience, training and learning. These are under cerebral control during learning. First demonstrated by Ivan Petrovitch Pavlov in hungry dog.

Examples: Learning of dancing, cycling, swimming, singing and driving, etc.

details.summary: Anatomy and physiology of the spinal cord and classification of reflex actions into inborn (unconditioned) reflexes and acquired (conditioned) reflexes demonstrated by Ivan Pavlov.

mcq.question: Conditioned reflex actions based on learning and past experience were first demonstrated in a hungry dog by which scientist?
mcq.explanation: Conditioned reflex actions were first demonstrated by Ivan Petrovitch Pavlov using a hungry dog.

subject: Biology
topic: Peripheral Nervous System and Cranial Nerves
text:
Peripheral Nervous System (PNS):

It is composed of 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves.

  • Cranial nerves emerge from brain, while spinal nerves arise from spinal cord. Different number of cranial nerves are present in different organism.
  • e.g. 10 pairs of cranial nerves are present in fishes and amphibians.
  • Number of cranial nerves found in rabbit is 12 (same as man) but 37 spinal nerves are present in rabbit.
  • The first 10 pairs are common for frog and rabbit.

List of Cranial Nerves:
tables:
| Cranial | Number | Function | Distribution |
|---|---|---|---|
| Olfactory | I | Sensory | Nose |
| Optic | II | Sensory | Retina of eye |
| Occulomotor | III | Motor | 4 muscles of eyeballs |
| Trochlear (smallest) | IV | Motor | Superior oblique muscle |
| Trigeminal (largest) | V | Mixed |  |
| Ophthalmic | ... | ... | Snout |
| Maxillary | ... | ... | Upper jaw |
| Mandibular | ... | ... | Lower jaw |
| Abducens | VI | Motor | External rectus |
| Facial | VII | Mixed | Neck, pinna, tongue, lower jaw |
| Vestibulocochlear (auditory) | VIII | Sensory | Internal ear |
| Glossopharyngeal | IX | Mixed | Tongue, pharynx |
| Vagus | X | Mixed | Larynx, heart, lungs, stomach, etc. |
| Spinal accessory | XI | Motor | Neck |
| Hypoglossal | XII | Motor | Neck and tongue |

details.summary: Comprehensive classification and details of the Peripheral Nervous System, comparing cranial and spinal nerve counts across humans, rabbits, and amphibians, alongside a detailed table of 12 cranial nerves.

mcq.question: Which of the following is the smallest cranial nerve in human anatomy?
mcq.explanation: Cranial nerve IV, the Trochlear nerve, is the smallest cranial nerve, whereas the Trigeminal nerve (V) is the largest.

subject: Biology
topic: Autonomous Nervous System and Sense Organs
text:
Autonomous Nervous System:

It was discovered by Langley. It is entirely motor and operates without conscious control.

Autonomic nervous system consists of two divisions:

  • (i) Sympathetic nervous system: This increases defence system of body against adverse conditions and active in stress conditions, e.g. pain, fear and anger.
  • (ii) Parasympathetic nervous system: It provides relaxation, comfort, pleasure at the time of rest and helps in the restoration and conservation of energy.

SENSE ORGANS:

The sensory organs (receptors) enable us to detect all types of changes in the environment and send appropriate signals to the CNS, where all the inputs are processed and analysed signals are then sent to different centres of brain.

details.summary: Covers the Autonomous Nervous System discovered by Langley, contrasting the functions of the Sympathetic and Parasympathetic nervous systems, and introduces the physiological role of Sense Organs.

mcq.question: Who discovered the Autonomous Nervous System?
mcq.explanation: The Autonomous Nervous System was discovered by Langley. It operates entirely as a motor system without conscious control.

subject: Biology
text:
Ears are a pair of stato-acoustic organs meant for both sensory functions, i.e., hearing and maintenance of body balance. The study of structure, function, and disease of the ear is called otology.

  • Location & Control: Located on the sides of the head. Hearing is controlled by the auditory area of the temporal lobe of the cerebral cortex.
  • Acoustic Range:
    • The measuring unit of sound frequency is the decibel. The human ear can listen to sounds of 60–80 decibels.
    • The human ear is sensitive to sound frequencies of 50–20,000 cycles/sec and is most sensitive to a frequency of 1,000–3,000 cycles/sec.

The human ear is divided into three parts:

  • (i) External Ear: Consists of the pinna (outer ear) and the external auditory meatus (auditory canal).
    • Pinna: Designed to collect sound waves.
    • Auditory canal: Contains fine hairs and specialized sebaceous glands called ceruminous glands, which secrete cerumen (ear wax) to prevent foreign particles from entering the ear.
  • (ii) Middle Ear (Tympanic Cavity):
    • The tympanic membrane (ear drum) separates the middle ear from the external ear.
    • Contains three auditory ossicles:
      • Malleus: Outer and hammer-shaped.
      • Incus: Middle and anvil/oval-shaped.
      • Stapes: Inner and stirrup-shaped, attached to the outer surface of the fenestra ovalis membrane. It is the smallest bone in the human body.
    • Eustachian Tube: A passage connecting the middle ear with the pharynx. It equalizes air pressure on both sides (external and middle ear) of the tympanic membrane.
  • (iii) Internal Ear (Membranous Labyrinth): Consists of a labyrinth of fluid-filled chambers within the temporal bone/lobe of the skull.
    • Divisions:
      • Bony labyrinth: Filled with a fluid called perilymph.
      • Membranous labyrinth: Contains endolymph; concerned with both balancing and hearing.
    • Internal ear components: (a) Body proper (utriculus and sacculus), (b) Semicircular canals, and (c) Cochlea.
    • Cochlea: A small snail-shaped structure. It makes 2½ turns in rabbits and 2¾ turns in humans.
    • Chambers of Cochlea: Divided into three chambers: scala vestibuli, scala media, and scala tympani.
    • Organ of Corti: Located in the scala media; it is the organ of hearing (discovered by Alfonso Corti).
  • Defects of Ear:
    • Otalgia: Earache (pain in the ear).
    • Acute infection of the middle ear.
    • Labyrinthine disease: Malfunction of the inner ear.
tables:
| Ear Region | Major Components | Primary Functions |
|---|---|---|
| External Ear | Pinna, External auditory meatus | Collects sound waves, secretes cerumen |
| Middle Ear | Tympanic membrane, Ossicles (Malleus, Incus, Stapes), Eustachian tube | Amplifies and transmits sound vibrations; equalizes air pressure |
| Internal Ear | Bony labyrinth (perilymph), Membranous labyrinth (endolymph), Semicircular canals, Cochlea | Hearing (Organ of Corti in scala media) and body equilibrium |
image_descriptions: Diagram titled 'Structure of human ear' illustrating anatomical sections: external ear showing pinna and external auditory meatus; middle ear depicting the tympanic membrane, tympanic cavity, and three ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) situated near the temporal bone; the Eustachian tube leading downwards; and inner ear structures including the semicircular canals, cochlea, vestibular nerve, facial nerve, internal auditory meatus, and cochlear nerve.

details.summary: Detailed anatomical overview of the human ear, covering external, middle, and internal ear structures, fluid compartments, acoustic ranges, and common disorders.

mcq.question: Which of the following structures in the human ear contains the 'Organ of Corti', the true organ of hearing?
mcq.explanation: The Organ of Corti is located inside the scala media of the cochlea and is responsible for converting auditory signals into nerve impulses.

subject: Biology
text:
The organ of sight is a pair of eyes situated in deep bony cavities called orbits or sockets of the skull. The eyes are sensitive detectors of light and are most sensitive to yellow colour. The study of the structure, functions, and diseases of the eye is called ophthalmology.

The eyeball is made basically of three concentric layers:

  • 1. Outermost Fibrous Layer: Composed of the sclera and cornea.
    • Sclera: Outermost, tough, and opaque white part that maintains the shape of the eyeball.
    • Cornea: Thin, transparent front portion of the sclera. It lacks blood vessels but is richly supplied with free nerve endings.
    • Conjunctiva: A thin, transparent layer covering the cornea. It refracts incident light rays to focus them on the retina.
  • 2. Middle Vascular Layer: Consists of the choroid, ciliary body, and iris.
    • Choroid: Chocolate-coloured layer pigmented with melanin, situated along the inner side of the sclera.
    • Iris: Formed of circular sphincter and radial dilator muscles; controls and adjusts the diameter/size of the pupil.
    • Pupil: The black aperture located in the center of the iris through which light enters the eyeball; regulates the intensity of incoming light.
  • 3. Internal Structures & Media:
    • Lens: Biconvex, transparent, circular, solid, and proteinaceous in nature.
    • Aqueous Humor: Fluid filling the anterior chamber between the cornea and the lens.
    • Vitreous Humor: Gelatinous fluid filling the posterior space between the lens and the retina.
tables:
| Eye Layer | Constituents | Distinctive Characteristics |
|---|---|---|
| Outermost Fibrous Layer | Sclera, Cornea | Tough, maintains shape; cornea is transparent and avascular |
| Middle Layer | Choroid, Ciliary Body, Iris | Pigmented with melanin; regulates light entry via pupil dilation/constriction |
| Refractive Media / Fluids | Conjunctiva, Lens, Aqueous Humor, Vitreous Humor | Focus light rays onto retina; maintain intraocular pressure |

details.summary: Covers the anatomical organization of the human eye, its three concentric layers (sclera/cornea, choroid/iris, and internal chambers), as well as ocular fluids.

mcq.question: Which transparent part of the human eye lacks blood vessels but is richly supplied with nerve endings?
mcq.explanation: The cornea is the anterior transparent portion of the fibrous tunic that lacks blood vessels (avascular) but possesses abundant nerve endings.

subject: Biology
text:
Retina: It is the innermost and incomplete layer of the eye. It consists of a nervous tissue layer and a pigmented layer. The image of an object is formed on the retina and is real and inverted.

The retina is composed of two types of cells: rod cells and cone cells.

  • Rods: Longer, slender, and filamentous. Cones are shorter and thicker. Rods are highly sensitive to dim light and contain a reddish-purple pigment called rhodopsin.
  • Cones: Sensitive to bright light, hence differentiate colours (i.e., red, green, blue).
  • Yellow Spot (Macula Lutea): Located at the exact centre of the retina. The fovea centralis is the area of sharpest vision due to a high concentration of cones.
  • Blind Spot (Optic Disc): Has no rods and cones cells; hence, no image forms in this region.
  • Tapetum Lucidum: Increases the sensibility of vision. It is made up of zinc, cysteine, and guanine. The eyes of carnivores like cat, dog, lion, seal, etc., glow in the night due to the tapetum lucidum.
  • Atropine: A chemical used by doctors to dilate the pupil.
  • Night blindness: Caused by the deficiency of rhodopsin in rod cells.
  • Colour blindness: Caused due to deficiency of cones.

Visual pigments for colour:

  • (a) Erythropsin: Sensitive to red
  • (b) Chloropsin: Sensitive to green
  • (c) Cyanopsin: Sensitive to blue

details.summary: Structure and function of the retina, detailing rod and cone cells, yellow spot, blind spot, tapetum lucidum, atropine, night blindness, colour blindness, and the specific colour pigments (erythropsin, chloropsin, cyanopsin).

mcq.question: Which visual pigment in the human eye is sensitive to red colour?
mcq.explanation: Erythropsin is the cone pigment sensitive to red light, while chloropsin is sensitive to green, cyanopsin to blue, and rhodopsin is found in rods for dim light vision.

subject: Biology
text:
Some common diseases of the eye are as follows:

  • Myopia (Short-sightedness): In this condition, the image of a distant object is formed in front of the retina. It is corrected by using a concave lens.
  • Hypermetropia (Long or Far-sightedness): The image of a nearer object becomes blurred as it is formed behind the retina. It is corrected by using a convex lens.
  • Astigmatism: Occurs due to irregular cornea or lens curvature; corrected by using cylindrical lens.
  • Cataract: An eye disease generally occurring in older people where the lens becomes opaque. It can be corrected by surgical operation and using a biconvex lens.
  • Conjunctivitis: Inflammation of the conjunctiva caused by bacteria.

details.summary: Covers eye defects and conditions including myopia, hypermetropia, astigmatism, cataract, and conjunctivitis along with their respective corrective lenses or causes.

mcq.question: Astigmatism is a visual defect caused by an irregular curvature of the cornea or lens. Which lens is used for its correction?
mcq.explanation: Astigmatism is corrected using cylindrical lenses.

subject: Biology
text:
Nose (Olfactory Organ): The nose is a sense organ for smell or olfaction. It contains mucus-coated olfactory (smell) receptors.

The nasal cavity is lined by olfactory epithelium lines. Olfactory epithelium contains three principal kinds of cells:

  • (i) Olfactory bipolar neurons
  • (ii) Columnar epithelial cells
  • (iii) Bowman's gland

details.summary: Anatomy and physiology of the human olfactory organ (nose), including the mucous lining and the three major cellular components of the olfactory epithelium.

mcq.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the three principal kinds of cells present in the olfactory epithelium?
mcq.explanation: Olfactory epithelium consists of olfactory bipolar neurons, columnar epithelial cells, and Bowman's glands. Parietal cells are found in the stomach wall.

subject: Biology
text:
Tongue (Gustatory Organ): Organs for gustation are taste buds, which are present mainly in the mucosa of taste papillae present on the upper surface of the tongue.

Taste buds are numerous on the tongue, but are also found on the soft palate, pharynx, and epiglottis. A papilla may contain few to many hundreds of taste buds. Taste buds are more numerous in children than in adults.

Location of taste buds for basic tastes:

  • Sweet: On the tip of tongue.
  • Salty: On upper surface of anterior half.
  • Sour: Lateral side of tongue.
  • Bitter: Near the base of tongue.

Bitter taste is evolved by many organic substances, i.e., quinine, morphine, caffeine, and urea.

details.summary: Details the anatomy of the tongue as a gustatory organ, taste papillae, distribution across soft palate and pharynx, and spatial map of basic tastes (sweet, salty, sour, bitter).

mcq.question: Which part of the tongue is primarily responsible for detecting bitter taste?
options: Near the base of the tongue
Anterior half of the upper surface
mcq.explanation: Taste buds sensitive to bitter taste are located near the base of the tongue.

subject: Biology
text:
In the vertebrate body, glands may be classified on the basis of the presence or absence of ducts into two types:

(i) Endocrine Glands

The word endocrine derives from Greek words, 'endo' meaning within and 'crines' meaning to secrete. The endocrine system is the collection of glands that produce hormones that regulate metabolism, growth and development, tissue function, sexual function, reproduction, etc.

  • The science dealing with the study of endocrine glands and their secretion is called endocrinology.
  • These glands do not have ducts (tubes) to carry their secretion to the target organs; hence, they are also called ductless glands.
  • Their secretion is called hormone or internal secretion.
  • These glands secrete their secretion directly into the blood for transportation to the sites of action (e.g., thyroid, pituitary, pancreas, hypothalamus, adrenal, etc.).

(ii) Exocrine Glands

  • These glands have ducts.
  • These glands secrete their secretions into ducts to carry them to sites of action (e.g., sweat and oil glands of skin, salivary gland, liver, etc.).

details.summary: Classification of vertebrate glands into endocrine (ductless) and exocrine (ducted) glands, along with functions, etymology, and representative examples.

mcq.question: Which of the following is an example of an exocrine gland?
mcq.explanation: Salivary glands possess ducts to convey their secretions to the site of action, classifying them as exocrine glands, whereas thyroid, pituitary, and adrenal are ductless (endocrine) glands.

subject: Biology
text:
Hormones:

  • These are the chemical messengers that can regulate biological processes. They are steroids, proteins, peptides of amino acid derivatives.
  • They can act as coenzymes.
  • These are the organic compounds secreted in small amounts by endocrine glands of the body.
  • Hormone was first discovered by Bayliss and Ernst H Starling in 1903.
  • Secretin was the first hormone to be discovered.

details.summary: Chemical nature, physiological role, and historical milestones of hormones, including discovery by Bayliss and Starling and identification of secretin as the first discovered hormone.

mcq.question: Which was the first hormone to be discovered in 1903 by Bayliss and Ernst H Starling?
mcq.explanation: Secretin was the first hormone discovered by Bayliss and Ernst H. Starling in 1903.

subject: Biology
topic: Endocrine Glands of Human and Pituitary Gland
text:
There are a total of nine endocrine glands in human beings. Most of them are common to both male and female:

  • (i) Pituitary (master gland)
  • (ii) Thyroid
  • (iii) Parathyroid
  • (iv) Thymus
  • (v) Adrenals (supra-adrenals)
  • (vi) Pancreas
  • (vii) Pineal gland
  • (viii) Gonads
  • (ix) Hypothalamus

Pituitary Gland:

  • It is the smallest gland, which is about the size of a pea, but plays a major role in the endocrine system.
  • It is also known as the master gland.
  • It is slightly larger in women than in men.
  • It is located in the region of the forebrain.
tables:
| Parts of pituitary | Hormones | Target organs | Actions/Effects |
|---|---|---|---|
| Anterior pituitary | Growth Hormone (GH) | All tissues | Normal body growth. |
| Anterior pituitary | Adrenocorticotropin Hormone (ACTH) | Adrenal cortex | Glucocorticoid secretion. |
| Anterior pituitary | Thyrotropin Stimulating Hormone (TSH) | Thyroid gland | Thyroxine secretion. |
| Anterior pituitary | Prolactin | Alveolar cells of mammary glands | Milk secretion. |
| Anterior pituitary | Follicle Stimulating Hormone (FSH) | Ovarian follicles | Growth of ovarian follicle and oestrogen secretion in females and spermatogenesis in male. |
| Anterior pituitary | Leuteinising Hormone (LH) | Testes or ovaries | Development of corpus luteum and progesterone secretion in females, testosterone secretion in males. |
| Intermediate pituitary | Melanocyte Stimulating Hormone (MSH) | Skin | Synthesis of melanin in the skin. |
| Posterior pituitary | Oxytocin (protein) | Uterus, mammary glands | Milk ejection, uterine contraction, contraction of smooth muscles. |
| Posterior pituitary | Vasopressin (ADH) | Kidneys and arteries | Hypertonic urine, absorption of water, arteriolar constriction. |
image_descriptions: Anatomical line diagram titled 'Human endocrine glands' illustrating male and female human outlines side-by-side. Pointers indicate the anatomical locations of major glands: Pineal body and Pituitary in the head/forebrain region; Thyroid and Parathyroid in the neck; Thymus in the upper chest; Stomach, Adrenal glands (atop the kidneys), Pancreas, Kidneys, and Intestine in the abdominal cavity; and Gonads differentiated by sex—Testes in the male and Ovaries in the female.

details.summary: Overview of the nine human endocrine glands and detailed anatomy and hormonal functions of the Pituitary Gland (anterior, intermediate, and posterior lobes).

mcq.question: Which hormone secreted by the posterior pituitary is responsible for milk ejection and uterine contractions?
mcq.explanation: Oxytocin is secreted by the posterior pituitary and acts on the uterus and mammary glands to cause uterine contractions and milk ejection.

subject: Biology
text:
Thyroid Gland:

  • It is the largest endocrine gland.
  • It is found on the ventral and lateral sides of the upper part of the trachea in the neck.
  • It is a brownish-red, shield-shaped, bilobed gland.
tables:
| Hormones | Target organs | Actions/Effects |
|---|---|---|
| Calcitonin (CT) | Bones, kidney | Fall in blood calcium, excretion of Ca2+. |
| Thyroxine | Heart, liver, kidney, skeletal muscles, mast cells. | Tissue metabolism, growth, IQ, differentiation of gonads, metamorphosis in amphibians. |

details.summary: Structure and hormonal profile of the thyroid gland, including actions of calcitonin and thyroxine on metabolism and calcium levels.

mcq.question: Which of the following is the largest endocrine gland in the human body?
mcq.explanation: The thyroid gland is the largest endocrine gland, located on the ventral and lateral sides of the upper trachea in the neck.

subject: Biology
text:
Parathyroid Glands:

  • These are four in number and are embedded within the thyroid glands.
  • They are small glands, oval-shaped and yellow-coloured, situated in the human neck.
  • The parathyroid gland produces parathyroid hormone (PTH) / Parathormone.
tables:
| Hormones | Target organs | Actions/Effects |
|---|---|---|
| Parathormone (PTH) | Bones, kidney | Rise in blood calcium level, phosphorus check of calcium secretion. |

details.summary: Overview of the parathyroid glands, their number, location embedded in the thyroid gland, and the role of parathormone (PTH) in raising blood calcium.

mcq.question: How many parathyroid glands are typically embedded in the human thyroid gland?
mcq.explanation: There are four parathyroid glands embedded on the surface of the thyroid gland in the human neck.

subject: Biology
text:
Pancreas:

  • It is a mixed gland (heterocrine gland) possessing both exocrine and endocrine functions, located within the curve of the duodenum.
  • Three kinds of cells are found in the islets of Langerhans, namely alpha, beta, and delta cells:
    • (i) α-cells (alpha-cells): Larger and peripheral cells; produce the hormone glucagon.
    • (ii) β-cells (beta-cells): Central and smaller cells; produce insulin, which is a peptide hormone.
    • (iii) δ-cells (delta-cells): Middle cells; produce somatostatin hormone.
tables:
| Hormones | Target organs | Actions/Effects |
|---|---|---|
| Insulin | All cells | Decreases blood sugar level, stimulates glycogenesis, increases stored protein in tissue. Hypersecretion results into diabetes mellitus. |
| Glucagon | Liver | Rise in blood sugar. |

details.summary: Dual endocrine and exocrine nature of the pancreas, cell types of the islets of Langerhans, and regulation of blood glucose by insulin and glucagon.

mcq.question: Which cells in the islets of Langerhans are responsible for the secretion of glucagon?
mcq.explanation: Alpha-cells (α-cells) are larger, peripheral cells within the islets of Langerhans that secrete glucagon to raise blood sugar levels.

subject: Biology
text:
Adrenal Glands

  • Our body has paired endocrine glands, located superior to kidneys. It is structurally and functionally divided into adrenal cortex and adrenal medulla.
  • It is also called as 4S gland because of its four functions including salt retention, sugar metabolism, as a source of energy and as a sex organ.

Hormones secreted by the adrenal gland are given in the table below:
tables:
| Hormones | Target organs | Actions/Effects |
|---|---|---|
| Glucocorticoids | Tissues, mast cells | Carbohydrate, fat and protein metabolism. |
| Mineral corticoids | Kidney | Sodium and potassium metabolism, water absorption. |
| Sex corticoids | Body cells | External sex characters. |
| Adrenaline and noradrenaline | Mast cells | Heartbeat, blood pressure rise, contraction and relaxation of muscles. |

details.summary: Adrenal glands are paired glands situated atop the kidneys, divided into cortex and medulla. Known as the 4S gland (salt retention, sugar metabolism, source of energy, sex organ), it secretes glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids, sex corticoids, and adrenaline/noradrenaline.

mcq.question: Why is the adrenal gland referred to as the '4S gland'?
options: It controls sight, smell, sound, and speech
It regulates salt retention, sugar metabolism, source of energy, and acts as a sex organ
It secretes four specific steroid hormones exclusively from the medulla
It regulates sleep, stress, secretion, and swallowing
mcq.explanation: The adrenal gland is designated as the 4S gland due to its key roles in salt retention, sugar metabolism, acting as a source of energy, and functioning as a sex organ.

subject: Biology
text:
Pineal Gland

  • It is a small gland in the brain derived from the embryonic ectoderm. It secretes hormones in direct response to nervous activity.
  • In man, it starts to degenerate at about age of 7 years.
  • In adult, it is largely a fibrous tissue.

Hormone secreted by pineal gland:

Thymus Gland

  • It is a lymphoid gland that plays an important role in the development of immune system.
  • It is situated in front of the heart.
  • Thymus is active in young ones, but gradually becomes inconspicuous after sexual maturity.
  • It arises from the endoderm of the embryo and consists of peripheral cortex and central medulla.

Hormone secreted by thymus gland:
tables:
| Hormone | Target organ | Action/Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Melatonin | Melanophores | Dispersion of melanin. |

| Hormone | Target organ | Action/Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Thymosin | — | Immune system of body produces lymphocytes. |

details.summary: Pineal gland develops from ectoderm, degenerates around 7 years of age, and secretes melatonin affecting melanophores. Thymus gland is an endodermal lymphoid organ in front of the heart producing thymosin for immune lymphocyte development, degenerating after sexual maturity.

mcq.question: Which hormone is secreted by the thymus gland to assist the immune system?
mcq.explanation: Thymosin is secreted by the thymus gland to stimulate the production of lymphocytes in the body's immune system.

subject: Biology
topic: Hypothalamus, Gonads, and Other Hormone-Secreting Tissues
text:
Hypothalamus

The complete endocrine system works more or less under the influence of hypothalamus.

  • It is located in the floor of forebrain.
  • Neurohormones were first discovered by Guillemin and Schally.

Gonads

  • The main function of gonads is to produce gametes.
  • They also secrete sex hormones.
  • Sex hormones are mostly steroids.
  • The testes in male and ovaries in females are gonads.

Other Secretory Tissues: Apart from these, hormones are also secreted from heart, kidney and gastro-intestinal tract.
tables:
| Hormones | Target organs | Actions/Effects |
|---|---|---|
| Thyrotropin releasing hormone | Thyroid, adrenal gland | Thyrotropin secretion, Corticotropin secretion |
| Corticotropin releasing hormone | Pituitary | Secretion of pituitary gonadotropin |
| Somatostatin | Pituitary | Initiation of growth hormone secretion |

| Endocrine gland | Hormones | Target organs | Actions/Effects |
|---|---|---|---|
| Testes | Testosterones | Male reproductive organ | Male secondary sex organs and external male characters. |
| Ovaries | Oestrogen | Female reproductive organ | Female secondary sex organ and external female characters. |
| Corpus luteum (ovaries) | Progesterone | Uterus, mammary glands | Pregnancy changes in female sex organs. |

| Organ | Hormone | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Heart | Atrial natriuretic factor | Dilation of blood vessels |
| Kidney | Erythropoietin | Erythropoiesis |
| Gastro-intestinal tract | Gastrin, Secretin, Cholecystokinin | Secretion of HCl; Action pancreas for the secretion of water acts on gall bladder and pancreas for bile juice secretion. |

details.summary: Hypothalamus acts as master regulator of endocrine glands; neurohormones discovered by Guillemin and Schally. Gonads produce steroid gametes and hormones (testosterone, oestrogen, progesterone). Heart secretes ANF, kidneys secrete erythropoietin, and the GI tract secretes gastrin, secretin, and cholecystokinin.

mcq.question: Which hormone secreted by the heart helps in the dilation of blood vessels?
mcq.explanation: Atrial natriuretic factor (ANF) is secreted by the heart walls and causes dilation of blood vessels.

subject: Biology
text:
REPRODUCTION IN ANIMALS

The process by which new individuals are produced from their parents is called reproduction. Reproduction is of two kinds:

  • Asexual reproduction: Production of offspring by a single parent without the formation and fusion of gametes.
    • Binary fission: It is the division of parent into two equal sized daughter cells.
    • Multiple fission: It is the division of parent cells into a number of daughter cells, e.g. Amoeba.
    • Budding: Formation of daughter cell from a small projection called bud, e.g. Hydra, sponges.
    • Fragmentation: Breaking up of animal's body into two or more pieces, each of which grows into a new individual, e.g. coelenterates.
  • Sexual reproduction: Production of offspring by two parents, male and female.
    • Syngamy: It involves fusion of two entire gametes to form a zygote.
      • Endogamy: (self-fertilisation) e.g. tapeworm.
      • Exogamy: (cross-fertilisation) e.g. frog and man.
    • Conjugation: Temporary pairing of two points, e.g. Paramecium.
image_descriptions: Flowchart showing classification of 'Reproduction'. It branches into 'Asexual reproduction' (Production of offspring by a single parent without the formation and fusion of gametes) and 'Sexual reproduction' (Production of offspring by two parents, male and female). Under Asexual reproduction, four types are listed vertically: 'Binary fission' (division into two equal sized daughter cells), 'Multiple fission' (division into a number of daughter cells, e.g. Amoeba), 'Budding' (formation of daughter cell from a small projection called bud, e.g. Hydra, sponges), and 'Fragmentation' (breaking up into two or more pieces, each growing into a new individual, e.g. coelenterates). Under Sexual reproduction, two branches occur: 'Syngamy' (fusion of two entire gametes to form a zygote, subdividing into Endogamy/self-fertilisation e.g. tapeworm and Exogamy/cross-fertilisation e.g. frog and man) and 'Conjugation' (temporary pairing of two points, e.g. Paramecium).

details.summary: Reproduction is classified into asexual (binary fission, multiple fission, budding, fragmentation) and sexual (syngamy consisting of endogamy and exogamy, and conjugation).

mcq.question: Which of the following is an example of an organism undergoing endogamy (self-fertilisation)?
mcq.explanation: Tapeworm is an example of an organism that exhibits endogamy (self-fertilisation), whereas frogs and humans exhibit exogamy (cross-fertilisation).

subject: Biology
text:
The male reproductive system consists of the following main parts:

  • Testes: These are the primary sex organ of males, which perform a dual role, i.e., function as an endocrine gland and also act as male sex organs. These are suspended in a thin skin bag called scrotal sacs.
  • Epididymis: It is a highly coiled, thin tube formed by the union of seminiferous tubules.
  • Penis: It is a muscular organ, richly supplied with blood. Externally, the penis has a bulge called glans penis, which is covered by prepuce (a skin fold).
  • Male can produce spermatozoa (sperm) throughout their life starting from the age of 13–14 years.
  • The growth of hairs on the body is due to male sex hormones, i.e., androgen (testosterone).
tables:
| Reproductive organs of male | Number | Function performed |
|---|---|---|
| Testes | 2 | To produce sperms and testosterone. |
| Sperm duct | 2 | To conduct the sperms from the testes to urethra. |
| Seminal vesicles | 2 | To secrete seminal plasma. |
| Epididymis | 2 | To temporarily store sperms and provide mobility. |
| Urethra | 1 | To conduct urine, sperms. |
| Prostate gland | 2 | To secrete an alkaline fluid to neutralise the acidity of urethra. |
| Cowper's gland | 2 | To secrete an alkaline white fluid. |
| Penis | 1 | To pass urine and deposite sperms in female genital tract. |
image_descriptions: Diagram of the Male Reproductive System showing the anatomical location and connections of the Urinary bladder, Ureter, Prostate gland, Seminal vesicle (behind bladder), Bulbourethral gland, Erectile tissue of penis, Vas deferens, Epididymis, Testis, Scrotum, Urethra, Penis, Glans penis, and Prepuce.

details.summary: Covers anatomical structures, functions, and organ count of the human male reproductive system including testes, epididymis, accessory glands, and penis.

mcq.question: Which gland in the male reproductive system secretes an alkaline fluid to neutralise the acidity of the urethra?
mcq.explanation: The prostate gland secretes an alkaline fluid that helps neutralize the acidity of the urethra.

subject: Biology
text:
The female reproductive system consists of the following parts:

  • Ovary: These are primary sex organs that produce female gametes (ovum) and several steroid hormones. After maturity, the ovary releases an ovum (egg cell) after every 28 days.
  • Lactation: Child is delivered after its development and mother produces milk to nourish the child.
  • Placenta: It is the connection between developing embryo and mother. It supplies blood, nutrition, etc., to the foetus.
  • Gestation period: The embryo develops for nine months in the uterus. This period is called the gestation period.
  • Amniocentesis: A technique to detect chromosomal abnormalities, if any, in the developing foetus by analysing the cells in the amniotic fluid. This technique is often misused to know the sex of the foetus. Ultrasound can also be used to detect the sex of the foetus.
tables:
| Reproductive organ of female | Number | Function performed |
|---|---|---|
| Ovaries | 2 | To produce ova and hormones. |
| Oviducts | 2 | To move the ovum towards uterus. |
| Uterus | 1 | To provide space for developing child. |
| Vagina | 1 | To receive the sperms. |
image_descriptions: Diagram of the Female Reproductive System depicting coronal cross-section of the Uterus, Cervix, Vagina, Fallopian tubes, Ovaries, Oviduct, Fimbriae, Follicles, Corpus luteum, Uterine wall, and Endometrium.

details.summary: Details female reproductive anatomy, key functions of ovaries, oviducts, uterus, vagina, and key developmental concepts such as lactation, placenta, gestation, and amniocentesis.

mcq.question: Amniocentesis is a technique primarily used for:
options: Determining the age of the mother
Detecting chromosomal abnormalities in the foetus
mcq.explanation: Amniocentesis is used to detect chromosomal abnormalities in the developing foetus by analyzing cells in amniotic fluid.

subject: Biology
text:
Key concepts regarding the menstrual cycle in human females:

  • Reproductive period: The reproductive period of a human female extends from puberty (9–13 years) to menopause (45–50 years).
  • Menopause: It is the stopping of ovulation and menses. It normally occurs between the ages of 45 and 50. In this stage, women lose the ability to reproduce. Menopause is characterised by hot flushes.
  • Menstruation: The periodic vaginal bleeding during the menstrual cycle is called menstruation.
  • Hormonal control: Menstrual cycle is controlled by FSH, LH, oestrogen, and progesterone.
  • Duration: On an average, the menstrual cycle is completed in 28 days.
  • Occurrence: It is absent during pregnancy, may be suppressed during lactation, and permanently stops at menopause.
  • Ovulation rate: About 13 mature eggs are released from two ovaries of a female in a year.

details.summary: Explains the phases, duration, hormonal control, and terminology of the human female menstrual cycle and menopause.

mcq.question: Which set of hormones controls the menstrual cycle in human females?
mcq.explanation: The menstrual cycle is regulated by follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), luteinizing hormone (LH), oestrogen, and progesterone.

subject: Biology
text:
Contraception is the prevention of union of sperm and ovum.

Some common contraceptive methods are as follow:

  • (i) Natural contraception: Avoid copulation during ovulation.
  • (ii) Mechanical contraception: Use devices to avoid union of sperm and ovum, e.g. condoms, diaphragm, Intra Uterine Devices (IUDs).
  • (iii) Chemical contraception: Fertilisation is avoided by the use of drugs, spermicidal creams, tablets, foam, etc.
  • (iv) Vasectomy: It is the surgical removal of sperm ducts (vas deferens) in males.
  • (v) Tubectomy: Cut and tied of Fallopian tubes in females.

details.summary: Covers five primary contraception methods: Natural (avoiding copulation during ovulation), Mechanical (condoms, diaphragms, IUDs), Chemical (drugs, spermicidal creams, foam), Vasectomy (surgical removal of vas deferens in males), and Tubectomy (cutting and tying of Fallopian tubes in females).

mcq.question: Which surgical contraceptive procedure involves cutting and tying the Fallopian tubes in females?
mcq.explanation: Tubectomy is the surgical method of contraception in females where the Fallopian tubes are cut and tied to prevent the egg from reaching the uterus.

subject: Biology
text:
Human population is growing fast and its present rate is about 2% per annum. Malthus (1798) gave the concept of human population. Study of human population is called demography.

  • (i) Biotic potential: The physiological capacity of organisms is called biotic potential.
  • (ii) Carrying capacity: The maximum number of individuals, which an environment can support or sustain is called carrying capacity.
  • (iii) Population growth: Determined by the number of organisms added to the population (through birth) minus the number of organisms lost (through death).
  • (iv) Zero population: When the number of individuals lost equals those added, resulting in stabilized population.

Growth Curves:

  • J-shaped curve: When there is no environmental resistance, a population grows exponentially and a J-shaped curve is obtained.
  • S-shaped curve: When environment resistance does not allow population growth to soar towards infinitely.
formulas: Population growth = (Number of organisms added through birth) - (Number of organisms lost through death)

details.summary: Examines human population growth rate (~2% per annum), Malthus' concept (1798), demography, biotic potential, carrying capacity, population growth equation, zero population, and the two major growth curves: exponential J-shaped curve and logistic S-shaped curve.

mcq.question: The maximum number of individuals that an environment can support or sustain is known as:
mcq.explanation: Carrying capacity is the maximum population size of a biological species that a particular environment can sustain indefinitely.

subject: Biology
topic: Health, Disease Factors, and Classification of Diseases
text:
Health: It is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being. Any deviation from this state results in a disease.

  • According to World Health Organisation (WHO) (1948), 'health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely an absence of disease'.
  • Basic factors contributing to good health: balanced diet, personal hygiene, and regular exercise.
  • Other factors with major impact on health: awareness about diseases and their effects on different functions of the body, vaccination against infectious diseases, proper disposal of waste, and maintenance of hygienic food and water resources.

Human Diseases:

A disease is an abnormal condition affecting the body of an organism; 'any change from normal state causing discomfort is called disease'. It is a specific condition associated with specific symptoms and signs.

Factors affecting human health are categorised into two groups:

  • (i) Intrinsic factors: Disease-causing factors within the human body, e.g. malfunctioning of organs (like heart, kidney, etc.), genetic diseases, hormonal imbalance, etc.
  • (ii) Extrinsic factors: Disease-causing factors that come from outside the human body, e.g. diseases caused by microorganisms, tobacco, alcohol, narcotics, and inadequate diet.

Pathogens:

  • Disease-causing organisms are called pathogens.
  • Various microorganisms responsible for infectious diseases are bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoans, worms, etc.
  • Pathogens enter the body by various ways, multiply, and disturb normal metabolic activities, thus shattering major organ systems.

Classification of Diseases:

Diseases are broadly classified into two types: Acquired diseases and Congenital diseases.

Acquired Diseases:

These diseases develop after birth and are not transferred from parents to offspring. They are classified into two main types:

  • (i) Communicable: Spread from one person to another person. Subdivided into:
    • Contagious: Spread by direct contact.
    • Non-contagious: Spread by indirect contact.
  • (ii) Non-communicable: Do not spread from one person to another person.
image_descriptions: Hierarchical flowchart titled 'Classification of Diseases': The root node 'Diseases' branches into two categories: 'Acquired diseases' and 'Congenital diseases'. 'Acquired diseases' further branches into: 1. 'Communicable (spread from one person to another person)', which splits into 'Contagious (by direct contact)' and 'Non-contagious (by indirect contact)'; 2. 'Non-communicable (do not spread from one person to another person)'.

details.summary: Detailed overview of health (WHO 1948 definition), contributing factors to health, definitions of disease, intrinsic vs extrinsic factors, pathogens, and the classification tree of diseases into congenital and acquired (communicable/non-communicable, contagious/non-contagious).

mcq.question: Which of the following is classified as an intrinsic factor causing disease?
mcq.explanation: Intrinsic factors originate from within the body, such as malfunctioning of organs (e.g., heart, kidney), genetic disorders, and hormonal imbalances, whereas pathogens, narcotics, and diet are extrinsic factors.

subject: Biology
text:
Communicable Diseases or Infectious Diseases: These diseases are caused by pathogens and can spread from an affected person to a normal person.

(i) Bacterial Diseases

Some of the common bacterial diseases are: Pneumonia (Streptococcus), cholera (Vibrio cholerae), tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis), tetanus (Clostridium tetani), leprosy (Mycobacterium leprae), food poisoning (Salmonella), plague (Yersinia pestis), etc.

  • Bacterium Staphylococcus present in the nasal passage causes food poisoning by producing a heat resistant toxin in the food.
  • Bacterium Salmonella typhi is a pathogenic bacterium that causes typhoid fever in human beings. It affects liver, pancreas, nervous system, gastrointestinal tract, kidney, heat, etc.
  • Bacterium Clostridium botulinum causes food poisoning in canned food.
  • Bacteria like Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae are responsible for pneumonia in human beings and infect alveoli of lungs.
  • Anthrax: It is an infectious disease caused by a bacteria called Bacillus anthracis. Anthrax cannot directly spread from one individual to other, it spread by its spores.
  • Diphtheria: It is an upper respiratory tract illness caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae, which is characterised by sore throat, low fever and an adherent membrane on the tonsils, pharynx and nasal cavity.
  • Pertussis (Whooping cough): It is a serious and common infection of children caused by Gram negative bacteria, Bordetella pertussis. It is an air borne infection with incubation period of 1-3 weeks.
  • DPT: A vaccine used against diphtheria, whooping cough, and tetanus.

details.summary: Overview of communicable bacterial diseases including causal organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Salmonella typhi, Clostridium botulinum, Bacillus anthracis, Corynebacterium diphtheriae, Bordetella pertussis, and prevention via DPT vaccine.

mcq.question: Which of the following vaccines provides combined protection against diphtheria, pertussis, and tetanus?
mcq.explanation: DPT is a trivalent vaccine used against diphtheria, whooping cough (pertussis), and tetanus.

subject: Biology
text:
(ii) Viral Diseases

Some of the common viral diseases are:

  • Poliomyelitis (polio), mumps (paramyxo virus), chickenpox (variola virus), measles (paramyxo virus), AIDS (HIV).
  • The virus causing dengue fever or break bone fever is an RNA virus of the family Flaviviridae. Symptoms of dengue include headache, muscle and joint pain.
  • Dengue causes platelet count in blood to decrease. It occurs mainly because this virus infects endothelial cells of bone marrow that give rise to platelets resulting in bone marrow suppression.
  • Conjunctivitis (also called pink eye or madras eye) is inflammation of the conjunctiva (the outermost layer of eye and inner surface of eyelids) caused by adenoviruses. It can also be caused by bacterial infection.
  • Rabies is a viral disease that causes acute encephalitis (inflammation of brain). Roughly 97% of human rabies cases come from dog bites, but rabid bats are also capable of causing this disease.
  • Hepatitis is a medical condition defined by inflammation of liver. It is caused by hepatitis viruses.
  • Influenza, commonly called as flu, is an infectious disease caused by RNA viruses of family Orthomyxoviridae.
  • Measles, also known as rubeola or morbilli, is an infection of the respiratory system caused by a virus, specifically a paramyxovirus of the genus Morbillivirus. Symptoms include fever, cough, runny nose, red eyes, etc.
  • Mumps is a viral disease of human species caused by mumps virus. Painful swelling of salivary glands (parotid gland) is the most typical symptom.
  • AIDS (Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome): It weakens the immunity of body. It spreads through sexual contact, transfusion of blood infected by AIDS virus, through infected needles, child gets diseases from mother's milk. Best way to avoid it is to adopt safe sex and use of sterilised syringes.

details.summary: Detailed notes on common viral diseases such as dengue, rabies, conjunctivitis, hepatitis, influenza, measles, mumps, and AIDS along with their respective viral families, transmission vectors, and clinical manifestations.

mcq.question: Which family does the RNA virus responsible for dengue fever belong to?
mcq.explanation: The virus causing dengue fever (breakbone fever) is an RNA virus belonging to the family Flaviviridae.

subject: Biology
text:
Antibiotics

Antibiotics are the chemical substances produced by certain microorganisms that kill or inhibit the growth of other microorganisms. Penicillin was the first antibiotic discovered by Alexander Fleming. It inhibits cell wall formation in bacteria.

  • Antibiotics inhibit the metabolic activities of other microorganisms, such as synthesis of cell wall, protein synthesis, nuclear membrane synthesis, etc.
  • The microorganisms which produce antibiotics (anti-microbial substance) are called antibiont.
  • The antibiotics can be of bacterial, fungal, or Actinomycetes origin.

Some of the antibiotics obtained from different sources are shown below in the given table:
tables:
| Antibiotics | Source |
|---|---|
| Penicillin | Penicillium notatum, P. chrysogenum |
| Streptomycin | Streptomyces griseus |
| Neomycin | Streptomyces fradiae |
| Tetracycline | Streptomyces erythraeus |

details.summary: Covers the definition, mechanism of action, discovery by Alexander Fleming, and major microbial sources of commercial antibiotics including Penicillin, Streptomycin, Neomycin, and Tetracycline.

mcq.question: Which microorganism is the biological source for the antibiotic Streptomycin?
mcq.explanation: Streptomycin is obtained from the Actinomycete bacterium Streptomyces griseus.

subject: Biology
topic: Diseases Caused by Protozoans, Worms, and Fungi
text:
Diseases Caused by Protozoans and Worms:

  • Malaria: Caused by Plasmodium sp. It is transferred to the host by means of vectors. Insects that can transmit diseases to humans are referred to as vectors (e.g., Anopheles serves as a vector for malaria, Culex for filaria, Aedes for dengue, and sandfly for kala-azar).
  • Kala-azar (Dum-dum fever): Caused by the protozoan Leishmania donovani, hence it is also called leishmaniasis. The infection to humans is caused by the bite of infected sandflies (Phlebotomus papatasi and P. argentipes).
  • Amoebiasis: Caused by Entamoeba histolytica in humans. This protozoan parasitises in the large intestine of man, occurring worldwide whenever sanitation and hygiene are poor.
  • Sleeping sickness (Trypanosomiasis): Caused by a flagellate protozoan parasite belonging to the class Mastigophora and genus Trypanosoma. It is transmitted by the blood-sucking tse-tse fly.
  • Ascariasis: A common helminthic infection (worm) caused by Ascaris lumbricoides. The disease is characterized by internal bleeding, muscular pain, fever, anaemia, and blockage of the intestinal passage.
  • Filariasis: Caused by filarial nematodes, specifically Wuchereria bancrofti.

Diseases Caused by Fungi:

  • Ringworm (skin problems)
  • Food poisoning (Aspergillus)
  • Athlete's foot

Sub-types of Communicable Diseases based on Mode of Infection:

  • Contagious Diseases: Transferred through simple contacts (e.g., smallpox, ringworm, chickenpox, influenza, measles, leprosy, etc.).
  • Non-contagious Diseases: Transferred through physical carriers such as air, water, food, etc. (e.g., cholera, taeniasis, ascariasis, typhoid, etc.). Some of these diseases are transmitted through disease carrier vectors (e.g., plague, AIDS, malaria, hepatitis, etc.).

details.summary: Covers communicable diseases caused by protozoans, parasitic worms (helminths), and fungi, including causative agents, vectors, symptoms, and classification based on modes of transmission (contagious vs non-contagious).

mcq.question: Which of the following insect vectors is responsible for transmitting Kala-azar to humans?
mcq.explanation: Kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis), caused by the protozoan Leishmania donovani, is transmitted to humans by the bite of infected sandflies belonging to the genus Phlebotomus.

subject: Biology
text:
Non-communicable Diseases or Non-Infectious Diseases:

These diseases remain confined only to the person who develops them. They can be categorized into four types:

  1. Organic (degenerative) diseases: Caused due to organ malfunctioning.
  2. Deficiency diseases: Caused due to deficiency of minerals, hormones, vitamins, and nutrients.
  3. Allergic diseases: Caused due to hypersensitivity of the body to foreign particles.
  4. Cancer: Caused due to uncontrolled division of certain cells of the body.

Diseases of Malfunctioning:

  • Improper functioning of heart – Cardiac failure.
  • Improper functioning of kidney – Kidney failure.
  • Improper functioning of bones – Osteoporosis.
  • Improper functioning of eyes – Myopia, hypermetropia, and cataract.

Deficiency Diseases:

  • Cretinism: In children, occurs due to deficiency of thyroxine hormone, which causes mental retardation.
  • Diabetes: Due to deficiency of insulin.
  • Dwarfism: Due to sluggish activity (hyposecretion) of the pituitary gland, leading to diminished bone growth.
  • Gigantism: Due to excessive activity (hypersecretion) of the pituitary gland, resulting in excessive growth of bones.
  • Goitre: Caused by deficiency of iodine in the diet, characterized by swelling of the thyroid gland.
  • Anaemia: A decrease in the number of RBCs or less than the normal quantity of haemoglobin in the blood, leading to hypoxia (lack of oxygen) in organs.

Allergic Diseases:

An unfavourable response of the body to certain foreign substances like dust, serum, drugs, fabrics, pollen, etc. Symptoms include sneezing, irritation of throat, itching, and skin rashes (e.g., asthma is caused by allergy).

Cancer:

Cancer is an uncontrolled growth of normal cells that have lost control over cell division, spreading throughout the body. Dividing cells form an abnormal mass of tissue called a tumour. Tumours can be benign or malignant.

Types of Cancers:

  • Carcinomas: E.g., lung cancer, breast cancer, cancer of pancreas and stomach. (Breast cancer is common among women, while lung cancer is common among smokers).
  • Sarcomas: E.g., bone cancer.
  • Leukemia: E.g., blood cancer.

Other Cancer Facts:

  • Radiations cause cancer, leukemia, and skin injuries; they damage genes or chromosomes, induce uncontrolled cell division, and destroy tissues, cells, and blood cells.
  • Cancer is common in older people because over time their genomes tend to accumulate more mutations.

details.summary: Comprehensive overview of non-communicable diseases, classified into degenerative, deficiency, allergic, and cancerous conditions, along with specific causes, symptoms, and classifications of tumours and cancers.

mcq.question: Which type of cancer originates in bone tissue?
mcq.explanation: Sarcomas are cancers arising from connective tissues, such as bones, whereas carcinomas affect epithelial tissues and leukemia affects blood-forming tissues.

subject: Biology
topic: Diseases Caused by Addictive Substances, Pollution, and Genetic Disorders
text:
Diseases Caused by Addictive Substances

  • Alcohol: Reduces alertness of mind and causes liver damage.
  • Narcotic drugs: Narcotic drugs are morphine, cocaine, heroin, hashish, ganja, opium, marijuana, barbiturates and LAD (Lysergic Acid Diethylamide).

Diseases Caused due to Pollution

  • Chemical pollution: Pneumoconiosis is caused by inhaling coal dust. Silicosis is caused by inhaling stone dust (silica). Asbestosis is caused by inhaling asbestos dust. Lung diseases and bronchitis are caused by smoke.

IMPORTANT POINTS TO REMEMBER

DOTS or directly observed treatment, short-course was launched by WHO as a strategy to control TB (Tuberculosis). It ensures a regular, uninterrupted supply of high quality anti-TB drug.

Congenital Diseases

These are anatomical or physiological abnormalities that come from birth. These diseases can be caused by genetic mutations or environmental factors. Diseases by genetic mutation can be transmitted to next generation, whereas diseases by environmental factors are non-transmissible.

Some common congenital diseases are phenylketonuria, alkaptonuria, haemophillia, sickle-cell anaemia, etc.

Chromosomal Aberrations

These are any variation from the 46 chromosome number of humans. These includes Turner's syndrom, klinfelter syndrom, etc.

details.summary: Covers health issues resulting from addictive substances, pollution-related respiratory ailments, WHO's DOTS strategy for tuberculosis, congenital disorders, and chromosomal aberrations.

mcq.question: Which of the following lung diseases is specifically caused by the inhalation of coal dust?
mcq.explanation: Pneumoconiosis is caused by inhaling coal dust, whereas silicosis is caused by silica/stone dust, and asbestosis by asbestos dust.

subject: Biology
text:
VACCINATION

Louis Pasteur coined the term 'Vaccine' and vaccination for the first time.

  • The word 'vaccination' has been derived from a Latin word 'vacca' which means cow.
  • A vaccine is either a cell suspension or a byproduct excreted by the cell.
  • These vaccines, when introduced into the body, stimulate the production of antibodies.
  • Serum is used for obtaining antibodies.
  • This introduction of harmless antigenic material into healthy person for providing acquired immunity against the disease is known as immunisation and vaccination.
