mcq.question: Ranikhet disease affecting poultry birds is caused by which of the following pathogens?
mcq.explanation: Ranikhet is a viral disease affecting poultry birds.

subject: Biology
text:
APPLIED BIOLOGY: FERTILISERS

Fertiliser is any material found naturally or formed synthetically and is applied to soil or plant tissues, to supply one or more plant nutrients essential to the growth of plants. They are of mainly two types:

1. Chemical Fertilisers

These are salt or an organic compound containing the necessary plant nutrients. They may be organic or inorganic, e.g. ammonium sulphate is an inorganic fertiliser, while urea is an organic fertiliser. If excess fertilisers are applied to a plant without water, crop will die due to the plasmolysis.

Chemical fertilisers can be classified into following types:

  • (i) Nitrogenous fertilisers: These are nitrogen containing fertilisers, e.g.
    • Ammonium nitrate [NH4NO3]
    • Ammonium sulphate [(NH4)2SO2]
    • Sodium nitrate [NaNO3]
    • Urea [NH2CONH2] (organic fertiliser)
  • (ii) Phosphatic fertilisers: These are phosphorus containing fertilisers, e.g.
    • Ammonium phosphate [(NH4)3PO4]
    • Ammonium hydrogen phosphate [(NH4)H2PO4]
    • Superphosphate [Ca2(H2PO4)2]
  • (iii) Potassium fertilisers: These are potassium containing fertilisers, e.g.
    • Potassium chloride [KCl]
    • Potassium nitrate [KNO3]

details.summary: Describes types and examples of chemical fertilisers including nitrogenous, phosphatic, and potassium fertilisers, along with the phenomenon of plasmolysis when overapplied without sufficient water.

mcq.question: What causes crops to die if excess chemical fertilizers are applied without sufficient water?
mcq.explanation: Excess chemical fertilizers increase the external osmotic concentration, causing water to exit plant cells via exosmosis leading to plasmolysis and eventual death.

subject: Biology
text:
Inorganic Fertilisers (Recap):

  • Potassium sulphate: [K2SO4]
  • Calcium Ammonium Nitrate (CAN): Also popularly known as Kisan Khad.
  • Complete Fertiliser: N, P, and K (Nitrogen, Phosphorus, and Potassium) are the macronutrients provided by inorganic fertilisers. Fertilisers supplying all three are termed complete fertilisers.

Biofertilisers:

The fertilisers which are biologically originated are referred to as biofertilisers. In other words, biofertilisers are those organisms which can bring about nutrient availability to crop plants. One of the important types of biofertiliser is manures.

Manures:

  • They are semi-decayed substances added to the soil to enhance soil fertility.
  • Decomposed products of organic wastes.
  • Improve various properties of soil:
    • Fertility
    • Aeration
    • Water holding capacity
    • Crumb structure
  • Traditionally in India, cow dung is widely used as manure.

Types of Manures:

  1. Farm Yard Manure (FYM): Consists of a mixture of cattle dung, crop residues, fallen leaves, twigs, etc.
  2. Composite Manure (Compost): Consists of rotten vegetables, garbage, sewage sludge, animal refuse, etc.
  3. Green Manure: Quick-growing crops cultivated and ploughed directly into the soil. These can increase the yield of the subsequent crop by 30–50%.

Green Manuring:

  • A type of cover crop grown primarily to add nutrients and organic matter to the soil.
  • Technique: Utilizing green manure, particularly leguminous plants such as Crotalaria juncea, Glycine max, and Indigofera linifolia.
  • Anabaena azollae (a cyanobacterium) is used as a biofertiliser in rice fields.
  • Sunnhemp plants are commonly used for green manuring in India.

Advantages of Manuring:

  • Improves soil fertility and enhances soil structure.
  • Enhances soil aeration capacity.
  • Helps in controlling pests, insects, mites, and the proliferation of weeds.

details.summary: Covers definition and types of manures including Farm Yard Manure (FYM), compost, and green manure crops (e.g., Crotalaria juncea, Sunnhemp), along with their soil enhancement advantages.

mcq.question: Which of the following inorganic fertilisers is commonly known as 'Kisan Khad'?
mcq.explanation: Calcium Ammonium Nitrate (CAN) is popularly referred to as Kisan Khad.

subject: Biology
topic: Sources of Biofertilisers and Biological Nitrogen Fixation
text:
Global Nitrogen Fixation Statistics:

  • Natural processes fix about 190 × 1012 g of nitrogen per year through biological nitrogen fixation.
  • Biological nitrogen fixation provides approximately 1750 million tonnes of nitrogen naturally and free of cost annually in the form of biofertilisers.

Main Sources of Biofertilisers:

1. Free-living Nitrogen-fixing Bacteria:

Non-symbiotic bacteria found abundantly in the rhizosphere (root-soil contact zone). Can be:

  • Aerobic: e.g., Azotobacter (maintains microaerobic conditions via a high rate of respiration); Gloeothece (evolves O2 photosynthetically during the day and fixes nitrogen during the night).
  • Anaerobic: Oxygen does not pose an inhibition issue due to its absence in their habitat. They can be photosynthetic (e.g., Rhodospirillum) or non-photosynthetic (e.g., Clostridium).

2. Symbiotic Nitrogen-fixing Bacteria:

  • Possess the enzyme complex nitrogenase, which reduces atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia.
  • Rhizobium: Forms nodules on the roots of leguminous plants.
  • Leghaemoglobin: An oxygen-binding haemoprotein present in high concentrations in the cytoplasm of infected nodule cells, giving the nodules a distinctive pink colour. It scavenges oxygen to protect the oxygen-sensitive nitrogenase enzyme.
  • Frankia: An Actinomycete that acts as a symbiont in non-leguminous trees and shrubs such as Alder, Ceanothus, and Purshia.

3. Free-living Nitrogen-fixing Cyanobacteria:

  • Examples include Anabaena, Nostoc, Aulosira, Cylindrospermum, and Trichodesmium.
  • Capable of adding 20–30 kg of nitrogen per hectare of soil and water.
  • Aulosira is the most active nitrogen fixer in rice paddy fields.
  • Cylindrospermum is predominantly active in sugarcane and maize fields.

4. Symbiotic Nitrogen-fixing Cyanobacteria:

  • Anabaena and Nostoc species are common symbionts in lichens, Anthoceros (bryophyte), Azolla (water fern), and Cycas coralloid roots.
  • The water fern Azolla hosts Anabaena azollae inside its fronds to fix nitrogen.
  • They proliferate extensively in rice paddy water and are widely inoculated into rice fields for natural biofertilisation.

details.summary: Detailed classification of biofertiliser organisms: free-living vs symbiotic bacteria (Azotobacter, Clostridium, Rhizobium, Frankia) and cyanobacteria (Aulosira, Anabaena azollae, Nostoc) highlighting leghaemoglobin and enzyme nitrogenase.

mcq.question: Which cyanobacterium is considered the most active nitrogen fixer in Indian rice fields?
mcq.explanation: Aulosira is known to be the most active free-living nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterium in rice (paddy) fields.

subject: Biology
text:
Mycorrhizae (sing. mycorrhiza) are the mutualistic association of a fungus and the roots of higher plants. Mycorrhizae are found in most groups of vascular plants.

There are two types of mycorrhizae listed as follow:

  • Ectomycorrhiza: The mycorrhizal fungi is present on the root surface only. The cortical cells are surrounded by a network of fungal hyphae called Hartig net. It is found in roots of oak, Pinus, peach, Eucalyptus, etc.
  • Endomycorrhiza: The mycorrhizal fungus enters the roots and spreads in the root cortex. It may be intercellular or intracellular.

The type of endomycorrhiza, which produce vesicles and arbuscules inside the cortical cells of roots are called VAM (Vesicular Arbuscular Mycorrhiza), e.g. orchids, common crop plants and grasses.

details.summary: Mycorrhizae represent a symbiotic association between fungi and vascular plant roots. Ectomycorrhizae form a Hartig net around cortical cells (e.g., Pinus, oak), while Endomycorrhizae penetrate inside root cortical cells. VAM (Vesicular Arbuscular Mycorrhiza) is an important type of endomycorrhiza.

mcq.question: The fungal hyphae network surrounding the cortical cells in ectomycorrhizae is known as:
mcq.explanation: In ectomycorrhiza, cortical cells of the root are surrounded by a network of fungal hyphae termed the Hartig net.

subject: Biology
text:
Weed: Wild plants, which grow along with a cultivated crop are called weeds.

  • Common weeds found in wheat and rice field are Phalaris minor (mandusi), Amaranthus (chaulai), Chenopodium (bathua).
  • Exotic weeds are Parthenium hysterophorus, Eichhornia, etc.
  • Most troublesome terrestrial weed is congress grass (Parthenium hysterophorus).

Weedicides: These are the chemical substances that are used to kill weeds.

Some weedicides are:

  • Butachloro
  • 2,4-D (2,4-dichlorophenoxy acetic acid)
  • MCPA (2-Methyl 4-Chloro, 1-Phenoxy Acetic acid)

details.summary: Weeds compete with cultivated crops; Parthenium hysterophorus (congress grass) is the most troublesome terrestrial weed. Weedicides like 2,4-D, MCPA, and butachloro are used for chemical eradication.

mcq.question: Which of the following exotic weeds is commonly known as congress grass and considered the most troublesome terrestrial weed?
mcq.explanation: Parthenium hysterophorus is commonly known as congress grass and is the most troublesome terrestrial weed.

subject: Biology
text:
Pesticides are used to destroy pests (pathogens, insects, rodents, etc.) by spraying the crop.

  • Biopesticides: Some microbes such as bacteria, fungi, viruses, protozoans, etc., and their products used for pest control are known as biopesticides. These are inexpensive, cause no pollution, pick no risk to human health and have a long term capability to control pests.
  • Common Pesticides: Warfarin sulphur, malathion, DDT (Dichloro Diphenyl Trichloroethane), BHC (Benzene Hexachloride), etc.
  • Important Facts on Pesticides:
    • DDT and 2, 4-D were mainly used during the Second World War.
    • Endosulfan is an organochlorine pesticide and acaricide used on plants and insects.
    • Bordeaux mixture a fungicide, composed of CuSO4, Ca(OH)2 was discovered by Millardet.
    • Methyl isocyanate gas, which is responsible for Bhopal gas tragedy (3rd Dec, 1984), is used for synthesising carbaryl (sevin).
    • Rotenone is obtained from roots of Derris eliptica and Lonechocarpus.
    • Fumigation is another method of pest control used mainly to kill pests attacking stored grains. The substances used for fumigation are known as fumigants, e.g. methyl bromide, iodoform.

details.summary: Pesticides target agricultural pests; biopesticides offer non-polluting microbial alternatives. Key historical and chemical compounds include Bordeaux mixture (CuSO4 + Ca(OH)2 discovered by Millardet), Endosulfan, Methyl isocyanate (Bhopal disaster), Rotenone (from Derris eliptica roots), and grain fumigants such as methyl bromide.

mcq.question: Bordeaux mixture, a widely used fungicide composed of CuSO4 and Ca(OH)2, was discovered by:
mcq.explanation: Bordeaux mixture is a fungicide composed of copper sulphate and calcium hydroxide, discovered by P. M. A. Millardet.

subject: Biology
text:
Animal husbandry is the science of rearing, caring, feeding, breeding, improvement and utilisation of domesticated animals. It is an agricultural practice of breeding and raising livestock.

The animals used for transport, milk, meat and agriculture are collectively called livestock.

On the basis of utility, the livestock can be categorised into the following categories:

  1. Milk yielding animals: Cows, buffaloes and goats provide us milk, which is used to obtain animal protein and serves as a perfect natural diet.
  2. Meat and egg yielding animals: Sheeps, goats, pigs, chicken, ducks and fowls provide us meat and eggs.
  3. Animals utilised as motive power: Buffaloes, horses, donkeys, bullocks, camels and elephants are used in transport and ploughing the fields.
  4. Wool giving animals: Sheeps are reared for obtaining wool.
  5. Miscellaneous uses: The hides of cattles are used for making a variety of leather goods.

details.summary: Animal husbandry deals with breeding and raising livestock. Domesticated livestock are categorised based on utility into milk-yielding, meat- and egg-yielding, draught/motive power, wool-bearing, and hide/leather-producing animals.

mcq.question: Which category of livestock includes animals like bullocks, camels, and donkeys utilised primarily for transport and ploughing?
mcq.explanation: Animals such as bullocks, camels, horses, and donkeys used for ploughing and transportation are classified as motive power animals.

subject: Biology
text:
Animal Breeding:

  • It is an important aspect of animal husbandry, which aims to increase the yield of animals and to improve the desirable qualities of produce.
  • Breed: A breed is a group of animals related by descent and similar in most characters like general appearance, features, size, configuration, etc.
  • Animal breeding can be classified as:
    • (i) Inbreeding: The crossing of closely related animals within the same breed for 4–6 generations is called inbreeding.
    • (ii) Outbreeding: Breeding between unrelated animals either of the same breed but not having common ancestors for 4–6 generations (called outcrossing) or of different breeds (cross-breeding) or even different species (interspecific hybridisation) is called outbreeding.

ARTIFICIAL INSEMINATION:

It is the process in which the stored semen of a superior male animal is introduced into the genital tract of a selected female animal by using suitable instruments, for carrying out reproduction, to get a better breed of the animal or to solve the problem of infertility.
image_descriptions: A highlighted informational box labelled with a checkmark icon titled 'ARTIFICIAL INSEMINATION', outlining the procedural definition, tools, and objectives including reproductive improvement and resolving infertility.

details.summary: Animal breeding focuses on increasing yield and improving desirable traits. It includes inbreeding (related animals of same breed for 4-6 generations) and outbreeding (outcrossing, cross-breeding, interspecific hybridisation). Artificial insemination introduces stored semen into the female reproductive tract.

mcq.question: Mating of animals within the same breed having no common ancestors on either side of their pedigree for 4 to 6 generations is referred to as:
mcq.explanation: Outcrossing is the practice of mating animals within the same breed that have no common ancestors for 4–6 generations.

subject: Biology
topic: Pisciculture, Poultry and High Yielding Breeds
text:
Pisciculture

The breeding, rearing and transplantation of fish by artificial means is called pisciculture. It involves raising fish commercially in tanks or enclosures usually for food.

Fishes are of two types:

  • Freshwater fishes: Rohu, Catla, carp, tirica, mali, singhara and calbasu.
  • Marine fishes: Bombay duck, conger eel, promphert, Salmon, Sardine, hilsa.

Fishes are the rich source of protein and vitamin (A and D).

Poultry

The term 'Poultry' means rearing of fowls, ducks, geese, turkeys and some varieties of pigeons, but more often is used for fowl rearing. Fowls are reared for food or for their eggs.

  • Poultry birds reared for meat are called broilers.
  • Layers are the female fowls raised for egg production.
  • The fowls may be categorised into two breeds:
    • Indigenous breeds: The term 'Desi' includes all indigenous fowls exhibiting great variations in their shape, size and colour, e.g., Assel, Ahagus, etc.
    • Exotic breeds: The term 'Improved' is applied generally to the exotic and comparatively modern breeds of chickens, e.g., white leghorn, Rhode island red, etc.

Some High Yielding Breeds of Animals

  • Cows: Karan Swiss, Sunandini, Jersey–Sindhi, Brown Swiss–Sahiwal, Friesion–Sahiwal, etc.
  • Buffalo: Murrah, Surti, Jaffarabadi, Nili, Nagpuri, etc.
  • Goat: Kashmiri, Gaddi, Bengal, etc.
  • Sheep: Gaddi, Lohi, Bikaneri, Gurez, Nillore, etc.
  • Pig: Large white Yorkshire, Middle white Yorkshire, etc.
  • Halstein: The cattle breed that produces highest amount of milk.
  • Pashmina: Fine wool obtained from mountain (Kashmiri) goat.

  • Exotic high egg yielding breeds of hens: White leghorn, Rhode island red, Black minorica, Plymoth rock and Light sussex.

subject: Biology
text:
Genetic Engineering

Biochemist Paul Berg is the father of genetic engineering.

Genetic engineering or genetic manipulation involves the introduction of foreign DNA or synthetic genes into the organism of interest, so as to obtain desired product.

  • Golden Rice: A variety of Oryza sativa produced through genetic engineering to biosynthesise β-carotene, a precursor of provitamin-A in the edible parts of rice. Two β-carotene biosynthesis genes were transformed into golden rice:
    • (i) ψ (psy) (phytoene synthase) from daffodil.
    • (ii) crt I from the soil bacterium Erwinia uredovora.
    • Later on, other modifications were developed, and golden rice was expected to reach the market by 2013.
  • Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR): Discovered by Kary Mullis (1985). It is a technique of amplification of DNA segment with the help of taq polymerase (isolated from Thermus aquaticus).
  • Restriction enzymes: These are used to cut DNA at specific sites, also called molecular scissors.
  • Bioasphalt: An asphalt alternative made from non-petroleum based renewable resources like sugar, natural tree and gum resins, etc.
  • Gene therapy: The insertion of genes into an individual's cells or tissues to treat disease(s).
  • Terminator technology: A technology used to alter seeds so that they fail to germinate after the first generation.
  • ELISA: Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay is a test for AIDS, which is based on Antigen-Antibody (Ag-Ab) reaction.

Some Achievements of Genetic Engineering

  • Sweet bug: A bacterium that turns coconut water into delicious confectionery. The bacterium is Acetobacter oxylinum.
  • Superbug: Prof Anand Mohan Chakraborty developed a new strain of oil-eating bacteria called 'Superbug' using species of Pseudomonas.
  • Organic foods: Foods produced by using methods free of inputs such as synthetic pesticides, chemical fertilisers, chemical additives, irradiation, etc.
  • Biodegradable plastic films (PSV): Made by blending polymers with an additive to provide oxidation or starch.
  • Humulin: The first human insulin produced by genetic engineering.

details.summary: Detailed overview of genetic engineering fundamentals, Father of Genetic Engineering (Paul Berg), Golden rice genes, PCR, restriction endonucleases, ELISA, bioasphalt, terminator technology, Superbug, Sweet bug, and Humulin.

mcq.question: Who developed the oil-degrading 'Superbug' bacterium using species of Pseudomonas?
mcq.explanation: Prof Anand Mohan Chakraborty developed the genetically engineered oil-eating bacterial strain known as 'Superbug' using species of Pseudomonas.

subject: Biology
text:
DNA Fingerprinting is a technique employed by forensic scientists to assist in the identification of individuals by their respective DNA profiles.

Principle: This technique is based upon the fact that the DNA constitution of an individual carries some specific sequences of nucleotides, which do not carry any information for protein synthesis. These are called VNTR regions, i.e., Variable Number Tandem Repeats or mini satellites.

Inventor: DNA fingerprinting was invented by Dr Alec Jeffreys.

Process:

  • Collection of sample (most preferably buccal swab).
  • RFLP (Restriction Fragments Length Polymorphism) analysis.
  • Southern blotting: DNA fingerprinting via Southern blotting is a quite laborious method that requires a large amount of undegraded sample, so the method was replaced by what is used today based on STR (Short Tandem Repeats) and PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction).

details.summary: DNA Fingerprinting is a forensic identification technique developed by Dr. Alec Jeffreys based on non-coding Variable Number Tandem Repeats (VNTRs), currently performed primarily using STR and PCR.

mcq.question: DNA fingerprinting was invented by which of the following scientists?
mcq.explanation: DNA fingerprinting was invented by British geneticist Dr Alec Jeffreys.

subject: Biology
text:
Cloning in biology is the process of producing similar organisms of genetically identical individuals that occur in nature when organisms such as bacteria, insects, or plants reproduce asexually.

Types of Cloning:

  • (i) Reproductive cloning: It is used for the production of offspring. In it, a new individual is created from a single cell by replacing the nucleus in an egg cell with the nucleus (containing the genetic material) from another cell of the body. The cloned egg cell grows and develops into an embryo. The embryo is implanted inside a surrogate mother's womb to mature and produce a viable foetus.
  • (ii) Therapeutic cloning: It is used for the development of embryonic stem cells. The inner cell mass of the blastocyst is then removed and used for the creation of an embryonic stem cell line that has the genetic make up of the donated nucleus.

Successfully Developed Clones:

  • Dolly: A sheep, the first mammal clone synthesised by Dr Wilmut, UK.
  • Noori: The world's first cloned Pashmina goat named Noori (an Arabic word referring to light). Funded by the World Bank, the clone project was jointly worked on by SKAUST and the Karnal-based National Dairy Research Institute (NDRI).
  • First Buffalo Calf: The world's first buffalo calf through the Handguided Cloning Technique was born on 6 February, 2009 at NDRI, Karnal.
  • Garima-II: Another cloned buffalo calf through the new and advanced 'Handguided Cloning Technique' was born at NDRI, Karnal.
image_descriptions: A highlighted informational box titled 'SUCCESSFULLY DEVELOPED CLONED' with a checkmark badge, listing historical cloning milestones including Dolly the sheep, Noori the Pashmina goat, and cloned buffalo calves at NDRI Karnal.

details.summary: Cloning creates genetically identical individuals via reproductive or therapeutic cloning. Notable cloned animals include Dolly (sheep), Noori (Pashmina goat), and Garima-II (buffalo calf via Handguided Cloning Technique at NDRI Karnal).

mcq.question: Which animal was the first mammal clone synthesized by Dr Wilmut?
mcq.explanation: Dolly the sheep was the first mammal clone synthesised by Dr Ian Wilmut in the UK.

text:
Stem Cell Therapy: The most promising use of stem cells is due to their ability to be modified into different functional adult cell types and serve as a potential source of replacement cells to treat numerous diseases.

Stem cell research involves the use of several different types of cells besides embryonic stem cells, such as adult stem cells from humans or animals, or stem cells from foetuses, umbilical cord, or amniotic fluid.

Embryonic, adult, foetal, umbilical cord, and amniotic fluid cells

subject: Biology
text:
A transgenic crop is a crop which contains and expresses a transgene (a gene that is transferred into an organism by genetic engineering). It involves the introduction of new DNA into a crop to confer a new superior trait. A popular term for the transgenic crop is genetically modified crops or GM crops.

Bt Crops: Bt crops are produced by inserting the toxic genes that code for a toxin directly into the genetic code of the crop in order to protect the crop from insects. Along with this, a section of gene known as a promoter (which encourages the crop to produce the toxin) and a marker (which is used to track and identify modified crops) are also introduced, e.g., Bt cotton, Bt brinjal, Golden rice, etc.

  • Bt Cotton: Created by using a bacterium, Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt). It produces a protein that kills certain insects, e.g., beetles, flies, budworm, etc.
  • Golden Rice: A transgenic rice biosynthesising β-carotene (a precursor to vitamin A, essential for eyesight) in the edible parts of rice.

Advantages of GM Crops:

  • Provides high nutrient-containing varieties, i.e., enriched in specific nutrients.
  • GM crops are more tolerant to cold, insect, drought, salinity, etc.
  • Resistance to pests, herbicides, and diseases.

details.summary: GM/Transgenic crops incorporate foreign DNA to express superior traits. Examples include Bt cotton (derived from Bacillus thuringiensis) and Golden Rice (synthesizes beta-carotene for vitamin A).

mcq.question: Golden Rice is genetically engineered to biosynthesise which precursor essential for human eyesight?
mcq.explanation: Golden Rice is biofortified with β-carotene, which acts as a precursor for Vitamin A essential for vision.

### Genetic Screening
- An experimental technique used to identify genes that may produce damaging changes in individuals.

content:

- **Father of Green Revolution globally:** Norman Ernest Borlaug (N. E. Borlaug).

subject: Biology
content:
### Operation Flood (White Revolution)
- Rural programme launched by India’s National Dairy Development Board (NDDB) in 1970.
- Focused on increasing milk production through high‑yielding breeds of cows and buffaloes.
- Resulted in India becoming the largest producer of milk and milk products, hence the term **White Revolution**.
