subject: Geography
topic: Composition and Relief Features of the Oceans
text:
Hydrosphere: The water components of the Earth is called Hydrosphere. It includes the oceans, seas, lakes, ponds, rivers and streams. The hydrosphere covers about 70% of the surface of the Earth.

Relief Features of the Oceans

  • Continental Shelf: The shallow submerged extension of the continent is called the continental shelf. Extends to a depth of 100 fathoms (1 fathom = 1.8 m). It has average width 70 km; average slope 17 ft/mile or about 1°. Continental shelf covers 7.5% area of the oceans. It extends over 13.3% of the Atlantic ocean, 5.7% of Pacific ocean and 4.2% of Indian ocean. In cases, where the mountains extend along the coast, the continental shelf will be narrower. About 20% petrol and gas are found here. They also provide the richest fishing ground in the world.
  • Continental Slope: Extends seawards from the continental shelf. It has depth—200-2000 fathoms (3660m) and average slope 20 to 50 degrees. The boundary between shelf and slope is known as Andesite Line, on the names of the Andesite rock. Continental slope covers about 8.5% of the total ocean area.
  • Continental Rise: Continental rise is an area at the foot of the slope, slightly rising due to the accumulation of debris transported over the slope. It has average slope— 0.5° to 1°. Oil deposits occur here.
  • Abyssal or the Deep Sea Plains: It is the deepest and most extensive part of the oceanic floor having average depth of 3000m to 6000m. It covers about 75.9% of total oceanic area. Parts of the Abyssal plains are occupied by raised ridges or submarine mountains and by very deep trenches or canyons.
  • Deeps/Trenches: Trenches are narrow and steep sides depressions. Trenches are formed, when two plates of the Earth’s crust are moving together and one is being pushed down below the other. Marina trench (challenger deep) is the deepest trench in the world situated in the NW Pacific oceans, near philippines. It is approx 11 km deep.
  • Oceanic Ridges: Oceanic ridges are of tectonic origin and they provide evidence in support of the Plate Tectonics Theory. They are formed by the volcanic activity along the spreading boundary of plates. These ridges are thousands of km long and hundreds of km wide mountain ranges on the oceanic floor. Their summits may rise above the sea level in the form of islands i.e. Iceland, Azores Island are such examples.
  • Coral Reefs: Coral reefs are formed due to accumulation and the compaction of skeletons of lime secreting organisms known as Coral Polyps. Corals are found mainly in the tropical oceans and seas because they require high mean annual temperature of ranging between 20°C to 25°C. Corals do not live in deeper waters due to lack of sufficient sunlight and oxygen. On the basis of nature, shape and mode of occurrence, the coral reefs are classified into three types:
    • Fringing Reefs: It develop along the continental margins or along the islands. The seaward slope is steep and vertical while the landward slope is gentle. These reefs run as a narrow belt of about 0.5 km to 2.5 km width. They are usually attached to the coastal land, but occasionally they are separated from the shore by a shallow and narrow lagoon called ‘Boat Channel’. This type of reefs are found near Rameshwaram in the Gulf of Mannar.
    • Barrier Reefs: Largest coral reefs off the coastal platform, but parallel to them. The reef lies at a distance away from the coast. Hence, a broad lagoon develops between the reef and the shore. They are hundreds of kilometer long and few kilometers wide. The Great Barrier Reef of Australia is the largest barrier reef in the world.

subject: Geography
text:
Atoll: A reef of narrow growing corals of horseshoe shape and crowned with plam trees is called an Atoll. Atoll partly or completely encloses a lagoon. It is formed around an island in an elliptical form on a submarine platform. Funafuti atoll of Ellice Islands is a famous atoll.

CORAL BLEACHING: When corals are stressed by changes in conditions such as temperature, light or nutrients, they expel the symbiotic algae living in their tissues, causing them to turn colourless, this phenomenon is known as Coral Bleaching.

details.summary: Definitions of Atoll and Coral Bleaching.

subject: Geography
text:
Salinity is defined as the total amount of salts and minerals in grams contained in 1 kg of sea water and is expressed as part per thousand. The oceanic salinity not only affects the marine organism and plant community, but also affects the physical properties of the ocean such as temperature, pressure, density, waves and currents.

  • Average salinity of seawater is about 35‰ and average salinity in Southern hemisphere is more than that of Northern hemisphere.
  • Iso-halines represent the salinity distribution in the surface of the sea. These are the lines joining places having an equal degree of salinity.
  • The main source of salinity is dissolution of the rocks of oceanic crust, which contains salts. Poles have minimum salinity because of addition of fresh water in the form of icebergs and excessive snowfall.
  • Variation in salinity causes vertical circulation of water.
  • Salinity also increases the density of water. More saline water freezes slowly while the boiling point of saline water is higher than the fresh water.
  • Salinity on an average decreases from equator to poles. The highest salinity is recorded near the tropics rather than the equator because of the heavy precipitation in the equatorial region.
tables:
| Controlling Factor | Relation with Salinity |
|---|---|
| Evaporation | Greater the evaporation, higher the salinity. |
| Precipitation | Higher the precipitation, lower the salinity. |
| Influx of river water | Big voluminous rivers pour down immense volume of fresh water into the oceans and salinity is reduced at the mouth. |
| Atmospheric pressure | Anticyclonic conditions with stable air and high temperature increases the salinity of the surface water of the ocean. |
| Circulation of oceanic water | Ocean currents affect the spatial distribution of salinity by mixing sea waters. |

details.summary: Definition, distribution, and controlling factors of oceanic salinity.

subject: Geography
text:
Waves: Waves are the oscillatory movements in water mainly produced by winds, manifested by an alternate rise and fall of the sea surface. The waves are the important agents of erosion in the coastal regions, where they carve out various landforms like caves, bays, gulfs, capes and cliffs.

Seismic waves or tsunamis are the waves caused by earthquakes in volcanic eruptions in the sea bottom. The tsunamis, which hit the coast in South-East Asia on 26th December, 2004, caused havoc in that region.

details.summary: Explanation of ocean waves and tsunamis.

subject: Geography
text:
Ocean Currents are continuous, directed movements of ocean water generated by forces such as breaking waves, wind, the Coriolis effect, temperature and salinity differences, and the gravitational pull of the Moon and the Sun.

  • Circulation: Clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere, anti-clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere.
  • Types:
    • Warm Ocean Currents: Flow from lower latitude to higher latitude.
    • Cold Ocean Currents: Flow from higher latitude to lower latitude.

details.summary: Overview of ocean current definitions and general circulation patterns.

subject: Geography
text:
North Pacific Ocean Currents

  • Warm Currents:
    • North Equatorial Current: Flows Westwards from Western coast of Mexico to the Philippines.
    • Kuroshio Current: Extension of North Equatorial current near Japan coast; flows towards North.
    • Alaska Current: Flows along the coast of British Columbia and the Alaska Peninsula.
  • Cold Currents:
    • Oyashio Current: Flows from Bering sea towards Japan from North pole and joins Kuroshio currents.
    • Okhotsk Current and Kuril Current: Flow down from sea of Okhotsk and join Kuroshio current to the North of Japan.
    • West Wind Drift: Flows towards Alaska.
    • Californian Current: Extension of Alaskan currents; completes clockwise circulation of water.

details.summary: Detailed list of warm and cold currents in the North Pacific Ocean.

subject: Geography
text:
South Pacific Ocean Currents

  • Warm Currents:
    • East Australian Current (Great Barrier Current): Flows towards East coast of Australia from equator towards Pole.
    • South Equatorial Current: Originates due to South East trade winds, flows Westwards, and bifurcates near New Guinea.
    • Counter Equatorial Current: Extends up to Panama Bay; flows exactly on equator from West to East.
  • Cold Currents:
    • Peruvian Current (Humboldt current): Flows from South towards equator on the coast of Chile and Peru.
    • West Wind Drift: Flows from Tasmania to Chile coast of South America.

details.summary: Detailed list of warm and cold currents in the South Pacific Ocean.

subject: Geography
text:
North Atlantic Ocean Currents

  • Warm Currents:
    • North Equatorial Current: Present between equator and 10°N.
    • Cayenne Current: Flows adjacent to French Guinea and enters into Caribbean Sea and Gulf of Mexico.
    • Florida Current: Cayenne current near Florida (US coast).
    • Antilles Current: Flows to the East of West Indies and other islands.
    • Gulf Stream: Flows from US coast towards North-West Europe under the influence of Westerly winds.
    • North Atlantic Drift: Gulf Stream bifurcates into North Atlantic drift (warm) and West Wind drift (cold) and Canaries current (cold).
  • Cold Currents:
    • Labrador Current: Originates in Baffin bay and Davis Strait and merges with Gulf Stream near Newfoundland (famous fishing zone, Grand Bank).
    • Irminger Current or Greenland Current: Flows between Greenland and Iceland and merges with North Atlantic drift.
    • Canaries Current: Flows along the Western coast of North Africa between Madeira cape verde and joins North equatorial current.
    • West Wind Drift: Flows towards UK.

details.summary: Detailed list of warm and cold currents in the North Atlantic Ocean.

subject: Geography
topic: Currents of South Atlantic and Indian Ocean
text:
South Atlantic Ocean

  • Warm Currents:
    • South Equatorial Current: Flows between equator and 10°S.
    • Brazilian Current: Flows to the East coast of Brazil from equator towards pole.
  • Cold Currents:
    • Falkland Current: Flows along the South-East coast of South America from South to North.
    • Benguela Current: Flows from South to North near the 'Cape of Good Hope'.
    • West Wind Drift: Continuance of Brazilian and Falkland current.
    • Guinea Current: Flows near coast of Guinea (Africa).

Indian Ocean

  • The Asiatic Monsoon: Influences the currents of the North Indian Ocean, while the currents of South Indian ocean are influenced by the atmosphere's anticyclonic circulation.

details.summary: Detailed list of currents in the South Atlantic and Indian Oceans.

subject: Geography
text:
• North Equatorial Current: Flows from East to West, reaches East coast of Africa, turns Southward, crosses the equator and becomes the Mozambique current.
  • Mozambique Current: Flows South along the East coast of Africa from the vicinity of the equator to about 35 degrees, where it is known as Agulhas stream.
  • Agulhas Stream: Flows Westward along the Southern West of Madagascar and joins the Mozambique current along the East African coast.
  • West Wind Drift Current: Flows across the Indian ocean to the South-West of Australia.
  • North-East Monsoon Drift: Flows along the coast of India during winter.
  • South-West Monsoon Drift: Flows along the coast of India during summer.
  • South Equatorial Current: A significant Pacific, Atlantic and Indian ocean current that flows East-West between the equator and about 20 degrees South.
  • Somalia Current: An ocean boundary current that runs along the coast of Somalia and Oman in the Western Indian ocean; analogous to the Gulf stream in the Atlantic ocean.

details.summary: Overview of major global ocean currents and their flow patterns.

subject: Geography
text:
The rises and fall of the sea level as a result of the forces between the Earth, the Moon and the Sun is called a Tide. The interval between two tides is 12 hrs and 26 min.

There are two types of tides:

  • Spring Tides: When the Earth, the Moon and the Sun are in a straight line (also called SYZYGY), the Sun enhances the gravitational pull of the Moon, creating a condition of higher high tides and lower low tides.
  • Neap Tides: When the Sun and Moon are at right angles to the Earth. The Sun partially contracts the pull of the Moon producing lower high tides.

details.summary: Definition and classification of tides including Spring and Neap tides.

subject: Geography
text:
Natural vegetation refers to those vegetations which grows naturally on the Earth's surface without any human interference.

  • Tropical Evergreen Rainforests: Characterised by long and evergreen trees with layered structure forming a canopy. Almost two-thirds of the world's flowering plants are found here. Hardwood trees like rosewood, teak, sal, ebony and mahogany are common. Found near the equator in Amazon basin, Zaire basin and South-East Asian region.
  • Tropical Deciduous Forests: Also known as Monsoon Forests. Found in regions having monsoon climate (India, Myanmar, Thailand, parts of Indonesia, Malaysia, Indo-China, Philippines). Trees shed leaves during dry season. Teak, sal, bamboo, khair, bargad, peepal are important trees.
  • Mediterranean Forests: Found in areas around Mediterranean Sea, Central Chile, South-West USA, Australia and Northern Africa. Xerophytic plants constitute natural vegetation. Known as 'Orchards of the World' for fruit cultivation (citrus fruits, oranges, figs, olives, grapes).
  • Coniferous Forests: Extend in a band across Northern North America and Eurasia. Largest terrestrial biome. Consist of tall, softwood evergreen trees (pine, spruce, fir, hemlock). Trees are conical shaped with needle shaped leaves.
  • Tropical Grasslands: Known as 'Savanna' in Africa and 'Campos' in Brazil. Grasses are very tall (3 to 4 metres). Scattered trees are thorny and have small leaves.
  • Temperate Grasslands: Known as Prairies in North America, Pampas in South America, Downs in Australia, Velds in South Africa and Steppes in Europe. Dominant plants are grasses and forbs (few cm to 2 m). Known as 'Bread Basket' due to maize and wheat cultivation.

details.summary: Classification of global natural vegetation types and their characteristics.

subject: Geography
text:
Tropical Deserts: These are located on the western margins of the continents between 15°-30° North and South of equator. These regions have hot and dry summers and receive very less rainfall. Vegetation is very scant, with succulent stems, long roots and leaves are reduced to spines.

Tundra: Tundra covers large area in North Canada, North Russia, North Sweden and Finland. The vegetation of tundra is mostly herbaceous, consisting of a mixture of mosses, grasses and forbs, alongwith some dwarf shrubs, trees and lichens. A permanently frozen layer of soil called permafrost restrict growth of plant roots.

details.summary: Description of Tropical Desert and Tundra biomes.

subject: Geography
text:
Agriculture: Agriculture is a primary economic activity. It includes both, cultivation of crops and rearing of animals, to provide food and other products. Agriculture is practised under different combination of physical and socio-economic conditions which gives rise to different types of agriculture systems.

Shifting Cultivation: It is also known as slash and burn cultivation as field to be cultivated is cleared by burning the vegetation. The cultivated patches are very small and cultivation is done with very primitive tools. This type of farming is widely practised by many tribes in the tropics, especially in Africa, South and Central America and South-East Asia.

Intensive Subsistence Agriculture: This type of agriculture is practised on wide scale in densely populated regions of monsoonal Asia. In this type of agriculture the farmer owns a small piece of land, grown crops with the help of his family members and consumes almost the entire farm produce with little surplus to sell in the market. This type of agriculture widely practised in Thailand, Myanmar, Vietnam, Cambodia and India.

Plantation Agriculture: Plantation agriculture is a form of commercial farming where crops are grown for profit. Large land areas are needed for this type of agriculture. It was introduced by the Europeans in colonies situated in the tropics. The major products of this type of farming are the tropical crops such as tea, coffer, rubber and oil palm etc has developed in parts of Asia, Africa and Latin America.

Extensive Commercial Grain Farming: It is commercial form of agriculture where entire operations from ploughing to harvesting are mechanised. Grain crops, especially wheat is grown under extensive farming methods. This kind of farming is done by developed countries like USA, Australia and Russia.

Mixed Farming: In this type of agriculture, equal importance is given to both crop cultivation and animal husbandry. It give earning to the farmers.

Nomadic Herding: It is a primitive subsistence activity, based upon rearing of animals on natural pastures. People in this system keep on moving along with their animals in search of grazing areas. In Africa, cattle are the most important livestock, while in Sahara and Asiatic deserts, sheep, goats and camels are reared. In the mountainous areas of Tibet and Andes, Yak and llamas are reared and in arctic and sub-arctic regions, reindeer is most important animal.

Mediterranean Agriculture: Specialised commercial farming practised in Mediterranean climatic region. Crops like wheat, barley and vegetables are grown for domestic consumption, while citrus fruits, olives and grapes are grown on commercial scale for export purpose. Main regions include countries on either side of Mediterranean in Europe, Southern California, Central Chile, South-Western South Africa and Western Australia.

subject: Geography
text:
It refers to rearing of animals for food and other human uses. The world 'Livestock' applies primarily to cattle, chickens, goats, pigs, horses and sheep. Poultry farmers keep chickens, turkeys, geese and other birds for meat and eggs.

  • Top Beef producer of world are USA, Brazil, European Union, China and India.
  • India is the world's largest producer of milk. It is the leading exporter of skimmed milk powder. The world's largest exportes of milk and milk products are New Zealand, the European Union, Australia and the United States.

DAIRY FARMING

  • It is highly capital intensive and advanced form of farm activity.
  • It is practised mainly near urban and industrial centres.
  • Denmark and Sweden have witnessed the maximum development of this type of farming.

Some animals like sheeps, goats and rabbits reared for wool production also. Australia is the leading producer of wool followed by New Zealand and China. Temperate grasslands like Steppes in Russia, Prairies in North America, Pampas in Argentina, Veldt in South Africa and Downs in Southern Australia supports highly intensive livestock industry.

details.summary: Overview of livestock, dairy farming, and wool production.

subject: Geography
text:
Fisheries constitute an important economic activity in the coastal regions of the world, especially in the temperate latitudes. Fisheries can be classified into two groups - fresh water fisheries and marine fisheries.

  • Around 90% of the fishes are caught from the sea while remaining is obtained from fresh water. The top ten largest fish producing countries in the world are China, Peru, India, Indonesia, USA, Chile, Japan, Thailand, Vietnam and Russia.
  • Major exporters of fish and fishery products in the world are China, Norway, Thailand, USA and Denmark and major importers of fish and fishery products are Japan, USA, Spain, France and Italy.

There are four major fishing grounds in the world:

  1. North-East Atlantic Region: Dogger Bank located in the North Sea is one of the most important fishing ground. Important species of this region are Cod and Herring.
  2. North-West Atlantic Region: Grand Bank and Georges Bank are important fishing grounds. Important species of this region are Cod, Lobster, Oyster and Herring.
  3. North-West Pacific Region: Countries involved in fishing in this region are China, Japan, Russia, North and South Korea.
  4. North-East Pacific Region: This region include coastal regions of Canada and USA. Important species of this region are Halibut, Sardine, Salmon and Tuna.

details.summary: Overview of global fisheries, major producers, exporters, and fishing grounds.

Minerals: A naturally occurring substance that has a definite chemical composition and physical properties is called mineral. Minerals are formed in different types of geological environments, under varying conditions. They are created by natural processes without any human interference.

subject: Geography
text:
Transport: Transport along with communication is considered as lifeline of an economy. The principle modes of transportation includes land transport, waterways, airways and pipelines.

Road Transport: Roadways are the most universal and accessible form of transportation. It is also very economical for short distances. Germany was the first country in the world to establish a nation wide highway network. USA has world's longest and biggest road network followed by China, India, Brazil and Russia. Pan-American Highway is the longest highway in the world.

Rail Transport: It is preferred mode of land transport for bulky goods passengers over long distances. The first train was started on 27th September, 1825 between Stockton to Darlington in England. United States has world's largest rail network, followed by Russia and China. Trans-Siberian Railway is the longest railway line in the world.

Air Transport: Air transport is the fastest but costliest mode of transport. The development of air transport started after the World War I. But the actual development of this transport took place after the World War II. Two types of services are performed by air transport: 1. Inter-Continental Global: This includes the longest services. e.g. services between the continents. 2. Continental Air Route: These services are performed among the countries within a continent. e.g. India-China.

details.summary: Overview of road, rail, and air transport systems, including historical facts and global rankings.

subject: Geography
text:
National Air Route: Perform services for long distance within the country. e.g. Mumbai-Delhi.

International Air Transport Authority (IATA):

  • It is an international trade body created over 60 years ago by a group of airlines. Today, IATA represents 240 airlines comprising 84% of total air traffic.
  • The organisation also represents, leads and serves the airline industry in general.

Water Transport:

  • Both ocean water transport and Inland water transport form the part of water transport.
  • Waterways are the most suitable and cheapest mode of transport for carrying international trade.

Important Sea Routes of the World:

  • North Atlantic Sea Route (Big Trunk): It links North-Eastern USA and North-Western Europe. It is busiest route in the world.
  • South Atlantic Sea Route: This route connects North America and Europe with South America.
  • Mediterranean-Indian Ocean Sea Route: It connects highly industrialised West European region with East Africa, South Africa, South-East Asia and Australia and New Zealand.
  • Cape of Good Hope Route: It connects West European and West African countries with Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay in South America.
  • North Pacific Sea Route: This route links the ports of West-coast of North America with those of Asia.
  • South Pacific Sea Route: This route is an important connecting link between South and North America with Australia, New Zealand and various Pacific islands via Panama Canal.

Major Canal System of the World:

  • Suez Canal: It was constructed in 1869. This is the largest canal in the world, that connects Port Said in North and Port Suez in South Linking Red Sea and Mediterranean Sea.
  • Panama Canal: It is constructed across the Panama Isthmus between Panama city and Colon, connecting the Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea.
  • Kiel Canal: This canal in Germany connects the North Sea with the Baltic Sea.
  • Manchester Shipping Canal: It connects Manchester with Eastham.
  • North-Sea Canal: It joins North-sea with Amsterdam.

details.summary: Overview of air and water transport systems, including major global sea routes and canal systems.

subject: Geography
text:
Inland Waterways:

  • Inland waterways were the chief mode of transportation before the advent of railways.
  • The major oceans of world are connected with each other thus, forming a continuous expanse of water providing links to most parts of the world.

Major Inland Waterways of the World:

  • Rhine Waterways: It is navigable for 700 km from Rotterdam (Netherlands) to Basel (Switzerland). This is world's most heavily used waterways.
  • Danube Waterway: Danube river rises in Black Forest and flow Eastward in Eastern Europe. It is navigable upto Taurna Severin.
  • Volga Waterways: It is an important waterways of Russia and is navigable for 11200 km. The Volga-Moscow Canal connects it with Moscow region and Volga-Don canal with Black sea.
  • Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Seaway: The Great lakes of North America, Superior, Hurie, Erie and Ontario are connected by Soo canal and Welland canal. Great Lakes along with estuary of St. Lawrence river form the waterways.
  • Mississippi Waterways: The Mississippi-Ohio waterway connects interior part of USA with Gulf of Mexico.

Races:

  • Race is a term used for large group of people with some basic inherited physical characteristics common. e.g. skin colour, hair, facial features, eye colour, head shape etc.
  • Four major human races are Caucasoid, Australoid, Mongoloid and Negroid.

subject: Geography
text:
Population refers to the whole number of people living in a country or region. Demography is the scientific study of human population.

Population Distribution

  • Population is not distributed evenly in all parts of the world. Some places have sparse (scattered) population and some have dense population.
  • Sparsely populated places tend to be difficult places to live. These are usually places with hostile environment e.g. desert areas of the world.
  • More than 75% of the world's population lives in the continents of Africa and Asia.

Population Density

  • Density is defined as number of persons in per unit area. The density varies not only from one country to another within a continent but also from one part to the other within a country.
  • The highest densities are found in North-Eastern USA, North-West Europe, South Asia, South-East Asia and East Asia.
  • The lowest densities are found in hot and cold deserts, areas around pole, high rainfall area near equator.

Demographic Variables

  • Birth Rate: Number of live births per 1000 population in a given year. High birth rate found in Africa while lowest is in Europe.
  • Death Rate: Number of deaths per 1000 population in a given year.
  • Infant Mortality Rate: The number of deaths of infants under per 1000 live births in a year.
  • Maternal Mortality Rate: The number of women who die as a result of pregnancy and child birth complications per 100000 live births in a year.
  • Total Fertility Rate: The average number of children that would be born alive to a women.
  • Population Pyramid: A bar chart that is arranged vertically to show the distribution of population by age and sex. Males are on the left and females on the right.

subject: Geography
text:
Doubling Time: The number of years required for the population of an area to double itself, at current rate of population growth.

Age-Dependency Ratio: The ratio of persons in the ages defined as dependent (under 15 years and over 64 years) to persons in the ages defined as economically productive (15-64 years).

Demographic Transition: It refers to shift of birth and death rates from high to low levels. The decline in fertility is always delayed leading to population growth.

Migration: Migration means the movement of people from one place to the other.

Types of Migration:

  • In the context of domestic migration, migration can be either in-migration or out-migration.
    • In-migration: The process of entering one administrative sub-division of a country from another sub-division.
    • Out-migration: The process of leaving one sub-division of a country to take up residence in another.
  • International migration can be classified into the following:
    • Emigration: It refers to the process of leaving one country to take up permanent or semi-permanent residence in another.
    • Immigration: It is a process of entering one country from another to take up permanent or semi-permanent residence.
  • Refugee: A person who is residing outside country of his/her origin due to fear of persecution for reasons of race, religion, nationality or political opinion.
  • Internally Displaced Person: A person who is forced to leave his/her home region due to unfavourable conditions, but does not cross any boundary.

subject: Geography
text:
Human Development:

  • Development means qualitative change, which is always value positive.
  • The concept of human development was introduced by Dr Mahbub-ul-Haq. Dr Haq has described human development as that development that enlarges people choices and improves their lives. The four pillars of human development are equality, sustainability, productivity and empowerment.

Human Development Index:

  • The Human Development Report is an annual milestone publication by the Human Development Report office of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP).
  • The Report was first launched in 1990 by the world renowned Pakistani economist Mahbub-ul-Haq and Indian Nobel laureate Amartya Sen.
  • Human development is measured in terms of life expectancy at birth, education and per capita income.
  • Norway has highest HDI ranking. India ranks 130th in the list.
  • (i) HDi ranking (2016)
  • (ii) India ranks 131
  • (iii) Norway topped the Index

subject: Geography
text:
India occupies a South-Central position in the Asian continent, looking across the Arabian sea to Arabia and Africa on the West and across Bay of Bengal to Myanmar, Malaysia and the Indonesian Archipelago on the East. Geographically, the Himalayan ranges keep India apart from the rest of Asia. India derives her name from river Indus.

Location

India is often described as a tropical country although a large part of India lies in sub-tropics. The territorial limits of the Indian mainland extend between 8° 4′ N and 37° 6′ N latitudes and 68° 7′ E and 97° 25′ E longitudes.

Area and Extent

  • India ranks 7th in the world in terms of area after Russia, Canada, USA, China, Brazil and Australia.
  • It has a total land area of about 3287263 sq km, i.e. about 33 lakh sq km.
  • It is second largest in terms of population and holds 17.4% of the total world population, the land area of India amounts only to 2.4% of the total world landmass.
  • India is the second largest country in Asia both in terms of area as well as population, after China.

Important Geographical Points

  • State with longest coastline is Gujarat.
  • Active volcanoes are in Barren island in Andaman and Nicobar islands.
  • Northern most point of India is Indira Col.
  • Southern most point is Indira point or Pygmalion point in Great Nicobar.
  • Southern most tip of mainland is Kanyakumari.
  • Eastern most point is Kibithu, Arunachal Pradesh.
  • Western most point is Guhar moti in Kutch, Gujarat.

subject: Geography
topic: Indian Standard Time and Physiographic Divisions
text:
Indian Standard Time (IST)

  • India has only one standard time.
  • India is 5.5 hours ahead of GMT/UTC, 4.5 hours behind Australian Eastern standard time and 10.5 hours ahead of American Eastern standard time.
  • The 82 1/2° E longitude that passes through Allahabad city is choosen as standard longitude for Indian standard time.

Relief and Physiographic Divisions

Physiography is the branch of geography, which studies the present relief features of the Earth’s surface or of natural features in their causal relationships. The physiographic diversity of India embraces fold mountains, flat plains and one of the oldest plateaus of the world. India is divided into five physiographic units:

1. The Himalayas

The Northern mountain wall is a series of high mountain ranges stretching over the Northern borders of India.

  • The geologically young and structurally fold mountain ranges, the Himalayas run in West-East direction from the Indus to the Brahmaputra.
  • They form an arc, which covers a distance of about 2400 km. Their width varies from 400 km in Kashmir to 150 km in Arunachal Pradesh.
  • The altitudinal variations are greater in the Eastern half than those in the Western half.

The Himalayas is classified into four longitudinal series of mountains, which are as follow:

  • i. Trans-Himalayas: North of the Greater Himalayas lie the Trans-Himalayas or the Tibet Himalayas. This section is older than Himalayas. This range acts as a watershed between rivers flowing towards South and those flowing towards North. These ranges are about 40 km wide and rise in height upto 5000 m. They include the Karakoram, Zanskar and Ladakh ranges.
  • ii. Greater Himalayas or Himadri: The Northern most important range is known as the Great or Inner Himalayas or the Himadri.
  • iii. Himachal Himalayas: The range lying to the South of the Himadri, forms the most rugged mountain system and is known as Himachal or Lesser Himalayas or Middle Himalayas.

details.summary: Details on Indian Standard Time and the classification of the Himalayan mountain ranges.

subject: Geography
text:
iv. Shivaliks: The outermost range of the Himalayas is called the Shivaliks. They extend over a width of 10-50 km and have an altitude varying between 900 and 1100 m. These ranges are composed of unconsolidated sediments brought down by rivers from the main Himalayan ranges located in North.

v. The Purvanchal: After crossing the Dihang Gorge, the Himalayas take a sudden Southward turn and form a series of comparatively low hills in the shape of crescent with it's convex side pointing towards the West. These hills are known as Purvanchal.

IMPORTANT PEAKS:

  • Highest mountain peak in India K2 or Godwin Austin (PoK).
  • Highest peak of India in Himalaya is Kangchenjunga.
  • Highest peak in Eastern Ghats Arma Konda (AP).
  • Highest mountain peak in Western ghats Annaimudi.
  • Highest peak in Aravali is Gurushikhar in Mount Abu.
  • Highest peak in Satpura and Mahadeo hills Dhupgarh.
  • Highest peak in Nilgiris Doda Betta.
  • Highest peak in Andaman and Nicobar Islands Saddle Peak.
  • Highest peak of Naga hills Saramati Peak.

subject: Geography
text:
2. The Great Indian Plain:

  • To the South of Himalayas and North of Peninsula lies the Great Plain of North India. It is an aggradational plain formed mainly by the work of 3 rivers systems viz, the Indus, the Ganga and the Brahmaputra.
  • This is the largest alluvial tract of the world, extending for a length of 3200 km and width varies between 150 to 300 km.

Regional division of Great Plain of India are as follows:

Punjab-Haryana Plain:

  • The western part of the Northern Plain is known as Punjab-Haryana Plain. Its Eastern boundary in Haryana is formed by the Yamuna river. It also includes North-Eastern part of Rajasthan.
  • Depositional processes by the rivers continuing since long, has united these doabs. However, this mass of alluvium is broken by bluffs, locally known as Dhayas.

Ganga Plain:

This is the largest unit of Great Plain of India. Depending upon its geological variations, this plain can be furthur sub-divided into the following three divisions:

(i) Upper Ganga Plain:

  • Compacting the upper part of Ganga plain, this plain is delimited by 300 m contour in Shivaliks in the North, the Peninsular body in the South and course of Yamuna river in the West and 100 m contour in East.
  • The gradient is comparatively steeper in the North.

(ii) Middle Ganga Plain:

  • To the East of upper Ganga plain, lies middle Ganga plain occupying Eastern part of Uttar Pradesh and Bihar.
  • This plain is drained by the Ghaghara, the Gandak and the Kosi rivers.

details.summary: Description of the Great Indian Plain, its formation, dimensions, and regional divisions including Punjab-Haryana Plain and the sub-divisions of the Ganga Plain.

subject: Geography
text:
The Peninsular plateau is a tableland composed of mainly Archean gneisses and schists. It was formed due to the breaking and drifting of the Gondwana land and thus making it a part of the oldest landmass. This region of the country is surrounded on three sides by water and thus is a Peninsular plateau.

The plateau has broad and shallow valleys and rounded hills. Narmada river, which flows into a Rift valley, divides the region into two parts namely, the Central Highlands in its North and the Deccan plateau in its South.

details.summary: Overview of the formation and physical characteristics of the Peninsular Plateau.

subject: Geography
text:
• The Deccan Plateau: It is the largest unit of the Peninsular plateau of India with an elevation of 600 m. It is higher in the South than in its North. It generally slopes from West to East and various big rivers of Southern India like Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri etc flow through it. Karnataka plateau with Archean formations lies to the South of Maharashtra plateau having rocks of lava origin in Northern Karnataka called Malnad region and the rest of the red soil region of the plateau called Maidan.
  • Meghalaya Plateau: It is extension of peninsular plateau, which has been separated by huge fault. Fault is between Rajmahal hills and Meghalaya plateau.
  • The Chotanagpur Plateau: It lies East of Baghelkhand in the state of Jharkhand covering some parts of Chhattisgarh and West Bengal. Its average elevation is 700 m above sea level. It is the storehouse of minerals and a large scale mining of iron, manganese, coal, uranium etc is done in this region. Damodar river valley is well-known for its coal deposits.
  • The Malwa Plateau: Largely in Western Madhya Pradesh and South-Eastern Rajasthan forms a triangular shape and is typical for having two systems of drainage.
  • The Marwar Uplands: The Marwar uplands of Eastern Rajasthan lie to the East of Aravalli ranges. They are made up of sandstones and limestones of the Vindhyan period.

details.summary: Detailed breakdown of various plateaus within the Peninsular region.

subject: Geography
text:
• The Aravalli Ranges: It runs North-East to South-West for 800 km from Delhi through Rajasthan to Palanpur in Gujarat. It has a lower elevation between Delhi and Ajmer, where it is characterised by a chain of discontinuous ranges. Gurushikhar (1722 m) is the highest peak of the range, located in Abu hills of Rajasthan.
  • The Vindhyan Ranges: It runs parallel to the Narmada Rift valley as an escarpment in an East-West direction from Jobat in Gujarat to Sasaram in Bihar for a distance of 1200 km.
  • The Satpura Ranges: It is a series of seven mountains that run in the East-West direction in between Narmada and Tapi rivers. It is an example of block mountain. Amarkantak is meeting point of Vindhyan and Satpura range.
  • The Eastern Ghats: These are discontinuous and irregular and dissected by rivers draining into the Bay of Bengal. The Eastern ghats stretch from the South of Mahanadi valley to the Nilgiris in the South. The Eastern ghats are comparatively broader and do not form a continuous water divide.
  • The Western Ghats or Sahyadris: Sahyadris form the Western edge of the Deccan plateau and lie parallel to the Western coast. They form a continuous water divide. It run continuously for 1600 km from Maharashtra to Kanyakumari and can be crossed through passes only. Highest mountain peak in Western ghat is Annaimudi. The Western ghats are higher than the Eastern ghats.

details.summary: Description of major mountain ranges in the Peninsular region.

subject: Geography
text:
The Peninsular plateau is flanked by a stretch of narrow coastal strips, running along the Arabian sea on the West and the Bay of Bengal on the East.

Eastern Coastal Plains

  • The plains along the Bay of Bengal, i.e. the Eastern coastal plains are wide and level.
  • In the Northern part, they are referred to as the Utkal plains and Northern Circars, while the Southern part is known as the Coromandel coast.

Western Coastal Plains

  • It runs almost parallel between Sahyadris and Arabian sea, from Kanyakumari to Surat.
  • North to South it has been classified as Kathiawar plain, Konkan plain, Karnataka plain and Malabar plain along the Kerala coast.

details.summary: Overview of Eastern and Western coastal plains of India.

subject: Geography
text:
• Also known as Thar or Great Indian desert, which covers Western Rajasthan and the adjoining part of Pakistan. Desert is called Marusthali.
  • The Eastern part of the Marusthali is rocky, while its Western part is covered by shifting sand dunes locally called dhrian.
  • The Eastern part of Thar desert upto Aravalli range is semi-arid plain, which is known as Rajasthan Bagar. It is drained by a number of seasonal streams creating fertile tracts locally known as Rohi.

details.summary: Geographical features of the Rajasthan Desert.

subject: Geography
text:
Lakshadweep Islands

  • These islands group lies close to the Malabar coast of Kerala. This group of 25 islands is composed of small coral islands.
  • The islands North of 11° N latitude are known as Amindivi islands and those South of it are Cannanore islands.

Andaman and Nicobar Islands

  • Andaman and Nicobar archipelago has been formed by the extension of the tertiary mountain chains of Arakan yoma. These islands lie close to equator and experience equatorial climate and have thick forest cover. Some of the islands are fringed with coral reefs.
  • The entire group of islands is divided into two broad categories—The Andamans in the North and the Nicobars in the South. The Great Andaman group of islands in the North is separated by the Ten Degree Channel from the Nicobar group in the South.

details.summary: Description of Lakshadweep and Andaman & Nicobar island groups.

subject: Geography
text:
India is blessed with hundreds of large and small rivers, which drains the length and breadth of the country. Water drains in two direction of the main water divide line of India. 90% of land water drains into Bay of Bengal and the rest drains into Arabian sea.

The Indian rivers are divided into following two major groups:

  • i. The Himalayan Rivers
  • ii. The Peninsular Rivers

The Himalayan Rivers

The Himalayan river system is divided into three major river system, which are as follow:

The Indus River System

  • The Indus, also known as Sindhu, is the Western most of Himalayan rivers in India. It is one of the largest river basins of the world covering an area of 1165000 sq km (in India it is 321289 sq km) and a total length of 2880 km (in India 1114 km).
  • It originates from a glacier near Bokhar Chu in the Tibetan region near Mansarovar lake. In Tibet, it is known as Singi Khamban or Lion’s mouth.
  • In Jammu and Kashmir, its Himalayan tributaries are Zanskar, Dras, Gartang, Shyok, Shingar, Nubra, Gilgit etc. Its most important tributaries, which join Indus at various places, are Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej.

The Ganga River System

  • The Ganga system is the second major drainage system of India. It rises in the Gangotri glacier near Gaumukh (3900 m) in the Uttarakhand. Here, it is known as the Bhagirathi. At Devprayag, the Bhagirathi, meets the Alaknanda, hereafter, it is known as the Ganga.
  • The Alaknanda has its source in the Satopanth glacier above Badrinath. The Alaknanda consists of the Dhauli and the Vishnu Ganga, which meet at Joshimath or Vishnu Prayag. The other tributaries of Alaknanda such as the Pindar joins it at Karna Prayag, while Mandakini or Kali Ganga meets it at Rudra Prayag.
  • The left bank tributaries of Ganga are Ramganga, Gomti, Kali or Sharda, Gandak, Kosi and Mahanadi. The right bank tributaries of Ganga are Yamuna and Son. Yamuna joins the Ganga at Allahabad.
  • Kosi is called as ‘Sorrow of Bihar’ while Damodar is called as ‘Sorrow of Bengal’ as these cause floods in these regions. Hooghly is a distributary of Ganga flowing through Kolkata.

The Brahmaputra River System

  • It is one of the largest river of the world. It is known as Tsangpo in Tibet, Dihang or Siang in Arunachal Pradesh, Brahmaputra in Assam and Jamuna in Bangladesh.

details.summary: Overview of the Indian drainage system, specifically the Himalayan river systems (Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra).

subject: Geography
text:
• Brahmaputra forms the largest number of riverine islands.
  • Majuli is the largest riverine island in the world.
  • The combined stream of Ganga and Brahmaputra forms the biggest delta in the world, the Sunderbans, covering an area of 58752 sq km. Its major part is in Bangladesh.
  • Brahmaputra is volume wise largest river of India, whereas lengthwise Ganga is the longest in India.
  • Tributaries of river are-Manar, Subanshri, Dibang and Lohit.
  • The Peninsular River System: The Peninsular drainage system is older than the Himalayan one. A large number of the Peninsular rivers are seasonal, as their flow is dependent on rainfall.
  • Most of the major rivers of the Peninsula such as Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Cauvery flow Eastwards and drain into the Bay of Bengal. These rivers make deltas at their mouths.
  • Narmada and Tapi are the only long rivers, which flow Westward and make estuaries rather than making a delta because of their swift flow and steep slopes. The drainage basins of the Peninsular rivers are comparatively smaller in size.

details.summary: Overview of Brahmaputra river characteristics and the general drainage patterns of the Peninsular River System.

subject: Geography
text:
A lake is an area of variable size that is filled with water and surrounded by land. Lakes from due to receding glaciers, plate tectonics, volcanism, meandering rivers, landslides and human damming. Man-made lakes are referred as reservoirs.

  • Wular lake (Jammu and Kashmir) is the largest fresh water lake in India. Tulbul Navigation Project is located on this.
  • Sambhar, Didwana, Lunkaransar, Panchpadra are some of the important saline lakes of Rajasthan.
  • Ukai reservoir (Gujarat) is a man-made lake on river Tapi. Ranapratap Sagar and Jawahar Sagar (Rajasthan) and Gandhi Sagar (Madhya Pradesh) are located on river Chambal. Govind Sagar (Himachal Pradesh) is a huge reservoir.
  • Nagarjuna Sagar (Andhra-Telangana) on river Krishna, Nizam Sagar (Telangana) on Manjra and Tungabhadra (Karnataka) on Tungabhadra are man-made lakes.
  • Govind Ballabh Pant Sagar (Chhattisgarh-Uttar Pradesh) has been constructed on Rihand. Stanley reservoir is located in Tamil Nadu on Kaveri.
  • Loktak lake (Manipur) is the largest fresh water lake in North-Eastern India. Keibul Lamjao is a floating national park located inside the lake.
  • Chilika lake (Odisha) is the largest lagoon in India. Kolleru lake (Andhra Pradesh) is a lake located around delta region. Pulicat lake (Andhra Pradesh) is a lagoon.
  • Vembanad is located in Kerala. Lonar lake is a crater lake located in Buldhana, Maharashtra.

subject: Geography
text:
• India has tropical monsoon type of climate. It is greatly influenced by the presence of Himalayas in the North as they block the cold masses from Central Asia. It is because of Himalayas that the monsoons shed their water in India.
  • The Tropic of Cancer (23.5°N) divide India into two almost equal climatic zones, namely; the Northern zone (sub-tropical) and the Southern zone (tropical).

details.summary: Brief overview of India's tropical monsoon climate and the role of the Himalayas and the Tropic of Cancer.

subject: Geography
text:
The warm temperature or the sub-tropical climate of the Northern zone gives it cold winter seasons and hot summer seasons. The Southern tropical climate zone is warmer than the North and does not have a clear cut winter season.

The Southern zone has the midday Sun almost vertically overhead at least twice every year and the Northern zone does not have the mid-day Sun vertically overhead during any part of the year.

There are various factors which influence the climate of India. Location and latitude plays an important role in affecting climate of India. Tropic of Cancer divides, India into tropical and sub-tropical climatic regions. Indian ocean influences the climate of peninsular.

Himalayan range protects India from bitterly cold and dry winds from Central Asia and moreover acts as barrier in bringing monsoonal rainfall. Heating of interior part during summer attracts monsoon winds and cause monsoon rainfall. In winter Western disturbance cause snowfall in mountains and rainfall in plains.

details.summary: Overview of Indian climatic zones, the role of the Tropic of Cancer, the Indian Ocean, and the Himalayan range in shaping India's climate.

subject: Geography
text:
Indian climate is characterised by distinct seasonality. Indian Meteorological Department (IMD) has recognised the following four distinct seasons:

  • The cold season or winter season.
  • The hot weather season or summer season.
  • The South-West monsoon season or rainy season.
  • The season of the retreating monsoon or cool season.

details.summary: Classification of Indian seasons as per the IMD.

subject: Geography
text:
India is a land of great variety of natural vegetation. Himalayas are marked with temperate vegetation; Western Ghats and Andaman and Nicobar islands have tropical rain forests; deltaic regions have tropical forests and mangroves; desert and semi desert areas are known for variety of bushes and thorny vegetation.

Tropical Forests

Tropical forests are divided into Moist Forest and Dry Forest.

Moist Forest

Moist forest can be classified as:

  • Tropical Wet Evergreen Forests: Found where annual rainfall exceeds 250 cm. Annual temperature is about 25-27°C, humidity exceeds 77%. Includes Western side of Western ghats, North-East to South-West direction across Arunachal Pradesh, upper Assam, Nagaland, Andaman and Nicobar. Species: white cedar, mesua, jamun, hopea, mahogany, ebony etc.
  • Tropical Semi-Evergreen Forests: Found in regions with 200-250 cm rainfall. Mean annual temperature 24-27°C, relative humidity about 75%. Includes Western coast, Assam lower slopes of the Eastern Himalayas, Odisha and Andamans. Species: aini, semul, kadam, rosewood, kusum etc.
  • Tropical Moist Deciduous Forests: Found in areas with 100 to 200 cm rainfall. Mean annual temperature about 27°C, relative humidity 60 to 70%. Includes areas along the Western ghats, a strip along the Shiwalik range including Terai and Bhabar from 77°E to 88°E, hills of Eastern Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Chhotanagpur and part of Odisha and West Bengal. Species: teak, sal, laurel, white chuglam, badam, mahua and bamboo etc.
  • Littoral and Swamp Forests: Occur in and around deltas, estuaries and creeks. Species: sundari, rhizophora, srwpines, sonnoratic etc. Can survive in fresh as well as brackish water.

Dry Forest

Dry forest can be classified as:

  • Tropical Dry Evergreen Forests: Found along the coasts of Tamil Nadu, short stature. Annual rainfall about 100 cm, mean annual temperature about 28°C, mean humidity about 15%. Species: khirni, jamun, tamarind, neem etc.
  • Tropical Dry Deciduous Forests: Similar to moist deciduous forests, shed leaves in dry season. Grow in 100-150 cm rainfall. Species: teak, axlewood, tendu, palas, bel etc.
  • Tropical Thorn Forests: Occur in areas of low rainfall and high temperature. Species: Khair, Neem, Babul, Cacti, Palas etc.

details.summary: Detailed classification of Indian natural vegetation into Tropical Moist and Dry forests with specific regional and species characteristics.

subject: Geography
text:
Sub-tropical Forest

Sub-tropical forest are of three types:

  • Sub-tropical Broad-leaved Hill Forests: Occur in the Eastern Himalayas to the East of 88°E longitude at altitudes varying from 1000 to 2000 m. Mean annual rainfall is 75 cm to 125 cm, mean annual temperature is 18°C-21°C. Species: Oaks, Chestnuts, Sals and Pines. Also occur in the Nilgiri and Palni Hills at 1070-1525 m above sea level (called shales).
  • Sub-tropical Moist Pine Forests: Found at the height of 1000 to 2000 m above sea level in the Western Himalayas between 73°E and 88°E longitudes. Chir is the most dominant tree.
  • Sub-tropical Dry Evergreen Forests: Found in the Bhabar, the Shivaliks and the Western Himalayas upto about 1000 m above sea level. Rainfall is between 50 to 100 cm. Species: Olive, Acacia, Modesta and Pistacia.

details.summary: Classification and characteristics of Sub-tropical forests in India.

subject: Geography
text:
Temperate Forest

Temperate forest is further divided into 3 types:

  • Montane Wet Temperate Forests: Grow at a height of 1800 to 3000 m above sea level. Mean annual rainfall is 150 cm to 300 cm, mean annual temperature is about 11°C-14°C and the average relative humidity is over 80%. Species: deodar, chilauni, Indian chestnut, birch, blue pine etc. Found in the higher hills of Tamil Nadu and Kerala, in the Eastern Himalayan region to the East of 88°E longitude.
  • Himalayan Moist Temperate Forests: Mainly composed of coniferous species such as pines, cedars, silver, firs, spruce etc. Found in the temperate zone of the Himalayas between 1500 and 3300 m. Rainfall varies from 150 cm to 250 cm.
  • Himalayan Dry Temperate Forests: Coniferous forests with xerophytic shrubs. Deodar, chilgoza, oak, olive etc are the main trees. Found in the inner dry ranges of the Himalayas.

details.summary: Classification and characteristics of Temperate forests in India.

subject: Geography
text:
Mangroves

Mangroves are very specialised forest ecosystem of tropical and sub-tropical regions of the world bordering sheltered sea-coasts. They occur all along the Indian coastline in the sheltered estuaries, tidal creeks, backwaters, salt marshes and mudflats.

Mangroves are dominated by salt tolerant halophytic plants of diverse structure and are invaluable marine nurseries for a large variety of fish and other marine fauna. They support a large variety of birds, amphibians and many other local arboreal, benthic and water creatures.

Mangroves have a dense network of aerial roots, which help to aerate the root system and anchor the tree. Sundari pines, canes and palms are common in deltas, cracks are often lined with Nipa.

details.summary: Characteristics and ecological importance of Mangrove forests.

subject: Geography
text:
SOIL

Soil is formed when rocks are broken down by the action of wind, water and climate. This process is called weathering.

Soil forms different layers of particles of different sizes called Horizons. Each layer is different from the other in thickness texture, colour and chemical composition.

Major Soils of India

  • Alluvial Soil: Covers the largest area in India (40%) and is the most important soil from agricultural point of view. Widespread in the Northern plains and the river valleys. Through a narrow corridor in Rajasthan, they extend into the plains of Gujarat. Geologically, the alluvium is divided into new alluvium which is known as Khadar and old alluvium, as Bhangar. The newer alluvium is sandy and light coloured, whereas, older alluvium is more clayey, dark coloured and contains lime concretions. The conglomerate deposits in piedmont area are generally known as Bhangar. This soil is suitable for rice, wheat, sugarcane, oil seeds and jute cultivation.
  • Black Soil/Regur Soil: The principal region of black soil is the Deccan plateau and its periphery. This is formed from Deccan basalt trap rocks and occur in areas under the monsoon climate, mostly of semi-arid and sub-humid types. This soil is characterised by dark grey to black colour, high swelling and shrinkage, plasticity, deep cracks during summer and poor status of organic matter, nitrogen and phosphorus while this is rich in lime, iron, magnesia and alumina. Impeded drainage and low permeability are the major problems. Cotton is mostly grown on this soil.

details.summary: Definition of soil, weathering, horizons, and characteristics of Alluvial and Black soils.

subject: Geography
text:
Red and Yellow Soils

  • Derived from granite, gneiss and other metamorphic rocks.
  • Formed under well-drained conditions.
  • High textured and contain low soluble salts.
  • Slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, well-drained with moderate permeability.
  • Poor in nitrogen, phosphorus, lime, and humus.
  • Covers large parts of Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, and Odisha.

Laterite Soil

  • Peculiar to India and some tropical countries with high temperature and heavy rainfall with alternating wet and dry periods.
  • During rainfall, silica is leached downwards and iron and aluminum oxide remains in the top layers.
  • More acidic in hilly areas than low areas; less fertile and poor in humus, nitrogen, phosphate, and calcium.
  • Found in Odisha, West Bengal, parts of Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Jharkhand, and Maharashtra.

Desert Soil

  • Occurs in North-Western India (Rajasthan, South Haryana, Punjab, Northern Gujarat).
  • Mostly derived from alluvium; pale brown to yellow brown, fine sandy to loamy fine sand, and structureless.
  • Low clay content and presence of alkaline Earth carbonates.
  • Productivity can be increased by adding organic matter and clay.

Swampy/Peaty Soil

  • Originate in areas of heavy rainfall with inadequate drainage.
  • Found at foot hills and in strips of varying widths at the foot of Himalayas in Jammu and Kashmir, Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, and West Bengal.

Saline Soil

  • Formed due to accumulation of soluble salts (chlorides and sulphates of calcium and magnesium).
  • Approximately 7 million hectares are salt-affected in India.

Forest Soil

  • Formed in forest areas where sufficient rainfall is available.
  • Structure and texture vary depending on the mountain environment.

details.summary: Overview of various soil types in India including their formation, characteristics, and geographical distribution.

subject: Geography
text:
Soil Erosion and Degradation

  • Soil Erosion: Destruction of the soil cover.
  • Soil Degradation: Decrease in soil fertility.
  • Wind and water are powerful agents of soil erosion.
  • Wind erosion is significant in arid and semi-arid regions.
  • Erosion by running water is significant in regions with heavy rainfall and steep slopes.

Agriculture in India

India is a vast country with a great variety of natural environments, providing conditions for a large number of crops.

Types of Farming

  • Subsistence Farming: Small, scattered holdings cultivated by family members using primitive tools. Focus is on food crops for personal consumption.
  • Plantation Farming: Capital-intensive, large-scale production of a single cash crop for sale. Requires managerial ability, technical know-how, fertilizers, and good transport. Practiced in Assam, sub-Himalayan West Bengal, Nilgiri, Anaimalai, and Cardamom hills.
  • Shifting Agriculture: Practiced by tribals in Assam, Meghalaya, Nagaland, Manipur, Tripura, Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh, Odisha, and Madhya Pradesh. Involves clearing forest land by felling and burning trees. Main crops: dry paddy, buck wheat, small millets, tobacco, and sugarcane. Causes large-scale deforestation and soil erosion.

details.summary: Covers soil degradation processes and different agricultural practices in India.

subject: Geography
text:
Organic Farming: A new trend of farming in which all input used for farming are natural, no chemicals are used. Green manures and compost are used. Sikkim is the first organic state of India.

Cropping Seasons: Three types of cropping seasons are found in India:

  • Kharif: It requires much water, long hot weather for their growth, grown in June with the arrival of South-East monsoon. e.g. rice, jowar, maize, cotton, groundnut, jute, tobacco, bajra, sugarcane, pulses etc.
  • Rabi: Grown in winter, required cool climate during growth and warm climate during germination of seeds and maturation. Sowing is done in November and harvested in April-May. e.g. wheat, gram and oilseeds like, mustard and rapeseed etc.
  • Zaid: A brief cropping season practised in irrigated areas, sown in February- March, harvested in June. e.g. urad, moong, watermelons.

subject: Geography
text:
India is capable of growing almost each and every crop due to varied climate, soil, and sunshine. Indian crops are divided into the following categories:

  • Food Crops: Rice, wheat, maize, millets, jowar, bajra, ragi, pulses, gram and tur.
  • Cash Crops: Cotton, jute, sugarcane, tobacco, oilseeds, groundnut, linseed, sesamum, castorseed, rapeseed and mustard.
  • Plantation Crops: Tea, coffee, spices, cardamom, chillies, ginger, turmeric, coconut and rubber.
  • Horticulture Fruits: Apple, peach, pear, apricot, almond, strawberry, mango, banana, citrus food and vegetables.

subject: Geography
text:
Resources: Human beings interact with nature through technology and create institutions to accelerate economic development. A resource is a source or supply from which benefit is produced.

Human Resources: Human beings themselves are essential components of resources. They transform material available in our environment into resources and use them. Human capital is sometimes used synonymously with human resources.

Natural Resources: Naturally occurring substances considered valuable in their relatively unmodified (natural) form. A resource's value rests in the amount of material available and the demand for it.

Classification of Natural Resources: Natural resources are mostly classified into renewable and non-renewable resources:

  • Renewable Resources: These resources can renew themselves if they are not over harvested but used sustainably. The rate of sustainable use of a renewable resource is determined by replacement rate and amount of standing stock of that particular resource.

details.summary: Definitions of resources, human resources, and natural resources, including the classification of natural resources into renewable and non-renewable.

subject: Geography
text:
Non-Renewable Resources: A natural resource which is present in a fixed quantity and it cannot be used again once it gets exhausted.

Mineral Resources: A mineral is an aggregate of two or more than two elements. A mineral has a definite chemical composition, atomic structure and is formed by inorganic processes. In economic geography, the term mineral is used for any naturally occurring material that is mined and is of economic value. Minerals generally occur in the Earth's crust in the form of ore.

The Mineral Regions of India:

  • The North-Eastern Peninsular Belt: Comprises of Chota Nagpur plateau, Odisha plateau and West Bengal. It is the richest mineral belt of India. Coal and Iron are very abundant in the region.
  • Central Belt: Comprises of Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh and Maharashtra. It contains deposits of manganese, bauxite, limestone, marble, coal, gems, mica, iron etc.
  • The Southern Belt: Comprises Karnataka plateau but extends upto Tamil Nadu upland. It is rich in ferrous minerals and bauxite but lacks in coal deposits.
  • The South-Western Belt: Includes Southern Karnataka, Kerala and Goa. It has deposits of iron-ore, garnet and China clay, Monazite sand etc.
  • The North-Western Belt: Extends along the Aravalis in Rajasthan and in adjoining part of Gujarat. It is rich in non-ferrous minerals (copper, lead, zinc), uranium, mica, precious stones, aquamarine and emerald etc.

subject: Geography
text:
Energy Resources in India: India is a fast growing country and therefore, the demand for the energy is also continuously growing. India has exploited almost all the sources of energy such as hydroelectricity, thermal energy, nuclear energy, solar energy, wind energy etc.

Energy Resources in India: The natural resources for electricity generation in India are unevenly dispersed and concentrated in a few pockets. Hydro resources are located in the Himalayan foothills and in the North-Eastern Region (NER). Coal reserves are concentrated in Jharkhand, Odisha, West Bengal, Chhattisgarh, parts of Madhya Pradesh, whereas lignite is located in Tamil Nadu and Gujarat. North Eastern region, Sikkim and Bhutan have vast untapped hydro potential estimated to be about 35000 MW in NER, about 8000 MW in Sikkim and about 15000 MW in Bhutan.

Conventional Sources of Energy: The conventional sources of energy are generally non-renewable sources of energy, which are being used since a long time. Conventional sources of energy are coal, petroleum and natural gas.

  • Thermal Energy: Thermal electricity is produced with the help of coal, petroleum and natural gas. About 65% of the total electricity produced is thermal in character. Thermal electricity has special significance in those areas, where geographical conditions are not very favourable for generation of hydroelectricity. It accounts for more than half of the installed capacity in 14 states.
  • Hydroelectricity: The hydroelectric power generation in India made a humble start at the end of the 19th century, with the commissioning of electricity supply in Darjeeling during 1897, followed by a hydropower station at Sivasamudram in Karnataka during 1902.
  • Atomic Energy: Nuclear power is fourth largest source of electricity in India after, thermal, hydroelectricity and conventional source of power.

Non-Conventional or Renewable Energy Sources:

Includes solar energy, wind energy, biomass energy, fuel cell, electric vehicles, tidal energy, hydrogen energy and geothermal energy. The Department of Non-Conventional Energy Sources was established in 1982. Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency was set-up in 1987. In 1992, DNES was converted into Ministry of Non-Conventional Energy Sources, renamed in 2006 as Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE).

Economic Activities:

  • Primary Activities: Dependent on environment (land, water, vegetation, minerals). Includes hunting, gathering, pastoral activities, fishing, forestry, agriculture, mining, quarrying.
  • Secondary Activities: Add value to natural resources by transforming raw materials into valuable products.
  • Tertiary Activities: Services including health, education, law, governance.
  • Quaternary Activities: Research, development, specialised knowledge and technical skills.
  • Quinary Activities: Services focusing on creation, re-arrangement and interpretation of new and existing technologies.

subject: Geography
text:
India has the fifth largest railway network in the World after the USA, Russia, China and Canada. The Indian railway operate in three different gauges.

  • It is the largest public sector undertaking of the country and it is the world's largest railway network under single management.
  • The first Indian railway line in India was operated for public traffic in 1853 between Mumbai and Thane over a distance of 34 km.
  • The first electric train in India was 'Deccan Queen', it was operated in 1929 between Bombay and Poona. The headquarters of Indian railway is in New Delhi.
  • The fastest train in India is the Vande Bharat Express, whose maximum speed is 180 km/hr.
  • Indian railways has the second biggest electrified system in the world after Russia. The total route covered is approximately 63000 km.
  • Vivek Express has the longest train route in India connecting Dibrugarh and Kanyakumari. It is 8th longest in the world.
  • The second longest train route is of 'Himsagar Express' from Jammu Tavi to Kanyakumari. It covers a distance of 3726 km and passes through ten states.
  • The oldest steam engine 'Fairy Queen' still runs on rail.
  • Uttar Pradesh has largest railway network in India.
  • Mumbai CST is busiest railway junction of India.
  • Railway track electrification was introduced in early 1920s. The first two sections from Victoria Terminus to Kurla and from Victoria Terminus to Bandra were electrified. About 26% of the rail lines have been electrified.
  • Anil Kakodkar Committee was constituted for Rail Safety in 2011.

subject: Geography
text:

text:
Population:

  • Population geography is closely related to demography. It is concerned with the study of demographic processes and their consequences in and environmental context.
  • Population density is the degree of compaction in population the closeness of persons living on a given surface, the spatial balance of their social and economic assets.
  • Population density shows the population pressure on land resource. There are various ways to measure population density such as crude or arithmetic density, nutritional or physiological density, agricultural density, economic density etc. Among them arithmetic density is mostly used.

details.summary: Introduction to demographic profile and population density concepts.

subject: Geography
text:
Factors affecting population distribution and density include physical factors (land forms, vegetation, soils, water supply), climatic factors (temperature, rainfall), availability of natural resources, and means of transport and communication.

  • Population growth: Change in population measured in absolute numbers or percentage. Components: fertility, mortality, migration.
  • Migration: Permanent, seasonal, or temporary shift of residence.
  • Population composition: Characteristics like age-sex composition, occupation, etc.

Demographic Characteristics of India:

  • India is one of the most populous countries.
  • Population is unevenly distributed; plains have more population than mountains, deserts, and forests.
  • 2011 Census: 121.01 crore population.
  • Most populous state: Uttar Pradesh (19.95 crore), followed by Maharashtra, Bihar, West Bengal, Andhra Pradesh.
  • Least populous state: Sikkim.
  • Average population density: 382 persons per sq km.
  • Lowest density: Arunachal Pradesh (17).
  • Highest density: Bihar (1102).
  • Union Territory highest density: Delhi (11297).
  • Union Territory lowest density: Andaman and Nicobar (46).

details.summary: Overview of Indian population distribution, density, and demographic factors based on the 2011 Census.

subject: Geography
text:
Growth of Population: Four phases identified in India's demographic history:

  1. Period of stagnant growth (before 1921)
  2. Period of steady growth (1921-1951)
  3. Period of rapid growth (1951-1981)
  4. Period of declining growth rate (after 1981)

The declining growth rate of population during 2001-2011 was 17.64%. Kerala registered the lowest growth rate (4.86%), whereas Daman and Diu registered the highest (53.54%).

Migration: A migrant is one enumerated in a census at a place other than their place of birth. Factors responsible: heavy pressure of population, poverty, high incidence of unemployment.

text:
Natural Hazards and Disaster Management:

  • A disaster is a result of natural or man-made causes that leads to sudden disruption of normal life, causing severe damage to life and property to an extent those available social and economic protection mechanisms are inadequate to cope.
  • Disaster management is the managerial function which deals with creating the framework within which communities to reduce vulnerability to hazards and cope with disasters.
  • As per origin, disasters can be classified into natural and man-made disasters. Based on generic disasters can be classified into five categories: water and climate, geological, biological, accidental and chemical, industrial and nuclear.

Natural Disaster: It is a major adverse event resulting from natural processes of the Earth; examples include floods, droughts, cyclones, landslides, volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, tsunamis and other geologic processes.

details.summary: Definitions and classifications of natural disasters and disaster management.

subject: Geography
text:
Earthquake:

  • An earthquake is a vibration or oscillation of the surface of the Earth caused by the elasticity or the isostatic adjustment of the rocks, beneath the surface of the Earth. Major earthquakes are usually caused by sudden movements along faults.
  • Earthquakes are by far the most unpredictable and highly destructive of all the natural disasters. There is a geographic-pattern of the earthquake around the world at the tectonic plate margins. Earthquakes that are of tectonic origin have proved to be the most devastating and their area of influence is also quite large.
  • Earthquake Zones of India: On the basis of the intensities or the destructiveness of the earthquakes, India is divided into four earthquake zones.
  • Zone IV and Zone V: Had experienced some of the most devastating earthquakes in India. Areas vulnerable to these earthquakes are the North-East states, areas to the North of Darbhanga and Araria along the Indo-Nepal border in Bihar, Uttarakhand, Western Himachal Pradesh (around Dharamshala) and Kashmir valley in the Himalayan region and the Kutch (Gujarat).
  • Zone III: Covers Southern and South-Eastern parts of Rajasthan, larger parts of Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Jharkhand and Northern and North-Western part of Odisha.

details.summary: Definition, causes, and seismic zoning of earthquakes in India.

subject: Geography
text:
Floods:

  • These are sudden and temporary inundation of a large area as an overflowing of rivers or reservoirs.
  • The common causes which can be responsible for over flowing of river are heavy rainfall, sediment deposition, deforestation, interference in drainage system, change in the course of river etc. Tsunami and cyclone are responsible for flood in coastal areas.

Flood Prone Zones in India:

  • In India, around 40 million hectare area is flood-prone, which is one eighth of the total area. The most flood prone areas are the Brahmaputra, Ganga and Indus basins.
  • As far as states are concerned, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal and Odisha are the most flood affected states followed by Haryana, Punjab and Andhra Pradesh.

subject: Geography
text:
Droughts:

It is either absence or deficiency of rainfall from its normal pattern in a region for an extended period of time leading to general suffering in the society.

On the basis of severity of droughts, India can be divided into the three regions, which are as follows:

  1. Extreme Drought Affected Areas: Most parts of Rajasthan, Marusthali and Kutch regions of Gujarat fall in this category.
  2. Severe Drought Prone Area: Parts of Eastern Rajasthan, most parts of Madhya Pradesh, Eastern parts of Maharashtra, interior parts of Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka plateau, Northern parts of interior Tamil Nadu and Southern parts of Jharkhand and interior Odisha.

text:
• It is a Japanese word which means Harbor waves.
  • Earthquakes and volcanic eruptions that cause the sea-floor, to move abruptly resulting in sudden displacement of ocean water in the form of high vertical waves are called tsunamis or seismic sea waves.
  • Earthquakes, volcanic eruptions and other underwater explosions (including detonations of underwater nuclear devices), landslides, glacier calvings, meteorite impacts and other disturbances above or below water all have the potential to generate a tsunami.
  • From the tsunami point of view, Pacific ocean is in the most dangerous position. The tsunami that occurred on the 26th of December, 2004 in the Sumatra island of Indonesia in the Indian ocean was the result of subduction of Indian plate below the Burmese plate.

subject: Geography
text:
The term landslide includes all varieties of mass movements of hill slopes and can be defined as the downward and outward movement of slope forming materials composed of rocks, soils, artificial fills or combination of all these materials along surface of separation by falling, sliding and flowing, either slowly or quickly from one place to another.

Landslides in India
  • Landslide and avalanches are among the major hydro-geological hazards that affect large parts of India. Besides the Himalayas, the North-Eastern hill ranges the Western Ghats, the Nilgiris, the Eastern Ghats and the Vindhyas in that order, covering about 15% of the landmass.
  • The Himalayas alone count for landslides of every fame, name and description big and small, quick and creeping, ancient and new. The North-Eastern region is badly affected by landslide problems of a bewildering variety.
  • A different variety of landslides, characterised by a lateritic cap, pose constant threat to the Western Ghats in the South, along the steep slopes overlooking the Konkan coast besides Nilgiris, which is highly landslide prone.

details.summary: Definition of landslides and their prevalence in various Indian geographical regions.

subject: Geography
text:
• Tropical cyclones are characterised by destructive winds, torrential rainfall and storm surges disrupt normal life with the accompanying phenomena of floods due to the exceptional level of rainfall and storm surge inundation into inland areas.
  • Cyclonic storms are more common in India's Eastern coast and Bangladesh, they routinely hit between April and November, causing deaths and widespread damage to property.
